k-j-stahlberg: Ståhlberg was born in Suomussalmi, in the Grand Duchy of Finland under Russian rule, the son of an assistant pastor, Johan Gabriel Ståhlberg. He was christened Carl Johan and later gave his forenames a Finnish form, as most supporters of Finnish language and culture did. His father died when he was a boy and the family moved to Oulu, where he excelled at a private Finnish lycée. He graduated in law from the University of Helsinki in 1889 and took his doctorate in 1893.

As a presenter of legislation for the Senate he was a constitutionalist who opposed the attempted Russification of Finland. He was dismissed as protocol secretary of the Senate's civil affairs subdepartment in 1902 for his strict legalism and opposition to legislation on compulsory military service. In 1905 he became a senator and helped draft the law that created the Parliament of Finland. From 1908 he was professor of administrative law at Helsinki.

In 1917 he chaired the Constitutional Council. After independence in December 1917, as the civil war and the quarrel between republicans and monarchists unfolded, he helped draft the proposals that became the Constitution of 1919. He favoured a republic and was not involved in Parliament's election of Prince Frederick Charles of Hesse as king in October 1918.

Parliament elected Ståhlberg President of the Republic on 25 July 1919, by 143 votes to 50 against Carl Gustaf Mannerheim. He pardoned most of the Red prisoners, despite criticism from White veterans and senior officers, and signed laws giving trade unions equal bargaining power and the Lex Kallio, which distributed land to former tenant farmers. He did not seek re-election in 1925.

In 1930 activists of the Lapua Movement kidnapped Ståhlberg and his wife, trying to send them to the Soviet Union; the incident hastened the movement's demise. He lost the 1931 presidential election by two votes in the third ballot. From 1946 he advised President J. K. Paasikivi. He died on 22 September 1952 and was buried in Hietaniemi cemetery. Finns regard him as the father of the Constitution and a defender of the rule of law.
ka-ahumanu: Kaʻahumanu, whose name means the Feathered Mantle, was born on 17 March 1768 in a cave called Puu Kauiki at Hāna on Maui. Her father Keʻeaumoku Pāpaʻiahiahi was a fugitive noble from the island of Hawaiʻi and became an adviser and friend of Kamehameha I, eventually serving as governor of Maui. Her mother was a daughter of King Kekaulike of Maui. Through her father she was a third cousin of Kamehameha, and her siblings included the governors John Adams Kuakini of Hawaiʻi and George Keʻeaumoku II of Maui. Her father arranged her marriage to Kamehameha when she was thirteen. He had many wives, but she became a favourite and encouraged his war to unify the islands.

When Kamehameha died on 8 May 1819, Kaʻahumanu announced that he had wished her to share governance with his 22-year-old son Liholiho, who became Kamehameha II. The council agreed and created the post of kuhina nui for her, similar to a co-regent. She continued in that role under Kauikeaouli, Kamehameha III. In the ʻAi Noa, or free eating, she and Keōpūolani, mother of Kamehameha II, ate at the same table as the young king, and she persuaded the high priest Hewahewa to support abolishing the kapu. Breaking the kapu had been a capital offence, but the king refused to put his mother to death, and the system collapsed.

Kauaʻi had never been conquered by force; its king Kaumualiʻi became a vassal of Kamehameha in 1810. Fearing that Kauaʻi would break away, Kamehameha II and Kaʻahumanu kidnapped Kaumualiʻi on 9 October 1821, and she married him by force. After he died in 1824 and a rebellion by his son Humehume was put down, she married his other son Kealiʻiahonui.

In April 1824 she publicly acknowledged her conversion to Protestant Christianity, was baptised on 5 December 1825 and took the name Elizabeth. She presented the first codified laws of Hawaiʻi, modelled on Christian ethics and the Ten Commandments. On 7 July 1827 she ordered the first Catholic missionaries to leave, and in 1830 she signed legislation forbidding Catholic teaching. She also banned the traditional hula in 1830; some chiefs ignored the ban after her death, but the dance was not performed openly again until the reign of Kalākaua in 1886. With Kamehameha III she negotiated the first treaty between Hawaiʻi and the United States in 1826. She died of an intestinal illness on 5 June 1832 in the Mānoa Valley near Honolulu.
ka-mate: Te Rauparaha composed Ka Mate as a celebration of life over death after his escape. On emerging from the pit into the sun he was grateful to Rangikoaea and her husband, Te Wharerangi, and the haka was the result. It was conceived as a brief, energising haka of the ngeri type, in which there are no set movements: the performers are free to extemporise their chanting and movement as they see fit, without any need to keep together.

The haka opens with a chant and then moves to its main body, which begins Ka mate, ka mate! Ka ora, ka ora!, rendered as it is death, it is death, it is life, it is life. The lines go on to a hairy man who brought back the sun so that it could shine once more.

Ka Mate is the best-known haka in New Zealand and abroad because a choreographed, synchronised version has traditionally been performed by the All Blacks, the national rugby union team, and by the Kiwis, the rugby league team, before test matches. Since 2005 the All Blacks have sometimes performed another haka, Kapa o Pango.

Before 1985 most players of European descent had no full training in the haka, and two Māori players, Buck Shelford and Hika Reid, changed the way it was delivered towards a style close to the original. In 2019 the team's haka leader, TJ Perenara, explained that in Wellington the team always performed Ka Mate, out of respect for Te Rauparaha and the lands he walked on.

Between 1998 and 2006 Ngāti Toa tried to register Ka Mate as a trademark to stop its commercial use without their permission. In 2006 the Intellectual Property Office of New Zealand refused, on the grounds that the haka had come to represent New Zealand as a whole. In 2009, as part of a wider settlement of grievances, the government agreed to record the haka's authorship and its significance to Ngāti Toa, without royalties or a veto on its performance, and in March 2011 the New Zealand Rugby Union reached an agreement with the iwi not to bring the haka's mana into disrepute.

On 14 November 2024 Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke of Te Pāti Māori tore a copy of the Treaty Principles Bill in half during its first reading in Parliament and led Ka Mate with her party, other opposition members and the public gallery. The Speaker, Gerry Brownlee, suspended the sitting for 20 minutes and suspended her from Parliament for 24 hours.
kaaba: The name Kaaba means cube in Arabic. In the pre-Islamic religions of Arabia many deities were represented by cubic stone carvings or cubic structures regarded as their abodes, with sacred zones around them. The Black Stone of the Kaaba has been compared to pre-Islamic stones called baetyls, often black and thought to be of meteoric origin. According to Islamic tradition, the Kaaba was rebuilt several times, notably by Ibrahim and his son Ismail. Scholars disagree about its standing before Islam: Christian J. Robin argues that it became prominent in the last decades of the 6th century, while Peter Webb argues that it largely played a local role in Western Arabia.

The Kaaba is a cuboid stone building at the centre of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, about 15 metres high, with sides of 12 and 10.5 metres. Inside, the floor is of marble and limestone, and the interior walls are clad with white marble halfway to the roof. Muslims consider it the House of God, and it determines the qibla, the direction of prayer. Early Muslims faced towards the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem before the direction changed to the Kaaba, which Muslims believe followed a Quranic revelation to Muhammad. Pilgrims circle it seven times anticlockwise in tawaf, which is required in both the hajj and the umrah.

Muhammad took part in the reconstruction of the Kaaba around 600 CE, after a fire and then a flood had weakened it. According to Ibn Ishaq, he settled a quarrel among the Meccan clans over who should set the Black Stone in place by having the elders raise it on a cloak and then setting it with his own hands.

The building was badly damaged by fire on 31 October 683 during the first siege of Mecca in the war between the Umayyads and 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, who rebuilt it. In 693 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan had al-Zubayr's building razed and rebuilt on the foundations laid by the Quraysh; its basic shape has not changed since. In 930 the Qarmatians sacked Mecca and took the Black Stone to al-Ahsa.
kaabu-empire: Mande-speaking people lived in the Senegambia centuries before the Mali Empire. Serer oral traditions call them the Soos, and they are believed to have moved south from the Western Sahara and the Tagant Plateau as the Sahara dried in the first millennium CE. A kingdom known as Kambutchi, ruled by the Jenung dynasty, existed in the region as early as the 7th century. When Mali expanded in the 13th century it brought a new warrior elite, the Nyancho, who were absorbed into the older Mande and Bainuk population, which in turn took on Mandinka political and social forms. Tradition names Tiramakhan Traore as the founder of Kaabu.

Mali declined after the middle of the 14th century, and in the early 16th century the rise of Koli Tenguella cut off its western lands. The Mandinka states of the region then formed a federation, whose provinces grew from three to seven and took in dozens of royal trading towns. Mansa Sala Sane moved the capital from Mampatim to the more central Kansala, the site of the sacred wood where the mansaba was crowned.

From 1776 the Torodbe clerics of the new theocratic state in the Futa Djallon waged jihad against Kaabu. Fula herders settled in Kaabu came to be treated as a possible fifth column, and as the slave trade declined the elites taxed the peasants harder, so the war had ethnic, religious and class sides. In 1867 Alfa Omar of Labé and Alfa Molo Balde besieged Kansala. At the end of the eleven-day Battle of Kansala, Mansaba Janke Waali Sanneh had the gunpowder stores set on fire, and the explosion killed the defenders and three quarters of the attackers. Fuladu became independent under Alfa Molo Balde, while kingdoms such as Kantora, Kiang, Niani and Wuli lasted until British and French rule.

Scholars disagree whether Kaabu was a kingdom, an empire or a federation. Power was decentralised, and people looked more to local leaders than to the distant mansaba. The ruler was chosen from the leaders of Jimara, Sama and Pachana, and only men of Nyancho blood on both sides could be elected; inheritance passed through the mother's line, following Bainuk custom. The principal tax, the kabunko, was paid in cloth woven from cotton grown by slaves, and the revenue paid for wars that captured more slaves. Mandinka was the language of rulers and trade, and the state was not Islamic: its chief shrine was that of the snake Tamba Dibi.
kaba-ye-zartosht: The tower stands 46 metres from the cliff, exactly opposite the tomb of Darius II. It is built of white limestone from Mount Sivand, laid without mortar and joined in places by dovetail joints, with shelves of grey-black stone and blind windows set into the walls so that it looks like a three-storeyed building. It is about 12 metres high, or 14.12 metres with its three-tiered platform, on a base about 7.30 metres square. A stairway of thirty steps leads to a single doorway and one dark room of 3.74 by 3.72 metres, once closed by a heavy two-panel door.

Its black-on-white stonework, its dovetail joints and its door resemble buildings of Pasargadae and of the reign of Darius I, so most scholars date it to the early Achaemenid period; a near twin, known as Solomon's Prison, stands at Pasargadae. Its purpose has long been disputed. Roman Ghirshman and Erich Schmidt held it a fire temple, though others note that the sealed room could not keep a fire burning; many take it for a royal tomb, likened to the Tomb of Cyrus; Henry Rawlinson and Walter Henning saw a treasury for religious documents; Heleen Sancisi Weerdenburg proposed a building for coronations.

The name, the Kaaba of Zoroaster, seems to date from about the fourteenth century, when ancient sites across Iran were attributed to figures of the Quran or the Shahnameh. Kartir's inscription calls the building bon-khanak, the foundation house.

European travellers such as Jean Chardin, Engelbert Kaempfer and Cornelis de Bruijn drew it in the seventeenth century, and Carsten Niebuhr described it in 1765. Ernst Herzfeld investigated the site in 1923, and the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago, led by Erich Schmidt, worked there between 1936 and 1939. On 1 June 1936 it found Shapur I's inscription, in Greek (70 lines), Arsacid Middle Persian (30) and Sassanian Middle Persian (35), telling of the death of Gordian III, the payment by Philip of half a million gold dinars and the capture of Valerian. Kartir's 19 lines, written around 280 under Bahram II, record his rise and his campaigns against Christianity, Manichaeism, Judaism, Buddhism and other religions.
kabaka-of-buganda: The word Kabaka means emissary, and tradition holds that at some point in the past an overseer sent from Bunyoro set himself up as an independent ruler. The king belongs to the royal clan, Olulyo Olulangira, whose men are called abalangira and women abambejja. It is often said that the Kabaka takes his clan from his mother, or that the royal family was matrilineal, but neither is true: like other Baganda, the royals trace their genealogy through the father, back to Kintu. The idea arose partly because the royal clan, unlike every other Baganda clan, has no totem.

According to Baganda tradition the kingdom has two kings, one spiritual and one secular. The spiritual king is represented by the Royal Drums, the regalia called Mujaguzo, which have their own palace, officials and guards; since they always exist, Buganda always has a king. A human prince must perform rites on the drums before he can be declared king, and the drums are sounded at royal births and at a king's death. In Buganda culture a king does not die but is lost in the forest, and the royal tombs, such as the Kasubi Tombs, show the entrance of that forest.

A further tradition began on the death of Kabaka Tebandeke. His cousin Ndawula Nsobya became the material king, while his only surviving son, Juma Katebe, took the spiritual priesthood once joined to the throne. The two lines have followed each other ever since.

Buganda has no crown prince. During a reign a special council studies the young princes, and on its advice the king chooses a successor, who receives a piece of bark cloth in secret. When the royal family views the dead king's body, the chosen prince lays the cloth over it and so reveals himself. The firstborn prince, called Kiweewa, may not become king, which protects him from rivals; the only exception came in 1888, during the religious civil war, when a Kiweewa was made king.
kabardians: The Kabardians, or Kabardinians, are one of the twelve major Circassian tribes, each represented by one of the twelve stars on the green-and-gold Circassian flag. They are also known as Kabardin, Kebertei or Kabarday. Along with the Besleney tribe they speak a distinctive dialect of Circassian. Historically they lived in Kabardia, a region of the north Caucasus, which partly corresponds to the present Russian republic of Kabardino-Balkaria.

Soviet administrative divisions placed Circassians under four designations and political units: Adygeans in Adygea, Cherkessians in Karachay-Cherkessia, Kabardians in Kabardino-Balkaria and Shapsugs in Krasnodar Krai. The four groups are essentially the same people, and the Cherkessians are mostly of the Kabardian and Besleney tribes.

Religions historically practised by Kabardians include the native Adyghe Xabze faith, Christianity and Islam. Kabardians also formed one of the earliest Christian communities in Europe, converting in the late 2nd and early 3rd centuries. Some Roman Catholic Kabardians may descend from families who reportedly converted from Orthodoxy during the 13th century. The majority had converted to Islam by the early 19th century, and most Kabardians today are either non-denominational or Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school. A small share still follows traditional Xabze beliefs, and Kabardians in the Mozdoksky District of North Ossetia and parts of Stavropol Krai are Orthodox Christians.

Kabardians are the largest Circassian group in the world and the largest in Russia, Turkey, Egypt and other countries. In 2002 around 520,000 lived in Kabardino-Balkaria and about 50,000 in Karachay-Cherkessia. More than a million live in Turkey, concentrated on the Uzunyayla plateau of Kayseri Province and around central Turkey, with villages also in the north-west and along the Black Sea coast. Significant populations live in Jordan, and there are communities in the United States.

Kabardians have also entered the wider history of the region. Maria Temryukovna became tsaritsa of Russia as the wife of Ivan the Terrible, and Alexey Cherkassky served as Chancellor of the Russian Empire under Empress Elizabeth. Bidar Kadın was imperial consort of Abdul Hamid II, and Servetseza Kadın the first wife of Abdulmejid I of the Ottoman Empire.
kabars: The Kabars, also called Qavars or Khavars, were Khazar rebels. Their rising against the Khazar Khaganate in the early 9th century was notable enough to be recorded by Constantine Porphyrogenitus in De Administrando Imperio. According to the historian Magocsi, a violent civil war in Khazaria in the 820s ended in their defeat, and the losers fled in two directions: northward to the Varangian Rus' in the upper Volga region near Rostov, and southward to the Magyars, who had formerly been loyal vassals of the Khazars.

Those who joined the Magyars went with the confederacy called Hét-Magyar, the seven Hungarians, from Levedia to Etelköz, while others under Khan-Tuvan sought refuge with the Rus'. Magocsi argues that Kabar refugees among the Varangian traders of Rostov raised the traders' prestige, so that by the 830s a new power centre, the Rus' Khaganate, had come into being. The name Kiabar on the Kievian Letter suggests that some Kabars settled in Kiev as well.

Known in Latin as Cowari, the Kabars served the Magyars as vanguard and rearguard. In 894 the Byzantine emperor Leo VI, at war with Simeon of Bulgaria, called in the Hungarians, who under Árpád crossed the Danube and attacked Bulgaria; the Bulgarians answered by setting the Pechenegs on their rear. Arnulf, duke of Carinthia, also sought Hungarian help against Svatopluk of Great Moravia. The Kabars took part in the invasion of Pannonia and the forming of the Principality of Hungary, and after Great Moravia collapsed the Hungarians settled in Hungary for good in 907.

A Turkic aristocracy among the Hungarians may explain why Byzantine protocol under Constantine Porphyrogenitus always called the Hungarian rulers Princes of the Turks. The religion of the Kabars is debated. At least part of the Khazar elite converted to Judaism, while most people of the khaganate stayed pagan. Since the conversion was begun by the ruler, scholars have doubted that rebels against him would have followed it, and the Kabars may have joined the Magyars before it took place. One theory links graves with Jewish symbols at Čelarevo in Serbia to them, and the remains and linguistic traces ascribed to them are likewise disputed.
kabir: The years of Kabir's birth and death are uncertain, and some historians favour 1398–1448 while others favour 1440–1518. Followers hold that he came from Satloka and appeared on a lotus flower. A few accounts say that as an infant he was found at Lahartara Lake by a Muslim weaver named Niru and his wife Nima, who raised him. He is believed to have become a disciple of the Bhakti poet-saint Ramananda in Varanasi, and the Persian text Dabestan-e Mazaheb, the earliest known text with biographical information, calls him a Bairagi, a Vaishnava yogi, and a disciple of Ramanand. His family is believed to have lived at Kabir Chaura in Varanasi.

Kabir's couplets suggest that he was persecuted for his views while alive, and he was said to have been threatened by both Hindus and Muslims. Legends describe him as an underdog who triumphs in trials before a sultan or a Brahmin, but many scholars doubt them, pointing to the lack of corroborating evidence. When he died, Hindus and Muslims both claimed him.

Kabir composed his poems orally in Sadhukkadi, a mixed language drawing on Khadi boli, Braj, Bhojpuri, Marwari and Awadhi, in simple words. He and his followers called them bāṇīs, utterances, and they include songs and couplets such as the dohe and the sākhī, a word meaning witness. Collections attributed to him include the Kabir Bijak, the Sakhi Granth and the Kabir Granthawali, and his verses form the largest non-Sikh contribution to the Adi Granth. Except for the Adi Granth, the versions differ considerably, and the Bijak was first written down in the seventeenth century, so scholars debate which poems are authentic.

Kabir attacked what he regarded as the follies of Hinduism and Islam alike and questioned the need for any holy book. Linda Hess holds that he is falsely presented as a synthesizer of the two religions, since he declared his independence from both. He taught that God is within every person and urged people to drop the ego. The Kabir panth, a Sant Mat sect that recognises him as its founder, arose centuries after his death, over the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and two temples to him stand in Varanasi, one maintained by Hindus and one by Muslims. Rabindranath Tagore's Songs of Kabir was first published in 1915.
kabirdham-district: Kabirdham district is one of the 33 administrative districts of Chhattisgarh state in central India, and was formerly known as Kawardha district. It covers 4,447.5 square kilometres, and the city of Kawardha is its administrative headquarters. Dindori District of Madhya Pradesh lies to the north, Mungeli and Bemetara districts to the east, Rajnandgaon District to the south, and Balaghat and Mandla districts of Madhya Pradesh to the west. The northern and western parts are surrounded by the Maikal mountain ranges of the Satpura range.

The present tehsil of Kawardha was a princely state, formed in 1751 by Mahabali Singh, the first zamindar of the Kawardha riyasat, who also founded Kawardha city. In 1895 it became Kawardha tehsil of Mandla district. In 1903 it was included in Bilaspur district, in 1912 it moved to Raipur district, and in 1948 it became part of Durg district. On 26 January 1973 the new district of Rajnandgaon was created and Kawardha became part of it. The other tehsil, Pandariya, was a zamindari until 1952, when it became a community block of Bilaspur district, and in 1986 it was raised to a tehsil.

On 2 July 1998 the government of Madhya Pradesh decided to create a new district, Kawardha, by combining the tehsil of Kawardha of Rajnandgaon district with the tehsil of Pandariya of Bilaspur district, and it came into existence on 6 July 1998. On 17 January 2003 the chief minister, Ajit Jogi, renamed it Kabirdham at the celebration of the sixth century of the birth of Dhani Dharm Das, founder of the Kabir panth in Chhattisgarh. Kawardha had been the Guru Gaddi seat of the Kabir panth from 1806 to 1903: the eighth Guru, Haq Nam Saheb, established it there in 1806, and the twelfth Guru, Ugr Nam Saheb, moved it to Damakheda in 1903.

The district is known for the Bhoramdeo Temple, nicknamed the Khajuraho of Chhattisgarh, 18 kilometres from Kawardha, and for the surrounding Bhoramdev Wildlife Sanctuary. The census of 2011 counted 822,526 people, of whom 96.13 per cent spoke Chhattisgarhi as their first language and 2.32 per cent Hindi. The district is divided into four tehsils: Kabirdham, Bodla, Sahaspur - Lohara and Pandariya.
kabuki: The history of kabuki is traced to 1603, when Izumo no Okuni, a former shrine maiden who may have served at Izumo-taisha, began performing with a troupe of young women in Kyoto. They gave a simple style of dance drama in pantomime on a makeshift stage in the dry bed of the Kamo River. In the earliest forms women played both men and women in comic playlets about ordinary life. Okuni was asked to perform before the Imperial Court, and rival troupes quickly formed.

The word is believed to derive from the verb kabuku, meaning to lean or to be out of the ordinary; the kabukimono were originally people bizarrely dressed, such as gangs of samurai. The characters for sing, dance and skill are ateji and do not reflect the etymology.

After women and young boys were banned from the stage in 1629, kabuki became the all-male form called yarō-kabuki. Male actors known as onnagata took over the women's roles, with young men preferred for their less obviously masculine appearance and higher voices. A kabuki stage has the hanamichi, or flower path, a walkway through the audience used for entrances and exits. Revolving stages and trap doors were introduced in the 18th century to produce sudden revelations and transformations.

Actors wear layered kimono in vibrant colours and the white oshiroi base. Kumadori make-up exaggerates facial lines into masks, with red for passion and heroism, blue or black for villainy, green for the supernatural and purple for nobility.

In the Genroku period the structure of the plays took the form still performed, and kabuki and the puppet theatre ningyō jōruri, later called bunraku, influenced each other. Chikamatsu Monzaemon was among the first professional kabuki playwrights; his The Love Suicides at Sonezaki, written for bunraku and adapted for kabuki, reportedly inspired copycat suicides and led to a government ban on plays about love suicides in 1723. The actor Ichikawa Danjūrō I is credited with the mie style of posing.  In 1842, under the Tenpō Reforms, the shogunate forced three theatres out of Edo into Asakusa and restricted the trade and socialising that went on in them.

After 1868 actors and playwrights worked to improve the reputation of kabuki, and the Emperor sponsored a performance on 21 April 1887. The occupying forces banned it briefly after the World War II, but the ban was rescinded by 1947. UNESCO inscribed it on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.
kabul: Kabul lies at an altitude of 1,791 m in a narrow valley of the Hindu Kush, along the Kabul River, in the eastern part of Afghanistan. South of the old city stand the ancient city walls and the Sher Darwaza mountain, and further east the ancient fortress of Bala Hissar. The city lies on the trade routes of Central Asia and South Asia and is traditionally seen as the meeting point between Tartary, Hindustan and Persia.

The origin of Kabul, who built it and when, is largely unknown, though it is believed to be over 3,500 years old. The Rigveda and the Avesta refer to the Kabul River and to a settlement called Kubha. Greek writers called it Kophen or Kophes. After Cyrus the Great annexed the Median Empire in 549 BCE, Kabul became part of the Achaemenid Empire and a centre of learning for Zoroastrianism, followed by Buddhism and Hinduism. An inscription on the tomb of Darius the Great lists it among the 29 countries of that empire.

After Alexander the Great annexed the Achaemenid Empire, the valley passed to the Seleucid Empire, which in 305 BCE ceded Gandhara, including the Kabul Valley, to the Maurya Empire. Trade flourished under Mauryan uniform weights and measures. Later empires that claimed Kabul include the Kushan, Ghaznavid, Ghorid and Timurid. In the 16th century the Mughal rulers used it as their summer capital, and it prospered.

Kabul became part of the Durrani Empire in 1747 and the capital of Afghanistan in 1776 under Timur Shah Durrani. British forces occupied it briefly in the First and Second Anglo-Afghan Wars. In the second half of the 20th century it was a stop on the hippie trail and was nicknamed the Paris of Central Asia. The Saur Revolution of 1978 and the Soviet intervention of 1979, which began a ten-year war, ended that period, and a civil war among mujahideen factions in the 1990s destroyed much of the city. The Taliban captured it in 1996.

Kabul is the capital and largest city of Afghanistan and has long been its political, cultural and economic centre. Its people speak mainly Dari and Pashto. Historical gardens and palaces include the Arg, Bagh-e Babur, Bagh-e Bala, Chihil Sutun, Darul Aman and Tajbeg.
kabyles: The name Kabyle comes from the Arabic qaba'il, meaning tribes, a word once used of mountain-dwelling peoples in Algeria generally. For the Kabyles specifically the older name is Zwawa, used since the medieval period for the tribes of Greater Kabylia and found in Ibn Khaldun. According to Mohamed Benrabah, the French first used Kabyle for all Berbers and only in the colonial era narrowed it to the people of Kabylia. Their own names for the region are Tamurt Idurar, Land of Mountains, and Tamurt n Iqbayliyen, Land of the Kabyle.

The Kabyles were among the few peoples of North Africa who stayed independent under the Carthaginians, Romans, Vandals, Byzantines and Ottoman Turks, and even after the Arab conquest they kept their mountains. Between 902 and 909 Kutama Berbers from Little Kabylia helped found the Fatimid Caliphate. The Zirids, a family of Sanhaja Berbers from the Kabyle mountains, later ruled much of the Maghreb, and the Hammadids, who broke from them, held Algiers, Béjaïa and other cities.

Under Ottoman rule the Kabyles lived mainly in three entities: the Kingdom of Kuku, the Kingdom of Ait Abbas and the principality of Aït Jubar. Kabylia was the last part of northern Algeria taken by the French, in 1854 to 1857, despite vigorous resistance, and leaders such as Lalla Fatma N'Soumer fought on until Mokrani's rebellion of 1871. The French took land from resisting tribes for colonists and deported many resisters, mainly to New Caledonia. Many Kabyles emigrated, including as workers to France, where Algerian migrants in the 1920s organised the first party for independence.

After independence in 1962 tensions with the central government recurred. Hocine Aït Ahmed founded the Socialist Forces Front in September 1963, and the army was sent into Kabylia; about 400 deaths were counted among the maquis. In 1980 months of protest, called the Berber Spring, demanded recognition of Berber as an official language. In 2001 the killing of a student, Massinissa Guermah, in custody set off the Black Spring, in which at least 126 people were killed. Tamazight was recognised in Algeria's constitution on 6 January 2016.

Kabyle villages were governed by assemblies called djemaas, which settled disputes and set customary law and which French administration preserved as part of an indirect system. The Kabyles speak Kabyle, a Berber language of the Afroasiatic family, spoken by about 3 million people in 2004. It was once written in the Libyco-Berber script, and since the 19th century in a Latin alphabet. They are mainly Muslim, with a small Christian minority. Their economy has rested on orchards, olive trees and crafts such as pottery and tapestry, and oral poetry, the asefru, is performed by imusnawen.
kabylia: Kabylia, in Kabyle Tamurt n leqbayel, is a mountainous coastal region of northern Algeria on the edge of the Mediterranean, part of the Tell Atlas, and the homeland of the Kabyle people. It covers, wholly or partly, nine provinces: Tizi Ouzou, Boumerdes, Bouira, Setif, Bordj Bou Arreridj, Jijel, Béjaïa, Mila and Skikda. The name comes from the Arabic qaba'il, meaning tribes, and during French colonial rule was used for the region's tribal groups before it became a regional name.

Three large mountain chains occupy most of the area: the maritime range in the north, the Djurdjura in the south, rising to 2,308 metres at Lalla Khedidja, and between them the Agawa range, the most populous, where Tizi Ouzou, the largest town of Great Kabylia, lies. Gouraya National Park and Djurdjura National Park are also in Kabylia.

The area was part of the Kingdom of Numidia. Its history appears in classical books from the fourth century CE with the revolt of the commander Firmus and his brother Guildon. Under the Romans, Vandals and Byzantines the Kabyles were among the few Imazighen of North Africa who remained independent, and during the Arab conquest they could temporarily keep their mountains. Between 902 and 909 the Kutama Berbers of Little Kabylia helped found the Fatimid Caliphate, in which Kutama power spread widely until al-Aziz Billah reduced their role in the army.

The French gradually took the region after 1830 despite vigorous resistance led by Faḍma n Sumer and Cheikh Mokrani. The Battle of Icheriden in 1857 marked a decisive French victory, though violence continued as late as Mokrani's rebellion of 1871. Much land was confiscated and given to French settlers, and many people were arrested and deported, mainly to New Caledonia. During the War of Independence from 1954 to 1962 the nationalists created a unified Kabyle territory, wilaya III. Kabylia was a main centre of the maquis and one of the areas most affected by French counter-insurgency, including the destruction of villages and the displacement of people. The FLN's first conference, at Soummam, took place there in 1956.

The Kabyles are a Berber people who speak Kabyle, the largest Berber language in Algeria, spoken by about 3 million people. Since the Berber Spring of 1980 they have been at the forefront of the campaign for recognition of Tamazight; it became a national language in 2002 and an official language in 2016. Traditional farming rests on olive trees and orchards and on crafts such as pottery. Béjaïa's port is the second biggest in Algeria. The region has dozens of zawiyas affiliated with the Rahmaniyya Sufi brotherhood.
kachin-people: The Kachin peoples, in Kachin Ga Hkyeng or red soil, are diverse ethnolinguistic groups living in the Kachin Hills of northern Myanmar, in Yunnan Province in China and in the Indian states of Arunachal Pradesh and Assam, about 1.5 million people in all. The term usually covers four to six groups: the Jingpo, the Zaiwa, the Lashi and the Lawngwaw or Maru, with the Rawang and the Lisu to a lesser extent. The name Kachin was probably used by Burmese and Shan speakers for the Jingpo before British rule, and in the colonial period became a wide administrative label. The peoples have no commonly agreed name for themselves.

Kachin oral history traces descent from Măjoi Shingra Bum, a mountain plateau to the north. Kachin historians place a migration from the Tibetan Plateau around 100 CE, while others date the arrival to the 5th century or, in earlier readings, the 17th.

In the highlands the Kachin stayed largely independent of the lowland states, raiding Shan and Burmese communities and suffering retaliation. In the 8th and 9th centuries the hills came under the influence of the Kingdom of Nanzhao, and later of powerful Shan states. As Shan power weakened, Kachin in the Hukawng Valley gained great influence and enslaved Shans. Under the Anglo-Singpho agreement of 1826 the British freed 6,000 slaves. From 1897 the British enlisted Kachin in the army and police, and in the Second World War irregular forces called the Northern Kachin Levies fought the Japanese for them.

Kachin State was established on 10 January 1947, and in February 1947 Kachin leaders took part in the Panglong Agreement led by Aung San. After his assassination the promised autonomy was not delivered, and Kachin leaders today regard the agreement as an unfulfilled obligation. The Kachin Independence Organisation was founded on 25 October 1960 and its army, the Kachin Independence Army, fought the Burmese military until a ceasefire on 24 February 1994. On 9 June 2011 fighting resumed, and by the end of a conflict that lasted two years an estimated 100,000 Kachin people were displaced.

The Kachin traditionally practise slash-and-burn farming in unirrigated hill fields, in contrast to the lowland Shan. Families form households within patrilineal clans called amyu, and mayu lineages give wives to a clan while dama lineages receive them. Traditional religion was a form of animism with sacrifices to nats; the Baptist missionary Josiah Cushing began a mission at Bhamo in the 1870s, and the first recorded baptism took place in 1882. Estimates of the share who now identify as Christian run from about two thirds to 90 to 95 per cent.
kachin-state: Kachin State covers 89,041 square kilometres. It is bordered by China to the north and east, by Shan State to the south, and by Sagaing Region and Arunachal Pradesh in India to the west. Besides Myitkyina, its capital, its important towns include Bhamo, Mohnyin and Putao. The state holds Myanmar's highest mountain, Hkakabo Razi, at 5,889 metres, and a large inland lake, Indawgyi Lake. Its economy is predominantly agricultural, and its minerals include gold and jade. Hpakant is well known for its jade mines, and Bhamo is one of the border trading points with China.

The Nanzhao Kingdom controlled much of Upper Burma, including the area of the present state, and the Dali Kingdom afterwards administered the lands of the Kachin people. The Qing dynasty briefly controlled it during the Sino-Burmese War of 1760. The region was historically inhabited by many groups, among them the Rawang, Lisu, Jingpo and Zaiwa, and the term Kachin was given by the British in the colonial period. Traditional society rested on shifting hill agriculture, with political authority held by chieftains, and the people were animist. The British accepted the autonomy of the Kachin Hills, though their forces carried out expeditions against the Kachin in 1892 and 1896.

On 12 February 1947 Aung San reached the Panglong Agreement with the Shan, Kachin and Chin peoples, which envisioned a Kachin State. Burma became independent on 4 January 1948, and the state was formed the same year from the former civil districts of Bhamo and Myitkyina and the northern district of Puta-o. The northern frontier was not demarcated until the 1960s. After the military coup of 1962 Kachin forces, who had formed a significant part of the Burmese army, withdrew and formed the Kachin Independence Army. The state was virtually independent from the mid-1960s through 1994, when an army offensive seized the jade mines and a ceasefire was signed.

Kachin State had a population of 1,689,441 in the census of 2014. Its mountain hinterlands are mostly Kachin, while the railway corridor and southern valleys are mostly Shan and Bamar. Buddhists form the largest religious community, with a large Christian minority. Burmese and Jingpho are the lingua francas, and a railway links Myitkyina with Mandalay.
kad-koy: Kadıköy is a municipality and district of Istanbul Province, covering about 25 square kilometres on the Asian side of the city, on the northern shore of the Sea of Marmara. It partly faces the historic centre of Constantinople across the Bosporus and is bordered by the districts of Üsküdar, Ataşehir and Maltepe. It was separated from Üsküdar in 1928, and the neighbourhoods of Bostancı and Suadiye, taken from Kartal in the same year, joined it.

Kadıköy is an older settlement than most on the Anatolian side of Istanbul. Chalcolithic finds of about 5500–3500 BCE come from the Fikirtepe Mound, and a port settlement of Phoenician date has also been found. Chalcedon was the first settlement the Greeks of Megara established on the Bosporus, in 685 BCE, a few years before Byzantium was founded across the strait in 667 BCE. It was called the city of the blind: Byzantium was said to have been founded after a prophecy that a capital would rise opposite it, since Chalcedon's people had failed to see the value of the Golden Horn. The fourth ecumenical council, the Council of Chalcedon, met there in 451.

Persians, Bithynians, Romans, Byzantines, Arabs, Crusaders and Turks held it in turn, and it was badly damaged during the Fourth Crusade. It came into Ottoman hands in 1353, a century before Constantinople, and so has the oldest mosque in Istanbul. After the conquest of 1453 it was a rural settlement outside the city's protection, placed under the jurisdiction of the Constantinople courts; the name Kadıköy, Village of the Judge, refers to Istanbul's first judge, Hızır Bey. Ottoman estimates of 1882 gave a population of 6,733: 2,695 Muslims, 1,831 Armenians, 1,822 Greeks, 249 Jews and smaller groups.

The population was recorded as 467,919 in 2023. The district is a residential, commercial and cultural area and a transport hub: the Haydarpaşa Terminal, opened in 1908 as the terminus of the Istanbul–Baghdad and Istanbul–Damascus–Medina railways, stands close to the centre, and ferries link it with the European shore. Marmara University has most of its buildings here. Kadıköy is the district where the club Fenerbahçe was founded and where the first football match in the Ottoman Empire was played. It remains the see of the Metropolis of Chalcedon of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople.
kadashman-enlil-i: Kadashman-Enlil was perhaps the 18th king of the Kassite dynasty of Babylon. His correspondence with Amenhotep III of Egypt, whom the letters call Nibmuareya, places him securely in the first half of the 14th century BCE by most standard chronologies. Five tablets of the Amarna letters, EA 1 to 5, belong to the exchange: three written by Kadashman-Enlil and two by the pharaoh.

In EA 1 Amenhotep assures him that his sister, a daughter of Kurigalzu I, has not died or been sent away as a minor concubine, and mocks the envoys as men unable to recognise her. In EA 3 Kadashman-Enlil complains of being left out of an invitation to a festival, and invites his brother king to the opening of his own new palace.

In EA 4 he protests that no Egyptian princess has been sent to him, quoting the reply that since earliest times no daughter of the king of Egypt had been given in marriage, and asks at least for a beautiful woman, while offering one of his own daughters in exchange for gold he needed for a building project. EA 5 lists the gifts the pharaoh would send for her, sealing the agreement.

His inscriptions are hard to tell apart from those of his descendant Kadashman-Enlil II, who ruled about a century later. Historians disagree whether building inscriptions at Isin, for the Egalmah of Gula, and bricks at Larsa recording the restoration of the Ebabbar temple of Šamaš belong to the earlier king, and finds from Nippur describing work on the Ekur, the temple of Enlil, could belong in part to either. An economic tablet from Nippur dated to his 15th year is assigned to him, and another names the 1st year of Burna-Buriash II after the 15th of his predecessor. An inscription on a block of lapis lazuli from Nippur suggests that Burna-Buriash II, his successor, may have been his son.
kadazan-dusun: The Kadazan-Dusun number almost a million people, concentrated in Sabah's West Coast Division, the upper Interior Division and Kudat Division, and in the Sandakan and Tawau divisions. Their tradition holds that they descend from the Nunuk Ragang, although not all the groups now counted as Kadazan-Dusun came from the same place. Other names they use for themselves are Mamasok and Momogun, meaning indigenous people and people of the land, sometimes combined as Pasok Momogun.

Dusun, meaning orchard people, was a Malay exonym used by the tax collectors of the Sultanate of Brunei for the agricultural peoples of northern Borneo; the Dusunic languages have no such word. Kadazan was the name used on the western coast, around Jesselton, Penampang, Papar and Beaufort, and was widely used by Roman Catholic missionaries from the 1880s. According to the Bobolian priestesses, Kadazan means people.

The British North Borneo Chartered Company grouped all these peoples under a single Dusun classification, and an early census of British North Borneo counted the Dusuns as the largest group, almost half the population. Article 9 of the company's royal charter of 1 November 1881 required its courts to have careful regard to the customs and laws of each people, above all in land, inheritance and marriage. Roman Catholic missionaries of the Mill Hill mission in the late 19th century made Christianity prominent among the Kadazans of Penampang and Papar and most Dusuns of Tambunan. Towards the end of British rule, Kadazan-Dusun parties governed Sabah.

The Kadazan-Dusun are known above all as farmers of wet rice and hill paddy, and the Kaamatan festival honours the paddy's spirit, Bambarayon. Customary law, adat, governs the gathering of forest produce and hunting while limiting over-exploitation, and the tagal system manages river fisheries. Their paramount leader is called Huguon Siou, brave leader.

Most are now Christians, mainly Roman Catholics, while some Dusuns of Ranau and the Bisaya of Beaufort, Kuala Penyu and Sipitang practise Islam; before conversion they followed a traditional religion, Momolianism, and practised headhunting, as did the Muruts. Music centres on the gong and the kulintangan, and the main dance of the Penampang Kadazan, the Sumazau, is performed by a man and a woman to seven or eight gongs.
kadi-burhan-al-din: Ahmad Burhan al-Din was born in Kayseri on 8 January 1345 into a family that had held the office of qadi for generations; his first ancestor in Anatolia was a Khwarezmian of the Salur tribe of the Oghuz Turks. His father, Shams al-Din Muhammad, was qadi of Kayseri and one of the viziers of the Eretnid ruler, and his mother, related to the Seljuk sultans, died when he was a year and a half old. Raised by his father, he mastered Persian and Arabic, Islamic law and logic, as well as horsemanship, swordsmanship and archery.

Although favoured by the Eretnid sultan, Burhan al-Din secretly joined the rising of local magnates in which Ghiyath al-Din was killed in 1365. As qadi of Kayseri he built close ties with the nomadic tribes, and by 1376 he was a powerful commander. Arrested by the Eretnid ruler Ala al-Din Ali when his ambitions were uncovered, he was freed by Hajji Ibrahim, the emir of Sivas, and in June 1378 the Eretnid emirs made him vizier. In 1381 he killed the ruler's deputy and proclaimed himself ruler, first as atabeg and then as sultan, striking his own coins and having the khutba delivered in his name.

His rule was a long struggle against the Ottomans, Mamluks, Karamanids, Aq Qoyunlu, Qara Qoyunlu and local emirs. He often pardoned defeated enemies to reduce their number, survived an assassination attempt in Sivas in 1383 and defeated the rulers of Amasya in 1384. In 1398 he was captured in a sudden attack by Qara Yuluk Osman and executed despite offering to give up Kayseri. His son Zeynal held power briefly before the Ottomans took Sivas.

Burhan al-Din wrote on Islamic law in Arabic, above all the Tarjih al-Tawzih, a commentary on the principles of jurisprudence, and a Sufi treatise, the Elixir of Happiness in the Mysteries of Worship, completed during the years 1395–1396, which he spent in Sivas. His divan of 1,500 ghazals and 119 tuyughs is the oldest such collection from Eastern Anatolia; the scholar Jan Rypka called him a poet of profane love. Scholars such as Mehmet Fuat Köprülü and Muharrem Ergin find in its language the features of Azerbaijani Turkic, and he is counted with Nasimi among the founders of Azerbaijani poetry.
kaduna-river: The Kaduna River is a tributary of the Niger that flows for 550 kilometres through Nigeria. Its name comes from the crocodiles that lived in the river and the land around it: kaduna is the Hausa word for crocodiles. In the Nupe language territory through which its southern section flows, including its confluence with the Niger, the river is called Lavun.

It rises in Plateau State on the Jos Plateau, 29 kilometres south-west of the town of Jos. In Kaduna State, which is named after it, the river turns to a south-westerly course and cuts through the city of Kaduna, dividing it into a northern and a southern section. It then enters Niger State, where it is dammed first at Shiroro and again at Zungeru, forming two fairly large reservoirs, before it turns sharply south and meets the Niger at the confluence south of Bida.

Most of the course runs through open savanna woodland, though the lower section has cut several gorges above the point where the river enters the wide floodplains of the Niger. The river is used for fishing and for the transport of local produce.

Studies have linked urban and industrial wastes to raised temperatures and heavy metal concentrations in the river, and untreated industrial waste dumped directly or through wastewater inflows has been identified as a source of pollution. Recurring floods at Kaduna led the federal government to set up a flood control project, and in 2022 flooding from the river did considerable damage to property in the surrounding area.
kaduna-state: Kaduna State lies on the northern high plains of Nigeria, in Sudan savanna country of scattered short trees, shrubs and grasses. The Kaduna River, a tributary of the Niger, flows through it. The most widespread explanation of the name is that it comes from the Hausa plural kadduna, crocodiles, which were once numerous in the river; another derives it from the Gbagyi name Odna for the river. The state borders seven others, among them Zamfara, Katsina and Kano to the north and Niger to the west.

The area holds sites of some of Africa's oldest civilisations, among them the Nok civilisation, which prospered from about 1500 BCE to about 500 CE. In the 9th century the geographer and historian Ya'qubi documented the Hausa kingdoms, which lasted until the region was incorporated into the Sokoto Caliphate in the early 1800s. Zazzau, the traditional state around Zaria, is said to have been founded in 1536, and Zaria is said to have been renamed after the younger sister of Queen Amina. The walls built in the time of Queen Amina are between 14 and 16 km long and are closed by eight gates.

Under British rule Lord Frederick Lugard moved the capital of the Northern Region from Zungeru to the city of Kaduna in 1916. In 1967 the old Northern Region was divided, and Kaduna became the capital of North-Central State, which was renamed Kaduna State in 1976. In 1987 the state was divided again, creating Katsina State. The state is thus the successor of the old Northern Region, and the many peoples within it have often been thought of simply as Hausa.

The capital is the city of Kaduna. About 59 to 63 ethnic groups live in the state, with the Hausa and Fulani the dominant ones; the main religions are Islam and Christianity, and some minority groups, mostly in the south, practise traditional worship. Cotton and groundnuts are the main crops. The state calls itself the Centre of Learning because of institutions such as Ahmadu Bello University at Zaria, established in 1962, and the Nigerian Defence Academy. The palace of the Emir of Zaria, the Zaria city walls and Lugard Hall are among its historic buildings.
kaesong: Kaesong lies in the centre of Korea and is the southernmost city of North Korea, close to the border with South Korea and just north of Kanghwa Island. It covers 1,309 km2. The urban district is surrounded by Songak Mountain, 489 metres high, and Pongmyong mountain, and most of the area consists of low hills. The Imjin River runs along the north-eastern border and the Ryesong River along the western. About 55% of the area is forested, mostly pine, and the frost-free period of 180 days is the longest in North Korea. The earliest signs of habitation date from the Neolithic era.

The area lay in the realm of the Mahan confederacy and was known as Busogap under Goguryeo. Baekje held it for about 100 years until 475, and it became part of Silla in 555 as Song'ak-gun. As Silla declined in the late 9th century, Kaesong fell in 898 to Gung Ye, the founder of the short-lived state of Taebong, and in 919 became part of Goryeo under its founder Wang Geon, enthroned as Taejo of Goryeo, who made it the national capital. It was renamed Gaegyeong in 960. During the second conflict of the Goryeo-Khitan War in 1010 the palace and houses were almost burnt down.

In 1198 a slave named Manjŏk gathered other slaves outside the city, but Ch'oe Ch'ung-hŏn suppressed the plot. When Yi Song-gye overthrew Goryeo in 1392 and founded Joseon, the capital was moved to Hanyang, the modern Seoul. Under Japanese occupation from 1910 to 1945 the city was called Kaijō. After the Second World War it lay mostly south of the 38th parallel, and the Korean People's Army took it in the first days of the Korean War. Ceasefire negotiations began there on 10 July 1951, and the Armistice of 27 July 1953 left Kaesong under North Korean control, the only city to pass from South to North Korea as a result of the war.

Kaesong was named a special city in October 2019. Called Songdo while it was the capital of Goryeo, it prospered as a trading centre that produced Korean ginseng, and it is now North Korea's light industry centre. It is home to the World Heritage Site Historic Monuments and Sites in Kaesong, which includes the remains of the Manwoldae palace, and the tombs of almost all the Goryeo kings, among them the reconstructed tomb of the founder Taejo. The Koryo Museum occupies the old Confucian academy of Songgyungwan, which began as the Gukjagam in 992. In 2009 the city had 192,578 inhabitants.
kafue-river: The Kafue rises at an elevation of 1,350 metres on a flat plateau of miombo woodland on the Congo–Zambezi watershed, in Zambia's North-western Province, 120 km north-west of Chingola. It begins as a trickle from marshy dambos and meanders sluggishly south-east. Past the Copperbelt towns of Chililabombwe, Chingola and Mufulira it turns south-west at Kitwe and then forms a maze of channels and lagoons on a swampy floodplain beside the Lukanga Swamp, where the combined wetland in the rains exceeds 6,000 square kilometres.

It then enters Kafue National Park, the second largest in Africa, and skirts the Busanga Plain, known for herds of buffalo, zebra and antelope. At the Itezhi-Tezhi Gap it turns east through a ridge about 100 metres high. Beyond lie the Kafue Flats, a floodplain about 240 km long and 50 km wide, home to tens of thousands of Kafue lechwe and many birds and formerly called Butwa after the Twa people. Below Kafue town the river drops 550 metres over 60 km in the Kafue Gorge and joins the Zambezi about 20 km north of Chirundu.

The river once flowed south all the way to Lake Makgadikgadi and on to the Limpopo, like the upper Zambezi, Okavango and Cuando. Uplift of the land and a rift valley changed this, and the Kafue cut the Itezhi-Tezhi Gap and turned east. The lower Zambezi, originally a separate river, cut back through the rift valleys and eventually captured it.

The Kafue Railway Bridge, opened in 1906 to connect Kafue with Mazabuka, was meant to be part of the Cape to Cairo Railway. The first road bridge was built across the Thames in London during the Second World War, dismantled afterwards and installed about 9 km downstream of the railway bridge; before that, road traffic crossed on a pontoon. The Itezhi-Tezhi Dam, built in 1977, forms a reservoir 50 km long, and a second dam at Kafue Gorge generates electricity.

The river is used for irrigation and hydroelectric power and is the most central and urban of Zambia's principal rivers: more than half of the country's people live in its basin. Sugar plantations around Mazabuka draw on it, notably the Nakambala Sugar Estate. Lochinvar and Blue Lagoon National Parks lie on the Kafue Flats, and the Hippo Pool near Chingola is a national monument.
kaga-province: Kaga Province (加賀国, Kaga no Kuni), abbreviated Kashū, lay in what is now the south and west of Ishikawa Prefecture in the Hokuriku region. It bordered Echizen, Etchū, Hida and Noto Provinces and belonged to the Hokurikudō Circuit. Under the Engishiki classification it ranked as a "superior country" in importance and a "middle country" in distance from the capital. Its provincial capital and provincial temple stood in what is now the city of Komatsu, and its Ichinomiya, the first shrine of the province, was the Shirayama Hime Shrine in what is now the city of Hakusan. No provincial nunnery appears to have existed.

The ancient Koshi Province was divided in 701, under the reforms of the Taihō Code, into Echizen, Etchū and Echigo. In 823 the two eastern districts of Echizen, Kaga and Enuma, were separated to form Kaga Province, the last province created under the ritsuryō system. In the same year the northern part of Enuma District became Nomi District, the southern part of Kaga District became Ishikawa District, and Kaga District itself was renamed Kahoku District. Despite its high rank, Kaga never developed a powerful local gōzoku clan and was divided into many shōen estates.

During the early Sengoku period the Ikkō-ikki held most of the province and established a loosely governed confederation there. Oda Nobunaga's general Shibata Katsuie eventually conquered the area, and it then passed under the control of Maeda Toshiie in the time of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. The Maeda clan kept it as Kaga Domain through the Edo period. From 1639 Enuma Domain and part of Nomi Domain were separated from Kaga Domain as the 100,000 koku Daishōji Domain, ruled by a junior branch of the Maeda.

After the Meiji Restoration and the abolition of the han system in 1871, Kaga was divided into Kanazawa Prefecture and Daishōji Prefecture, which were merged with Fukui Prefecture. In 1872 they were divided out again and joined with Nanao Prefecture, the former Noto Province, to form today's Ishikawa Prefecture. Etchū Province was united with Ishikawa in 1876 and separated again in 1883.
kagawa-prefecture: Kagawa occupies the northeast corner of Shikoku, a relatively narrow prefecture between the mountains of the island and the sea. The Sanuki Mountains run along its southern border with Tokushima Prefecture, and Ehime Prefecture lies to the west. Its coast on the Seto Inland Sea faces Okayama Prefecture on Honshu, to which it is joined by the Great Seto Bridge. It includes Shōdoshima, the second-largest island of the Seto Inland Sea. At 1,877 square kilometres it is the smallest prefecture of Japan by area. Takamatsu is its capital and largest city, and other major cities are Marugame, Mitoyo and Kan'onji.

Kagawa was formerly known as Sanuki Province. For a brief period between August 1876 and December 1888 it was made part of Ehime Prefecture. Yashima, a mountain in Takamatsu, was the battlefield of one of the best-known struggles between the Heike and Genji clans, the Battle of Yashima. Many of its towns were created after 1999 through mergers, as part of a national effort to reduce the number of small towns and villages.

The prefecture had a population of 949,358 in 2020, about 7.1 per cent lower than in the census of 2000. Sanuki udon is its best-known local food, and in 2008 there were over 700 udon restaurants in the prefecture. Kagawa was the first place in Japan to cultivate olives successfully, and it has produced olive goods since 1908. Sites include Ritsurin Garden and Takamatsu Castle in Takamatsu, Marugame Castle, the Konpira Shrine at Kotohira and the Kanamaruza Kabuki Theatre. The island of Naoshima holds several art museums, and Zentsūji and Yashima-ji are temples on the Shikoku Pilgrimage. Setonaikai National Park covers part of the coast.
kagera-region: Kagera Region covers 35,686 square kilometres, of which 27 percent is water, including parts of Lake Victoria, Lake Ikimba, Burigi and Ngono, and the Kagera River. The river forms the region's border with Rwanda and gives it its name. Hills run parallel to the lake shore from north to south. Rainfall is heaviest along the shore, about 2000 mm a year at Bukoba, and falls to about 500 mm in the west. The region lies on the Kivu Rift, the western branch of the East African Rift, and a magnitude 5.9 earthquake struck it on 10 September 2016, killing 17 people.

For about five centuries Kagera was home to nine kingdoms with highly hierarchical societies, among them Karagwe, Misenye, Bugabo, Ihangiro, Bukara and Biharamulo. Their kings, called omukama, lived in elaborate palaces and were respected as the direct link to the gods of their kingdoms. Women held special respect in traditional ritual. When a king died, a sister chosen from among his sisters took part in the crowning of the next king as the sister to the nation, and a head of a family had a female counterpart to share the authority of his inheritor.

Germany colonised Tanzania in 1885 and favoured the Haya, the people of Bukoba and Muleba districts. The local kings nevertheless kept their power, and some, such as Kahigi, gave up their territories by collaborating with the Germans. In 1897 and 1898 the local medical officer, Dr M. Zupitza, met a plague outbreak in Kiziba and, working with Dr Robert Koch, confirmed that it had the same cause as the outbreak in Bombay. After authority passed to the British following World War I, Lutheran missionaries began work in the region, and other Christian denominations followed.

In the colonial period the area was called West Lake and belonged to Lake Province. After independence it became the West Lake Region, and it took the name Kagera after the war that began with Uganda's attempted annexation of the region. President Nyerere regarded the kingdoms as detrimental to national unity, and they ended after independence.

Bukoba is the regional capital, about 1,500 kilometres from Dar es Salaam. Kagera is one of Tanzania's 31 regions, and its 2022 census population was 2,989,299. Agriculture is the main economic activity, and the region is one of the country's largest coffee producers. Its protected areas include Burigi-Chato, Rumanyika-Karagwe, Ibanda-Kyerwa and Rubondo Island national parks.
kagera-river: The Kagera River, also called the Akagera River or the Alexandra Nile, forms part of the upper headwaters of the Nile and carries water from its most distant source. Its total length is 597 kilometres, measured from its source in Lake Rweru in Rwanda. The section named Kagera begins in Burundi, flowing out of that lake. It runs east along the borders of Rwanda with Burundi and Tanzania to a confluence with the Ruvubu River, close to the northernmost point of Lake Tanganyika. Its waters thus come from two major tributaries, the Nyabarongo of Rwanda, which feeds Lake Rweru, and the Ruvubu of Burundi. It is unknown which of the two is longer and so the ultimate source of the Nile.

From the confluence the Kagera flows north along the Rwanda-Tanzania border, over the Rusumo Falls, an important crossing point between the two countries, and through Akagera National Park. It then turns east along the Tanzania-Uganda border and empties into Lake Victoria in Uganda. It is the largest single inflow into the lake, contributing about 6.4 billion cubic metres of water a year, about 28 percent of the lake's outflow. The river gives its name to the Kagera Region of Tanzania and to Akagera National Park. Its basin is rich in fish, and because of its many waterfalls and rapids the sections of the basin are separated from one another.

Richard Kandt was the first European to reach the source of the Kagera, in 1898. The river has featured prominently in the histories of the countries it runs through, particularly Rwanda. In 1894 the German Gustav Adolf von Götzen crossed it at the Rusumo Falls, which marked the Rwandan colonial era, officially begun in 1899. In 1916, during the First World War, the Belgians defeated the Germans and entered Rwanda by the same route.

During the Rwandan genocide of 1994, thousands of Tutsis and Hutu political moderates were murdered on the river's banks, and the Kagera was used to dispose of the corpses. It carried the bodies into Lake Victoria, where they washed up in Uganda and created a serious health hazard, for which a state of emergency was declared in affected areas.
kagome-kagome: The most common reading of the words runs: Kagome, kagome, the bird in the cage, when, oh when will it come out? In the evening of the dawn, the crane and the turtle slipped. Who is behind you now? The song is usually written as a single line without punctuation, so with its odd phrasing and ambiguous words it is unclear which phrases belong together; the evening of the dawn may answer the question of when the bird will come out, or set the scene for the slipping of the crane and the turtle.

The words vary from region to region, and many versions are recorded in writing. Common variants replace yoake no ban ni, in the evening of the dawn, with yoake no bannin, the watchman of the dawn, and ushiro no shoumen, the front of the back, with ushiro no shounen, the boy behind. Who wrote the words and the tune is not known.

The song works through wordplay. Kagome is a pivot word that can mean to surround, a basket woman, a woven bamboo pattern with gaps, or to crouch. The bird in the basket then turns the opening sound towards kamome, a seagull, so that the child in the middle becomes a bird caught in a cage. The evening after dawn reverses the order of night and morning, and the slipping of the crane and the turtle, two auspicious creatures, suggests a failure. The last line asks who stands in front although behind.

Because its original meaning is lost, the song has drawn much academic interest and many theories. Japanese dictionaries adopt the plainest one, that the words describe the game alone, with the Oni as the caged bird waiting to change places. Other readings take it as the lament of a prostitute without freedom, as the grudge of a pregnant woman pushed down the stairs in an inheritance dispute, as the fate of a prisoner facing escape or execution, or as an account of spiritual awakening. Single phrases have been read as a fence round an execution ground, a shrine maiden, or a severed head asking who killed it.
kagoshima: Kagoshima lies at the south-western tip of the island of Kyūshū, on the north-eastern part of the Satsuma Peninsula, and its area includes the whole of Sakurajima. It sits on the bay of the Aira Caldera beneath the stratovolcano Sakurajima and has been nicknamed the Naples of the Eastern world for its bay, warm climate and volcano. Ash from Sakurajima falls constantly on the city, and residents have developed ways of coping, such as schoolchildren wearing helmets against volcanic debris. The kanji of its name mean deer child island, but the source of the name is not clear.

Shimazu Ujihiza of the Shimazu clan moved into the area around 1340, and the city lies in ancient Satsuma Province, the centre of Shimazu territory from the late Kamakura period. Francis Xavier first reached Japan by landing at Kagoshima on 15 August 1549, on the coast of what is now Gionnosu. Kagoshima was a significant centre of Christian activity until bans were imposed in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

In the Edo period (1603–1868) Kagoshima became the seat of the Shimazu's Satsuma Domain, one of the most powerful and wealthiest domains in the country. Satsuma also controlled the semi-independent kingdom of Ryūkyū, and a special embassy building housed Ryūkyūan emissaries in the city. The domain was a centre of anti-Tokugawa sentiment.

In 1863 the British Royal Navy bombarded Kagoshima to punish the daimyō of Satsuma for the Namamugi Incident, the murder of a British merchant on the Tōkaidō the year before, for which the domain had refused to pay an indemnity. Many leaders of the Meiji Restoration and the Boshin War came from Satsuma. Nineteen young men of Satsuma broke the shogunate's ban on foreign travel and visited industrial sites in the United Kingdom, and a statue outside the train station honours them. Tōgō Heihachirō, who led the Grand Fleet of the Imperial Japanese Navy in the Russo-Japanese War, was born in Kagoshima.

The 1914 eruption of the volcano spread ash across the city with relatively little disruption. On the night of 17 June 1945 120 B-29 bombers dropped incendiary and cluster bombs, destroying 44.1 per cent of the built-up area; the city was targeted for its naval port and its position as a railway terminus. The municipality was founded on 1 April 1889, and on 1 November 2004 five neighbouring towns, among them Sakurajima, were merged into it.

Kagoshima is the capital of Kagoshima Prefecture and its largest city by a wide margin, with an estimated 583,966 people in 2024. Its economy centres on light manufacturing, tourism and commercial fishing, and the Kyushu Shinkansen linked it to Hakata Station in Fukuoka in 2011.
kagoshima-prefecture: Kagoshima Prefecture lies at the south-western tip of Kyushu, on the Satsuma and Ōsumi peninsulas, which are separated by Kagoshima Bay. It also includes a chain of islands, most importantly the Amami Islands, stretching a few hundred kilometres to the south-west, so that its coastline runs to 2,632 kilometres including 28 islands. Its position made it a gateway to Japan at various times in history. Active and dormant volcanoes are found across the prefecture. Sakurajima, which rises out of Kagoshima Bay opposite the city, sends up a steady trickle of smoke and ash. In its major eruption of 1914 the island mountain spilled enough material to become permanently joined to the mainland.

The prefecture corresponds to the ancient provinces of Ōsumi and Satsuma, together with the northern part of the Ryukyu Islands, known as Satsunan. Its territory formed the core of the Satsuma Domain, ruled from Kagoshima Castle, one of the most important domains of the Edo period and of the Meiji Restoration. The region played a key role in that Restoration through Saigō Takamori, and the city of Kagoshima was an important naval base in Japan's wars of the 20th century and the home of Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō. The Satsuma lord Shimazu Nariakira is said to have introduced the deep-fried fish cake satsuma-age from the Ryūkyū Kingdom.

The city of Kagoshima is the capital and largest city, and most of the economy is concentrated there and in the area of the former Satsuma Province. The eastern part, the former Ōsumi Province, is mostly rural. The prefecture has strong agricultural roots, and its best-known products include green tea, sweet potatoes, radishes, Berkshire pork and Black Wagyu beef. It has more than a hundred distilleries of shōchū, one of Japan's most traditional drinks. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency has facilities here, including the country's main launch site on Tanegashima. The people speak the distinctive Satsugū dialect, mutually unintelligible with standard Japanese, though most speakers know both.
kagyu: Kagyu, in Tibetan bka' brgyud, means Oral Lineage or Whispered Transmission, and it is one of the four major schools of Tibetan Buddhism. Its lineages begin in Tibet with Marpa Lotsawa (1012–1097), a householder who trained as a translator and travelled three times to India and four times to Nepal in search of teachings. His principal teachers were the siddhas Nāropa, from whom he received the close lineage of mahāmudrā and tantric teachings, and Maitrīpāda, from whom he received the distant lineage. Nāropa had been the chief disciple of Tilopa, who had received Four Lineages of Instructions, and Nāropa codified them as the Six Dharmas of Naropa.

Marpa gave his main lineage to Milarepa (1040–1123), and Milarepa's student Gampopa (1079–1153) became the central figure. Marpa, Milarepa and Gampopa are together considered the founders of the school in Tibet.

The main teachings of the Kagyu are Mahamudra and the Six Dharmas of Naropa. Gampopa, a Kadampa monk, combined the monastic discipline and stages-of-the-path teaching of the Kadam order with the teachings he had received from Milarepa. He founded Daklha Gampo Monastery and established a celibate monastic order, in contrast to Marpa and Milarepa, whose tradition consisted mainly of householders and hermits practising in solitude. This lineage became known as Dagpo Kagyu, and most major Kagyu lineages can be traced through Gampopa.

Later writers spoke of Four Major and Eight Minor lineages of the Dagpo Kagyu. The four major branches were the Karma Kagyu, founded by Düsum Khyenpa, 1st Karmapa Lama (1110–1193), the Barom Kagyu, the Tshalpa Kagyu and the Phagdru Kagyu, founded by Phagmo Drupa Dorje Gyalpo (1110–1170). The eight minor ones derive from Phagmo Drupa's disciples and include the Drikung Kagyu, from Drigung Monastery, and the Drukpa lineage. These terms date only from writings of the 19th century, and they do not measure size: the Drikung school was probably the largest and most influential in the 13th century.

The independent schools surviving today are chiefly the Karma Kagyu, the Drikung Kagyu and the Drukpa lineage. The Karma Kagyu is the largest and is headed by the Karmapa. The Phagmodrupa declined between 1435 and 1481 and were eclipsed by the Rinpungpa of Tsang, who supported the Karma Kagyu. The Tshalpa Kagyu was absorbed by the Gelug in the 15th century. Marpa's transmission of the Guhyasamāja Tantra, through Tshurton Wangi Dorje, passed in time to Tsongkhapa, founder of the Gelug. In the 19th century Jamgon Kongtrul gathered the surviving initiations of Marpa's teachings in the Kagyu Ngak Dzö. After the death of the 16th Karmapa in 1981, his followers disagreed over the identity of his successor.
kahal-zur-israel-synagogue: The name means Congregation Rock of Israel. Its founders were Portuguese and Spanish Sephardic Jews who had fled forced conversion and taken refuge in Dutch Brazil, joined by New Christians already living in the colony, who possibly helped to build it. In 1630 Moses Cohen Henriques had led a Jewish contingent to the island of Itamaracá and from there to Recife; after retiring from privateering for the Dutch around 1636, he helped his brother Abraham Cohen establish the synagogue.

From 1636 to 1654 the synagogue stood on the site of houses 197 and 203 of the Rua do Bom Jesus, formerly the Rua dos Judeus, the Street of the Jews, in the old city of Recife. It served a community of about 1,450 Jews, with the cantor Josue Velosino and the rabbi Isaac Aboab da Fonseca, who was sent to Recife in 1642. In 1654 the Dutch surrendered to the Portuguese only after the Jews were guaranteed safe passage, and Aboab da Fonseca, Cohen Henriques and most of the colony's Jews left.

The original building survived until the early 20th century, when it was torn down. An archaeological excavation later confirmed the site, and in 2001 the two-storey house then standing there was turned into a Jewish museum, designed to resemble the synagogues Sephardic Jews built in the 17th and 18th centuries. It shows a Torah and a bema, and excavated parts of the first synagogue, among them its mikveh. Families hold weddings and Bnei Mitzvot there for its link with the long history of Jews in Brazil, and a Jewish festival held each November draws around 20,000 visitors to the street.
kahnawake: Kahnawake lies on the south-west shore of the Saint Lawrence River where it narrows, across from Montreal. Its name comes from the Mohawk word kahnawà꞉ke, place of the rapids, after the people's former village of Caughnawaga near the rapids of the Mohawk River in present-day New York; the nearby Lachine Rapids also shaped the choice. Its people call themselves Kanien’kehá꞉ka, People of the Flint, and their nation was historically the most easterly of the Haudenosaunee, the Keepers of the Eastern Door.

The first Haudenosaunee settlement near Montreal was founded on Jesuit land near La Prairie by a group of Oneida, joined over the next decade by Mohawk refugees from Ossernenon and by Onondaga, Wendat and Algonquians. The village moved towards the Lachine Rapids in 1675, again in 1690 and 1696, and in 1715 to its present site. In 1680 the French Crown granted the Jesuits the Seigneurie du Sault-Saint-Louis, which was meant to be closed to European settlement, but the Jesuits let French settlers take land there. New France kept a garrison at the village to guard the south-west approach to Ville-Marie.

In 1907 thirty-three Kahnawake men died in the collapse of the Quebec Bridge. In the first half of the 20th century many ironworkers moved with their families to Brooklyn, where they called their neighbourhood Little Caughnawaga. In 1955 the government expropriated 1264 acres for the Saint Lawrence Seaway, cutting the community off from the river despite its appeals to the courts and the United Nations. During the Oka Crisis of 1990 people from Kahnawake blocked the Honoré Mercier Bridge in support of Kanesatake, and on 28 August 1990 a crowd stoned a convoy of women, children and elders leaving the reserve.

The Kahnawà꞉ke Mohawk Territory is a self-governing First Nations reserve of 48.05 square kilometres, with a resident population slightly above 8,000 and many members living elsewhere. Its people, once speakers of Kanien'kéha and French, now mostly speak English. It holds three National Historic Sites of Canada: Fort St-Louis, the Jesuit Mission of St-François-Xavier and the Caughnawaga Presbytery.
kahone: Kahone is a town and urban commune near Kaolack in Senegal, and a centre of Serer culture and history. Its name comes from Ka-Woon, a Serer religious site and place of worship where the Serer venerated a founding ancestor. The name is older than the Guelwar maternal dynasty and its member Mbegane Ndour, the founder of the Kingdom of Saloum, and it was given to the future capital of the kingdom.

In the 14th century the Mandinka Guelowar clan migrated north from Kaabu after losing a succession dispute. According to Rokhaya Fall, the clan founded several small chiefdoms north of the Gambia River, and the home of one of its leaders, Kéno Mbèye, became a meeting place that grew into Njoob, capital of a state called Mbey. Others hold that this tradition concerns a royal princess, one of three sisters who were the maternal ancestors of the three Guelowar families of Saloum, and that the Serer country of Mbey existed before the Guelowar arrived.

In the late 15th century Mbey and its prosperous salt works fell under the influence of a Toucouleur marabout named Elibana. The Siin-Siin leader Mbegane Ndour attacked and killed him, founded the Serer kingdom of Saloum and gave its capital the name Kahone, which remained the kingdom's political and religious centre for several centuries. Kahone was once far more important than neighbouring Kaolack, but in the 20th century the roles were reversed as Kaolack grew into a port and railway hub, and Kahone was reduced to a sub-prefecture of Kaolack.

The town lives mainly from farming. An annual royal festival brings together the O Maad, the Serer king, the Djaraaf, his prime minister, and other dignitaries, with pageants celebrating the history of Saloum and the Serer. Kahone has a mosque and a Catholic mission, and around it lie ancient tombs, stone circles, megaliths and large burial mounds planted with baobab trees. Official estimates gave it 5,852 inhabitants in 2007.
kahramanmaras: Kahramanmaraş is the administrative centre of Kahramanmaraş Province in the Mediterranean region of Turkey.
