The city lies on a plain at the foot of Mount Ahır, 568 metres above sea level, and the Ceyhan River, which rises in the mountains around the Elbistan Plain, is its most important hydrological feature. Historically it was known as Marash, Maraş in Turkish, and Germanikeia in Greek. After 1973 Maraş was officially renamed Kahramanmaraş, adding kahraman, the Turkish word for heroic, to commemorate the Battle of Marash.

In the early Iron Age, from the late 11th century BCE to about 711 BCE, the city was the capital of the Syro-Hittite state of Gurgum, called the Kurkumaean city by its Luwian inhabitants and Marqas by the Assyrians. In 711 BCE Gurgum was annexed as an Assyrian province and named Marqas after its capital. The Romans called the city Germanicia Caesarea. In Byzantine times Germanikeia was the seat of an eparch, one of whom took part in the First Council of Nicea. It was lost to the Muslims in the 7th century, and under al-Mansur the whole Christian population of the Germanikeia valley was deported and resettled at Ramla in Palestine.

After the fall of the Armenian kingdoms in the 11th century, the city became a stronghold for exiled Armenians and the capital of the short-lived principality of Philaretos Brachamios. His successor, the Armenian general Tatoul, hosted the exhausted army of the First Crusade for four days. According to Matthew of Edessa, an earthquake destroyed the city on 29 November 1114 and killed 40,000 people.

It passed between the Danishmends, Seljuks and Crusaders, among them Tancred, who retook it in 1107. From 1337 to 1515 it was ruled by the Beylik of Dulkadir as vassals of the Mamluk Empire before being annexed to the Ottoman Empire. In 1525–6 it had 1,557 adult males, a total population of 7,500, all Muslims, and a substantial number of non-Muslims migrated there later, mainly in the 19th century.

In 1915 about 20,000 Armenians from Marash were deported. During the Turkish War of Independence the French army occupied Maraş, and in February 1920 Turkish nationalist forces regained control, followed by a massacre of the Armenian population. The official French report said the victims did not exceed 5,000. In December 1978 the Maraş Massacre of leftist Alevis, incited by the Grey Wolves, left more than 100 dead and contributed to the declaration of martial law and the 1980 coup.

Kahramanmaraş had 571,266 inhabitants in 2022 and is populated mostly by Turkish and Kurdish people, with a small Armenian population. The earthquakes of 6 February 2023 had their epicentre in Pazarcık and Elbistan in the province and destroyed much of the city.
kahuna: A kahuna might be versed in agriculture, canoe building or any other skill or field of knowledge, and the secrecy surrounding their knowledge has been compared to that of the Freemasons and the guild masters of medieval Europe. Communities called on them to bless new buildings and construction projects or to officiate at weddings. The book Tales from the Night Rainbow lists forty types of kahuna, twenty of them in healing alone, among them the kahuna hāhā, an expert who diagnosed sickness or pain by feeling the body.

Classes of kahuna in pre-contact Hawaii included the kahuna kilokilo, a reader of skies and omens; the kahuna kalai wa‘a, a canoe maker; the kahuna ho‘okele, a navigator; the kahuna kumu hula, leader of a hula group; the kahuna ka‘a kaua, a war strategist; and the kahuna lawelawe iwi, who cared for the bones of the dead.

Of Fornander's ten branches of the priesthood, the ʻAnāʻanā, Hoʻopiopio and Hoʻounāunā were said to bring death or injury to others by prayer, and the Hoʻokomokomo and Poʻi ʻUhane to use spirits for divination and possession, while the Kuhikuhi puʻuone located sites for heiau, or temples. Kahuna nui usually lived in places such as Waimea Valley, known as the Valley of the Priests, and were given slices of land running from the mountain to the sea.

Craft kahuna were never prohibited, but as native Hawaiian culture declined many died without passing on their knowledge; when the Hōkūleʻa was built to sail to the South Pacific, the master navigator Mau Piailug of Satawal was brought to Hawaii to reteach navigation. King Kamehameha IV, in his translation of the Book of Common Prayer, used kahuna for Anglican priests and kahunapule for lay and ordained ministers.

Outsiders distorted the word into a witch or wizard. In the 1959 film Gidget the Big Kahuna was the leader of a group of surfers, and the figure became commonplace in the beach party films of the 1960s; the Hawaiian surfer Duke Kahanamoku rejected the title because he knew its original meaning. The New Age system called Huna uses kahuna for a person of priestly or shamanic standing, which has shaped English dictionary definitions. The Native Hawaiian scholar Lisa Kahaleole Hall wrote that Huna bears absolutely no resemblance to any Hawaiian worldview or spiritual practice.
kaibara-ekken: Kaibara Ekken, also read Ekiken and known as Atsunobu, was born on 17 December 1630 into a family of advisers to the daimyō of Fukuoka Domain in Chikuzen Province. He went with his father to Edo in 1648 and in 1649 was sent to Nagasaki to study Western science. At his father's urging he continued his studies there as a rōnin from 1650 to 1656, then re-entered the service of the Kuroda, which allowed him to study further in Kyoto. After his father's death in 1665 he returned to Fukuoka.

His two main contributions were a study of nature that blended Western natural science with Neo-Confucianism, and the rendering of the complex writings of Neo-Confucianism into vernacular Japanese. His science kept to botany and materia medica and was concerned with natural law; the Yamato honzō of 1709 was a seminal study of Japanese plants, and the German Japanologist Philipp Franz von Siebold later called him the Aristotle of Japan.

As an educator he turned the ethics of Zhu Xi into easy manuals of conduct, among them Precepts for Children and the Yōjōkun of 1713. He also wrote on Shinto, in the Jingikun and a treatise on the non-divergence of Shintō and Confucianism, as well as a history of Dazaifu Shrine. His synthesis of Confucian ideas and Western science influenced the formation of Shinto, especially State Shinto, and shared concerns with the Kokugaku movement.

Kaibara died on 5 October 1714, and his Taigiroku, The Record of Great Doubts, appeared after his death the same year. The Greater Learning for Women (Onna daigaku), long his best-known book, is argued by modern scholarship to have been prepared by other hands, although the oldest surviving copy, of 1733, ends with the words as related by our teacher Ekiken Kaibara, and its colophon says it was written from his lectures.
kaidu: Kaidu was the posthumous son of the Mongol prince Kashin, a son of Ögedei Khan, and so belonged to the House of Ögedei. Ögedei died in 1241 and was followed by his widow Töregene as regent, then by Güyük Khan. In 1251 the throne passed to a Toluid, Möngke Khan, and Kaidu, then about 16, was one of the few Ögedeid princes the new regime favoured. Möngke invested him with Qayaliq, southeast of Lake Balkhash, in 1252.

Despite this favour, Kaidu arrested Möngke's envoy, the judge Shi Tianlin, in 1256 and held him for twenty years. In the civil war of 1260 to 1264 between Kublai Khan and Ariq Böke he is said to have supported Ariq Böke, though this is not certain. Excluded from Kublai's partition of the Mongol territories, he entered a long conflict with Kublai and Kublai's Ilkhanid allies.

After Ariq Böke's defeat in 1264, Kublai summoned Kaidu to court, but Kaidu stayed away. In 1268 Kublai incited Baraq, khan of the Chagatai, to attack him. Baraq won at first, but Kaidu, helped by Möngke-Temür of the Golden Horde, defeated him on the Jaxartes. Peace was made at a kurultai, with two-thirds of Transoxiana going to Baraq. Kaidu then encouraged Baraq to invade Ilkhanid Persia, where he was beaten at Herat on 22 July 1270 and died in August 1271. The Chagatayid princes submitted to Kaidu.

In 1282 Kaidu installed Baraq's son Duwa as khan of the Chagatai Ulus, and the two cooperated for two decades. A princes' revolt against Kublai in 1276 freed Kaidu to deal with opposition in the west. With Duwa he took Beshbaliq in 1286, forcing Kublai's troops out of Uighuria and the Tarim Basin, and in 1289 he briefly held Karakorum before retreating before Kublai.

Kublai's commanders Bayan and Tuq Tuqa then won reverses against Kaidu. After Kublai's death in 1294, his successor Temür Öljeitü Khan turned more forces against him. In 1300 Temür's nephew Qayishan defeated Kaidu, and on 3 September 1301 Kaidu was wounded in a serious defeat at Mount Tiejiangu. A follow-up fight with Duwa's reinforcements ended roughly in a draw. Kaidu died late in 1301.

He appears to have aimed to re-establish the Ulus of Ögedei and assert its control over the Chagatai. His long opposition to the great khans allowed an effectively independent Mongol state in Central Asia to emerge, and helped the other khanates become independent too. His elder son Chapar succeeded him, but Duwa forced Chapar to surrender by early 1307, largely ending the Ulus of Ögedei as a power. Kaidu is said to have relied for military advice on his daughter Qutulun.
kaifeng: In 361 BCE King Hui of Wei moved the Wei capital to Yi and built the city of Daliang. After Qin conquered Wei, Daliang was destroyed apart from a mid-sized market town renamed Junyi. Under the Han it was the capital of the Kingdom of Liang, ruled by Liu Wu, who restored the walls and made it a centre of music, art and gardens. The nearby Qifeng was renamed Kaifeng to avoid the naming taboo of Emperor Jing of Han. In the early 7th century, as Bianzhou, the city became a commercial hub when it was joined to the Grand Canal. During the Five Dynasties it was capital of four successive dynasties, and the Song made it their capital in 960 as Dongjing.

Under the Song, Kaifeng became the largest and most prosperous city in China, at the intersection of four major canals and surrounded by three rings of walls. It probably held between 600,000 and 700,000 people and is believed to have been the largest city in the world from 1013 to 1127. The memoir Dongjing Menghualu recalls its night and dawn markets, restaurants and theatres, and Zhang Zeduan's painting Along the River During the Qingming Festival depicts its bustle. The Iron Pagoda of Youguo Temple, built in 1049, is the oldest landmark of the city, and Su Song's astronomical clock tower used an escapement two hundred years before they appeared in the clockworks of Europe.

In 1127 the Jurchen Jin took the city and carried off the Song imperial family and officials; Zhao Gou escaped and the court never moved back. The Jin court itself moved to Kaifeng in 1214 to resist the Mongols, and in 1233 the city fell to them after a ten-month siege. Kaifeng was vulnerable on the Yellow River floodplain: five major floods struck between 1375 and 1416. In 1642 the Ming army flooded the city during a siege by rebels, and only 30,000 of its 370,000 people remained.

Kaifeng was rebuilt in 1662 and again after the flood of 1841, and was the capital of Henan until 1954. It is one of the Eight Ancient Capitals of China, having been the capital eight times, and has long been home to the Kaifeng Jews, the oldest Jewish community in China.
kailasa-temple-ellora: The Kailasa temple, also called Cave 16, is the largest of the 34 Hindu, Buddhist and Jain cave temples and monasteries of the Ellora Caves, which stretch for over two kilometres along a sloping basalt cliff. It has no dedicatory inscription, but it was certainly commissioned by a Rashtrakuta ruler. Most scholars attribute it to Krishna I, who reigned from about 756 to 773 CE, on the strength of two grants.

The Vadodara copper-plate of about 812-813 CE names Krishnaraja as patron of the Kailasanatha temple, and the Kadaba grant seems to credit him likewise. The attribution is not completely certain, because neither inscription is physically connected to the caves. Hermann Goetz argued that work began under Krishna's predecessor Dantidurga and continued under later kings, while M. K. Dhavalikar concluded that the main part was finished under Krishna I.

The temple was carved from the top downward out of the rock face, and archaeologists believe it was sculpted from a single rock. The top of the structure over the sanctuary stands 32.6 metres above the court below. A two-storeyed gateway opens into a U-shaped courtyard measuring 82 metres by 46 metres at the base, edged by a columned arcade three storeys high with large sculpted panels. Within it stand the central shrine of Shiva, with a Dravidian shikhara and a flat-roofed mandapa on 16 pillars, and an image of Nandi, his bull.

Five detached shrines include three to the river goddesses Ganga, Yamuna and Saraswati. The base of the hall shows scenes from the Mahabharata and Ramayana, and one of its best-known sculptures shows Ravana attempting to lift Mount Kailasa. Its style shows Chalukya and Pallava influence, and the main shrine resembles the Virupaksha Temple at Pattadakal.

A medieval Marathi legend, first recorded in the Katha-Kalpataru of Krishna Yajnavalki, tells of a queen who vowed to fast until she saw the top of a temple, and of an architect named Kokasa who carved the shikhara first and finished it within a week. Dhavalikar suggests that Kokasa was the chief architect and that the temple was first called Manikeshwar. Dhavalikar also estimated that 250 labourers could have cut the temple in about five and a half years. According to the Bijapur historian Rafi al-Din Shirazi, the Kailasanatha was an ancient wonder, and the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb called it a marvellous place for strolling.
kailasanathar-temple-kanchipuram: The name means Lord of Kailasa, and the temple was built in the Smartha tradition of worship of Shiva, Vishnu, Devi, Surya, Ganesha and Kartikeya. It rose during the Pallava expansion of Kanchipuram, after Narasimhavarman I had extended the kingdom into Tamil, Andhra and Kannada lands. Earlier temples had been built of wood or cut into caves and boulders, as at Mahabalipuram. Mahendravarman III, son of Narasimhavarman II, completed the front façade and the gopuram, and further additions and restorations followed in later centuries. Local belief holds that the temple sheltered the rulers in time of war, with a secret tunnel as an escape route.

The foundations are of granite and the superstructure and carvings of sandstone. At first only the sanctum with its pyramidal vimana and a separate mandapa stood; later an ardhamantapa joined the two, a change said to have marred the design. The four-storey vimana is square in plan, and its outer faces carry miniature shrines in sala, kuta and panjara forms. The sanctum holds a sixteen-sided Shivalinga of black granite, and 58 small shrines with Somaskanda reliefs line the niches of the compound wall. Rearing lions project from the pillars and walls in many directions.

The carvings depict forms of Shiva such as Tripurantaka, Lingodbhava, Bhikshatana and Dakshinamurthy, together with themes from Vaishnavism, Shaktism and Vedic deities; an Ardhanariswara seated on a bull is held the finest. The courtyard cells keep murals in a style also found at the Ajanta Caves, among the earliest Hindu mural art in Tamil Nadu.

The temple set a pattern for later temples in South India, and Raja Raja Chola I is believed to have drawn on it for the Brihadeeswara Temple. Its walls carry inscriptions in early scripts, including the earliest stone record of the twenty-eight Saivagamas, in which Rajasimha states his Shaiva faith. Devotees crawl through a narrow circumambulatory passage entered by the Gate of Death and left by the Gate of Birth. The Archaeological Survey of India maintains the site, and Maha Shivaratri is its largest festival.
kainai-nation: The people's own name, Káínaa, comes from aká, many, and nínaa, chief: Akáínaa means many chief, and Káína many chief people. The English name Blood goes back to the Plains Cree, their enemies, who called them mihkowiyiniw, stained with blood. The Kainai speak a language of the Blackfoot group, in a dialect closely related to those of the Siksika and Piikani. When treaties such as Treaty 7 were signed, they lived on the Oldman, Belly and St. Mary rivers west of Lethbridge, Alberta.

In pre-treaty times a society called the iikunuhkahtsi was responsible for punishing misdeeds. The band government numbered 18,465 members in 2024, against 11,791 in December 2013. Its reserve, Blood 148, covers 1,410 km2 about 200 kilometres south of Calgary; ammolite mining there has uncovered mosasaur fossils, which are stored at the Royal Tyrrell Museum but belong to the nation.

In 1960 the National Film Board of Canada filmed the Kainai Sun Dance for the documentary Circle of the Sun, with the permission of tribal leaders who feared the ceremony might be dying out; its 1973 documentary Kainai dealt with the building of a factory on their land. The Kainai News, published in southern Alberta by the Blood Indian Tribe and later by Indian News Media, was one of Canada's first aboriginal newspapers. Its first editor was Caen Bly, a granddaughter of Senator James Gladstone, and it carried editorial cartoons by Everett Soop.

The nation held the first buffalo dialogue in 2009 and in September 2014 became one of the original eight signatories of the Buffalo Treaty. In 2017 a federal court ruled that the Crown had underestimated the band's population, leaving the reserve smaller than it should have been; it could be enlarged by 421 square kilometres or the claim settled in cash. In July 2019 the nation received a $150 million settlement of a claim over Crown mismanagement of its ranching assets.

The nation is governed by an elected council of twelve to fifteen members with one chief, serving four-year terms; Jim Shot Both Sides, chief from 1956 to 1980, was the last of the hereditary chiefs. In 2015 the reserve was policed by the Blood Tribe Police, with 31 officers. Among its enterprises is the mining of ammolite, a gem found only in the Bearpaw Formation and sold to Asia for feng shui. Its communities include Standoff, Moses Lake, Fish Creek, Levern and Old Agency.
kainji-dam: The dam was built by Impregilo, a consortium of Italian civil engineering contractors, between 1964 and 1968. Its total cost was estimated at US$209 million, and one quarter of that sum went to resettling the people displaced by the dam and by its reservoir, Kainji Lake.

Including its saddle dam, which closes off a tributary valley, Kainji Dam extends for about 10 kilometres; the main section across the outflow to the Niger is 550 metres long. Most of the structure is of earth, but the centre section, which houses the hydroelectric turbines, was built of concrete and stands 65 metres high. A single lock chamber can lift barges 49 metres. The lake behind it is about 135 kilometres long and about 30 kilometres across at its widest point.

The power station was designed for a capacity of 960 megawatts, but only 8 of its 12 turbines were installed, which reduced it to 760 megawatts. The dam supplies electricity to all the large cities of Nigeria, and some of its power is sold to neighbouring Niger. Occasional droughts have made the river's flow unpredictable and lowered its output. The lake supports irrigation and a local fishing industry.

The dam's handling of floods has drawn criticism. In October 1998, in response to flooding upstream, a torrent of water released from the dam burst the river banks and flooded nearly 60 villages; domestic animals drowned and dikes and several farms were washed away. Dam officials were blamed for waiting too long before opening the gates and then releasing too much water.
kairouan: Kairouan, in Arabic al-Qayrawān, takes its name from an Arabic word meaning military group or caravan, borrowed early from the Middle Persian kārawān. The city lies 50 km from the east coast of Tunisia, west of Sousse, 75 km from Monastir and 184 km from Tunis, and it has a hot semi-arid climate. It is the capital of the Kairouan Governorate. Its Great Mosque of Sidi-Uqba, one of the largest Islamic monuments in North Africa, covers more than 9,000 square metres.

The foundation dates to about 670, when the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi, acting for Caliph Mu'awiya, chose a site in dense forest as a military post for the conquest of the West. A Byzantine garrison town, Kamounia, had stood there before. Berber resistance continued under Kusaila, whose troops killed Uqba at Biskra about fifteen years later, and under a woman called Al-Kahina, who was killed and her army defeated in 702. A mass conversion of the Berbers to Islam followed.

Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab recaptured Kairouan at the end of the 8th century, and in 800 Caliph Harun ar-Rashid confirmed him as emir of Ifriqiya. His Aghlabid dynasty ruled until 909 and made Kairouan its capital. The Aghlabids built the great mosque and a university, which made the city a centre of Islamic learning.

After the Fatimids overthrew them in 909 they moved first to Raqqada and then to Al Mahdiyah, and Kairouan lost importance. The Zirids, ruling for the Fatimids after these had moved to Egypt, governed again from Kairouan, until in 1045 they declared independence and allegiance to Baghdad. As punishment the Fatimids sent the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym, who took and destroyed the city in 1057, and it never regained its former importance.
The city began to emerge from its ruins under the Hafsids in the 13th century. The French took it in 1881, after which non-Muslims could enter and live there, which they had been forbidden to do.

The old city and its monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1988. Besides the Great Mosque they include the Mosque of the Three Doors, founded in 866, and the Aghlabid basins of the 9th century, a water system with a storage capacity of 68,800 cubic metres. The city had about 187,000 inhabitants in 2014, and its Jewish community, a centre of Talmudic scholarship from the late 8th century to the early 11th, has left only a cemetery.
kaiser: Kaiser is derived directly from the Roman emperors' title of Caesar, which came from the personal name of the Julii Caesares, a branch of the gens Julia to which Gaius Julius Caesar belonged. It has been suggested, on the strength of an anecdote in Suetonius, that Caesar himself once used his cognomen as a title, but this is thought unlikely. The Hindi and Urdu Kaisar-i-Hind, used of the British Emperor of India, shares the Latin origin but comes through Persian Kaysar, not from the German word.

The Holy Roman Emperors called themselves Kaiser, combining the imperial title with that of King of the Romans, which the designated heir took before the imperial coronation. They saw their rule as a continuation of that of the Roman emperors. From 1452 to 1806, except in 1742 to 1745, only members of the Habsburg family held the title.

The Holy Roman Empire was dissolved in 1806, but the Habsburgs kept the title, and from 1804 their head was Kaiser of Austria. In 1867 the empire became Austria-Hungary, with the emperor also King of Hungary. Four Habsburg kaisers ruled the Austrian Empire: Franz I (1804 to 1835), Ferdinand I (1835 to 1848), Franz Joseph I (1848 to 1916) and Karl I (1916 to 1918). In central Europe Franz Joseph is still remembered with high respect as Der Kaiser, because of his long reign before the First World War.

When Germany was unified without Austria in 1871 there was debate over the monarch's title. The first kaiser preferred Kaiser von Deutschland, Emperor of Germany, but Chancellor Bismarck's choice, Deutscher Kaiser, German Emperor, was adopted, since it did not claim rule over all German lands and so would not offend Austria. Three Hohenzollern kaisers held it: Wilhelm I (1871 to 1888), Friedrich III, who ruled for 99 days in 1888, and Wilhelm II (1888 to 1918), in whose reign the monarchy ended near the close of the First World War.

During the First World War anti-German feeling gave the word, especially as applied to Wilhelm II, strongly negative associations in English-speaking countries. In Central Europe it entered everyday speech through Franz Joseph: Kaiserwetter is sunny weather, linked to the sunshine on his birthday on 18 August, and Kaiserschmarrn is a sweetened pancake named for him. Kaiserjäger and Kaiserschützen were elite units of the Austro-Hungarian army. Der Kaiser is also the nickname of the footballer Franz Beckenbauer.
kaiseraugst: Kaiseraugst is a municipality in the district of Rheinfelden in the canton of Aargau, along the Rhine. It is named after the ancient Roman city of Augusta Raurica, whose ruins are nearby. The prefix Kaiser, meaning imperial, refers to the fact that from medieval times the town formed part of the Habsburg territory of Further Austria, whereas the neighbouring village of Augst belonged to the canton of Basel in the Old Swiss Confederacy. The two villages separated in 1442. The municipality covers 4.91 square kilometres, about a third of it forest and two fifths built up.

About 300 CE, after the loss of the Limes Germanicus and the right bank of the Rhine, the Roman army built a fort near Augusta Raurica. Called Castrum Rauracense, it was intended as the headquarters of the legio I Martia and to protect a ford over the Rhine. In the 4th century it grew in importance because it commanded a bridge on the road from Gaul to the Danube. An amphitheatre, probably the youngest known Roman amphitheatre, was built there around 337 to 341. The emperors Constantius II and Julian assembled their armies at the fort before marching against the Alemanni.

After the Roman Empire collapsed the fort stayed occupied as local Germanic tribes moved in. The fort and the neighbouring church became the seat of a bishop, first mentioned in 346, but in the 7th century the bishop moved to Basel and the settlement declined. A village called Augusta is first mentioned in 752. In 894 the East Francian King Arnulf granted the church to his vassal Anno, and it later passed to the Abbey of St Gall and then to the Basel Münster. The original church of 400 CE was replaced by a new building in 1749.

In the early 1960s a nuclear power plant was planned at Kaiseraugst. The population strongly opposed it and occupied the site in 1975. After the Chernobyl disaster the Swiss government and Kaiseraugst Nuclear Energy AG agreed to abandon the project.

Kaiseraugst has a little over five thousand inhabitants, most of whom speak German. The Roman city of Augusta Raurica with the Castrum Rauracense is a Swiss heritage site of national significance, and the whole village is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites. Another Roman amphitheatre was discovered during building work in December 2021. The village lies on the Bözberg railway line and is served by the Basel S-Bahn.
kaitai-shinsho: On 4 March 1771 the students of Rangaku medicine Sugita Genpaku, Maeno Ryōtaku and Nakagawa Jun'an watched dissections of executed criminals at the Kozukappara execution grounds. Sugita and Maeno each owned the Ontleedkundige Tafelen, the Dutch version of Johann Adam Kulmus's Latin Tabulae Anatomicae, and Sugita, struck by its accuracy, proposed translating it. They began the next day.

Only Maeno could read Dutch, and his vocabulary was limited; there were no dictionaries, and the interpreters were far away in Nagasaki, so the work went forward in a way compared to code-breaking. In 1773 they issued a five-page flyer, the Kaitai Yakuzu, to test the response of the authorities. The court physician Katsuragawa Hosan put the finished book before the shogunate, and Odano Naotake, a samurai artist from Kakunodate recommended by Hiraga Gennai, drew the figures.

The book, issued by the publisher Suharaya Ichibee, has four volumes of text in kanbun and one of illustrations. Maeno did most of the translating and Sugita put it into classical Chinese. Besides Kulmus, the translators consulted works by Bartholini, Blankaart and others, and left out the long footnotes that fill more than half of Kulmus's book. The volumes run from the skeleton and joints through the head and senses, the chest, heart and vessels, and the digestive organs to the kidneys, genitalia, pregnancy and muscles. Maeno is named only in the dedication; accounts differ on why he withheld his name.

The translation advanced both medicine and the understanding of Dutch in Japan, and helped the rise of scholars such as Ōtsuki Gentaku. Its translators coined words still in use, among them shinkei for nerve, nankotsu for cartilage and dōmyaku for artery, though many other terms written in Chinese characters soon disappeared. As a first attempt it had many mistranslations, and Ōtsuki Gentaku published a revised version, the Chōtei Kaitai Shinsho, in 1826. Late in life Sugita told the story of the work in Rangaku Koto Hajime, which shaped later writing on the modernisation of Japanese medicine.
kak-tiliw-chan-yopaat: Kʼakʼ Tiliw Chan Yopaat was formerly known by several names, among them Cauac Sky, Kawak Sky, Butsʼ Tiliw and Butzʼ Tiʼliw. Quiriguá was then a vassal of Copán. In 734, on Altar M at Quiriguá, he gave himself the title kʼuhul ajaw, declaring the city's independence from Copán, and to formalise his sovereignty he received the Kʼawiil sceptre.

The most important event of his reign, and of Quiriguá's history, came in 738, 9.15.6.14.6 in the Mayan calendar, when his forces defeated Copán. Its ruler, Uaxaclajuun Ubʼaah Kʼawiil, formerly known as 18 Rabbit, was captured and later beheaded. Copán's inscriptions then fell silent for 20 years, and the captured king is not mentioned again. Quiriguá became a fully autonomous city that controlled the main trade route from the Caribbean into the Maya world.

The defeat led to Copán's decline but opened a golden age for its former dependent: for the next 38 years the stonecutters of Quiriguá made zoomorphs and stelae celebrating its king. Among them is Stele E, carved from a single stone and 10.7 metres high, the tallest stele of the Maya world. When Frederick Catherwood and John Lloyd Stephens came upon these monuments in 1840, they helped to dispel the European belief that the Indigenous peoples of the region had been less advanced.

The evidence points to his death in 785, and a carved stone now known as Zoomorph G seems to have served as his funeral marker. Two later rulers of Quiriguá are known, Sky Xul and Jade Sky, each of whom reigned for about ten years.
kakawin: The pattern of heavy and light syllables in a kakawin line is called its guru laghu. A syllable with a long vowel (ā, ī, ū, ö, e, o, ai and au) is always long, and so is a syllable whose vowel is followed by two consonants. The last syllable of a line may be either long or short, an anceps. In notation a long syllable is marked with a dash and a short one with U. In one metre, for example, each line has 19 syllables in a fixed sequence of long and short.

That metre opens the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha, whose first line reads ambĕk sang paramārthapaṇḍita huwus limpad sakêng śūnyatā. In a tentative English translation, its first stanza describes one who knows the Highest Knowledge, whose thought has leapt from the emptiness, who seeks not to satisfy his senses or gain worldly things but the happiness of the world, and who stands just a wayang screen away from the Mover of the World.

Dated poems include the Kakawin Śivagŗha of 856 and the Kakawin Ramayana of about 870. Mpu Kanwa wrote the Kakawin Arjunawiwaha around 1030, and Mpu Sedah and Mpu Panuluh the Kakawin Bharatayuddha in 1157. The Kakawin Nagarakṛtâgama, also called the Desawarnana, was written by Mpu Prapanca in 1365.

Several poets are known by more than one work. Mpu Tantular wrote the Kakawin Sutasoma and the Kakawin Arjunawijaya, and Mpu Tanakung the Kakawin Siwaratrikalpa and the Kakawin Wrtasañcaya. The Kakawin Kunjarakarna is by Mpu Dusun and the Kakawin Sumanasantaka by Mpu Monaguṇa. Other notable kakawin include the Kakawin Adiparwa, the Kakawin Bhomantaka, the Kakawin Hariwangsa, the Kakawin Krsnayana and the Kakawin Smaradhana.
kakegawa-castle: Kakegawa Castle is a hirayama-style castle, raised on a small hill in the centre of Kakegawa. The town had been an important post station on the Tōkaidō highway between Kyoto and eastern Japan since the Heian period, and its position made it a strategic point for holding the eastern half of Tōtōmi Province. The first castle was built by Asahina Yasuhiro, a retainer of the warlord Imagawa Yoshitada, and it stayed with later generations of the Asahina clan.

After the Imagawa clan's defeat at the Battle of Okehazama, its former lands were divided between Takeda Shingen of Kai and Tokugawa Ieyasu of Mikawa. The castle passed to the Tokugawa after a siege of five months. The surrounding district was contested between the Tokugawa and the Takeda for many years, but the castle stayed in Tokugawa hands until the Takeda clan fell.

After the Battle of Odawara in 1590, Toyotomi Hideyoshi made Tokugawa Ieyasu give up his domains in the Tōkai region for the Kantō. Kakegawa went to Hideyoshi's retainer Yamauchi Kazutoyo as the centre of a new domain of 51,000 koku, later 59,000. He rebuilt the castle completely to the latest designs, and its present layout and much of its stone walls and moats date from his time. Under the Tokugawa shogunate the Yamauchi were moved to Kōchi in Shikoku, and Kakegawa Domain passed first to Hisamatsu Sadakatsu, then to a series of fudai daimyō clans, ending with seven generations of the Ōta clan.

The Yamauchi keep was destroyed by an earthquake in 1604 and rebuilt in 1621. The Ansei Tōkai earthquake of 1854 did extensive damage. Many buildings were rebuilt by 1861 and served as local government offices after the Meiji Restoration, but the keep was left in ruins.

The Ni-no-Maru Goten, the daimyō's mansion built by Ōta Sukekatsu after the earthquake, survives and was registered as an Important Cultural Property in 1980, as do parts of the moats and walls, a guardhouse and the drum house. A gate of the main bailey built in 1659 is now the main gate of the temple of Yusan-ji in Fukuroi. In April 1994 the keep and parts of the innermost bailey were rebuilt by the original methods from a few surviving diagrams, the first keep in post-war Japan reconstructed in wood in this way, at a cost of 1 billion yen raised largely through public donation.
kakusthavarma: Kakusthavarma, also written Kakusthavarman, was a son of King Bhageerath, the third ruler of the Kadamba dynasty. When his father died the throne passed to his elder brother Raghu, and Kakusthavarma became Yuvaraja, or crown prince. As heir apparent he held a court of his own, perhaps at Palashika, the present-day Halasi, from where he is known to have issued land grants. In due course he succeeded his brother as king.

His reign is noted above all for its marriage alliances. The marriage of one daughter, read as a marriage into the imperial Gupta family, is counted the most important. It is also likely that another daughter married the Vakataka prince Narendrasena: Vakataka records describe Narendrasena's wife, Ajjhitabhattarika, as a princess of the Kuntala country, which probably corresponds to the Kadamba kingdom. Through such ties the Kadambas stood in close diplomatic relations with the great royal houses of India. The Talagunda and Halmidi inscriptions praise the king as a formidable warrior.

He appears also to have been a builder and a patron of both secular architecture and religious causes. He is described as owning numerous palaces adorned with gopuras. The Talagunda pillar inscription of his son Santivarma records that he had a great water tank made near a Shiva temple at which Satakarni and other kings of the past had worshipped. His own leanings seem to have been Jain: his grant at Halasi opens with an invocation to Jinendra, the lord of the Jinas, and he probably patronised a Jain temple there.

On his death the kingdom appears to have been divided among his descendants. One son, Santivarma, succeeded him at Banavasi and ruled the northern part of the realm. Another, Krishnavarma I, seems to have founded a junior branch of the dynasty at Triparvatha, in the south. The height of Kadamba power under Kakusthavarma was therefore followed by a kingdom held in two lines.
kakuyids: The Kakuyids were a Shia Muslim dynasty of Daylamite origin, related to the Buyids. Scholars hold that they were kin of Sayyida Shirin, a princess of the Daylamite Bavand dynasty who married the Buyid amir Fakhr al-Dawla. The founder's father, Rustam Dushmanziyar, was her uncle; he had served the Buyids and received lands in the Alborz to guard them against the local rulers of neighbouring Tabaristan. From this tie the founder was often called Ibn Kakuya or Pisar-i Kaku, meaning son of the uncle.

Ala al-Dawla Muhammad began as a Daylamite military leader in the service of the Buyid amirate of Jibal and owed the governorship of Isfahan to Sayyida Shirin. Mafarrukhi, an 11th-century local historian of Isfahan, suggests that he held the city at least as early as 1003. Over time he became in effect independent of the Buyids, though at times he acted as their ally: Shams al-Dawla turned to him for help against a revolt in Hamadan.

After Shams al-Dawla died and Sama' al-Dawla succeeded him, the Kakuyids took Hamadan in 1023 or 1024 and went on to seize Hulwan from the 'Annazids. Musharrif al-Dawla, the Buyid ruler of Fars and Iraq, forced them out of Hulwan, but they kept Hamadan, and peace between the two houses was eventually sealed by a marriage alliance. In 1041 Faramurz succeeded his father at Isfahan, while his brother Garshasp I ruled Hamadan, Nihawand, Borujerd and western Jibal until 1048.

The Seljuks took Isfahan after a year-long siege in 1051 or 1052. Faramurz was nonetheless given Yazd and Abarkuh in fief, and the family governed these provinces into the 12th century; their rule there is remembered for the building of mosques, canals and fortifications. His son Ali, who ruled Yazd from the 1070s to 1095, married Arslan Khatun Khadija, a daughter of Chaghri Beg, in 1076–1077. The last ruler, Garshasp II, succeeded in 1095 and was killed at the Battle of Qatwan in 1141.
kalaburagi: Kalaburagi lies on the Deccan Plateau, at an elevation of 300 to 750 metres in the district, which the Krishna and Bhima rivers cross. The soil is mainly black soil, and the district's main crops are groundnuts, rice and pulses. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with a rainy season brought by the south-west monsoon from late June to late October and dry winters from late November to February.

The earliest recorded name of the region dates from the 6th century, when the Chalukyas called it Kalburgi, roughly 'rocky land' in Kannada. The Rashtrakutas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas kept the name until 1321, when the region was annexed by the Delhi Sultanate, which renamed it Gulbarga, 'city of flower gardens', from the Persian gul and bagh. The Kakatiya power was subdued in 1308, and the whole Deccan passed under Delhi.

A revolt of the officers appointed from Delhi led to the founding of the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347 by Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah, who chose Gulbarga, also called Hasanabad, as his capital. When the sultanate ended in 1527 it broke into five Deccan sultanates, Bijapur, Bidar, Berar, Ahmednagar and Golconda, and the Gulbarga area was divided between Bidar and Bijapur. Golconda, the last of them, fell to Aurangzeb in 1687, and Gulbarga passed to the Mughal Empire.

Early in the 18th century Asaf Jah I, one of Aurangzeb's generals, formed the kingdom of Hyderabad, which took in most of the area. In 1948 Hyderabad State joined the Indian Union, and in 1956 the Gulbarga district became part of the new Mysore State. The state government restored the name Kalaburagi in 2014.

The city is the headquarters of Kalaburagi district and division. The Jama Masjid inside the fort was built in 1367 by a Persian architect named Rafi, during the reign of the Bahmani king Mohammed Shah I. Other Bahmani monuments include the Haft Gumbaz and the Shor Gumbad, and painted floral, geometric and calligraphic designs decorate the domed tombs of Sufi saints and of Sultan Firuz Shah Bahmani. Buildings in the city, with others in the region, were placed on UNESCO's tentative list as Monuments and Forts of the Deccan Sultanate in 2014. The 2011 census counted 533,587 people, of whom 55 per cent gave Kannada as their first language and about 36 per cent Urdu.
kalakaua: Kalākaua was born on 16 November 1836 in Honolulu, on the island of Oʻahu, to Caesar Kaluaiku Kapaʻakea and Analea Keohokālole. His family belonged to the aliʻi class of Hawaiian nobility and was a collateral branch of the reigning House of Kamehameha. At four he began his education at the Chiefs' Children's School, where he and his classmates, among them the future kings Kamehameha IV, Kamehameha V and Lunalilo, had been proclaimed eligible for the throne. He later held military and court posts and married Kapiʻolani on 19 December 1863.

Kamehameha V died on 12 December 1872 without naming a successor, so the legislature chose the next king. Kalākaua, who had led the Young Hawaiians, a group whose motto was "Hawaiʻi for the Hawaiians", was elected to the throne in 1874 against Queen Emma. He was sworn in quickly, in a hasty ceremony, and held a coronation in 1883. At his coronation and his birthday jubilee of November 1886 the hula, until then banned in public, became a celebration of Hawaiian culture.

In 1875 he helped negotiate the Reciprocity Treaty, which let sugar and other products into the United States duty-free; he opposed ceding any land, and the treaty was signed without any. Between 1880 and 1887 he sent 18 students abroad for further education. In 1881 he circumnavigated the globe in 281 days to encourage the importation of contract labour for the plantations, and his sister Liliʻuokalani acted as regent in his absence. He also ordered the old palace destroyed and replaced by ʻIolani Palace.

Extravagant spending and his plans for a Polynesian confederation played into the hands of annexationists. In 1887 he was pressured to sign the Bayonet Constitution, which made the monarchy little more than a figurehead position.

Kalākaua sailed for California on the USS Charleston on 25 November 1890, with Liliʻuokalani again named regent. He died on 20 January 1891, and she became the last monarch of Hawaiʻi. His reign is generally regarded as the first Hawaiian Renaissance, for his influence on Hawaiian music and his efforts to reinvigorate Hawaiian culture.
kalamata: Kalamata is the second most populous city of the Peloponnese after Patras, and the capital and chief port of Messenia. It lies on the Nedon River at the head of the Messenian Gulf. The modern name probably comes from a church title, the Virgin Mary with beautiful eyes, or else from the older name Kalamai, meaning reeds. The city occupies the site of ancient Pharae, mentioned by Homer.

Kalamata is first mentioned with its modern name in the 10th-century Life of St. Nikon. The medieval town lay inland, at the foot of Mount Taygetos, and prospered in the 11th and 12th centuries as capital of the fertile Messenian plain. After the Fourth Crusade it was conquered in 1205 by the Frankish lords William of Champlitte and Geoffrey of Villehardouin and became part of the Principality of Achaea, the centre of the Villehardouins' patrimony. Prince William II of Villehardouin was born and died there. It came under the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea only in 1428.

The Ottomans occupied Kalamata in 1481. In 1659 the Venetian commander Francesco Morosini took it, plundered it and carried off its able-bodied men to row in the Venetian galleys. He returned in 1685 at the start of the Morean War, and Venice ruled it as part of the Kingdom of the Morea until the Ottomans reoccupied it in the war of 1715.

Kalamata was the first city taken by the Greeks in the Greek War of Independence. On 23 March 1821 revolutionary forces under Theodoros Kolokotronis, Petros Mavromichalis and Papaflessas occupied it. In 1825 the Ottoman officer Ibrahim Pasha destroyed the city. It was rebuilt in independent Greece and became one of the most important ports of the Mediterranean. It was liberated on 9 September 1944, and an earthquake in 1986 killed 20 people.

Kalamata is known for the Kalamatianos dance, black Kalamata olives and olive oil, and exports raisins and olives. The 2021 census recorded 58,816 inhabitants in the city proper. Its sights include the Villehardouin castle, the Church of the Holy Apostles, where Mavromichalis declared the revolt of 1821, and the cathedral of the Ypapanti, consecrated in 1873. It is the seat of the Metropolitan Bishop of Messenia.
kalbid-dynasty: The Kalbids descended from the Arab tribe of Banu Kalb, whose members often served as governors and officials in Ifriqiya in the Umayyad period. Their fortunes declined under the Aghlabids, who favoured the rival Qays–Mudar group, but when the Fatimids conquered Ifriqiya in 909 the Kalb, an important military and religious support of the new regime and allies of the Kutama Berbers, quickly gained influence. The Muslim conquest of Sicily had begun in 827, when an Aghlabid fleet under Asad ibn al-Furat landed at Mazara; Palermo fell in 831 and Syracuse in 878.

After a revolt on the island was put down, the Fatimid caliph appointed al-Hasan al-Kalbi emir of Sicily, and the dynasty ruled on as the caliphs' proxies after they moved their capital to Cairo in 969. Raids into southern Italy continued, and in 982 Abu'l-Qasim defeated a German army under Otto II at the Battle of Stilo in Calabria. A steady decline began under Yusuf al-Kalbi (990–998), who left the island to his sons and opened the way to interference by the Zirids of Ifriqiya.

Under al-Akhal the dynastic quarrels deepened, with factions seeking help from Byzantium or the Zirids, and under Hasan as-Samsam (1040–1053) Sicily broke up into small lordships. The Normans under Roger I of Sicily arrived in 1061 and completed their conquest in 1091; Muslims remained important in the administration, army and economy of the Norman kingdom until the 12th century.

The Kalbids worked to make Sicilian society Muslim: in 962 fourteen thousand children were circumcised in a single ceremony. After a Byzantine offensive was crushed at Rametta in 965, the caliph al-Mu'izz had the emir regroup the inhabitants from 967 into a few towns, one to a district, each with a castle and a Friday mosque, spreading both Islam and the dynasty's Shiite message. Palermo became an important Mediterranean centre, trading between the Near East, North Africa and Amalfi, Pisa and Genoa, and lemons, Seville oranges, sugar cane, cotton and mulberries came with new irrigation.
kaleb: Kaleb, a name taken from the biblical Caleb, was the king's given name; his regnal name was Ella Asbeha, which Greek writers rendered as Elesbaan or Hellestheaios. On his coins and in the inscriptions he left at Aksum, as well as in Ethiopian king lists and lives of saints, he calls himself the son of Tazena. An inscription at Aksum, RIE 191, names him as Kaleb Ella Asbeha, son of Tazena.

Procopius, John of Ephesus and other contemporaries describe his invasion of Yemen around 520 against the Himyarite king Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar, known as Dhu Nuwas, a Jewish convert who was persecuting the Christian community of Najran. After much fighting the king was killed and Kaleb appointed a native Christian, Sumyafa Ashwa, as his viceroy. Around 525 Sumyafa Ashwa was deposed by Abraha, who made himself king, and according to Procopius Kaleb's attempts to recover the territory failed. The historian Stuart Munro-Hay judged that Aksum overextended itself, calling the venture its swan-song as a great power in the region.

At home his reign saw the integration of the Agaw tribes of what are now Wag and Lasta. Cosmas Indicopleustes mentions a governor of Agau whom Kaleb entrusted with guarding the caravan routes from the south. The Byzantine ambassador Nonnosus met him in 530.

Ethiopian tradition holds that Kaleb abdicated, gave his crown to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem and retired to a monastery. Three sons, Gebre Meskel, Israel and Gebre Krestos, are recorded as reigning after him, and sources disagree about the struggle for the succession. Because he protected the Christians of Najran, Cardinal Caesar Baronius added him to the Roman Martyrology as Saint Elesbaan in the sixteenth century. A ruined structure at Aksum said to be his tomb, beside one said to be his son Gabra Masqal's, was examined by Henry Salt, cleared by the Deutsche Aksum-Expedition in 1906 and excavated in 1973.
kalenjin-people: The Kalenjin languages form a branch of the Southern Nilotic group within the Nilo-Saharan family, and the Kalenjin are classed as Highland Nilotes. Archaeological and linguistic evidence places the cradle of the Nilotic languages in the Nile Valley, and a southward migration that began around 500 BCE brought the ancestors of the Kalenjin to the Rift Valley of Kenya. There they had close contact with Southern and Eastern Cushitic-speaking communities, from whom they adopted the age-set system (ipinda), circumcision and many words for livestock and social organization.

Kalenjin oral traditions point to an origin called Misiri, often interpreted as ancient Egypt. The scholar Kipkoeech Arap Sambu has argued for Egyptian and Semitic roots of Kalenjin words, while many historians attribute such similarities to ancient contact between Nilotic, Cushitic and Semitic peoples. Oral traditions of other East African communities point to Kalenjin-speaking groups in the region before the 19th century, the earliest being the Lumbwa on the lower slopes of Mount Kenya.

Colonial administrators and scholars first called these peoples the Nandi-speaking peoples, and the Nandi and Kipsigis, prominent in the early colonial period, gave their names to the whole. Under the Orkoiyot Koitalel Arap Samoei the Nandi waged a guerrilla resistance to British rule, sabotaging the construction of the Uganda Railway between 1895 and 1905.

The name Kalenjin, a Nandi expression meaning I tell you, was proposed in 1944 by fourteen students at Alliance High School led by Taaitta Arap Toweett. It had gained currency in the Second World War through the radio broadcaster John Arap Chemallan, who used it as a catchphrase for African soldiers, and Nandi and Kipsigis servicemen began to use it as a collective identity. The Kalenjin Union was founded in Eldoret in 1948.

The Kalenjin comprise some twenty or more groups, among them the Kipsigis, Nandi, Pokot, Keiyo, Marakwet, Tugen, Sabaot and the Sebei of Uganda. The 2019 Kenyan census counted 6,358,113 Kalenjin, the third-largest ethnic group after the Kikuyu and the Luhya. Traditionally herders, many, especially the Kipsigis and Nandi, now farm maize and wheat, and the Kericho and Nandi highlands are central to Kenya's tea industry.

Circumcision and initiation (yatitaet and tumdo) mark the passage from boyhood to manhood and remain a key part of Kalenjin identity. Almost all Kalenjin today belong to an organised religion, the great majority Christian. Daniel arap Moi, president of Kenya from 1978 to 2002, was Kalenjin, and since the mid-1960s a large share of Kenya's international honours in distance running has gone to Kalenjin athletes.
kalevala: The Kalevala is a 19th-century compilation of epic poetry by Elias Lönnrot, drawn from Finnish, Karelian and Ingrian folklore and mythology. Before the 18th century this runic song was common throughout Finland and Karelia, but it began to disappear in western Finland as European rhymed poetry spread. The nationalist and linguist Carl Axel Gottlund hoped for a Finnish epic in the manner of the Iliad, Ossian and the Nibelungenlied that would stir national feeling. Lönnrot, a physician, botanist and linguist, was district health officer of Kainuu from 1833 and made eleven field trips in fifteen years.

The work opens with the Finnish creation myth. The Earth is made from the shards of the egg of a sotka bird, and the first man, Väinämöinen, is born to Ilmatar, the Holy Spirit of the Heaven. Väinämöinen is a shamanistic hero with a magical power of song, associated with the kantele. The smith Ilmarinen forged the dome of the sky and the Sampo, a device that brings its possessor great fortune and whose precise nature is still debated. The land of Väinölä is set against Pohjola, whose mistress is Louhi, and the poems tell of voyages and quarrels between them and of the making and robbery of the Sampo.

The first version, the Old Kalevala, appeared in 1835 and 1836 with 12,078 verses in thirty-two poems. The standard version, published in 1849, has fifty poems and 22,795 verses. Lönnrot also compiled a lyrical companion collection, the Kanteletar, in 1840.

How much of the text is Lönnrot's own is still argued. He merged variants and characters, left out verses that did not fit and wrote connecting lines. The historian Väinö Kaukonen estimated that about 3 per cent of the lines are Lönnrot's own composition, 14 per cent his compositions from variants, 50 per cent verses kept mostly unchanged and 33 per cent unedited oral poetry.

The Kalevala is regarded as the national epic of Finland and Karelia and was important in forming Finnish national identity and in the language struggle that led to independence from Russia in 1917. It has been translated over 150 times into more than 60 languages. Composers from Filip von Schantz to Jean Sibelius, whose Kullervo dates from 1892, took subjects from it, and Akseli Gallen-Kallela is the painter most associated with it.
kalgoorlie: Kalgoorlie, also called Kalgoorlie-Boulder, lies in the Goldfields-Esperance region of Western Australia, 595 km east-northeast of Perth at the end of the Great Eastern Highway. The urban area takes in the historic townsite of Boulder. It lies on the traditional lands of the Kapurn people, and languages of the Kapurn family, including Kalaamaya, are still spoken there. The name comes from the Wangai language of the Eastern Goldfields, and sources give it several meanings, among them an Aboriginal dog chasing a kangaroo, a local shrub and the edible silky pear. The climate is hot semi-arid, with an average annual rainfall of 260 mm.

In the winter of 1893 the prospectors Patrick Hannan, Tom Flanagan and Dan Shea were travelling to Mount Youle when a horse cast a shoe, and they noticed signs of gold near what is now the Mount Charlotte mine. Hannan filed a Reward Claim on 17 June 1893 and hundreds of men swarmed to the place, first called Hannan's Find. The government chose the name Kalgoorlie in August 1894, after an official had warned that the native name sounded too much like Coolgardie.

Boulder, gazetted in 1896, took its name from the Great Boulder lease, registered in August 1893 by Sam Pearce and William Brookman. The calaverite found in the rush was at first ignored as a kind of fool's gold and used for buildings and paving; when it was found in 1896 to be a compound of tellurium and gold, nearly every structure of the previous three years was demolished to extract it.

The population was 2,018 in 1898 and 6,790 by 1903. The Eastern Goldfields Railway reached Kalgoorlie in 1896 and a standard-gauge line to Port Augusta in 1917. The goldfields as a whole had more than 200,000 people in the 1890s, and complaints of neglect by the government in Perth led to a proposal for a new state, Auralia, which lapsed when the rush ended. The Town of Kalgoorlie and the Shire of Boulder amalgamated in 1989.

The water pipeline designed by C. Y. O'Connor, bringing water from Mundaring Weir near Perth, ends at Kalgoorlie, and the Golden Pipeline Heritage Trail follows it. The concentrated area of mines around Hannan's find is called the Golden Mile. The Fimiston Open Pit, or Super Pit, about 3.6 km long and over 600 metres deep, was formed in 1989 by consolidating many underground mines. The city has ornate heritage buildings, among them the Town Hall and historic hotels on Hannan Street, and had an estimated urban population of 29,072 in 2021.
kalhora-dynasty: The Kalhora were a Sindhi Muslim dynasty whose power lay in Sindh, in present-day Pakistan, and whose rule also reached the northern half of Kutch. Their rule began when the Mughals, by royal decree, gave Yar Muhammad Kalhoro the title of Khuda Yar Khan and made him subahdar of upper Sindh. After his death his son was also appointed subahdar of Sehwan, and so came to oversee most of Sindh. Their capital was Khudabad until 1768, when it moved to Hyderabad.

The dynasty gave way before the invasion of Nader Shah, and Ahmad Shah Durrani then conquered Sindh in 1748-1750, making it a vassal of the Durrani Empire. The Kalhora nawabs fought in the Third Battle of Panipat on the side of the victorious coalition. Ghulam Shah Kalhoro brought stability to Sindh by restructuring the state, but his successors could not hold it for long, and the Talpur mirs overthrew them at the Battle of Halani.

Abdul Nabi Kalhoro, the last Kalhora ruler, was overthrown in 1783. He went on to govern Layyah and Bhakkar from 1787 to 1790, after defeating the Jaskani tribe. When the Afghan ruler Timur Shah died in 1793, his successor Zaman Shah demanded from Abdul Nabi arrears of one lakh and twenty thousand rupees. Abdul Nabi did not pay or obey the Afghan court, and his jagir was cancelled and granted to Nawab Muhammad Khan Saddozai.

According to Ḳāniʿ, who visited their court, the Kalhora spoke Sindhi there. Their army was divided into two main groups. The Sariwal were the men best at ambushing an enemy camp, while the Sarfarosh were the finest fighters, who specialised in swordsmanship.
kaliakra: The headland lies in the Southern Dobruja region, 12 kilometres east of Kavarna, 60 kilometres north-east of Varna and 65 kilometres south-west of Mangalia. It sits on the Via Pontica, a major bird migration route from Africa into eastern and northern Europe, and its reserve shelters rare breeding birds such as the pied wheatear, saker falcon and lesser grey shrike, while dolphins and cormorants can be seen offshore. The name is Byzantine Greek, from words meaning beautiful and headland; its Thracian name was Tirizis.

The earliest settlement dates to the 4th century BCE, when the Thracian Tiris lived here. Strabo placed here the capital of Lysimachus, Alexander's general and ruler of Thrace. A second wall was built inland in the Hellenistic era, round towers were completed in 341 and 342, and in the later 4th century a third wall 2.90 metres thick went up still farther from the tip. In the 5th and 6th centuries the fortress was one of the 15 cities of the province of Scythia, and some researchers see a decline in the 7th century.

The site flourished in the second half of the 14th century as capital of the despotate under Balik and Dobrotitsa, whose town struck its own coins and whose galleys fought in the Black Sea, the first navy built by native rulers. The principality fell to the Ottomans in 1393 and 1394. The Vlach voivode Mircea Stari held the surrounding lands briefly in 1402, and in 1444 the knights of King Vladislav III were stopped near the cape. In 1791 Admiral Fyodor Ushakov's squadron defeated Hussein Pasha's larger fleet offshore.

Remains of the walls, the water supply, the baths and the prince's residence survive on the tip of the headland. The first lighthouse was built in 1866, and the present one in 1901. An obelisk at the entrance, the Gate of the 40 Maidens, recalls the legend of forty Bulgarian girls who tied their hair together and leapt into the sea rather than be captured by the Ottomans, and a monument to Ushakov was raised in 2006.
kalidasa: Little is known of Kalidasa's life beyond what can be inferred from his poetry and plays. His name means servant of Kali. His works cannot be dated precisely, but they were most likely written during the Gupta era. Several ancient and medieval books say he was a court poet of a king named Vikramaditya. A king of that name is said to have ruled from Ujjain around the 1st century BCE, though some scholars think he is not historical, and other Ujjain kings took the title, notably Chandragupta II (r. 380–415 CE). The most popular theory places Kalidasa in the reign of Chandragupta II.

Scholars have placed his birthplace in Bengal, Kashmir, Vidarbha and Malava. V. V. Mirashi argues for Ujjayini because the poet describes it with such affection; in the Meghaduta the cloud is told not to miss it even if it means a detour. Lachhmi Dhar Kalla argued for Kashmir from the plants, animals and landscape in the works. His name is first mentioned, with that of the poet Bhāravi, in the Aihole inscription of 634 CE in Karnataka.

Most modern scholars attribute seven works to Kalidasa: two epic poems, the Kumārasambhava and the Raghuvaṃśa; two lyric poems, the Meghadūta and the Ṛtusaṃhāra; and three plays, the Abhijñānaśākuntalam, the Mālavikāgnimitram and the Vikramōrvaśīyam. The Kumārasambhava describes the birth and youth of Pārvatī, her marriage to Śiva and the birth of their son Kumāra, and the Raghuvaṃśa tells of the kings of the Raghu dynasty. The Meghadūta describes a Yakṣa sending a message to his lover by a cloud.

In the Abhijñānaśākuntalam, King Duṣyanta meets and marries Śakuntalā; a curse makes him forget her until he sees the ring he gave her, which she has lost. It is generally regarded as a masterpiece and was among the first Sanskrit works translated into English, by Sir William Jones in 1791, after which it was received with wonder by Herder and Goethe. A large number of other works have been wrongly attributed to him.

According to legend Kalidasa was once a simple cowherd who gained learning through the blessing of the goddess Kali. The 7th-century writer Bāṇabhaṭṭa praised his sayings as sweet as honey-laden flowers, and Jayadeva called him the lord of poets. His influence extends to all later Sanskrit works, and the earliest surviving commentaries on his works are those of the Kashmirian scholar Vallabhadeva in the 10th century.
kalina-people: The name Caribe was first recorded by Christopher Columbus. It is often said to mean brave warrior, but this is considered a folk etymology; the name more likely comes from a Cariban word meaning person. Early Spanish colonisers called the groups they considered hostile Caribs and those they thought friendly Arawak. The Kalina call themselves Kalina or Karìna, which in their language also means person, and the name Galibi, a form of Caribe, has been used since at least the 19th century.

By 1998 archaeologists had found 273 Amerindian sites on 310 square kilometres of land by the Sinnamary River, some about two thousand years old. Before 1492 the Kalina seem to have held the coast from the mouth of the Amazon to that of the Orinoco, sharing it with the Arawak, whom they fought as they expanded. They travelled widely by land and sea to trade and marry, and went to the Essequibo to collect pebbles of red porphyry, takuwa, which women prized for polishing pottery.

The Kalina first took Europeans for spirits of the sea, Palanakiłi, a name they have used for white people since. Violence by European soldiers and diseases from the Old World brought a steep fall in their numbers, while iron axes and machetes replaced their stone axes and hardwood machetes. In Suriname they lived in the same area as the colonists, under a peace treaty dating from 1686. In Guyana plantation owners paid Kalina to capture Indigenous slaves and to recapture escaped African slaves. In July 1882 fifteen Kalina of one family from Sinnamary and Iracoubo were taken to Paris and exhibited at the Jardin d'Acclimatation, as others were in 1892.

Most Kalina live in villages along rivers and coasts, the largest share of them in Venezuela; in French Guiana they are a majority only at Awala-Yalimapo. Their Cariban language is spoken by over 10,000 people but remains mainly oral, with no fewer than nine ways of writing even the name Kalina. Mourning for a relative may last a year or more and ends with the Epekotono, a public celebration with body painting, music, dancing and the burning of the dead person's belongings. Kasiri, a cassava beer, belongs to their feasts, and their music is mostly percussion, with the sanpula drum and maracas.
kalinago: The Kalinago may have been related to the mainland Caribs, or Kalina, of South America, but they spoke an unrelated language, Kalinago or Island Carib, which linguists classify as Arawakan rather than Cariban. Early missionary accounts held that Caribs from South America had conquered and displaced the island's earlier inhabitants, the Igneri. Linguistic and archaeological evidence contradicts a mass migration and conquest. Irving Rouse and others suggest that a smaller group from the mainland arrived without displacing the islanders and took on the local language while keeping traditions of a South American origin.

At the time of Spanish contact the Kalinago were among the dominant groups in the Caribbean, living across the Windward Islands, Dominica and the southern Leeward Islands, including Guadeloupe. Columbus recorded the name Caribe. The Taínos told him the Caribs were fierce warriors and cannibals who raided them. By the middle of the 16th century resistance in the Greater Antilles was largely quashed. In the Lesser Antilles the Kalinago kept their independence against the Spanish and later the French and English, helped by the lack of gold and the heavy Spanish casualties.

In the 17th century they regularly attacked English and French plantations in the Leeward Islands. In 1660 France and England signed the Treaty of Saint Charles with the Island Caribs, which left only Dominica and Saint Vincent as reserves, but the English ignored it. By 1763 the British had annexed Saint Lucia, Tobago, Dominica and Saint Vincent. On Saint Vincent the Kalinago intermarried with free West African captives, forming the Black Caribs, or Garifuna, who were expelled to Honduras in 1797.

Stories of cannibalism come from Spanish accounts, and there is no hard evidence for it. Historians such as Hilary McD. Beckles suggest the stories were an ideological campaign to justify violent expeditions against the Kalinago. The English word cannibal comes from karibna, an Island Carib word that meant person.

The Kalinago and their descendants live in the Antilles, notably in Dominica, where the Kalinago Territory on the east coast was granted by the British government in 1903. The people elect their own chief, and the name Carib was officially changed to Kalinago in Dominica in 2015. Canoes are important in their material culture and economy. The Garifuna, who share common ancestry with the Kalinago, live mainly in Central America.
kalinga-war: Kalinga was an independent kingdom on the east coast, in the present-day state of Odisha and the northern parts of Andhra Pradesh. It was a prosperous region with ports and a skilled navy, and its people had traded offshore as far as Southeast Asia. Its culture blended tribal religions, Śramaṇa traditions such as Buddhism, Jainism and Ajivika, and Brahmanism, which existed side by side. The region had been under the Nanda Empire of Magadha until the fall of the Nanda Empire in 321 BCE, and Ashoka's grandfather Chandragupta Maurya had possibly tried to conquer it and been repulsed.

Ashoka set out to annex Kalinga once he was securely established as emperor. Some scholars argue that Kalinga was a strategic threat to the Mauryas, since it could interrupt communications between the capital Pataliputra and the possessions in the central Indian peninsula, and it also controlled the coastline for trade in the Bay of Bengal.

According to Ashoka's own edicts, the war was completed in the eighth year of his reign, probably in 261 BCE. It was the only major war he fought after his accession. The Greek historian Megasthenes, at the court of Chandragupta Maurya, reported that the ruler of Kalinga had a powerful army of infantry, cavalry and elephants. According to the archaeologist Dilip K. Chakrabarti, the Mauryan army marched to Kalinga through Sarguja, a route Samudragupta later followed in his own campaign against Kalinga. It is presumed that the battle was fought on the Dhauli hills, on the banks of the Daya River.

Ashoka recorded the result himself in Rock Edict 13. It states that the Kalingans were conquered eight years after his coronation, that one hundred and fifty thousand were deported, that one hundred thousand were killed and that many more died from other causes. The edict says that he came to feel a strong inclination towards the Dharma and deep remorse for having conquered the Kalingans.

Ashoka, already a Buddhist who was not actively engaged in the faith, devoted the rest of his life to ahimsa (non-violence) and to dharma-vijaya, victory through dharma. The conquest ended the military expansion of the empire that had begun under Chandragupta Maurya, and an era of more than 40 years of relative peace followed.
kaliningrad-oblast: Kaliningrad Oblast covers 15,125 square kilometres and is bordered by Poland to the south, Lithuania to the north and east, and the Baltic Sea to the west. It has sea access, so it is described as a semi-exclave. It is mainly flat, with its highest point, Gora Dozor, at 230 metres. The river Pregolya, its largest, drains through the Vistula Lagoon into the Baltic, and the Curonian Lagoon is shared with Lithuania. The port of Baltiysk is Russia's only Baltic port that remains ice-free all year. The oblast also holds amber, and many Russians call it the Amber Land.

The area was inhabited by the Old Prussians and other Western Balts before the Teutonic conquest in the 13th century, after which Germans settled it extensively. The Teutonic Order founded Königsberg in 1255 on the site of a destroyed Sambian settlement called Tvanksta, naming it for Ottokar II of Bohemia. The Lithuanian-inhabited areas of the Teutonic State were known as Lithuania Minor, which covered all of the modern oblast until the 18th century, and the Old Prussians died out through Germanisation in the first half of the 18th century. In 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg secularised the Order's Prussian branch and made himself ruler of the Duchy of Prussia, the first Protestant state in Europe, with Königsberg as its residence.

Königsberg was a place of Polish and Lithuanian printing, including the first Lithuanian grammar and the first Polish translation of the New Testament, and its Albertina University received a royal privilege from King Sigismund II Augustus in 1560. In 1807, after the defeat at Jena–Auerstedt, the Prussian court fled to Königsberg, and the battles of Eylau and Friedland were followed by the Treaties of Tilsit.

The territory was the northern part of East Prussia and overwhelmingly German. After the defeat of Nazi Germany in the Second World War the Soviet Union annexed it into the Russian SFSR. The flight and expulsion of the Germans left it largely empty until Soviet citizens, mostly ethnic Russians, were settled there. When Lithuania became independent in 1990 and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the oblast was cut off from the rest of Russia, and land links now cross neighbouring states. Königsberg Cathedral was restored in the 1990s.

Kaliningrad Oblast is a federal subject of Russia, with its largest city and administrative centre at Kaliningrad, formerly Königsberg. Its population is roughly one million, and Russians form the large majority. Before 1945 the region was overwhelmingly Lutheran.
kalinjar-fort: The fort stands on an isolated, flat-topped outcrop of the Vindhya Range near the border between Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh, rising 244 m above the surrounding plain. The village of Tarahati, also called Kalinjar, lies at its northern foot. The name comes from the Sanskrit kāla, time, and was later linked with Shiva as lord of time. Hindu legend holds that Shiva came here after drinking the poison of the Samudra Manthan and conquered death, and the hill was a place of pilgrimage long before it was fortified: the Mahābhārata names it three times, and Gupta-period seals point to a Shiva temple there.

Kalinjar appears to have been under Gurjara-Pratihara control by 836 and changed hands several times in the mid-900s, passing to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna III and then to the Kalachuris of Tripuri. The Chandelas under Yashovarman took it before 954, and by 998 his son Dhanga called himself lord of Kālañjara. In 1023 Mahmud of Ghazni attacked it and received tribute. In 1202 or 1203 the Ghurid general Qutb ud-Din Aibak besieged it; Paramardi apparently offered tribute but died, and the garrison surrendered on 27 April 1203.

Humayun besieged the fort in 1530. In 1545 Sher Shah Suri attacked the Baghela raja Ram Chand and his Bundela allies there and was mortally wounded when one of his own cannons exploded, though he lived long enough for his men to take the fort. He was buried for a time on a hillock east of the fort before being moved to his tomb at Sasaram. Ram Chand later retook Kalinjar, but in 1569 Akbar's commander Majnun Khan Qashqal forced him to surrender for lack of water. In the early 18th century the Peshwa Bajirao captured it from the Mughals, and the Marathas used it to levy chauth on the surrounding lands.

Seven gates line the northern approach, the first dated by an inscription to 1673. The chief building is the Nilakantha Temple, a cave shrine with a blue linga and, beside it, a rock-cut figure of Kala-Bhairava about 7 m tall. Three Bundela palaces survive, and the Raja Aman Singh Palace serves as a site museum. The fort forms part of a National Geo-Heritage Site.
kalisz: Kalisz lies on the Prosna river in the south-east of Greater Poland, the region regarded as the cradle of the Polish state, and with Poznań is one of its two traditional capitals. Its name is thought to come from the archaic word kal, meaning swamp or marsh. Roman-era finds in the area suggest a stop on the Amber Trail to the Baltic Sea.

Excavations show an early medieval settlement of the Piast period, and the modern town was most likely founded in the 9th century as a castellany and minor fort. In 1106 Bolesław III Wrymouth captured it for his domain. Between 1253 and 1260 it was incorporated under the German town law of Środa Śląska, a variant of Magdeburg law, and during the fragmentation of Poland it formed a separate duchy under a local branch of the Piast dynasty.

The Statute of Kalisz of 1264, issued by Bolesław the Pious, protected Jews at a time of persecution in Western Europe, and in later centuries Poland became a destination for Jewish migration.  In 1314 Ladislaus the Short made it capital of the Kalisz Voivodeship. Casimir III the Great signed a peace treaty with the Order there in 1343.

Kalisz was annexed by Prussia in the Second Partition of 1793, regained by Poles after the Greater Poland uprising of 1806 and, after Napoleon's fall, became a provincial capital of Congress Poland. In August 1914 German forces shelled the city and burned it to the ground, although the Russian troops had left without a fight; of about 68,000 inhabitants only 5,000 remained a year later, and much of the centre was rebuilt by the war's end.

After the German invasion of 1939 the city was annexed by Germany. The Wehrmacht executed Polish defenders in the city and at Winiary, and the Intelligenzaktion targeted the Polish intelligentsia. The Germans set up a Germanisation camp for Polish children taken from their parents. About 30,000 local Jews were murdered by the end of the war, and 20,000 local Catholics were murdered or expelled. The population in 1945 was 43,000, about half the pre-war figure.

Kalisz is the second-largest city of the Greater Poland Voivodeship, with 97,905 residents in December 2021, and is the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Kalisz, created in 1992. It is a historical burial site of Piast dukes and medieval Polish monarchs.
kalka: The name of the town comes from Kalika Maa, the goddess Kali, its ruling deity. The central part of the town was established by Pundir Rajputs, and the area was under them and governed by local Rajput zamindars. British India acquired Kalka from the princely state of Patiala in 1843 as a stopover and depot for Simla, the summer capital of the Raj. In 1846 it was transferred to Shimla district and in 1899 to Ambala district.

In the 1800s the British took the land from the local zamindars for railway development, which gave the town an economic boost. It became the junction of the Delhi-Panipat-Ambala-Kalka railway line and the Kalka-Shimla railway, which was begun in 1898 and opened to traffic in 1903. By 1901 Kalka, administered as a notified area, had a population of 7,045, a railway workshop and a market for ginger and turmeric. Its municipal committee was created on 11 April 1933.

Kalka lies on National Highway 5 between Chandigarh and Shimla, near Solan, and is the gateway to Himachal Pradesh. Pinjore is to its south and the industrial village of Parwanoo to its north. The census of 2011 counted 34,314 people in Kalka and 86,550 in the urban area made up of Kalka, Pinjore and Parwanoo. The local language is Baghati, though Punjabi, Haryanvi and Hindi are also used. Hinduism is the main religion, followed by 81.54 per cent of the population, and Sikhism the second, at 13.02 per cent.

Kalka railway station is the northern terminus of the Delhi-Kalka line, with broad gauge towards Chandigarh and narrow gauge towards Shimla. The Kalka-Shimla Railway is on UNESCO's World Heritage list. The ancient temple of Kali on National Highway 22 draws worshippers during Navratri, and a fair is held there each year in March and April. Oral tradition holds that the Pandavas of the Mahabharata built the original temple during their exile. Nearby is the Chandimandir Cantonment, home of the Western Command of the Indian army.
kalka-shimla-railway: The idea of connecting Shimla by rail was first raised by a correspondent to the Delhi Gazette in November 1847. Shimla became the summer capital of British India in 1864 and the headquarters of the Indian army, so twice a year the entire government had to be moved between Calcutta and Shimla by horse- and ox-drawn carts. The opening of the broad-gauge Delhi–Kalka line in 1891 made a branch to Shimla feasible. Surveys were made in 1884, 1885, 1892, 1893 and 1895, and after much debate an adhesion line was chosen in preference to a rack system.

Construction was begun by the privately funded Delhi-Ambala-Kalka Railway Company after a contract with the secretary of state on 29 June 1898. The government gave the land free but no financial aid. Herbert Septimus Harington was chief engineer and Sujan Singh Hadaliwale chief contractor. The line opened on 9 November 1903 and was dedicated by Viceroy Lord Curzon. The estimated cost of 8,678,500 rupees had doubled by the opening. The Indian Army thought the 2 ft gauge too narrow, so the contract was revised on 15 November 1901 and the line was regauged to 2 ft 6 in.

The route climbs from 656 metres at Kalka to 2,075 metres at Shimla, through 20 stations and more than a hundred tunnels, the longest at Barog. The first locomotives were two small engines from the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, replaced from 1902 by ten 0-4-2T engines built by Sharp, Stewart and Company.
