kandake: Kandake, also written kadake or kentake (Meroitic kdke), was one Meroitic term for a queen or queen mother of Kush, attested for six or seven women. Some were rulers, while others were most likely wives of a king; a kandake might also be the king's sister or another close female relative. She sometimes had her own court, may have held land, and could act as regent until her son came of age. A kandake who ruled in her own right also bore the title qore, the same title carried by male rulers.

Royal women were represented in the ceremonies that ensured the continuity of kingship. The stelae of Tanawetamani, Harsiyotef and Nastasen show each king accompanied at his enthronement by his mother and wife, and Taharqo's coronation stelae suggest his mother travelled to attend. In Meroitic art queens often stand alone at the front of stelae and sculptures in regal dress. Bas-reliefs of about 170 BCE show the kentake Shanakdakheto in armour wielding a spear; she ruled as an independent sovereign with her husband as consort.

Much of this evidence came to light after George Reisner excavated the royal cemeteries at El Kurru and Nuri in 1917-19. Strabo reports that the kandake Amanirenas attacked Syene, today's Aswan, in Roman territory in 25 BCE, and that Augustus destroyed Napata in retaliation; Cassius Dio says the Roman general Petronius took Napata and other cities.

Greek and Roman writers mistook the title for a name, and the form Candace comes from the New Testament (Acts 8:27), where Philip the Evangelist baptises a treasury official of Candace, queen of the Aethiopians. The Alexander romance of Pseudo-Callisthenes tells of a Candace of Meroë who faced Alexander the Great, though Alexander never went further south than the oasis of Siwa. Later Ethiopian king lists also give queens the title Kandake, but no archaeological or epigraphic evidence shows its use in Ethiopia, and historians suggest such claims followed King Ezana's conquest of Meroë in the 4th century CE.
kandariya-mahadeva-temple: Khajuraho was once the capital of the Chandela dynasty, whose rulers built temples there to Hindu deities and to the Thirthankaras of the Jain religion. The Kandariya Mahadeva, a name meaning the Great God of the Cave, was built in the reign of Vidyadhara (r. c. 1003-1035 CE). He fought Mahmud of Ghazni in 1019 and again in 1022, when Mahmud's siege of the fort of Kalinjar failed and the two rulers parted after a truce. Vidyadhara marked his success by building the temple to his family deity, Shiva. An inscription on a pilaster of the mandapa names its builder as Virimda, read as a pseudonym of Vidyadhara.

The temple stands in the western group, the largest of Khajuraho's three, on a plinth 4 metres high; it is 31 metres long, 20 metres wide and 31 metres tall. Steep steps lead to the entrance, where a torana, an intricately carved garland cut from a single stone, recalls a Hindu wedding procession. Inside, three mandapas rise successively in height and width towards the sanctum, which holds a Shiva linga and is ringed by passages with balconies; its dim light gives a cave-like atmosphere. The superstructure rises like a mountain, symbolic of Mount Meru, its contour recalling Mount Kailasa, where Shiva resides.

The exterior is covered with sculpture in three vertical layers: gods and heavenly beings, among whom Agni is prominent, musicians and apsaras, and in the niches erotic figures in mithuna postures, the Saptamatrikas or seven mother goddesses, Ganesha and Virabhadra. A sardula, a creature with a lion's face and human limbs, appears in a lower panel.

The temple is considered one of the best examples of temples preserved from medieval India. In 1986 the temples of Khajuraho, the Kandariya Mahadeva among them, were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List for their artistic creation and as testimony to the culture of the Chandelas, which was dominant until the Muslim invasion of 1202.
kanem-bornu-empire: The Kanem–Bornu Empire was based around Lake Chad and at various times ruled areas that are now parts of Nigeria, Niger, Cameroon, Libya, Algeria, Sudan and Chad. Its early history is poorly known. It is believed to have been founded around the year 700, though later and earlier dates have been proposed, in the lands between Lake Chad and the Bahr el Ghazal. The Duguwa dynasty ruled from the capital Njimi in Kanem and used the title mai. The empire was sustained by the trans-Saharan trade. The name Kanem–Bornu is a modern historians' name, an amalgamation of the empire's two central regions, and not a name the state used itself.

In the 11th century the empire converted to Islam and the Sayfawa dynasty replaced the Duguwa. The mai Dunama II Dibalemi brought it to its height in the 13th century. It controlled Saharan trade routes and exported salt, ivory, slaves and animal products. In the 14th century economic factors and conflict with the Bilala led to the loss of Kanem, and Umar I Idrismi re-centred the empire in Bornu. After a century of instability the mai Ali I Gaji founded Ngazargamu, around 1472, as a permanent capital. The empire reached its peak under Idris IV Alooma in the late 16th century and began a slow decline in the 17th.

The Fula jihads of the early 19th century nearly ended it and moved the centre of regional power west to the Sokoto Caliphate. The al-Kanemi dynasty, ruling as shehus, replaced the Sayfawa. In 1893 the Sudanese slave raider Rabih az-Zubayr defeated Bornu armies and took Kukawa, which was plundered and burned, its 120,000 to 200,000 inhabitants killed, enslaved or dispersed. The al-Kanemi dynasty was restored in 1900 under colonial suzerainty, and in 1902 the territories were absorbed into the French, British and German colonial empires.

The mai was variously equated to an emperor or a king, and after the conversion rulers were also called sultan and emir. Any son of a mai could succeed, which led to succession conflicts and civil wars, and hardly any mai was fully secure. Perhaps in the 13th century the empire moved to a feudal system with a class of princes and a large system of titles. The mai held audience from a wooden cage called the zanadir. All land belonged formally to the sovereign, who granted fiefs under the chima system to courtiers, princes, princesses and clerics. Most fiefs returned to the ruler at the holder's death. The Borno and Dikwa emirates in Nigeria survive as remnants of the regime.
kanesh: Kültepe, Turkish for ash-hill, lies about 20 km northeast of the modern city of Kayseri on the Central Anatolian plateau. The site has two parts: a circular mound, about 500 m across and some 20 m high, and a lower town to its northeast. The mound was inhabited, with breaks, from the Early Bronze Age through the Roman Empire, while the lower town was occupied only from the last decades of the third millennium BCE to the early sixteenth century BCE. Its ancient name appears as Kaneš in Assyrian inscriptions of the 20th and 19th centuries BCE and as Neša in later Hittite ones.

In the early second millennium BCE a kārum, the Assyrian word for a trading district, was established in the lower town. Local officials set it aside for Assyrian merchants, who could trade there without paying taxes as long as the goods stayed inside. Soldiers and merchants from Assyria lived there for hundreds of years, exchanging local tin and wool for luxury goods, foodstuffs, spices and woven fabrics from the Assyrian homeland and Elam.

It appears to have been the administrative and distribution centre of the whole network of Assyrian colonies in Anatolia, and the trade was run by families rather than the state. The kārum was destroyed by fire at the end of its two main levels, II and Ib, and its inhabitants left most of their possessions behind.

Local kings reigned at Kaneš in this period, among them Ḫurmili, Paḫanu, Inar and Waršama. Uḫna, king of Zalpuwa, raided the city and carried off its Šiuš idol. Pitḫana, king of Kuššara, then conquered Neša in the night, and his son Anitta made it his capital and recovered the idol. In the 17th century BCE Anitta's descendants moved their capital to Hattusa, founding the line of Hittite kings, and the Hittite language was called Nešili, the Neša tongue.

Over 22,000 cuneiform tablets have been recovered, mainly from the kārum, and only about forty from the mound. Written in Old Assyrian, they record trade between the colony and Assur and between merchants and local people, and they are the oldest documents from Anatolia. Their Hittite loanwords and names are the oldest record of any Indo-European language. The letters of women such as the businesswomen Zizizi and Taram-Kubi show their part in the trade. Ernest Chantre began excavating in 1893, Bedřich Hrozný found over 1,000 tablets in 1925, and Tahsin Özgüç led the Turkish excavations begun in 1948 until 2005. The site was placed on Turkey's tentative World Heritage list in 2014.
kangaba: Kangaba is believed to have been founded in 1050 by Mandinka people, and it was at first a vassal state of the Ghana Empire. Once known as Kaba, the area later became a core province of the Mali Empire. According to the list of rulers in John Stewart's African States and Rulers, the state's capital was at Kiki from 1050 to 1090, at Dodu until 1200 and at Kangaba itself from 1200 to 1237.

The same list begins with Taraore, who ruled from about 1050, and names among his successors Baraonendana, Hamama and Di Jigi Bilali. Around 1200 the throne passed to Keita Nari fa Majan, the father of Sundiata Keita, and then to Sundiata's half-brother Danagaram Tumo. After a brief period of Soninke rule from 1228 to 1230, Sundiata Keita, also known as Mari Jata I, took power. After his victory at the Battle of Kirina in 1235 he proclaimed the Manden Charter, called the Kouroukan Fouga after the field near Kangaba where it was made, which some regard as perhaps the oldest constitution in the world.

Kangaba is a town, commune and the seat of the Kangaba Cercle in the Koulikoro Region of south-western Mali. At the centre of its large public square, the bara, stands the Kamablon, a sacred circular mudbrick building with a conical roof built in 1653, the oldest of its kind in the Manden cultural zone. Its re-roofing every seven years gathers the traditional castes, the founding dynasties of the Mali Empire and griots who recite the region's oral history, and in 2009 the ceremony was inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
kangra-fort: The fort, also called Kot Kangra, stands on a hillock between the Manjhi and Banganga rivers in the foothills of the Dhauladhar range, 20 kilometres from Dharamsala. It was built by the Katoch dynasty of Rajputs. Its oldest surviving remains are Jain and Hindu temples of about the 9th and 10th centuries, and the earliest recorded mention of the fort is Mahmud of Ghazni's invasion of 1009.

Muhammad bin Tughluq captured it in 1337 and Firuz Shah Tughluq in 1351, and Khawas Khan Marwat, a general of Sher Shah Suri, in 1540. Raja Dharam Chand submitted to Akbar in 1556 and gave up his claim to it. In 1620 Jahangir killed Raja Hari Chand and annexed the Kangra kingdom, and his forces under Nawab Ali Khan, aided by Raja Jagat Singh, took the fort; Jahangir visited it in 1621, and a mosque was built inside.

In 1783 the son of the Mughal governor Saif Ali Khan surrendered the fort to Jai Singh Kanhaiya of the Kanhaiya misl. Raja Sansar Chand II, who had sought it, besieged it with Maha Singh of the Sukerchakia misl and Jassa Singh Ramgarhia, and in 1786 gained it by treaty. From 1807 a Gurkha army under Amar Singh Thapa besieged it, and Sansar Chand turned to Maharaja Ranjit Singh, who drove the Gurkhas back and took the fort and its 66 villages on 24 August 1809. Ranjit Singh added its outer gate.
The British took it after a six-week siege in the First Anglo-Sikh War, ending on 28 May 1846, and kept a garrison there until the earthquake of 4 April 1905 damaged it heavily.

The fort covers 463 acres. A long, narrow passage climbs from a courtyard between two gates of the Sikh period through the Ahani and Amiri gates and the Jehangiri Darwaza. The Darsani Darwaza, flanked by defaced figures of the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna, opens onto a courtyard with shrines of Lakshmi-Narayana and Ambika Devi and a Svetambara Jain temple. Its granite image of Rishabhanatha bears an inscription in Śāradā script dating its consecration to 854 CE; since 1978 it has stood in its own shrine, where Jainas keep the right to worship. The Archaeological Survey of India protects the site.
kangxi-emperor: The Kangxi Emperor was born on 4 May 1654 in the Forbidden City, Beijing, the third son of the Shunzhi Emperor, and was given the personal name Xuanye. He was enthroned on 7 February 1661 at the age of seven, though his era name Kangxi was first used on 18 February 1662. Four regents appointed by his father held actual power: Sonin, Suksaha, Ebilun and Oboi. After Sonin died, Oboi put Suksaha to death and became sole regent, an arrangement the young emperor and the court accepted for some years.

In 1673 three Ming generals who had aided the Qing, Wu Sangui, Geng Jingzhong and Shang Zhixin, controlled large fiefs in the south and west. Against the advice of most of his advisers, Kangxi tried to make them give up their lands, and the result was a rebellion lasting eight years. He relied mainly on Han Chinese Green Standard Army soldiers, granted clemency to common people caught up in the war, and won in 1681. In later years he blamed himself in part for the loss of life.

In 1683 Qing ships under Admiral Shi Lang defeated the Ming loyalist forces of the Kingdom of Tungning off Penghu, and Zheng Keshuang surrendered Taiwan. Border conflicts with the Tsardom of Russia on the Amur ended with the Treaty of Nerchinsk in 1689, which set a border between Russia and China. Against the Dzungar Khanate the emperor campaigned in person. In 1720 a larger expedition took Lhasa from the Dzungars, who had held it for three years.

At court Kangxi ordered the compilation of the Kangxi Dictionary, the Complete Tang Poems and the Complete Classics Collection of Ancient China, and persuaded scholars still loyal to the Ming to work on the dictionary without formally serving the Qing. He welcomed Jesuits such as Ferdinand Verbiest, who ran the imperial observatory, and in 1692 issued an Edict of Toleration for Catholicism. That tolerance ended with the Chinese Rites controversy.

The succession was disputed for years. His son Yinreng was named crown prince at the age of two, but was later deposed, and the princes quarrelled over the throne in what is known as the Nine Lords' War. Kangxi died on 20 December 1722 at the age of 68. According to official records he had summoned seven sons to his bedside, and the fourth prince, Yinzhen, became the Yongzheng Emperor. His reign of 61 years is the longest of any Chinese emperor, and began the High Qing era.
kanhoji-angre: Angre was born at the fort of Suvarnadurg to Ambabai and Tukoji; his father served there under Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj with a command of 200 posts. His origins are disputed. To the British he was of Siddi descent, to Portuguese sources a man of humble birth who had served a Hindu master, and to his family history a Kshatriya Maratha; the Dutch historian Rene Barendse judged that he was most likely a Koli. He grew up among Koli sailors and learned seamanship from them.

Little is known of his early life except that he took part in exploits at sea with his father. His career as a commander began in 1685, when the fort commander of Suvarnadurg tried to defect to the Siddi of Janjira. The young Angre seized the fort and captured him, and Chhatrapati Sambhaji Maharaj made him its commander.

After the death of Admiral Sidhoji Gujar around 1698 Angre held the Maratha navy together. In the Maratha succession dispute he first backed Tarabai. In 1713 he defeated and captured the Peshwa Bahiroji Pingale, sent against him by Shahu, and took the forts of Lohagad and Rajmachi. Balaji Vishwanath then negotiated terms: Angre released the Peshwa and pledged allegiance to Shahu, and received ten forts, sixteen fortified posts and the titles Vizarat Mal and Sarkhel.

From Vijaydurg, where a dockyard built and armed his ships, and from Kolaba at Alibaug, he controlled the coast from Sawantwadi to Mumbai. His fleet of grabs and gallivats was manned by Koli, Bhandari and Kharvi seamen, with Europeans, generally Dutch, commanding his best vessels. On 4 November 1712 his ships took the yacht Algerine of William Aislabie, governor of Bombay, releasing it on 13 February 1713 for 30,000 rupees. Governor Charles Boone's attacks on Vijaydurg and Khanderi failed, as did a joint Portuguese and British expedition of 29 November 1721 under Commander Thomas Mathews, and a Dutch attack on Vijaydurg in 1724.

Angre died on 4 July 1729; his tomb stands at Alibag. His son Sekhoji kept up the war at sea until his death in 1733, after which the holdings were divided between Sambhaji and Manaji. The family's power on the coast ended in February 1756, when the East India Company and the Peshwa Balaji Bajirao took Gheriah and captured Tulaji. The Western Naval Command of the Indian Navy was named INS Angre in his honour on 15 September 1951.
kanishka: Kanishka belonged to the Kushan dynasty and was a descendant of Kujula Kadphises, who founded the Kushan Empire. The Rabatak inscription lists his line: Kujula Kadphises was his great-grandfather, Vima Taktu his grandfather and Vima Kadphises his father. He was of Yuezhi ethnicity, and his native language was probably Tocharian.

Earlier scholars believed he took the throne in 78 CE and that this year began the Saka calendar era. Historians no longer regard it as the date of his accession, and Falk estimates that he came to the throne in 127 CE.

Kanishka's empire extended from southern Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, north of the Amu Darya, to northern India as far as Mathura, and it included Kashmir, where the town of Kanishkapur still contains the base of a large stupa. The Rabatak inscription claims that he held Pataliputra, and a Buddhist text known through a Chinese translation of 472 refers to his conquest of that city. His hold over Central Asia is less well established, although several of his coins have been found in the Tarim Basin.

Around 127 he replaced Greek with Bactrian as the official language of administration. His early coins carry Greek legends and Greek deities such as Helios and Selene, while later coins carry Bactrian legends and Iranian deities such as Mithra and Nana. Both are written in a modified Greek script with an extra letter for the sound sh.

Kanishka never converted to Buddhism but gave it royal sponsorship. Buddhist tradition says he presided over the 4th Buddhist Council in Kashmir, with Vasumitra and Ashwaghosha, and holds that he was close to the scholar Ashvaghosha. He encouraged both the Gandhara school of Greco-Buddhist art and the art of Mathura. His coins with Buddhist figures are rare, well under one percent of the total.

His chief Buddhist monument was the Kanishka Stupa at Puruṣapura, now Peshawar. Archaeologists who found its base in 1908 and 1909 estimated a diameter of 286 feet, or 87 metres, and Chinese pilgrims such as Xuanzang reported a height of 600 to 700 Chinese feet. The reliquary found beneath it is dated to the first year of his reign in 127 CE, though recent scholars attribute it to his successor Huvishka. Buddhist monks of Gandhara carried Mahayana teachings to China from the middle of the 2nd century, and the Kushan monk Lokaksema, about 178, became the first translator of Mahayana scriptures into Chinese.
kannada: Kannada, like Malayalam and Tamil, is a South Dravidian language and a descendant of Tamil-Kannada, from which it derives its grammar and core vocabulary. Its history is divided into Old Kannada, from 450 to 1200, Middle Kannada from 1200 to 1700, and Modern Kannada from 1700. It has been influenced by Sanskrit and Prakrit and has many Sanskrit loan words.

The earliest Kannada inscriptions date from the middle of the 5th century. The Halmidi inscription, usually dated to about 450, is the earliest well-attested full-length stone inscription in Kannada, and its existence indicates that the language had become an administrative one by then.

Kannada is spoken mainly in Karnataka in south-western India, where it is the official and administrative language, and by minorities in neighbouring states. It had 43.7 million native speakers in India at the 2011 census, and it has been declared a Classical language of India. It is written in the Kannada script, which evolved from the 5th-century Kadamba script. The script is syllabic and almost entirely phonetic, with forty-nine letters. The canonical word order is subject–object–verb.

Kannada was the court language of many dynasties of South India and the Deccan, including the Kadambas, the Western Ganga dynasty, the Rashtrakutas, the Hoysalas and the Vijayanagara Empire. The oldest known literary work is the Kavirājamārga, a work on poetics linked to the Rashtrakuta king Nṛpatuṅga Amoghavarṣa I in about 850. Pampa, regarded as the first poet of Kannada, was one of the three gems of Jaina literature along with Ponna and Ranna.

The vacana tradition of Śaiva devotional writing, with Basavanna, Allama Prabhu and Akka Mahadevi, emerged around the turn of the second millennium in the common language. Between the 13th and 18th centuries literature turned to devotional themes, and the Haridāsas, among them Kanakadāsa and Purandaradāsa, spread bhakti literature through music. Kannada literature has received eight Jnanpith Awards, the most of any Indian language.
kannauj: Archaeological discoveries show that the site was inhabited by the Painted Grey Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware cultures, c. 1200-600 BCE and c. 700-200 BCE. In the Vedic period it is said to have been the capital of the Panchala Kingdom under King Vajrayudha. Under the names Kuśasthala and Kanyakubja it appears in the Mahabharata and the Ramayana and in the work of the grammarian Patanjali (c. 150 BCE).

According to the Valmiki Ramayana it was founded as Mahodaya by King Kushanabha, and it took the name Kanyakubja, 'city of hunchbacked maidens', after the wind god Vayu made Kushanabha's hundred daughters hunchbacks when they refused him. Early Buddhist literature places it on the trade route from Mathura to Varanasi and Rajgir, and the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang visited it.

After the Gupta Empire declined in the 6th century, the Maukhari dynasty of Kannauj broke away and took control of large areas of northern India. Under Emperor Harsha (r. 606 to 647 CE) of the Vardhana dynasty, who made it his capital, it became the foremost city of northern India, a large and prosperous city with many Buddhist monasteries according to Xuanzang. Harsha died without an heir, and Maharaja Yashovarman then seized power.

Between the 8th and 10th centuries the city was the focus of the three-sided struggle between the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Palas and the Rashtrakutas. The Pratihara ruler Vatsaraja defeated Indrayudh and then the Pala ruler Dharmapala, but the Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva took Kannauj, the furthest northern expansion by a South Indian ruler. Nagabhata II later made it the capital of the Gurjara-Pratihara Empire, which became the leading power in northern India in the 9th century.

Mahmud of Ghazni captured it in 1018. Chandradeva founded the Gahadavala dynasty there around 1090, and his grandson Govindachandra raised it to what a source calls unprecedented glory. Muhammad Ghori killed Jayachandra at the Battle of Chandwar in 1193, and the glory of imperial Kannauj is said to have ended with the conquest by Iltutmish. On 17 May 1540 Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun at the Battle of Kannauj.

Kannauj is a city of Uttar Pradesh and the administrative headquarters of its district. It is known as India's perfume capital, with more than 200 distilleries making attars, such as rose, jasmine and khus, by the ancient deg and bhapka method of hydro-distillation in copper stills. Its perfume received a Geographical Indication tag in 2014. It has given its name to the Kannauji dialect, and had a population of 84,862 at the 2011 census.
kannur: Kannur lies on the coast of the Laccadive Sea, 280 kilometres north of Kochi and 146 kilometres south of Mangalore, at an elevation of about one metre on a sandy shore. The city has an 8-kilometre seashore and a 3-kilometre beach at Payyambalam. Its climate is a very wet tropical monsoon one, with heavy rain from the southwest monsoon and an annual average of 3,438 millimetres. At the harbour of Mappila Bay stand St Angelo Fort on one side and the Arakkal palace on the other.

The earliest traces of settlement are rock-cut caves, dolmens and megalithic burial sites of the Neolithic age. In the Sangam period (1st to 5th century CE) a powerful kingdom was based at Ezhimala nearby, and the ancient port of Naura named in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea is identified with Kannur. Kerala Muslim tradition places some of the oldest mosques of the Indian subcontinent in Kannur, Madayi and Dharmadom, linking them to the legend of the Cheraman Perumals.

Kannur was the headquarters of Kolathunadu, one of the four most important dynasties of the Malabar Coast, with the Zamorin of Calicut, the Kingdom of Cochin and the Kingdom of Quilon. In the late medieval period the Arakkal kingdom held rights over the city and the Laccadive Islands. St Angelo Fort was built in 1505 by Dom Francisco de Almeida, the first Portuguese viceroy of India. The Dutch captured it in 1663, it was sold to the Arakkal family in 1772, and the British seized it in 1790.

Kannur served as the East India Company's military headquarters on India's west coast until 1887. Its municipality, formed on 1 November 1866, was one of the first modern municipalities in Kerala. Because the Company preferred Madras and Cochin as its main stations, the town lost much of its earlier standing. Under British rule it was best known for Thalassery pepper.

Kannur is the administrative headquarters of Kannur district and became a municipal corporation in 2015. At the 2011 census its municipal area had 232,486 inhabitants, and the local language is Malayalam. It holds Kerala's only cantonment board and, at Ezhimala, the Indian Naval Academy. The district is the main centre of the ritual art Theyyam, and handloom weaving earned the city the name Manchester of Kerala. Kannur International Airport opened on 9 December 2018.
kano-state: Kano State is in the north of Nigeria. It was created on 27 May 1967 from the former Northern Region and borders Katsina State on the north-west, Jigawa State on the north-east, Bauchi State on the south-east and Kaduna State on the south-west. A part of it became Jigawa State in 1991. The state capital is Kano. The Hausa and Fulani make up most of the population, Hausa is the dominant language, and Hausa and Fulfulde are the official languages. The state observes Sharia law within the framework of the Nigerian constitution. It has 44 local government areas.

The area was the site of several kingdoms and empires. The Kingdom of Kano was centred on Dalla Hill from about 1000 to 1349. In 1349 the Sultanate of Kano was established when Yaji I converted to Islam and became its first sultan. Kurmi Market opened in 1463 and helped the city of Kano become a centre of commercial activity in Hausaland. It is still open, and its importance is reflected in the state's nickname, Centre of Commerce. In the 16th and 17th centuries the sultanate became one of the most powerful Hausa kingdoms.

After the Fulani jihad of 1804 to 1808 the Kano Emirate replaced the sultanate. Emir Ibrahim Dabo made administrative reforms to increase commerce, and leaders encouraged traders to move from Katsina, taking advantage of raids from the Hausa Sultanate of Maradi. The British Empire conquered the Kano Emirate in 1903 and incorporated it into the Northern Nigeria Protectorate. The main ethnic groups in pre-colonial Kano were the Hausa, Fulani, Barebari (Kanuri), Tuareg, Arabs and Nupe.

Kano has many large markets, including Kurmi, Kantin Kwari, Sabon Gari and Dawanau, and many specialise in products such as textiles or grain. The dye industry has contributed to the economy since the 19th century. During the colonial period and for several years after independence, the groundnuts grown in the state were one of the country's major sources of revenue. Millet, cowpeas, sorghum, maize and rice are grown for local use, and groundnuts and cotton for export and industry. Industries include textiles, tanning, footwear, plastics and pharmaceuticals. Attractions include Kurmi Market, Kano's city wall, Gidan Rumfa, the emir's palace, the Kano Museum and Dalla Hill.
kansas: Kansas is a landlocked state on the Great Plains, bordered by Nebraska to the north, Colorado to the west, Oklahoma to the south and Missouri to the east. It is generally considered the geographic centre of the contiguous United States, with Lebanon in Smith County approximately the centre. Its highest point is Mount Sunflower, at 1,231 m. The name comes from the Kansas River, named after the Kansa or Kaw people, and ultimately from the Algonquian term Akansa, which referred to the Quapaw.

Before European colonisation the area was occupied by the Caddoan Wichita and later the Siouan Kaw. In the east, people generally lived in villages along the river valleys, while those in the west were semi-nomadic and hunted large herds of bison. The first European to enter present-day Kansas was the Spanish conquistador Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, who explored the area in 1541. Between 1763 and 1803 the territory was part of Spanish Louisiana. Most of modern Kansas was acquired by the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, and the south-west was ceded after the Mexican–American War in 1848.

From 1812 to 1821 Kansas was part of the Missouri Territory. The Santa Fe Trail crossed it from 1821 to 1880, carrying manufactured goods from Missouri and silver and furs from Santa Fe, and wagon ruts from the trail are still visible in the prairie. The first settlement of non-Indigenous people took place in 1827 at Fort Leavenworth, and settlement quickened in the 1850s during the political wars over slavery.

The Kansas–Nebraska Act officially opened Kansas to settlement in 1854. Conflict then broke out between abolitionist Free-Staters from New England and pro-slavery settlers from neighbouring Missouri over whether it would be a free or a slave state, a period known as Bleeding Kansas. Kansas entered the Union as a free state on 29 January 1861, whence the unofficial nickname The Free State. The Homestead Acts of 1862 brought further settlers, and the cattle trade of the 1870s drew some of the best-known figures of the Wild West to the west of the state. From 1887 Kansas women could vote in city elections and hold certain offices.

Topeka is the capital and Wichita the most populous city, while the largest urban area is the Kansas City metropolitan area, which straddles the border with Missouri. The 2020 census counted 2,937,880 people. Nearly 90 per cent of the land is devoted to agriculture, with wheat, corn, sorghum and soybeans among the main crops, and the state also has a large aerospace industry. Kansas is the setting of Dorothy Gale's home in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900), and its state anthem is Home on the Range, written by Brewster Higley.
kanto-region: The Kantō region is commonly defined as the Greater Tokyo Area together with seven prefectures: Chiba, Gunma, Ibaraki, Kanagawa, Saitama, Tochigi and Tokyo. The Kantō Plain, the largest plain in Japan, makes up just over 45 percent of its land area, and hills and mountains form its land borders. Tokyo Bay is enclosed by the Bōsō and Miura peninsulas, the Arakawa and Edo rivers flow into the bay, and the Kinugawa and Tone rivers reach the Pacific at Inubōsaki. The highest point is Mount Nikkō-Shirane on the border of Tochigi and Gunma. The Sagami Trough, the epicentre of two Kantō earthquakes, passes through Sagami Bay.

The name means east of the barrier, and is generally taken to mean the land east of the Hakone Barrier; its counterpart, Kansai, lies to the west. Kamakura was the political capital of the first military government in Japanese history, the Kamakura shogunate, established by Minamoto no Yoritomo and in power from 1185 to 1333. Its political functions returned to Kyoto in 1392.

In 1591 Tokugawa Ieyasu gave up his five provinces of Mikawa, Tōtōmi, Suruga, Shinano and Kai and moved his soldiers and vassals to eight new provinces in Kantō. The decision was proclaimed on the day Toyotomi Hideyoshi entered Odawara Castle after the Hōjō clan surrendered following the Siege of Odawara of 1590. Ieyasu assigned his premier vassals to large areas of the former Hōjō lands, which historians such as Kawamura read as an effort to bring order to the newly subdued population and to guard against the Satomi clan. Ieyasu made Edo, then an underdeveloped town, his seat of power.

In the Edo period Kantō became a centre of modern development. The Great Kantō earthquake of 1923, in the late Taishō period, claimed more than 100,000 lives and ravaged the Greater Tokyo area. In World War II, Operation Coronet, part of the proposed Allied invasion of Japan, was scheduled to land on the Kantō Plain.

Kantō contains Tokyo, the capital and largest city of Japan, and is the centre of the country's politics and economy. Its population was 43,509,179 at the census of 1 October 2025, more than a third of Japan's total. Rice is the principal crop on the farmed part of the plain, while the zone around Tokyo and Yokohama grows garden produce for the metropolitan market.
kanva-dynasty: The Kanva dynasty, also called the Kanvavamsha, ruled Magadha after it overthrew the Shunga dynasty. Its kings were Brahmins who traced their descent from the sage Saubhari, and the dynasty took its name from the gotra of its first ruler, Vasudeva Kanva. Vasudeva began as a minister of the Shunga emperor Devabhuti, whom he assassinated before taking the throne.

He allowed the Shunga kings to go on ruling in obscurity in a corner of their former dominions. Puranic literature places the Kanva court in Pataliputra, the former Shunga capital, but their coins are found mainly in and around Vidisha in Central India, which had also been the seat of the later Shungas.

There were four Kanva rulers. Vasudeva was succeeded by his son Bhumimitra, who ruled for fourteen years. Coins bearing the legend Bhumimitra have been found in the Panchala region, and copper coins marked Kanvasya have turned up at Vidisha and at Kaushambi in the Vatsa realm. Bhumimitra's son Narayana ruled for twelve years, and Narayana's son Susharman was the last king.

According to the Puranas, the Satavahanas brought the dynasty to an end, and they name Balipuccha, founder of the Andhra dynasty, as the killer of the last king. Numismatic and archaeological evidence does not support this account. Scholars regard the defeat by the Satavahanas as a local event in Central India. After it the Magadha empire came to an end, and coin and inscription evidence suggests that Magadha later came under the hegemony of the Mitra dynasty of Kaushambi, which lasted from the 1st century BCE until the 2nd century CE.
kanye: Kanye lies 83 kilometres south-west of Gaborone, on a series of hills that form a natural protective barrier against the sands of the Kalahari Desert. The hills extend into the Bushveld region of South Africa, and the most notable is Kgwakgwe hill. A deep natural gorge, Pharing Gorge, is reputed to have served as a hiding place for villagers during the Mfecane wars of the 19th century. The village also has two natural dams, Mmamokhasi and Mmakgodumo.

The Ngwaketse, a Tswana people, first settled the area in the 1790s under their paramount chief Makaba, who moved his people to Kanye after losing a battle to the neighbouring Kwena and fortified the existing hill with stone walls. Around 1798 an alliance of Rolong and Griquas attacked Kanye, but the Ngwaketse repelled them and killed their leader. European traders and hunters began visiting in the early 19th century, and began to settle after Gaseitsiwe became chief of the Ngwaketse in 1845.

In June 1854 Robert Moffat passed through on his way to the Matabele and found the town completely destroyed as a result of the wars with the Boers, with the Ngwaketse living in the ruins. By the 1860s it had been rebuilt and was prospering as a trading centre for ivory, skins and ostrich feathers. The London Missionary Society established a formal mission in 1871, and a small British-run police station followed in 1887, two years after the Bechuanaland Protectorate was set up. In 1899, during the Second Boer War, the Ngwaketse allied with the British. In the early 20th century Kanye became the first village in the protectorate to introduce irrigation projects and public standpipes, and an asbestos mine opened in the 1920s.

Kanye is the traditional capital of the Ngwaketse and the administrative centre of the Southern District, and the longest continuously occupied tribal capital in the country. It had a population of 48,028 at the 2022 census. The village is divided into wards, each with a kgosana responsible for its cultural administration. It lies on the A10 road to Gaborone and on the A2 highway, part of the Trans-Kalahari Corridor linking Walvis Bay in Namibia with Pretoria in South Africa. Quett Masire, president of Botswana from 1980 to 1998, was born in Kanye on 24 July 1926 and buried there.
kaolack: Kaolack lies on the north bank of the Saloum River, about 100 kilometres from its mouth, on the N1 road. It is the capital of the Kaolack Region, which borders The Gambia to the south. It is an important regional market town and has a hot semi-arid climate, with a short rainy season and a long dry season. Its neighbourhoods include Léona, which holds much of the city centre, Médina Baye, Saam, Ndorong and Thiofoke, a Serer village that existed before Kaolack and was ruled by the Guelowar dynasty.

Kaolack is the successor city to Kahone, the historic capital of the kingdom of Saloum, which stood about 8 kilometres upriver and was made up of separate neighbourhoods under different dignitaries. Kaolack was one of these. One tradition says it was founded by two brothers of Fulani origin from Macina in Mali, Sega and Massar. Another says that a princess of Baol took shelter there under the Maad Saloum Mbegan Ndour, married him and founded the cult of the Nile monitor, called mbossé in Wolof, the totem of the city.

French interest in the Saloum grew in the early 19th century, when lawful goods were sought to replace the slave trade. By mid-century the kingdom grew peanuts, and with the king's permission the French built a fortified factory on the riverfront at Kaolack, better placed for shipping than Kahone. They laid out a first grid of lots in 1860 in what became the Escale neighbourhood. A rail spur from the port to the Dakar-Niger line in 1911 made the town boom as a peanut processing and export centre, and its population rose from 5,600 in 1925 to 44,000 in 1934.

Kaolack is Senegal's main peanut trading and processing centre, with an oil plant and port at Lyndiane and salt pans across the river. It had 298,904 inhabitants at the 2023 census. It is also a major centre of the Ibrahimiyya branch of the Tijaniyya Sufi order. Allaaji Abdulaay Ñas opened a first major lodge in the Léona neighbourhood in 1910, and his son Ibrahim Niass moved the community to Médina Baye in the early 1930s. The Léona Niassène mosque is one of the largest in Senegal.
kapan: Kapan lies in the narrow valley of the Voghji River on the southeastern slopes of the Zangezur Mountains, between the Bargushat and Meghri ridges, on the northern slopes of Mount Khustup, which at 3,201 metres is the highest peak of the region. Its elevation is 750 to 1,050 metres. The name comes from the Classical Armenian kapan, meaning mountain pass. It later became Ghap'an, which was in use until 1991, when the older form was restored.

The area was first mentioned in the 5th century as a small settlement among the properties of the Siunia dynasty, in the Baghk' canton of Syunik, the ninth province of historic Greater Armenia. Prince Dzagik fortified it in the late 9th and early 10th century, and it became the residence of the Dzagikian princes. By the end of the 10th century Prince Smbat II moved to Kapan and founded the Kingdom of Syunik, proclaiming himself king under the protectorate of the Bagratid Kingdom of Armenia. As its capital Kapan flourished in the 11th century, reaching around 20 thousand inhabitants, mostly Armenians with a prominent Jewish minority, and was a centre of trade, crafts and metallurgy.

In 1103 Seljuk invaders ruined it; the historian Stephen Orbelian says they began their massacres in the Jewish quarter. After the kingdom fell in 1170 Syunik suffered Seljuk, Mongol, Aq Qoyunlu and Kara Koyunlu invasions between the 12th and 15th centuries.

In the early 16th century Kapan became part of the Erivan Province of Safavid Iran. In 1722 the noble families of Syunik united in an Armenian principality of Kapan, and the military leader David Bek began the campaign against the Iranians and the invading Ottoman Turks, helped by thousands of local Armenians including Avan Yuzbashi and Mkhitar Sparapet. The centre of his struggle was the Baghaberd Fortress northwest of Kapan and the Halidzor Fortress, where he died in 1728.

In 1813 Syunik became part of the Russian Empire under the Treaty of Gulistan. In the first half of the 19th century Russian and German engineers and workers came to work in the region's copper mines, and Greek specialists arrived in 1850.

Kapan is a town in southeastern Armenia and the capital of Syunik Province, which was formed in 1995 after Armenia's independence. The town received city status in 1938 and was a major mining and industrial centre of Soviet Armenia, known as Kafan in Russian. It is almost entirely Armenian and its population was 43,190 in 2011. Heritage monuments in the area include the Baghaberd Fortress and a medieval bridge dating from 871.
kapilendra-deva: Accounts of his origins differ. The Madala Panji, the chronicle of the Jagannath Temple in Puri, says he was known as Kapila Rauta, of the Surya Vamsa line, and grazed cattle with a Brahmin named Kasia, who foretold that he would be king after a cobra was seen shading his head as he rested. He later begged near the Vimala Temple at Puri and was adopted by the Eastern Ganga king Bhanudeva after a divine dream. The Raghudevapuram copper plate grant traces the family to his grandfather Kapileswara, a lieutenant in the Ganga army.

He took the throne with support inside the kingdom while Bhanu Deva IV was away on an expedition in the south, and was proclaimed with a Rājyābhiṣēka ceremony at Old Bhubaneswar, starting an era known as Kapilabda. Vassal rulers such as the Matsarvamshi of Oddadi and the Shilavamshis of Nandapur refused to accept him; he put them down by force, and the rebels were suppressed by 1440.

His minister Gopinath Mahapatra met the threat from the Jaunpur Sultanate and drove back the Sultan of Bengal; Gajapati forces then took lands west of the Ganga, including the fort of Gar Mandaran, and Kapilendra took the title Gaudeshwara, Lord of Gauda. In the south a first campaign of 1444 was abandoned, but in 1446 his eldest son Hamvira Deva defeated the Reddis of Rajahmundry, and after August 1453 his army crossed the Krishna and occupied Kondavidu. A victory over the Bahmani forces at Devarakonda in 1458 made Telangana a vassal state.

An invasion of Bidar in 1461 ended in retreat when Husain Sharqi of Jaunpur invaded Odisha. Hamvira Deva took the capital of Vijayanagara and made Mallikarjuna Raya pay yearly tribute, and inscriptions at Shrirangam say he advanced as far as Tiruchirappalli, Thanjavur and Arcot.

Kapilendra called himself Routaray, the servant-king of Jagannath. He enlarged the Puri temple, built its two concentric walls, the Kurma Prachira and Meghanada Prachira, and began the Chandan Jatra festival, while also building the Kapilesvara Temple in Bhubaneswar. He wrote a Sanskrit play, Parshuram Bijaya. Under him Odia was used as an administrative language and the poet Sarala Das wrote the Odia Mahabharata. He reduced taxes and warned his officials that injustice would be punished with exile.
kapp-putsch: The Kapp Putsch, or Kapp-Lüttwitz Putsch, aimed to undo the German Revolution of 1918-1919, overthrow the Weimar Republic and set up an autocratic government. Right-wing nationalist and militarist circles opposed the republic and promoted the stab-in-the-back myth, which held that civilians had undermined an undefeated army. Under the Treaty of Versailles, in force from 10 January 1920, Germany had to reduce its land forces to 100,000 men, although in early 1919 more than 250,000 men were enlisted in the volunteer Freikorps. On 29 February 1920 Defence Minister Gustav Noske ordered the disbandment of two of the most powerful of them, the Marinebrigade Loewenfeld and the Marinebrigade Ehrhardt.

Hermann Ehrhardt, commander of his Marinebrigade of 5,000 to 6,000 men, declared that it would refuse dissolution, and General Walther von Lüttwitz said he would not accept its loss. On 10 March Lüttwitz demanded of President Friedrich Ebert the dissolution of the National Assembly, new elections and his own appointment as supreme commander. Ebert and Noske refused. Lüttwitz then brought in Wolfgang Kapp, Erich Ludendorff and others, and Ehrhardt's brigade marched on Berlin from the evening of 12 March. Noske asked the senior commanders to defend the government buildings and was turned down. General Hans von Seeckt is reported to have said that Reichswehr does not fire on Reichswehr.

The cabinet fled and called a general strike, and the brigade reached the Brandenburger Tor within minutes of its departure. Kapp declared himself Chancellor and Lüttwitz became Minister of Defence. There was no military resistance, but the strike, which began in Berlin on 14 March and spread over the Reich, involved up to 12 million workers. Gas, water and power stopped in Berlin, civil servants refused to cooperate, and the putsch collapsed on 17 March. Lüttwitz resigned on 18 March. As the Marinebrigade left Berlin it fired machine guns on a hostile crowd, killing twelve civilians. Kapp fled to Sweden in April and Lüttwitz to Hungary.

The putsch led to violence elsewhere. In the Ruhr a Red Ruhr Army of about 50,000 workers rose against the republic, and the Reichswehr and Freikorps suppressed it in early April, killing over 1,000 workers, many in summary executions. In Mecklenburg-Schwerin 91 people died in violence tied to the putsch. Most putschists received an amnesty: of 705 cases against civilians only that of Traugott von Jagow ended in a guilty verdict. Noske was forced to resign on 22 March. The election of the first republican Reichstag was brought forward to 6 June 1920, and these events polarised the electorate and shifted the majority.
kapuas-river: The Kapuas rises near the centre of Borneo, between the western slope of the Müller Mountain Range and the southern slope of the Upper Kapuas Range. It runs for about 165 kilometres through mountainous country and then falls only 50 metres over the 902 kilometres from Putussibau to the delta. Its basin covers more than two thirds of West Kalimantan. A second river of the same name rises on the other side of the Müller Mountain Range and flows south to join the Barito.

Some 350 kilometres from its source a group of lakes, among them Luar, Sentarum and Belida, lies beside the river and is linked to it by many channels. When monthly rainfall exceeds about 300 millimetres the river overflows into the lakes at up to 1,000 cubic metres a second, which prevents heavy flooding downstream. The delta has five arms, of which the northernmost, the Big Kapuas, is the widest, and silt extends 50 to 60 kilometres from the coast. Pontianak lies on the equator near the delta.

The river is the main waterway connecting the centre of the island with its western coast. It is up to 27 metres deep, and ships drawing three metres can reach Sintang, 465 kilometres from the mouth, while those drawing two metres can reach Putussibau. Logging and the rafting of timber take place along its length, and fishing is common near the lakes and the delta. The largest tributary is the Melawi, which joins near Sintang; others are the Landak, Sekayam, Ketungau, Tawang, Bunut and Embaloh.

The climate is warm and very humid, with annual rainfall between 2,863 and 5,517 millimetres, and the discharge peaks in April and November, when the level can rise ten to twelve metres overnight. The river has about 300 fish species, more than any other river basin in Indonesia, a diversity partly explained by a link some 6,000 years ago, when it was a tributary of the Sunda River, with the rivers of Sumatra, Java and the Malay Peninsula. Two national parks, Betung Kerihun and Danau Sentarum, lie on its banks.
kapudan-pasha: The Kapudan Pasha, also called the Kapudan-ı Derya or Captain of the Sea, was the grand admiral of the Ottoman Navy. The title itself is attested only from 1567 onwards; earlier names for the supreme commander of the fleet include Derya Bey, bey of the sea, and Re'is Kapudan, head captain. The Oxford English Dictionary regards kapudan as a form of the Italian capitano, and pasha comes from the Persian padishah.

The rank of Derya Bey began under Bayezid I, who reigned from 1389 to 1402. After the conquest of Constantinople in 1453, Mehmed II raised Baltaoğlu Süleyman Bey to sanjak bey for his efforts against the Byzantines in the Golden Horn, giving him the sanjak of Gallipoli, the principal naval base, and the districts of Galata and İzmit, whose tax consisted of ship timber.

The success of Hayreddin Barbarossa raised the Kapudan Pasha to the ranks of beylerbey and vizier in 1535, with territories expanded into the Eyalet of the Archipelago and Algiers. His successors held these lands but fell to the rank of two-horsetail vizier for several centuries. The Kapudan Pasha usually worked from Galata and Gallipoli in winter and sailed annually in summer. His official residence was in the Divankhane in the Imperial Arsenal on the Golden Horn, though he was often away, as governing the Eyalet of the Archipelago meant visiting its provinces in person every year.

Beyond naval command he held gubernatorial authority over most of the Aegean islands, responsible for their administration, tax collection and shipbuilding resources. In the 17th century Evliya Çelebi reported an annual income of 885,000 silver akçe, and leasing Aegean islands to tax farmers added about 300,000 kuruş in the 18th and 19th centuries.

The post's heyday was the 16th century, when a succession of capable holders brought Ottoman naval power to its height and for a time secured Ottoman supremacy in the Mediterranean. In theory only a serving admiral, a chief of the Imperial Arsenal or at least the sanjak bey of Rhodes could hold it, but from the turn of the 17th century the appointment of court favourites and people without military or naval experience marked the beginning of Ottoman naval decline.

The Tanzimat reforms reduced the Eyalet of the Archipelago in rank and in 1848 gave its governance to the wali of Rhodes, leaving the Kapudan Pashas solely military servicemen. A total of 161 captains served until 13 March 1867, when the post was abolished and replaced by ministers of the Ottoman Naval Ministry.
kapunda: Kapunda lies on the Light River near the Barossa Valley. Quarries near the town yield marble from dark blue to white, used to face Parliament House in Adelaide. A railway from Adelaide opened in 1860 and was extended to Eudunda and Morgan in 1878, and the Corporate Town of Kapunda was established in 1865. Local firms made farm and mining machinery, and the pastoralist Sidney Kidman, who once owned 68 properties, lived in the town and held annual horse sales there.

Francis Dutton and Charles Bagot, who both ran sheep in the area, found outcrops of copper ore in 1842 and bought 80 acres around them. Surface ore was removed early in 1844, and by the end of that year mining had gone underground. The ore was first shipped to Swansea in Wales, but Welsh smelters later came to South Australia and it was smelted locally by 1851. A steam pumping engine was installed in 1847 and replaced by a larger one in 1851.

Work stopped in 1851 under the impact of the Victorian gold rush and resumed in 1855. In 1865 a Scottish company leased the mine, switched to open-cut methods and replaced smelting with the cooking of the ore with salt to make copper chloride. Copper prices fell in 1877 and the mine closed in 1879. The miners were typically Cornish, the labourers Irish and the smelter specialists Welsh, while German farmers had already settled at nearby Bethel. In the 1850s Irish labourers formed a communal settlement of around 500 people at Baker's Flat, in the form of a traditional Irish clachan, and resisted attempts from the 1870s to evict them.

Kapunda had 2,633 people at the 2021 census and produces wheat, barley and oats. Since 1988 its southern entrance has been marked by the 8-metre statue of Map Kernow, a Cornish miner, rebuilt by its creator Ben van Zetten after a fire in 2006. The Kapunda Historical Society runs a museum in the old Baptist Church of 1866.
kapyl: Kapyl is first mentioned in 1274. It was a walled town that was noteworthy by the 14th century and is listed in the atlas of Ortelius of 1574. In the 14th century it belonged to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. In 1395 it passed to Prince Vladimir Olgerdovich and his heirs, the Olelkovich family, who kept it until 1612. It was then part of the dowry of Zofia Olelkowicz Słucka, and one of seven fortified towns left to her husband Janusz Radziwill on her death in 1612. Tatars attacked it numerous times, and it was sacked at least once in the 16th century.

On 27 August 1652 King John II Casimir Vasa granted Kapyl Magdeburg rights and a seal showing a hunting horn on a gold field. He also established local markets and an annual horse and cattle fair. Weaving, including velvet, became established in the 16th century and gave rise to six guilds. Its town rights were confirmed in 1658, 1665 and 1706. After the Second Partition of Poland in 1793 Kapyl became part of the Russian Empire, and from 1832 it was a personal holding of Prince Wittgenstein.

Towards the end of the 19th century Kapyl had over 350 houses and over 2,000 inhabitants, most of them Jewish; by 1900 the Jewish population was 2,671. Its institutions included three schools, churches including a Calvinist church, and two synagogues. In 1924 it became the capital of Kapyl District. In an operation named Erntefest II, which ended in February 1943 and was officially aimed at Soviet partisans, German forces killed 2,325 inhabitants of the Slutsk-Kapyl area against six German soldiers lost. A 19th-century church is among the district's major monuments. Kapyl is the administrative centre of Kapyl District in the Minsk Region of Belarus, and has a sister city in Joniškis, Lithuania.
kaqchikel-people: Kaqchikel tradition tells its political history as a series of dawns (saqarik), each a step away from dependence on other groups, above all the K'iche'. In the first, the Kaqchikel formed an alliance with the K'iche', kept through the marriage of Kaqchikel men and K'iche' women; in the second they and their allies moved to present-day Chichicastenango, under K'iche' rule. In the third, the K'iche' allowed the Kaqchikel elite a government of their own, and around 1430 they founded their first capital, Chi Awär. The fourth dawn brought independence and the founding of Iximche around 1470.

Like the neighbouring K'iche', the Kaqchikel of Iximché were governed by four lords, Tzotzil, Xahil, Tucuché and Acajal, responsible for administrative, military and religious affairs. The Acajal, also known as Chajoma, kept their political autonomy, and the ruins of Mixco Viejo have been identified as their capital. The Kaqchikel recorded their history in the Annals of the Cakchiquels, also called the Memorial de Sololá.

As enemies of the K'iche' Kingdom, the Kaqchikel helped the Spaniards conquer it, and Pedro de Alvarado took Iximché in 1524. The first colonial capital of Guatemala, Tecpán Guatemala, was founded near Iximché on 25 July 1524; after several Kaqchikel uprisings it was moved to Ciudad Vieja, near Antigua Guatemala, on 22 November 1527.

The Kaqchikel are Guatemala's third largest Maya group, about one sixth of its Maya population. They live mainly in the departments of Sololá, Chimaltenango, Sacatepéquez, Guatemala, Baja Verapaz and Escuintla, and there are communities in the state of Chiapas in Mexico and, after recent migrations, in Campeche. Their language belongs to the Quichean branch of the Mayan languages and is closely related to the Tzutujil language. Kaqchikel migrants to the United States, where they are usually counted as Latino or Hispanic, often keep their language, food, clothing and customs, and some reject a Latino identity for their Indigenous one.
kara-khanid-khanate: The Kara-Khanid Khanate grew from a confederation formed in the 9th century by Karluks, Yagmas, Chigils, Tuhsi and other peoples living in Zhetysu, the western Tian Shan and western Xinjiang around Kashgar. The Karluks were nomads from the western Altai Mountains who, by 766, had forced the Turgesh to submit and made Suyab on the Chu their capital. At the end of the 8th century they converted to the Church of the East. The date of its foundation and the name of its first khan are uncertain. By one reconstruction the first ruler was Bilge Kul Qadir Khan. Its history is reconstructed from fragmentary and often contradictory written sources and from studies of coinage.

In the mid-10th century the Kara-Khanids converted to Islam and adopted Muslim names while keeping Turkic titles such as Khan and Ilek. Between 990 and 992 Hasan Bughra Khan took Bukhara, though he died in 992 and the Samanids returned. By 999 Nasr, son of Ali, had taken Samarkand and Bukhara. The Samanid lands were divided between the Ghaznavids, who gained Khorasan and Afghanistan, and the Karakhanids, who received Transoxiana, so that the Oxus became the boundary.

The state was divided into appanages centred on Balasagun, Kashgar, Uzgen and Samarkand, and internal warfare led to a formal split into Eastern and Western khanates in the 1040s. In 1089 the Seljuks took Samarkand, and the Western Khanate was their vassal for about half a century. In 1141 the Qara Khitai defeated the Seljuk Sultan Ahmad Sanjar and the Kara-Khanids at the Battle of Qatwan near Samarkand. The Karakhanids stayed in power as Qara Khitai vassals, serving as tax collectors in Samarkand and Kashgar. In 1212 the Khwarazmshah Muhammad executed the Western ruler Uthman and extinguished the Western Khanate, and the Eastern line ended when rebels killed Prince Yusuf in Kashgar in 1211.

The court language at Kashgar and other centres, called Khaqani, remained Turkic, though court culture was almost entirely Persian. Mahmud al-Kashgari wrote the first comprehensive dictionary of Turkic languages, the Dīwānu l-Luġat al-Turk, in Arabic in 1072-76, and Yusuf Balasaghuni wrote the Kutadgu Bilig, a work of advice for princes. Ibrahim Tamghach Khan founded the earliest known madrasa in Central Asia, at Samarkand. The Kalyan minaret in Bukhara, built by Muhammad Arslan Khan, survives. Rulers used titles such as Tamghaj Khan, meaning Khan of China, and the Cambridge World History describes the state as the first of the Islamic Turco-Iranian states.
kara-koyunlu: The Qara Qoyunlu, or Black Sheep Turkomans, were a Turkoman, culturally Persianate, Muslim dynasty that ruled from about 1374 to 1468. Their name means those with black sheep, probably from a black sheep painted on their flags. The ruling family descended from the Baharlu branch of the Yıwa tribe of the Oghuz Turks, which held territory north of Lake Van and Mosul by the fourteenth century. Other tribes of the confederation included the Saadlu, the Karamanlu, the Dukharlu and the Jagirlu. The Oghuz dialect they spoke is connected by a number of researchers with the Azerbaijani language.

The Qara Qoyunlu became vassals of the Jalayirid Sultanate from about 1375. In 1400 Timur defeated them, and Qara Yusuf fled to the Mamluk Sultanate in Egypt. Released after Timur's death in 1405, he defeated the Timurid Abu Bakr at the Battle of Nakhchivan on 14 October 1406 and, on 20 April 1408, Miran Shah at Sardrud. The conquest of Tabriz and the execution of Shaykh Uways Jalayir in 1410 secured independence, and in the same year the Qara Qoyunlu took Baghdad and Armenia. After Qara Yusuf died in 1420 the Timurid Shah Rukh defeated his son Qara Iskander, and in 1436 made Jahan Shah, Iskander's brother, his vassal.

Jahan Shah was crowned on 19 April 1438 and became independent after Shah Rukh's death in 1447. He took Sultaniya, Hamadan and Qazvin, and in 1452–1453 Isfahan, Shiraz and Yazd; in 1458 he occupied Herat for some months. His reign was troubled by rebellious sons. In 1466 his attempt to take Diyarbakır from the Aq Qoyunlu failed, and he died in the Battle of Chapakchur in 1467. By 1468 the Aq Qoyunlu under Uzun Hasan had defeated the Qara Qoyunlu and conquered Iraq, Azerbaijan and western Iran. Armenian sources record heavy taxes, devastation and captivity under Iskander and Jahan Shah, though Jahan Shah approved the move of the Catholicos's seat to Etchmiadzin in 1441.

The state's organisation followed that of the Jalayirids and the Ilkhanids, and Persian was the language of diplomacy, poetry and court. Jahan Shah wrote poetry in Azerbaijani and Persian. His buildings include the northern iwan of the Darb-e Imam in Isfahan, from 1453, and the Blue Mosque in Tabriz, completed in 1465, whose tilework may have influenced the later blue-and-white tiles of Mamluk and Ottoman buildings. His son Pir Budaq, governor of Fars and Baghdad, was active in the making of refined manuscripts. Sultan Quli, founder of the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda, and Bairam Khan of the Mughal service belonged to the Qara Qoyunlu.
kara-mustafa-pasha: Kara Mustafa Pasha was of Turkish origin, the son of a sipahi, a cavalryman, and was born in the village of Mirince near Merzifon. He was brought up in the household of the Köprülü family, who were of Albanian origin, and was educated by Köprülü Mehmed Pasha and married into the family. Within the household he served as letter-carrier to the grand vizier and as armourer, and then entered the sultan's household as master of the horse. European observers described him as greedy and intransigent, though some, such as the Dutch agent Colyer, found him agreeable at first. He also made many enemies in the Ottoman army and palace.

In 1659 he became governor of Silistria. Within ten years he was acting as deputy for his brother-in-law, the grand vizier Köprülüzade Fazıl Ahmed Pasha, when the latter was absent from court. As commander of ground troops in a war against Poland he negotiated a settlement with John Sobieski in 1676 that added the province of Podolia to the empire. When Fazıl Ahmed Pasha died in the same year, Kara Mustafa succeeded him as grand vizier.

He then led campaigns against the Tsardom of Russia to support the Cossack state, an Ottoman vassal, and placed Ottoman garrisons in many cities in Ukraine. He took the fortress of Chigirin and fought Grigory Romodanovsky on the Dnieper between 14 and 20 August. Neither commander won decisively, and logistical difficulties on the steppe forced Mustafa to withdraw. After the battle he took the fortress of Kaniv by siege.

In 1683 Kara Mustafa marched north into Austria, on his own initiative and without the knowledge of Sultan Mehmed IV; his army lacked heavy siege cannon. By mid-July about 100,000 men were besieging Vienna, which was held by some 10,000 Habsburg soldiers, and by September he had taken part of the walls. On 12 September 1683 a Polish army under King John III Sobieski won the Battle of Vienna with a flank attack by its Winged Hussars. The Ottomans retreated into Hungary, much of which was later conquered by the Habsburgs and their Holy League allies.

Mehmed IV ordered him executed, and on 25 December 1683 he was strangled with a silk cord at Belgrade. Historians describe him as either a capable tactician or a reckless commander. His birthplace was renamed Karamustafapaşa in his honour.
karabakh: Karabakh extends from the highlands of the Lesser Caucasus down to the lowlands between the rivers Kura and Aras. It is usually divided into Highland Karabakh, Lowland Karabakh (the steppes between the two rivers) and the eastern slopes of the Zangezur Mountains. No official designation fixes the whole of its extent. Its widest historical bounds are those of the Karabakh Khanate of the 18th century, which ran from the Zangezur Mountains along the Aras to its meeting with the Kura, and north along the Kura as far as what is now the Mingachevir reservoir.

The name Karabakh is first recorded in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries in Georgian and Persian sources, and became common after the Mongol conquest of the 1230s. It is generally believed to combine the Turkic kara, black, with the Iranian bagh, garden, though other explanations have been proposed, including kara in the sense of large. Place names in the region form several layers, Turkic, Armenian, Iranian and Russian, and for centuries sedentary Armenians and nomadic Turkic and Kurdish herders used two overlapping sets of names for the same places.

The region is believed to have been conquered by the Kingdom of Armenia in the 2nd century BCE and organised as parts of the provinces of Artsakh, Utik and southern Syunik. After the partition of Armenia by Rome and Persia in 387 CE, Artsakh and Utik became part of the Caucasian Albanian satrapy of Sassanian Persia. After the Arab invasions several Armenian princes established their dominance in the highlands, ruling as vassals through the House of Khachen and later the Melikdoms of Karabakh. From the 11th century Oghuz Turkic tribes settled the region and moved between winter pastures in the lowlands and summer pastures in the highlands.

The Abbasid Caliphate, Bagratid Armenia, the Mongol Ilkhanate, the Jalayirid Sultanates, the Qara Qoyunlu, the Aq Qoyunlu and Safavid Iran held the highlands in turn between 821 and the early nineteenth century. The Ottoman Empire ruled Karabakh in 1578–1605 and again in 1723–1736. In 1747 Panah Ali Khan, a chieftain of the Javanshir clan, seized control after the death of Nader Shah and founded the Karabakh Khanate. Qajar Iran re-established its rule several years later, and the region then passed to the Russian Empire under the Treaty of Gulistan, with Shusha as its most prominent city.

After 1917 Karabakh was disputed between the new republics of Armenia and Azerbaijan, and in 1921 the Bolsheviks decided it would remain within Soviet Azerbaijan. In 1923 the Armenian-inhabited highlands became the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast. In February 1988 its Supreme Soviet voted to unite with Armenia, and a war followed after the Soviet Union's collapse. A further war in 2020 ended with a ceasefire signed on 10 November 2020.
karabakh-movement: Nagorno-Karabakh was the only autonomous region of the Soviet Union whose ethnic majority matched that of a neighbouring republic but which was not allowed to join it. Its Armenians complained of economic neglect, the closing of churches and schools, limits on teaching Armenian history and the settling of Azerbaijanis in the region; their share of its population fell from 84.4% in 1959 to 76% twenty years later. In periods of change, as in 1945, 1965 and 1977, they petitioned Moscow for transfer to Soviet Armenia, and in August 1987 some 75,000 Armenians signed a petition to Mikhail Gorbachev.

The movement is traditionally dated from a demonstration in Stepanakert on 13 February 1988. On 20 February the Soviet of the autonomous oblast voted 110 to 17 to ask for the region's transfer to Armenia, which the journalist Thomas de Waal called truly revolutionary, and crowds in Yerevan's Theater Square doubled day by day. In March activists in Karabakh founded Krunk, which used strikes as a political weapon, and the Karabakh Committee of intellectuals was formed in Yerevan in May.

Moscow refused to change the borders: the Presidium of the USSR Supreme Soviet rejected the transfer in July 1988. The Sumgait pogrom of 27–29 February 1988 was followed by violence in Kirovabad that November and in Baku in January 1990. After the Armenian earthquake of 7 December 1988 the members of the Karabakh Committee were arrested and taken to Moscow; they were freed on 31 May 1989. In January 1989 Moscow placed the region under a special administration answerable to the central government.

The committee's following became the Pan-Armenian National Movement, which won a majority in the parliamentary election of 20 May 1990. Levon Ter-Petrosyan was elected chairman of the Supreme Council on 4 August 1990, and Armenia declared independence on 23 August. In 1991 Soviet and Azerbaijani forces deported Armenian villagers in Operation Ring, the Nagorno-Karabakh Republic was proclaimed on 2 September, and in November Azerbaijan voted to abolish the region's autonomy. By 1992 the conflict had become the First Nagorno-Karabakh War.

About 350,000 Armenians fled Azerbaijan, and some 167,000 Azerbaijanis left Armenia from the autumn of 1988. Armenians regard the movement as a struggle for national liberation, and it was the largest public mobilisation in the Soviet Union since the 1920s.
karachay-cherkessia: Karachay-Cherkessia lies on the slopes of the north-western Caucasus, stretching 140 kilometres from north to south and 170 kilometres from east to west, and mountains cover 80 per cent of its territory. Mount Elbrus, at 5,642 metres the highest peak in the Caucasus, stands on its border with Kabardino-Balkaria. The republic borders Krasnodar Krai, Stavropol Krai, Kabardino-Balkaria and Georgia. A total of 172 rivers flow through it, the largest being the Kuban, the Bolshoy Zelenchuk, the Maly Zelenchuk, the Urup and the Laba, and it has about 130 glacial mountain lakes.

The Karachay-Cherkess Autonomous Oblast was founded on 12 January 1922, in the early years of the Soviet Union. On 26 April 1926 it was divided into the Karachay Autonomous Oblast and the Cherkess National Okrug, which became an autonomous oblast in 1928. In November 1943 the Karachay Autonomous Oblast was abolished; the Karachay were accused of collaboration with the Nazis and 70,000 of them were deported to the Kazakh and Uzbek republics. Most of their territory was divided between Stavropol Krai and the Georgian SSR, and the remaining area, populated by the Cherkess, remained the Cherkess Autonomous Oblast.

On 9 January 1957, after the rehabilitation of the Karachay, the Cherkess oblast was merged with the restored Karachay territory in the former borders of the Karachay-Cherkess Autonomous Oblast. It became an Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic on 3 July 1991. In January 1992 Boris Yeltsin was prepared to accept its division, and a commission on forming three autonomous regions, Karachay, Cherkess and Batalpashinsk, was set up. According to official results a referendum on 28 March 1992 produced a majority against splitting, and on 9 December 1992 the republic was recognised as the Karachay-Cherkess Republic.

The Karachay-Cherkess Republic is one of Russia's ethnic republics, in the North Caucasian Federal District, with its capital at Cherkessk. The Karachays, a Caucasian Turkic people, form the largest group, followed by Russians, Cherkess and Abazins. It has five official languages: Russian, Abaza, Cherkess (Kabardian), Karachay-Balkar and Nogai. At the Special Astrophysical Observatory on the Zelenchuk River stands the BTA-6 telescope, the largest in the world from 1975 until 1993, and the large radio telescope RATAN-600.
karachi: Karachi lies on the coastline of Sindh province in southern Pakistan, along the Karachi Harbour, a natural harbour on the Arabian Sea. It is built on a coastal plain with scattered rocky outcroppings, hills and marshlands, and mangrove forests grow in the brackish waters around the harbour and farther south-east towards the Indus River Delta. West of the city is Cape Monze, known locally as Ras Muari, an area of sea cliffs, sandstone promontories and beaches. Two small ranges, the Khasa Hills and the Mulri Hills, lie within the city in the north-west. They are barren, part of the larger Kirthar Range, and reach a maximum height of 528 metres.

The region has been inhabited for millennia. Upper Paleolithic and Mesolithic sites have been excavated in the Mulri Hills on the northern outskirts, and their earliest inhabitants are believed to have been hunter-gatherers who left ancient flint tools. The region is believed to have been known to the ancient Greeks and may have been the site of Barbarikon, an ancient seaport at the nearby mouth of the Indus. Karachi may also be the place called Ramya in ancient Greek texts.

The modern city was reputedly founded in 1729 as the fortified village of Kolachi-jo-Goth during the rule of the Kalhora dynasty, said to be named in honour of Mai Kolachi, whose son slew a man-eating crocodile. The shortened name Karachee was first used in a Dutch report of 1742 about a shipwreck near the settlement. The village greatly increased in importance with the arrival of the East India Company in the mid-19th century, following the annexation of Sindh. The colonial administration began substantial projects to turn it into a major seaport and to connect it to the railway network of South Asia.

At independence in 1947 Karachi was the largest city in Sindh, with an estimated 400,000 people and a slim Hindu majority. After the partition of British India, hundreds of thousands of Muslim refugees arrived from India while nearly all its Hindu residents left. Karachi served as the federal capital of Pakistan from 1947 to 1959 and grew rapidly, attracting migrants from across the country and other parts of South Asia.

Karachi is the capital of Sindh and the largest city in Pakistan, with about 20 million people according to the census of 2023. It contains the country's two largest seaports, the Port of Karachi and Port Qasim, and its busiest airport, Jinnah International Airport. It is one of the most linguistically, ethnically and religiously diverse cities in Pakistan. Among its landmarks are Frere Hall, Empress Market and St. Patrick's Cathedral, which brought the first neo-Gothic buildings to the city, and Wazir Mansion, the birthplace of Muhammad Ali Jinnah, now a museum.
karad: Karad lies at the confluence of the Koyna and Krishna rivers, known as the Pritisangam; both rivers rise at Mahabaleshwar, about 100 km away. The town stands at an average elevation of 566 metres, 302 km from Mumbai, 162 km from Pune and 74 km from Sangli. National Highway 48 runs through it, and its railway station lies about 4 km from the town on the line from Mumbai to Miraj, Sangli and Kolhapur.

The town was originally called Karhatak, meaning elephant market. According to the Mahabharata, Sahadeva, one of the Pandavas, lived there, and local tradition holds that Lord Rama set foot on its land. About five kilometres to the southwest are the Karad Caves, also called the Agashiv Caves, which contain early Buddhist symbols.

The first capital of the Shilaharas was probably at Karad during the reign of Jatiga II, as their copper plate grant of Miraj and Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita show, and they are sometimes called the Shilaharas of Karad. Their capital later moved to Kolhapur. Among the Shilaharas of Kolhapur, Gonka is described as the Lord of Karhad, Miraj and Konkan. Near the town stands a mosque built by Sultan Ali Adilshah, who reigned from 1557 to 1580.

Karad is known as the sugar bowl of Maharashtra for the many sugar factories around it and is an educational centre of western Maharashtra; the Government College of Engineering was founded there in 1960. The 2011 census counted 74,355 people in the town and its surrounding villages, most of whom are Hindu and speak Marathi. The samadhi of Yashwantrao Chavan, the first chief minister of Maharashtra, stands at the rivers' confluence, and the town hosted the 76th Akhil Bharatiya Marathi Sahitya Sammelan in 2003.
karadorde: Đorđe Petrović was born on 14 November 1768 in the village of Viševac in the Šumadija region of Ottoman Serbia, the eldest of five children in an impoverished family. His father had been a highwayman, or hajduk, in his youth and was by then a peasant farmer. Like most of his contemporaries Petrović was illiterate. He worked as a shepherd in adolescence and in 1785 married Jelena Jovanović; they had seven children, six of whom reached adulthood. In 1787 the family settled in the Habsburg monarchy, fearing persecution by Ottoman janissaries.

After the Austro-Turkish War of 1788–1791 began he joined the Serbian Free Corps, a volunteer militia armed and trained by the Austrians, was decorated for bravery and rose to sergeant. The Treaty of Sistova of 1791 returned the captured territory to the Ottomans, and the rebels were crushed by 1792. He took refuge again in Austria, then returned to Šumadija as a livestock merchant.

In January and February 1804 renegade janissaries known as Dahis killed between 70 and 150 Serbian chieftains. Karađorđe, who narrowly escaped, was unanimously elected leader of the uprising by the surviving chiefs that February, and held the title of Grand Vožd from 14 February 1804 to 3 October 1813. Within six months most Dahi leaders were captured and executed. The rebels beat Ottoman regulars at Ivankovac in August 1805, and by 1806 held all the major towns of the Pashalik, including Belgrade, and expelled their Muslim inhabitants. Muslims, combatants and non-combatants alike, were killed.

He was feared for a volatile temper and, according to the military historian Brendon A. Rehm, personally killed 125 people. In 1806 he ordered his own brother Marinko hanged. He refused the extensive autonomy offered by Selim III because Russia had promised to aid the rebels. Infighting and Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 weakened them, and he fled Serbia in October 1813.

Austria arrested him and handed him over to the Russians, who gave him refuge in Bessarabia. He returned to Serbia in secret in July 1817 and was killed shortly afterwards by agents of Miloš Obrenović, who feared that his reappearance would make the Ottomans renege on concessions agreed after the Second Serbian Uprising of 1815. The murder began a decades-long feud between the Karađorđević and Obrenović houses, ended in June 1903 when officers killed King Alexander Obrenović and Karađorđe's grandson Peter Karađorđević took the throne.
karaikal: Karaikal is a port city and the administrative headquarters of Karaikal District, the second-largest city in the Union Territory of Puducherry after Pondicherry.
