It lies at the centre of a small coastal enclave, bounded on the north by Mayiladuthurai district, on the south by Nagapattinam district and on the west by Tiruvarur district, all in Tamil Nadu, and on the east by the Bay of Bengal. The enclave is flat, covered by a thick mantle of alluvium and by the distributaries of the Kaveri, whose branches, among them the Arasalar, supply its irrigation.
The origin of the name is uncertain. The Imperial Gazetteer of British India gives it as fish pass, and another suggestion is a canal built of lime mix, though no trace of such a canal survives.

In 1738 Sayaji, the exiled Rajah of Thanjavur, promised Karaikal to the French in exchange for their help. The transfer took place only in 1739, with the help of Chanda Sahib of Arcot. In 1749 Pratap Singh ceded 81 more villages to the French during their siege of Thanjavur, a grant confirmed by treaty in 1754. The town changed hands several times in the conflicts between the French and the British. On 5 April 1760 British forces captured it after a ten-day defence, defeating the governor Pierre Renault.

Karaikal was restored to French control in 1817, after the Napoleonic Wars, and the French held it, despite occasional British interruptions, until 1954, when it was de facto incorporated into India. With Mahé, Yanaon, Chandernagor and Pondichéry it was integrated de jure in 1962.

Karaikal is known for Karaikal Ammaiyar, a Shaivite saint and Bhakti poetess among the sixty-three nayanmar, who lived there around the 5th century CE. Her temple holds each summer the Mangani, the Mango Festival, the town's main feast, and shares the Chandra Theertham tank with the Kailasanathar and Nithyakalyana Perumal temples. A dargah formed after the death in 1829 of Mastan Saheb, a Bukharan Sufi cleric, and a procession known as Kanduri is held there each year. Agriculture and fishing are the district's main sources of income, along its 26 kilometres of coast. The 2011 census counted 200,222 people in the district.
karakalpaks: The name means black kalpak, or black hat. Many accounts link the Karakalpaks with the Cherniye Klobuki, a Turkic confederation of the 11th century whose name also means black hat in Russian and who were mercenaries of the Kievan Rus; but there is no archaeological or historical evidence for a connection. The Karakalpaks, Uzbeks and Kazakhs are regarded as subgroups of the same Uzbek Confederation, which arose in the 15th century after the Golden Horde collapsed.

Documents from the reign of Abdullah Khan of Bukhara (1583–1598) mention Karakalpaks near Sighnaq on the lower Syr Darya. Recent archaeological evidence suggests that they formed as a confederation of tribes in the late 15th or the 16th century on the Syr Darya or its Zhany Darya outlet, near the Kazakhs of the Lesser Horde, which would explain why their language and customs resemble those of the Kazakhs.

The 18th century was the most difficult time in their political development. Many Kazakh clans became subject to the Kalmyks, and many Karakalpaks fled to the lower Syr Darya. In that century they settled along the lower Amu Darya and in its delta on the southern shore of the Aral Sea. Since 1810 their fate has been closely tied to that of the Khiva Khanate, and under its rule the poor were hired as farm labourers by the rich and by officials. The annexation of the region to Russia did not end exploitation, according to the literature.

About 900,000 Karakalpaks live worldwide, and more than 770,000 of them in Karakalpakstan in north-western Uzbekistan, where Nukus is the capital. They are not the largest group in their homeland, as Uzbeks increasingly outnumber them. Their language belongs to the Kipchak–Nogai group of Turkic languages, with Kazakh and Nogai, and is written in Cyrillic and Latin letters; before the Soviet period it was rarely written, in a modified Perso-Arabic script. Karakalpaks are mainly followers of the Hanafi school of Sunni Islam, and dervish orders such as the Kubrawiya are common.

The oral tradition includes legends of Alexander the Great, Genghis Khan and Dede Korkut, and of fortresses such as Ayaz-Kala. The 19th-century poets Ajiniyaz and Berdakh wrote of the hard life of the people and their dissatisfaction with the feudal order. The drying of the Aral Sea has destroyed the local fishing industry and much of the grazing and farmland in the north of the delta.
karakoram-highway: The Karakoram Highway, also called the KKH, National Highway 35 and the China–Pakistan Friendship Highway, was built jointly by the governments of China and Pakistan. It was completed in 1979 and opened to the public in 1986. Pakistan at first favoured a route through the Mintaka Pass, but in 1966 China recommended the steeper Khunjerab Pass instead, noting that Mintaka would be more exposed to air strikes. On the Pakistani side the road was built by the Frontier Works Organisation, using the Pakistan Army Corps of Engineers.

The work was costly in lives: about 810 Pakistanis and about 200 Chinese workers died, mostly in landslides and falls. More than 140 of the Chinese dead are buried in the Chinese cemetery in Gilgit. The route follows one of the many paths of the ancient Silk Road.

The highway runs about 1,300 km. Its Pakistani section is 806 km long and meets the Indus River at Thakot, then follows it to Jaglot, where the Gilgit River joins it. There the Hindu Kush, the Himalayas and the Karakoram meet. The road passes through Gilgit, the capital of Gilgit–Baltistan, and the valleys of Nagar and Hunza, and reaches the Chinese border at the Khunjerab Pass, at a maximum elevation of 4,714 m. It is one of the highest paved roads in the world.

On the Chinese side the road follows the Sarykol valley west of the Tarim Basin from Kashgar, enters the canyon of the Gez River and passes Karakul Lake and the peak of Muztagh Ata before descending to Tashkurgan. The highway crosses the collision zone between the Eurasian and Indian plates and has strategic importance for Pakistan and China.

The highway gives access to Gilgit and Skardu, the hubs for mountaineering in Gilgit–Baltistan, and to glaciers such as the Passu and Minapin. More than 50,000 rock carvings stand along it, concentrated at ten major sites between Hunza and Shatial; the earliest are dated to between 5000 and 1000 BCE. Daily bus service between Gilgit and Kashgar began on 1 June 2006.

In January 2010 a massive landslide above Karimabad in the Hunza Valley created Attabad Lake, which flooded more than 20 km of the highway and cut through traffic to China. Goods crossed the lake by boat until a new route with five tunnels and several bridges, built by the China Road & Bridge Corporation from 2012, was inaugurated on 15 September 2015.
karakorum: The Orkhon valley had been a centre of the Xiongnu, Göktürk and Uyghur empires. The Göktürks placed the seat of power, Ötüken, in the nearby Khangai Mountains, and the Uyghur capital Karabalgasun lay 27 kilometres north-west of where Karakorum later stood. The site suited the Mongols: it was central to the growing empire, the climate in the late Medieval Warm Period gave abundant grass, the Orkhon ran north to south where most rivers run east to west, and its symbolic importance as a former seat of power expressed Mongol control over the region's largely non-Mongol population.

In 1218–1219 Genghis Khan gathered his troops at a place called Karakorum for the campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire, and the foundation of a city is usually dated to 1220. Until 1235 it seems to have been little more than a yurt town. After defeating the Jin, Ögedei Khan had walls and a fixed palace built; the Tumen Amgalan Ord, the Palace of Myriad Peace, was decreed in 1235 and finished within a year. Ögedei encouraged the empire's elite to build houses near it. Möngke Khan enlarged the palace and had the great stupa temple completed. An enslaved Parisian goldsmith, Guillaume Boucher, made the Silver Tree for the central courtyard, with silver fruit, four golden serpents and a trumpet-sounding angel, which dispensed drinks to guests.

William of Rubruck, a Flemish Franciscan envoy, reached the city in 1254. He thought the royal abbey at Saint-Denis ten times grander than the palace, yet described a cosmopolitan and religiously tolerant town with four gates, quarters for the Saracenes and for the Cathai, twelve temples, two mosques and a Nestorian church. After the empire divided in 1260, Khubilai Khan favoured Dadu, and Karakorum became a provincial administrative centre. Kaidu took it in 1277 and was driven out the next year, and it prospered again in the first half of the 14th century.

After the Yuan fell in 1368 Karakorum housed Biligtü Khan from 1370. Ming armies occupied it in 1372 and in 1380 took and razed it. It was inhabited at the start of the 16th century, when Batu-Möngke Dayan Khan made it a capital again, but after changing hands between Oirads and Chinggisids it was finally abandoned. In 1585 Abtai Sain Khan built the Erdene Zuu Monastery from its stones and bricks. Nikolai Yadrintsev conclusively identified the site in 1889, and the German-Mongolian excavations of 2000–2004 suggest that the building Soviet and Mongolian excavators took for Ögedei's palace was the great stupa temple. The ruins lie in the Orkhon Valley World Heritage Site.
karaman: Karaman lies in Central Anatolia, north of the Taurus Mountains and about 100 km south of Konya, at an average elevation of 1,039 metres. It has a cold semi-arid climate with hot, dry summers, cold, snowy winters and almost 3,000 hours of sunshine a year. The city takes its name from Karaman Bey, one of the rulers of the Karamanid dynasty. Its earlier name, Laranda, comes from the Luwian Larawanda, meaning a sandy place, and in Hittite times it was known as Lānda.

Little is known of the early history of Laranda. It is first named in the writings of Diodorus Siculus, who says that Perdiccas and King Philip, after defeating Ariarathes I of Cappadocia, set out to punish Laranda and Isauria for killing Balacrus, the general whom Alexander the Great had appointed satrap of the region. Laranda was destroyed, later became a seat of Isaurian pirates and for a time was controlled by Antipater of Derbe, until Amyntas of Galatia killed him. In the early third century CE it was the seat of a bishop, Neon, who approved the preaching of the layman Euelpis there. It belonged to the Roman and then the Byzantine Empire until the Seljuks captured it in the early 12th century.

Frederick Barbarossa occupied the city in 1190 and the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia held it from 1211 to 1216. Karaman Bey took it in 1256 and gave it his name, and from 1275 it was the capital of the Karamanid beylik. The Sufi preacher Bahaeddin Veled arrived in 1222 with his family, and the emir had a madrasah built for them. His son Rumi married his wife Gevher Hatun in Karaman, and Rumi's mother died there in 1224. The Ottoman Empire conquered the Karamanids in 1468 and moved the capital of the province to Konya in 1483.

Karaman is the seat of Karaman Province and had 175,390 inhabitants in 2022. From the Karamanid period it keeps the ruins of a castle and some walls, two mosques and a madrasah. The Aktekke Mosque, also called the Mader-i Mevlana Cami, built in 1370 to replace the original madrasah, holds the graves of Rumi's mother and other family members. The poet Yunus Emre, who lived about 1238 to 1320, spent his later years in Karaman and is believed to lie buried beside the Yunus Emre Mosque.
karamanoglu-mehmed-bey: Shams al-Din Mehmed Bey was born at Ermenek in 1245 or 1246, the eldest son of Karim al-Din Karaman, the soubashi of the region around Ermenek, Mut, Silifke, Gülnar and Anamur, and he became the third ruler of the Karamanids. When his father died in 1263, Sultan Kilij Arslan IV of Rum arrested his children and his brother Bunsuz. After the sultan's death in 1266 Muʿīn al-Dīn Parwāna took full power and released them, except for Ali, who was kept in Kayseri.

Mehmed and his brothers joined Hatiroghlu Sharaf al-Din's revolt against the Mongols, and Sharaf al-Din granted him the lands his father had ruled. He extended them towards the Mediterranean coast and destroyed a Mongol force of 200 men at Ulukışla. Bedreddin Ibrahim, the former subaşı he had displaced, marched against him with a Mongol unit of 2,000 men and refused an offer of 100,000 dinars; the Karamanids wore the army down in the mountains and defeated it at the Göksu Pass.

Opposing Sultan Kaykhusraw III, who ruled under Mongol suzerainty, Mehmed besieged Konya with Ala al-Din Siyavush, known as Jimri, who claimed to be a son of Sultan Kaykaus II. His Turkmen troops burned the Atpazari and Chashnigir gates and entered the city on 12 May 1277. The regent Emin al-Din Mikail was captured, made to reveal the treasury and executed with Melik al-Sawahil Baha al-Din. Siyavush was enthroned on 15 May, and Mehmed became vizier and issued the edict on the Turkish language, which replaced Persian and Arabic in the palace and official correspondence.

The sons of Sahib Ata Fahreddin raised an army against him with fifty thousand dirhams paid to the Germiyanid Turkmens. At Değirmençayı near Akşehir, Mehmed met Taceddin Hüseyin in a duel in a stream and his men beheaded him, and the Germiyanid Turkmens fled. A siege of Afyonkarahisar failed. His hold on Konya lasted 37 days: as a Mongol army approached he and Jimri left the city, and near Mut the Mongols ambushed him, killing him with two of his brothers and a cousin. His brother Güneri succeeded him. Karamanoğlu Mehmetbey University in Karaman is named after him.
karamchand-gandhi: The Gandhi family came from the village of Kutiana in what was then Junagadh State. In the early 18th century Lalji Gandhi moved to Porbandar and entered the service of its ruler, the Rana, and later generations served as civil servants there. Karamchand's father, Uttamchand, became diwan in the early 19th century under Rana Khimojiraj. After the Rana died suddenly in 1831, his widow, Rani Rupaliba, ruled as regent for their 12-year-old son Vikmatji, fell out with Uttamchand and sent him back to his ancestral village. Vikmatji took the throne in 1841 and restored Uttamchand as diwan.

Karamchand in turn became chief minister to the prince of Porbandar, advising the royal family and hiring other officials, and he later served as diwan of Rajkot. He had very little formal education and knew little of geography or history, but his practical experience made him a capable administrator. He was said to be kind and generous but also bad-tempered. He did not grow rich: his income covered the household's expenses, with enough to eat, a number of servants and a few good pieces of furniture.

He married four times. His first three wives died, two of them soon after giving birth to daughters. In 1857 he married Putlibai, and they had three sons, Laxmidas, Karsandas and Mohandas, the youngest of his children, and a daughter, Raliatbehn. All his children married during his lifetime.

In 1885 Karamchand fell seriously ill with a fistula. Putlibai and the children, Mohandas above all, nursed him, but the doctors' treatments failed, and the family doctor refused the surgery he suggested. He died on 16 November 1885, aged 63. Mohandas, then sixteen, later recalled that he had been massaging his father's legs that night when his uncle Tulsidas sent him to bed, and that within moments a servant called him back to find his father dead.
karanis: Karanis lay at what is now Kom Aushim, in the north-east corner of the Faiyum Oasis. The town covered roughly 60 hectares, and its peak population is estimated at 4,000, though it may have been as much as three times greater. It was one of several towns of the Arsinoites nome founded by Ptolemy II Philadelphus. Its dry conditions are ideal for preserving papyri, which became the main interest of its early excavators.

The town stagnated in the late Ptolemaic period until Augustus, recognising the Faiyum's farming potential, sent workers to clean the canals and restore the dikes, and Karanis expanded northwards. Roman veterans settled in the Faiyum towns, but only two Latin papyri have been found at Karanis against a great many Greek ones, which suggests the veterans were Greek, or at least from the Eastern empire. Peace brought prosperity to its landholders into the second century, followed by recessions in the late second and the second quarter of the third century. Radiocarbon dates from stored seeds show the town was still inhabited at least through the sixth century; it was gradually abandoned around the Sasanian conquest of Egypt.

Two limestone temples in Egyptian style stood in the town. The south temple was dedicated under Nero to the crocodile gods Pnepheros and Petesouchos and had a dining room where weddings and banquets could be held. The north temple, built in the early Roman period, has an altar that fits a crocodile mummy and a figure of a hawk-headed crocodile, probably the god Soknopaios.

Farmers digging the mound for sebbakh fertiliser destroyed much of the site's context, and Bernard Pyne Grenfell and Arthur Surridge Hunt, who dug there in 1895, thought it too plundered to repay work. Francis W. Kelsey of the University of Michigan led excavations aimed at knowledge rather than collections; their papyri, mostly tax records, are in the University of Michigan Papyrus Collection. Later work has been done by Cairo University, the French Institute, Virginia Commonwealth University and the URU Fayum Project. The Kom Aushim Museum, built on the site in 1974, displays finds from Karanis and the Faiyum.
karashahr: Karashahr, called Yanqi in Chinese sources, lies on the Kaidu River about 24 kilometres west of Lake Bosten in Xinjiang. The lake, about 1,000 square kilometres, has been noted since Han times for its fish. In classical times the city stood on the branch of the Silk Road that ran along the northern edge of the Taklamakan Desert. It was originally known in the Tocharian languages as Ārśi, and later as Agni, perhaps from the Sanskrit word for fire. Its neighbours were the related states of Kucha to the west, Turfan to the east and Krorän to the south.

Han sources describe Yanqi as a large and important kingdom, controlled by the Xiongnu until the Han dynasty extended its influence in the late 2nd century BCE. From the 1st century BCE the Ārśi converted to Buddhism. After Yanqi attacked and killed the Chinese Protector General Chen Mu in 75 CE, General Ban Chao made a punitive campaign in 94 CE, and the king was beheaded. A source describes it as having 15,000 households and 52,000 individuals. Agnideśa became a tributary of Tang China in 632, and in 644 Emperor Taizong attacked it after it allied with the Turks. One of the Four Garrisons of Anxi was based there.

By the mid-9th century the Uyghur Khaganate had conquered the area, the Tocharian languages were fading, Islam gained ground and the town became known by the Turkic name Karasahr, "black city". From the mid-13th to the 18th century it was part of the Chagatai Khanate. The Jesuit Bento de Góis stayed three months in 1605 in the kingdom he called Cialis, and the British traveller Francis Younghusband visited in 1887.

Yanqi is the seat of Yanqi Hui Autonomous County in the Bayingolin Mongol Autonomous Prefecture. It lies on China National Highway 314 and the Southern Xinjiang Railway, and had 31,773 people in 2006, of whom 16,032 were Han, 7,781 Hui and 7,154 Uyghur. It has many mosques.
karatay-madrasa: The madrasa stands at the foot of the citadel hill in Konya, across from the ruins of the Seljuk palace and in view of the Alâeddin Mosque. Its founder, the vizier Jalal al-Din Qaratay, who died in 1254, built it during the joint rule of the brothers Kayqubad II, Kaykaus II and Kilij Arslan IV, next to the Küçük Karatay Medrese, which no longer exists. Because it was built after the Mongol invasions of Anatolia, its design is not strictly Seljuk. With the Karatay Han, a caravanserai completed in the 1240s, it is the largest surviving monument of Konya and its region.

Shams al-Din Ahmad Aflaki, a biographer of Rumi, recorded gatherings of both Sufis and scholars there, yet the endowment deed required that its teacher of Islamic law be a Hanafi, likely because the Seljuk rulers were largely Hanafi. The tile work was probably coordinated by Muhammad al-Tusi, a master ceramicist from Tus in Khurasan who also decorated the Sırçalı Medrese.

The rectangular building measures about 31.5 by 26.5 metres and is entered through a vestibule at its southeast corner. Its ornate stone portal, with Arabic inscriptions, geometric and floral motifs, alternating bands of grey and white marble and a muqarnas canopy, is not joined to the body of the building. It resembles the portal of the Alâeddin Mosque and is likely the work of craftsmen from northern Syria in the 1220s, so it may have been built earlier and reused.

The vestibule leads to a domed hall 12 metres square with a square water basin in the middle and an oculus about 5 metres wide at the summit. The dome and the Turkish triangles below it are covered with tiles and tile mosaic, mostly black and turquoise, with geometric motifs and interlacing Kufic inscriptions. Students' rooms opened off the hall, and on its west side an iwan, flanked by two domed rooms, probably served as the main classroom. The southern room holds a cenotaph, most likely the founder's.

Since 1954 the building has been a museum of tile art, while stone and wood pieces are shown in the İnce Minareli Medrese, also in Konya. The collection grew with finds from the Kubadabad Palace, the royal summer residence on the shore of Lake Beyşehir, excavated since the 1960s. The students' rooms, ruined by the 20th century, were reconstructed in the 1970s, and the building was restored again in 2006.
karatepe: Karatepe, Turkish for Black Hill, lies in the Taurus Mountains on the right bank of the Ceyhan River, about 23 km from the district centre of Kadirli, within Karatepe-Aslantaş National Park. The ancient city of Cilicia controlled a passage from eastern Anatolia to the north Syrian plain. Its two monumental gates carry reliefs of hunting, war and a boat with oars, and pillars of lions and sphinxes flank them.

Karatepe became an important Neo-Hittite centre after the collapse of the Hittite Empire in the late 12th century BCE. Its bilingual inscription, composed in Phoenician and then translated into Hieroglyphic Luwian, names its author as Azatiwada, ruler and founder of the town, and commemorates its foundation. Azatiwada called himself a subordinate of Awarikus, king of Adanawa (Adana), the ancient kingdom of Ḫiyawa, and the inscription records the kings of Adana from the house of Mopsos. The Cinekoy inscription, discovered more recently, also names a king Awariku, who may have been the same ruler or one of his dynasty.

The site was examined during the Oriental Institute of Chicago's survey of the Amuq Valley in 1936. A team led by Helmuth Theodor Bossert (1889–1961) excavated it from 1947 to 1957, revealing the walled city; restoration and further soundings went on for many years, and in the late 1990s Halet Çambel (1916–2014) led work on a palace. The inscription has served archaeologists as a Rosetta Stone for the Luwian glyphs.

Across the river lies Domuztepe (Aslantaş), inhabited from the Neolithic period and substantially flooded after the building of the Aslantaş Dam. There Bossert and B. Alkım found a statue base with two bulls in 1947, and Halet Çambel found a Storm God stele in 1982. The statue base is now in the Karatepe Museum, and the artefacts of Karatepe are shown in the Karatepe-Aslantaş Open-Air Museum.
karatoya-river: The name of the river joins two Vedic Sanskrit words, kará, meaning hand as an instrument of action, and tóya, meaning water. Known in its upper reaches as the Phuleshwari, it rises in the Baikunthapur forests in the extreme north-west of Jalpaiguri district in West Bengal, India, and for some distance forms the boundary between Dinajpur and Rangpur districts in Bangladesh. It then meanders through Rangpur and Bogura.

In the south of Bogura district it receives the Halhalia, and the united stream is known as the Phuljhur. Flowing south past Raiganj and Shujapur, it is joined by the Ichhamati at Nalka, passes the village of Ullapara and meets the Hurasagar at Narnia. Under the name of the Hurasagar it passes close to Shazadpur and Hera and joins the Jamuna near Bera.

The Puranas mention the Karatoya and give it a high repute for sanctity. Also called Sadānīrā, always full of water, it marked the easternmost boundary of Aryavarta and was the eastern boundary of the old kingdom of Pundravardhana, the country of the Paundras. In the classical period it formed the western boundary of Kamarupa, and later of the Kamata kingdom.

According to the Siyar-al-Mutakhkhirin, in the early 1100s the Ganges was three times smaller than the Karatoya. Van den Brouck's map of Bengal of about 1660 shows it flowing into the Ganges, and before the destructive floods of 1787 it carried a great volume of Teesta water to the Atrai and the Ganges. James Rennell mapped the region's rivers in the late 1700s.

After the main stream of the Teesta was diverted to the east in 1787, the Karatoya and the Phuljhur gradually silted up and became rivers of minor importance. One channel that joins the Baral, 48 kilometres east of Pabna, is still called both the Buri Teesta, or old Teesta, and the Karatoya. Traces of another old channel claimed for the Karatoya are pointed out in the Chatmohar thana, where the Baral appears to have obliterated it.
karel-capek: Karel Čapek was born on 9 January 1890 in Malé Svatoňovice and grew up in Úpice, where his father, Antonín Čapek, was a doctor at the textile factory. His mother, Božena Čapková, collected local legends, songs and stories. He was the youngest of three children and remained especially close to his brother Josef, a painter, with whom he lived and worked throughout his adult life.

Expelled from a school in Hradec Králové for taking part in an illegal students' club, he finished secondary school in Prague in 1909. He studied philosophy and aesthetics at Charles University, with some time in Berlin and Paris, and took his doctorate in 1915. Spinal problems kept him out of military service in the First World War.

Čapek began as a journalist. With Josef he edited Národní listy from October 1917 to April 1921, and then both joined Lidové noviny. Through his circle of Friday garden parties for Czech intellectuals he came to know Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, whose conversations with him became the book Talks with T. G. Masaryk.

His first international success was R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots, 1920), which was translated into English in 1922 and performed in the United Kingdom and America by 1923. He wrote that his brother Josef proposed the word robot, from the Czech robota, meaning forced labour or drudgery; he had first thought of laboři. His other works include The Insect Play, The Makropulos Affair, Krakatit, the novels Hordubal, Meteor and An Ordinary Life, War with the Newts (1936), travel books and The Gardener's Year. By the mid-1930s he was an outspoken anti-fascist, the first president of the Czechoslovak PEN Club, and had also opposed communism.

In 1938 France and the United Kingdom refused to defend Czechoslovakia against Nazi Germany. Čapek declined an offer of exile in England, although the Gestapo had named him public enemy number two. While repairing flood damage at the family's summer house he caught a cold, which became pneumonia; he suffered from spondyloarthritis and smoked heavily. He died on 25 December 1938.

When Nazi agents came to arrest him after the German invasion, they found he was dead and arrested his wife, the actress Olga Scheinpflugová, instead. Josef died in Bergen-Belsen in April 1945. Čapek was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature seven times. Ivan Klíma credits him with bringing written Czech closer to the spoken language, and the Czech PEN Club awards a Karel Čapek Prize.
karel-doorman: Karel Willem Frederik Marie Doorman was born in Utrecht on 23 April 1889 and raised as a Roman Catholic in a military family. He and his brother Lou were commissioned as midshipmen in 1906. In 1910 he became an officer and went to the Dutch East Indies aboard the cruiser Tromp, and from January 1912 to December 1913 he served on survey vessels mapping the coastal waters of New Guinea.

In 1915 Doorman joined the Aviation Service and became one of the first Dutch naval officers to earn pilot's wings. He trained pilots at Soesterberg and from 1918 at the Naval Air Base De Kooy in Den Helder, which he commanded from 1919 to 1921, and in 1922 he was made a Knight of the Order of Orange-Nassau for his work in organising naval aviation. Budget cuts and an arm injury ended his flying, and from 1921 to 1923 he attended the Higher Naval School in The Hague.

He then served at sea and ashore: as gunnery officer and later first officer of De Zeven Provinciën, in command of the mine-layer Prins van Oranje and the destroyers Witte de With and Evertsen, and as chief of staff at Den Helder. In 1937 he went out as a captain to command the cruisers Sumatra and Java, and in August 1938 he became Commander of Naval Aviation in the Dutch East Indies. He was promoted to rear admiral on 16 May 1940.

In early 1942 Doorman led the remnants of the ABDA Combined Striking Force. On 3 February Japanese bombers forced his ships back from Makassar, and on 19 February his attacks failed to stop the Japanese landing on Bali in the Battle of Badung Strait.

In the Battle of the Java Sea, which lasted with interruptions for over seven hours, his outnumbered squadron was almost wholly destroyed. Following navy tradition, Doorman chose to go down with De Ruyter when a Japanese Long Lance torpedo sank her. He is remembered for the signal I am attacking, follow me, a loose rendering of his order All ships, follow me; one source doubts he said the words. He was posthumously made a Knight 3rd class of the Military William Order, and four Dutch navy ships have borne his name.
karelia: Karelia stretches from the White Sea coast to the Gulf of Finland and contains the two largest lakes in Europe, Lake Ladoga and Lake Onega. The Karelian Isthmus lies between the Gulf of Finland and Lake Ladoga. The River Svir is usually thought of as its traditional southern border, and the River Kymi as the historic western border, which separated the Karelians from the Häme Finns in the Middle Ages.

During the Early Middle Ages settlers from western Finland mixed with the local population to form the Karelian ethnic group. Sweden and the Novgorod Republic fought bitterly over Karelia from the 13th century. The Treaty of Nöteborg of 1323 divided it: Sweden received the southern Karelian Isthmus and most of South Karelia, with Viborg as the capital of its province, while Novgorod held the northern isthmus and North and Ladoga Karelia.

By the Treaty of Stolbovo of 1617 large parts of Russian Karelia were ceded to Sweden, and conflict between the new Swedish rulers and the local people led thousands of Karelians to emigrate to Russia. The Treaty of Nystad of 1721 ceded a portion of Karelia to Russia, and the Treaty of Åbo of 1743 ceded South Karelia. After Russia occupied Finland in the Finnish War, these provinces, Old Finland, were incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Finland in 1812. Finland declared independence in 1917, and the Treaty of Tartu of 1920 confirmed the border. The Russian part became a Karelian autonomous republic of the Soviet Union in 1923.

The Winter War of 1939 ended with the Moscow Peace Treaty of March 1940, which handed a large part of Finnish Karelia to the Soviet Union and forced over 400,000 people to relocate within Finland. Finland retook the territory in the Continuation War of 1941 to 1944, occupied much of East Karelia, and was forced out in 1944. It lost its fourth biggest city, Viipuri, its industrial heartland along the River Vuoksi, and access to the fishing waters of Lake Ladoga. One eighth of Finland's citizens became refugees. About one million people in Finland can trace their roots to that area.

Karelia is divided between north-western Russia, in the Republic of Karelia and Leningrad Oblast, and Finland, in the regions of South Karelia, North Karelia and the eastern part of Kymenlaakso. The Republic of Karelia was formed in 1991 from the Karelian autonomous republic. Its capital is Petrozavodsk.
karelian-assr: The Karelian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, also called Russian Karelia or East Karelia, was formed within the Russian SFSR by a resolution of the All-Russian Central Executive Committee of 27 June 1923 and a decree of 25 July 1923, out of the Karelian Labor Commune. Until 1936 it was called the Autonomous Karelian Soviet Socialist Republic. Its capital was Petrozavodsk, and in 1927 it was divided into districts that replaced the old volosts.

Before the Great Purge its leaders, mostly socialist Finnish immigrants, followed a policy of indigenization under the long-time leader Edvard Gylling. Finnish was the main language of education and administration, with Russian second. It is believed that Gylling, a Finnish socialist, wished to create a Red Finland in Soviet Karelia after the defeat of the Reds in the Finnish Civil War, and Finnish propaganda called the republic the Gyllingian Empire.

In the Great Purge and the NKVD's Finnish Operation Gylling and the rest of the Finnish leadership were removed in 1935, and he was later executed. Russification replaced indigenization: a heavily Russified standard for written Karelian was introduced and speaking Karelian or Finnish in public was banned. In June 1938 Gennady Kupriyanov became First Secretary and promised in his inaugural speech to exile Finns from Petrozavodsk. At least 9,100 Finns were sentenced to death, and estimates of the total death toll run as high as 30,000 or 40,000. In 1938 the Kandalakshsky District passed to the Murmansk Oblast.

From 1940 to 1956 the republic was merged with territory annexed from Finland as the Karelo-Finnish Soviet Socialist Republic, a union republic, although only a small part of its population was Karelian or Finnish. Some later historians see this as a convenient means of facilitating the incorporation of more Finnish territory. After the downgrading of 1956 the compulsory study of Finnish was abolished in 1958, though Finnish remained an official language. Poyakonda passed to the Murmansk Oblast in 1987.
On 9 August 1990 the republic declared state sovereignty and was renamed the Karelian Soviet Socialist Republic. On 13 November 1991 it became the Republic of Karelia, a federal subject of Russia.
karen-national-union: After Myanmar's independence in January 1948, KNU leaders told local organisers to form defence militias, grouped under the Karen National Defence Organisation, and early in 1949 the KNU launched its armed campaign against the government. Its first aim was independence; since 1976 it has called instead for a federal system. In 1953 Mahn Ba Zan and other leaders founded the communist-influenced Karen National Unity Party (KNUP), whose members dominated the KNU by 1960 and reorganised its army along Maoist lines.

Resistance came from the Thai border, where S'gaw Karen commanders such as Shwe Hser and Bo Mya held sway. In 1966 Bo Mya seized the Dawna Range and much of the border and ordered KNUP cadres out, maintaining an army of about 10,000 men by taxing illegal trade with Thailand. Mahn Ba Zan reconciled with him in 1967, and by 1970, after KNUP defeats in the Irrawaddy Delta, the KNU was the dominant body of the Karen movement. Bo Mya led it from 1976 to 2000.

After the failed 8888 Uprising of 1988, the expanded Myanmar Army offered rebel groups the choice of cooperation or destruction. In 1994 Buddhist soldiers, citing discrimination by the overwhelmingly Christian leadership, broke away under the monk U Thuzana as the Democratic Karen Buddhist Army, which agreed a ceasefire with the army and fought the KNU. The KNU headquarters fell at Manerplaw in 1995, and its secretary-general Padoh Mahn Sha La Phan was shot dead in Mae Sot, Thailand, on 14 February 2008. By 2009 its fighting force had fallen to around 3000 to 5000 soldiers.

A ceasefire was signed in Hpa-an in January 2012, and on 15 October 2015 the KNU signed the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement. After the 2021 coup its Brigade 5 overran an army base near the Thai border on 27 March 2021, killing ten soldiers, and the army answered with airstrikes on Karen villages. On 28 August 2025 the junta declared the KNU an unlawful association and a terrorist group, and on 14 November 2025 the KNU and its allies recaptured the border town of Mawdaung, held by the junta since 1990.

The KNU Congress, its supreme legislative body, meets every four years to elect the president, vice-president, general secretary and central committees. The seven KNU districts elect their own chairmen every two years, and these chairmen and the brigade commanders sit on the Central Standing Committee, which provides the ministers of 14 departments, among them defence, education and health. An eleven-member Central Executive Committee runs its daily affairs.
karen-people: The Karen, also called the Kayin, consist of about 20 subgroups, the largest of which are the S'gaw and the Pwo. A pan-Karen identity is a relatively modern creation, established in the 19th century with the conversion of some Karen to Christianity and shaped by British colonial policies. In pre-colonial times the Burmese and Mon kingdoms recognised two categories: the lowland Pwo, called Talaing Kayin, regarded as original settlers, and the highland S'gaw, called Bamar Kayin, who were subordinated or assimilated by the Bamar.

Karen legends speak of a river of running sand that their ancestors crossed. Many Karen take it to be the Gobi Desert, but most scholars read it as rivers carrying sand, perhaps the sediment-laden Yellow River. The linguists Luce and Lehman estimate that Tibeto-Burman peoples such as the Karen migrated into present-day Myanmar between 300 and 800 CE.

Baptist missionaries brought Christianity to Myanmar from 1830 and converted many Karen. The first Karen convert, Tha Byu, was baptised in 1828 by George Boardman. After Myanmar was annexed as a province of British India in 1886, the colonial authorities favoured Christian Karen, who gained military recruitment and seats in the legislature. During the Second World War many Karen villages were destroyed and massacres committed by both the Japanese and the Burma Independence Army, and Karen soldiers supported the British in Operation Character in 1945.

At the Panglong Conference of 1947 the Karen attended only as observers. In February 1947 the Karen National Union was formed at a Karen Congress of 700 delegates. After independence in January 1948 it tried at first to coexist peacefully with the Burman majority. In January 1949 the Karen general Smith Dun was removed as army chief of staff, and the Karen National Defence Organisation rose in insurgency, coming close to capturing Yangon and holding out for 111 days at the Battle of Insein. The union first aimed at an independent Karen homeland called Kawthoolei and since 1976 has called for a federal system.

The Karen languages are Tibeto-Burman and comprise three mutually unintelligible branches: Sgaw, Eastern Pwo and Western Pwo. They are unusual in the family in having subject-verb-object word order, probably through the influence of Mon and Tai languages, and are written in a modified form of the Mon-Burmese script.

Most Karen are Theravada Buddhists who also practise animism, and about 15 to 30 per cent are Christian. Karen animism holds that every person is embodied by thirty-seven spirits, called k'lar, and that death comes when all of them leave.
karenni-people: The Karenni, also called the Kayah or Kayah Li, are a Karenic-speaking ethnic group native to Kayah State in Myanmar. The name Karenni means "red Karen" in Burmese. The term Karennies is used for all the peoples native to the region of Kayah State, which are counted as nine sub-tribes: the Kayah, Padaung (Kayan), Geko, Geba, Zayein, Bre, Manu-Manau, Yintale and Yinbaw. Several of these, including the Geko, Geba, Padaung and Yinbaw, belong to Kayan, a subgroup of the Karenni region, while the Bre and the Manu-Manau belong to the Kayaw subgroup.

The Karenni States were a collection of small states inhabited by Karenni people and ruled by petty princes called myozas. They included Kantarawadi, the only state whose ruler was promoted to saopha or sawba, a title comparable to maharaja in India, as well as Kyebogyi, Bawlake, Nammekon and Naungpale. They had feudal ties to the Burmese kingdom but were independent until British rule in Burma. They bordered the Shan States of Mong Pai, Hsatung and Mawkmai to the north, Thailand to the east and the Papun district of Lower Burma to the south.

In 1875 the British government formally recognised and guaranteed the independence of the Karenni States in a treaty with the Burmese king Mindon Min, by which both parties recognised the area as belonging neither to Burma nor to Great Britain. The states were therefore never fully incorporated into British Burma. In 1892 their rulers agreed to accept a stipend from the British government, and the states were recognised as tributary. A garrison of military police was stationed at the village of Loikaw. In the 1930s the Mawchi Mine in Bawlake was the most important source of tungsten in the world.

The Constitution of the Union of Burma of 1947 proclaimed that the three Karenni States would be amalgamated into a single constituent state, Karenni State, with the possibility of secession from the Union after ten years. In 1952 the former Shan state of Mong Pai was added and the whole was renamed Kayah State, possibly with the intent of driving a wedge between the Karenni and the rest of the Karen people in Karen State, both of whom were fighting for independence.
kargil-war: Before the Partition of India in 1947 Kargil was a tehsil of Ladakh. The Indo-Pakistani War of 1947–1948 ended with the Line of Control dividing Ladakh district, and after the war of 1971 the two states signed the Simla Agreement promising not to engage in armed conflict over that boundary. In the 1990s separatist activity in Kashmir and the nuclear tests that both countries conducted in 1998 made the atmosphere increasingly belligerent. In February 1999 the two governments signed the Lahore Declaration, promising a peaceful bilateral solution to the Kashmir dispute.

During February 1999 the Pakistan Army sent forces to occupy posts on the Indian side of the Line of Control. Special Services Group troops and four to seven battalions of the Northern Light Infantry, a paramilitary regiment, set up bases on 132 vantage points. Pakistan at first blamed independent Kashmiri insurgents, but documents left by casualties and later statements by its Prime Minister and army chief showed the involvement of its paramilitary forces. By the second week of May an ambush of a patrol led by Captain Saurabh Kalia, who had acted on a shepherd's tip-off, exposed the intrusion. Indian estimates of the number of infiltrators rose from some militants on 12 May to over 1,000 by 21 May.

The task of repelling them fell to the 15th Corps. In the Batalik sector an assault on Point 5203 on 6 June led to heavy casualties, and the point was captured on 21 June. The Indian Army, later supported by the Indian Air Force, recaptured a majority of the positions, while the Indian Navy prepared to blockade Pakistani ports in Operation Talwar. President Bill Clinton refused to intervene until Pakistan removed all its forces from the Indian side. After the Washington accord of 4 July 1999, in which Nawaz Sharif agreed to withdraw Pakistani troops, most fighting stopped. On 27 July Pakistani forces asked for a flag meeting to collect their dead and agreed to abide by the ceasefire.

Pakistan was heavily criticised abroad for instigating the war, and its claim that Kashmiri freedom fighters were responsible failed. Two soldiers received the Nishan-E-Haider, its highest military honour, which confirmed the army's role. Pakistani casualties are hard to determine: Pervez Musharraf stated that 357 soldiers were killed, while Nawaz Sharif later said over 4,000. India awarded four Param Vir Chakras and eleven Maha Vir Chakras. The Kargil Review Committee under K. Subrahmanyam led to a large-scale restructuring of Indian intelligence. The Kargil War was one of only two major conventional wars between nuclear-armed states, the other being the Sino-Soviet border conflict.
kariba-dam: The dam was planned and built by the Government of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, a federal colony within the British Empire that existed from 1953 to the end of 1963. Northern Rhodesia had decided earlier in 1953 to build a cheaper dam on the Kafue River, closer to its Copperbelt. Southern Rhodesia, the richest of the three territories, objected and insisted on Kariba, whose capacity was also much higher.

Cogefar-Impresit built the double curvature arch between 1955 and 1959 at a cost of 135 million dollars for the first stage, with only the Kariba South power cavern. The Kariba North cavern was not finished until 1977 because of largely political problems, bringing the total to 480 million dollars. Eighty-six construction workers died. Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother opened the dam on 17 May 1960.

The dam stands in the Kariba Gorge, 128 metres tall and 579 metres long. Lake Kariba extends for 280 kilometres and holds 185 cubic kilometres of water. Each country has a power station on its own bank. The southern station, Zimbabwe's, has operated since 1960 with six 125 MW generators, and in March 2018 two new 50 MW turbines raised it to 1,050 MW. The northern station, Zambia's, has run since 1976 with four 150 MW generators, expanded to 960 MW by December 2013. Together they supply 2,010 MW to the Copperbelt and parts of Zimbabwe. The dam is operated by the Zambezi River Authority, owned equally by Zimbabwe and Zambia.

The reservoir forced the resettlement of about 57,000 Tonga people living along the Zambezi on both banks. The British author David Howarth described schools and cooperative markets provided for them in Northern Rhodesia, while the anthropologist Thayer Scudder wrote that most remained development refugees, some on degraded land. The American writer Jacques Leslie, in Deep Water (2005), judged it the worst dam-resettlement disaster in African history. The displaced people formed the Basilwizi Trust in 2002 to promote development projects. From 1958 to 1961 Operation Noah removed around 6,000 large animals threatened by the rising water, and the dam controls 90 percent of the Zambezi's runoff.

In March 2014 engineers warned that erosion of the bedrock by the spillway torrents had weakened the foundations. A rehabilitation project begun in 2017 set out to reshape the plunge pool and rebuild the spillway gates. Drought left the reservoir at 12 percent of capacity in January 2016 and at 1 percent in January 2023.
karijotas: Karijotas was one of the sons of Gediminas, Grand Duke of Lithuania, and a member of the House of Gediminas. According to the Polish historian Jan Tęgowski he was probably born between 1305 and 1308. He was baptised before 1349, taking the name Michal, and from 1341 he held Navahrudak as its duke, together with Vawkavysk.

In 1349 Algirdas, the grand duke, sent him with two sons, Aikštas or Eikšis of Eišiškės and Simeon of Svislach, to Jani Beg, Khan of the Golden Horde, to negotiate an alliance against the Teutonic Knights and the rising principality of Moscow. Jani Beg instead handed Karijotas over to Simeon of Moscow for a ransom. The date of his death is uncertain. He is last mentioned in writing in the treaty of 1358 between the dukes of Mazovia and Kęstutis and his brothers, and is no longer named in 1366, where he would have been expected.

It is unclear how many children Karijotas had; the number given varies between four and ten. Reliable information survives for four sons, Aleksander, George, Konstantin and Fedir, who helped Algirdas defeat the Tatars at the Battle of Blue Waters in 1363 and received Podolia in return. Aleksander, who died about 1380, took part in the Galicia–Volhynia Wars between his uncle Liubartas and Casimir III of Poland; in 1366 Casimir gave him Volodymyr in Volhynia, which Liubartas recaptured after Casimir's death.

George first assisted Aleksander and was poisoned in 1375 soon after accepting an invitation to rule Moldavia. Konstantin moved to Hungary after the Union of Krewo of 1385 and died there around 1389. Fedir, who died in 1414, became ruler of all Podolia once his brothers were dead around 1389, but in 1392 he defied Vytautas the Great and fled to Hungary, where he ruled Mukachevo and built Palanok Castle. Dmitri Bobrok is also often listed as one of his sons.
karikala-chola: Karikala was the son of Ilamcetcenni, king of Uraiyur. His name has been read as the man with the charred leg, recalling a fire in his youth, while some scholars take kari and kalan to mean slayer of elephants. The Poruṇarāṟṟuppaṭai tells the legend: his father died soon after his birth, the child was passed over and exiled, a state elephant found him hiding at Karuvur, and his enemies imprisoned him and set the prison on fire. He escaped with a scorched leg and, helped by his uncle Irum-pitar-thalaiyan, defeated them. The Pattinappalai tells of his escape without the burnt limb.

According to the Poruṇarāṟṟuppaṭai, Karikala defeated the Pandya king and the Chera king Uthiyan Cheralathan at Venni, along with eleven minor chieftains; the Chera king, wounded in the back, starved himself to death. Venni, now Kovilvenni near Needamangalam, about 25 km from Thanjavur, established him among the three crowned kings. At Vahaipparandalai, a battle the poet Paranar mentions, he defeated a confederacy of nine chieftains. He is said to have moved the Chola capital from Uraiyur to Puhar, which gave access to the sea and foreign trade.

Later traditions add wider conquests. Legends say he won the whole of Ceylon and used Sinhalese prisoners to build the Kaveri works, and Telugu Chola inscriptions in Andhra tell of a war with the Pallava king Trilochana, who refused to help raise the Kaveri's banks. The Silapathikaram has him march north and carve his tiger emblem on the Himalayas, and the Kalingattuparani repeats the story. The Grand Anicut, or Kallanai, a dam of unhewn stone 329 metres long across the main stream of the Kaveri, is credited to him and is still in use.

A lament by the poet Karungulal Adanar mourns him as a king who stormed forts, fed his minstrels and performed the Vedic sacrifice with his queen. His dates are uncertain: Nilakanta Sastri placed his reign in 190 CE, while V. R. Ramachandra Dikshitar held that the Karikala of the Silapathikaram and the Karikala of Sangam poetry were two different kings. The Thiruvalangadu plates of Rajendra Chola I include him in the Chola genealogy, and many Telugu dynasties, among them the Kakatiyas and the Telugu Chodas, claimed descent from him.
karim-khan-zand: Karim Khan was born about 1705 in the village of Pari, then part of the Safavid Empire. He belonged to the Zand tribe, a small and little-known tribe of Laks, a branch of the Lurs, concentrated in the Malayer district. In 1732 Nader Qoli Beg, who had restored Safavid rule and become the de facto ruler of the country, marched into the Zagros to subdue the tribes. He killed the Zand chief Mehdi Khan Zand and 400 of his kinsmen at Pari and moved the survivors to Abivard and Dargaz in Khorasan, where able men such as Karim Beg were taken into Nader's army. When Nader became shah in 1736, Karim served as a cavalryman of low standing.

Nader Shah was murdered in 1747, and the Zands under Karim Khan went back to western Iran. In 1748/49 Karim Khan allied with Zakariya Khan and fought the Bakhtiari chieftain Ali Mardan Khan Bakhtiari. In May 1750 they took Isfahan together, and on 29 June a 17-year-old Safavid prince, Abu Turab, was declared shah as Ismail III, as a cover for restoring the dynasty. Karim Khan was made commander of the army and charged with conquering the rest of Iran.

The partners soon quarrelled. Ali Mardan had the governor Abu'l-Fath Khan Bakhtiari deposed and killed and pillaged Fars. Karim Khan returned to Isfahan in January 1751 and defeated him in a battle in Chaharmahal, in which Ismail III and Zakariya Khan changed sides. Ali Mardan was beaten again near Nahavand and withdrew to Baghdad, and later campaigns against him ended with Karim Khan in control of all Iran except Khorasan, where Shahrukh, the grandson of Nader Shah, ruled.

Karim Khan did not take the title of shah, preferring Vakil al-ra'āyā, Representative of the People. His rule, from 1751, is described as a time when Iran recovered from 40 years of war, with renewed security and prosperity. The years from 1765 to his death mark the height of Zand rule. Relations with Britain were restored and the East India Company was allowed a trading post in southern Iran. He made Shiraz his capital and ordered several building projects there.

In 1775 and 1776 a Zand army under his brother Sadeq Khan besieged Basra, which surrendered on 16 April 1776 after an encirclement of more than a year. Karim Khan died on 1 March 1779 after six months of illness, most likely from tuberculosis, and was buried in the Nazar Garden in Shiraz. Civil war followed, and none of his descendants ruled as effectively. The last of them, Lotf Ali Khan, was killed by the Qajar ruler Agha Mohammad Khan, who became sole ruler of Iran.
karimnagar: Karimnagar, formerly known as Elagandula, is a city and district headquarters in the Indian state of Telangana. It stands on the banks of the Manair River, a tributary of the Godavari. In earlier times the place was known as Veligandula and Tellakandula, and the poet Veligandala Narayya, the principal disciple of the poet Potana, came from here. During the Nizam era the village was given its present name by Syed Karimuddin, the qiladar, or fort commander, of Elgandala.

During the Asaf Jahi dynasty (1724–1948) Karimnagar was part of Hyderabad State under the Nizams. The region grew in importance because of its strategic location and its part in agriculture, trade and military activity. It became a district in 1905. In the 1920s the District Collector, Sir John Hunter, oversaw the building of the clock tower that still stands in the city centre, and in 1937 Janab Shaikhaan Sahab built the Karimnagar Kaman to mark the Nizam's Silver Jubilee.

After the annexation of Hyderabad State into the Indian Union in 1948 the district became part of the reorganised Hyderabad state. On 1 November 1956 the Telugu speaking region of that state was merged with Andhra state to form Andhra Pradesh, and on 2 June 2014 Karimnagar became part of the newly formed state of Telangana.

Karimnagar had 397,447 inhabitants within its corporation limits at the 2011 census. Telugu is the main language, and Urdu is also widely spoken. The spring festival of Bathukamma is typical of the region. The city is nationally known for its silver filigree, a local silverware handicraft, and its economy rests on agriculture, industry and services, with granite quarries on its outskirts and paddy and cotton as the main crops. The Lower Manair Dam, with a capacity of 24.5 thousand million cubic feet, can irrigate 400,000 acres.
karkheh-river: The Karkheh, also written Karkhen, is a river in Khūzestān Province in southwest Iran, the region of ancient Susiana. It rises in the Zagros Mountains and passes west of Shush, the ancient Susa. In ancient times it fell into the Tigris just below that river's confluence with the Euphrates, very near the Iran-Iraq border. In modern times it approaches within 16 kilometres of the Dez River, turns southwest and then, northwest of Ahvaz, turns northwest and is absorbed by the Hawizeh Marshes, which straddle the Iran-Iraq border.

The river was known in ancient times as the Choaspes and also as the Eulæus, and in Hebrew as the Ulai; the Book of Daniel mentions it (8:2 and 8:16). Its peculiarly sweet water was reserved for the use of the Persian kings. It should not be confused with the Choaspes in modern Afghanistan, which flows into the Indus.

The ancient names are conjectural, because the river's bed has changed in historic times and because a nearby watercourse, the Shaur, confuses the identification. The Karkheh flows a kilometre or two west of Susa, while the Shaur runs parallel a few kilometres to the east and flows into the Dez River. When both are in flood, the whole area south of Susa can be inundated as their waters mingle. The Karkheh may at some earlier time have joined the eastern end of the Shaur, and the Shaur may be the one anciently called the Choaspes. The timing of these changes is not known with certainty.

The Karkheh Dam and hydro-power plant stand on the river. In 2007 the endangered Persian fallow deer was reintroduced to its historical habitat along the Karkheh, in the Dez and Karkheh protected areas.
karkota-dynasty: Scholars disagree on how the dynasty began, though it is held to have followed the rule of the Hunas in Kashmir. In Kalhana's account Durlabhavardhana, a man of low caste, served Baladitya, the last king of the second Gonanda dynasty, who had no son and married his daughter Anaṅgalekhā to him so that his land would not pass to in-laws. After Baladitya's death Durlabhavardhana took the throne with a minister's help and claimed descent from the Naga king Karkotaka. Atreyi Biswas rejects this story as fictitious, and the early chronology of the Rajatarangini remains disputed.

Kalhana gives Durlabhavardhana thirty-six years and his son Durlabhaka Pratapaditya fifty, a reign of growing trade with neighbouring states. Candrapida, known to the Tang annals, sent an embassy to Emperor Xuanzong of Tang in 713 asking for help against Arab invasions, and in 720 received the title King of Kashmir; he was killed by his brother Tarapida. Lalitaditya Muktapida, who ruled from 724/725 to 760/761, is credited by Kalhana with conquests across India, Afghanistan and Central Asia. Aurel Stein dismissed these as mythology, and Tansen Sen, comparing Chinese and Tibetan sources, agrees with him.

Jayapida ruled for 31 years and is also said to have campaigned far afield, though the claims lack support from other sources; Kalhana describes his later years as harsh towards the Brahmins. Under the young Cippatajayapida, crowned in 837/8, power lay with the five brothers of his mother Jayadevi, who after his murder around 840 fought one another while setting up puppet kings of the Karkota line. Avantivarman, son of Sukhavarman, finally deposed Utpalapida with the help of the minister Sura.

The Karkotas built many shrines to Vishnu but let Buddhism flourish, and their foundations include Buddhist monasteries, Buddha statues and new towns and capitals such as Pratāpapura, Parihasapura and Jayapura. Coins and cowrie shells served as money, and the state levied customs, market and other taxes. The court of Jayapida, where Vāmana was a minister and Udbhaṭa chief scholar, gave rise to a school of literary criticism in Kashmir, and Damodaragupta wrote the Kuttanimata there. Lalitaditya's reign is considered the height of Kashmiri sculpture, and Ratnākara's Haravijaya, written under Cippatajayapida, is the largest surviving mahākāvya.
karl-august-von-hardenberg: Hardenberg was the eldest of eight children of Christian Ludwig von Hardenberg, a Hanoverian colonel who later became field marshal and commander-in-chief of the Hanoverian army. He was born at Essenrode Manor near Hanover, his maternal grandfather's estate. After studying at Leipzig and Göttingen he entered the Hanoverian civil service in 1770 and, on the advice of George III, travelled widely, studying the workings of the Holy Roman Empire at Regensburg.

In 1774 he married Countess Christiane von Reventlow. Her affair with the Prince of Wales caused a scandal that forced him out of Hanoverian service. In 1782 he joined the service of the Duke of Brunswick, where his zeal for reform made him unpopular with the orthodox clergy and the conservative estates. His wife's conduct again made his position untenable, and he divorced her.

In 1792 Hardenberg was appointed administrator of the principalities of Ansbach and Bayreuth, which had passed to Prussia after the last margrave abdicated. He reformed traditional anomalies there and worked to extend Prussian influence in southern Germany. During the French Revolutionary Wars he became Prussian envoy and, as plenipotentiary at Basel, signed the peace with the French Republic in 1795. Summoned to Berlin in 1797 by King Frederick William III, he took an important post in the cabinet, and on 14 April 1804 he succeeded Count Haugwitz as foreign minister.

He would have preferred an alliance with France, but Napoleon's march of three corps through Ansbach changed the king's mind. After Austerlitz, the Treaty of Schönbrunn of 15 December 1805 gave Prussia Hanover in return for all its territories in southern Germany, and Napoleon, who disliked Hardenberg, secured his retirement. The Treaty of Tilsit later required his dismissal again.

Hardenberg was recalled to Berlin as chancellor on 6 June 1810, after Stein's forced retirement. He carried out Stein's reorganisation: the military system was reformed, serfdom abolished, municipal institutions fostered, and the civil service opened to all classes. He signed the first Peace of Paris in 1814 and was made a prince on 3 June 1814. He was Prussia's chief representative at the Congress of Vienna, though he failed to win the whole of Saxony.

His influence then fell behind that of Klemens von Metternich. Before the Carlsbad conference of 1819 he signed a convention with Metternich that the historian Heinrich von Treitschke judged a surrender of a voice in Prussia's internal affairs. Though he saw the need for constitutional reform, Hardenberg drifted with the tide against liberalism, and the constitutions he drafted never appeared. He died at Genoa on 26 November 1822.
karl-donitz: Karl Dönitz was born on 16 September 1891 in Grünau, near Berlin, the son of an engineer, Emil Dönitz, and Anna Beyer. He enlisted in the Imperial Navy in 1910 and was commissioned in 1913. In the First World War he served on the light cruiser SMS Breslau, which was transferred to the Ottoman Navy in August 1914 and operated from Constantinople against Russian forces in the Black Sea.

He transferred to the submarine service in October 1916, commanded UC-25 and then UB-68 in the Mediterranean, and on 4 October 1918, after technical difficulties, scuttled the boat and was captured by the British. He was a prisoner of war until 1919 and returned to Germany in 1920. His attack on a convoy near Malta in 1918 led him to the idea of U-boats operating in groups, the wolfpack.

Dönitz continued in the navy of the Weimar Republic, commanding torpedo boats and, from 1934, the cruiser Emden. After the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935 allowed submarines, he commanded the Weddigen flotilla of three boats. On 1 October 1939 he became Commander of the Submarines as a rear admiral. He had only 57 boats at the start of the war, of which 27 could reach the Atlantic, and torpedo failures plagued his commanders early on.

After Germany declared war on the United States on 11 December 1941 he launched Operation Drumbeat against shipping off North America. On 30 January 1943 he replaced Erich Raeder as Commander-in-Chief of the navy and became a grand admiral. From May 1943 the Allied navies, with hunter-killer groups, took the initiative. In all, 648 U-boats were lost, and around 30,000 of the 40,000 men who served in them died.
Dönitz was a dedicated Nazi and supporter of Hitler, and he formally joined the Nazi Party on 1 February 1944. On 30 April 1945, under Hitler's will, he was named his successor as head of state.

On 4 May 1945 Admiral Hans-Georg von Friedeburg, for Dönitz, surrendered German forces in the Netherlands, Denmark and north-western Germany to Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery. Dönitz then authorised Alfred Jodl to sign the instrument of unconditional surrender at Reims on 7 May. The Flensburg Government was dissolved on 23 May, when Dönitz was arrested. At the Nuremberg trials he was found not guilty of conspiracy but guilty of planning and waging wars of aggression and of crimes against the laws of war, and he was sentenced to ten years.

He was released on 1 October 1956, lived at Aumühle and published his memoirs, Zehn Jahre, Zwanzig Tage, in 1958. In them he argued that he was not a politician and so not morally responsible for the regime's crimes. He died on 24 December 1980.
karl-gunther-prince-of-schwarzburg-sonde: Karl Günther was born in Arnstadt on 7 August 1830, the third child of Hereditary Prince Gonthier Frederick Charles and his first wife, Princess Marie of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt. The death of his elder brother in 1833 put him in direct line for the throne, and when his grandfather abdicated on 19 August 1835 he became hereditary prince.

In 1850 he began studying law and literature at the University of Bonn and entered the Prussian Army as an Oberleutnant, becoming a Rittmeister two years later and a Major in 1855. On 12 June 1869 he married Princess Marie Gasparine of Saxe-Altenburg, daughter of Prince Eduard of Saxe-Altenburg, at Altenburg.

He succeeded on 17 July 1880, when his father abdicated because of an eye condition, and also became head of the House of Schwarzburg. His reign saw improvements to the principality's education, with the opening of a state school and a teacher-training college.

His marriage was childless, and his heir was his younger brother, Prince Leopold. In 1890 the brothers caused a scandal in Germany when they came to blows after Karl Günther suggested that Leopold, who wished to marry, take a commoner if no royal woman would have him. Under a family pact of 7 September 1713, the territory of an extinct branch passed to the surviving one, but the junior Rudolstadt line was also dying out. On 21 April 1896 Karl Günther, Leopold and their cousin Günther Victor agreed to admit their morganatic relative Prince Sizzo of Leutenberg to the princely house with full rights of succession, which became law on 1 June 1896.

A serious hunting accident in 1906 left him confined to a hospital bed for the rest of his life. Leopold died the same year, and when Karl Günther died in a sanatorium in Dresden on 28 March 1909, the throne passed to Günther Victor.
karl-i: Charles was born on 17 August 1887 at the Castle of Persenbeug in Lower Austria, the son of Archduke Otto Franz and Princess Maria Josepha of Saxony. He was raised a devout Catholic and, unusually for the imperial family, attended a public gymnasium, the Schottengymnasium, before entering the army. From 1906 to 1908 he served as an officer chiefly in Prague, where he studied law and political science. On 21 October 1911 he married Princess Zita of Bourbon-Parma. He became heir presumptive in 1914 when his uncle Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated at Sarajevo, an event that precipitated the First World War.

Charles succeeded his grand-uncle Franz Joseph on 21 November 1916, took the title of Supreme Commander of the army on 2 December and was crowned King of Hungary on 30 December. In 1917 he secretly began peace negotiations with France through his brother-in-law Prince Sixtus of Bourbon-Parma, but the Allies insisted that Austria recognise Italian territorial claims and he refused. When the Sixtus Affair leaked in April 1918, Charles denied involvement until French Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau published letters signed by him. Foreign minister Count Czernin resigned, and Austria-Hungary had to give Berlin full control of its armed forces, factories and railways.

From the start Charles favoured a third, Croatian, political entity beside Austria and Hungary, but the Hungarian Parliament vetoed the proposals. On 14 October 1918 he issued a People's Manifesto, and on 29 October the Croatian Sabor ended all ties with Hungary and Austria. On 11 November 1918 he issued a proclamation recognising the Austrian people's right to determine the form of the state and relinquishing every participation in the administration, although the word abdication was never used. He wrote privately that he had not abdicated and never would. In April 1919 the National Assembly dethroned the Habsburgs and banished him from German-Austria for life.

Charles went into exile in Switzerland and in 1921 made two attempts to reclaim the Hungarian throne, which failed largely because the regent, Admiral Miklós Horthy, refused his support. He was arrested and, on 19 November 1921, arrived at his last place of exile, the Portuguese island of Madeira, where he died of respiratory failure on 1 April 1922. Historians have been mixed in their judgements. Helmut Rumpler called him far too weak for the challenges facing him, while others see a brave and honourable man who tried to stop the war. The Catholic Church beatified him in 2004.
karl-i-prince-of-liechtenstein: Karl I of Liechtenstein was born on 30 July 1569, the elder son of Hartmann II, Baron of Liechtenstein, and Countess Anna Maria of Ortenburg. Emperor Rudolf II appointed him chief intendant, an important court position, which he held until 1607. He became a Catholic in 1599. In 1600 he married Anna Maria Šemberová, Baroness of Černá Hora and Lady of Aussee, and they had at least four children, among them Karl Eusebius, born on 11 April 1611, who became Prince of Liechtenstein.

In a dispute over land between Rudolf II and the heir presumptive, Archduke Matthias, Karl sided with Matthias. He played a leading role as adviser and supporter of Matthias in the coup against Rudolf, and in thanks the then Hungarian King Matthias made him a hereditary prince in 1608. As an adviser he rivalled Melchior Khlesl, Bishop of Vienna, who in the end prevailed and became the minister-favourite of Matthias, king and later emperor. In 1605 Karl established at Feldsberg in Lower Austria the first branch north of the Alps of the Hospitaller Order of Saint John of God. When Matthias was succeeded in 1619 by Emperor Ferdinand II, the Catholic monarch whose religious policy triggered the Thirty Years' War, Karl's reconversion proved advantageous.

For further aid at the Battle of White Mountain, Ferdinand II appointed Karl proconsul and vice-regent of Bohemia in 1622 and gave him the Order of the Golden Fleece. He received the Duchy of Troppau and, on 15 March 1622, the Silesian Duchy of Jägerndorf, together with much confiscated Protestant rebel property. He died in Prague on 12 February 1627.

His title of prince was only honorary, since the family held no territory with semi-sovereignty in the Holy Roman Empire. The territory of Liechtenstein was first purchased in 1699 and 1712 and declared a principality in 1719, whereby the princes became its monarchs.
karl-kautsky: Karl Kautsky was born in Prague on 16 October 1854. His father Johann was a Czech theatrical scene designer and his mother Minna Jaich an actress and writer, and the family moved to Vienna in 1863. After a year at the Melk seminary, which he found oppressive, he attended the Academic Gymnasium in Vienna from 1866 to 1874, a mediocre student whose interests ran to the Paris Commune and to history and philosophy. For two years from 1868 he considered himself a Czech nationalist. At about twenty he joined the Austrian Social Democratic Workers' Party in January 1875, and he became a Marxist in the early 1880s while in exile in Zurich.

In 1883 Kautsky founded Die Neue Zeit, which he edited until 1917 and which became the most prestigious international Marxist journal. From 1885 to 1890 he lived mainly in London and became a close friend of Friedrich Engels. After the Anti-Socialist Laws lapsed he wrote the theoretical section of the SPD's Erfurt Program of 1891, with Eduard Bernstein writing the short-term demands. From 1896 he defended orthodoxy against Bernstein's revisionism.

In August 1914 he urged the SPD's parliamentary group to abstain on war credits, and when it voted for them he broke with the party and in 1917 co-founded the Independent Social Democratic Party of Germany. After the revolution of 1918 to 1919 he chaired the Socialization Commission, and he criticised the Bolsheviks in The Dictatorship of the Proletariat (1918). He rejoined the SPD in 1922, drafted its Heidelberg Program in 1925 and moved to Vienna in 1924. He fled to Amsterdam after the Anschluss of 1938 and died there on 17 October 1938.

Kautsky held that a socialist revolution was inevitable but could not be forced, and that a socialist party should organise workers and win reforms within parliamentary democracy until conditions were ripe. After the Russian Revolution of 1905 he took a centrist position between reformism and radicalism, and he opposed the council system in 1918 as undemocratic. He also tried to join Marxism with Darwin, arguing that humanity inherited communist instincts of solidarity from its animal ancestors. Leszek Kołakowski called him the chief architect and embodiment of Marxist orthodoxy, and he was known in his time as the Pope of Marxism.
karl-ludwig-sand: Sand was born on 5 October 1795 to Gottfried Christoph Sand and Dorothea Johanna Wilhelmina Schöpf. He attended the Latin school at Wunsiedel from 1804 and from 1810 the Gymnasium at Hof, where he lived with its rector, Georg Heinrich Saalfrank, a friend of his Enlightened Protestant family. When the school closed under Montgelas's reforms he followed his teacher to the New Gymnasium in Regensburg, finishing in September 1814, and in November entered the University of Tübingen. In 1815 he volunteered under Major von Falkenhausen, took part in the Battle of Waterloo and reached Paris, returning traumatised and disillusioned.

At the University of Erlangen in 1816 Sand founded the Burschenschaft Teutonia with his friend Georg Friedrich Christoph Dittmar; its 80 students met at castle ruins they called Ruttli. The destruction of Ruttli by the rival Landsmannschaft and Dittmar's drowning in 1817 deepened his depression. From 1817 he studied at the University of Jena, heard Jakob Friedrich Fries, Heinrich Luden and Lorenz Oken, and was among the students at the Wartburg festival, where Kotzebue's History of the German Empires was burned.

In a diary entry of 5 May 1818 he called Kotzebue a traitor to the nation. On 23 March 1819, calling himself Henry, he visited Kotzebue's house in Mannheim, returned that afternoon and stabbed him repeatedly. Seeing Kotzebue's four-year-old son watching, he stabbed himself, handed a servant his written statement and stabbed himself again in the street, but survived.

The Mannheim Hofgericht sentenced Sand to death on 5 May 1820, and he was beheaded by the executioner Franz Wilhelm Widmann on 20 May. Through his execution he became a martyr to many German nationalists who sought a united German state. The Carlsbad Decrees that Metternich's meeting produced outlawed the Burschenschaften and barred their members from public office, teaching and study at the universities. Alexandre Dumas wrote of his life and published excerpts from his journals and letters after visiting Widmann's son in Mannheim in 1838, Alexander Pushkin recalled him in the poem The Dagger, and three German films have told his story.
karl-marx: Karl Marx was born on 5 May 1818 to Heinrich Marx and Henriette Pressburg at Brückengasse 664 in Trier, then part of the Kingdom of Prussia. His family was originally Jewish but had converted to Christianity before his birth. His father, a lawyer, had converted to the state Evangelical Church of Prussia to keep his career after Prussia annexed the Rhineland and Jewish emancipation was abrogated. Heinrich was a man of the Enlightenment and a classical liberal who took part in agitation for a constitution and reforms.

Marx was the third of nine children and became the eldest son when his brother Moritz died in 1819. He was baptised into the Lutheran Church on 28 August 1824. His father educated him privately until 1830, when he entered the Gymnasium zu Trier. Its headmaster, Hugo Wyttenbach, employed many liberal humanists, and in 1832 police raided the school and found literature promoting political liberalism among the students. Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841, then turned to radical journalism.

In Paris Marx wrote his Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844 and began a close collaboration with Friedrich Engels. After moving to Brussels they were active in the Communist League. In London Marx wrote the Grundrisse notebooks and the three volumes of Das Kapital, the second and third of which Engels published after his death, in 1885 and 1894. He became a leading figure in the International Workingmen's Association, and in 1875 wrote the Critique of the Gotha Programme.

His thought drew on Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel's dialectic, on the classical political economy of Adam Smith and David Ricardo, and on French socialist thought. Unlike Hegel, who saw spirit driving history, Marx argued for the primacy of matter over idea. He held that societies develop through class conflict, in capitalism between the bourgeoisie who control the means of production and the proletariat who sell their labour power for wages, and he criticised utopian socialists for relying on small-scale communities.

Marx died on 14 March 1883 and was buried in Highgate Cemetery. His ideas had a profound impact on world politics after the Russian Revolution of 1917. His followers have often disagreed over how to interpret him, and tendencies including Leninism, Marxism–Leninism, Trotskyism, Maoism and Luxemburgism each claim to be his most accurate interpreter. In scholarship his work contributed to the birth of modern sociology, and Isaiah Berlin considered him the true founder of the discipline in so far as anyone can claim the title.
karl-philipp-prince-of-schwarzenberg: Karl Philipp was born on 18 or 19 April 1771 in Vienna, one of thirteen children of Johann Nepomuk Anton of Schwarzenberg and Marie Eleonore, Countess of Öttingen-Wallerstein; seven of the children did not reach adulthood. The family held land in Franconia and Bohemia and was close to the House of Habsburg, and in 1788 he entered the Austrian army as a lieutenant. In 1789 he fought against the Ottoman Empire in the Austro-Turkish War, and he became a major in 1792.

In the French Revolutionary War Schwarzenberg served in the advance guard of Prince Josias of Coburg in 1793. At Le Cateau-Cambrésis in 1794 his charge at the head of his regiment, supported by twelve British squadrons, broke a French corps of around 25,000 men and captured 32 guns, and he was decorated with the Knight's Cross of the Military Order of Maria Theresa. He became a general-major in 1796 and a Generalleutnant in 1799. In 1809 he led a cavalry division at the Battle of Wagram, which the Austrians lost.
