On 19 January 1990 mosques issued declarations that Pandit men had to leave Kashmir, convert to Islam or be killed. According to a number of authors about 100,000 of some 140,000 Pandits left the valley; others give higher figures. A Jammu and Kashmir government report counted 219 members of the community killed in the region between 1989 and 2004. Many refugees lived in camps in Jammu, and by 2011 only an estimated 2,700-3,400 Pandits remained in the valley.

The community is divided into three subcastes, which probably took shape in the 14th century: the Guru or Bāchabat, priests; the Jotish, astrologers; and the Kārkun, historically employed mainly by the government, to which most belong. All three dine and teach together, but only the Jotish and Kārkun intermarry. Major festivals are Shivratri, called Herath in Kashmiri, and Navreh, the lunar new year, and the Mata Kheerbhawani shrine at Tullamulla is among the holiest. Pandits traditionally eat mutton and fish but not beef or pork. Descent is reckoned in the male line, with family names such as Kaul, Dhar, Raina and Sapru.
kashta: Kashta succeeded Alara as king of the Kushite dynasty in ancient Nubia. His name, k3š-t3, means of the land of Kush and is often translated simply as The Kushite. He is thought to have been either Alara's brother or unrelated to him; the older view, going back to Dunham and Macadam, that both kings married their sisters rests on no clear evidence, as the historian Morkot points out. His only known wife was Pebatjma, and his children are thought to have included Piye, Shabaka, Queen Khensa and Amenirdis I.

Kashta ruled Nubia from Napata, 400 km north of present-day Khartoum, while extending control over Upper Egypt. The key step was the installation of his daughter Amenirdis I in Thebes as presumptive God's Wife of Amun, in line to succeed Shepenupet I, the daughter of Osorkon III; this legitimised the Kushite takeover of the Thebaid. The scholar László Török thinks Kushite garrisons were probably stationed in Thebes, and that the takeover was peaceful, since the descendants of Osorkon III, Takelot III and Rudamun kept a high social status there.

A stela of his reign bearing his prenomen Nimaatre was found at the temple of Khnum at Elephantine, attesting his control of that region. The length of his reign is unknown. Some sources credit him as founder of the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty, as the first Kushite king known to have extended his kingdom's influence into Upper Egypt. Under his rule the Kushite population between the third and fourth Cataracts of the Nile rapidly adopted Egyptian traditions, religion and culture.

Kashta was buried at el-Kurru, the royal cemetery that also holds the tombs of several of his successors. His pyramid lies in a row of at least eight east of the older tumulus tombs, beside one presumed to be Pebatjma's, while a further row holds the pyramids of Piye, Shabaka and Tanutamani. Piye, his successor, went on to conquer Egypt.
kashtiliash-iv: Kaštiliašu IV was the twenty-eighth Kassite king of Babylon and succeeded Šagarakti-Šuriaš, who may have been his father; he ruled for eight years. He may have resided in the Palace of the Stag and the Palace of the Mountain Sheep at Dur-Kurigalzu, named in a jeweller's archive of the time. At least 177 economic texts are dated to his reign, recording items for a chariot, flour, dates, oil and salt for offerings, and butter and oil received at the expense of the governor of Nippur.

Tension with Assyria may have been building for some time. The Hittite king Tudḫaliya, defeated by the Assyrians at the Battle of Nihriya, named the king of Babylon as his equal in a treaty with his vassal Šaušgamuwa of Amurru, hinting at an understanding between them. Kaštiliašu also gave land, and presumably asylum, to a Hurrian fugitive from Assyria's vassal Ḫanigalbat, and reconfirmed a land grant first made by Kurigalzu II for service in an earlier war against Assyria.

According to the Tukulti-Ninurta Epic, the Assyrian king was provoked by a treacherous attack that broke a treaty between their ancestors Adad-nīrāri I and Kadašman-Turgu. Tukulti-Ninurta claimed to have captured Kaštiliašu single-handed and to have trod on his neck as on a footstool. He demolished the walls of Babylon, massacred many of its people, carried off the statue of Marduk from the Esagila temple and called himself king of Sumer and Akkad. A letter found at Dūr-Katlimmu tells of a Babylonian king, perhaps Kaštiliašu, travelling into exile with his wife and a large retinue.

Written entirely from the Assyrian side, the epic casts Kaštiliašu as the transgressor of an oath whom the gods had abandoned. Chronicle P says Tukulti-Ninurta ruled Babylon through governors for seven years, though the order of events is disputed. After his overthrow Kidin-Hutran III, king of Elam, led two incursions into Babylonia, explained either as loyalty to the fallen Kassite dynasty or as raids exploiting the over-extended Assyrians. When Assyrian rule there collapsed, the Kassite nobles rebelled and put Kaštiliašu's son, Adad-šuma-ušur, on the throne.
kasimbazar: Cossimbazar lies in Murshidabad district on the triangle of land between the Hooghly, Padma and Jalangi rivers, which English documents until the early 19th century called the island of Cossimbazar, naming the Hooghly itself the Cossimbazar river. According to the historian Irfan Habib, the name Qāsimbāzār probably comes from Qāsim Khān, governor of the Bengal Subah early in the reign of Shah Jahan.

The town's history cannot be traced back before the 17th century, but it was important long before the foundation of Murshidabad. After Satgaon declined when the mouth of the Saraswati river silted up, Cossimbazar became the great trading centre of Bengal, unchallenged until the foundation of Calcutta. The first English agency of the East India Company was set up there in 1658, and from 1667 the chief of the factory sat ex officio on the council. Armenian merchants also settled there and built St. Mary's Church in 1758.

Nearness to Murshidabad, the capital of the Nawabs of Bengal, brought wealth and political weight but also danger. In 1757 the factory was the first of the company's to be taken by the Nawab Siraj-ud-dowlah, and its resident and his assistant Warren Hastings were taken prisoner to Murshidabad. The town later became the seat of the Maharajas of Cossimbazar, descendants of Kanta Babu, Hastings's moneylender, who built a palace there partly of carved stone from the palace of Chait Singh of Benares.

In 1811 the town was still known for its silks, hosiery and ivory work. Its climate worsened, probably through endemic malaria, cultivated land shrank and jungle spread, and in 1813 a sudden change in the course of the Hooghly left a swamp around the old wharves. The population was 3,538 in 1829 and only 1,262 in 1901.

Cossimbazar is now a suburban area of Berhampore in the Indian state of West Bengal, on the Sealdah–Lalgola railway line. Its Dutch cemetery, with graves from 1721, a British cemetery holding the grave of Hastings's first wife Mary, the Armenian church, restored in 2005, and two mansions of local landlords survive.
kasimov: The first inhabitants of the area were a Finnic tribe called the Meshchyora, later assimilated by Russians and Tatars. The Vladimir-Suzdal ruler Yuri Dolgorukiy founded the town in 1152 as Grodets, then Gorodets Meshchyorsky. The Mongols destroyed it in 1376, and it was soon rebuilt as Novy Nizovoy. After the Battle of Suzdal in 1445, in which Grand Duke Vasily II was taken prisoner, the Meshchyora lands were given to Oluğ Möxämmäd, Khan of the Kazan Khanate, as a ransom for the sovereign's life.

In 1452 Vasily II, Grand Prince of Moscow, gave the town to the Kazan prince Qasim, who served as tribute inspector of the Great Horde and then entered Russian service. By other accounts Qasim and his brother Yosif fled from Kazan after losing a contest for the throne to their brother Mäxmüd. After 1471 the town was known as Qasim city, and it remained the capital of the Qasim Khanate until the khanate was absorbed into Russia in 1681.

A group of Tatars settled in Kasimov in the 15th century and are now known as Qasim Tatars. They speak the Mishar dialect, mixed with the Middle Tatar dialect of the Tatar language. In the 19th century the town became known for its waiters, who staffed many of the hotels of St Petersburg. In the 17th century it was divided in three: the Old Town and the Tatar Town, ruled by the khan and Tatar noblemen, the Yamskoy Town of Russian commoners, ruled from Moscow, and the Marfin Town, ruled by the Kasimov voivodes.

Historical buildings include the Khan's Mosque, with a limestone minaret dated either to 1467 or to the 1550s, the mausoleum of Shahghali Khan of 1555 and that of Afghan Moxammad Khan of 1658. Four Russian Orthodox churches also stand there: the Church of the Epiphany, St Nicholas Church and Trinity Church of the 17th century, and the Cathedral of the Ascension of the 19th century.
kaskaskia: The name Kaskaskia derives from the old Miami–Illinois word for a katydid, kaaskaaskia, which later appeared in the Peoria and Miami dialects as kaahkaahkia; Gravier's early 18th-century Illinois dictionary already gives caskaskia as both the insect and an Illinois nation. The Kaskaskia were one of about a dozen related tribes of the Illiniwek Confederation, whose lands reached from modern Arkansas through eastern Missouri and most of Illinois into Iowa. Their first contact with Europeans reportedly took place in 1667 at a Jesuit mission station near present-day Green Bay, Wisconsin.

In 1703 the French established a permanent mission, settlement and fort at Kaskaskia, in the Illinois Country of New France, which became the capital of Upper Louisiana. From the start it was a mixed community: in 1707 its population was estimated at 2,200, most of them Illinois Indians living somewhat apart, and of 21 children baptised there before 1714, 18 had Indian mothers and 20 French fathers. In 1718 the larger Fort de Chartres was built nearby, and the French brought African slaves from Saint-Domingue to work in the lead mines.

As allies of France, the Illinois fought the Iroquois, Sioux, Meskwaki, Quapaw, Chickasaw, Cherokee and Osage, and epidemics of European diseases, which historians believe caused the most deaths, cut their numbers further. Early French explorers had estimated them at 6,000 to more than 20,000; by 1763 only a fraction remained. After a Peoria warrior killed Pontiac in 1769, the Ottawa, Sauk, Meskwaki, Miami, Kickapoo and Potawatomi devastated the Illinois and occupied their lands along the Illinois River, though some historians question this account of the retaliation.

From 1766 the British kept a small detachment at Kaskaskia, garrisoned in the former Jesuit compound and called Fort Gage after Fort de Chartres was abandoned in 1772. During the American Revolutionary War, George Rogers Clark captured the town and the fort on 4 July 1778.

The descendants of the Kaskaskia, together with the Wea and Piankeshaw, are enrolled in the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma, a federally recognised tribe. Their name survives in the Kaskaskia River, in Kaskaskia College near Centralia and in Kaskaskia, the first capital of Illinois, while the city of DuQuoin is named after Jean Baptiste DuQuoin, a Kaskaskia chief of their later history.
kassaman: Under French rule the native population of Algeria was given very few political rights for a century. A nationalist movement began in the 1920s and gained strength after World War II, when a government commitment to grant French Algeria autonomy failed to materialise. A prominent member of the movement was Moufdi Zakaria, a Mozabite Berber poet affiliated with the Algerian People's Party. He was jailed and tortured on several occasions between the 1920s and 1962.

He wrote the words in April 1955, during one of these imprisonments, in Barberousse Prison. Since he had no paper or writing instruments, he reportedly wrote the lyrics with his own blood on the walls of his cell. The music was composed by the Egyptian composer Mohamed Fawzi, who was asked to take on the task after two earlier submissions by other composers, one of them by Mohamed Triki, had been rejected.

The lyrics read as a war song. They promote nationalist ideals on the front line, glorify the actions of the National Liberation Front and present armed uprising as the only route to independence. The song alludes to France, the former colonial ruler, in connection with the violent struggle for independence, and foretells that a day of reckoning will come for it. Usually only the first verse is performed, for brevity, as at sporting events.

The words and music were officially adopted in 1962, the year in which the Évian Accords were signed. They paved the way for a referendum in which Algerians voted overwhelmingly for independence, which was then granted. Although Kassaman was intended only as a provisional national anthem, it has endured. In November 2008 an amendment to Article 5 of the Constitution of Algeria declared it immutable, given its association with the country's revolution, and confirmed that the anthem comprises all of its verses, ending the discussion of whether the unfavourable reference to France was still appropriate.
kassel: Kassel lies on both sides of the Fulda River in northern Hesse. It was first mentioned in 913, when King Conrad I signed two deeds there, in a place called Chasella or Chassalla, a fortification at a bridge over the Fulda. The origin of the name is unproven: it may come from the ancient Castellum Cattorum, a castle of the Chatti, or from words meaning a valley and a hall. A deed of 1189 shows that Cassel had city rights, though the date they were granted is not known. The first castle was built in 1277 and later replaced by a Renaissance palace that burned down in 1811.

In 1567 the Landgraviate of Hesse, until then centred in Marburg, was divided among four sons, and Kassel became the capital of Hesse-Kassel and a centre of Calvinist Protestantism in Germany. Strong fortifications protected the Protestant stronghold, and the Rosicrucian Fama Fraternitatis was first published there in 1617. In 1685 Landgrave Charles gave refuge to 1,700 Huguenots, in the new borough of Oberneustadt. In the late 18th century Hesse-Kassel sold auxiliary troops to the British crown to help suppress the American Revolution, and the money financed palaces. The Brothers Grimm lived in Kassel in the early 19th century, where they collected and wrote most of their fairy tales.

Napoleon annexed the Electorate, and Kassel was the capital of the Kingdom of Westphalia under his brother Jérôme from 1807. The Electorate was restored in 1813 and annexed by Prussia in 1866, after it sided with Austria in the Austro-Prussian War. Kassel then ceased to be a princely residence but became an industrial centre and railway junction, home of Henschel & Son, the largest locomotive maker in Germany at the end of the 19th century. After the Battle of Sedan in 1870 Napoleon III was held prisoner at Wilhelmshöhe Palace.

In the Second World War a subcamp of Dachau provided forced labour for the Henschel works, which included tank plants. The heaviest bombing destroyed 90 per cent of the downtown area, killed some 10,000 people and left 150,000 homeless. The US 80th Infantry Division took the city in house-to-house fighting from 1 to 4 April 1945. Most old buildings in the centre were not restored, and large parts of the inner city were rebuilt in the style of the 1950s, though the Museum Fridericianum was restored. Kassel had 201,048 inhabitants in December 2020 and has a university. The Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the documenta exhibitions of contemporary art are held there.
kassite-dynasty: The Kassites, called kaššû in Mesopotamian texts and possibly the Kossaioi of later Greek sources, were a people of unknown origin; it has been suggested that they came from the Zagros Mountains. In 1595 BCE the Hittite king Mursili I defeated Samsi-Ditana of Babylon and carried off the statue of Marduk from the Esagila temple, ending the Amorite dynasty. According to the Babylonian king list, Agum II then took over Babylon as the tenth ruler of a Kassite line founded by Gandas. It took the Kassite kings more than a century to consolidate their power, under conditions that remain unclear.

The 14th and 13th centuries BCE were the dynasty's height. Its kings bore the title of great king and exchanged letters, emissaries and gifts of gold with the rulers of Egypt, Hati, Mitanni and Assyria, as the Amarna letters record, in the Middle Babylonian form of Akkadian. When Ashur-uballit I of Assyria broke free from Mitanni in 1365 BCE, a long rivalry with the north began. After his grandson Kara-hardash was murdered, Ashur-uballit invaded and placed Kurigalzu II on the throne. Conflict lasted over a century and culminated when Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria defeated Kashtiliash IV, sacked Babylon and deported thousands of people.

The Kassite kings kept Babylon's traditions rather than replacing them. They used the new title king of Karduniash beside older ones, acted as warriors, judges and builders of temples, and gave high offices to members of the royal family. Horses and the light chariot were apparently a Kassite specialty. Royal land grants, recorded on the carved boundary stones called kudurrus, are the best documented part of the economy, while the largest archive, some 12,000 tablets from Nippur, is mostly unpublished. Surveys suggest a slow recovery in which small villages came to outnumber towns.

Marduk grew steadily in importance in the pantheon, and the original Kassite deities, such as the storm god Burias, gained little place in it. Akkadian entered the scribal schools, and Standard Babylonian took shape as the classic literary form of the language. A king named Kurigalzu founded the new city of Dur-Kurigalzu, whose palace and temples are the only monumental complex of the period yet found.
kassites: The origin of the Kassites is uncertain. Several names thought to be Kassite appear in economic documents of the Ur III period, but their origin there is ambiguous, and many historians place their original homeland in the Zagros Mountains. One theory makes them a Caucasian people akin to the Hurrians with an Indo-European ruling element; another, disputed, derives them from the region of the Caspian Sea. Their language is most likely an isolate, related to neither Indo-European nor Semitic languages, though some linguists propose a link to Hurro-Urartian. The earliest person with a Kassite name in Babylonia is recorded in 1770 BCE, and a year name of Samsu-iluna of Babylon refers to a campaign against the Kassite army.

After the Hittite sack of Babylon in 1531 BCE the Kassites took control of Babylonia, which they held until about 1155 BCE on the short chronology. Their rulers regained the idol of Marduk, returned it to Babylon and made him the equal of the Kassite god Shuqamuna; they renamed the city Karanduniash. The fall of the First Sealand dynasty in 1460 BCE left a power vacuum that they filled. After the Hittites destroyed Mitanni in the early 14th century BCE, Assyria rose, and the Kassites, Hittites and Assyrians formed a three-way balance with Elam and Egypt exerting influence, joined by trade, treaties and intermarriage. Fourteen of the Amarna Letters are exchanges between the pharaoh and the Kassite king.

Under Kurigalzu I, in the mid-14th century BCE, the Kassites conquered Elam and sacked Susa. He also founded the new city of Dur-Kurigalzu, with palaces and temples to Enlil, Ninlil and Ninurta. Conflict with Assyria continued for centuries, and for a time early in the reign of Tukulti-Ninurta I Assyria had the upper hand. The Elamites of the Shutrukid dynasty finally conquered Babylonia in the 12th century BCE and carried off the statue of Marduk. According to the Assyrian Synchronistic Chronicle, which is not considered reliable, the last king, Enlil-nadin-ahi, was taken to Susa in 1155 BCE and died there.

Kassite Babylonia was ruled by kings through a bureaucracy supported by an aristocracy of chariot warriors, and their arrival coincided with the introduction of the horse-drawn chariot. Over the centuries the Kassites were absorbed into the Babylonian population, and eight of the last kings bore Akkadian names. After the dynasty was overthrown the provincial administration continued, and the country remained united under the Second Dynasty of Isin. About 12,000 documents of the period have been recovered, only about a tenth of them published; kudurrus, stone stelae recording land grants, are another major source. Groups called Kassites, known to the Greeks as Cossaei, lived in the mountains for centuries and were a target of Alexander the Great's last winter campaign, in 324/323 BCE.
kastamonu: Kastamonu lies at an elevation of 904 metres in the southern part of Kastamonu Province in northern Turkey, and it is the seat of the province and of its central district. Several explanations of its name are given. One derives it from Paphlagonia, the Greek name for the Black Sea region, whose Paphlagonians dominated it about 1000 BCE. Another derives it from Kastama, a name for the same region in the Hittite period. A third combines Gas, the Kashkas who were among the first settlers, with Tumanna, the name of a city or region there, and a fourth combines the Latin kastra, castle, with the Komnenos dynasty of Byzantine emperors.

Ibn Battuta visited the city, called it one of the largest and finest cities, with abundant commodities and low prices, and stayed forty days. The city's best-known Sufi saint is Sheikh Shaban Veli, who died in 976 AH, or 1569 CE. In the early 20th century nickel was mined in the area around Kastamonu.

On 23 August 1925 Mustafa Kemal, later known as Atatürk, began the Dress Code Revolution at Kastamonu with a speech on the hat and dress reform during a visit to the city, given in the building of the Republican People's Party. The building is now the Archeological Museum of Kastamonu, which also exhibits the possessions Atatürk used on that visit.

Kastamonu has a population of 125,622 at the 2021 count. Its Kastamonu Lisesi, also known as Abdurrahman Paşa Lisesi, was the first modern high school established in Anatolia in the late Ottoman Empire. Kastamonu University was founded in 2006 by uniting colleges, schools and institutes that had belonged to Ankara University and Gazi University. The city is the main railway terminus of the West Black Sea region. Taşköprü, in the province, is known for kuyu kebabı, a lamb dish slow-cooked in a sealed pit.
kasubi-tombs: The site covers around 26 hectares on Kasubi hill, about 5 kilometres north-west of the centre of Kampala. A royal palace there was built in 1882 by Muteesa I, the 35th kabaka of Buganda, to replace one built by his father Ssuuna II in 1820, and it became a royal burial ground on his death in 1884. It is one of 31 royal tombs across the kingdom since its founding in the 13th century. Traditionally a king's body was buried in one place and his jawbone, believed to hold his soul, had a separate shrine; Kasubi is unusual in holding the tombs of four kabakas: Muteesa I, Mwanga II, Daudi Chwa II and Sir Edward Muteesa II.

A gatehouse leads to a small courtyard, the drum house holding the royal drums, and then to the circular main courtyard on the hilltop, enclosed by a reed fence. Opposite the entrance stands the main building, Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, 31 metres in circumference and 7.5 metres high. It is circular, with a dome of thick thatch resting on 52 rings of palm fronds, which stand for the 52 clans of the Baganda, over a frame of wooden poles, reed wattle and daub. Steel, concrete and brick were added in a renovation of 1938, largely hidden behind traditional materials.

The tombs lie in a sacred forest inside the building, hidden by a barkcloth curtain, on floors covered with lemon grass and palm-leaf mats. Around the courtyard stand houses for the kabaka's widows, who tend the graves, and for royal officials, among them the Nalinya, the spiritual guardian. The Ngo clan makes and decorates bark cloth there and the Ngeye clan keeps up traditional thatching. Bark cloth fig trees mark the boundary.

The kingdom of Buganda managed the site until Milton Obote abolished it in 1966, and again after it was reinstated in 1993. The site became protected under Ugandan law in 1972. It remains an important spiritual and political place for the Baganda. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in December 2001, describing it as an outstanding example of building with purely vegetal materials in the region.

On 16 March 2010 fire almost completely destroyed the main buildings, though the inner sanctum, with the remains of the kabakas, was reported intact. The site was placed on the list of World Heritage Sites in Danger in July 2010. Reconstruction began in 2014, with funds raised by a campaign called Etofaali and by Japan.
kasugayama-castle: Kasugayama was a yamashiro, a mountain castle of the Sengoku period, in the Nakayashiki neighbourhood of Jōetsu. It spread over two ridges at the summit of Mount Kasuga, 180 metres high, and had no stone walls: it was made of many enclosures, or kuruwa, with earthen or clay ramparts and dry moats, cut as terraces at different levels on the mountain. It stood at the centre of a network of smaller forts within two to six kilometres.

The core, just below the peak, held a watch tower, a Buddhist temple, Uesugi Kenshin's residence and a garden. On the south ridge was the fortified residence of his adopted son Uesugi Kagekatsu, with that of the retainer Kakizaki Kageie below it; on the north ridge lived the retainer Naoe Kagetsuna, and just below the centre Kenshin's other adopted son, Uesugi Kagetora. Smaller enclosures held retainers, barracks and warehouses.

An older castle on the site dates to the 14th century, but little is known of it. The castle was probably built by Nagao Tamekage and passed to Nagao Harukage, whose younger brother, born Nagao Kagetora and later known as Uesugi Kenshin, became its lord in 1548. Kenshin set out from it against Takeda Shingen at the Battle of Kawanakajima in 1561.

After Kenshin's death in 1578, Kagekatsu won the castle in a brief fight with Kagetora over the inheritance. Weakened by wars with Oda Nobunaga and the Odawara Hōjō clan, the Uesugi submitted to Toyotomi Hideyoshi. After their transfer, Hori Hideharu, son of Hori Hidemasa, took the castle and dug a large water moat round its town, the jōkamachi, as the local people resented the Uesugi's departure. In 1600 he moved his seat to Fukushima Castle near the port of Naoetsu, and by 1607 Kasugayama was deserted.

The ruins have been protected as a National Historic Site since 1935. No buildings survive on the grounds, but one gate is preserved at the nearby Rinsen-ji temple, which has a small museum. Kasugayama Shrine was founded at the foot of the mountain in 1901, and the inner bailey, about 20 minutes' walk above it, looks out over Jōetsu, the Kubiki Plain and the Sea of Japan.
kasur: Kasur is a city south of Lahore in the Pakistani province of Punjab, near the border with India, and the headquarters of Kasur District. Its name comes from the Arabic and Persian qasur, meaning palaces or forts. The city is an aggregation of fortified hamlets overlooking the alluvial valleys of the Beas and Sutlej rivers. According to a legend, it was founded by Prince Kusha of the Ramayana, son of Rama and Sita, but historical records reject an ancient founding and date it to 1525, when it began as a fortified settlement.

The region was agricultural, with forests, in the time of the Indus Valley civilisation, and was ruled in turn by the Maurya Empire, the Indo-Greek kingdom, the Kushan Empire, the Gupta Empire and others. In 1005 Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni took over the region, and Sufi missionaries sent there made Punjab predominantly Muslim. The Kheshgi tribe of Pashtuns, migrating from Kabul in 1525 in the reign of Babur, built small forts and established the Kheshgi chieftaincy. Kasur grew into a town of fortified hamlets called kots, and under Mughal rule it flourished in commerce and trade. It became the home of the Sufi saint and poet Bulleh Shah, who is buried in a large shrine there.

After the decline of the Mughal Empire the region fell into a power vacuum, and Ahmad Shah Durrani captured Kasur. The Sikhs sacked the city in 1747 under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and again in 1763. Ranjit Singh of the Sikh Empire captured it in 1807 in the Battle of Kasur. In the First Anglo-Sikh War the city was occupied by Company forces on 10 February 1846. Under British rule canals irrigated large areas of the district, and riots in April 1919 after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre destroyed civic infrastructure, including the railway station.

After the formation of Pakistan in 1947 the Hindus and Sikhs of Kasur migrated to India, while Muslim refugees from India settled there. The population is overwhelmingly Punjabi-speaking, with Urdu the second language. Kasur emerged after independence as a major centre of leather tanning, and it remains known as the burial place of Bulleh Shah.
kasym-khan: His full name was Muhammad Qasim bin Janibek Khan, shortened as a ruler's name to Qasim Khan. He was the fourth khan of the Kazakh Khanate. Although Burunduk Khan held the title of khan, control of the government had already passed into Qasim's hands, and he eventually sent Burunduk into exile; Burunduk died in Samarkand. When Qasim's brother Adik Khan died, Qasim married his widow, Sultana Nigar Khanim, a daughter of Yunus Khan of Moghulistan.

Early in his reign Qasim fought his cousin Muhammad Shaybani for control of the Desht-i-Kipchak. After Shaybani and the Uzbeks suffered heavy losses in battles near Lake Balkhash, the Uzbek Khanate agreed to give the Kazakhs all the former Uzbek lands north of the Syr Darya. The Kazakh Khanate held these lands until the 18th century, when it came under attack from the Tsardom of Russia in the north, the Emirate of Bukhara in the south and the Dzungars in the east.

He is credited with the first written law code of the Kazakhs and with some of the first written records of the Kazakh language, which used the Arabic script until the early 20th century. A devout Muslim and a patron of the arts, he oversaw the building of many mosques and mausoleums, especially in northern Kazakhstan. Sunni Islam, which had begun to spread over the steppe in the 13th century, became firmly established under him and the Shaybanid rulers before him. Towards the end of his reign he allied with the Timurid prince Babur, who shared his enmity towards Muhammad Shaybani.

Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat, governor of Kashmir, wrote at length of Qasim's successes in the Tarikh-i-Rashidi, and counted him, after the Ottoman sultan Selim I and the Safavid shah Ismail I, among the most powerful rulers of the eastern Islamic world. Qasim had three sons by two wives: Abu'l Khair by Sultan Nigar Khanum, and Haqnazar and Muhammed by Khanyk Sultan Khanum. Muhammed, the eldest, succeeded him as khan, and Haqnazar reigned long after.
kataragama: Kataragama lies in Uva province, 228 km southeast of Colombo, in a dry region surrounded by jungle, and adjoins Yala National Park. The Sinhalese name is commonly read as village in the desert, from katara, desert, and gama, village, while some scholars derive it from Karthikeya Grama, the village of Kartikeya, an explanation not all accept. The Manik Ganga, the River of Gems, is used for ritual bathing, and local people hold that its waters heal. The deity is held to reside on the hill of Wædahiti Kanda just outside the town.

The surrounding area has evidence of human habitation at least 125,000 years ago, and of Mesolithic and Neolithic settlement. The Mahavamsa names a town, Kajjaragama, whose dignitaries came to receive the sacred Bo sapling sent from Ashoka's Mauryan Empire in 288 BCE. Kataragama served as the capital of a number of kings of the Ruhuna kingdom and sheltered kings from the north when South Indian kingdoms invaded. Archaeological evidence suggests the Kiri Vehera was built or renovated in the first century BCE. The area is believed to have been abandoned around the 13th century.

By the 15th century the town drew Hindu pilgrims from India and Sri Lanka, and by the 16th century its shrine was identified with Skanda-Kumara, a guardian deity of Sinhala Buddhism. Scholars such as Paul Younger and Heinz Bechert suggest that the rites of the temple's native priests reflect Vedda practices, and that Buddhists and Hindus took over a Vedda sacred place in the medieval period.

Kataragama is one of the 16 principal places of Buddhist pilgrimage in Sri Lanka; the Bo tree behind the temple is held to be one of eight saplings of the Sri Maha Bodhiya at Anuradhapura. Hindu devotees perform kavadi, and the nearby shrine of Sella Katirkamam is dedicated to Ganesha. The annual festival in July and August, which celebrates the god's marriage to a Vedda princess, swells the town of about 18,220 people, recorded in 2012, to a few hundred thousand.
kate-sheppard: Kate Sheppard was born Catherine Wilson Malcolm on 10 March 1848 at Liverpool, to Scottish parents. After her father died in 1862 she lived with an uncle, a Free Church of Scotland minister at Nairn, who instilled in her the values of Christian socialism. In 1868 the family sailed for New Zealand, arriving at Lyttelton in February 1869. In Christchurch she joined the Trinity Congregational Church and became part of the city's intellectual life. She married the shop owner Walter Allen Sheppard on 21 July 1871, and their only child, Douglas, was born in 1880. She taught Sunday school and served on the YWCA's committee.

Her activism began after the American temperance speaker Mary Leavitt toured New Zealand in 1885. Sheppard helped found a Christchurch branch of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, and when petitions on women's issues were rejected she concluded that politicians would ignore women while they could not vote. In 1887 she became the union's national superintendent for franchise and legislation. A suffrage bill failed by one vote that year. In 1888 she published the pamphlet Ten Reasons Why the Women of New Zealand Should Vote, sending a copy to every member of the House of Representatives, and later Should Women Vote?

Her first petition, with 10,085 signatures, was presented in 1891, and a second, with 20,274, followed. The third, presented in 1893, carried 31,872 women's signatures, the largest petition presented to Parliament up to then. The Electoral Bill of 1893 passed the Legislative Council by 20 votes to 18 on 8 September, and Governor David Boyle signed it on 19 September. By the election on 28 November, 88 percent of women had enrolled and nearly 70 percent voted. Women could not stand for Parliament until 1919.

In 1896 Sheppard became the first president of the National Council of Women of New Zealand, and she edited the union's journal The White Ribbon. She spent time in England, promoting suffrage there, and later withdrew from politics because of ill health while continuing to write. She revived the National Council in 1918. She died at Christchurch on 13 July 1934, aged 86, leaving no living descendants. Her portrait has appeared on the New Zealand ten-dollar note since 1991, and a memorial to her stands in Christchurch.
kateb-yacine: Kateb Yacine was born in Constantine, into a scholarly maraboutic Chaoui Berber family from Sedrata. His birth name was Yacine Kateb, but he said he had grown so used to teachers calling out surnames first that he took Kateb Yacine as a pen name. His father was a lawyer and the family followed his postings. He attended the Quran school at Sedrata in 1937, the French school in Lafayette in Little Kabylie in 1938, and in 1941 became a boarder at the colonial collège of Setif.

In his third year there he took part in the demonstrations of 8 May 1945, which ended in a massacre of Algerians by the French army and police, between six and eight thousand according to the figures given, forty-five thousand according to nationalists. Three days later he was arrested and imprisoned for two months. From then on he was a partisan of the nationalist cause. He was expelled from the collège and sent by his father to the high school in Bône. His first collection of poetry appeared in 1946.

Kateb went to Paris in 1947 and joined the Algerian Communist Party that May. He published Nedjma ou le Poème du Couteau in the Mercure de France and worked as a journalist at Alger Républicain from 1949 to 1951. After his father died in 1950 he worked as a longshoreman in Algiers, and he lived in Paris until 1959. His play Le cadavre encerclé was published in Esprit in 1954 and banned in France. The novel Nedjma appeared in 1956. During the war of independence he was forced abroad by harassment from the DST. He returned to Algeria in 1962 and, in 1967, left for Vietnam and wrote L'Homme aux sandales de caoutchouc, a play celebrating Ho Chi Minh.

In 1970 he settled in Algeria and gave up writing in French, turning to popular theatre, epics and satires in dialectal Arabic. With the Théâtre de la Mer of Bab El Oued, from 1971, he toured Algeria for five years, playing to workers, farmers and students. He was criticised for stressing Berber tradition and the Tamazight language, and for liberal positions on gender equality. He regarded French as the Algerians' spoil of the war for independence. He received the Grand prix national des Lettres in France in 1987. He died on 28 October 1989, leaving unfinished a work on the Algerian riots of October 1988.
kateri-tekakwitha: Kateri Tekakwitha was born around 1656 in the Mohawk village of Ossernenon, in what is now northeastern New York. Her name, Tekakwitha, means she who bumps into things in Mohawk. Her father, Kenneronkwa, was a Mohawk chief, and her mother, Kahenta, was an Algonquin woman who had been captured in a raid, adopted into the tribe and earlier baptised by French missionaries. When Tekakwitha was around four, her parents and brother died of smallpox. She survived with facial scars and impaired eyesight and went to live with her father's sister and her husband, a chief of the Turtle Clan.

In 1666 the French burned the three Mohawk villages, and the peace that followed required the Mohawks to tolerate Jesuit missionaries. At eleven she met the Jesuits Jacques Frémin, Jacques Bruyas and Jean Pierron. Pressed to think of marriage around thirteen, she refused.

In the spring of 1674 she told the Jesuit Jacques de Lamberville of her wish to become a Christian. He baptised her on Easter Sunday, 18 April 1676, giving her the name Catherine, of which Kateri is the Mohawk form. Some Mohawks opposed her conversion and accused her of sorcery, and others stoned and harassed her. She fled about 200 miles to the Christian mission of Sault Saint-Louis, Kahnawake, near Montreal, and joined it in 1677.

At Kahnawake she practised severe penances, which some priests opposed because of her poor health. With her friend Marie Thérèse Tegaianguenta she tried to found a Native religious order, which the Jesuits rejected. In 1679, on the Feast of the Annunciation, she consecrated herself to Jesus as her husband.

Tekakwitha died on Holy Wednesday, 17 April 1680, in the arms of Marie-Thérèse. The Jesuits Claude Chauchetière and Pierre Cholenec wrote her biographies in 1695 and 1696. She is often called the Lily of the Mohawks.

The cause for her canonisation was begun by American Catholics at the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1885, and some 906 Native Americans signed letters supporting it. Pope John Paul II beatified her on 22 June 1980 and Benedict XVI canonised her on 21 October 2012, the first Native American woman of North America to be canonised.
kathiawar: The peninsula covers about 61,000 square kilometres and faces the Arabian Sea on the south and south-west. From the heads of its two gulfs the Little Rann of Kutch and the waste tracts of Khambhat, half salt morass and half sandy desert, reach inland towards each other, so that only one narrow neck on the north-east joins Kathiawar to the mainland of Gujarat. Two belts of hill country cross it, and nine rivers drain it radially; they carry little water outside the monsoon months, and dams have been built on some of them. Most of the natural vegetation is dry scrub. The region has also been called Sorath.

The name Kathiawad seems to derive from the early settlements of the Kathis, who entered Gujarat from Sindh in the early centuries of the Common Era; Saurashtra comes from Sanskrit words meaning good nation. In the reign of Chandragupta Maurya the region was governed by Pushyagupta, and under Ashoka by the Yavana Tushaspa. The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, of the first century CE, calls the coast Syrastrene and describes a fertile country yielding wheat, rice, sesame oil, clarified butter and cotton cloth, with many cattle. The Junagadh rock inscription attributed to Rudradaman I, dated to 150 CE, also mentions the region.

After Indian independence in 1947, 217 princely states of Kathiawar, among them the former Junagadh State, were merged on 15 February 1948 into the United State of Kathiawar, renamed Saurashtra State in November 1948. Vallabhbhai Patel spent much time persuading the princes; Maharaja Krishnakumar Sinhji of Bhavnagar State was the first to offer his state. Rajkot was the capital and Uchharangray Navalshankar Dhebar the first chief minister. On 1 November 1956 Saurashtra was merged into Bombay state, and when that state was divided along linguistic lines in 1960 it became part of Gujarat.

The region now comprises eleven districts of Gujarat, with part of Ahmedabad district; historically it also took in Diu. Gir National Park and its surroundings hold the last remaining population of Asiatic lions, and the peninsula has two further national parks, the Blackbuck National Park at Velavadar and the Marine National Park in the Gulf of Kutch. Severe droughts have repeatedly left farmers without crops or drinking water. A campaign to build check dams from the late 1990s raised water tables, but in 2019 a severe drought struck again and water had to be brought by tanker from the Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada River.
kathmandu: Kathmandu lies in the northwestern part of the Kathmandu Valley, north of the Bagmati River, at an elevation of about 1,324 metres. The city covers 50.7 square kilometres and is bounded by Lalitpur, also called Patan, with which it forms one urban area surrounded by a ring road. It is dissected by eight rivers, of which the main one is the Bagmati. The valley is an ancient lake basin with fertile soil and flat terrain, which helped form a society based on agriculture.

Its position between India and China made it an important trading centre. Trade flourished along an offshoot of the Silk Road linking India and Tibet, and Lhasa Newar merchants of Kathmandu conducted trade across the Himalaya and helped spread art styles and Buddhism across Central Asia.

Archaeological excavations in Kathmandu have found evidence of ancient civilisations. The oldest finding is a statue from Maligaon dated to 185 CE. The excavation of Dhando Chaitya uncovered a brick with an inscription in Brahmi script, which archaeologists believe is two thousand years old. Historically the valley was known as the Nepal Mandala and was the cultural and political hub of the Newar people. From ancient times until the medieval period Kathmandu was known as Kantipur, which derives from Sanskrit words meaning beauty and place, giving the sense of city of light.

The name Kathmandu comes from Kasthamandap, a public pavilion made of wood, from the Sanskrit words for wood and pavilion. It was rebuilt in 1596 in the period of King Lakshmi Narasimha Malla, and according to legend all its timber came from a single tree. The earliest Western reference to the city is in the account of the Portuguese Jesuit Father Joao Cabral, who passed through the valley in the spring of 1628 and was received by the king, probably Lakshminarasimha Malla. He reported that they reached Cadmendu, the capital of the kingdom of Nepal.

Kathmandu is the capital and largest city of Nepal and its main governmental, financial, industrial and cultural centre. The 2021 census recorded a population of 845,767, with approximately 4 million in the surrounding metropolitan area. Its people are multi-ethnic, with a Hindu majority and a significant Vajrayana Buddhist presence. Since 1985 it has hosted the headquarters of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation.

Hindu and Buddhist practice has influenced the monuments of the city over the centuries. In 2006 UNESCO declared seven groups of monuments in the valley a World Heritage Site, among them Durbar Square, Swayambhu Mahachaitya, Bouddha and Pashupatinath.
kathmandu-valley: The Kathmandu Valley is a bowl-shaped valley in the Himalayan mountains of Nepal, at the crossroads of ancient civilisations of the Indian subcontinent and the wider Asian continent. Historically the valley and adjoining areas formed a confederation known as the Nepal Mandala. Until the 15th century Bhaktapur was its capital, when Kathmandu and Lalitpur were established as two further capitals. The name Kathmandu comes from Kasthamandap, a wooden pavilion in Kathmandu Durbar Square built in 1596 by King Lakshmi Narasimha Malla, said to contain no iron nails or supports.

The Newars are the indigenous inhabitants and the creators of the valley's historic civilisation, and their language is Newar, not to be confused with Nepali. The valley's trademark is the multiple-roofed pagoda, which may have originated there. A Newar artisan, Araniko, travelled to the court of Kublai Khan in the 13th century and influenced styles in China and Tibet.

The valley's origin is explained in legend. According to the Swayambhu Purana it was once a lake called Nagahrada, inhabited by Nagas. Vipassi Buddha planted a lotus seed in it, which grew into a radiant manifestation of the primordial Buddha called Svayambhu, and the bodhisattva Manjushri drained the lake by cutting a gorge. In a Hindu account Krishna drained the lake by cutting through the southern hills with his Sudarshana Chakra.

Kathmandu, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur and a ring of smaller cities form the largest urban agglomeration in Nepal, with about 5 million people. The valley has at least 130 important monuments, including pilgrimage sites for Hindus and Buddhists. UNESCO made it a World Heritage Site in 1979, with seven component sites, among them Pashupatinath Temple, Boudhanath Stupa and Swayambhunath.
kathua: Kathua lies at the foothills of the Sivaliks at an average elevation of 393 metres. The Sivalik hills and the snow-capped Kailash Kund range stand to the north, and the city is surrounded by three rivers: the Ravi is 7 km down from the town, and the Ujjh about 11 km along the Jammu highway. The town itself stands on the banks of a khad, the Dogri word for a seasonal stream, which divides it into two boroughs, Parliwand, meaning the other side, and Orliwand, meaning this side. The large Ranjit Sagar Lake lies 25 km away and cools the climate.

The climate is monsoon-influenced and humid subtropical. Rainfall averages around 1,700 millimetres a year, mainly in the monsoon of July and August and in winter, when western disturbances bring rain. Summers are hot, with temperatures that may reach 40 degrees, and winter nights can fall below 0. Kathua has no snowfall, and temperatures stay 3 to 4 degrees lower than at Jammu.

Kathua is the headquarters of Kathua district and a municipal council of 27 wards, in the Jammu division of Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, a region whose status is disputed. It lies along NH-44 and is linked by rail to the major cities of India. Jammu Airport is the nearest major airport. An army cantonment adjoins the city, and its industrial area includes a textile park, a biotechnology and pharmaceutical research park and cement works.

The municipal council and its outgrowth areas had a population of 59,688, with a literacy rate of 86.46%. Dogri is the mother tongue of most people, alongside Hindi, and Urdu predominates in official documents together with English. Hinduism is the largest religion, followed by over 91% of the people, with Sikhism second at 4.75% and Islam and Christianity smaller.
kato-kiyomasa: Katō Kiyomasa was born in what is now Nakamura-ku, Nagoya, to Katō Kiyotada, whose wife Ito was a cousin of Toyotomi Hideyoshi's mother. His father died while he was young, and he soon entered Hideyoshi's service, receiving a stipend of 170 koku in 1576 at the age of 15. He fought at the Battle of Yamazaki in 1582 and at Shizugatake in 1583, where his achievements made him one of Hideyoshi's Seven Spears of Shizugatake and brought 3,000 more koku. In 1584 he fought at Komaki and Nagakute against the Tokugawa. After the Kyūshū campaign of 1587 he was granted 250,000 koku in Higo, roughly half the province, with Kumamoto Castle as his residence.

Kiyomasa was one of three senior commanders in the Imjin War against Joseon Korea (1592–1598). Together with Konishi Yukinaga he captured Seoul, Busan and many other cities, defeated the last Korean regulars at the Battle of the Imjin River and pacified Hamgyong. He held two Korean princes hostage to force lower officials to surrender. A noted castle-builder, he built strategic Japanese-style castles in the lands he took, among them Ulsan, whose siege, begun on 22 December 1597, was his best-known battle: he defended it against a Chinese army under Yang Hao said to number 60,000. Ishida Mitsunari did not report his bravery to Hideyoshi. Like other daimyō he brought captive Korean potters back to Kyūshū.

After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 a group of seven generals including Kiyomasa turned against Mitsunari over his reports of the Korean war, and Tokugawa Ieyasu mediated. Kiyomasa then sided with Ieyasu, and in the Sekigahara campaign of 1600 he fought Mitsunari's allies on Kyūshū and took a number of castles. As a reward he received the other half of Higo, bringing his income to nearly 500,000 koku.

In his later years Kiyomasa tried to mediate between Ieyasu and Toyotomi Hideyori. In 1611, on a sea voyage to Kumamoto after one such meeting, he fell ill and died shortly after he arrived. He was buried at Honmyō-ji in Kumamoto and is enshrined at many Shinto shrines, among them Katō Shrine in Kumamoto. His son Katō Tadahiro succeeded him, but Tokugawa Iemitsu confiscated the fief and exiled him in 1632 on suspicion of conspiracy. A devoted follower of Nichiren Buddhism, Kiyomasa encouraged Nichiren temples in his lands. He is noted for brutally suppressing Christianity and clashed with Konishi Yukinaga, who held the other half of Higo and was a Christian. In 1910 he was posthumously promoted to junior third court rank.
kato-yoshiaki: As a retainer of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Katō fought at the Battle of Shizugatake in 1583 and was soon counted among the shichi-hon-yari, the Seven Spears of Shizugatake. He was also one of Hideyoshi's seven most trusted and experienced generals. He took part in the naval fighting at the Siege of Shimoda during the Odawara Campaign of 1590 and fought along the coast of the southern Korean peninsula in both Korean campaigns.

After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 Katō was one of seven generals, with Fukushima Masanori, Katō Kiyomasa, Ikeda Terumasa, Hosokawa Tadaoki, Asano Yoshinaga and Kuroda Nagamasa, who turned against Ishida Mitsunari, reportedly angered by his reports underrating their deeds in the Imjin War. Warned in advance, Ishida Mitsunari escaped from Osaka Castle to Fushimi Castle, where the generals surrounded him. Tokugawa Ieyasu refused to hand him over, arranged a review of the assessment of the Battle of Ulsan Castle and had his son Yūki Hideyasu escort Ishida Mitsunari to Sawayama Castle.

Historians read the affair differently. A popular account treats it as a plot to kill Ishida Mitsunari; Watanabe Daimon sees a legal dispute in which Tokugawa Ieyasu acted as mediator, while others place it within the wider rivalry between the Tokugawa faction and its opponents. The seven generals went on to support Tokugawa Ieyasu against the Western army in the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, after which Katō's fief was doubled from 100,000 koku to 200,000.

Katō, who in his later career served as lord of the Aizu Domain, died on 7 October 1631. In 1917 Emperor Taishō posthumously granted him the courtesy title of junior third rank. He has been portrayed on film by Kim Kang-il in The Admiral: Roaring Currents of 2014 and by Kim Sung-kyun in Hansan: Rising Dragon of 2022.
katsushika-hokusai: Hokusai's date of birth is unclear but is often given as 31 October 1760, in the Katsushika district of Edo. It is believed his father was Nakajima Ise, a mirror-maker for the shōgun. He began painting around the age of six. At twelve he was sent to work in a bookshop and lending library, at fourteen he became an apprentice to a woodcarver, and at eighteen he entered the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō, a master of ukiyo-e, which then concentrated on courtesans and kabuki actors. He published his first prints, of kabuki actors, in 1779.

After Shunshō's death in 1793 Hokusai explored other styles, including European ones known to him from French and Dutch copper engravings, and was expelled from the Katsukawa school by Shunkō, the chief disciple. In his own words, the embarrassment he suffered at Shunkō's hands motivated the development of his style. He turned from actors and courtesans to landscapes and the daily life of people of many social levels, a breakthrough for ukiyo-e. He used at least thirty names in his lifetime.

By 1800 he had taken the name Katsushika Hokusai, meaning north studio, in honour of the North Star, a symbol of a deity in his Nichiren Buddhism, and he published two collections of landscapes. He taught about 50 pupils over his life. On 5 October 1817 he painted the Great Daruma, 18 by 10.8 metres, in Nagoya before a large crowd. Between 1804 and 1815 he illustrated books with the novelist Takizawa Bakin.

In 1811 he took the name Taito. The first volume of the Hokusai Manga, a collection of drawings of objects, plants, animals and ordinary people, appeared in 1814 and was an immediate success; by 1820 twelve volumes had been produced. After 1820, as Iitsu, he made Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji in the early 1830s, including The Great Wave off Kanagawa. From 1834, as Gakyō Rōjin Manji, the Old Man Mad About Art, he produced One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji.

A fire in 1839 destroyed Hokusai's studio and much of his work,. At 83 he went to Obuse in Shinano Province at the invitation of a wealthy farmer, and he kept working almost until the end. He died on 10 May 1849 and was buried at the Seikyō-ji in Tokyo. Hokusai's prints were collected by European artists including Degas, Gauguin, Manet and van Gogh. Claude Debussy is believed to have been inspired by The Great Wave in La Mer, which first appeared in 1905.
kattegat: The Kattegat is a sea of roughly 24,000 square kilometres, bounded by the Skagerrak in the north, Jutland in the west, the Danish Straits and Zealand in the south and the Swedish provinces of Bohuslän, Västergötland, Halland and Scania in the east. The Baltic Sea drains into it through the Danish Straits. Its main islands are Samsø, Læsø and Anholt, and the cities and ports on its shores include Gothenburg, Aarhus, Aalborg, Halmstad, Varberg and Frederikshavn.

It is rather shallow, mostly less than 25 metres deep with an average of 22 metres, and dangerous to navigate because of sandy and stony reefs and shifting currents. The Baltic Current carries fresher water north along the Swedish coast, while a deeper current brings salt water in from the Skagerrak. The sea is therefore stratified into two layers, separated by a halocline at an average depth of 15 metres. Tides change the water level by only 15 to 30 centimetres.

According to Danish reference works, the name comes from the Dutch katte, cat's, and gat, passage. Captains of the Hanseatic fleets in the late Middle Ages compared the Danish Straits to a passage so tight that even a cat would have difficulty squeezing through, because of the many reefs and shoals. An archaic name for the Kattegat together with the Skagerrak was the Norwegian Sea or Jutland Sea, and its ancient Latin name was Sinus Codanus.

Control of and access to the Kattegat has been important throughout the history of international seafaring. Until the completion of the Eider Canal in 1784 it was the only sea route into and out of the Baltic region. From 1429 the Danish royal family, and later the state of Denmark, profited greatly from the Sound dues, a toll charged for passage through the Øresund. Copenhagen sheltered and repaired ships and offered trade and protection from piracy. The dues were lifted in 1857.

Boundaries differ by authority. A convention signed by Denmark, Norway and Sweden on 31 December 1932 drew the line with the Skagerrak from Skagen to Vinga Lighthouse, and other definitions place it further north or south, so that Gothenburg lies on the Kattegat under some and on the Skagerrak under others. Artificial channels, dredging and a network of lights now protect the heavy international traffic on the sea.

In the northern Kattegat, cold seeps known as bubbling reefs rise in shallow water, built up by methane and carbonate into pillars up to 4 metres tall. They are protected as a Natura 2000 habitat. Since the 1950s a bridge across the Kattegat joining Jutland and Zealand has been proposed.
kauai: Kauaʻi has an area of 1,456 square kilometres, making it the fourth largest of the Hawaiian Islands, and lies 117 kilometres northwest of Oʻahu across the Kauaʻi Channel. It is about five million years old, the oldest of the main islands, though Niʻihau is older. Its highest peak is Kawaikini at 1,598 metres, and Mount Waiʻaleʻale, 1,569 metres high, has an average annual rainfall of 11.7 metres on its east side, one of the wettest spots on earth. Rain has carved deep valleys and canyons with many waterfalls, and the flow of the Waimea River formed Waimea Canyon, about 910 metres deep.

It is uncertain when people first reached the Hawaiian Islands. Early archaeological studies suggested that Polynesian explorers from the Marquesas or Society Islands arrived as early as 600 CE, with a second wave from Tahiti around 1100, while later analyses suggest the first settlers came between 900 and 1200. Kauaʻi had its own dialect of Hawaiian, which still survives on Niʻihau.

In January 1778 the British navigator James Cook arrived at Kauaʻi by accident during his third voyage, the first recorded contact between a European and the indigenous people of the islands. By 1795 Kamehameha I had united most of the islands in the Kingdom of Hawaii, but Kauaʻi stayed independent. His attempt to conquer it in 1796 was cancelled because of stormy seas, and a second invasion planned from Oʻahu was cancelled after an epidemic broke out among his forces. In 1810 Kaumualiʻi, who had ruled Kauaʻi since 1803, agreed to be Kamehameha's vassal and to cede the island on his death by making Kamehameha's son his heir.

In 1816 Georg Anton Schäffer, a German working for the Russian-American Company, involved Kaumualiʻi in a plan to place Kauaʻi under the protection of the Russian Empire, and a fort was built at Waimea in 1817. On Kamehameha's orders Kaumualiʻi dismissed the Russians. From 1835 sugarcane plantations were the island's most important industry for about a century; the last, the Gay & Robinson Plantation, stopped planting in 2008.

Kauaʻi calls itself the Garden Isle and holds Waimea Canyon State Park and Nā Pali Coast State Park. It forms most of Kauaʻi County, which also includes Niʻihau, Kaʻula and Lehua, and its population was 73,298 in 2020.
kaub: Kaub lies on the right bank of the Rhine in the district of Rhein-Lahn-Kreis in Rhineland-Palatinate, about 50 kilometres west of Wiesbaden, and is part of the municipality of Loreley. It is connected to Wiesbaden and Koblenz by railway. The restored castle of Gutenfels stands on a hill above the town, and the castle of Pfalzgrafenstein, known as the Pfalz, sits on a rock in the middle of the river. According to legend the Palatine countesses awaited their confinement in the Pfalz, but in reality it served as a toll-gate for merchandise on the Rhine. Historically the town's trade consisted mainly of the wines of the district.

Kaub is first mentioned in 983. It originally belonged to the lords of Falkenstein. In 1260 the Counts of Katzenelnbogen divided their county and selected the inhabitants of Kaub, and in 1277 the town passed to the Rhenish Electorate of the Palatinate. It received civic rights in 1324. In 1477 it was passed as a deposit to the Counts of Katzenelnbogen again, but that family died out in 1479.

On New Year's night 1813 to 1814 Blücher crossed the Rhine at Kaub with the Prussian and Russian armies in pursuit of the French, and the town has a statue of the general. From 1919 to 1923 Kaub was part of the temporary Free State of Bottleneck.

Kaub is home to the Kaub gauging station, a decisive measuring point for the water level of the Rhine. The town lies at the shallowest part of the Middle Rhine, which ships carrying freight from the North Sea ports must pass on their way to the south-west of Germany. When the gauge falls to 78 centimetres, a low-water threshold is declared, and at that level four times as many barges are needed to carry the same volume of goods as at the high level of 250 centimetres. The town has a Roman Catholic and an Evangelical church.
kaunas: Kaunas stands at the confluence of Lithuania's two largest rivers, the Nemunas and the Neris, near the Kaunas Reservoir, the largest body of water in the country. Its name is of Lithuanian origin and most likely derives from the personal name of an unknown ruler of the castle, a name taken from an adjective meaning one who likes to fight. A 16th-century legend in the Bychowiec Chronicle instead says that it was founded by Romans led by a patrician named Palemon, who fled from the Emperor Nero, and that his son Kunas built a fortress at the confluence.

A settlement stood on the site of the Old Town by the 10th century at the latest. Kaunas was first mentioned in written sources in 1361. The brick Kaunas Castle defended its residents against the Teutonic Order, and with the castle at Grodno it was one of only two brick castles on the Nemunas, which was the main front line between the Crusaders and the Lithuanians. In 1408 Vytautas the Great granted Kaunas city rights and chose its coat of arms, which shows an aurochs. After the third partition of the Polish–Lithuanian state in 1795 the city passed to the Russian Empire, and Napoleon's Grand Army passed through it twice in 1812, devastating it both times.

After Vilnius was occupied by the Red Army in 1919, the Lithuanian government made Kaunas its main base, and it became the temporary capital when Vilnius was annexed by Poland. It held that position until 28 October 1939. In June 1940 the Soviet Union occupied and annexed Lithuania. On 29 June 1941 over 9,200 Jews were murdered in the Kaunas pogrom, and nearly 50,000 people, over 30,000 of them Jews, were killed at the Ninth Fort during the Nazi occupation. The Red Army took the city on 1 August 1944, and the region became a centre of the partisan war against Soviet rule, which ended by 1953.

Kaunas is the second-largest city in Lithuania after Vilnius and the capital of Kaunas County. It is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Kaunas. The interwar city was known for its Art Deco and Lithuanian National Revival architecture, and in 2023 it became a World Heritage Site.
kaupang: Kaupang lay on a beach by the Viksfjorden, a branch of the Larviksfjorden, near the present-day village of Tjøllingvollen in Larvik Municipality. The Viking hall of Skiringssal stood just inland from the fjord, and written sources indicate that the area was an important royal seat in the 8th and 9th centuries. The name is Old Norse for a market-place, from kaup-, to buy, and angr, a fjord harbour, so that it means something like buy harbour.

Archaeological evidence suggests that Kaupang may have been the first proto-urban settlement of any significance in Norway. Excavation has shown a centre of crafts and commerce with around 1,000 inhabitants, varied craft production and extensive trade with foreign lands, dealing in iron, soapstone and perhaps fish. Why the town was abandoned is unknown.

The first excavations were made in 1867 by Nicolay Nicolaysen, who mapped one of the grave-fields around the settlement, dug 79 grave mounds and found a cremation cemetery dated largely to the 10th century. Charlotte Blindheim began excavating in 1947 and published her last work in 1999. From 2000 to 2002 the University of Oslo's Institute for Archaeology, Conservation and Historical Studies dug at the site under Dagfinn Skre, followed by a smaller excavation of the harbour area in 2003. Four possible houses were found, with hearths, pits and postholes, and the results appeared in three books between 2007 and 2011.

Kaupang has been described as Norway's most important monument of the Viking Age. Many of the approximately 100,000 finds from its excavations, among them Arab silver coins, a gold coin from Dorestad, hundreds of glass beads, gold and bronze jewellery, pottery, weapons and tools, have been displayed at the University of Oslo.
kausambi: Kosambi, as the city is called in Pali, stood on the Yamuna upstream of its confluence with the Ganges at Prayaga, a position that made it a centre of trade for the Vatsa kingdom, one of the sixteen mahajanapadas. It was the main halt for traffic coming to Kosala and Magadha from the south and the west, and Buddhist texts place it thirty leagues by river from Benares. Buddhist commentaries derive its name either from the hermitage of the sage Kusumba or from the neem trees that grew around it.

Excavations show a fortified town of irregular oblong plan, with gates on the east, west and north sides, bastions, and a moat on three sides still visible in the north. Dense brickwork shows how closely the city was built. A palace excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India was built in six phases from the 8th century BCE to the 2nd century CE; its last phase used true arches and was destroyed by fire, leaving a layer of ash.

Occupation may go back to the 12th century BCE. The date of the great rampart is disputed: James Heitzman places it in the 7th to 5th centuries BCE, while G. R. Sharma, who excavated the site in 1949 and from 1951 to 1956, dated it to between 1025 and 955 BCE. In the Buddha's time the city's king was Parantapa, followed by his son Udena, and it held four Buddhist monasteries given by leading citizens, among them the Kukkutārāma and the Pāvārika-ambavana. Tradition says the Buddha spent his ninth rainy season there, and a schism among its monks over a minor rule drove him to retreat alone to the Pārileyyaka forest.

Kosambi remained an urban centre through the Mauryan and Gupta periods. Ashoka's schism edict addresses its officials, warning that monks or nuns who break the unity of the Sangha must wear white and live outside it. Pushyamitra Shunga may have moved his capital there. Jain texts place four events in the life of Padmaprabha, the 6th Tirthankara, at Kauśāmbī and say Mahavira visited it five times. More than three thousand stone sculptures have been recovered from the city and nearby sites.
kavad-i: Kavad was born in 473, a son of the Sasanian shah Peroz I. The nobles crowned him in 488, at the age of 15, to replace his deposed and unpopular uncle Balash. He inherited an empire at its lowest ebb. Drought, famine and defeats by the Hephthalites had emptied the treasury, since the Hephthalites had seized large parts of the eastern provinces and exacted heavy tribute, and rebellions were under way in Armenia and Iberia. The nobility and clergy acted as king-makers. For his first five years Kavad was tutored by Sukhra, who was the real ruler, and in 493 Kavad exiled him to Shiraz.

Kavad turned to the priest Mazdak, whose movement called for the sharing of wealth and property and loosened marriage laws, and used it to curb the nobility and clergy. Royal granaries were distributed and land was shared among the lower classes. The nobles deposed him and imprisoned him in the Castle of Oblivion in Khuzestan, replacing him with his brother Jamasp. He escaped with the help of his wife and his friend Siyawush, fled east and regained the throne with a Hephthalite army, in 498/9.

In his second reign he began reforms later completed by his son Khosrow I: a poll tax, a review of taxable land, and a division of the empire into four frontier regions, each under a spāhbed. By the 520s he no longer needed Mazdak and withdrew his support; the Shahnameh tells of the killing of Mazdak's followers under Khosrow, though the story's validity is uncertain. When the Byzantine emperor Anastasius I refused subsidies, Kavad invaded in 502, starting the Anastasian War, took Amida after a three-month siege, and made peace in 506. By 513 he had retaken Khorasan from the Hephthalites.

In 528 the Iberian War began with the Byzantines, partly because they would not recognise Khosrow as Kavad's heir. It was largely indecisive, though the Sasanians lost at Dara and Satala. Kavad died of an illness on 13 September 531 while his army besieged Martyropolis. Khosrow I succeeded him and executed his brothers and their offspring after a plot to put another Kavad on the throne. Historians regard Kavad's reign as a turning point and him as one of the most effective Sasanian kings; the Iranologist Nikolaus Schindel called him a genius in his own right, even if of a somewhat Machiavellian type.
kavad-ii: Kavad II was born Sheroe, a son of Khosrow II and Maria, a Byzantine woman whom some Eastern sources considered a daughter of the emperor Maurice. Byzantine sources do not report that Maurice had such a daughter, and the historian Nikolaus Schindel thinks Maria more likely belonged to the Sasanian aristocracy. Khosrow II's war on the Byzantines, begun in 602, had turned against him by 627, when Emperor Heraclius was seizing territory in Adurbadagan. Sheroe was held in a fortress outside Babylon with some brothers.

After the Byzantines sacked Dastagird on 6 January 628, Khosrow II fled to Ctesiphon and planned to crown his son Mardanshah as heir. Learning of this, Sheroe wrote to the general Gurdanasp, leader of the opposition, promising to make peace with the Byzantines and to raise the conspirators' rank.

The conspirators staged the coup on the night of 23 and 24 February 628, having first assured themselves through envoys that Heraclius would talk peace. Khosrow II was found hiding in the palace gardens and imprisoned, and Sheroe took the throne on 25 February as Kavad. His backers pressed him to kill his father, and Khosrow II was executed on 28 February 628 by Mihr Hormozd. Kavad II also had all his brothers, seventeen or eighteen, executed, at the urging of his minister Piruz Khosrow; his sisters Boran and Azarmidokht reproached him, and he is said to have felt remorse.

He sent envoys to Heraclius, addressing him as brother in a letter that survives in part in the Chronicon Paschale. Most of Khosrow's conquests were to be given up, ending the war of 602 to 628, though the general Shahrbaraz refused to withdraw from Byzantine territory. Kavad II also let the Church of the East again nominate its own catholicos, a privilege lost since 609.

Kavad II died of the Plague of Sheroe, which al-Masudi said killed at least a third of Iran's population; sources differ on whether he ruled six, seven or eight months. His seven-year-old son Ardashir III succeeded him under the regent Mah-Adhur Gushnasp.

Al-Tabari judged him a bad ruler, while the Chronicle of Seert is kinder. Michael Bonner and Touraj Daryaee blamed the killing of his brothers for the disruption of the succession, whereas Schindel suggests it may have averted a civil war and that a longer reign might have prevented the collapse of the Sasanian state and the Arab-Islamic conquest.
kawit: Kawit lies at the base of the hook-shaped shoreline of Manila Bay that runs out to the tip of Cavite City, 13 kilometres from Imus and 23 kilometres from Manila. Its name comes from the Tagalog kawit or kalawit, a hook or a larger fishing device, which suggests both the shape of the coast and the town's traditional fishing life. A legend instead tells of a blacksmith hammering a hook who answered a Spanish visitor's question with kawit, the word that became Cavite.

Before the Spanish arrived Kawit was the most thriving settlement of the area, and it gave the Spanish their first anchorage in the province, from which colonisation and Christian missions spread. It was established as a town in 1587, or by law on 1 August 1600. The Spanish called it Cavite el Viejo, Old Cavite, to tell it from Cavite la Punta, the port and naval base that is now Cavite City. Sailors on shore leave made it a red-light district, until Saint Mary Magdalene was made its patroness under the Jesuits. The 1818 census counted 1,855 native families and 55 Spanish-Filipino families.

Cavite el Viejo once took in present-day Kawit, Cavite City, Noveleta and Imus, which grew and became municipalities of their own. Emilio Aguinaldo, born there, was the municipality's chief executive from 1895 to 1897, and the Battle of Binakayan-Dalahican, one of the Filipino victories of the Revolution, was fought in the town. The Philippine Independent Church built a shrine to Saint Michael the Archangel at Binakayan in 1902, and in 1907 Act No. 1718 of the Philippine Commission gave the town its present name.

Kawit is an urban municipality of the province of Cavite, divided into 23 barangays, with 123,631 people in the 2024 census. Aguinaldo's house is preserved as the Aguinaldo Shrine. Every Christmas Eve the Maytinis Festival reenacts Mary and Joseph's search for shelter in the streets, ending at the 400-year-old St. Mary Magdalene Church.
kayah-state: Kayah State, also called Karenni State, lies in eastern Myanmar. It is bounded on the north by Shan State, on the east by Thailand's Mae Hong Son Province, and on the south and west by Kayin State. Its area is 11,670 square kilometres, and its capital is Loikaw. The relief is mountainous, and the Salween River crosses the state. The Lawpita Dam, built in 1950 under a reparation agreement with Japan, produces a quarter of the hydroelectric power generated in Myanmar. The Karenni, also known as Red Karen or Kayah, a Sino-Tibetan people, form the majority of the population, with Bamar, Shan and Karen minorities.

The Karenni States were a group of states, among them Kantarawadi, Kyebogyi and Bawlake, south of the Federated Shan States and east of British Burma. In 1875 Britain and the Burmese king Mindon Min recognised the area as belonging neither to Burma nor to Britain, so the states were never fully incorporated into British Burma. In 1892 their rulers accepted a stipend and were recognised as tributary. In the 1930s the Mawchi Mine in Bawlake was the most important source of tungsten in the world.

The 1947 Constitution of the Union of Burma provided that the three states be amalgamated into one constituent state, Karenni State, with the possibility of secession after ten years. Karenni accounts say that the central government then invaded, and on 9 August 1948 the leader U Bee Htu Re began a resistance, remembered as Karenni Resistance Day. He was assassinated on 8 September 1948 by central government militia, a date remembered as Karenni Martyr's Day. In 1952 the former Shan state of Mong Pai was added and the whole renamed Kayah State, possibly, according to one view, to drive a wedge between the Karenni and the Karen people in Karen State, both of whom were fighting for independence.

In 1957 pro-independence groups formed the Karenni National Progressive Party, backed by its own army, the Karenni Army, which has fought ever since apart from a brief ceasefire in 1995. In 1996 the State Law and Order Restoration Council stepped up its campaign with a population transfer, forcibly moving villagers to relocation sites to deprive the pro-independence forces of support, and the Myanmar government has been accused of massive human rights violations in the region.

Kayah State is the smallest of Myanmar's seven states, with a population of 286,738 in the 2014 census, though it is larger than Yangon Region. The Karenni, Shan, Intha, Bamar and Pa-O live in different parts of the state, and ethnolinguists distinguish many groups. In the 2014 census Buddhists made up 49.9 per cent of the population and Christians 45.8 per cent.
kayak: The original kayaks (Inuktitut qajaq, Yup'ik qayaq, Aleut iqyax) were developed by the Inuit, Yup'ik and Aleut, who used them on inland lakes, rivers and the coastal waters of the Arctic Ocean, North Atlantic, Bering Sea and North Pacific. Western Alaskan Natives built the frame of wood, while the eastern Inuit used whalebone because their landscape had no trees. The oldest surviving kayaks are in the North America department of the State Museum of Ethnology in Munich, the oldest dating from 1577.

Subarctic peoples made several kinds of boat for different purposes. The Aleut baidarka was built with two or three cockpits to carry hunters, passengers or goods. The umiak was a large open-sea canoe of seal skins and wood, between 5.2 and 9.1 m long, originally paddled with single-bladed paddles by more than one paddler.

The traditional kayak has an enclosed deck and one or more cockpits, each seating one paddler, which sets it apart from an open-deck canoe. The cockpit is sometimes covered by a spray deck that keeps out waves and splashes. The paddler's body is part of the structure, and design is largely a matter of trade-offs, such as directional stability against manoeuvrability and stability against speed. In general a longer kayak is faster and tracks better, and a shorter one turns more easily.

Modern kayaks are usually made of fibreglass or of rotationally moulded polyethylene and are mostly commercial products, rather than boats built by their users. They serve touring, racing, whitewater, surf, fishing and recreational purposes, and the term is now applied even to sit-on-top craft and inflatables that look little like the traditional boat.

Contemporary traditional-style kayaks trace their origins mainly to the native boats of Alaska, northern Canada and south-west Greenland. John MacGregor introduced a kayak to England and Europe in 1860. Folding kayaks with collapsible wooden frames covered in rubberised canvas, called foldboats, became widely popular in Europe from 1907, when Johannes Klepper and others began to mass-produce them. By 1929 Klepper and Company were making 90 foldboats a day, and by the mid-1930s an estimated half a million were in use in Europe. First Nation masters of the roll taught that technique to Europeans in these years.
