Kayaks were adapted for military use in the Second World War, mainly by British Commandos and special forces; the Royal Marines Boom Patrol Detachment made what is perhaps the best-known use of them in the Operation Frankton raid on Bordeaux harbour.
kayan-people-borneo: The Kayan are counted among the Dayak peoples and are grouped with the Kenyah and the Bahau as the Apo Kayan; they also belong to the wider Orang Ulu, the upriver people. They may number around 200,000, speak a Malayo-Polynesian language of the Austronesian family, and are distinct from the Kayan people of Myanmar. Their oral history places their origin on the Kayan River in North Kalimantan.

In historic times they spread south into Sarawak, settling on the middle Baram, the Bintulu and the Rajang, and clashed with the Iban, who were moving north at the same time. From 1863 Iban migrants on the upper Saribas and Rajang attacked Kayan settlements, and such wars and headhunting raids displaced many peoples. In the 17th century the Kayan sub-group Uma Apan moved into east Borneo, converted to Islam and gave rise to the Bulungan people and the Sultanate of Bulungan.

Kayan farming rests on shifting cultivation of upland rice, with sago, corn, yams, pumpkin and tobacco; sago was gathered in years of famine. They fish, hunt with the sumpitan and raise pigs and chickens, keeping dogs for hunting and ritual. Their smiths make the Malat sword, long their chief item of exchange, and they build boats and carve wood. Women tattooed girls and women to mark womanhood, and both sexes stretched their earlobes. Parap, improvised sung poetry, greets guests, and Tekna', a sung epic, carries village history.

Traditionally they lived in longhouses on river banks, up to 300 metres long and holding as many as 100 families. Society had three estates that married within themselves: the aristocrats, the commoners called panyin, and the slaves, dipen. The leader was usually chosen from the nobility.

The old religion centred on a feast of collected heads, with warrior initiations and funerals; headhunting and human sacrifice ended early in the 20th century. In the 20th century some Kayan converted to Christianity, while others took up Adat Bungan, a reform of the indigenous religion that began among the Kenyah Lepo' Tau of Long Nawang after World War II. Since the 20th century outside influence has made many practices fade, and younger Orang Ulu have made efforts to revive them.
kayapo: The Kayapo live over a vast area of the states of Pará and Mato Grosso in Brazil, south of the Amazon River and along the Xingu River and its tributaries, which has given them the nickname the Xingu. They are one of the subgroups of the Mebêngôkre nation, a name meaning people from the water's source. The name Kayapo came from neighbouring peoples in the early 19th century and means those who look like monkeys, probably after a men's ritual with monkey masks. Subgroups include the Xikrin, Gorotire, Mekranoti and Metyktire, and an estimated 8,638 Kayapo lived in 2018, up from 7,096 in 2003. Their villages typically have about a dozen huts, with a central hut where the men meet to discuss community matters.

In the 18th century, in the north-east of the present state of São Paulo, the Kayapo first met Portuguese-Brazilian bandeirantes, who were seeking gold, precious stones and Indigenous slaves, and as a result the Kayapo left the area and moved west. The Brazilian government contacted the Kayapo in the 1950s and 1960s with the intention of making peace.

The Kayapo speak a language of the Jê family, in several dialects, and value oratory so highly that they call themselves those who speak beautifully, Kaben mei. A beautiful name is a sign of wealth, and a naming ceremony requires enough food for a celebration. Men and women wear intricate black body painting, which they say mimics the insects from which their ancestors learned the ways of life. Chiefs wear headdresses of yellow feathers representing the rays of the sun, and women shave a V into their hair. They practise shifting cultivation by slash and burn, growing sweet potatoes, yams, taro, manioc and papaya, and use about 250 food plants and 650 medicinal plants.

Their land is arguably the largest tropical protected area in the world, covering 11,346,326 hectares. In the village of Gorotire the Kayapo agreed to gold mining in return for a share of the proceeds and demarcation of their territory. Mining brought money and better housing, education and health, but also mercury pollution that decimated fish, and disease. The Kayapo used forceful tactics to expel loggers and miners in some areas.

In 1987 the government proposed hydroelectric dams on the Xingu, among them the Belo Monte Dam. Under the leadership of Paulinho Paiakan the Kayapo organised the Altamira Gathering, which drew worldwide media attention and put pressure on the World Bank and the Brazilian government. Sting appeared at the demonstration and in 1989 founded the Rainforest Foundation Fund. In 1992 Conservation International Brazil began a partnership with the Kayapo community of A'Ukre to protect a stand of mahogany.
kayastha: The earliest known reference to the term dates from the Kushan Empire, when it became a common name for a writer or scribe. In Sanskrit literature and inscriptions it denoted the holders of a class of government offices, and it may derive from kaya, treasury, and stha, to stay, perhaps first naming an officer of the royal treasury. An inscription of the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I, dated 442 CE, uses prathama-kāyastha, chief officer, as a title, and the Yājñavalkya Smṛti and the Vishnu Smriti describe kayasthas as record-keepers and accountants, not as a jāti.

Modern scholars explain the rise of this class of administrators by the growth of the state, a more complicated system of taxation and the spread of land grants that had to be documented. The historian Chitrarekha Gupta notes that the earliest inscriptions naming a lekhaka or kayastha are associated with Buddhism.

From the ninth century, and perhaps earlier, Kayasthas began to consolidate into a distinct caste. A kāyastha assists a judge in the Mṛcchakatika, and in the Mudrarakshasa the Kayastha Śakaṭadāsa is a trusted man of the Nanda king's prime minister. In Kashmir they ran the administration and collected revenue, and Kshemendra's Narmamālā, written under King Ananta, lists their offices. After the Muslim conquest of India they mastered Persian, the language of the Mughal courts, and some converted to Islam, forming the Muslim Kayasth community of northern India.

In Bengal, Kayasthas had been the dominant landholding caste before the conquest and kept that role, serving the Mughals as treasury officials and ministers; according to Abu al-Fazl most of the Hindu zamindars of Bengal were Kayasthas. Under the British Raj they qualified for the highest offices open to Indians, and in 1911 Bengali Kayasthas and Bengali Brahmins owned 40% of the Indian-owned mills, mines and factories in Bengal.

The Kayasthas are a cluster of regional communities: the Chitraguptavanshi Kayasthas of the north, who trace their descent to the 12 sons of the god Chitragupta, the Bengali Kayasthas, the Chandraseniya Kayastha Prabhus of Maharashtra and the Karanas of Odisha. Their place in the varna order has never been uniform. British courts ruled differently by region, the Allahabad High Court holding in 1890 that Kayasthas were Kshatriyas and the Calcutta High Court that Bengali Kayasthas were shudras; the census of 1931 classed them as upper caste.
kayes: Kayes lies in western Mali on the Sénégal River, about 420 kilometres north-west of Bamako, and is the capital of the administrative region of the same name. It had 127,368 inhabitants at the 2009 census. The name derives from the Soninke language, and several etymologies are possible: kharré, a low humid place that floods in the rainy season, kayé, a type of grass, or khayé, the Soninke name for the rhun palm.

The climate is hot and semi-arid, with all the rainfall between June and October, around 650 millimetres a year. The town is nicknamed the pressure cooker of Africa for its extreme heat, which the iron-rich mountains around it are said to increase.

The area around Kayes was historically part of the Soninke states of Diarra and Gajaaga. The important trading centre of Goundiourou, known in Arabic sources as Ghiyaru, stood just across the river and was later rebuilt just south of the modern city. Kayes itself was founded in the second half of the 19th century, when Guéssé Sidy, a prince of Khasso, established a base to protect the western approaches to the kingdom's capital, Medina.

Before French expansion Kayes was still a small village. In 1881 the French chose it for a fort and barracks, the headquarters of their presence in the central Sudan, since Medina was difficult to reach by boat. By 1886 the post was fortified, and by 1889 a market town of 6,000 people had grown up around it. Kayes was the furthest point reachable by boat on the Sénégal, and the French built a railway from there to Bafoulabe, completed in 1890, which reached Bamako in 1904. A line to Thiès, begun in 1907 and interrupted by the First World War, was completed in 1923.

In 1892 Kayes became the capital of the French Sudan. Bamako replaced it as capital of the state of Haut Sénégal-Niger on 17 October 1899 and of all French Sudan in 1908. During the Second World War part of Poland's gold reserve, evacuated in 1939, was stored in Kayes for several years before being sent to the United States in 1944.

Kayes lies on the Route Nationale 1, 612 km by road from Bamako and 96 km from the border with Senegal, and has an international airport and a station on the Dakar-Niger Railway. The area is rich in gold and iron. Sites nearby include the Fort du Médine, the Félou Falls, the Gouina Falls, the tata of Koniakari built by El Hadj Umar Tall, and the Manantali Dam.
kaykaus-i: Kaykaus I was the eldest son of Kaykhusraw I. When his father died at the Battle of Alaşehir in 1211, his two younger brothers, Kayferidun Ibrahim and the future Kayqubad I, challenged his succession. Kayqubad won some support from neighbours of the sultanate, among them Leo I, king of Cilician Armenia, and the independent ruler of Erzurum, Tughrilshah, who was his uncle. Kayferidun put the newly acquired port of Antalya at risk by seeking help from the Cypriot Franks.

Most of the emirs supported Kaykaus, who seized Kayseri and then Konya from his base in Malatya, which brought Leo over to his side. He soon captured both brothers and secured the throne. He also made peace with Theodore Laskaris, the Byzantine emperor of Nicaea, which ended hostilities between the two states.

His most significant gain was the Black Sea port of Sinop. In 1214 Turkmen tribesmen captured Alexios, Grand Komnenos of the Empire of Trebizond, on a hunting trip outside the city and handed him to the sultan. He bought his freedom with Sinop and the vassalage of the Trapezuntine territory to the east. The Seljuqs thus gained a Black Sea outlet to match Antalya on the Mediterranean, and a wedge was driven between Trebizond and Nicaea. Kaykaus appointed an Armenian, Rais Hetoum, to govern the mixed Greek and Turkish population, and ordered churches in the city converted to mosques. Between April and September 1215 the walls were rebuilt under the Greek architect Sebastos, with fifteen emirs contributing to the cost.

Kaykaus allied with al-Afdal, an exiled Ayyubid and a son of Saladin, who offered him Aleppo in return for help in regaining his power. In 1216 Kaykaus attacked Aleppo in support of al-Afdal, his vassal, and was defeated by al-Ashraf. He was working towards an alliance with Badr al-Din Lu'lu', emir of Mosul, against the Ayyubids when he died in 1220, and the alliance collapsed.

He built a madrasa in Ankara in 1212 and in 1217 the Şifaiye Medresesi in Sivas, designed as a hospital and medical school. His mausoleum stands in its south eyvan under a conical dome, and the facade bears a poem by the sultan in blue faience tiles. According to Rustam Shukurov, Kaykaus and his brother Kayqubad, who spent considerable time in Constantinople with their father, very probably shared Kaykhusraw I's dual Christian and Muslim and Turkic, Persian and Greek identity.
kaykaus-ii: Kaykaus was the eldest of the three sons of Kaykhusraw II. His mother, Prodoulia, was a Byzantine Greek and may have had him baptised as a child, as Christian wives and concubines of the Seljuk harem often did with their sons. He was still young when his father died in 1246 and could do little against the Mongol conquest of Anatolia; the Mongol commander Baiju pressed him over late tribute and demanded new pastures for the Mongol cavalry.

After the Mongols defeated him at the Battle of Aksaray, Kaykaus fled in 1257 with his children and followers to the Empire of Nicaea. Emperor Theodore II Laskaris received him at Sardis and gave him 400 soldiers under Isaac Doukas Mourtzouphlos, in return for Laodicea, Chonae and two small fortresses, and with them he recaptured Iconium. He lost the city again on 12 August 1261 and, after his defeat at Sivrihisar by Kilij Arslan IV and the Mongol general Alijaq, fled from Attaleia to Constantinople with his family, his uncles, the Sufi Sarı Saltık and many of his court.

Under Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos tensions grew, and Kaykaus joined a plot to depose him. When it was uncovered he was caught trying to escape and imprisoned at Ainos; his commander Ali Bahadur was executed. His brother Kayqubad appealed to Berke Khan of the Golden Horde, whose forces invaded Thrace in the winter of 1264 and 1265 and besieged Ainos until Kaykaus was handed over.

Berke gave him an appanage in the Crimea and his daughter Urbay Khatun as a wife, and he died there in exile in 1279 or 1280. The researcher Rustam Shukurov describes him as holding a dual Christian and Muslim identity. He remained popular among the Turkmen of Anatolia, and in 1280 his son Masud II won the Seljuk throne. His son Constantine Melik stayed in Byzantine service, founding a Christian branch of the family, and the later rebel Sheikh Bedreddin claimed descent from him.
kaykhusraw-i: Kaykhusraw I was the eleventh and youngest son of Kilij Arslan II, and his date of birth is unknown. His name is based on that of the hero Kay Khosrow of the Shahnameh. His mother was of Byzantine ancestry: Christian Greek women were the dominant origin of the slave-concubines in the Seljuk harem. He received a good education and learned Persian, Arabic and Greek besides his native Turkish. He married a daughter of Manuel Maurozomes, who later held the castles of Chonae and Laodicea as his vassal.

In 1192/93 Kaykhusraw returned the Byzantine nobleman Theodore Mangaphas to Emperor Isaac II after receiving assurances about his treatment. In 1196 his brother Rukn al-Din Suleiman Shah advanced quickly on Konya, and Kaykhusraw fled to Constantinople. He lived there from 1197 to 1203 and was possibly baptised. A mathnawi he wrote himself compares his fate in these years to that of the Iranian hero Jam (Jamshid), who went into exile after losing his divine fortune (farr).

After Suleiman's death and the accession of Kilij Arslan, Kaykhusraw forced his way into Konya, removed Kilij from power and was enthroned a second time. In 1207 he seized Antalya from its Niceaen garrison, which gave the sultanate a port on the Mediterranean, and in that year he founded a mosque there.

Kaykhusraw was killed at the Battle of Antioch on the Meander in 1211, and his body was taken to Konya and buried in his family's ancestral tomb. His son Kayqubad I, born to the daughter of Manuel Maurozomes, ruled from 1220 to 1237, and his grandson Kaykhusraw II from 1237 to 1246.

He wrote poetry in Persian, and Muhammad ibn Ali Rawandi (died after 1207) dedicated to him his chronicle of the Seljuk Empire, Rahat al-sudur wa-ayat al-surur. According to Rustam Shukurov, Kaykhusraw had a dual Christian and Muslim identity, further complicated by his dual Turkic and Persian and Greek ethnic identity.
kaykhusraw-ii: Ghiyath al-Din Kaykhusraw ibn Kayqubad was the son of Sultan Kayqubad I and Mahpari Khatun, a Byzantine Greek by origin. Although he was the eldest, his father chose as heir a younger son, 'Izz al-Din. In 1226 Kayqubad gave him the newly annexed Erzincan, and he took part with the general Kamyar in the conquest of Erzurum and Ahlat. He married Tamar, a daughter of Queen Rusudan of Georgia, who as Gurju Khatun became Queen of Queens. On Kayqubad's death in 1237 he seized the throne with the support of the great emirs, and Sa'd al-Din Köpek, who excelled at political murder, guided his early reign.

Kaykhusraw captured Diyarbekir from the Ayyubids in 1241. At home the preacher Baba Ishak stirred the Turkmen of Anatolia to revolt from the borderland of Kafarsud in the eastern Taurus Mountains. The rebels destroyed Seljuq armies at Malatya and Amasya and took the regions of Kayseri, Sivas and Tokat before they were defeated near Kırşehir, with Frankish mercenaries credited by Simon of Saint-Quentin. Between 1240 and 1243 silver dirhams struck at Sivas and Konya in his name bore a lion and sun, which some read as the constellation Leo, Tamar's sign, and others as the sultan and his wife.

In 1243 the Mongols under Bayju took Erzurum. Kaykhusraw gathered allied contingents from Armenia, Nicaea, Trebizond and Aleppo, and on 26 June 1243 met the Mongols at the pass of Köse Dağ with an army of 80,000. A feigned retreat disorganised it, and it was routed. The Mongols took Sivas and sacked Kayseri but did not move on Konya. His vizier Muhadhdhab al-Din negotiated, and the sultan returned as a vassal paying a heavy annual tribute.

Kaykhusraw died in 1246 leaving three young sons, Kaykaus II, Kilij Arslan IV and Kayqubad II. He had named Kayqubad his successor, but the vizier Shams al-Din Isfahani set all three on the throne as co-rulers. One account holds that his failure to name a competent successor was the real blow to the dynasty, since power passed from Seljuq princes to court administrators.
kayqubad-i: Alā ad-Dīn Kayqubād was born about 1192, the second son of the Seljuk sultan Kaykhusraw, who gave him the title malik and the governorship of Tokat while he was young. When the sultan died after the battle of Alaşehir in 1211, Kayqubad and his elder brother Kaykaus struggled for the throne.

Kayqubad had allies in Leo I, king of Cilician Armenia, and in his uncle Tughrilshah, ruler of Erzurum, but most of the emirs supported Kaykaus. He fled to the fortress at Ankara and sought help from the Turkman tribes of Kastamonu, but was soon caught and imprisoned by his brother in a fortress in western Anatolia. Kaykaus died unexpectedly in 1219 or 1220, and Kayqubad was released and became sultan.

Kayqubad expanded the sultanate at the expense of the Mengujek Beylik and the Ayyubids, and established a Seljuk presence on the Mediterranean by taking the port of Kalon Oros, later renamed Ala'iyya after him. He reduced Cilician Armenia to a vassal state and, in 1221 or 1222, launched a naval attack on Sudak that defeated the combined forces of the Rus and the Cumans. Jalal al-Din Mangburni, fleeing the Mongol destruction of the Khwarezmian Empire, unsettled Anatolia, and Kayqubad first sought an alliance against the Mongols.

When it failed he defeated Jalal al-Din at the Battle of Yassıçimen, between Sivas and Erzincan, in 1230, and established Seljuk rule over Erzurum, Ahlat and the Lake Van region. The Artuqids and the Ayyubids of Syria recognised his sovereignty. In 1234 he defeated the allied Ayyubid forces under al-Kamil, took Siverek, Urfa, Harran and Raqqa, and forced the Komnenos dynasty of the Empire of Trebizond to renew its pledges of vassalage. He also captured several fortresses in Georgia, and the queen of Georgia gave her daughter Tamar in marriage to his son Kaykhusraw II.

Kayqubad died at Kayseri on 31 May 1237, given poison at a feast; poison was later found in DNA analysis of his bones. He was the last of his line to die independent. Kaykhusraw II took the throne and had his half-brothers Rukn al-Din and Kilij Arslan and their mother strangled.

Kayqubad built a large number of mosques, medreses, caravanserais, bridges and hospitals, completed the Seljuk Palace in Konya, and built the Kubadabad Palace on Lake Beyşehir, the castle and Red Tower at Alanya and the citadel walls of Konya. After the Mongol invasion the people of Anatolia looked back on his reign as a golden age, and later beylik rulers traced their pedigrees to him.
kayseri: The city lies on a low spur at the foot of Mount Erciyes, a dormant volcano that rises to 3,917 metres, more than 1,500 metres above the city's mean altitude. In antiquity the mountain was Mount Argaeus. The site stood at a crossing of trade routes: that from Sinope to the Euphrates, and the Persian Royal Road from Sardis to Susa during more than two centuries of Achaemenid rule. In Roman times a route from Ephesus to the east crossed it as well.

Kayseri has been equated with the early Hittite kingdom of Kussara, mentioned in early Assyrian trading records, and a first period of prosperity is dated to about 2000 BCE, when it served as a trading post between Assyrians and Hittites. As Mazaca it was the residence of the kings of Cappadocia. According to Armenian tradition it was founded by Mishak. In 14 CE the last king, Archelaus, renamed it Caesarea in Cappadocia in honour of Augustus. In the fourth century Basil of Caesarea founded there a large complex of charitable institutions, a monastery and churches, known as the Basiliad.

From the mid-seventh century Arab attacks on Cappadocia became common and the city was besieged several times; Muawiyah took it temporarily in 647. The Seljuk ruler Alp Arslan demolished the city and massacred its population in 1067, and it stood uninhabited for about half a century. The Danishmendids rebuilt it in 1134. Under the Sultanate of Rum, from 1178 to 1243, it was one of the sultanate's most important centres, until it fell to the Mongols in 1243. In 1277 Sultan Baybars, after his victory at Elbistan, entered the city and massacred its Christians while sparing the Muslim inhabitants. The Eretnids held it in the fourteenth century and the Ottomans took it in 1515.

The Seljuk period left the Hunat Hatun Complex, the Kiliç Arslan Mosque, the Grand Mosque and the Gevher Nesibe hospital. The Grand Mosque was begun by the Danishmend emir Melik Mehmed Gazi and finished by the Seljuks. During the Turkish War of Independence the building of the Kayseri Lyceum housed the Turkish Grand National Assembly while the Greek army advanced on Ankara.

Kayseri is the capital of Kayseri province in Central Anatolia. Its huge basalt walls, dating to the reign of Justinian in the sixth century, were repeatedly repaired by Seljuks, Ottomans and later authorities. The suburb of Talas was the ancestral home of Calouste Gulbenkian, Aristotle Onassis and Elia Kazan, and the architect Mimar Sinan was born in 1490 at Ağırnas nearby. The archaeological site of Kanesh-Kültepe lies 20 km to the north-east. Public investment in the 1920s and 1930s brought a textile factory and an aircraft factory to the city, and its merchants later built an industrial base.
kaysone-phomvihane: Kaysone Phomvihane was born on 13 December 1920 in Naxeng village, Savannakhet Province, in what was then French Indochina. His father, Nguyễn Trí Loan, a Vietnamese, was a civil servant in the French colonial administration, and his mother, Nang Dok, was a Lao farmer. He studied in Hanoi, first medicine and then law, without completing a degree. He later said he became a revolutionary at sixteen out of patriotism. In Hanoi he joined student activities linked to the Indochinese Communist Party and protested against the Japanese occupation, and he received his first military and political training from the Viet Minh.

On 23 August 1945 Kaysone took part in seizing power from the Japanese in Savannakhet. On 20 January 1949 he founded the Lao Issara army, forerunner of the Lao People's Army, and in August 1950 became Minister of Defence in the resistance government formed under Souphanouvong. The Lao People's Party was founded on 22 March 1955 at Nameo village and elected him general secretary. Although Souphanouvong was the movement's public leader, real power lay with Kaysone. After fighting resumed in 1964 he moved the leadership into caves at Viengxay, where they withstood American bombing. The party was renamed the Lao People's Revolutionary Party in 1972.

After the fall of Saigon in April 1975 the party took power with little bloodshed. On 2 December 1975 Kaysone presided over the session that proclaimed the Lao People's Democratic Republic and became its first prime minister. He kept Laos closely allied with Vietnam, and sided with it in the split with China in 1978. At the Fourth Party Congress in November 1986 he launched chintanakan mai, the New Economic Mechanism, which gradually opened the economy to market forces within a socialist framework.

In October 1990 three officials who had called for a multiparty system and free elections were arrested; Kaysone held to Marxism-Leninism and the party's monopoly of power. At the Fifth Party Congress in March 1991 he became party chairman, and in August 1991 the Supreme People's Assembly adopted the first constitution and elected him president. He died in Vientiane on 21 November 1992, aged 71, and was given a state funeral with Buddhist rites.

In Laos he is revered as a Father of the Nation. Statues of him were placed in every provincial capital, and a museum in his honour was built in Vientiane. In January 2016 the party's Tenth Congress placed Kaysone Phomvihane Thought alongside Marxism-Leninism as its ideological foundation.
kazakh-famine-of-1930-1933: Kazakhs were traditionally nomads who moved herds across the steppe with the seasons, and meat and dairy foods were the basis of survival through long winters. The destruction of nomadic pastoralism began in the 19th century with the Russian conquest of Central Asia, when authorities auctioned fertile land to attract Russian peasants. After the Russian Revolution, grain requisitioning combined with drought led to an earlier Kazakh famine of 1919–1922. A severe cold spell, the jut of 1927 to 1928, left cattle unable to graze.

In 1928 Soviet authorities began a campaign to confiscate cattle from richer Kazakhs, called bai, known as Little October; Kazakhs themselves decided who was a bai. More than 10,000 bais may have been deported. Nomads were forced onto collective farms, which reduced grazing. Between 1929 and 1932 a third of the republic's cereals were requisitioned, and a third of the livestock was confiscated between 1930 and 1931. Pianciola holds that Kazakhs were consciously sacrificed when livestock went to Moscow and Leningrad. The famine began in late 1930 under First Secretary Filipp Goloshchyokin.

Food aid was selectively distributed, and some went to European workers instead. Between 665,000 and 1.1 million Kazakhs fled to China, Mongolia, Afghanistan, Iran, Turkey and Soviet republics, taking an estimated 900,000 head of cattle. Fugitives were classified as class enemies and shot, and 30 percent of refugees died of epidemics and hunger. Some of the starving resorted to cannibalism. Census returns show the number of Kazakhs in Kazakhstan falling from 3,637,612 in 1926 to 2,181,520 in 1937.

Kazakhs fell from about 60 percent of the republic's inhabitants to 38 percent. Herds fell by 80 percent, and two thirds of surviving Kazakhs were sedentarized. Soviet textbooks later called the crisis the years of the great dzhut, a natural disaster. In 1991 the Kazakhstan parliament created a commission under the historian Manash Kozybayev, which reported that the tragedy could be designated a politics of genocide. Other scholars treat it as part of the wider Soviet famine driven by Joseph Stalin's collectivization. A monument to the victims was built in 2017, and 31 May is a day of remembrance.
kazan: Kazan lies at the confluence of the Volga and the Kazanka rivers. In Tatar a kazan is a cauldron, and the name perhaps describes the topographic basin around the city. Its central part is divided by the Bolaq canal and Kaban Lakes into two districts: the Kazan Posad, historically Russian, on the hill, and the Old Tatar Quarter, historically Tatar, between the canal and the Volga, where the mosques stand. Its symbol is Zilant, a mythical dragon-like creature, and the first official coat of arms was approved on 18 October 1781.

According to the official version adopted today, the city is more than 1,000 years old, with an estimated date of the urban settlement of 1004 to 1005. The dating rests on finds in the Kazan Kremlin, among them a Czech coin, remains of masonry and a wooden city fence, and handicrafts.

In 1552 Tsar Ivan the Terrible conquered the city after a siege. During the governorship of Alexander Gorbaty-Shuysky most of the Tatar residents were forcibly Christianised or deported, and mosques and palaces were ruined. The survivors were moved 50 kilometres away, and Tatars in Russian service were settled in the Tatar Bistäse near the city wall. Several great fires destroyed much of the city, and after one of them, in 1579, the icon Our Lady of Kazan was discovered there.

In 1708 the Tsardom of Kazan was abolished and Kazan became the seat of Kazan Governorate. After a visit by Peter the Great it became a centre of shipbuilding for the Caspian fleet. Pugachev's Rebellion, which began in 1773, seized and largely destroyed the city, which was rebuilt under Catherine the Great.

In 1918 Kazan was the capital of the Idel-Ural State, which the Bolshevik government suppressed, and in August of that year the Czechoslovak Legions briefly occupied it. In 1920 it became the centre of the Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic. From the Treaty of Rapallo of 1922 until 1933 the German and Russian armies jointly ran the Kama tank school there.

Kazan is the capital and largest city of Tatarstan, with over 1.3 million inhabitants, and the most populous city on the Volga. It is known for the mix of Tatar and Russian cultures. The Kazan Kremlin, a citadel declared a World Heritage Site in 2000, holds the five-domed Annunciation Cathedral of 1561 to 1562 and the Söyembikä Tower, named after the last queen of Kazan.
kazanlak: Kazanlak lies in Stara Zagora Province, in the middle of the Kazanlak Valley at the foot of the Balkan Mountains. The valley formed in the Quaternary Period, when the Balkan and Sredna Gora ranges rose, and hot mineral springs near Ovoshtnik, Yagoda and Pavel Banya mark its fault line. It is drained by the Tundzha river, which rises in the highest part of the Balkan east of Mount Botev and flows on to join the Maritsa. The average altitude is 350 m, and the soils suit oil-producing crops and herbs.

The oldest settlement in the area of the modern town dates from the Neolithic, in the sixth to fifth millennium BCE. In the fourth and third centuries BCE the lands on the upper Tundzha lay within the dominion of the Thracian ruler Seuthes III and held an important place in Hellenistic Thrace. The Thracian city of Seuthopolis was uncovered near Kazanlak when the Koprinka Reservoir was built. Close to it stands a Thracian tomb with a vaulted brick tholos, a narrow corridor and a round burial chamber, painted with murals of a Thracian couple at a ritual funeral feast. It belongs to a large necropolis, in a region where more than a thousand tombs of kings and aristocrats are found.

After the liberation of Bulgaria the town numbered about 9,000 people in the 1880s, and it grew steadily by migration from the countryside, passing 60,000 at its peak in 1985. The Iskra chitalishte, a reading centre founded in 1860, holds a library, theatre, cinema and museum, and it hosted the first Bulgarian opera, Siromahkinya. The Iskra Town History Museum was founded on 29 June 1901 by Peter Topuzov.

Kazanlak is the centre of rose oil extraction in Bulgaria, and the oil-producing rose of Kazanlak is one of the country's widely recognised national symbols. The town's Rose Museum began as a small exhibition in 1967 and became an independent museum in 1969. The Thracian tomb has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1979. Nearby, the Shipka National Park preserves the battlefield of the Russian-Turkish Liberation War of the 1870s, with the Freedom Monument opened in 1934.
kazanlak-tomb: The Thracian Tomb of Kazanlak is a vaulted-brickwork beehive, or tholos, tomb near the town of Kazanlak in central Bulgaria. It is part of a large royal Thracian necropolis in the Valley of the Thracian Rulers, near the ancient Thracian capital of Seuthopolis, in a region where more than a thousand tombs of royalty and members of the Thracian aristocracy can be found. The tomb lies in the Kazanlak Valley, enclosed between the Balkan Mountains to the north and the Sredna Gora range to the south.

The site consists of a narrow corridor leading to a round, domed chamber of the size required for the burial. Both are painted with murals in fresco, showing a Thracian couple at a ritual funeral feast. The walls were painted a sanguine or dark reddish colour.

The dome mural shows a seated couple, on separate ornate chairs, grasping each other's wrists as others approach in a procession with trays and various items. Horn musicians play as they walk. Saddled horses are led or held without riders, an attendant holds the team of horses drawing an awaiting chariot, and a chariot race in progress is depicted at the top of the dome. The border at the base of the dome has cattle skulls draped with scarves across their horns, alternating with an equilateral-cross design interpreted as a flower. Other bands include an egg-and-dart pattern of Hellenistic style.

The art historian Lyudmila Zhivkova interprets the shared gesture of the central figures as a moment of tenderness and equality, but not all specialists share that reading. The paintings are the best-preserved artistic works of the Hellenistic period in Bulgaria, and the monument has been on UNESCO's World Heritage list since 1979. To protect the delicate paintings the tomb is closed to the public, and a full-size exact replica was built nearby for visitors. The seated woman of the mural appears on the reverse of the Bulgarian 50 stotinki coin issued in 2005.
kazembe: Around 1740 the first Mwata, Ng'anga Bilonda, left the Luba-Lunda kingdom of Mwata Yamvo, about 300 km west of the Luapula, in pursuit of Mutanda, who had drowned his father Chinyanta and his uncle. Mwata was at first a title equivalent to general. Under Mwata Kazembe II Kanyembo Mpemba the group crossed the Luapula, conquered the Shila of the valley and set Luba or Lunda aristocrats over them as chiefs, while adopting the language of their Bemba allies. The kingdom prospered from the fisheries of Lake Mweru and the Mofwe Lagoon and from the copper of Katanga.

Portuguese expeditions came from 1796 onward, among them Francisco José de Lacerda e Almeida, who died there in 1798, and António Gamito in 1831, hoping for a trade route between Angola and Mozambique; Mwata Kazembe III Lukwesa Ilunga and IV Kanyembo Keleka Mayi rebuffed them. Arab and Swahili traders came for copper, ivory and slaves, and David Livingstone visited the capital in 1867. From the 1860s Msiri took over Kazembe's copper and ivory trade, founded the Yeke Kingdom and conquered much of its territory.

In 1894 the Luapula valley was divided between British North-Eastern Rhodesia and the Congo Free State, confining Mwata Kazembe's rule to the eastern bank. When Mwata Kazembe X refused British taxes and defeated an armed incursion, Alfred Sharpe and Robert Codrington sent troops in 1899 who burnt his capital and killed a number of his people. He accepted British rule, rebuilt his capital at Mwansabombwe and ruled under the system of indirect rule.

On the Luba model, the Mwata stands over the senior chiefs Lukwesa, Kashiba, Kambwali and Kanyembo, appointed from his family, and one of them may succeed him. He rules with a council, which became the Lunda Native Authority in colonial times. Mwata Kazembe XIV Shadreck Chinyanta Nankula, called the first modernizing Mwata, built schools and clinics in the 1940s. The kingdom's functions today are those of local government and custom, and the Mutomboko Festival, held at the end of July since 1971, recalls the migration and the conquest of the valley in its dances.
kazi-nazrul-islam: Nazrul Islam was born on 24 May 1899 in Churulia, in the Burdwan district of the Bengal Presidency, into a Bengali Muslim family. His father, Kazi Faqeer Ahmed, was the imam and caretaker of the local Pirpukur mosque. After his father's death in 1908, at the age of ten, Nazrul took his place as caretaker and later worked as muezzin. Attracted to folk theatre, he joined a travelling group run by his uncle Fazle Karim, for which he acted and wrote songs, poems and plays, among them plays on characters of the Mahabharata. Through this work he began to study Bengali and Sanskrit literature and the Puranas.

He joined the British Indian Army in late 1917 and left in 1920, settling in Calcutta, where he published his novel Bandhan-hara in 1920. His poem Bidrohi, The Rebel, and his publication Dhumketu, The Comet, made him known as the Rebel Poet and drew him into the independence movement. In 1930 his book Pralayshikha was banned and he was charged with sedition; he was jailed and released in 1931, after the Gandhi–Irwin Pact.

Lacking formal education, Nazrul did not follow the conventions of Rabindranath Tagore and faced criticism from Tagore's followers, though he looked to Tagore as a mentor. He introduced the ghazal into Bengali and used many Arabic and Persian words. Between 1928 and 1935 he published ten volumes with 800 songs, over 600 of them based on classical ragas. His songs, nearly 4,000 in all, are known as Nazrul Gīti. He also directed a film and from 1939 supervised music programmes for Calcutta Radio.

Nazrul wrote that quarrels between religions were those of priests and imams, not of ordinary Hindus and Muslims, and opposed religious, caste and gender bigotry; fundamentalists condemned his views. In the early 1940s he began to lose his voice and memory, and in Vienna the neurosurgeon Hans Hoff diagnosed Pick's disease, judged incurable.

On 24 May 1972, with the consent of India, Bangladesh brought him to Dhaka. He was given Bangladeshi citizenship in February 1976 and died on 29 August 1976. He received the Padma Bhushan in 1960. His writings inspired Bengalis in the Bangladesh Liberation War.
kazimierz-michalowski: Kazimierz Józef Marian Michałowski was born in Tarnopol on 14 December 1901, the grandson of Emil Michałowski, the town's mayor. He studied classical archaeology and art history at the Jan Kazimierz University in Lwów and later in Berlin, Heidelberg, Paris, Rome and Athens, and took part in French excavations at Delphi, Thasos and Delos. His doctorate of 1926, supervised by Edmund Bulanda, dealt with the Niobids in Greek art. In 1931 he founded the Department of Classical Archaeology at the University of Warsaw, which he headed until he retired in 1972.

In 1936 he began excavations at Edfu with the French Institute for Eastern Archaeology, the first in the Mediterranean world with Polish archaeologists. Taken prisoner in the September campaign of 1939, he lectured on Egyptology to fellow prisoners in the camp Oflag II-C Woldenburg. After the war he was dean and pro-rector at the University of Warsaw and in 1960 opened the Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology in Cairo, which he headed until his death.

His teams worked at Myrmekion in Crimea, at Tell Atrib, and from 4 May 1959 at Palmyra, where they found a hoard of jewellery and 27 gold solidi. At Kom el-Dikka in Alexandria they uncovered the first ancient theatre found in Egypt, and at Deir el-Bahari a funerary temple of Thutmose III. He chaired the UNESCO experts who oversaw the cutting of the temples of Ramesses II at Abu Simbel into 30-tonne blocks and their rebuilding, and from 1965 he dug at Nea Paphos in Cyprus, where a mosaic of Theseus and the Minotaur came to light.

Michałowski died in Warsaw on 1 January 1981 and was buried at Brwinów. He coined the term Nubiology for the study of ancient Nubia. The Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology and the Faras Gallery of the National Museum in Warsaw bear his name, as do streets in Częstochowa, Malbork and Słupsk, and his bust stands in the gardens of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. He received honorary doctorates from Strasbourg, Cambridge and Uppsala.
kazys-grinius: Kazys Grinius was born on 17 December 1866 at Selema, near Marijampolė, in Congress Poland, then part of the Russian Empire, the third of eleven children of a farmer with 15 hectares. At school he helped publish a newspaper inspired by the first Lithuanian newspaper Aušra and smuggled banned Lithuanian publications from Prussia. He studied medicine at Imperial Moscow University and led a secret society of Lithuanian students. After practising as a doctor in Marijampolė and elsewhere, he helped found the Lithuanian Democratic Party in 1902, and was jailed several times by the Tsarist authorities for cultural activism.

During the First World War he worked in the northern Caucasus, where he cared for Lithuanian refugees. At Kislovodsk, on 8 October 1918, Bolshevik forces shot his wife and fatally injured his daughter. He returned to Lithuania in November.

Grinius led a bloc of the Popular Socialist Democrats and the Peasant Union at the elections to the Constituent Assembly in April 1920, and on 19 June 1920 became prime minister. His government signed a peace treaty with the Soviet Union, settled the border with Poland and saw Lithuania accepted into the League of Nations; it also reformed taxes and founded Vytautas Magnus University. The coalition broke up and he resigned in 1922. He helped prepare the permanent constitution and sat in the Seimas as a defender of press freedom and minority rights.

The Third Seimas elected him President on 7 June 1926. He signed a non-aggression pact with the Soviet Union that recognised Lithuanian rights to the Vilnius region, and ended martial law. On 17 December 1926, his birthday, nationalists took control of the military and civilian institutions, arrested him and Mykolas Sleževičius and installed a new government under Antanas Smetona. Grinius resigned to 'save Lithuania from possible misfortunes'. Smetona's party said a Communist takeover was imminent; Grinius's memoirs say this was false.

Grinius returned to medicine in Kaunas. In 1942, under German occupation, he signed a memorandum protesting repression of the local population, Jews included, and was deported to Selema. From October 1941 to spring 1942 he and his wife Kristina hid a Jewish acquaintance, Dmitry Gelpernas, and he was recognised as Righteous Among the Nations in 2016. In 1944 he emigrated to the West, in 1947 to the United States, and he died in Chicago on 4 June 1950. His remains were buried near Selema in 1994.
kde-domov-muj: The song was written by Josef Kajetán Tyl for his comedy Fidlovačka and set to music by František Škroup. Tyl is said to have considered leaving it out of the play because he doubted its quality. It nevertheless soon became the most popular song of Fidlovačka, which gained popularity among Czechs who were seeking to revive their identity within the Habsburg monarchy, and it quickly became their unofficial patriotic anthem.

Soon after Czechoslovakia was formed in 1918, the first verse of the song became the Czech part of the national anthem, followed by the first stanza of the Slovak song Nad Tatrou sa blýska, with official translations into German and Hungarian. During the German-occupied Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia from 1939 to 1945 the state kept the song as its anthem. It was usually played alongside the German anthems, the Deutschlandlied and the Nazi Horst-Wessel-Lied.

When Czechoslovakia split in December 1992, the Czech Republic kept Kde domov můj and Slovakia kept Nad Tatrou sa blýska. Slovakia extended its anthem with a second verse, but the Czech anthem was adopted unextended, in its single-verse version, and its lyrics are fixed in Czech Act No. 3/1993.

The melody has been taken up by other composers. Johann Strauss the Younger included its motif in his Slaven-Potpourri of 1847, and in 1882 Antonín Dvořák used it in his overture to Šamberk's play Josef Kajetán Tyl, which is often performed alone as Domov můj, a concert work of some ten minutes. Rainer Maria Rilke paid tribute to it in two poems in German, published in 1895.

Otakar Jeremiáš orchestrated the anthem in three versions, for large orchestra in 1930, for small orchestra in 1932 and for organ and orchestra in 1932, and they are still performed. In 2008 the Czech government released an official recording of the anthem by the National Theatre Opera Chorus and Orchestra, in four versions.
kealakekua-bay: The bay lies about 12 miles (19 km) south of Kailua-Kona, and the area around it was settled over a thousand years ago. Its name comes from the Hawaiian ke ala ke kua, the god's pathway, and it was the focus of extensive Makahiki celebrations. Hikiau Heiau, a luakini temple, stands at the south end; the village of Kaʻawaloa, with the Puhina O Lono Heiau and royal residences, stood at the north. The cliff above the bay, part of it named the sacred cliffs of Keōua after Keōua Nui, holds burials of Hawaiian royalty.

James Cook's ships Resolution and Discovery sighted the bay on 17 January 1779, during the Makahiki, and Cook estimated that several thousand people lived in its two villages. On his return the theft of the Resolution's jolly boat and his taking of wood from a sacred enclosure brought relations to a crisis. Cook tried to take the chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu hostage, fighting broke out on the shore and Cook was stabbed; in the skirmishing that followed dozens of Hawaiians were killed by musket and cannon fire.

In 1782, after Kalaniʻōpuʻu's death, Kamehameha I fought his rival Keōua Kuahuʻula at the battle of Mokuʻōhai just south of the bay. George Vancouver anchored there in February 1793 with John Young as interpreter, and on 25 February 1794 he negotiated a treaty with the island's leaders on his ship, though the British parliament never acted on it.

After the ʻAi Noa ended the kapu system in 1819, Keaoua Kekuaokalani gathered the defenders of the old religion at Kaʻawaloa and was defeated at the Battle of Kuamoʻo. The temples then fell into disrepair, a church was built at Kaʻawaloa in 1824, and in 1825 Lord Byron of HMS Blonde set up a monument to Cook and took away many sacred objects.

A white stone monument built in 1874 on the order of Archibald Cleghorn, and deeded to the United Kingdom in 1877, marks the approximate place of Cook's death; it can be reached only by water or on foot. About 180 acres around the bay became the Kealakekua Bay State Historical Park in 1967, the bay itself a Marine Life Conservation District in 1969, and the area was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1973. Hawaiian spinner dolphins use the bay to rest, feed and raise their calves.
keban-dam: The dam was first proposed in 1936 by the newly founded Electric Affairs Survey Administration, but work began only in 1966. The French-Italian consortium SCI-Impreglio built it, and estimates of its cost range from US$85 million to US$300 million. Filling began in 1974 and displaced about 25,000 people. Weak bedrock beneath the dam later forced a temporary lowering of the lake so that extensive reinforcement could be carried out. Though not built as part of the Southeastern Anatolia Project (GAP), the dam is now a full component of it.

Keban is a combined rockfill and concrete gravity dam run by the State Hydraulic Works (DSİ). It is 1,097 metres long, and its crest stands 207 metres above the riverbed; eight turbines can produce 1,330 MW. The reservoir holds 30.6 cubic kilometres and covers 675 square kilometres, flooding the valleys of the Murat River and the Karasu, from which the Euphrates rises. Its height and the high rainfall keep evaporation low. The dam was not meant for irrigation, yet in 1999 63,872 hectares were watered from the lake.

While the reservoir filled, Turkey kept the river flowing at 450 cubic metres per second, as agreed with Syria and Iraq. Syria was filling the reservoir of its new Tabqa Dam at the same time, and in 1975, in a drought, Syria and Iraq quarrelled over the water reaching Iraq; Saudi Arabia mediated the dispute.

From 1968 to 1974 the Euphrates and Murat valleys were surveyed and excavated before the flooding. The narrow rock valleys held no sites, so the work centred on the two places where the Murat valley opens out. In the Aşvan region the British Institute of Archaeology at Ankara excavated Aşvan Kale and three smaller sites. On the Altınova plain survey found 36 sites, the largest being Norşuntepe, dug by a German team under Harald Hauptmann; other mounds there included Tepecik, Korucutepe, Değirmentepe and Körtepe. The late Roman Karamagara Bridge, an early pointed-arch bridge, now lies under the water.
kebra-nagast: The Kebra Nagast is divided into 117 chapters and is clearly a composite work, which Edward Ullendorff called a gigantic conflation of cycles of tales. According to the colophon on most copies, it was written in Coptic, translated into Arabic in 1225, and then put into Ge'ez by a team of Ethiopian clerics, which has led scholars to date its composition to between 1314 and 1322.

Other sources attribute it to a fourteenth-century writer, Nebura'ed Yeshaq of Aksum. Many scholars doubt that a Coptic version ever existed. Its sources include the Hebrew Bible, the Book of Enoch, the Book of Jubilees, Syriac works, rabbinical material and patristic writings. Historian Stuart Munro-Hay noted that no record shows Ethiopian monarchs claiming descent from Solomon before the 13th century.

The text is framed as a debate among the 318 fathers of the First Council of Nicaea on the question of what the glory of kings consists in. It centres on Queen Makeda, known as the Queen of Sheba, who travels to Jerusalem after hearing of Solomon's wisdom and there turns from worship of the sun to the God of Israel. Solomon tricks her into sleeping with him and gives her a ring, and she bears Menelik on the way home.

At 22 Menelik visits Solomon and is recognised by the ring. The young men sent home with him take the Ark of the Covenant from the Temple, and Menelik learns on the journey that it is with him. The Ark flies him home, and Makeda abdicates in his favour. A later part of the work is a collection of prophecies, with a marked anti-Jewish tone, which ends by foretelling that Ethiopia's power will eclipse that of Rome.

Modern scholarship holds that the stories were largely created to legitimise the Solomonic dynasty's rise to power in the 13th century, which ended the Zagwe dynasty. Harold G. Marcus calls the work a pastiche of legends, and David Northrup calls the descent from Solomon and Sheba a myth. Many Ethiopian Christians nevertheless hold it to be historically reliable, and Ullendorff described it as the repository of Ethiopian national and religious feelings.

The Jesuit Pedro Páez translated much of it in the early 1620s. James Bruce brought a copy home from Gondar, which is now in the Bodleian Library, and the full text was first published by Carl Bezold in 1905. E. A. Wallis Budge's English translation appeared in 1922 and 1932.
kedarnath: Kedarnath lies in the Himalayas about 3,583 metres above sea level, on a barren stretch of land beside the Mandakini River, near the Chorabari Glacier. It is 223 kilometres from Rishikesh and about 86.5 kilometres from Rudraprayag, and the nearest roadhead is at Gaurikund, about 16 kilometres away. Behind the town and its temple stand Kedarnath peak at 6,940 metres and the Kedar Dome at 6,831 metres. Heavy snow closes the temple in winter. From November to April the palanquin carrying the idol of Kedarnath is taken to the Omkareshwar Temple in Ukhimath, and priests and summer residents move to nearby villages.

The name means Lord of the Field, from the Sanskrit kedara, field, and natha, lord. The Kashi Kedara Mahatmya says that the crop of liberation grows here. The construction of the temple is credited to the Pandava brothers of the Mahabharata, though that epic names no place called Kedarnath. One of the earliest references is in the Skanda Purana, from about the 7th or 8th century, which names Kedara as the place where Shiva released the waters of the Ganga from his matted hair, so forming the Ganges.

The temple is said to have been rebuilt by Adi Shankaracharya. Hagiographies based on Madhava's Sankshepa-Shankara-Vijaya say the 8th-century philosopher died near the Kedarnath mountains, while others, based on Anandagiri's Prachina-Shankara-Vijaya, say he died at Kanchipuram. The ruins of a monument to his purported resting place stand at Kedarnath. By the 12th century the site was a prominent pilgrimage centre, mentioned in the Kritya-kalpataru of the Gahadavala minister Bhatta Lakshmidhara.

Kedarnath is a town in Rudraprayag district and the most remote of the four Chota Char Dham pilgrimage sites. The 2011 census recorded a population of 830, though the numbers of pilgrims between May and October run into thousands a day. Nearby are the Bhairavnath Temple, whose deity is believed to protect the town in winter, the glacier-lake Chorabari Tal, the Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary and the Adi Shankaracharya Samadhi. On 16 and 17 June 2013 flash floods destroyed much of the town and killed thousands of people, but the temple itself survived.
kediri-kingdom: The kingdom grew out of the division of Airlangga's realm. In 1042, according to the tradition, Airlangga split Kahuripan into two parts, Janggala and Panjalu (Kadiri), and abdicated in favour of his sons to live as an ascetic; he died seven years later. The Marimbong Inscription of 1264 places the boundary between the two regions at the Bengawan River. In the early inscriptions the name Panjalu was used more often than Kediri. Kadiri comes from an Old Javanese word meaning to stand alone or be independent. The capital, Daha or Dahanapura, is thought to have stood in the western Brantas River valley, near the modern city of Kediri.

Jayabhaya (1135–1159) is remembered for a reign that is considered the golden age of Old Javanese literature. Mpu Sedah's Kakawin Bharatayuddha, a Javanese version of the Mahabharata, was written in 1135 and perfected by Mpu Panuluh, who also wrote the Hariwangsa and the Gatotkacasraya. Under Kameçvara, Mpu Dharmaja wrote the Smaradhana, and the story of the king and his wife Çri Kirana lies behind the Panji cycle, which spread through Southeast Asia as far as Siam.

The last king, Kertajaya (1194–1222), was fighting the brahmins in 1222, and they asked for protection from Ken Arok, ruler of Tumapel. The decisive battle took place near the village of Ganter, where Ken Arok's troops destroyed Kertajaya's. Kediri became a vassal of Tumapel, or Singhasari, under regents. In 1292 Jayakatwang rebelled against Singhasari and killed its king Kertanegara. He rebuilt Kediri, but it lasted only a year before a combined attack by Yuan dynasty troops and Raden Wijaya, who later founded Majapahit.

Chinese sources describe a society based on rice cultivation, animal farming and the spice trade. Daha lay inland near the fertile Brantas valley, and Kediri inherited irrigation systems from Airlangga's Kahuripan, among them the Wringin Sapta dam. The economy was partly monetised, with silver coins issued by the royal court. The Chinese author Chou K'u-fei, writing in 1178, reported that offenders paid fines in gold, except thieves and robbers, who were executed, and that the bride's family received a bride price.

A water festival was held in the fifth month and a festival in the mountains in the tenth, with flutes, drums and wooden xylophones. Chou Ju-kua, writing around 1225, named Srivijaya and Java as the two powerful kingdoms of the archipelago and found Buddhism and the Brahmin religion practised in Java.
keelung: Keelung lies in the northern part of Taiwan Island and covers 132.76 square kilometres. Mountains to the east, west and south separate it from its neighbouring county, while the northern part faces the ocean and has been a deep-water harbour since early times. The city is nicknamed the Rainy Port, with yearly rainfall averaging upwards of 3,700 millimetres, an effect related to the Kuroshio Current.

The Ketagalan were its first inhabitants. The Taiwanese name Ke-lâng, written with characters meaning rooster cage, is more likely derived from Ketagalan than from the shape of a mountain. In 1875 the late Qing authorities gave it the new official name Jilong, meaning base prosperous.

The Spanish expedition to Formosa in the early 17th century made the first contact with the West, and the Spanish built San Salvador de Quelung, a fort serving as an outpost of the Manila-based Spanish East Indies. From 1642 to 1661 Keelung was under Dutch control. The Dutch East India Company took over the Spanish fort, reduced its size and renamed it Fort Noort-Hollant. After Koxinga attacked Fort Zeelandia, the Dutch returned in 1663, but they left in 1668 after harassment by aboriginals, when trade with Qing China through Keelung fell short of their hopes.

In 1863 the Qing Empire opened Keelung as a trading port, and the city developed quickly on placer gold and high-quality coal from the Keelung River basin. An earthquake and tsunami in 1867 caused serious damage and cost hundreds of lives. During the Sino-French War the French attempted an invasion in the Keelung Campaign (1884–85). Liu Mingchuan, who led the defence of Taiwan, recruited Aboriginals to serve with the Chinese soldiers, and the Qing forces pinned the French down at Keelung for eight months before the French withdrew.

After the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895 handed Taiwan to Japan, a five-phase construction of Keelung Harbor began. By 1916 its trade exceeded that of Tamsui and Kaohsiung. The city was upgraded in 1924, and in the Pacific War it was nearly destroyed by Allied bombers. After the handover to the Republic of China in October 1945 the city and harbor were rebuilt, and by 1984 the harbor was the seventh largest container harbor in the world.

The Keelung Ghost Festival dates to 1855, when rival clans that had fought bitterly agreed to bury their dead together and keep the peace through competition in folk performances. It was the first folklore custom included in Taiwan's national cultural heritage list. The National Taiwan Ocean University stands in the city.
kefalonia: Kefalonia, also written Cephalonia, is the largest of the Ionian Islands and the sixth-largest island in Greece, after Crete, Euboea, Lesbos, Rhodes and Chios. The main island covers 773 square kilometres. Its highest mountain is Mount Ainos, at 1,628 metres, whose summit is covered with Greek fir and black pine and is a national park. Argostoli and Lixouri are its largest towns. The island lies just south-east of a major active fault zone where the Eurasian and Aegean plates meet, and a series of thrust faults is responsible for its continuing uplift.

Archaeological finds on the island go back to about 40,000 years before the present, and a survey in the Leivatho area has found dozens of sites from the Palaeolithic to the Venetian period. The Mycenaean era is represented in the small archaeological museum of Argostoli. In antiquity the people lived in four cities, Cranii, Sami, Pale and Pronnoi, which formed a federation called the tetrapolis. Legend explained the island's name through Cephalus, who helped Amphitryon of Mycenae in a war and was rewarded with the island of Same.

In the late Roman Empire Cephalonia belonged to the province of Achaea, and the four ancient cities survived into late antiquity, with Sami probably the capital. In 1222 the Frankish Crusaders established the Diocese of Kefalonia-Zakynthos. Turkish rule lasted until 1500, when a Spanish-Venetian army captured the island, a rare Venetian success in the Second Ottoman-Venetian War. Refugees from the lost Venetian fortresses of Modon and Coron and colonists from Crete arrived, and Venetian pressure for olive plantations led to the first exports of olive oil to Venice.

When France conquered Venice in 1797, Cephalonia became part of the French département of Ithaque. In 1798 a combined Russian and Turkish fleet forced the French out, and from 1799 to 1807 the island belonged to the Septinsular Republic, nominally under Ottoman sovereignty but protected by Russia. In 1864 it joined the Greek state with the other Ionian Islands.

In the Second World War Axis forces occupied the island, mostly Italian troops until late 1943. After Italy's armistice in September 1943 the Italian division Acqui, having voted in a referendum among its soldiers, fought the German forces that came to take control, which prevailed after the siege of Argostoli. The earthquake of 1953 was so destructive that of 200 olive presses working before it, thirteen remain. Argostoli is the seat of administration, and Cephalonia is a regional unit of the Ionian Islands region. Tourism, begun in the early 19th century, grew widely from the 1980s.
kehl: Kehl lies in the region of Baden on the Rhine, at the confluence with the smaller Kinzig, directly opposite Strasbourg. It has around 38,000 inhabitants and is the third-largest city of the Ortenaukreis after Offenburg and Lahr. Four bridges join it to Strasbourg: the Passerelle des Deux Rives for pedestrians and cyclists, the Bridge of Europe, the Beatus-Rhenanus Bridge for the tramway, and the Rhine Bridge for the railway. The Jardin des Deux Rives extends on both banks, and the two cities share some municipal services.

The village of Kehl was first mentioned in 1038, and the first permanent bridge to Strasbourg was completed in 1338. France took the place in 1678 as part of Strasbourg's defences, and in 1683 the architect Vauban turned it into a fortress. Louis XIV had annexed the Imperial City of Strasbourg in 1681, and the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697 confirmed this but restored the territories on the right bank to the Empire, so that Kehl passed the following year to the Margraviate of Baden. On 7 May 1770 Marie Antoinette was handed over by Austria to France on an island in the Rhine near Kehl, later called the Kommissionsinsel.

Kehl received town rights in 1774 from Charles Frederick, Margrave of Baden. It was badly damaged in the French Revolutionary Wars, above all in the Rhine Campaign of 1796, with two battles of Kehl and an Austrian siege that ended in its surrender on 9 January 1797. It was returned to Baden in 1803 and again in 1815, when the fortress was dismantled. The first port facility was built between 1842 and 1847, and the first railway bridge in 1861 gave a direct link from Paris to Vienna.

Under the Treaty of Versailles the harbour was placed under French administration for seven years. In September 1939 the population was evacuated to the Black Forest, since Kehl lay in the so-called Red Zone. On 10 November 1938 the synagogue was broken into and its ritual objects destroyed, Jewish men were deported to Dachau, and the building was demolished in 1939. France administered Kehl after the war and released it in stages between 1949 and 1953.

Kehl is a border city in Baden-Württemberg with a large Rhine port, the Häfen Kehl, and the seat of the Kehl University of Applied Sciences. Tramway line D from Strasbourg was extended to Kehl station in 2017 and to the town centre in 2018.
keir-hardie: James Keir Hardie was born on 15 August 1856 in a two-roomed cottage at Newhouse, Lanarkshire. His mother, Mary Keir, was a domestic servant and his stepfather, David Hardie, a ship's carpenter. The family moved to Govan, and at seven Hardie became a message boy for the Anchor Line Steamship Company, which ended formal schooling; his parents taught him to read and write in the evenings. At ten he went to work in the mines as a trapper, opening and closing a door for a ten-hour shift. He later became a hewer, read Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus, took up preaching and temperance work, and was blacklisted by mine owners as an agitator.

In 1879 Hardie became an organiser of the miners at Hamilton and was chosen National Secretary at a conference in Dunfermline. He took part in the Lanarkshire strike of 1880 and the Ayrshire strike of 1881, both formally failures. In August 1886 he became Organising Secretary of the new Ayrshire Miners Union at a salary of £75 a year. Disillusioned with Gladstone's Liberals, he stood in the Mid Lanarkshire by-election of April 1888, and in August 1888 became first secretary of the Scottish Labour Party.

In 1892 he won West Ham South, defeating the Conservative George Banes by 5,268 votes to 4,036, and entered Parliament in a tweed suit and deerstalker hat. He helped found the Independent Labour Party in 1893 and lost his seat in 1895 after a speech attacking the monarchy. In 1900 he helped form the Labour Representation Committee and was elected for Merthyr Tydfil. After 29 Labour MPs were elected in 1906 he became their parliamentary leader, and he resigned in 1908 in favour of Arthur Henderson.

Hardie then campaigned for women's suffrage, self-rule for India and an end to segregation in South Africa. He opposed the First World War and tried with other socialists to organise an international general strike against it; his meetings met heckling, though he wrote in November 1914 that he had never dissuaded men from enlisting. After a series of strokes he died of pneumonia in a Glasgow hospital on 26 September 1915, aged 59. His biographer Kenneth O. Morgan described him as a pioneer and hero of the Labour Party. His childhood home at Holytown is preserved, and streets, estates and buildings across Britain bear his name.
keith-holyoake: Holyoake was born at Mangamutu near Pahiatua in the Wairarapa, into a family related to the secularist George Holyoake, and was raised in the Plymouth Brethren church. After his father's death he left school at 12 to work on the family hop and tobacco farm at Riwaka, his mother continuing his education at home. Farming associations drew him into politics: he won the Motueka seat for the Reform Party at a by-election in 1932, the youngest member of Parliament at 28, helped to found the National Party, lost his seat in 1938 and returned for Pahiatua in 1943.

Under Sidney Holland he was Minister of Agriculture for eight years from 1949, encouraging farm mechanisation and a campaign that nearly eliminated the rabbit pest, and in 1954 became the first formally appointed Deputy Prime Minister. He succeeded Holland two months before the 1957 election, which Labour under Walter Nash won by two seats. He returned to power in 1960, campaigning against the Black Budget of 1958, and served as his own Minister of Foreign Affairs.

His government created the Office of the Ombudsman, passed the Crimes Act 1961 abolishing capital punishment, published the Hunn Report on the state of Māori, and introduced a form of voluntary unionism. It accepted a mixed economy and a long period of prosperity, negotiated a limited free trade agreement with Australia in 1965, banned nuclear weapons from New Zealand territory in 1963 and sent forces to Vietnam, cautiously at first. After a narrow victory in 1969 the government came to seem careworn, and he resigned in 1972 in favour of Jack Marshall.

In 1977 Robert Muldoon's government had him appointed Governor-General, which opponents called a political appointment; Labour's leader Bill Rowling said he would remove him. His conduct was acknowledged to be impartial, and his term was limited to three years because of his age. He became a Knight of the Garter in 1980. Known as Kiwi Keith, he died in Wellington on 8 December 1983 and is the only New Zealand politician to have been both Prime Minister and Governor-General. He counted Kinloch, the town he developed on Lake Taupō, his proudest achievement.
keladi: Keladi is a temple town in Sagara Taluk, about 8 km from the town of Sagara. Its principal building is the double temple of Rameshwara and Virabhadra, a large and plain structure in the Hoysala-Dravida style. Two mounds called Kalte at the entrance to the town are pointed out as the scene of the human sacrifices told in the story of its founding.

Keladi is the place from which the Ikkeri chiefs derived their origin, and tradition tells it thus. Two brothers, Chavuda Gowda and Bhadra Gowda, lived in the village of Hale-bayal with two servants, Yadava and Murari, who worked their fields. When a cow was seen shedding her milk over an ant-hill, Chavuda Gowda dug into it, found a linga and built a small temple over it. The servants later ploughed up an old sword, which leapt out as a serpent to kill any crow that perched on the shed; Chavuda Gowda kept it and named it Nagaramuri.

The plough then struck a cauldron of treasure. In a dream Chavuda Gowda was told to offer a human sacrifice and take it, and the two servants volunteered on condition that their memory be preserved; they were beheaded with Nagaramuri. With this wealth the brothers raised a small force and subdued the neighbouring villages, but they were seized on the king's order and held in custody at Vijayanagar.

Through the court musicians they offered to punish a rebellious Palegar near Balihalu. Having killed him, they were released, confirmed in the places they had taken and given a royal seal, and the town of Keladi was founded with the temple of Rameshwara. Later, while the chief was hunting, a hare turned on his hounds, a sign of heroic virtue in the soil, and he moved his town to that spot, calling it Ikkeri.

His son, with the sanction of the Vijayanagar sovereign Sadasiva Raya, took the name Sadasiva-Nayak. After the Battle of Talikota broke up the Vijayanagar Empire, the Keladi Nayakas created an independent kingdom, whose rulers included Shivappa Nayaka, Chennamma and Basava Raja. It remained independent until Hyder Ali annexed it to the Kingdom of Mysore.
keladi-chennamma: Chennamma was born in the household of Siddappa Shetty, a merchant of the Kundapur region, and married King Somashekara Nayaka in 1667. After his death she took charge of the administration of the Keladi Nayaka kingdom, also called the Ikkeri Nayakas, and governed it for 25 years from Keladi near Sagara. She adopted one of her close relatives, Basavappa Nayaka, who succeeded her as Hiriya Basappa Nayaka.

Her reign is regarded as a period of administrative consolidation and economic stability. She kept the Shist land revenue system of Shivappa Nayaka but gave tax holidays to farmers who cleared new forest land in the Malnad. The state kept its monopoly on black pepper, the main export, and by the Treaty of Barkur with the Portuguese in 1678 she kept sovereignty over the coastal ports while collecting fixed customs duties. A devout Veerashaiva, she granted the village of Kuduvalli tax-free to the Sringeri Sharada Peetham in 1691 and let the Portuguese build churches at Mirjan, Honnavara, Chandavara and Kalyanpura.

When Chikka Devaraja of Mysore took several Ikkeri territories, among them Magadi, Kadur and Channarayadurga, the queen, as regent for her adopted son Basava Raja, defeated the Mysore army at Vasudhare and recovered Kadur, Banavara, Hassan and Belur. Expecting Mughal attack, she moved the treasury and records to the mountain fortress of Bidanur (Nagara) and strengthened it with stone-lined water channels and granaries for long sieges.

In late 1689 Chhatrapati Rajaram I, fleeing to Gingee after Aurangzeb's execution of his half-brother Sambhaji, reached Bidanur pursued by a Mughal army under Kasim Khan. Chennamma gave him supplies and an escort through the Malnad forests. Aurangzeb then sent Kasim Khan to besiege Bidanur, but in the monsoon-drenched Western Ghats her Bedar infantry raided the Mughal supply lines, and after heavy losses the Mughals withdrew. A treaty of 1690 recognised the autonomy of Keladi.

Channagiri is named after her. She is counted, with Rani Chennabhairadevi, Abbakka Rani, Kittur Chennamma, Belawadi Mallamma and Onake Obavva, among the foremost women warriors of Karnataka, and her life is the subject of Keladi Chennamma, a Kannada historical series on Suvarna TV.
keladi-nayakas: The dynasty, also called the Nayakas of Bednore, was based at Keladi in the present-day Shimoga district. Its founder, Chaudappa Nayaka, originally Chauda Gowda, came from the village of Pallibailu near Keladi, the son of farmers, and rose to be a feudatory of the Vijayanagara Empire. His successor Sadashiva Nayaka earned the title Kotekolahala from Aliya Rama Raya for his part in the battle of Kalyani, brought the coastal provinces under his direct rule and moved the capital to Ikkeri, some 20 km from Keladi. The rulers were of the Vokkaliga and Banajiga castes and Veerashaivas by faith.

After the fall of Vijayanagara in 1565 the Nayakas became independent rulers of the Malnad hills of the Western Ghats, most of the Karnataka coast and the plains along the Tungabhadra River. Hiriya Venkatappa Nayaka refused tribute to the Penukonda rulers by 1613, defeated the Portuguese in 1618 and 1619 and received the Italian traveller Pietro Della Valle at Ikkeri in 1623. Under Virabhadra Nayaka the Bijapur army plundered Ikkeri, and his uncle Shivappa Nayaka deposed him in 1645. Shivappa's campaigns against Bijapur, Mysore and the Portuguese, whose coastal forts he captured, brought the kingdom to its largest extent, and his revenue schemes were later praised by British officials.

Keladi Chennamma, who ruled from 1672 to 1697, sheltered the Maratha Rajaram when he fled the Mughal army. Wars with local chieftains and Mysore and harassment by the Marathas drained the treasury, and Queen Virammaji was defeated and confined by Hyder Ali until the Peshwa Madhavrao I freed her in 1767.

The Nayakas built temples at Ikkeri and Keladi in granite, mixing late Kadamba, Hoysala, Vijayanagara and Dravida styles, with yali pillars of rearing lions and horses; the Aghoreshwara temple at Ikkeri and the Rameshwara temple at Keladi are the best examples. They spread Veerashaivism through the hills and the coast, with sixty-four mutts in Dakshina Kannada alone, while granting land to other faiths and appointing Nawayath Muslims to office. Basavappa Nayaka wrote the Sanskrit encyclopedia Sivatattva Ratnakara, and a member of the family founded the Haleri Kingdom of Coorg.
kelso-abbey: The monks came from Tiron, near Chartres in France, and had first entered Scotland around 1113 under the patronage of David I, then Prince of the Cumbrians, in the reign of his brother Alexander I. Why they left their first site near Selkirk is not known for certain, but David, by then King of Scots, was making Roxburgh, where he also set up the royal mint, the economic and administrative centre of southern Scotland. Building seems to have begun at once, and by 1143 the abbey was far enough advanced to be dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary and Saint John.

The king's son Henry, Earl of Northumbria, was buried there in 1152, and John, abbot from 1160 to 1180, was the first abbot in Scotland granted the mitre. Once the Scottish crown lost its hold on Northumbria, Roxburgh lay close to the border, and during the Wars of Scottish Independence the abbey was repeatedly attacked and repaired by its monks; from 1299 to 1307 its abbot was an English appointee, Thomas de Durham. In 1460 James II was killed in an accident within sight of the abbey, and the infant James III was hastily crowned there.

After the attacks of the Rough Wooing in the 1540s, Henry VIII's Italian engineer Archangelo Arcano drew up plans to turn the abbey into a bastion fort. The Scottish Reformation of 1560 ended the community's official standing, and after further damage the abbey was declared derelict in 1587. Its estates became the secular lordship of Holydean, granted in 1607 to the last commendator, Robert Ker of Cesford. A parish kirk occupied part of the ruins from 1647 to 1771, while townspeople took its stone for buildings in Kelso, and in 1805 most of the remaining ruins were cleared away.

Only the west tower with its crossing and transepts and part of the infirmary still stand; records of 1517 in the Vatican archives suggest the complete church had two crossings, a rare double-cruciform plan. A memorial cloister to the 8th Duke of Roxburghe, designed by Reginald Fairlie, was added in 1933. The ruins are cared for by Historic Environment Scotland, which repaired them after a closure in 2022, and lie on the Borders Abbeys Way.
kemalism: Kemalism, also called Atatürkism, grew out of the efforts to save the Ottoman Empire that began chiefly with the Tanzimat reforms of the 19th century. The Young Ottomans tried to build an Ottomanism that would check the rising ethnic nationalisms, and after their suppression under Sultan Abdul Hamid II the Young Turks took up their legacy. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk spent his formative years in Salonica. In the army he joined the Committee of Union and Progress, abandoned Ottoman nationalism for Turkish nationalism and adopted a secular outlook.

His defence of Gallipoli in the First World War made his career, and after the Ottoman defeat he led the Turkish War of Independence against the Allies' planned partition of Anatolia and Eastern Thrace. By 1923 his government in Ankara had abolished the Ottoman monarchy and proclaimed a Republic.

Atatürk described his ideology as based on science and reason and avoided dogma. It rests on six principles, symbolised by the Six Arrows: republicanism, populism, nationalism, laicism, statism and reformism. Republicanism replaced dynastic rule with popular sovereignty and constitutional limits on government. Populism rejected class conflict in favour of national unity, and it also meant state supervision of religious schools and organisations. Laicism, closer to French laïcité than to the Anglo-American idea of secularism, aims to keep religion out of government and the reverse.

Its first steps were the abolition of the caliphate in March 1924 and the replacement of the Shaykh al-Islām by the Presidency of Religious Affairs. In 1926 the mejelle and shari'ah law codes gave way to an adapted Swiss Civil Code and penal codes modelled on German and Italian ones.

Statism meant that the state regulated economic life and entered fields private enterprise would not, and after the Great Depression it took an active part in investment, notably in infrastructure, power stations and iron and steel. Nationalism defined every citizen as a Turk, and reformism treated the changes as irreversible.

The six principles were written into the Turkish constitution as state ideology on 5 February 1937. The Republican People's Party, which Atatürk founded on 9 September 1923, carried them for decades, and later constitutions in 1961 and 1982 kept secularism, nationalism and democracy.

Abroad, observers in Germany, France, Britain and several countries farther east followed the Turkish transformation closely in the 1920s and 1930s. The Bolsheviks saw Kemalists as allies against Western imperialism.
