Historian Şükrü Hanioğlu calls Kemalism a scientifically sanctioned version of Turkish nationalism, drawing on Enlightenment ideas, positivism and republicanism.
kempten: Kempten is the largest town of the Allgäu, in Swabia, Bavaria. It is one of the oldest urban settlements in Germany. The area was possibly first settled by Celts, and the Greek geographer Strabo mentions a town of the Celtic Estiones named Kambodunon, which is considered the oldest written reference to any German city. No archaeological evidence has yet been found that this Celtic settlement existed.

In 15 BCE Roman troops led by Nero Claudius Drusus and his brother Tiberius conquered and destroyed the existing Celtic settlement. The town, Latinized as Cambodunum, was rebuilt on a classical Roman plan with baths, a forum and temples, first in wood and then in stone after a fire that destroyed almost the whole town in 69. It possibly served as capital of the province of Raetia in the first century before Augsburg took that role. The Alemanni destroyed it in 233, and the settlement moved to the Burghalde hill above the river Iller. In the middle of the 5th century the last Roman troops left and the Alemanni took the town over entirely.

The Franks destroyed the town again in 683, because it had supported an uprising against the Frankish kingdom. Around 700 two Benedictine monks from the Abbey of Saint Gall, Magnus von Füssen and Theodor, founded Kempten Abbey, the first monastery in the Allgäu. It became one of the most privileged of the Frankish Empire with the support of Charlemagne's wife Hildegard. After Magyar raids, Ulrich of Augsburg, who was also abbot, began rebuilding the monastery and the town in 941.

In 1213 Emperor Frederick II made the abbots members of the Reichstag and granted the Abbot of Kempten the title of Duke. In 1289 King Rudolf I granted privileges to the settlement in the valley, making it the Free Imperial City of Kempten. The last property rights of the abbots in the city were sold in 1525, and from then two independent cities of the same name lay side by side. Conflict grew when the Imperial City turned Protestant in 1527, in opposition to the Catholic abbey. Both were destroyed during the Thirty Years' War, by imperial forces and Swedish troops respectively. The abbey and the city came under Bavarian rule in 1802–03, and in 1819 the two cities were united.

Kempten had about 68,000 inhabitants in 2016. Among its sights are St Lorenz Basilica, commissioned in 1652 by the abbot Roman Giel of Gielsberg and acknowledged as the first large church built in Germany after the end of the Thirty Years' War, the Duke-Abbots' Residence, St Mang Church and the Archaeological Park Cambodunum, where excavations in the late 19th century and again in the 1950s uncovered the foundations of the Roman town.
ken-arok: The story of Ken Arok's life comes from the Pararaton, a semi-mythical literary work on the kings of Java. It makes him the son of the Brahmin Sri Jayamerta and of Ken Endok, born to a poor family on the bank of the Brantas River in East Java. His parents placed the infant in the river in the hope that a wealthier family would find him, but he was found by a thief, Lembong, who taught him his skills, and he grew into the most cunning thief in Kediri.

The rishi Mpu Lohgawe persuaded him to abandon his life of crime, proclaimed him an avatar of Vishnu and found him a place as an attendant of Tunggul Ametung, the powerful ruler of the Tumapel area. When Ken Arok glimpsed Tunggul Ametung's wife, Ken Dedes, his teacher told him it was a sign that she would bear a royal dynasty and that whoever married her would be a king.

To kill Tunggul Ametung, Ken Arok ordered a kris from the smith Mpu Gandring. Impatient at the months of rituals still needed, he took the unfinished weapon and stabbed its maker, who with his last breath cursed him and seven generations of his descendants to die by it. Ken Arok gave the kris to another attendant, Kebo Ijo, who showed it to everyone in Tumapel, then stole it back one night, stabbed Tunggul Ametung to death and left it at the scene. When Kebo Ijo was accused, Ken Arok killed him, married Ken Dedes and proclaimed himself ruler of Tumapel.

After his victory over Kertajaya, Kediri became a fief of the new kingdom. Ken Arok took the title Sri Ranggah Rajasa Bhatara Amurwabhumi, the rainbow king of the universe and all lands, and claimed to be a son of Siwa. His kingdom was centred at Singasari, now in Malang, about 50 kilometres east of Kediri.

His rule was short. Anusapati, son of Ken Dedes and Tunggul Ametung, had long suspected Ken Arok of his father's death, and on finding out the truth he killed him, according to legend with the kris of Mpu Gandring; Anusapati was in turn killed with the same kris by his stepbrother Panji Tohjaya. The kings of Majapahit were believed to descend from Ken Arok, and since Ki Ageng Pemanahan, founder of Mataram, claimed Majapahit blood, so did the Mataram rulers and the kingdoms of Surakarta and Jogjakarta formed when Mataram split in 1755. His story remains popular in Central and East Java.
kenesary-kasymov: Kenesary was born into the noble and wealthy Genghisid Töre clan. His grandfather Ablai Khan had been one of the most significant rulers of the Kazakh Khanate, and his grandmother was a daughter of the Dzungar Khuntaiji Galdan Tseren. By his elder wife Aikumis he had six children. His younger brother, the batyr Nauryzbai, a son of their father Kasym by his second wife, became one of his closest associates.

Russian influence over the Kazakh juzes had grown through the 18th century. In 1731 Abul Khair Khan of the Junior Juz recognised a Russian protectorate, and in 1740 Ablai, khan of the Middle Juz, also became a Russian subject. Later khans were appointed by the Russian government, and lines of forts, among them Orenburg, Petropavlovsk, Akmolinsk and Semipalatinsk, moved ever deeper into the steppe.

Kenesary demanded that Russia restore the Kazakh statehood of Ablai Khan's time, abolish its taxes and withdraw from the forts it held. The envoys he sent with letters to the Governor-General of Western Siberia and to Tsar Nicholas I were captured and punished. His rising drew in Kazakhs of all three juzes, with Nauryzbai leading detachments, and in May 1838 his forces captured the Akmolinsk Prikaz. Besides resisting Russian colonisation, it aimed to free the Kazakhs of the southern regions from the rule of the Kokand Khanate.

As khan from 1841 he briefly held an independent state of his own. In 1847 he died at the hands of Kyrgyz manap chieftains, and historical sources suggest that his severed head was sent to the Russians.

Soviet historians described him as the leader of a reactionary feudal-monarchist movement that sought to separate Kazakhstan from Russia; in Kazakhstan today he is honoured at the state level as the leader of a rebellion against the Russian Empire. He is the model for the Tatar khan Feofar in Jules Verne's novel Michael Strogoff. In 1969 Ilyas Esenberlin made him the subject of Khan Kene, the third part of his trilogy Nomads, and in 2008 Kazpost issued a stamp of Abilhan Kasteev's portrait of him.
kengtung: Kengtung, also spelt Kyaingtong, with the classical name Tungapuri, is a city in Shan State, Myanmar. It is the principal town of Kengtung Township and the former seat of Kengtung State, a minor principality, and it is the largest city and the capital of eastern Shan State. It lies on National Highway 4 and on the Asian Highway routes AH2 and AH3.

Because of its closeness to China and Thailand it has several names: Tai Khun and Tai Lue speakers call it Jeng Tung, Thai speakers Chiang Tung and Chinese speakers Jingdong. The town has several lakes, the largest of which is Naung Tung Lake in the western part of the city. Its climate is tropical wet and dry, with a dry season from December to April and a wet season from May to November.

The early history of Kengtung is made up of myths and legends. Oral tradition of the Tai people holds that the ancient city was founded in the distant past by the Tai Lue as the original inhabitants of the region, and was later re-established by a grandson of King Mangrai after he defeated the Tai Lue. The migration of the Chiang Mai dynasty in the 13th century, which founded a kingdom later named Lanna, gave Kengtung a different type of Tai population from the rest of Shan State, the Tai Khün.

Like other major towns of the Shan Plateau, Kengtung was home to a Shan saopha, or sawbwa, and was the capital of Kengtung State. In 1905 Sao Kawng Kiao Intaleng built the Kengtung Palace. From 1942 until the end of the Second World War the Thai Phayap Army seized and occupied the city, which became the headquarters of the Saharat Thai Doem territory. The regional military command of the Tatmadaw has its headquarters in the town today.
kenjutsu: Kenjutsu is an umbrella term for the schools of Japanese swordsmanship, especially those that predate the Meiji Restoration. It means "sword techniques", as opposed to kendo, "the way of the sword", and it grew out of the samurai class of feudal Japan. The curved sword now known as the katana was developed in the Heian period. The oldest schools still in existence date to the Muromachi period (1336–1573), a time of long inter-state warfare, and three major ones emerged then: Kage-ryū, Chujō-ryū and Tenshin Shōden Katori Shintō-ryū. On Okinawa the art of Udundi, practised by the noble Motobu family of the Ryukyu Kingdom, is the only surviving sword system.

Practice varies by school but commonly includes battlefield techniques without an opponent and paired kata. Kata training has always been the mainstay, though later schools added sparring. Many schools train with the wooden sword (bokutō or bokken), shaped to a style's principles, and some use the fukuro shinai, a bamboo sword covered in leather or cloth, which dates to the 15th century. Many syllabi teach a paired long and short sword, called nitōjutsu. Miyamoto Musashi (1584–1645), who advocated it in The Book of Five Rings, was its best-known exponent, but the Katori school, founded about 1447, and Tatsumi-ryu, founded in 1504–1521, taught two swords before him.

In the Edo period (1603–1868) more than 500 styles were recorded. In the 19th century the bamboo shinai and protective armour (bōgu) allowed full-speed sparring with less risk of injury. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 dissolved the samurai class, and kenjutsu declined for about twenty years until rising national confidence revived the sword arts, especially in the military and police. In 1886 the police gathered kata from various schools into a standard set, and in 1912 the Dai Nippon Butoku Kai, founded in 1895, issued an edict with ten kata as a core curriculum. That curriculum evolved into modern kendo.
kennebec-river: The river rises in Moosehead Lake in west-central Maine, where its East and West Outlets join at Indian Pond, and is joined at The Forks by the Dead River. It flows south past Madison, Skowhegan, Waterville, Augusta, Hallowell and Gardiner into Merrymeeting Bay, a freshwater tidal bay it shares with the Androscoggin River, and reaches the Gulf of Maine below Bath. Below the fall line it has no rapids, so tides and saltwater fish such as the Atlantic sturgeon reach as far as Waterville. Its name comes from the Eastern Abenaki for a large body of still water.

Samuel de Champlain charted the river as far as present-day Bath in 1605, and in the 1600s the Abenaki village of Norridgewock stood on its banks. The settlers of the Popham Colony built the Virginia of Sagadahoc, the first oceangoing vessel built in the New World by English-speaking shipwrights, and the trading post at Cushnoc followed in 1628. In the 17th century the river was for a time the western boundary of Cornwall County, Province of New York.

After England's conquest of Acadia in 1710, New France still claimed Maine east of the Kennebec and set up a Catholic mission at Norridgewock. In Father Rale's War (1722–1725) Abenaki warriors resisted English encroachment, until a militia raid on Norridgewock in August 1724 killed as many as 40 inhabitants, among them women and children, and the Jesuit Sebastien Rasle; the raiders burned the village and were paid bounties for scalps. Some 1,110 soldiers followed the river on Benedict Arnold's expedition to Quebec in 1775.

Ocean ships once reached Augusta, and the river served as a trade corridor into interior Maine, carrying logs to sawmills and paper mills and ice cut in winter for shipment south. Bath, known as the City of Ships, had at least 19 major shipbuilding firms in 1854 and still has the Bath Iron Works. The Edwards Dam of 1837 was removed in 1999, letting migratory fish return, and rafting through the gorge below Harris Station Dam began in 1976. A flood on 1 and 2 April 1987 destroyed 215 homes.
kenneth-kaunda: Kenneth Kaunda was born on 28 April 1924 at Lubwa Mission in Chinsali, Northern Rhodesia, the youngest of eight children. His father, the Reverend David Kaunda, a Church of Scotland missionary and teacher born in Nyasaland, died when Kenneth was a child. His mother, Helen Nyirenda Kaunda, was also a teacher and the first African woman to teach in colonial Northern Rhodesia. He trained at the Munali Training Centre in Lusaka from 1941 to 1943 and became a teacher.

Kaunda entered politics in 1949 and in 1953 became Secretary General of the African National Congress under Harry Nkumbula. Kaunda broke with Nkumbula and founded the Zambian African National Congress in October 1958. It was banned in March 1959 and he served nine months in prison. He was elected president of its successor, the United National Independence Party (UNIP), in January 1960. UNIP won the elections of January 1964, and on 24 October 1964 he became the first president of independent Zambia.

The new state had a very poorly developed school system, with about a hundred university graduates, and Kaunda invested heavily in education; the University of Zambia opened in 1966. In April 1968 the Mulungushi Reforms began to bring foreign-owned companies under national control, and a number of mining firms were nationalised. From 1973 rising oil prices and falling copper prices cut state income and left Zambia in debt to the International Monetary Fund. Kaunda banned all parties except UNIP, and the Choma Declaration and a new constitution made Zambia a one-party state. He promoted an ideology he called Zambian Humanism.

He supported the movements against white minority rule in Rhodesia, South West Africa, Angola and Mozambique, allowing groups such as the African National Congress, ZAPU and SWAPO to operate from Zambia. The TAZARA Railway to Dar es Salaam, completed in 1975, gave Zambia a trade route that did not cross white-ruled territory.

After riots in 1990 and a failed coup attempt, Kaunda yielded to demands for multiparty politics. In the elections of 1991 Frederick Chiluba of the Movement for Multiparty Democracy won 75 percent of the vote to his 24. Kaunda handed power over on 2 November 1991, the second mainland African head of state to leave office peacefully after losing a free multiparty election. He retired from politics in 1998 and later worked against the spread of HIV/AIDS. He died on 17 June 2021, aged 97, and Zambia observed 21 days of national mourning.
kenneth-macalpin: Kenneth MacAlpin is believed to have been born around 810 on Iona. According to the traditional genealogy his father was Alpín mac Echdach, king of Dál Riada, but modern historians are sceptical about Alpín's reign, and the genealogy rests on a manuscript written under Malcolm III in the 11th century. A tradition makes Kenneth's grandmother a Pictish princess, a sister of Constantine I and Óengus II, which under Pictish custom would have given him a claim to the Pictish throne. His brother Donald I succeeded him. Dál Riada was mountainous and infertile, and it had lost its western territories in the Hebrides to Vikings.

The Chronicle of the Kings of Alba says Kenneth defeated the Picts and ruled them for 16 years. Most modern historians accept 843 as the year he became king of the Picts, though the Pictish king lists suggest the Pictish kingdom may have fallen in 849 or 850. Sources do not detail the conquest, and a later legend tells of a Pictish nobleman killed treacherously at a feast at Scone. After it, Scots from Dál Riada migrated in large numbers into Pictish lands, and the Picts' language and institutions quickly disappeared. In 848 or 849, according to the Chronicle, Kenneth moved relics from the abbey on Iona, where Viking raids made life untenable, to Dunkeld, and the Stone of Scone was moved to Scone.

Kenneth invaded Lothian in Northumbria six times and razed Melrose and Dunbar, while Britons from Strathclyde burnt Dunblane and Vikings ravaged the country from Clunie to Dunkeld. He married his daughters to the kings of Strathclyde and Ireland. The Chronicle of Melrose calls him one of the first Scottish lawgivers, but no laws survive.

Kenneth died in 858, most likely on 8 February, at Forteviot, of a tumour according to the Chronicle of the Kings of Alba, and was buried on Iona. His brother Donald I succeeded him by tanistry, and then his sons Causantín and Áed ruled in turn. The Alpínid dynasty, formed in this period, ruled until the beginning of the 11th century. Tradition makes him the founder of Scotland, but the current academic consensus is that he was not the first king of Alba. Like his immediate successors he bore the title king of the Picts, and Donald II was the first to be called king of Alba. Historians argue that his chief achievement was founding a new dynasty.
kenroku-en: The garden's beginnings are uncertain. One account starts with the Tatsumi water channel, completed in 1632 by Maeda Toshitsune, the third daimyō, whose water later fed the garden's winding streams. Another holds that it began in 1676, when the fifth daimyō, Maeda Tsunanori, built a house on the slope facing Kanazawa Castle and named its garden Renchitei, the lotus pond garden. Lords and retainers used it for banquets, viewing the moon and the autumn maples, until a great fire destroyed nearly all of it in 1759; the Shigure-tei teahouse of 1725 survived.

Restoration began in 1774 under the 11th daimyō, Harunaga, who made the Emerald Waterfall and the Yūgao-tei teahouse, now the oldest building in the garden. In 1822 the 12th daimyō, Narinaga, laid out streams drawn from the Tatsumi Waterway, and the 13th, Nariyasu, added more streams and enlarged the Kasumi Pond, completing the garden's present form. It was designated a National Site of Scenic Beauty in 1922 and a National Site of Special Scenic Beauty in 1985.

Matsudaira Sadanobu named the garden in 1822, drawing on a classical Chinese text on the gardens of Luoyang that listed six attributes of a perfect landscape: spaciousness, seclusion, artifice, antiquity, waterways and panoramas. These form contrasting pairs that are hard to unite, and the garden sets open areas such as the shores of Kasumi Pond against secluded ones such as Tokiwaoka Hill, while its viewpoints look out over the Sea of Japan and the Iozan mountains.

A strolling garden of over 25 acres, it holds about 8,750 trees of 183 plant species. Among its features are one of the oldest fountains in Japan, worked by natural water pressure, the two-legged Kotoji stone lantern, a symbol of Kanazawa, the Flying Geese Bridge of eleven red stones, and the Kaiseki Pagoda, said to have been given to the Maeda by Toyotomi Hideyoshi. In winter ropes called yukitsuri support the branches against heavy snow.
kente-cloth: The name comes from kɛntɛn, basket in the Asante dialect of Akan, for its basket-like pattern; the Akan also call the cloth nwentoma, woven cloth. Ashanti folklore tells of weavers who invented kente by copying the patterns of Anansi the spider. Spindle whorls and dye holes from Begho and Bono Manso, dated to the 14th–18th centuries, are the oldest evidence of handloom weaving in southern Ghana. Asante oral tradition credits a man from Bonwire with bringing a loom from Bono Gyaman in the reign of Nana Oti Akenten in the 17th century; another oral source places its invention in the reign of Osei Kofi Tutu I.

Early Asante cloths of blue and white cotton stripes resemble Bondoukou cloths, but the colourful kente was an Asante innovation, woven from dyed thread and from imported silks that were unravelled. The Danish agents Nog and L.F. Rømer recorded that Asantehene Opoku Ware I encouraged craft work in the 18th century and set up a factory for weaving. In 1817 Thomas Edward Bowdich found Asante cloths in all varieties of colour and pattern. The Ewe weave a version of their own from double-woven bands, with Keta as its centre in the 18th century.

Kente is woven by hand on a wooden loom in strips of silk and cotton that are sewn together. Weaving is traditionally men's work, learnt over years of apprenticeship to a master weaver. There are hundreds of patterns, each with a name or message drawn from proverbs, historical events, chiefs, queen mothers or plants, and Ghanaians choose a cloth as much for its name as for its colours. Adweneasa, I've exhausted my skills, fills every block of plain weave with weft patterns and needs three heddles. Colours carry meanings: gold royalty and wealth, black the ancestors and mourning.

Mass-produced prints with kente patterns have spread across Africa, and kente stoles are worn at graduations, mostly by African Americans and others of the African diaspora. In December 2024 UNESCO recognised kente cloth as intangible cultural heritage, and in September 2025 Ghana gained geographical indication status for it: only cloth woven by traditional techniques in approved communities such as Bonwire, Agotime Kpetoe and Sakora Wonoo may now be sold as kente.
kenya-african-national-union: The party grew out of the Kenya African Union, formed in 1944 to voice African grievances against the British colonial administration and to recruit more widely than the Kikuyu Central Association. Jomo Kenyatta became its president in 1947. During the state of emergency declared against the Mau Mau rebellion in October 1952, the union was banned and Kenyatta was imprisoned in 1953. When the ban on national movements was lifted, the revived union merged on 14 May 1960 with Tom Mboya's Kenya Independence Movement and the Nairobi People's Convention Party, with James Gichuru as chairman, Mboya as secretary general and Oginga Odinga as vice chairman.

Its rival, the Kenya African Democratic Union, spoke for the smaller peoples grouped as KAMATUSA and for the European settlers against the Luo and Kikuyu who made up most of KANU's members. KANU wanted immediate independence and universal suffrage, while its rival favoured federalism, which the British backed and which entered the independence constitution. Kenyatta was released in 1961; KANU won the elections of 1963, Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963, and Kenyatta became prime minister. KANU then removed the federal provisions, and its rival dissolved itself into KANU in 1964.

The Kenya People's Union, a leftist party formed in 1966 under Oginga Odinga, was banned after the unrest that ended in the Kisumu massacre, and no new opposition party was formed after 1969. When Kenyatta died in August 1978, Daniel arap Moi became president on 14 October as KANU's sole nominee. After the constitution was amended in June 1982, single-party rule lasted until parliament repealed it in December 1991. Moi and KANU won the multiparty elections of 1992 and 1997, the second with 109 of 212 seats.

In 2002 the party's candidate, Uhuru Kenyatta, lost to Mwai Kibaki of the National Rainbow Coalition, ending 24 years of Moi's rule. KANU later split into factions, backed Kibaki in the disputed election of 2007, lost Kenyatta and his supporters after 2011 and entered a four-party coalition for the 2013 elections.

At its founding KANU held politicians of many views, among them advocates of African socialism. After Sessional Paper No. 10 of 1965 and the resignation of the left allied to Odinga, it pursued a mixed economy with state-run parastatals and kept Kenya on the side of the West in the Cold War. Its national chairman, secretary general and vice chairmen are elected by a national delegates conference.
keoladeo-national-park: The park lies 2 kilometres south-east of Bharatpur and 55 kilometres west of Agra, and covers about 29 square kilometres. It is known locally as Ghana, a mosaic of dry grassland, woodland, swamp and seasonal wetland on the eastern edge of the land that becomes desert. A third of it is wetland with mounds, dykes and open water, which alternately wets and dries and so suits waterfowl. The uplands have tall and short grasses, and pockets of kadam woodland. The park holds 379 species of flowering plants, and the wetland is part of the Indo-Gangetic plain.

The wetland is regulated by people. It also protects Bharatpur's settlements from flash floods and gives pasture to local livestock. Water remains only in some depressions, and tube wells pump water into small hollows to save seeds, spores and other aquatic life, which helps in years of drought.

The area was a private duck-shooting preserve of the Maharaja of Bharatpur, and tradition dates its development as a reserve to 1899. Through the efforts of the ornithologist Salim Ali it became a bird sanctuary, and it was designated a Ramsar site in October 1981. It was established as a national park on 10 March 1982 and made a World Heritage Site in 1985 as a wetland of international importance for migratory waterfowl and the wintering ground of the rare Siberian crane.

Some 2,500 cattle and water buffalo had grazed there until grazing was banned in November 1982. The ban caused resentment and an attempted forced entry; police opened fire and eight people were killed. Without grazing, an amphibious grass blocks the channels, and the Rajasthan government has rejected a proposal to allow limited grazing. A project of 1992 to 1995 by India, Russia, the International Crane Foundation and the Wild Bird Society of Japan tried to build a resident Siberian crane population from captive-bred birds, and did not reach its aim. The last Siberian cranes recorded arrived in the winter of 2001–02.

More than 370 bird species have been recorded, and the park is an important staging ground for waterfowl arriving in the Indian subcontinent and leaving for breeding grounds in the western Palearctic. Common waterfowl include gadwall, shoveler, bar-headed goose, painted stork, spot-billed pelican and sarus crane. It also has 27 mammal species, among them nilgai, chital, sambar and blackbuck, and seven of Rajasthan's ten species of turtle. The park is a World Heritage Site and a Ramsar wetland, and water supply from the Ajan Bund reservoir has been irregular.
keopuolani: Keōpūolani was born at Pahoehoe of Pāpōhaku, near present-day Wailuku on Maui, and was known in early childhood as Kalanikauikaʻalaneo; her later name means Gathering of the Clouds of Heaven. Her father Kīwalaʻō was the son of King Kalaniʻōpuʻu of Hawaiʻi island, and her mother, Kekuʻiapoiwa Liliha, a half-sister of Kamehameha I, shared a mother with Kīwalaʻō: High Chiefess Kalola of Maui. She lived for a time at Hāna before returning to Wailuku.

When Kamehameha defeated the Maui forces of Kalanikupule at Kepaniwai in 1790, while her great-uncle King Kahekili II was on Oʻahu, Kalola fled with her family towards Oʻahu, but sickness halted them on Molokaʻi. Kalola offered her granddaughter as a future bride, and recognition of Kamehameha as ruler of Maui, in exchange for peace.

Her rank gave her unquestioned social and political influence, and the marriage strengthened Kamehameha's claim after he had overthrown her father, his cousin. When chanters spoke her name, listeners bared themselves above the waist, and even Kamehameha removed his malo in her presence. She kept the kapu strictly but was mild to those who broke it, and they often fled to her for protection. Perhaps eleven or twelve children were born to her, of whom only three survived; her sons were raised by others, but, breaking the custom of hānai, she kept her daughter Nāhiʻenaʻena by her side.

After Kamehameha's death in 1819 she mostly stayed out of politics but generally supported Kaʻahumanu as Kuhina Nui. She married High Chief Hoapili, who carried Kamehameha's remains by canoe to a secret place on the Kona coast. After the missionaries arrived in 1820 she was among the first of the aliʻi to become Christian, adopted western clothing and learned to read and write, and in 1823 she declared that royalty would no longer take several spouses.

She fell ill in August 1823. The missionary William Ellis spoke for the church at her baptism, and she took the Christian name of Harriet Stewart, wife of the missionary Charles Stewart. She died in the early evening of 16 September 1823 and was buried after a public funeral at Hale Kamani in Lahaina. In 1837 Kamehameha III moved her body to the sacred island of Mokuʻula, and her remains were perhaps later reburied at Waiola Church.
keraites: The Keraites first appear in history as the ruling faction of the Zubu, a large confederacy of tribes that dominated Mongolia during the 11th and 12th centuries and often fought the Liao dynasty of north China, which controlled much of Mongolia at the time. Their language is disputed. Names and titles of early leaders, such as Toghrul and the title buiruk ('commander'), are Turkic, and many scholars classify them as a Turkic people. Others, among them Vasily Bartold and Boris Vladimirtsov, hold that they spoke a Mongolic language, and Tao Zongyi listed them about 1366 among the 72 Mongol peoples.

After the Zubu broke up, the Keraites kept their dominance on the steppe. Their khanate had a central faction, which served as the khan's army and was drawn from many tribes, and an outer faction of tribes that pledged obedience but lived on their own pastures. Toghrul reigned from the 1160s to 1203 and became the blood-brother (anda) of Yesugei; Genghis Khan called him khan etseg, 'khan father'. In 1196 the Jin dynasty gave him the title Wang, hence Wang Khan. Fearing the growing power of Temüjin, the future Genghis Khan, he plotted with Jamukha against him.

In 1203 Temüjin defeated the Keraites, and Toghrul was killed by Naiman soldiers who did not recognise him. Temüjin dispersed the survivors among the other Mongol tribes. He married Toghrul's eldest niece Ibaqa, and his son Tolui married another niece, Sorghaghtani Bekhi, who became the mother of Möngke Khan and Kublai Khan.

The Keraites were converted to the Church of the East early in the 11th century. According to accounts by Mari ibn Suleiman and Bar Hebraeus, the khan, lost in a snowstorm about 1007, saw a vision of Saint Sergius of Samarkand and promised to become a Christian. He wrote to Abdisho, Metropolitan of Merv, and the king and 200,000 of his people were baptised. William of Rubruck, who visited Mongolia in 1254–1255, found the faith mixed with shamanism and Manicheism. Some versions of the Prester John legend identify that king with Toghrul.

Remnants of the Keraites lived along the Kara Irtysh in the late 14th century and were dispersed in the 1420s in the Mongol-Oirat wars fought by Uwais Khan. Afterwards they disappear as an identifiable group, though they are proposed as part of the ancestry of Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Bashkir and Nogai groups.
kerala: Kerala is mainly a strip of coastal plains wedged between the Western Ghats and the Laccadive Sea, 38,863 square kilometres in area, with Karnataka to the northeast and Tamil Nadu to the east. Geographically it falls into three regions: the cool eastern highlands, the central midlands of rolling hills and the western coastal lowlands.

In Hindu tradition the land was won from the sea by the sage Parashurama, the sixth avatar of Vishnu, who threw his axe across the water so that the sea withdrew to where it landed. Archaeology shows Neolithic dolmens in the Marayur region and rock engravings in the Edakkal caves in Wayanad from about 6000 BCE. Sumerian records are said to show Kerala as a spice exporter from at least 3000 BCE, and Babylonians, Assyrians and Egyptians were drawn to the Malabar Coast in the 3rd and 2nd millennia BCE, as were Arabs and Phoenicians.

The word Kerala first appears as Keralaputra, son of the Cheras, in an edict of the Maurya emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. The Cheras were the earliest major dynasty of the region and rose through maritime commerce, but often faced invasion from the Chola and Pandya dynasties. A second Chera kingdom, c. 800 to 1102, was founded by Kulasekhara Varman and governed most of present-day Kerala and parts of Tamil Nadu, with a flourishing of art, literature, trade and the Bhakti movement. Most historians hold that Malayalam descends from a dialect of early middle Tamil and became a distinct language between the 9th and 13th centuries.

Vasco da Gama arrived at Kappad, near Kozhikode, in 1498, and the Zamorin of Kozhikode allowed the Portuguese to trade, which led to a factory and fort. In 1947 the princely states of Travancore and Kochi acceded to India, and on 1 July 1949 they merged as Travancore-Cochin. On 1 November 1956 the Malabar district and the Kasargod taluk were joined to it, and its four southern taluks went to Madras State, forming Kerala under the States Reorganisation Act. The first elections in 1957 produced a Communist-led government under E. M. S. Namboodiripad, among the earliest democratically elected Communist governments in the world.

Kerala is a state of southern India with its capital at Thiruvananthapuram, and 33 million people at the census of 2011. Malayalam is the most widely spoken language and, with English, an official one. Hinduism is practised by more than 54 per cent of the people, followed by Islam and Christianity.
kerameikos: The Kerameikos lies north-west of the Acropolis and takes in a wide area both inside and outside the ancient city walls, on either side of the Dipylon Gate and by the banks of the Eridanos River. Its name comes from the deme of the Kerameis, the potters, and from the Greek word kéramos for pottery clay, from which the English word ceramic derives. The Inner Kerameikos was the potters' quarter within the city, sited there because of the clay carried down by the Eridanos. The Outer Kerameikos covered the cemetery and the Demosion Sema, the public graveyard just outside the walls, where Pericles delivered his funeral oration in 431 BCE.

The area was originally marshland along the Eridanos and was used for burial as early as the 3rd millennium BCE. It became an organised cemetery from about 1200 BCE, and cist graves with offerings from that period have been found. After the Persian sack of Athens in 480 BCE the new city wall of 478 BCE changed the area. At the suggestion of Themistocles the funerary sculptures were built into it, and two large gates were set up: the Sacred Gate and the double-arched Dipylon Gate, with state graves beside it for prominent figures including Pericles and Cleisthenes.

Inside the walls, between the two gates, stood the Pompeion, where the procession of the Panathenaic Festival gathered and the nobility of Athens ate the sacrificial meat. The army of the Roman dictator Sulla razed it and much else near the Sacred Gate in his sack of Athens in 86 BCE, an episode Plutarch called a bloodbath. A storehouse built on its site in the 2nd century CE was destroyed in the invasion of the Heruli in 267 CE, and a new Festival Gate built about 500 CE was destroyed in raids by Avars and Slavs at the end of the 6th century, after which the Kerameikos fell into obscurity.

The site was rediscovered when a Greek worker dug up a stele in April 1863. Excavations began in 1870 under the Greek Archaeological Society and have continued since 1913 under the German Archaeological Institute at Athens. Work on the Kerameikos metro station revealed a pit holding 89 individuals, dated by pottery to 430 to 426 BCE and widely linked to the Plague of Athens. The Kerameikos Museum, with the largest collection of burial-related objects in Greece, stands on the site.
kerbogha: Kerbogha was a Seljuk Turk who owed his success to his military talent. He supported Terken Khatun, the wife of Malik-Shah I, and her four-year-old son Mahmud I, who was installed on the throne at Baghdad. Sent with an army to secure Isfahan and arrest Berkyaruq, he saw Mahmud's supporters defeated by Berkyaruq's forces at Isfahan in January 1093. Later he joined Berkyaruq, and in 1094 he was sent to fight Tutush I, who had declared himself sultan in Syria. He was imprisoned with his brother Altuntaş at Aleppo and then Homs, and released on Tutush's death by Fakhr al-Mulk Radwan.

In 1095 Kerbogha served under the Abbasid caliph al-Mustazhir in an attempt to reconquer Aleppo. In 1096 he captured Harran, Nisbis and Mosul, ending Uqaylid rule there. In 1098, hearing that the Crusaders were besieging Antioch, he gathered his troops and left Mosul on 31 March. On the way he tried to retake Edessa, recently conquered by Baldwin I, so as to leave no Frankish garrison behind him. He besieged it for three weeks without result before going on. When he arrived around 7 June, the Crusaders had held Antioch since 3 June, and he began to besiege them in turn.

On 27 June the Crusaders sent Peter the Hermit as emissary to propose that the two sides settle their differences by a duel; Kerbogha, feeling secure, refused. Inside the city, Peter Bartholomew claimed to have found the Holy Lance through a vision, which revived the Christian army. In Kerbogha's army, made up of semi-nomadic Turkmen and levies from Mosul, the Jazira, Palestine and Damascus, quarrels among the emirs took precedence over unity. What united them was fear that his real aim was to conquer all their lands.

On 28 June Bohemond, the leader of the Christian army, decided to attack, and the emirs chose to humble Kerbogha by abandoning him at the critical moment. He was surprised by the organisation and discipline of the Crusader army, and his strategy of dividing his forces failed. He was quickly routed and retreated to Mosul.

Despite his defeats at Edessa and Antioch, his position in Mosul was not challenged for the rest of his life. He spent time raising Imad ad-Din Zengi, the namesake of the Zengid dynasty, who took power in Mosul in 1127 after a series of Seljuk vassals had ruled following Kerbogha's death in 1102.
kerch: Kerch lies on the Kerch Peninsula in the east of Crimea, on the Kerch Strait that gives access to the Sea of Azov. The Greek city of Panticapaeum stood on Mount Mithridat near the mouth of the Melek-Chesme river, which was navigable in Bosporan times. Its position at the intersection of trade routes between the steppe and Europe made it grow rapidly, exporting grain and salted fish and also making wine and minting its own coins.

Panticapaeum subdued nearby cities and by 480 BCE had become the capital of the Kingdom of Bosporus. For a short time, under Mithradates VI Eupator, it was the capital of the much larger Kingdom of Pontus. The Huns devastated the city in 375. From the 6th century it was Byzantine, and Emperor Justinian I had a citadel named Bospor built. In the 7th century the Khazars took it and called it Karcha, and it served as a major port of the Khazar slave trade. The Church of St. John the Baptist, founded in 717, is said to be the oldest church in Ukraine.

After the fall of Khazaria to Kievan Rus', Kerch became the centre of a Khazar successor state whose ruler, Georgius Tzul, was deposed by a Byzantine-Rus expedition in 1016. The city became the Genoese colony of Cerco in 1318, and in 1475 it passed to the Ottoman Empire, under which it decayed and became a slave market. Russia received Kerch and the fortress of Yenikale by the Treaty of Kuchuk-Kainarji in 1774.

British forces devastated the city in 1855. In the Second World War the Germans took it in November 1941, the Red Army retook it on 31 December 1941, and the Germans occupied it again in 1942. It returned to Soviet control on 11 April 1944. The occupiers killed about 15,000 citizens and deported another 14,000.

Archaeological digs began under Russian auspices in the middle of the 19th century, and finds from Kerch are in the Hermitage, the Louvre and the British Museum. The Great Mithridates Staircase, with 428 steps, was built in 1833 to 1840. A memorial stands at the Adzhimushkay catacombs, where thousands of soldiers and refugees sheltered and fought during the occupation.
kerch-strait: The Kerch Strait connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov and separates the Kerch Peninsula of Crimea in the west from the Taman Peninsula in the east, the westernmost extension of the Caucasus Mountains. It is about 35 kilometres long, between 3.1 and 15 kilometres wide, and up to 18 metres deep. Its most important harbour, the city of Kerch, gives it its name, and it has also been called the Straits of Taman and the Straits of Yenikale, after the Yeni-Kale fortress at Kerch.

The Cimmerian Strait, as it was called in Greek, honoured the Cimmerians, steppe nomads who lived nearby, and the Romans knew it as the Cimmerian Bosporus. In antiquity it seems to have held a group of islands cut by arms of the Kuban River, then called the Hypanis, and various sounds that have since silted up. Like the Thracian Bosporus, it was regarded as a boundary between Europe and Asia, although most geographers, among them Posidonius, Strabo and Ptolemy, placed that boundary at the river Tanais, the Don.

The Battle of Kerch Strait, fought in 1790 during the Russo-Turkish War, ended in a Russian victory. In the Second World War the Kerch Peninsula saw desperate fighting between the Red Army and Nazi Germany, which grew more intense in the coldest months, when the strait froze and troops could cross on the ice. In spring 1943 Hitler ordered a road and rail bridge 4.8 kilometres long across the strait. A cable railway entered service on 14 June 1943, but the bridge was never finished, and the Wehrmacht evacuated the Kuban bridgehead in September 1943.

The Soviets built a provisional railway bridge in 1944, and moving ice floes destroyed it in February 1945. A train and vehicle ferry service began in 1954 between Port Krym and Port Kavkaz. Because the strait is shallow at its narrowest point, the Kerch–Yenikale Canal was dredged through it. Its main channel takes vessels up to 215 metres long with a draft of up to 8 metres, with a pilot, and large ships pass in alternating one-way convoys, a procedure unchanged under Soviet, Ukrainian and Russian jurisdiction. Fishing is a major activity, and Taman Bay is a main fishing ground.
kerei-khan: Kerei was born in 1424. In the late 1450s part of the nomadic population, led by Janibek and Kerei, broke away from the rule of the Uzbek khan Abu'l-Khayr and migrated to Moghulistan, settling in the valleys of the Chu and Talas rivers, where the khan of Moghulistan offered them support against their opponents. Around 200,000 nomads joined the movement, and its strength alarmed Abu'l-Khayr. He set out on a campaign against Moghulistan in 1468 but died suddenly on the way.

His son Sheikh Haidar succeeded him, but all of Abu'l-Khayr's opponents combined against the new khan, whose short reign ended when the Siberian Khan Ibak murdered him. Kerei then took supreme power in the eastern Dasht and appointed his brother Janibek ruler of the west wing. The two khans still had to fight the Shaybanids for power over the eastern steppe, and Kerei and his followers fought for an independent state. Kerei was killed in that conflict; the sources mention him for the last time in the events of the winter of 1473.

The secession led by Kerei and Janibek is seen as an important link in the chain of events that produced the Kazakh Khanate and the Kazakh nationality itself. From the end of the 15th century the name Kazakh took on a political sense, designating the domains created by the two khans, and from the beginning of the 16th century, after part of the tribes moved with Shaibani Khan into Maverannahr, an ethnic one.

Why Kerei and Janibek broke away, and where the khanate first took shape, are unknown, and a number of authors date its formation to the turn of the 15th and 16th centuries, treating the migration as only its beginning. On 1 June 2010 a monument to Kerei and Janibek by the sculptor Renat Abenov was unveiled in Astana, near the Museum of the First President of Kazakhstan.
kerkennah-islands: The Kerkennah Islands lie in the Gulf of Gabès, off the east coast of Tunisia and east of Sfax. The group covers 160 square kilometres, and the land is low, rising no more than 13 metres above sea level. The main islands are Chergui and Gharbi. Remla, on Chergui, is the main town, and a port called Kraten lies in the north. The climate is warm and dry, with strong prevailing winds that cross the mainland first and arrive hot. The vegetation is mostly tall xerophytic and often halophytic plants, such as palms and saltbushes.

The natives of Tunisia and Kerkennah first settled the islands. As the Roman Empire spread, the Romans used Kerkennah as a port and look-out point to watch activity offshore. In 2 BCE Augustus exiled Sempronius Gracchus, a lover of Julia the Elder, to the islands for 14 years. The Greeks called the islands Cercina and Cercinna, and Strabo and Ptolemaeus wrote that the city on the island bore the same name.

Athenius, bishop of Cercina, was among the Catholic bishops whom the Arian Vandal king Huneric summoned to Carthage in 484. The see was on the most easterly island of the group and is now listed by the Catholic Church as a titular see. The monastery that Saint Fulgentius of Ruspe built in 532 has been placed on one of the islets, although a recent argument identifies it with Kneiss island. In the Second World War the Battle of the Tarigo Convoy was fought near the islands on 16 April 1941. Drought in the 1980s left the islands short of clean water and irrigation, and many islanders moved to the mainland, the nearest city being Sfax.

Kerkennah had a population of 15,501 in 2014. Agriculture is slight, and the islanders keep chickens and goats for their own use. Fishing, especially for octopus, is the main industry, and the catch is exported to mainland Tunisia and nearby countries. Tourism is limited, since the islands lack broad sandy beaches, but many mainland Tunisians spend holidays there. The archipelago is an important wintering area and migration stopover for birds and is classed by BirdLife International as an Important Bird Area. It is also home to an endemic gerbil subspecies, Gerbillus simoni zakariai.
kerma: Kerma was the capital city of the Kingdom of Kerma, which had its roots in the pre-Kerma culture of present-day Sudan from 3500 BCE. It is one of the largest archaeological sites in ancient Nubia and has produced decades of excavation, including thousands of graves and tombs and the residential quarters of the main city around the Western, or Lower, Deffufa. The site was first settled by hunter-gatherers around 8350 BCE. It was mostly abandoned between 5550 and 5150 BCE, possibly because of a decreased flow of the Nile, and again between 4050 and 3450 BCE.

Agriculture developed around 3000 BCE and a cultural tradition began around Kerma. A state society formed between 2550 and 1550 BCE. The city grew into a large urban centre built around a great adobe temple, the Western Deffufa, built after 1750 BCE. Copper metallurgy appears from about 2200-2000 BCE. The settlement is divided into Pre-Kerma (c. 3500-2500 BCE), Early Kerma (c. 2500-2050), Middle Kerma (c. 2050-1750), Classic Kerma (c. 1750-1580) and Final Kerma (c. 1580-1500), followed by a late period under Egyptian New Kingdom influence. By 1700 BCE the city had a population of at least 10,000. Its artefacts are marked by blue faience, which the Kermans learned to work independently of Egypt, and by glazed quartzite and architectural inlays.

The cemetery holds over 30,000 graves, with larger graves ringed by smaller ones, which suggests social stratification. At its southern boundary four burial mounds extend more than 90 metres in diameter and are believed to be the graves of the city's final kings. Egyptian pottery, scarab seals and amulets in the burials point to extensive trade with Egypt. After the sacking of Kerma, the cemetery was used for the kings of the 25th, or Napatan, dynasty of the Kingdom of Kush.

George Reisner of Harvard and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, led the first major excavations in 1913-1916 and treated Kerma as an Egyptian satellite. Excavations by Charles Bonnet and the University of Geneva from 1977 to 2003 showed instead a vast independent urban complex that ruled most of the Third Cataract for centuries, with houses, workshops, palaces and a bronze forge. In 2003 Bonnet's team found black granite statues of Twenty-fifth Dynasty pharaohs near Kerma, which are displayed in the Kerma Museum.
kerman: Kerman lies on a large, flat plain on the high margin of the Lut Desert, in the south-central part of Iran, about 800 km south-east of Tehran. The city stands 1,755 m above sea level and is surrounded by mountains, those to the south and south-east snow-capped all year round. It has a cold desert climate, with hot summers, cool to cold winters and scarce rain, an average of 148 mm a year. The archaeological areas of Jiroft and Tappe Yahya lie south of the city.

Kerman was founded as a defensive outpost under the name Veh-Ardashir by Ardashir I, the founder of the Sasanian Empire, in the 3rd century CE. After the Battle of Nahāvand in 642 the city came under Muslim rule. Abbasid authority over the region was weak, and in the tenth century power passed to the Buyid emirs; Mahmud of Ghazni took the region and city in the late tenth century. The name Kerman was adopted at some point in the tenth century.

Under Seljuk Turkish rule in the 11th and 12th centuries Kerman remained virtually independent and conquered Oman and Fars. When Marco Polo visited in 1271 it had become a major trading centre linking the Persian Gulf with Khorasan and Central Asia. Afterwards the city was sacked many times by various invaders, but it expanded rapidly under the Safavid dynasty, when carpets and rugs were exported to England and Germany.

The city suffered its worst reprisals at the end of the 18th century. When Kerman fell to Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar, he was angered by the popular support the city had given Lotf Ali Khan. Many of its men were killed or blinded, and a pile of 20,000 eyeballs was heaped before the victor.

Kerman is the capital of Kerman province and of its county, and the largest city of the province. Its population was 537,718 at the 2016 census. Carpet weaving is one of its main industries, and its carpets are known internationally; cotton textiles and goat-wool shawls are also made. The Kerman Fire Temple houses the only Iranian anthropology museum dedicated to Zoroastrianism, for the city has a small Zoroastrian minority beside its mostly Muslim population.
kermanshah: Kermanshah stands in western Iran, 525 kilometres from Tehran, and is the capital of its province, county and district. Its name comes from the Sasanian title Kirmanshah, King of Kerman, held by Prince Bahram, son of Shapur III, when he governed the province of Kirman. Having succeeded his father as Bahram IV, he is said to have founded the city in 390 and his title was applied to it. In Iranian mythology the city's construction is instead attributed to Tahmuras, third king of the Pishdadian dynasty.

The Kermanshah area was occupied from the Lower Paleolithic onward. Hand axes have been found east of the city, and the only skeletal remains of Neanderthal Man discovered in Iran came from caves and a rock shelter in Kermanshah province. It was also one of the first places where settlements such as Asiab, Ganj-Darreh and Sarab were established, between 8,000 and 10,000 years ago, and the first pottery of Iran was made at Ganj-Darreh, near Harsin. The city itself contains four archaeological mounds, among them Chogha Golan and Tappa Gawri.

Under the Sasanians it was a summer resort for the kings. Under Seljuk rule in the 11th century it became a cultural and commercial centre of western Iran. The Mongols under Hulegu sacked it in 1257, shortly before the sack of Baghdad. The Safavids fortified the town, and the Qajars repulsed an Ottoman attack during the reign of Fath Ali Shah (1797–1834). The Ottomans occupied Kermanshah in 1723–1729 and 1731–1732. In the First World War it was occupied by the Imperial Russian Army in 1914 and the Ottoman Army in 1915, and evacuated in 1917 when British forces arrived. It was heavily damaged in the Iran–Iraq War of 1980 to 1988.

The city has the largest Kurdish population in Iran. Its people speak Kermashani, a variety of Southern Kurdish, and Kermanshahi Persian. Most are Shia Muslims, with Sunni Muslims, Christians and followers of Yarsanism also living there. The Kermanshah Grand Bazaar was built around 1820, when Prince Mohammad Ali Mirza Dowlatshah of the Qajar dynasty governed the city.

Taq-e Bostan, 5 kilometres from the centre, is a series of Sasanian rock reliefs, among them Ardashir II's and Shapur III's investitures and the armoured equestrian figure of Khosrow II. Nearby is the Behistun Inscription, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, which Henry Rawlinson had transcribed in 1835 and 1843 and which was crucial in deciphering cuneiform.
kerosene: Distilling petroleum into kerosene was first written about in the ninth century by the Persian scholar Rāzi, whose Kitab al-Asrar describes two methods, using an alembic, for making what he called naft abyad, white naphtha. Distillation was repeated until the product was clear and safe to burn. Kerosene was also made at the time from oil shale and bitumen. Coal oil was known to chemists by the 1700s as a byproduct of coal gas and tar, but it burned smokily, so the market for indoor lamps outside the cities went to whale oil, especially that of sperm whales.

The Canadian geologist Abraham Pineo Gesner claimed to have shown in 1846, in Charlottetown, a process of distilling a clear lamp fuel from coal. He coined the name kerosene from the Greek roots for wax and oil. In 1848 the Scottish chemist James Young began distilling coal, especially torbanite, and named one liquid paraffine oil because it congealed like paraffin wax. He patented his process in 1850 and built the first truly commercial oil works at Bathgate in 1851. Gesner moved to Long Island in 1854, obtained his patent that year and registered Kerosene as a trademark.

In 1851 Samuel Martin Kier of Pennsylvania began selling lamp oil to miners, distilled from the crude oil that fouled his salt wells. The Polish pharmacist Ignacy Łukasiewicz showed his lamps during an emergency operation on 31 July 1853 and set up a refinery near Jasło in 1859. Edwin Drake's well in western Pennsylvania in 1859 let refiners side-step the coal-oil patents, and by the 1860s the American illuminating oil industry had switched to petroleum. The name lost its proprietary status and became the generic kerosene.

Kerosene was a fire risk: in 1880 nearly two of every five fires in New York City were caused by defective kerosene lamps. The American whaling fleet peaked at 199 ships in 1858, and only 39 sailed in 1876. Electric lighting displaced kerosene in cities from the late 19th century, and in 1909 motor fuels overtook it as the main use of refined petroleum in the United States. It stayed in use in stoves, heaters, tractors and, in highly refined form, jet engines.

Kerosene is a low-viscosity, clear liquid of hydrocarbons with 6 to 20 carbon atoms per molecule, taken by fractional distillation of petroleum between 150 and 275 °C. It is called paraffin in the United Kingdom, South Africa and East Africa, and the Primus stove of 1892 burns it.
kertanegara: Kertanagara was the fifth ruler of Singhasari, the son of King Wisnuwardhana. The dynasty had come to power in 1222, when its first ruler, Ken Arok, overthrew the Kediri Kingdom. Kertanagara effectively held power from 1254 and formally succeeded on his father's death in 1268. He followed a mystical Tantric blend of Hinduism and Buddhism, presented himself as a god-king embodying Shiva and Buddha, and held many religious festivals.

Under him Singhasari reached the height of its power. He put down rebellions in Java by Cayaraja in 1270 and Mahisha Rangkah in 1280, made Bali a vassal in 1284, allied with Champa and extended Javanese involvement in the spice trade with the Maluku Islands. The Pamalayu expedition brought the Melayu Kingdom of eastern Sumatra under his control, and lands in Madura and Borneo offered their submission. When envoys of Kublai Khan arrived in 1289 to demand tribute, he had their faces branded and their ears cut and sent them back to China, and in 1292 Kublai ordered a punitive naval expedition.

Before it arrived, Jayakatwang, prince of Kediri and one of Singhasari's strongest vassals, rebelled while most of the Javanese army was overseas. A diversionary attack drew the remaining troops north, and Jayakatwang struck the undefended capital from the mountainous south. Kertanagara was killed with many courtiers in his palace in May or June 1292.

His son-in-law Raden Wijaya escaped to Madura and founded the settlement that grew into Majapahit. Through his daughter Gayatri Rajapatni, Kertanagara became ancestor of the Rajasa dynasty that ruled it. In 1351 Gajah Mada issued an inscription for a funerary temple dedicated to him. Kertanagara had already named the idea of Nusantara, a united archipelago, in the Mula Malurung inscription of 1255, and used the term Cakravala Mandala Dvipantara in 1275; historians suggest Gajah Mada took him as a model in his own aim of uniting the islands.
kesh-temple-hymn: Fragments of the hymn came to light among tablets from the temple library at Nippur held by the University of Pennsylvania Museum. Hugo Radau published one in 1909, and Stephen Herbert Langdon translated a four-sided prism from Nippur in the Ashmolean in 1913 as A Liturgy to Nintud, Goddess of Creation, reading its refrain as a reference to the creation of man and woman. George Aaron Barton rejected that reading in 1918: he saw no allusion to the creation of man, only to Nintu as the mother of mankind.

Further copies were found at Isin, Kish, Susa and Ur, and others are in Istanbul, the Louvre, the British Museum and the Walters Art Museum. Miguel Civil produced the latest composite text in 1992. Robert D. Biggs translated a very archaic version from Tell Abu Salabikh and found surprisingly little deviation, except in spelling, from copies some eight centuries later, concluding that the Old Babylonian text faithfully reflected one fixed in Sumerian tradition for centuries.

The hymn has 134 lines in eight songs, or houses, each ending with three rhetorical questions: whether anything as great as Kesh, its hero Acgi or its lady Nintud will ever be seen. It opens with Enlil coming forth from his house and speaking the praises of Kesh, which the goddess Nisaba records on tablets.

Later lines liken the temple to the moon, set its foundation on the Abzu, describe its oxen and sheep, gate, courtyard and walls, and tell of drums and a bull's horn sounded at its ceremonies. It ends with a fourfold warning: draw near to the city, to the house Kesh, to Acgi and to Nintud, but do not draw near.

Scholars have read the text in several ways. Victor Hurowitz called it a temple building hymn, and Charpin and Todd noted that it presents itself as the work of gods handed to humans, which gave it legitimacy. Raymond de Hoop compared its metaphors with the sayings on Joseph and Judah in Genesis 49. Wilfred G. Lambert noted that the Kesh sanctuary was the centre of the goddess's cult from the Early Dynastic period into the Old Babylonian Dynasty, after which it lost its importance.
keshab-chandra-sen: Sen was born on 19 November 1838 into an affluent Bengali Baidya family of Calcutta whose roots lay in Garifa on the Hooghly. His grandfather Ramkamal Sen was a pro-sati activist and an opponent of Ram Mohan Roy. His father, Peary Mohan Sen, died when he was ten, and he was raised by an uncle and studied at Hindu College. In 1855 he opened an evening school for working men's children, and he worked briefly as a clerk in the Bank of Bengal before leaving to devote himself to literature and philosophy.

In the Brahmo Samaj of Debendranath Tagore he wrote for the Indian Mirror and helped found the Albert College in 1862. By 1865 he had come to believe that only Christian doctrine could renew Hindu society, and an open break with Tagore over Christian practices followed. His address of 1866, Jesus Christ, Europe and Asia, led many to expect his conversion and won the interest of the Viceroy, Sir John Lawrence. In 1870 he spent six months in England, met Queen Victoria and preached Love for the Sovereign, the view that British rule served a divine purpose, which drew heavy criticism at home.

The Special Marriages Act of 1872 deepened resentment among Brahmos. Around 1875 he clashed publicly with the reformer Annette Akroyd, as he opposed teaching women subjects such as mathematics, philosophy and science, and the radical party opened its own school for women, the Hindu Mahila Vidyalaya. Those who left him in 1878 founded the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj.

From 1876 Sen came under the influence of Ramakrishna, whom he made known to a wider audience through his New Dispensation journal. In 1881 he announced the New Dispensation, holding that all the established religions of the world are true; he called God Mother, adopted the homa and arati rites and composed a hymn of 108 names of God. Brahmo opponents denounced it as anti-Brahmo. In his last illness he wrote The New Samhita. He died on 8 January 1884, and over 2000 people attended his Hindu funeral.
kestutis: Kęstutis was a son of the Grand Duke Gediminas. His younger brother Jaunutis succeeded their father as Grand Duke, and Kęstutis conspired with his brother Algirdas to remove him, and they succeeded. They divided their holdings into an eastern and a western sphere, with Algirdas concentrating on the east and Kęstutis on the west. The Duchy of Trakai arose from this division. Kęstutis organised the defence of western Lithuania and Samogitia against the Teutonic Knights and raided the Order in return; during his rule the Teutonic raids into Lithuania reached their peak.

Kęstutis wielded great influence under Algirdas, and the two appear to have been co-rulers as Grand Dukes, Algirdas being the dominant one. In 1349, to avoid further clashes with the Order, he began negotiations with Pope Clement VI for the conversion of Lithuania and was promised royal crowns for himself and his sons. The intermediary, the Polish King Casimir III, attacked Volhynia and Brest in October 1349 and ruined the plan. On 15 August 1351 Kęstutis agreed with King Louis I of Hungary to accept Christianity and give military aid in exchange for a crown, confirming it with a pagan ritual; he did not intend to comply and ran away on the way to Buda.

In March 1361 he, his son Patrikas and Algirdas took the Teutonic castles of Eckersberg and Johannisburg. Kęstutis was captured in a skirmish at Lake Ublik and held in Malbork Castle. Two attempts to arrange his release failed, probably because the ransom was too high. About half a year later he escaped, with the help of his servant Alfas, by breaking a hole in a wall three metres thick and riding out dressed as a Teutonic knight.

After Algirdas died in 1377, Jogaila became Grand Duke and Kęstutis recognised him, in effect ruling for the young man. On 31 May 1380 Jogaila signed the secret Treaty of Dovydiškės with the Teutonic Order, promising not to intervene if it attacked Kęstutis. In August 1381, once he learned of the treaty, Kęstutis took Vilnius while Jogaila was away and declared himself sole Grand Duke; Jogaila swore loyalty and was released with Kreva and Vitebsk.

In June 1382 the people of Vilnius, led by the merchant Hanul of Riga, let Jogaila's army in, and Jogaila allied with the Order. When the armies met near Trakai, both sides agreed to negotiate, and Kęstutis and his son Vytautas were arrested and held at Kreva. Five days later Kęstutis was found dead. Jogaila claimed he had hanged himself, but few believed it. Jogaila gave him a pagan funeral in Vilnius, and Vytautas escaped and was made co-ruler in 1401.
keta: Keta was an important trading post from the 14th century to the late 20th. The Somey Ewe were the first people of the area. The Anlo Ewe, who in the 17th century migrated from Ketu in Benin by way of Adja Tado and Notsie in Togo, settled it: according to tradition Awanyedor and Akaga, sons of Torgbui Wenya, the founder of the Anlo State, left Anloga to found Keta as a fishing village. The town was also known as Quittah or Agudzeawo, meaning Easterners in old Ewe.

The Danes, who hoped to trade there without interference from rival European nations, first set up a factory to sell alcohol and, after the Anlo-Danish War, the Sagbadre War of 1784, built a fort whose trade made Keta flourish, though their power reached no further than its guns. In June 1790 a Danish official who had killed the chief of Keta years before was killed near Denu. The Danes hired the people of Anloga to punish Keta; a staged fight became a real one, and a war between Keta and Anloga in 1794 ended in Keta's defeat and weakened the Anlo.

Missionaries of the North German Missionary Society landed at nearby Dzelukofe on 2 September 1853. From 1874 the Hausa Constabulary was based at Keta, and a community of Hausa traders grew up. In 1887, when the writer R. Austin Freeman was a medical officer there, an epidemic of black water fever killed forty per cent of the European population. The first Orange Lodge in Ghana, Pride of Keta, was founded in 1917 by R. E. Sharlley, a postal worker.

Keta, a town of 23,207 people, is the capital of the Keta Municipal District. Since the early 20th century it has suffered tidal waves, flooding and erosion: the Bremen Factory and a coconut plantation near the high-water mark in 1907 had been swept away by 1924, and the sea has reached Queen Street and the fort. The Keta Lagoon, the largest in Ghana with 300 km2 of water, lies in a protected wetland and is a stopping point for migratory birds and a breeding ground for sea turtles.
ketapang: The town stands on the delta of the Pawan River and takes its name from the local Malay word for the ketapang tree, Terminalia catappa; in Teochew it is called Tau-pang, and Kayong is its nickname. Officially it is not a city but the district of Delta Pawan, which holds most of the government offices and businesses of Ketapang Regency and is therefore treated as its capital. Benua Kayong District borders it to the south and forms part of the urban area across the river, while Muara Pawan District lies to the north.

In 1936, under Dutch rule, Ketapang became one of the districts, or afdelingen, of the residency of Western Borneo. In 1956 it became an autonomous regency of the province of West Kalimantan, led by a regent, or bupati. The regency once held the whole of Gunung Palung National Park, a rainforest park reached from the town, but most of it passed to the new regency of Kayong Utara, or North Kayong, created in 2007. The Tanjungpura Royal Cemetery, the burial place of the kings of Tanjungpura, lies about three hours' journey from the town.

Ketapang is a town of many peoples: besides Malay and Dayak inhabitants it has large Chinese, Madurese and Javanese communities, and most of its Chinese residents are of Teochew or Hakka descent, Teochew being the main dialect among them. Its industries produce palm oil, rubber and wood, and alumina, bauxite, zircon sand and lead are mined in the area. The town is served by Rahadi Oesman Airport and has a polytechnic, opened in 2008. Among its sights are the Chinese temple of Tua Pek Kong and the peat forest of Pematang Gadung, home of wild orangutans.
ketevan-the-martyr: Ketevan was the daughter of Prince Ashotan Bagration of Mukhrani and married Prince David Bagration of Kakheti, who reigned as David I from 1601 to 1602. After his death she devoted herself to church building and charity. In 1605 David's brother Constantine I killed his father, King Alexander II, and seized the crown with Safavid support. Ketevan rallied the nobles of Kakheti against him, and the usurper died in battle. According to the Safavid official and chronicler Fażli Ḵuzāni, she treated his surviving followers and Qizilbash officers with mercy, had the wounded cared for and compensated the Muslim merchants who had suffered in the war.

Ketevan then negotiated with Shah Abbas I, the overlord of Georgia, to have her young son Teimuraz I confirmed as king, and she governed as regent from 1605 to 1614. In 1614 Teimuraz sent her to the shah as a negotiator, and she gave herself up as an honorary hostage in a vain attempt to spare Kakheti from attack by Iranian armies. She was held at Shiraz for several years. In revenge for Teimuraz's defiance, Abbas ordered her to renounce Christianity, and when she refused she was tortured to death with red-hot pincers on 13 September 1624.

Portuguese Augustinian missionaries who witnessed her death secretly took part of her relics to Georgia, where they were buried at the Alaverdi Monastery; the rest were said to lie in the Augustinian church at Goa. Patriarch Zachary of Georgia canonised her, with her feast on 13 September. Teimuraz told her martyrdom in his poem The Book and Passion of Queen Ketevan of 1625, and Andreas Gryphius in his tragedy Catharina von Georgien of 1657.

Georgian delegations worked with the Archaeological Survey of India from 1989 to find her grave in the ruined convent at Old Goa. Bone fragments found near the window named in the Portuguese sources carried a mitochondrial haplogroup, U1b, absent in India but present in Georgia, and in 2013 one was judged consistent with a Georgian woman. India handed relics to Georgia on 9 July 2021. A tiled panorama of her martyrdom was found at the Graça Convent in Lisbon in 2008.
keti-koti: Ketikoti, also spelled Keti Koti, is officially called Dag der Vrijheden in Dutch, the Day of the Freedoms. The day is also known as Manspasi Dei or Prisiri Manspasi, meaning Emancipation or Emancipation Festival, and in Dutch as Kettingsnijden, chain cutting. The Sranantongo name can be rendered either as the chain is cut or as the chain is broken. It marks Emancipation Day in Suriname, the date in 1863 when slavery was abolished in the colony.

Abolition did not bring full freedom at once. Until 1873 the formerly enslaved were held to a mandatory transition period of ten years, during which they had to work on the plantations for minimal pay and under state-sanctioned force; anyone found outside without a pass could be jailed. After 1873 many left the plantations where their families had worked for several generations and moved to the city of Paramaribo. It was the former slave owners who were compensated: for the 32,911 people released in Suriname they received ƒ 9,867,780, a sum put at about €250 million in 2020.

On 1 July 1955 Ketikoti officially became a public holiday in Suriname. On 30 June 1963 a statue of Kwakoe was unveiled in Paramaribo, the capital, to commemorate the abolition of slavery. The day has also taken root in the Netherlands, where by 2009 several cities hosted activities, making it a day of celebration and remembrance across the country.

Since 2002 the Kingdom of the Netherlands has had an official memorial to slavery, the Nationaal Monument Slavernijgeschiedenis (National Monument Slavery History), which stands in the Oosterpark in Amsterdam. The organisers of the Keti Koti festival also use the occasion to press the Dutch government for reparations and for research. Each year the festival returns to the date on which slavery was abolished in Suriname and the Dutch Caribbean in 1863.
kexholm: Priozersk, formerly Kexholm, lies on the north-western shore of Lake Ladoga, at the estuary of the northern arm of the Vuoksi River on the Karelian Isthmus. Its main landmark, the Korela Fortress, has been the centre of the Karelians of the isthmus and, from time to time, the north-western outpost of the Russians or the eastern outpost of the Swedes. Russians knew the place as Korela from the Middle Ages, and Karelians and Finns as Käkisalmi.

The earliest recorded mention of the place is from 1143. It was part of the Vodskaya pyatina of the Novgorod Republic, and Novgorod taxation documents of 1500 list 183 houses in Korela. The Swedes captured Korela twice, in 1578 for seventeen years and in 1611 for a hundred years. In the Swedish Empire the fortress was called Kexholm, and the region became the County of Kexholm. Russia secured the area during the Great Northern War and kept the Swedish name, as Keksgolm. Wars and fires hurt the civilian population, and when the town gained its first court house in 1800 it had only 400 inhabitants.

In 1812 Tsar Alexander I incorporated Keksgolm, with the rest of Old Finland, into the autonomous Vyborg Governorate, later known as Viipuri Province. Finland became independent in 1917, and the town grew with a railway and, in 1929, two sawmills and a wood pulp mill. The Winter War began on 30 November 1939 with a Soviet attack, and Finland ceded the town in the Moscow Peace Treaty of 1940. Finland regained it in the Continuation War of 1941 to 1944, but its people were evacuated again at the end of the war. On 1 October 1948 it was renamed Priozersk and settled mainly by Russian, Belarusian and Ukrainian migrants.

Priozersk is the administrative centre of Priozersky District in Leningrad Oblast, Russia, and had 18,777 inhabitants in 2021. The ramparts and towers of the Korela Fortress survive on the bank of the Vuoksi, with a small museum inside, and the town has thirty-three cultural heritage monuments of federal significance, most of them part of the fortress.
kgb: The KGB was formed in March 1954 under Ivan Serov, after a restructuring of the MVD that followed the fall of Lavrentiy Beria in June 1953. It was the direct successor of earlier Soviet secret police agencies, including the Cheka, the OGPU and the NKVD. Attached to the Council of Ministers, it held what was called union-republican jurisdiction: similar agencies operated in each republic apart from the Russian SFSR, where the KGB itself was headquartered. It was a military service governed by army laws and regulations, and its operational personnel held army-style ranks.

Within the Soviet bloc the KGB monitored public and private opinion and possible plots. It was instrumental in crushing the Hungarian Revolution of 1956, when Serov personally supervised the "normalization" of the country after the invasion. Before the Red Army's invasion that ended the Prague Spring in 1968, it infiltrated Czechoslovakia with illegal residents disguised as Western tourists, who were to spy on supporters of Alexander Dubček's government and plant evidence that right-wing groups backed by Western agencies planned a coup.

It also prepared hardline members of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia, such as Alois Indra and Vasiľ Škultéty, to take power. In Poland in the 1980s it infiltrated Solidarity and the Catholic Church and coordinated the declaration of martial law with Wojciech Jaruzelski, but Solidarity weakened the Polish government by 1989. On 27 December 1979 KGB special forces, the Alpha and Zenith groups, joined by a GRU battalion and paratroopers, stormed the Tajbeg Palace in Kabul and killed Hafizullah Amin.

Under Vladimir Kryuchkov, chairman from 1988, the KGB led the coup attempt of August 1991 against President Mikhail Gorbachev. Its failure and the collapse of the Soviet Union led to the dissolution of the KGB on 3 December 1991. Its successors in Russia were the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) and what became the Federal Security Service (FSB).

The KGB had two main parts, the organs and the troops. The organs handled intelligence, counter-intelligence and military counter-intelligence. The troops, separate from the armed forces, included the Border Troops, the Governmental Signals Troops and the Kremlin Regiment, with the special forces Alpha and Vympel. The First Chief Directorate ran foreign espionage, and its Directorate S ran illegals, agents working under deep cover abroad. The Second Chief Directorate handled counter-intelligence and internal political control. The Fifth, which dealt with artistic, political and religious dissent, was renamed Directorate Z in 1989. Abroad, legal residents worked from embassies under diplomatic immunity, while illegals had no such protection.
khabul-khan: Khabul Khan, also called Qabul or Kabul Khan, was born in the 1090s or around 1100, a son of Tumbinai Khan and great-grandson of Khaidu, and head of the Borjigin obog. His twin brother, Khaduli Barlas, is counted as an ancestor of Timur, founder of the Timurid Empire. In his time the Jurchens of Manchuria founded the Jin dynasty in 1115 and, allied with the Song dynasty, had taken much of the territory of the Khitan-led Liao dynasty by 1122.

In 1135 Khabul Khan was invited to the court of Emperor Taizong of Jin, where, by the well-known story, he pulled the emperor's beard. The Jin army pursued him into southern Mongolia, but he escaped and came back with a larger force to pillage Jin territory. When a Jin army entered Mongolia to conquer the lands of Emperor Dezong of Liao, founder of the Qara Khitai, Khabul Khan organised a Mongol confederation and led the successful defence.

This confederation, the Khamag Mongol or Whole Mongol, rested on four core clans, the Khiyad, Taichuud, Jalairs and Jurkhin, and is sometimes seen as a predecessor of Genghis Khan's empire. After their defeat the Jurchens recognised him in 1146 or 1147 as paramount ruler of the Mongols, though they still regarded him officially as their vassal. He is also said to have expanded his tribe and suppressed the Tatar tribes, and his reign saw the first attempts to unite the Mongols politically.

Khabul Khan died in 1148. Although he had seven sons, he named as his successor Ambaghai, a son of Sengun Bilge of the Taichuud clan. His eldest son was Okin-barkhakh; his second, Bartan the Valiant, was the father of Yesugei and so the grandfather of Genghis Khan. A third son, Mongler, was the father of Buri the wrestler.
khabur-river: The Khabur is the largest perennial tributary of the Euphrates in Syria. It begins in Turkey, but the karstic springs around Ras al-Ayn are its main source of water. Several wadis join it north of Al-Hasakah, creating what is known as the Khabur Triangle or Upper Khabur area, and it meets the Euphrates near the town of Busayrah. Annual rainfall in the basin falls from over 400 millimetres in the north to under 200 in the south, which has made the river a vital water source for agriculture throughout history. Its tributaries, among them the Jaghjagh, the ancient Mygdonius, mostly carry water for only part of the year.

Excavations and surveys since the 1930s show that the valley has been occupied since the Lower Palaeolithic. Excavated sites include Tell Halaf, Tell Brak, Tell Leilan, Tell Mashnaqa, Tell Mozan and Tell Barri.
