A distinctive painted pottery of northern Mesopotamia and Syria in the early 2nd millennium BCE is called Khabur ware, and the river region is associated with the rise of the Kingdom of the Mitanni.

In ancient times the river was known in Akkadian and Amorite as ḫabur. Classical writers called it the Chaboras, the Aborrhas or the Aburas, and described it as a large river of Mesopotamia flowing into the Euphrates at Circesium. The Hebrew Bible says that Tiglath-Pileser took the Reubenites, the Gadites and half the tribe of Manasseh into exile at Halah, Habor, Hara and the River Gozan, and the identification of the Khabur with the Habor is not contested.

Xenophon's Corsote, visited by Cyrus the Younger, is placed by Robin Waterfield at the meeting of the Khabur and the Euphrates, though other authors are cautious about its location. In the 7th and 8th centuries monasteries of the Tur Abdin, such as Qartmin, owned farmland in the upper valley, where the monk Simeon planted 12,000 trees.

The Khabur River Project, begun in the 1960s, built three dams in the basin as part of an irrigation scheme that also includes the Tabqa Dam on the Euphrates. Two of them, Hasakah West and Hasakah East, stand on tributaries between Ras al-Ayn and Al-Hasakah, and a third, Hassakeh South, on the river itself 25 kilometres south of Al-Hasakah. The valley holds about 16,000 square kilometres of farmland and is Syria's main area of wheat cultivation.
khafre: Khafre was the brother and successor of King Djedefre. Some scholars think his mother was Queen Meritites I, because an inscription says she was honoured under Khafre; others argue that it shows only that she died during his reign, and he may instead have been a son of Queen Henutsen. He had several wives and at least twelve sons and three or four daughters. Queen Meresankh III, a niece of Khafre, was the mother of Nebemakhet, Duaenre, Niuserre, Khentetka and Shepsetkau. Hekenuhedjet bore Sekhemkare, and Menkaure and Khamerernebty II may have been children of Queen Khamerernebty I.

There is no agreement on the date of his reign. The Turin King List leaves its length blank and Manetho gives 66 years, but most scholars place it between 24 and 26 years. They rely on the will of Prince Nekure, a son of Khafre, which is dated to the Year of the 12th Count, and on a painted date, the Year of the 13th occurrence, on a casing stone of mastaba G 7650.

Khafre built the second-largest pyramid at Giza, called Wer(en)-Khafre, meaning Khafre is Great. A small subsidiary pyramid beside it holds a burial whose owner is not clear. His valley temple stood close to the Nile, next to the Sphinx temple, and inscriptions at its entrance mention Hathor and Bubastis. The Great Sphinx of Giza is said to date to his time, because it lies close to his temple complex and resembles his statues in the face. It may have been carved as a guardian of his pyramid and a symbol of royal power, and it was deified in the New Kingdom.

More statues survive of Khafre than of any other Old Kingdom ruler, almost all from Giza. A hall of the valley temple has 23 depressions in the floor where life-size statues stood, and one is wider than the rest. It has been suggested that the 24 statues related to the hours of the day. Auguste Mariette found nine of them in 1860, with fragments of a tenth in a pit, and they are now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

Greek writers described him differently. Manetho called him Sûphis II, while Herodotus and Diodorus, writing more than 2,000 years later, portrayed him as a tyrant who ruled for 56 years and was followed by Menkaure, who restored peace and piety.
khai-dinh: Khải Định was born Nguyễn Phúc Bửu Đảo on 8 October 1885, the son of Emperor Đồng Khánh, but he did not succeed his father immediately. Before him the French had exiled two emperors, Thành Thái and Duy Tân, for their resistance to the colonial regime. They then chose Bửu Đảo because his father had been the most submissive of the Nguyễn collaborators with the protectorate and had opposed any independence movement. He married his first wife, Trương Như Thị Tịnh, in 1907, when he was still Duke of Phụng Hóa. She left him in 1915 and became a nun.

Bửu Đảo became the nominal ruler of Annam on 18 May 1916, after the exile of Duy Tân, and took the reign name Khải Định. He said he wanted to restore the prestige of the empire, but his close collaboration with the French made that impossible, and he has been described as a figurehead who followed colonial instructions to give legitimacy to French policies. His consort Hồ Thị Chỉ was a daughter of Hồ Đắc Trung, who became Annam's Minister for Public Instruction. His son Nguyễn Phúc Vĩnh Thụy, the later Emperor Bảo Đại, had been born in 1913 to the concubine Hoàng Thị Cúc.

Khải Định was unpopular. The nationalist leader Phan Châu Trinh accused him of selling out his country while he lived in imperial luxury and the people were exploited. Nguyễn Ái Quốc, later known as Hồ Chí Minh, wrote a play called The Bamboo Dragon that ridiculed him as all ceremony and no power. Nationalist leaders also mocked his visit to France in 1922 to see the Marseilles Colonial Exhibition.

His unpopularity reached its peak in 1923, when he authorised the French to raise taxes on Vietnamese peasants, partly to pay for his palatial tomb, which caused great hardship. He also signed orders for the arrest of nationalist leaders such as Phan Bội Châu, who were forced into exile, and followers who were captured were beheaded. Khải Định had poor health, like his father, and died of tuberculosis in the Imperial City of Huế on 6 November 1925, at the age of forty.
khajuraho: The name of the town, anciently Kharjuravahaka, comes from the Sanskrit word kharjur, meaning date palm. The region belonged to many kingdoms and empires. The earliest known power to hold Khajuraho was the Vatsa, followed by the Mauryans, Sungas, Kushans, Nagas of Padmavati, the Vakataka dynasty, the Guptas, the Pushyabhuti dynasty and the Gurjara-Praitharas. Architecture and art began to flourish in the region under the Guptas, and their successors continued the tradition.

The Chandelas ruled the area from the ninth century as subjects of the Gurjara-Praitharas. In the reign of Dhanga, c. 950 to 1002, they became independent, and many important temples were built in this time. The Chandelas suffered fatal blows from the Chahamanas of Shakambhari in 1182 and from Qutb al-Din Aibak in 1202. Khajuraho declined to a small village as they moved their activities to the forts of Mahoba, Kalinjar and Ajayagarh.

Ibn Battuta visited Khajuraho and described temples and a few ascetics there. Sikander Lodi damaged some temples in 1495, and by the 16th century the place was insignificant. The military surveyor C. J. Franklin is said to have rediscovered it in 1819, though the credit for bringing it back to wider attention goes to the British army captain T. S. Burt, who visited in 1838. Alexander Cunningham was the next significant visitor, between 1852 and 1855. Khajuraho has the largest group of medieval Hindu and Jain temples in India, known for erotic sculptures, and the Khajuraho Group of Monuments has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986.
khakas-people: The Khakas, or Khakass, speak the Khakas language and live in the Republic of Khakassia in Russia. They are described as direct descendants of the ancient cultures of southern Siberia, among them the Andronovo culture, Samoyedic peoples, the Tagar culture and the Yenisei Kyrgyz culture.

They were historically known as Kyrgyz, and their own name for themselves is Tadar. The name Khakas was given after the Russian Revolution by the Soviet authorities, a newly formed name based on the Chinese name for the Kyrgyz, Xiaqiasi. Under the empire they were also called Minusinsk Tatars, Abakan Tatars and Yenisei Turks, and the names Khongorai and Khoorai were once applied to them.

The Yenisei Kyrgyz were made to pay tribute under a treaty between the Dzungars and the Russians in 1635, and the Dzungar Oirats forced them into submission. Some were moved into the Dzungar Khanate, and in 1761 the Qing moved them from Dzungaria to north-eastern China, where they became known as the Fuyu Kyrgyz. Russian agrarian settlers arrived in the Minusinsk region, and in the 1820s gold mines were opened around Minusinsk, which became a regional industrial centre.

During the nineteenth century many Khakas took on Russian ways of life and most were converted to Russian Orthodox Christianity. A movement for autonomy appeared in the Revolution of 1905. After the Soviets came to power, the Khakas National District was set up in 1923, and several groups, the Beltir, Sagai, Kachin, Koibal and Kyzyl, were combined into one people. The district became the Khakas Autonomous Oblast in 1930 within Krasnoyarsk Krai, and the Republic of Khakassia took its present form in 1992.

Traditionally the Khakas practised nomadic herding, agriculture, hunting and fishing, and the Beltir specialised in handicraft. Herding sheep and cattle is still common. In the 1989 census the Khakas numbered 78,500, about 12 per cent of the republic's population. Most are Orthodox Christians today, and traditional shamanism, linked with Tengrism, continues; many Christians combine it with their faith, and several societies for the traditional religion exist.
khalaf-ibn-ahmad: Khalaf was born in the middle of November 937 to Abu Ja'far Ahmad and Banu, a daughter of the second Saffarid amir, Amr ibn al-Layth. From 957 or 958 at the latest he was recognised as heir, and his name appeared on his father's coins. When his father was murdered in Zarang at the end of March 963, Khalaf rode to Bust, whose governor backed him, and took the capital from the rival Saffarid Abu Hafs, who fled to Samanid Khurasan. He then named Abu'l-Husayn Tahir ibn Muhammad his co-ruler.

While Khalaf made the Pilgrimage, the caliph al-Muti confirmed him in Sistan at Baghdad in 965, but Abu'l-Husayn Tahir would not give up power, and Khalaf twice needed Samanid armies against him until his death in 970. Tahir's son Husayn then pressed his claim. With Samanid support he defeated Khalaf in August 979 and besieged him in Zarang for probably three years. A truce of 983 left Khalaf in the fortress of Taq; he broke it, won over the Ghaznavid Sebuktigin with a bribe and made peace with Husayn on 25 December 983.

Sole amir for the first time in twenty years, Khalaf gained his name as a scholar and patron of learning, and probably received his title Wali 'l-Dawla from the caliph al-Qadir, whom he recognised in 991. He took Bust in 986 but had to give it back. His sons 'Amr and Tahir each rebelled against him and died in prison. After Tahir's attack on Ghaznavid lands in 998, Mahmud of Ghazna trapped Khalaf in 1000 and made him pay an indemnity and put Mahmud's name before his own on his coins.

His rule had grown unpopular, and after Tahir's death the commander of Tahir's army invited Mahmud to take Sistan. Khalaf withstood a siege at Taq until Mahmud came in person, joined by the townspeople of Zarang, and forced him to surrender. He was held in Farighunid Guzgan until rumours of contact with the Karakhanids led to his removal to Gardez, where he died. His fall ended Saffarid rule over Sistan.
khalchayan: Khalchayan lies near the modern town of Denov, in the valley of the Surkhan Darya, a northern tributary of the Oxus, the modern Amu Darya. The building is thought to have been a small palace or a reception hall, and the site is usually attributed to the early Kushans or to their ancestors, the Yuezhi or Tocharians. Its interior walls were decorated with clay sculptures and paintings, which are dated to the mid-1st century BCE but are thought to show events going back as far as the 2nd century BCE.

Galina Pugachenkova excavated the site between 1959 and 1963. The panels show scenes of Kushan life: battles, feasts and portraits of rulers. Some are thought to show the Kushans fighting a Saka tribe, the Yuezhi drawn with a majestic bearing and the Sakas with side-whiskers in more or less grotesque poses. Among the sculptures is the bust of a Parthian king, which its date and a likeness on coins suggest may be Vardanes I. Tacitus wrote that Vardanes took refuge among the Bactrians after failing at the siege of Seleucia around 35 CE, which would date the portrait to about 45 to 47 CE, perhaps under the Kushan ruler Kujula Kadphises.

The art historian Benjamin Rowland held that the art of Khalchayan derives ultimately from Hellenistic art, possibly by way of the cities of Ai-Khanoum and Nysa, and that it resembles the later art of Gandhara and may even have stood at its origin. He pointed to the likeness between the head of a Yuezhi prince from Khalchayan and Gandharan heads of Bodhisattvas, and argued that through Kushan patronage this Bactrian art lived on for centuries in Gandhara. The Chinese researcher Duan Qingbo has noted that the style and building techniques of the statues closely resemble those of the earlier Terracotta Army.
khalid-bin-barghash: Sayyid Khalid bin Barghash Al-Busa'id was born in 1874 in Zanzibar, the second son of Barghash bin Said, the second Sultan of Zanzibar. In July 1890, by the Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty, Germany recognised a British protectorate over the islands of Zanzibar and Pemba. When Sultan Ali bin Said was ailing early in 1893, the British consul Rennell Rodd judged Khalid, despite his strong claim as the son of Barghash, undesirable as a successor.

When the sultan died on 5 March 1893, Khalid entered the palace, let in by his aunt Bi. Zemzem binti Sa'id bin Sultan. Rodd at once landed 200 marines with machine guns and threatened to blow open the palace doors; after entry was forced, Khalid was marched off to his house under arrest, and Hamad bin Thuwaini was installed as sultan on conditions Rodd had prepared.

Khalid seized power again on the sudden death of his cousin Hamad bin Thuwaini in August 1896; many suspect that Khalid had him poisoned. Britain refused to recognise him, citing a treaty of 1866 under which a new sultan could accede only with British assent. In the Anglo-Zanzibar War that followed, Royal Navy vessels shelled his palace for 38 minutes before a surrender was received. Some 500 men of his retinue were casualties, martial law was imposed and several Omani sheikhs suspected of complicity were deported to Machakos. Khalid fled by a back door to the German consulate, which German sailors guarded.

In October 1896 the German consul Albrecht von Rechenberg informed the British consul Basil Cave that Khalid would be sent to Dar es Salaam without setting foot on Zanzibar, and the SMS Seeadler took him there. In German East Africa he received political asylum and lived in a grand house with the privileges of an exiled royal, allowed to fly the red flag of the sultanate.

During the First World War British forces captured him, arguably at Dar es Salaam, in 1917, and exiled him to Saint Helena and later to the Seychelles, where he was denied his property around Mombasa and its revenues. In 1922 Winston Churchill, as Secretary of State for the Colonies, allowed him to live in Mombasa, where he died on 19 March 1927. His son Majid helped Frederick Johnson compile his Standard Swahili–English Dictionary.
khalid-ibn-al-walid: Khalid ibn al-Walid belonged to the Makhzum clan of the Quraysh, Mecca's pre-Islamic aristocracy, which was strongly opposed to Muhammad. His father, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, arbitrated local disputes in Mecca, and his uncle Hisham was known as the lord of Mecca. Khalid's cousin Abu Jahl led the Makhzum in the war against Muhammad until the rout at the Battle of Badr in 624, where about twenty-five of Khalid's paternal cousins were killed. In 625 Khalid played the instrumental part in defeating the Muslims at the Battle of Uhud.

He embraced Islam in 627 or 629, and the later date is thought perhaps more trustworthy by the historian Michael Lecker. Muhammad made him a commander and gave him the title Sayf Allah, the Sword of God.

After Muhammad's death in June 632, Khalid supported Abu Bakr's succession as caliph and led the Ridda wars against rebel tribes. In late 632 he defeated the forces of Tulayha at the Battle of Buzakha, giving the Muslims most of Najd, and in 633 he overcame the prophet-claimant Musaylima of the Banu Hanifa in the Yamama. Sources record the execution of the Tamimite chieftain Malik ibn Nuwayra, which has been judged differently by historians.

He then marched into Sasanian Iraq in 633 with about 1,000 warriors. Early in 634 Abu Bakr ordered him to Syria. He crossed a waterless stretch of the Syrian Desert in six days and five nights, with between 500 and 800 men, using camels to carry water. The Muslims then won at Ajnadayn, Fahl, Damascus and Yarmouk in 636, and conquered most of Syria. Afterwards Khalid was removed from supreme command by Umar, for reasons the sources give variously, among them his independence and Umar's fear that his fame might breed a personality cult. He remained a lieutenant of Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah at the sieges of Homs and Aleppo in 637 and 638.

In 638 Umar had Khalid questioned over rumours that he had lavishly distributed war spoils, and dismissed him from his governorship of Qinnasrin. He died in Medina or Homs in 642. Early sources rate him the most effective commander of the conquests, but also give a mixed view of him, citing his part at Uhud and his reputation for brutal actions against Arab tribes during the Ridda wars. Sunni tradition honours him as a hero, while Shia tradition portrays him more critically. Homs has been known since the Ayyubid period as the site of his tomb and mosque.
khalifa-bin-hamad-al-thani: Khalifa bin Hamad Al Thani was born in Doha on 17 September 1932, the son of Sheikh Hamad bin Abdullah Al Thani and grandson of the emir Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani. In 1957 he was appointed minister of education, and he then became deputy emir. He was named heir apparent on 24 October 1960. In the 1960s he also served as prime minister and minister of finance.

On 22 February 1972 Khalifa became emir by seizing power from his cousin Ahmad bin Ali Al Thani in a bloodless coup. Many Western news outlets called it an overthrow, while the Qatari population regarded it merely as a succession of power. He began by reorganising the government and limiting the financial privileges of members of the ruling family. He appointed a foreign minister and an adviser for day-to-day affairs, and on 19 April 1972 he amended the constitution and enlarged the cabinet with more ministers.

Diplomatic relations were established with a number of foreign countries at ambassadorial level. His reorganisation sharply reduced the traditional powers of the heir apparent and gave all power to himself. The cabinet was reshuffled for the first time on 18 July 1989, when most ministers were replaced and it came to have 15 members, and again on 1 September 1992, when it grew to 17.

Oil revenue rose through production-sharing agreements with foreign companies: with the Standard Oil Company of Ohio in January 1985, with Amoco in February 1986 and with the French state-owned Elf Aquitaine in January 1989. In the middle of 1991 gas production began in the North Field, the world's largest single field of non-associated gas. Qatar also built an industrial base to reduce its dependence on oil.

In June 1995, while Khalifa was staying in Geneva, his son Hamad bin Khalifa seized power in another bloodless coup on 27 June. Hamad accused his father of treason and demanded that Interpol arrest him, charging him with four counts that included his execution.

Khalifa lived in France until 2004, when he returned to Qatar for the funeral of his wife, Sheikha Moza bint Ali Al Thani, after nine years in exile. He had five sons and thirteen daughters by four wives, and his son Hamad was emir from 1995 to 2013. Khalifa died on 23 October 2016 at the age of 84, and Qatar declared three days of national mourning.
khalifa-bin-harub: Khalifa bin Harub Al-Busaidi was born on 26 August 1879 in Muscat, Oman. His father, Harub bin Thuwaini, was a son of Thuwaini bin Said, Sultan of Muscat and Oman, and his mother was Turkiya bint Turki Al Busaidi. In 1900 he married Sayyida Matuka bint Hamud Al-Busaid, daughter of the seventh Sultan of Zanzibar and sister of the eighth; he later took a second wife, Sultana Nunu. He became the ninth sultan on 9 December 1911.

Zanzibar's sovereignty was limited during his reign. The sultan kept ceremonial authority and influence over religious and cultural affairs, while Britain controlled foreign policy, defence and the major decisions of administration. Khalifa kept a cooperative relationship with the British through both world wars, and the monarchy survived those decades. Roads and ports were extended, public health services and the administration improved, and clove plantations, the backbone of the economy, grew.

A devout Muslim, he was a patron of mosques, madrasahs and the Islamic courts of the qadis, and he supported the spread of formal education, including schools for Arabs and Africans, encouraging both Islamic and modern secular learning. On a journey to Uganda he visited Makerere University on 30 April 1954. Britain made him a knight of several orders, from the KCMG in 1914 and the KBE in 1919 to the GBE in 1935, the GCMG in 1936 and the GCB in 1956.

Khalifa died on 9 October 1960 at the age of 81, after a reign of about 48 years and 10 months, the longest of any Sultan of Zanzibar. He was succeeded by his eldest surviving son, Abdullah bin Khalifa, who reigned until his own death in 1963. Part of the museum in the Sultan's Palace in Zanzibar is dedicated to him.
khalifa-bin-zayed-al-nahyan: Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan was born on 7 September 1948 at Qasr Al-Muwaiji, Al Ain, in Abu Dhabi, then part of the Trucial States. He was the eldest son of Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan and Hassa bint Mohammed Al Nahyan, and spent most of his childhood in Al Ain. He studied first at a small school his father founded at Muwaiji around 1956, and later graduated from the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst. He regularly attended his father's majlis, where he gained experience of governance.

When his father became emir of Abu Dhabi in 1966, Khalifa was appointed the ruler's representative in the Eastern Region and head of the Courts Department in Al Ain. On 1 February 1969 he was named crown prince and next day head of the Abu Dhabi Department of Defense, where he oversaw the build-up of the Abu Dhabi Defense Force, which after 1971 became the core of the armed forces of the United Arab Emirates.

After the federation was founded he became the second deputy prime minister of the UAE on 23 December 1973 and chairman of the Executive Council of Abu Dhabi in January 1974. In March 1976 he helped found and then led the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority, and in May of that year became deputy commander of the armed forces. In the late 1980s he headed the Supreme Petroleum Council.

Khalifa carried out some presidential duties from the late 1990s, when his father's health failed. He succeeded as ruler of Abu Dhabi on 2 November 2004, and the Federal Supreme Council elected him president of the UAE the next day. He drew cultural and academic institutions to Abu Dhabi, among them the Louvre Abu Dhabi, New York University Abu Dhabi and Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi, and he established Etihad Airways.

In 2009 he directed billions of dollars of emergency funds to Dubai, and on 4 January 2010 the tower then called Burj Dubai was renamed the Burj Khalifa in his honour. After a stroke in January 2014 he kept ceremonial powers while his half-brother Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan ran daily affairs. Khalifa died on 13 May 2022, aged 73, and was buried at Al Bateen Cemetery in Abu Dhabi. Mohamed bin Zayed succeeded him as ruler and was elected president the next day.
khalilullah-i: Khalilullah I, also known as Sultan-Khalil, succeeded his father Ibrahim I as Shirvanshah, the king of Shirvan. After the death of the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Qara Yusuf in 1420, many of the peoples he had conquered, once vassals of the Timurid Empire, swore fealty to Timur's son Shah Rukh. Khalilullah was among them, and he married a daughter of the Timurid prince Abu Bakr ibn Miran Shah, who was Qara Yusuf's widow.

In 1425 his brothers Kay-Qubad, Ishaq and Hashim led a revolt against him, which he put down with Shah Rukh's help. In 1432 he gave sanctuary to Yar Ali, a son of the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Iskandar. This seems to have provoked Iskandar's invasion of Shirvan in 1433/4, which reached as far as Darband before he returned to Azerbaijan with loot and captives. Khalilullah appealed to the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uthman Beg, who in response invaded Qara Qoyunlu-ruled Armenia and took Erzurum in the spring of 1434.

Between 1456 and 1459 the Safavid leader Shaykh Junayd allied himself with the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan by marrying his sister Khadija Begum. With Uzun Hasan's support Junayd raided northern Anatolia, around Trebizond, and Circassia, but in March 1460 he was killed by Khalilullah's forces in a battle near Tabarsaran.

Khalilullah died in 1465, after a reign of almost half a century, and was buried in the city of Baku. He was succeeded by his son Farrukh Yasar. His grave did not remain undisturbed: in 1500, after the Safavid conquest of Shirvan, the Safavid commander Khadem Beg Talish had his body dug up, burned and publicly scattered.
khalkha-mongols: The Khalkha have been the largest subgroup of the Mongols in what is now Mongolia since the 15th century. Dayan Khan created the Khalkha Tumen from Mongols living in central Mongolia and the north of Inner Mongolia, and organized it as one of three tumen of the Left Wing. He installed his fifth son Alchu Bolad and his son Geresenje over the Khalkha. The first became the founder of the Five Khalkha of Southern Mongolia, the second of the Seven Khalkha of Northern Mongolia, which the Manchus called Inner and Outer Khalkha. The meaning of the name is uncertain; one reading links it to a word for shield, and Mongols have also linked it to the river Khalkhin Gol.

The Seven Khalkha fought regularly against the Oirats in the west. Geresenje's descendants formed the houses of the Tüsheet Khan, the Zasagt Khan and the Setsen Khan, and in 1725 the Yongzheng Emperor gave Tsering independence from the house of the Tüsheet Khan, forming the house of the Sain Noyon Khan. They kept their independence until they sought help from the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty against the Dzungar leader Galdan Khan in 1688. The Five Khalkha of the south were eventually conquered by the rising Manchus.

In Qinghai, Tsogtu Khong Taiji moved there with his subjects after 1624 and attacked the dGe-lugs-pa monasteries. The Fifth Dalai Lama summoned the Oirat Güshi Khan, whose 10,000 men crushed Tsogtu's 30,000 at Ulaan-Khoshuu in early 1637, and Tsogtu was killed. In the north, from 1628 the Russians advanced into Transbaikalia. Khalkha khans protested in 1652 and raided as far as Bratsk and Nerchinsk from 1666, but Galdan's invasion in 1688 ended their resistance and sent more Mongol refugees into Russian control.

The Khalkha led the Mongolian independence movement of the 20th century and established the independent state of Mongolia in the north. The Thirteen Khalkha of the Far North are its major group, numbering 2,659,985, or 83.8 percent of the population of Mongolia. Small Khalkha banners remain in Inner Mongolia, Qinghai and Rehe in China. The Selenge Mongols, cut off from their Khalkha kinsmen by the new border and mixed with displaced Buriats and Khori, gradually accepted the Russian designation Buriat and no longer keep a Khalkha identity, culture or language.
khalq: The People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan held its First Congress on 1 January 1965, when twenty-seven men met at Nur Muhammad Taraki's house in Kabul and elected him Secretary General, with Babrak Karmal as his deputy. The two men disagreed on strategy. Taraki held that revolution could come in the classical Leninist way, through a tightly disciplined working-class party; Karmal thought Afghanistan too undeveloped for that and favoured a national democratic front of patriotic and anti-imperialist forces.

Khalq was also the name of the faction's newspaper, whose first edition sold 20,000 copies before the authorities closed it on 23 May 1966 as anti-Islamic, anticonstitutional and antimonarchical. Hafizullah Amin, who trained teachers in the late 1950s and early 1960s, used that work to radicalise a generation of them, laying the ground for Khalq's following in rural Pashtun areas. From 1973 Amin took over recruitment in the armed forces, and by April 1978 Khalq outnumbered Parcham by two or three to one.

When the government arrested the party's leaders on 25 April 1978, Amin, the last to be taken, used the delay to order Khalqi officers to rise. On 27 April troops under Colonel Mohammad Aslam Watanjar took Kabul, and air force squadrons under Colonel Abdul Qadir attacked the palace, where President Mohammad Daoud Khan and most of his family, women and children among them, were killed. In power, the Khalqists began a land reform, carried out brutal crackdowns on dissent through the AGSA (later KAM) security police, and refused to recognise the Durand Line as the border with Pakistan.

The rivalry between Taraki and Amin ended in September 1979 with Taraki's murder, after which Amin purged his opponents. By the end of that year there were 400,000 Afghan refugees, mostly in Pakistan. Soviet forces then killed Amin and installed Karmal.

Because Khalqis filled most of the officer corps, the Soviets had to rebuild the army with them, and many resented the favour shown to Parcham; some assisted the Mujahideen. In December 1989, 127 Khalqist officers were arrested for an attempted coup, and in March 1990 the Khalqist Defence Minister Shahnawaz Tanai led another attempt, with the cooperation of Gulbuddin Hekmatyar, which failed. After April 1992 former Khalqists joined Hekmatyar, the Taliban or other warlords; according to western diplomatic sources, Tanai gave the Taliban a cadre of trained officers.
khalsa: The word khalsa comes from an Arabic word meaning pure or sincere. Under Mughal rule it first meant land held directly by the emperor, not granted to lords as jagir. Before Guru Gobind Singh, the Sikh community was organised through agents called masands, who collected revenue. Khalsa came to mean loyalty directly to the Guru and not to these intermediaries, who were increasingly seen as corrupt. The term appears in letters of earlier Gurus, such as Guru Hargobind, who referred to a congregation as the Khalsa of the Guru.

According to the popular account, Guru Gobind Singh gathered the Sikhs at Anandpur Sahib on 13 April 1699, the day of Vaisakhi. He drew his sword and asked for a volunteer willing to give his head, and five men came forward in turn.

Each was taken into a tent, and the Guru returned with a bloodied sword; in the end all five emerged unharmed, and the blood was that of goats. He called them the Panj Pyare, the first Khalsa, and initiated them with amrit, water and sugar stirred with a double-edged sword. He then asked them to initiate him, and his name changed from Gobind Rai to Gobind Singh.

Initiation is called Amrit Sanchar or Khande di Pahul, and anyone of any previous religion, caste or age may take it. A male initiate takes the name Singh, meaning lion, and Kaur became the compulsory name for women in the twentieth century. The Khalsa wear the Five Ks: uncut hair, a wooden comb, an iron or steel bracelet, a sword or dagger, and short breeches. Its rules forbid tobacco and intoxicants, adultery, and meat slaughtered in the Muslim manner, and a member who breaks them must be initiated again. The collective body of initiated Sikhs is known as the Guru Panth.

The creation of the Khalsa abolished existing social divisions, and conservative followers protested; many left the ceremony. A Mughal newswriter, Ghulam Mohyiuddin, reported to the emperor that the Guru had abolished caste and custom and bonded his followers into one brotherhood. In October 1708 Banda Singh Bahadur was sent to lead the Khalsa against the Mughals.

Later the Dal Khalsa, a coalition army, fought the Mughals and Afghans, which led to the misls and then to the Sikh Empire. By the death of Ranjit Singh in 1839 its army was assessed at 120,000 men with 250 artillery pieces. Today Sikhs respect the Khalsa although not all are initiated, and it displays martial skills at the festival of Hola Mohalla.
kham: Kham is one of the three traditional Tibetan regions, with Amdo in the northeast and Ü-Tsang in central Tibet. Its terrain is a series of mountain ridges and gorges, the Hengduan Mountains, running from northwest to southeast, and the Mekong, Yangtze, Yalong and Salween rivers flow through it. Tibetans have called it the Four Rivers and Six Ranges. The early trading route between central Tibet and China ran through Kham. Most residents speak Khams Tibetan, while at least a third speak Qiangic languages, a family of twelve interrelated languages not closely related to it. The Khampas were governed locally by chieftains and monasteries and are reputed warriors, known for marksmanship and horsemanship.

Troops of the Tibetan Empire's Yarlung dynasty were sent east in the 7th century to establish Kham as Tibet's eastern frontier, and King Songtsen Gampo, who reigned from 629 to 649, built twelve border-taming temples there. After the Tibetan Empire broke into independent kingdoms in the mid-9th century, Kham was never controlled by a single king but remained a patchwork of kingdoms, tribes and chiefdoms, with Buddhist monasteries alongside secular rulers. Its main independent polities included Chakla, Degé, Lingtsang, Nangchen and Lhatok. In 1639 Güshri Khan, a supporter of the Dalai Lama, invaded with Mongolian troops and defeated the King of Beri.

After the Qing army defeated the Dzungars, the frontier moved in 1725 or 1726 to the Dri River, the upper Yangtze, and the chieftains east of it received the title of tusi. From 1837 the chieftain Gompo Namgyal of Nyarong made himself the leading power in the region, until a Tibetan army defeated and killed him by 1865. Between 1904 and 1911 the Qing commander Zhao Erfeng, nicknamed the Butcher of Kham, executed monks, destroyed monasteries and replaced local leaders with Chinese magistrates. In 1932 an agreement between the warlord Liu Wenhui and Tibetan forces divided Kham into an eastern part under Chinese administration and a western part under Tibet, and an eastern area became Xikang Province in 1939.

In 1950 the People's Liberation Army invaded western Kham, which became the Qamdo Territory and was merged into the Tibet Autonomous Region in 1965; Xikang was merged into Sichuan in 1955. Kham now includes 50 counties: 25 in the eastern Tibet Autonomous Region, 16 in Sichuan, six in Qinghai and three in Yunnan. The border between Sichuan and the Tibet Autonomous Region remains at the Yangtze.
khambhat: Khambhāt lies on an alluvial plain at the northern end of the Gulf of Khambhāt, in Anand district, Gujarat. The gulf is noted for the extreme rise and fall of its tides, which can vary by as much as thirty feet near the town. The soil is silt deposited by the Mahi River. Some have thought the city to be the Camanes of Ptolemy, and James Tod derived its name from the Sanskrit Khambavati, the City of the Pillar. The town is known for its halvasan sweet, sutarfeni, agate stone and kites.

Cambay was a flourishing city and the seat of an extensive trade, noted for silk, chintz and gold stuffs. The Arab traveller al-Mas'udi visited in 915 and called it a very successful port. Marco Polo, who called it Cambaet, noted in 1293 that it was a busy port with a king of its own. Indigo and fine buckram were products of the region, and much cotton and leather was exported. In the early 1340s Ibn Battuta remarked on its architecture and cosmopolitan population, observing that most inhabitants were foreign merchants who competed in building houses and mosques. Niccolò de' Conti, visiting about 1440, gave the circumference of its walls as twelve miles.

The Portuguese Duarte Barbosa, in the early sixteenth century, found a busy and rich city of Muslims and Hindus, with ships sailing to the Sultanate of Mogadishu with cloths and spices and returning with gold, wax and ivory. The difficulty of reaching the town as the gulf silted up gradually ended its commerce, which by 1900 was chiefly in cotton. Cambay State, a princely state of British India with an area of 350 square miles, was founded in 1730 as the Mughal Empire broke up. General Goddard took Cambay in 1780, it was restored to the Marathas in 1783, and the Peshwa ceded it to the British by the treaty of 1803.

Khambhāt was long a centre of Jainism and holds old Jain temples and collections of Jain palm-leaf manuscripts. It is perhaps the only place in India where the Harappan craft of agate bead making survives as a living tradition, although the town has no stone deposits of its own and obtains its stones from the Rajpipla hills, about 200 km away. Folklore credits the craft to Baba Ghor, a saint from Ethiopia, while the archaeological record traces it to the nearby Harappan outpost of Lothal. The 2011 census gave the town 201,964 inhabitants, of whom 72.88 per cent were Hindus, 23.87 per cent Muslims and 2.50 per cent Jains.
khami: Khami, also written Khame, Kame or Kami, is a ruined city 22 km west of Bulawayo in Zimbabwe. It was once the capital of the Kingdom of Butua of the Torwa dynasty. The settlement developed from the architectural form that emerged at Great Zimbabwe in the 13th century and from the local Leopard's Kopje culture, whose builders made platforms of rough walling on which houses were set. The area is riverine and hot, and malaria was a problem. Building platforms made the houses cooler and, for the royal families living in the built-up areas, removed the danger of malaria.

The stone at Khami is laminar granite mixed with dolerite, harder to quarry than the biotite granite found at other sites in Zimbabwe, and it yields shapeless blocks. More than 60 per cent of the quarried stone would not have been of building quality, and even shaped blocks did not suit free-standing dry stone walls, so the builders made gravity retaining walls without mortar.

Khami was the capital of the Torwa dynasty for about 200 years from around 1450 and appears to have been founded when the state at Great Zimbabwe disappeared. It was conquered, traditionally in 1683, by Changamire Dombo, who led an army of Rozvi rebels from the Mwenemutapa state. The Rozvi made another site of the Khami phase, Danamombe (Dhlo-Dhlo), their new capital. In the 1830s Nguni speaking Ndebele raiders displaced the Rozvi from Khami and many of their other sites.

The site has seven built-up areas occupied by the royal family, with open areas in the valley for commoners. The platforms, rising 2 to 7 metres, carried clay huts and courtyards. The Hill Complex was the king's; its terraces of rough walling were covered with dressed stone decorated in checkerboard, herringbone or cord patterns, and lean inwards so that gravity would not bring them down. The retaining wall of the precipice platform, 6 metres high and 68 metres long, bears a checkerboard design along its whole length.

Khami is a national monument and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. Among the ruins stands a Christian cross, believed to have been placed by a contemporary missionary. In the early 2000s the National Museums and Monuments of Zimbabwe began a programme of recording and conservation that stabilised and restored terrace walls on the Main, Cross and North platforms, with volunteers taking part between 2000 and 2007.
khana-ratsadon: Under King Prajadhipok (Rama VII), the absolute monarchy of the Chakri dynasty faced serious economic problems and threats from the British and French Empires, while the urban middle classes of Bangkok grew and began to demand more rights. In February 1927 seven Siamese students met for five days at a hotel on the Rue Du Sommerard in Paris and founded the group. Among them were Lieutenant Plaek Khittasangkha, later Luang Phibulsonggram, a student at the School of Applied Artillery in France, and Pridi Banomyong, a law student at the Institut d'Études Politiques de Paris, whom they made their president.

Calling themselves the promoters, they adopted Six Principles: the supreme power of the Thai people, national security, economic welfare, equality, rights and liberties, and public education for all. To achieve them they resolved to overthrow the absolute monarchy, using force if necessary. Back in Siam they recruited 102 members in four branches: civilians under Laung Praditmanutham, the navy under Group Commander Luang Sinthusongkhramchai, junior army officers under Major Luang Phibulsonggram and senior officers under Colonel Phraya Phahonphonphayuhasena.

By 1933 the party had made Siam a single party state, and it produced six prime ministers from its ranks. In power it intensified assimilation of the Chinese community: laws of 1938 and 1939 barred Chinese from certain professions, trades and residential areas, and the Nationality Law was amended in 1939 to require those seeking citizenship to adopt Thai names, send their children to Thai schools, speak Thai and renounce allegiance to China. Factional rivalry split the party into a civilian wing under Pridi Banomyong and a military wing under Marshal Pibulsongkram, and it declined at about the end of the Second World War.

Later governments played down the party's significance. Sala Chaloem Thai was demolished in 1989, and after the 2014 coup several landmarks linked to the party were removed without explanation. The last surviving member, Lieutenant Krachang Tularak, died on 24 June 2009.

A brass plaque marking the 1932 revolution in the Royal Plaza went missing in April 2017 and was replaced with one praising the Chakri dynasty, and in 2019 statues of Phraya Phahon and Plaek Phibunsongkhram were removed from an army base in Lopburi Province renamed after King Bhumibol. Historians such as Chatri Prakitnonthakan called the removals ideological cleansing by the conservative establishment. During the 2020 protests young demonstrators set a new plaque in Sanam Luang, and one group called itself Khana Ratsadon 2563.
khandesh: Khandesh lies in the north-western corner of Maharashtra, bounded by the Satpura Range to the north, the Berar region to the east, the Hills of Ajanta to the south and the northernmost ranges of the Western Ghats to the west. Its main feature is the Tapti River, which, unlike most rivers of the Deccan, flows westward to the Arabian Sea. The Tapti receives thirteen principal tributaries in Khandesh, among them the Girna, Bori and Panjhra, but none is navigable, and its deep bed long made irrigation difficult. The richest tracts lie on the alluvial plain north of the river, while the wooded hills of the north and west are home to the Bhil people.

The Markandeya Purana and Jain texts call the region Abhiradesa, and inscriptions and oral traditions record the rule of the Abhiras there. In 1295 Ala-ud-din Khilji of Delhi took Khandesh from the Chauhan ruler of Asirgarh, and Delhi dynasties held it until Malik Raja founded the independent Farooqui dynasty in the late 14th century. Under the Mughals, whose army under Akbar overran the region and took Asirgarh, Burhanpur was the capital of the Khandesh Subah. Shah Jahan introduced Todar Mal's revenue system around 1640, and the mid-17th century has been called the time of Khandesh's highest prosperity, owing to trade in cotton, rice, indigo, sugarcane and cloth.

Maratha raids began in 1670, and a century of unrest followed until the Peshwa ousted the Mughals in 1760 and granted parts of the region to the Holkar and Scindia rulers. After Baji Rao II surrendered to the British in June 1818, fighting continued in Khandesh, one of the last of the Peshwa's former lands to come fully under British control. It became a district of the Bombay Presidency and in 1906 was divided into East Khandesh, headquartered at Jalgaon, and West Khandesh, headquartered at Dhule.

After Bombay State was divided in 1960, East and West Khandesh became the Jalgaon and Dhule districts of Maharashtra, and Dhule was later split to form Nandurbar district. The Khandeshi language, named after the region and sometimes counted as a dialect of Marathi, is widely spoken there, and the region is known for growing bananas.
khanty: In the second millennium BCE the lands between the Kama and the Irtysh were home to a Proto-Uralic-speaking population that had contacts with Proto-Indo-European speakers to the south. The woodland people of this region are held to be ancestors of the Ugrian inhabitants of Trans-Uralia, though other researchers place the Khanty origin in the southern Ural steppe, from which they moved north about 500 CE. The Khanty probably appear in Russian records as Yugra around the 11th century, when they dealt with hunters and merchants from Novgorod. The name Ostyak comes from the Khanty words for a person from the Ob.

In the 11th century Yugra was a name for numerous tribes, each with its own centre and chief, and each divided into two exogamic phratries whose members counted as blood relatives. Clans later replaced this structure, and each clan leader, called a knyazets, negotiated with the Russian realm. Khanty princes joined Russian campaigns and received the right to collect yasaq, or tribute, from two Khanty districts, until Russia withdrew these privileges when they were no longer needed. Some Khanty princedoms were partly included in the Siberia Khanate from the 1440s to the 1570s.

After the Russian conquest of Siberia, missionaries and officials ordered idols destroyed, held mass baptisms, punished those who disobeyed the church and took Khanty children as hostages to be converted. Conversions were largely superficial and driven by economic incentives, so Native practices continued within Khanty belief. In the Soviet period the Khanty were among the few Indigenous peoples of Siberia to receive an autonomous okrug. In the 1930s the state moved to collectivise them, executing tribal chiefs as kulaks and then shamans. Children were taken to Russian-speaking boarding schools, which provoked the Kazym rebellion of 1933.

The Khanty traditionally lived by fishing, taiga hunting and reindeer herding, and as trappers they relied heavily on gathering. In winter they lived in stationary huts of earth and branches in permanent villages. In spring they moved to hunting and fishing grounds and built temporary shelters of birch bark and poles. Most Khanty today are Orthodox Christians who combine this with traditional beliefs. The Bear Celebration is held after a successful bear hunt and lasts five or six days, with over 300 songs and performances. Khanty literature began in the first half of the 20th century, and their language belongs to the Ugric branch of the Uralic family, closest to Mansi and Hungarian.
khaqani: Afzal al-Dīn Badīl ibn ʿAlī ibn ʿOthmān, known as Khāqānī, was born about 1120 in Shirvan, on the border of the Persianate world, into a carpenter's family. His mother was a former slave-girl of Nestorian Christian faith who had converted to Islam. By his own account she was a descendant of the great Philippus, which Minorsky took to mean the third-century Roman emperor Philip the Arab.

He lost his father early and was raised by his uncle, the physician Kāfi-al-Din ʿOmar. His poems suggest he may have been a child prodigy, since several can be dated to his early youth, when he was already eulogist of Manuchihr III. He first wrote under the pen name Haqaiʿqi, and later took Khaqani from Khaqan, the title of the Shirvanshahs.

Khaqani decided to make the pilgrimage to Mecca against the wishes of his patron, and was caught at Beylagan. Charged with insubordination, he was imprisoned for five or seven months in a fortress at Shabaran, near Darband, and was condemned to further imprisonments until he escaped in 1156-7 and travelled through the Middle East. The journey gave him material for the Tohfat al-ʿErāqayn, a mathnawi of over three thousand verses that serves as an autobiography. He also composed his qasida The Portals at Madāʾen, in which the ruins of the Sasanian palace near Ctesiphon prompt a warning about the transience of royal courts.

On his return Akhsitan I, successor of Manuchihr, detained him at once, and from this imprisonment came his habsiyāt, or prison poetry, of which five poems describe the ordeal. Between 1173 and 1175 he wrote odes on a Shirvan victory over the Russians, mentioning the destruction of 73 Russian ships. He lost his first wife and his son Rashid-al-Din, and wrote elegies for them. After a second pilgrimage he left court life and settled in Tabriz, where his gravestone gives his death as Shawwal 595, which is July 1199.

His Divān holds qasidas, strophic poems, ghazals and quatrains, and about sixty letters survive. His verse is dense, with rare words and allusions to astrology, medicine, theology and history, and Ali Dashti called him the inaccessible poet. His praise poems of Muhammad earned him the title Hassānu'l-ʿAjam, the Persian Hassan. He lived in a partly Christian milieu, had contact with Byzantine, Armenian and Georgian royalty, and used Christian imagery with, in Lewis's words, an insider's knowledge. He presented Shirvan as heir of the Sasanian and Samanid monarchies. Jan Rypka placed him in the front ranks of Persian literature, and his work influenced Nezami Ganjavi and Jami.
kharak-singh: Kharak Singh was born in Lahore on 22 February 1801, the son of Ranjit Singh and his second wife, Datar Kaur, daughter of Ran Singh Nakai of the Nakai Misl. His father named him Kharak, wielder of the sword, after a warrior of the Dasam Granth, and it was his birth that persuaded Ranjit Singh to proclaim himself Maharaja of Punjab. As a boy he was married to Chand Kaur, daughter of Jaimal Singh Kanhaiya, a match meant to keep the Kanhaiya Misl from opposing the heir, and in 1816 he was formally made Yuvraj, crown prince.

He was given commands from boyhood. In 1812 he was sent against the chiefs of Bhimber and Rajouri and received Jammu as his jagir; in 1818 he led, with Misr Diwan Chand, the expedition that defeated Nawab Muzaffar Khan at Multan; and he commanded a battalion at the Battle of Shopian, after which he kept Srinagar from being plundered. In 1839 his father gave him Kashmir.

On Ranjit Singh's death he was proclaimed maharaja and was crowned at Lahore Fort on 1 September 1839. He commissioned a Sanskrit astronomical manuscript, the Sarvasiddhantattvacudamani. His tutor Chet Singh Bajwa gained great influence over him, which set him against the prime minister, Dhian Singh, and rumours spread that the two were planning to sell the Punjab to the British and disband the Sikh army. Chet Singh was murdered in the maharaja's presence on 9 October 1839, and Kharak Singh's son Nau Nihal Singh became the real ruler.

Deposed and imprisoned, Kharak Singh was, by one account, poisoned with white lead and mercury, and he died in Lahore on 5 November 1840; the official announcement blamed a sudden illness, while most contemporaries believed Dhian Singh responsible. Two of his wives committed sati on his pyre. British writers such as Alexander Burnes called him an imbecile, but Claude Martin Wade, at the Lahore court for 16 years, described a man of mild and humane disposition. His samadhi stands in Lahore near those of his father and son.
kharg-island: Kharg Island is a coral outcrop in the Persian Gulf, about 25 to 28 kilometres off the Iranian coast and about 55 kilometres north-west of Bushehr, to whose province it belongs. It is around 8 kilometres long and 4 to 5 kilometres wide. The surrounding waters are deep, and it is one of the few islands in the Gulf with its own supply of fresh water. The island's name has also been recorded as Khark, Kharaj and Kharej.

The Hudud al-'Alam mentions Kharg around 982 CE as a source of pearls, and it served as a stopover for ships sailing between India and Basra. The geographer Yaqut visited in 1218. The Portuguese claimed it in 1507 under Afonso de Albuquerque and Tristão da Cunha. In 1753 the Dutch East India Company agent Baron Tiddo Frederik van Kniphausen paid 2,000 rupees to Mir Nasáir, ruler of Bandar Rig, for perpetual ownership, and made the island a free port. The Dutch built a trading post and Fort Mosselstein. A church was built in 1757, and a Carmelite priest served what was then the largest Catholic community in Persia.

In January 1766, after relations with local peoples worsened, Mir Muhanna, governor of Bandar Rig, seized the fortress and forced the Dutch out for good. The British occupied the island briefly in 1837 and again from December 1856, during the Anglo-Persian War. Reza Shah Pahlavi used Kharg as a place of exile for political opponents. Work on oil reservoirs began in 1956, and a terminal fed by a pipeline from the Gachsaran field was inaugurated on 8 November 1960. By around 1975 it was the world's largest offshore crude-oil terminal. The Iraqi air force bombed it heavily between 1982 and 1986.

Kharg holds a number of archaeological sites. In 2007 a cuneiform inscription in Old Persian, dated to between 550 and 330 BCE, was found carved on a coral rock. Its authenticity and meaning have been disputed, and it was damaged in 2008. A ruined Christian complex, the Kharg Monastery, measures about 96 by 85 metres and has a chapel and 19 monks' cells. Daniel T. Potts dates it from ceramic evidence to the 8th and 9th centuries, while Marie-Joseph Stève suggested a founding as early as the 7th century. Rock-cut tombs, megalithic tombs and Zoroastrian and Christian burials have also been studied.
kharga-oasis: The Kharga Oasis lies in the Western Desert, about 200 km west of the Nile valley. Its name is Arabic for the outer. To the ancient Egyptians it was the Southern Oasis, to the Greeks the outer, and to the Romans Oasis Magna, and in Coptic it was the Oasis of Hib. It is the largest of the oases of the Libyan Desert in Egypt, in a depression about 160 km long and between 20 and 80 km wide. The climate is hot desert, with no rain in the extreme summers and warm winters with cool nights. Kharga is also the name of the main town, the capital of the New Valley Governorate.

A trade route called Darb El Arba'īn, the Way of Forty, ran through Kharga as part of a long caravan road between Middle Egypt and the Sudan, from the Al-Fashir area of Darfur to Asyut on the Nile, about 1,800 km. It was probably used from the Old Kingdom for gold, ivory, spices, wheat, animals and plants, and it was cheaper and safer than the river route. Herodotus described it as a road traversed in forty days, which gave it its name. The Romans built a chain of mud-brick fortresses to protect it, some small outposts and some guarding large cultivated settlements, a few of them with small stone temples.

After the Council of Ephesus condemned Nestorius in 431 he was removed as Patriarch of Constantinople and exiled to a monastery in the Great Oasis of Hibis, where he lived for the rest of his life. He was injured in a raid by desert bandits and seems to have survived there until at least 450. There he wrote the Bazaar of Heracleides, the only one of his works to survive in full. The English explorer W. G. Browne stopped at Kharga with a caravan to Darfur and left on 7 June 1793. In 1930 the archaeologist Gertrude Caton-Thompson uncovered the Palaeolithic history of the oasis.

The Temple of Hibis, a temple of the Saite period, stands about 2 km north of the modern town in a palm grove and was erected largely about 500 BCE. A second temple of the first millennium BCE stands at Dush in the south. The Christian cemetery of El Bagawat was in use from the 3rd to the 7th century and is one of the earliest and best preserved in the ancient world. Serious archaeological work began in 1976 with Serge Sauneron of the Institut Français d'Archéologie Orientale. Kharga is the most modernised of Egypt's western oases, with little of its old architecture left, and had an estimated population of 87,482 in 2023.
kharkiv: Kharkiv stands on the banks of the Kharkiv, Lopan and Udy rivers, which flow into the Siverskyi Donets watershed in north-eastern Ukraine. It is the main city of the historic region of Sloboda Ukraine, also called Slobozhanshchyna. The name probably comes from the river Kharkiv, which is attested earlier than the fortress; a folk etymology connects it to a Cossack founder called Kharko.

The earliest historical references to the region are to Scythian and Sarmatian settlement in the 2nd century BCE. In the 8th to 10th centuries the Khazar fortress of Verkhneye Saltovo stood about 40 km east of the modern city. In the 12th century the area belonged to the Cumans, and from the mid-13th century to the Golden Horde. In 1654 settlers arrived on the banks of the Lopan and Kharkiv rivers and rebuilt and fortified an abandoned settlement. In 1765 Kharkiv became the seat of a separate Sloboda Ukraine Governorate, and an imperial university was decreed in January 1805.

In December 1919 the Bolsheviks made Kharkiv the capital of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. Ukrainian replaced Russian as the largest recorded nationality, though Russian remained the dominant spoken language. In the 1930s the city was a centre of Ukrainian writing, nicknamed a Literary Klondike, and over 100 of these writers were repressed in the Stalinist purges, an event called the Executed Renaissance. German forces occupied Kharkiv from 1941, with an interval in 1943, and under their rule its Jewish population was systematically destroyed. The city was liberated on 23 August 1943. In the referendum of 1 December 1991, 86 per cent of Kharkiv Oblast approved Ukrainian statehood.

Kharkiv is the second-largest city of Ukraine and the administrative centre of Kharkiv Oblast, with a population of 1,430,885 in 2023. Machinery, electronics and military hardware have been its leading industries, and it has many research institutes. Principal landmarks include the Dormition Cathedral, built in the 1680s and rebuilt in the 1820s and 1830s, the Annunciation Cathedral, completed on 2 October 1888, the Derzhprom building in Freedom Square and the Kharkiv Railway Station.
khartoum: Khartoum stands at the confluence of the White Nile, flowing north from Lake Victoria, and the Blue Nile, flowing west from Lake Tana in Ethiopia. The meeting place is known as al-Mogran. The two rivers divide the metropolitan area into three parts: Khartoum proper, Khartoum North and Omdurman, linked by bridges. The site is flat, at about 385 metres above sea level, with a hot desert climate and a very short rainy season. One proposed origin of the name is the Arabic khurṭūm, trunk, probably for the strip of land between the rivers.

Khartoum was established in 1821, 24 km north of the ancient city of Soba, as an outpost of the Egyptian army, soon after Muhammad Ali Pasha had incorporated Sudan into his realm. Egypt moved its colonial government there in 1823, and the settlement grew into a regional centre of trade on the caravan route from Ethiopia to Egypt and a focus of the slave trade. Floods destroyed most of the city in 1854, and it was rebuilt in mud and stone instead of thatch and straw.

The Siege of Khartoum began on 13 March 1884, when troops of the Mahdi, Muhammad Ahmad, besieged the Egyptian garrison under the British General Charles George Gordon. The Mahdists took the city on 26 January 1885 and annihilated the garrison. Many inhabitants were massacred or enslaved, the survivors were deported to the newly founded Omdurman, and Khartoum was largely destroyed and abandoned.

After the reconquest of 1898 Khartoum became the capital of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. Herbert Kitchener, Governor-General from September 1898, rebuilt it on a street plan in the shape of the Union Jack. The Gordon Memorial College opened in 1903, and a railway to Port Sudan was completed in 1919. Khartoum became the capital of independent Sudan in 1956.

Khartoum is the capital and most populous city of Sudan, and Greater Khartoum is the country's largest urban area. It is an economic and trade centre with rail lines from Port Sudan, El Obeid and Wadi Halfa. The National Museum of Sudan, founded in 1971, holds two Egyptian temples, from Buhen and Semna, moved there when Lake Nasser was flooded. The city also has the Khalifa House Museum and the University of Khartoum, and it saw heavy fighting and destruction in the civil war that began in April 2023.
khas-people: The Khas have been linked with the Khasas of ancient Hindu literature. The linguist George Abraham Grierson held that most of the people of the lower Himalaya from Kashmir to Darjeeling who speak Aryan languages descended from the Khasas of the Mahabharata, and Pliny the Elder named a people called the Casiri among the peoples of India. Historians disagree on their origins: Baburam Acharya placed them in a homeland stretching from Kashmir to Nepal, while Rahul Sankrityayan saw them as a wave of the same people as the Shakas. Early linguistic evidence of Nepali points to the arrival of Khas speakers from the west or north-west in what is now western Nepal.

The Katyuri dynasty of Kumaon, of Khas origin, ruled from Joshimath and later Baijnath between 700 and 1065 CE. The Khasa kings of western Nepal and Uttarakhand formed the Malla kingdom, which lasted from the eleventh century until it collapsed and splintered into local chiefdoms during the fourteenth. In Kashmir the 12th-century Rajatarangini of Kalhana names the Lohara dynasty as Khas and calls the rulers of Rajapuri lords of the Khasas.

Until the 19th century the Gorkhali called their country Khas Desh. The legal code of 1854 issued by Prime Minister Jung Bahadur Rana, himself a Khas, treated the Khas as a community within the Gorkha kingdom, and he relabelled them Chhetri. Wealthier Khas families had Brahmin priests initiate them into the high-caste Chhetri order, while those who did not became known as Matwali Chhetris. Jung Bahadur also decreed that the language once called Khas kura be called Gorkhali, and it later became the Nepali language.

In Nepal the Khas today include hill Brahmins, the Thakuri and Chhetri, and occupational groups such as the Kami, Damai and Sarki; Nepal's constitution counts Bahun, Kshetri, Thakuri and Sanyasi citizens as Khas Arya for electoral purposes. The name itself is passing out of use because of negative stereotypes attached to it. Most Khas are Hindu, and some follow Buddhism or Christianity. They also had a sect of Shaivism of their own, the Masto religion, in which twelve gods held to be sons of Shiva were worshipped across the Western Himalaya, and Deuda songs and dances are performed at festivals in the Sudurpashchim and Karnali provinces of Nepal.
khasekhemwy: Khasekhemwy is normally placed as the successor of Seth-Peribsen, though some Egyptologists think he followed Sekhemib-Perenmaat and that a king Khasekhem ruled between them; most scholars hold that Khasekhem and Khasekhemwy are the same person. According to one view, he changed his name after defeating Seth-Peribsen and reuniting Upper and Lower Egypt after a civil war between the followers of Horus, led by himself, and the followers of Seth led by Peribsen. Others believe he defeated Peribsen only after returning from putting down a revolt in Nubia. The Palermo Stone first calls him the Dual King in his 13th year, so the country was reunited by his 12th year.

Wilkinson's study of the Palermo Stone gives him a reign of about 18 years, falling roughly between 2690 and 2670 BCE, while Manetho gives thirty years and the Turin King List twenty-seven; both are considered unreliable because they were written long after his death.

The Palermo Stone records a census of gold and fields in alternate years, the making of a copper statue called High is Khasekhemwy in his 15th year, and ship-building at Duadjefa in his 17th. An inscription on a stone vase records him fighting the northern enemy within Nekheb, which suggests that Lower Egypt nearly took the capital Nekhen.

Khasekhemwy is the only Egyptian king known to have both Horus and Seth on his serekh. He began with the Horus name Khasekhem, the powerful one has appeared, and later added the symbol of Seth and changed his name to Khasekhemwy, the two powers have appeared, with the addition that the two powers are at peace with him. Some Egyptologists see this as an attempt to unify the two factions, but after his death Seth was dropped from the serekh for good. He was the earliest Egyptian king known to have built statues of himself.
A life-size limestone statue from Hierakonpolis, found by Flinders Petrie in 1896 and now in the Ashmolean Museum, shows him in the White Crown; its base records 47,209 slain northern rebels.

He built in stone at el-Kab, Hierakonpolis and Abydos and built enclosures at Nekhen and at Abydos, the mud-brick structure known as Shunet ez Zebib. He may also have built the Gisr el-Mudir at Saqqara.

Khasekhemwy was buried in Tomb V, the last royal tomb built in the Umm el-Qa'ab necropolis. The trapezoidal tomb is some 70 metres long and divided into 58 rooms, and its central chamber of quarried limestone was long considered the oldest masonry structure in the world. Though looted in antiquity, it still held a gold and sard sceptre and fine stone vessels. His wife Nimaathap was the mother of Djoser, and the final years of the Second Dynasty prepared the way for the Third.
khatyn-massacre: Khatyn, a village of 26 houses in Lahoysk district of the Minsk region, about 50 km from Minsk, suffered a fate common in occupied Belarus. At least 5,295 Belarusian settlements were burned by the Nazis, often with all their inhabitants, as punishment for helping partisans; in the Vitebsk region 243 villages were burned twice. Over 2,000,000 people, almost a quarter of the population, were killed in Belarus during the three years of occupation.

On 22 March 1943 men of Schutzmannschaft Battalion 118, made up mostly of Ukrainian and other Soviet collaborators, were repairing a telephone line near Kozyri, 6 km from Khatyn, when Soviet partisans attacked them, killing four policemen, among them the company commander Hauptmann Hans Woellke. The partisans fled towards Khatyn. Platoon commander Vasyl Meleshko called for help from the SS-Sonderbataillon Dirlewanger, to which the battalion was subordinated. Meanwhile 26 of a group of woodcutters detained at Kozyri were killed near the village of Guba when they panicked and tried to flee.

Dirlewanger's men under SS-Sturmbannführer Praefke and the battalion under Hryhoriy Vasiura surrounded Khatyn and shelled the partisans sheltering there; by the afternoon 34 partisans had been killed. The surviving villagers were driven into a shed, which was covered with straw and set on fire, and those who broke out through the doors were cut down by machine guns. The village was looted and burned. Eight inhabitants survived, among them the smith Yuzif Kaminsky and several children.

Bruno Pavel, the officer who ordered the massacre, was tried at the Riga Trial in 1946 and executed. Meleshko was executed in 1975, and Vasiura, tried in Minsk in 1986, in 1987; his trial received little publicity, as Soviet leaders worried about unity between the Belarusian and Ukrainian peoples. In 1969 Khatyn became the national war memorial of the Byelorussian SSR, with a statue of Kaminsky carrying his dying son and a Cemetery of villages of 185 tombs. The historian Norman Davies argues that the Soviet authorities used it to create confusion with the Katyn massacre.
khayr-al-nisa-begum: Khayr al-Nisa Begum was the daughter of Mir Abdollah Khan II, the Marashi ruler of Mazandaran, whose family claimed descent from the fourth Shi'a Imam, Zayn al-Abidin, and had ruled the province since the mid-14th century. She was related to Khan Ahmad Khan of Gilan. In 1565–66, after her cousin Mir Sultan-Murad Khan murdered her father, she fled to the Safavid court, where she was married to Mohammad Khodabanda, son of Shah Tahmasp I. The wish to avenge her father stayed with her for the rest of her life. Her royal title, Mahd-i Ulya, means the highest-ranked cradle.

When Ismail II died in 1578, Mohammad Khodabanda became shah. He was a weak-willed ruler, and his sister Pari Khan Khanum, allied with factions of the Qizilbash army, expected to control him, but his wife took charge of his affairs from the start. The couple reached the outskirts of Qazvin on 12 February 1578, where Pari Khan Khanum met them in a gilded litter with 4,000–5,000 guards and attendants. Warned of her power by Mirza Salman Jaberi, Ismail II's former vizier, Mahd-i Ulya resolved to have her killed. Khalil Khan Afshar, Pari Khan Khanum's former tutor, had her strangled; her uncle Shamkhal Sultan was executed, and Ismail II's infant son Shoja al-Din Mohammad Safavi was murdered.

From February 1578 Mahd-i Ulya governed Iran in practice. She built a network of support by appointing friends and relatives to high posts and favoured the Persian Tajiks over the Qizilbash. Her chief aims were to advance her elder son Hamza Mirza at the expense of his brother Abbas, and to take revenge for her father. As his killer was dead, her supporters seized and killed his son Mirza Khan on his way to Qazvin, although Qizilbash leaders had promised him safe-conduct.

The angered Qizilbash petitioned the shah to remove her or face revolts. He considered exiling her and even offered to abdicate and retire to Shiraz, but she refused to give way. A group of Qizilbash conspirators then accused her of a love affair with Adil Giray, brother of the Crimean Tatar khan, who was held captive at court. They burst into the harem on 26 July 1579 and strangled her with many of her retinue and family; Adil Giray was killed as well.
khazar-khaganate: The Khazars were a confederation of different Turkic-speaking peoples, and their precise origins and nature are uncertain, because no record in the Khazar language survives and the state was multilingual and polyethnic. The ruling elite probably spoke an eastern variety of Common Turkic, while the subject tribes appear to have spoken Oghuric languages. An embryonic Khazar state began to form sometime after 630, from the breakdown of the First Turkic Khaganate of the Göktürks, whose ruling clan was the Ashina. A later Khazar ruler named Joseph, in his reply to Hasdai ibn Shaprut, wrote that the Khazars descended from Kozar, one of the ten sons of Togarmah.

For most of its history Khazaria was a buffer state between the Byzantine Empire, the nomads of the northern steppes and the Umayyad and Abbasid Caliphates, having earlier served as Byzantium's proxy against the Sasanian Empire. In the 7th and 8th centuries the Khazars fought a series of wars with the caliphates. In 652 Arab forces advanced on the Khazar capital, Balanjar, but were defeated with heavy losses. Around 830 a rebellion broke out, and three Kabar tribes, probably the majority of the ethnic Khazars, joined the Hungarians and moved to Etelköz, between the Carpathians and the Dnieper.

In the 9th century Varangian Rus' began probing south down the waterways the Khazars controlled, partly in pursuit of the Arab silver that flowed north through the Khazar and Volga Bulgar trading zones. The fortress of Sarkel, built with Byzantine technical help, and an autonomous Khazar coinage from around the 830s may have been defences against the Varangians and the Magyars. Around 900 the Byzantines began encouraging the Alans to attack Khazaria in order to weaken its hold on Crimea and the Caucasus.

Sviatoslav I of Kiev and his allies conquered the capital, Atil, and by most accounts the campaign left Khazaria devastated, with at best a minor rump state. Khazars fade from the sources after a conflict in 1106, and by the 13th century they survived in Russian folklore only as Jewish heroes.

Khazaria had a dual leadership, typical of Turkic nomads, of a khagan-bek and a khagan. According to Arabic sources, the khagan-bek managed and commanded the military, while the greater khagan's role was mainly sacral. The original religion was probably Tengrism, which focused on the sky god Tengri and included horse sacrifices and offerings to fire, water and the moon.

The population included pagans, Jews, Christians and Muslims. Evidence suggests the ruling elite converted to Rabbinic Judaism in the 8th century, but the extent of the conversion is uncertain, and archaeological evidence for it remains elusive. Scholars view with scepticism the nineteenth-century theory that Ashkenazi Jews descend from Khazars.
khedive-of-egypt: Khedive, a term of Persian origin, was the title that distinguished the ruler of Egypt from other Ottoman governors, called walis. Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman officer, was recognised as governor of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, established de facto autonomy from the sultan, and by 1841 secured recognition of his descendants' right to hold the office of viceroy. His successors were his son Ibrahim, his grandson Abbas I, his son Muhammad Sa'id, and then Isma'il Pasha, a son of Ibrahim, who took the throne in 1863.

A firman of 8 June 1867 granted Isma'il the title of khedive from the Ottoman sultan Abdulaziz. It came with near-complete control of Egypt's internal affairs and the right to negotiate certain international agreements. In return for doubling his tributary payments to Istanbul, Isma'il also won the right to change the order of succession to primogeniture. A second firman, of 8 June 1873, let him take foreign loans and removed limits on the size of the army. Egypt was not independent: it remained an autonomous tributary state of the Ottoman Empire.

Three men held the title. Isma'il (1863–1879) pursued European-style modernisation and sought to expand Egypt's rule along the Nile and the African coast of the Red Sea, but his army was defeated by the Ethiopian Empire at the Battles of Gundet in 1875 and Gura in 1876. His costly projects brought heavy foreign debt, and the European powers pressed the sultan to depose him, which happened on 29 June 1879. His son Tawfiq (1879–1892) saw European influence reimposed and the Urabi revolution suppressed when Britain invaded in 1882. The British then took control of the country, with Tawfiq restored.

Abbas II (1892–1914) grew hostile to the British. When the Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in the First World War, Britain proclaimed a Sultanate of Egypt and abolished the Khedivate on 5 November 1914. Abbas II, on a state visit to Vienna, was deposed in his absence and banned from returning. His uncle Hussein Kamel took the title of sultan on 19 December 1914.
kherlen-river: The Kherlen, also known as the Kerülen, is 1,254 kilometres long and is one of the two longest rivers in Mongolia, together with the Orkhon River. It rises on the southern slopes of the Khentii Mountains, near the mountain of Burkhan Khaldun in the Khan Khentii Strictly Protected Area, about 180 kilometres north-east of Ulaanbaatar. The area is a watershed between the Arctic and Pacific basins. The Tuul River drains to the Arctic side, while the Kherlen and the Onon belong to the Pacific side, and the area is therefore called the Three River Basins.

From its source the river flows mostly eastward through the Khentii province. Farther downstream it crosses the eastern Mongolian steppe, passing Ulaan Ereg and Choibalsan, and enters China. It ends in Hulun Nuur after a further 164 kilometres. Its mean streamflow fell by more than half between 2000 and 2008 when compared with earlier decades.

Hulun Lake normally has no outlet. In years of high precipitation it may overflow at its northern shore, and the water then reaches the Ergune River after about 30 kilometres. The Ergune forms the border between Russia and China for about 944 kilometres, until it meets the Amur River. Counted together, the Kherlen, Ergune and Amur make a system 5,052 kilometres long.

On the Kherlen lies the Khuduu Aral, a plain 30 kilometres long and 20 kilometres wide. It is described as the site of Genghis Khan's palace, Ikh Aurag. Near it is a small lake rich in carbonate, soda and chlorine, whose water has a reputation for treating nerve disorders.

Near the city of Choibalsan, in the Dornod province of far north-eastern Mongolia, the river feeds several soda lakes, among them the Tsaidam lakes, the Gurvany lakes and Shar Burdiin. They are closed lakes fed by groundwater, lying in basins formed in basalt, pyroclastic material and rhyolite erupted late in the Cretaceous. The climate is semi-arid, with a mean annual precipitation of 207 millimetres, so the groundwater is recharged only by the largest rainfalls and by snowmelt.

Several of these lakes are exceedingly rich in uranium. At Shar Burdiin, the most highly evaporated of them, a concentration of 62.5 micromoles has been measured, which may be the highest naturally occurring figure reported for surface water. The source of the uranium is uncertain. Possibilities are the breakdown of volcanic glass and wind-blown salts, since dust storms are frequent in spring when the lakes are driest.
khevsurs: The Khevsurians are an ethnographic group of Georgians who live mainly in Khevsureti, on both sides of the Caucasus chain in the watersheds of the rivers Aragvi and Argun; some villages in Khevi, Ertso-Tianeti, Kakheti (Shiraki) and Kvemo Kartli (Gardabani) are also Khevsurian. They speak the Khevsurian dialect of the Georgian language. They are first mentioned in manuscripts of the 10th century, and in 1745 Vakhushti Bagrationi described them in his Description of the Kingdom of Georgia.

The old Georgian chronicle names Khevsureti and Pshavi together as Pkhovi and their people as Pkhoveli. Describing the north-eastern part of Heret-Kakheti, Vakhushti wrote that those now called Pshav Khevsur had earlier been called Pkhoelni, and the neighbouring Kists still call Khevsureti Pkhia or Pkhye, which means the same as Pkhoeli.

In the autumn of 1811 the Khevsurians and the Ingush joined the uprising that broke out in Kakheti under the fugitive Georgian prince Alexander. Between 1951 and 1953 the Soviet authorities forcibly resettled many Khevsurs from their mountain homeland to designated lowland areas. The official reasons were better access to public services and their joining collective farms with other groups of the area.

Khevsurs who lived through the resettlement describe it as traumatic and destabilising. Many were sent to places with too few resources, which led to social and physical conflict with other resettled groups such as the Tatars and Kakhetians. The Khevsurians had long kept their traditional clothing, weapons and polyphonic music, but since the resettlements elements of their culture, among them traditional dress and religious practices, are in danger of being lost.
khilafat-movement: In the late 19th century the Ottoman sultan Abdul Hamid II launched a pan-Islamist programme to protect his empire from Western attack and dismemberment, and sent an emissary, Jamaluddin Afghani, to India. The cause of the Ottoman ruler stirred religious feeling among Indian Muslims.
