As caliph the sultan was nominally the supreme religious and political leader of all Sunni Muslims, although that authority had never actually been used. The Ottoman Empire, which sided with the Central Powers in the First World War, was defeated. The victorious Allied Powers promised to protect the sultan's status as caliph, but under the Treaty of Sèvres of 1920 Palestine, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq were severed from the empire.

To its founders and followers the Khilafat was not a religious movement but a show of solidarity with Muslims in Turkey. Mohammad Ali and his brother Shaukat Ali, joined by leaders such as Hakim Ajmal Khan, Mukhtar Ahmed Ansari, Hasrat Mohani and Abul Kalam Azad, formed the All India Khilafat Committee, based in Lucknow. In 1920 it published the Khilafat Manifesto, calling on the British to protect the caliphate and on Indian Muslims to unite.

In 1920 the Khilafat leaders allied with the Indian National Congress, and Mahatma Gandhi and they promised to work together for the Khilafat and for Swaraj. The Khilafatists became a major part of the non-cooperation movement, which began with a boycott of legislative councils, government schools and colleges, and foreign goods and the surrender of titles. Gandhi and the Ali brothers were swiftly arrested. Indians also gave donations, including funds for the government of Mustafa Kemal at Ankara. The movement weakened as Muslims divided between the Congress, the Khilafat cause and the Muslim League.

The movement ended in 1922 with the end of the non-cooperation movement. Turkish revolutionaries under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk replaced the Treaty of Sèvres with the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923, and the Republic of Turkey abolished the caliphate in 1924. The leadership fragmented, and the Ali brothers joined the Muslim League.

The period of 1919 to 1922 is widely seen as the heyday of Hindu-Muslim unity, and the movement is described as a milestone in the growth of Muslim nationalism and of civil disobedience in India. Muhammad Ali Jinnah left the Congress after his warnings against entangling the secular independence movement with the religious elements of the Khilafat movement went unheeded. Critics questioned whether a campaign centred on the Ottoman caliphate was compatible with a movement for the unity of Indians of all religions, and some argue that its religious rhetoric concealed a weak and uncertain religious agenda.
khitans: The Khitans inhabited, from the 4th century, an area corresponding to parts of modern Mongolia, north-east China and the Russian Far East. They are described as descended from the proto-Mongols through the Xianbei, and spoke the now-extinct Khitan language, which is related to the Mongolic languages. Their own origin myth, recorded in the History of Liao compiled in the 14th century, tells of a sacred man on a white horse and a heavenly woman in a cart drawn by a grey ox, whose eight sons became eight tribes. The eight tribes shared power by rotating the leadership every three years.

The Khitans sent tribute to the Northern Yan and Northern Wei, were defeated by the Northern Qi in 553, and submitted to the Sui dynasty in 584. In the early 7th century the Dahe clan united the tribes in a federation able to raise 34,000 troops. After a rebellion ended Dahe supremacy in 730, a new confederation placed a khagan from the Yaonian clan at its head, though its military chief held greater power. The Tang governor An Lushan invaded Khitan territory in 751 and 755 and later led a rebellion that included Khitan troops.

Abaoji, who had united the Khitan tribes, founded the Liao dynasty, whose territory took in northern and north-eastern China, Mongolia and parts of the Korean Peninsula and Siberia. The Khitan language, origin myth, shamanic religion and nomadic way of life endured the change to an imperial state. After the Jurchen invasion ended the Liao in 1125, many Khitans followed Yelü Dashi west and founded the Qara Khitai, which lasted nearly a century until the Mongol Empire overran it in 1218. Through them the name Khitai came to mean China to neighbouring peoples, and it reached medieval Europe as Cathay.

The nomadic Khitans originally lived by stockbreeding, fishing and hunting; under Chinese influence they took up farming, growing panicled millet, and built cities. They wrote their language in two independent scripts, the large and the small, which have not been fully deciphered. Their shamanism gave animals an important place: hunters offered a sacrifice to the spirit of the animal they hunted. Khitan women learned to hunt, ride and shoot, and elite women such as Shulü Ping, Empress Yingtian, took part in military affairs and commanded armies. The Daur people of north-east China are regarded as their genetic descendants.
khiva: Khiva is a city of about 93,000 people in Khorazm Region, Uzbekistan. According to archaeological data it was established around 2,500 years ago, and in 1997 it marked its 2,500th anniversary. It is the former capital of Khwarezmia, the Khanate of Khiva and the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic. Its inner town, Itchan Kala, was the first site in Uzbekistan and in Central Asia to be inscribed on the World Heritage List, in 1991. The scholar Al-Biruni (973–1048) was born in either Khiva or the nearby city of Kath. The origin of its name is unknown, and a traditional story attributes the city to Shem, a son of Noah.

The Eastern Iranian language Khwarezmian was spoken in Khiva in its early history. Turkic peoples replaced the Iranian ruling class in the 10th century, and the region gradually came to have a majority of Turkic speakers. The earliest records of the city are in Muslim travel accounts of the 10th century, although archaeology shows habitation in the 6th century. By the early 17th century Khiva was the capital of the Khanate of Khiva, ruled by the Uzbek Kongirad dynasty.

From the 17th century Khiva developed as a slave market, and with Bukhara it was known for centuries as a major centre of the slave trade. In the first half of the 19th century about 30,000 Persians and an unknown number of Russians were enslaved there before being sold, and many were put to work on the construction of buildings in the walled Itchan Kala.

In 1873 the Russian general Konstantin von Kaufman attacked Khiva, which fell on 28 May. The Russian Empire controlled the khanate, but it let Khiva remain a nominally quasi-independent protectorate. The last khan of the ruling dynasty was removed in 1919, and Khiva became the capital of the short-lived Khorezm People's Soviet Republic (1920–1924), which was incorporated into the USSR in 1924.

Khiva is split into two parts. The inner town, Itchan Kala, is encircled by brick walls, with foundations believed to date to the 10th century and present walls from the late 17th century, up to 10 metres high. It retains more than 50 historic monuments and 250 old houses, mostly of the 18th or 19th century. The Juma Mosque was rebuilt in 1788–89 and its hypostyle hall keeps 112 columns taken from older buildings. The blue tower of Kalta Minor was begun in 1851 by Mohammed Amin Khan and left unfinished when he died.
khmelnytsky-uprising: In 1569 the Union of Lublin gave the Ruthenian voivodeships of Volhynia, Podolia, Bracław and Kiev to the Crown of Poland within the new Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Bohdan Khmelnytsky was born to a noble family and attended a Jesuit school, probably in Lviv. After service against the Ottoman Empire and a period of captivity in Constantinople, he returned as a Registered Cossack and settled at his estate of Subotiv. His life changed when Aleksander Koniecpolski, heir of a magnate estate, tried to seize his land. In 1647 Daniel Czapliński harassed Khmelnytsky on Koniecpolski's behalf and raided Subotiv twice, and his son Yurii was badly beaten. Appeals to the king in Warsaw failed.

On 25 January 1648 Khmelnytsky and 400 to 500 Cossacks attacked the Sich on Mykytyn Rih. Registered Cossacks joined him, and the Cossack Rada elected him hetman by the end of the month. He allied with the Crimean Khanate. In April and May Cossack and Tatar forces won the first victories. Talks in June under Adam Kysil led to Khmelnytsky's demands for more Registered Cossacks and the return of churches to the Orthodox. The Commonwealth army of 35,000 to 40,000, encumbered by a baggage train, was routed at Pyliavtsi on 23 September 1648. In January 1649 Khmelnytsky entered Kyiv in triumph.

Fighting resumed in 1649 and 1651, and in June 1652 at Batih a Cossack and Tatar force killed the field hetman Marcin Kalinowski and half of his hussars. On 11 October 1653 the Zemsky Sobor of Muscovy decided to accept the Zaporozhian Host under the tsar, and the Treaty of Pereyaslav followed in early 1654. The Swedish invasion of the Commonwealth in 1655, known as the Deluge, further changed the war. Sources disagree on when the uprising ended: 1654, 1655 or Khmelnytsky's death in 1657.

The uprising is generally considered a Cossack victory, since it ended Polish-Lithuanian rule over much of the Ukrainian lands and created the Cossack Hetmanate. The struggle to consolidate the victory, outside pressure and divisions after Khmelnytsky's death led to a period known as the Ruin. It eventually led to the incorporation of eastern Ukraine into the Tsardom of Russia, and with the Swedish and Russian invasions it ended the Polish Golden Age.

The war brought mass atrocities against civilians, especially Poles, Jews and Catholic and Uniate clergy, by rebels, and reprisals by the Polish army and nobility. Jews, who often leased estates, were seen by peasants as immediate oppressors, and many Jews regard these events as the biggest national catastrophe since the destruction of the Temple. Population loss in the whole Commonwealth from 1648 to 1667, which includes later wars, is estimated at about 4 million.
khmer-empire: The empire called itself Kambuja or Kambujadeśa, the country of the sons of Kambu, and grew out of the earlier civilisation of Chenla. Its beginning is conventionally dated to 802, when the Khmer prince Jayavarman II declared himself chakravartin, universal ruler, and devaraja, god king, in a consecration ritual on Mount Mahendraparvata, now Phnom Kulen. He also declared Kambuja independent of a place the inscriptions call Java.

No written records of the Angkor period survive other than stone inscriptions. Knowledge of the Khmer civilisation comes from excavation, temple foundation steles, the reliefs on temple walls, which show daily life, markets, military marches and palace life, and the reports of Chinese diplomats, notably Zhou Daguan, who stayed at Yaśodharapura in 1296 and 1297.

Under Suryavarman II, who reigned from 1113 to 1150, the empire united internally and Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu, was built over 37 years. His campaigns against Champa and Dai Viet were unsuccessful, though he sacked Vijaya in 1145. In 1177 a Cham fleet raided and looted the capital in a naval battle on the Tonlé Sap, and the king Tribhuvanadityavarman was killed. The Greater Angkor Region had perhaps 700,000 to 900,000 people at its peak in the 13th century.

By the 14th century Kambuja was in long decline. Historians point to the shift from Hinduism to Theravada Buddhism, constant power struggles among princes, in which eleven of the 27 rulers lacked a legitimate claim, vassal revolt, foreign invasion, plague and ecological breakdown. A period of strong monsoon rains followed by severe drought damaged the water works. The last Sanskrit inscription dates to 1327, and the fall of Angkor to the Ayutthaya Kingdom in 1431 traditionally marks the end.

The Khmers relied heavily on rice, grown on plains irrigated by canals and barays, or giant reservoirs and on fish from the Tonlé Sap. Barter was the main form of exchange until the 13th century, when Zhou Daguan recorded rice, grain, Chinese coins and cloth for small transactions and gold and silver for the largest.

Society was arranged in a hierarchy reflecting the Hindu caste system. Commoners, rice farmers and fishermen, formed the large majority, kshatriyas formed the governing elite, and brahmins, traders and artisans made up other classes, with slaves at the bottom. Hinduism was the main religion, with Vishnu and Shiva most revered, followed by Buddhism, and Theravada Buddhism, introduced from Sri Lanka in the 13th century, came to prevail even among the lower classes.
khmer-rouge: The name Khmers rouges, French for red Khmers, was coined by Norodom Sihanouk in the 1960s for the communist-led dissidents of Cambodia. The movement grew from earlier communist parties, beginning with the Indochinese Communist Party, whose members were almost all Vietnamese. In the 1950s Khmer students in Paris organised a communist movement of their own, and men and women from its ranks later took command of the party apparatus. Pol Pot, who went to Paris in 1949, rose to the leadership in the 1960s.

The Kampuchea Revolutionary Army was built up in the forests of eastern Cambodia in the late 1960s, supported by the People's Army of Vietnam, the Viet Cong, the Pathet Lao and the Chinese Communist Party. Though it first fought Sihanouk, it supported him after Lon Nol overthrew him in 1970 and set up the pro-American Khmer Republic.

The Khmer Rouge won the Cambodian Civil War despite a massive American bombing campaign, and captured Phnom Penh in April 1975. Its leaders, Pol Pot, Nuon Chea, Ieng Sary, Son Sen and Khieu Samphan, at once began forcibly evacuating the major cities, and in 1976 the country was renamed Democratic Kampuchea. China was the main foreign supporter, providing at least 90 per cent of the foreign aid. Inside the party, purges began early, and returning intellectuals were treated with suspicion, and some were sent straight to the Tuol Sleng prison.

Fearing Vietnam, Pol Pot ordered a pre-emptive invasion on 18 April 1978. In December 1978 Vietnamese forces and Heng Samrin's Kampuchean United Front for National Salvation invaded, and they captured Phnom Penh on 7 January 1979. The Khmer Rouge fled to Thailand and fought on until 1989. Thousands of guerrillas surrendered under an amnesty a year after the monarchy was restored in 1993, and the movement finally surrendered completely in 1999. In 2014 the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia sentenced Nuon Chea and Khieu Samphan to life imprisonment for crimes against humanity.

The Party Centre led by Pol Pot defeated other regional leaders in a power struggle in 1976. Its ideology combined communism with a strongly xenophobic Khmer nationalism that idealised the Khmer Empire. It sought to abolish money, trade and private property at once, and aimed for self-sufficiency through collectivisation, a Super Great Leap Forward. This led to widespread famine, and thousands died of treatable diseases such as malaria because even medicine had to be home-made.

The regime murdered hundreds of thousands of perceived opponents and targeted Buddhist monks, educated people and minorities, among them the Chinese, Vietnamese and Cham. The Cambodian genocide led to the deaths of 1.5 to 2 million people, about a quarter of the population. At Tuol Sleng, known as S-21, of an estimated 15,000 to 30,000 prisoners only seven survived.
khmu-people: Linguistic, cultural and historical evidence suggests that the Khmuic peoples descend from a single people who may have been among the first to settle northern Indochina. They once held a far larger area, including lowlands of present-day Thailand and Laos, until the Mon and Khmer empires and the later arrival of Tai peoples absorbed them or pushed them into the hills. There they came to live above the rice-growing lowland Lao and below the Hmong and Mien of the highest ground, farming by shifting cultivation. Their name is thought to come from kymhmuʔ, meaning people.

About 88 per cent of the Khmu live in northern Laos, across ten provinces, and they outnumber even the Lao in five of them, among them Luang Prabang, Phongsaly and Oudomxay. Smaller groups live in Vietnam, where they are an officially recognised ethnic group, in Thailand's Nan Province and in Xishuangbanna in China, where they are classed as a subgroup of the Bulang. Migration into northern Thailand for farmland and work in the teak trade began as much as 200 years ago. Others came to Thailand and the United States as refugees from the Vietnam War, and most of those in the United States settled in California.

The Khmu language belongs to the Austro-Asiatic family and has many dialects, broadly Western and Eastern, which are mostly mutually intelligible; most speakers also use the language of the dominant group around them. The Khmu divide themselves into subgroups called tmowy, set apart mainly by dialect, and the Khmu Roek of the higher hills keep older customs others have dropped. Villages grow sticky rice, maize, bananas and vegetables, much of the work done in common, and elders settle disputes. Traditional belief honours the house spirit Hroi gang, treats the village as a ritual space guarded by taboos, and gives each family a protecting totem such as a boar or an eagle. Bronze drums were beaten at harvest rituals to ask the sun to shine.
khoja-niyaz: Khoja Niyaz was born in a small mountain village in Kumul Prefecture, Xinjiang. At eighteen he joined a 1907 uprising of peasants and mountaineers against Shah Maqsud, the hereditary ruler of Kumul under Qing China. After its defeat he fled to the Turpan region, studied at the Astana religious school, where he came to know the brothers Maksut and Mahmut Muhiti, and then made the Hajj to Mecca, taking the title Hajji.

In 1912 he joined another rising against the Kumul Khanate, led by Temur Halpa, as an adviser. After Governor Yang Zengxin had Temur Halpa killed at a banquet on 6 September 1913, he fled again. In 1916 he reached Jarkent in Russian Semiryechye, where after the Russian Revolution he helped organise Uyghur self-defence groups and met the revolutionary Abdulla Rozibakiev.

He returned to Xinjiang in 1923 and organised underground groups in Ghulja and Urumchi. After the death of Shah Mahsut in March 1930 he became adviser to the new ruler of Kumul, but Governor Jin Shuren abolished the khanate and settled Han Chinese migrants from Gansu there. This sparked the Kumul Rebellion of 1931, in which the Hui warlord Ma Zhongying joined Khoja Niyaz and Yulbars Khan; the Mongolian People's Republic also sent him winter clothing, tents and 120 rifles.

By February 1933 the provincial government held no more than 10% of Xinjiang. After Ma Zhongying seized the arsenal of Jimsar on 28 May 1933, Khoja Niyaz turned to General Sheng Shicai, signing an alliance on 4 June 1933 that recognised his claim to the lands south of the Tengri Tagh, and the Soviets armed him. Defeated by Tungan troops at the Battle of Toksun, he took the presidency of the Turkic Islamic Republic of East Turkestan, which broke that agreement. The republic fell to Tungan forces and Soviet intervention by June 1934.

Sheng Shicai then made him Vice-Chairman of the Xinjiang government, but he was kept apart from his troops in Urumchi under the watch of Soviet agents, and his request to meet Stalin was refused. After the rebellion of the 6th Uyghur Division under Mahmut Muhiti in 1937 he was arrested in November of that year. He and 120 followers were labelled counter-revolutionaries and Japanese agents, charges he called fabrications of Sheng Shicai, and he was sentenced to death with Moscow's approval. His last words were reported as: "I will die, but my People will continue to live."
kholop: The word is first mentioned in a chronicle under the year 986. It is related to Slavic words for a man or a boy, such as the Ukrainian khlopets, the Polish chłopiec and the Slovak chlap, a synonym for man. A shift between the meanings young person and servant, in either direction, is common, as in the English use of boy for a domestic servant.

In Kievan Rus' the status and kinds of kholops were set out in the Russkaya Pravda, a legal code of the late Kievan period. Besides killing or selling his kholop, a master could hand him over to settle a debt, and he was answerable if the kholop insulted a freeman or stole. Until the late 15th century kholops made up the majority of the servants working lordly lands. Some, mainly house serfs, joined the ranks of the princely servants, including those in military service, or took up trades, farming or administrative work.

Through the 16th century the place of kholops in the corvée economy of the Principality of Moscow shrank as landowners relied more on the labour of peasants. At the turn of that century service-class kholops appeared and spread across the country. The boevye kholopy, or combat kholops, formed the armed retinues and bodyguards of large and medium landowners from the 16th to the 18th century and served alongside noblemen as a considerable part of the landed army, equipped as mounted archers, usually in cheap quilted armour and caps. In the late 17th century there were also kholops settled on the land, who ran their own households and paid a due called chynsh, similar to quitrent.

The kabala people of the 15th to 17th centuries fell into heavy debt bondage after taking a loan and served their creditor until it was repaid. Their status was governed by the general laws on kholops, the Sudebnik of 1550 and the Sobornoye Ulozheniye of 1649. A decree of 1 February 1597 bound such a kholop to serve until the creditor's death, and in time all kinds of kholop were placed in the kabala category; the agreements were written in kabala books.
khongirad: The Khongirad are often identified with the ancient Wuku or Wugu tribe of Tang dynasty records, and their name first appears in the Secret History of the Mongols as ongirad. Mongolian historians derive it from khun, swan, and ard, people, the swan being a totem of Mongolian peoples such as the Buryats; other scholars link it to words for a raven or for a brown or chestnut coat colour. Their origin myth tells of three brothers born of a golden vessel, Jurluq Mergen, Quba Shira and Tusbu Da'u, whose descendants split in feuds into the Ikires, Olkhonud, Karanut, Gorlos and Qongliyuts.

In the Mongol legend of Ergune Khun, the Khongirad were among the peoples descended from the warriors Kiyan and Negus, who escaped an enclosed valley by melting an iron vein in its mountains; their liability to gout was explained by their ancestors burning their feet on the hot iron as they fled first.

The Mongol royal line traced its descent from Alan Qo'a, a woman of the Kharlas clan, an offshoot of the Khongirad. Khabul Khan took Khongirad wives, and Yesugei, the father of Genghis Khan, obtained his Onggirat wife by stealing her from another man. Under the Yuan dynasty the tribe held the title Prince of Lu, built Yingchang city in present-day Inner Mongolia in 1271, and used its place behind the throne to press the Golden Horde into peace with Kublai in the 1280s and Tokhta Khan into accepting the Great Khan's supremacy in 1304.

After the death of Toghan Temur, the last Yuan emperor, a body of Khongirat and Olkhunut surrendered to the Ming dynasty in 1371. In the west, the Sufi dynasty of Khwarazm ruled under the Jochids and Timur until Timur subjected it. In the Khanate of Khiva, Qongirat inaks became the real rulers in the 18th century, and their descendants took the title of khan in 1804.

Khiva's last khan, Sayid Abdullah, abdicated on 2 February 1920, and its territory was incorporated into the Soviet Union in 1924. Descendants of the Khongirad live among the people of Mongolia and the Yugurs of Gansu, and a few among the Karakalpaks and the Uzbegs. The Qoñyrat tribe of the Kazakh Middle Juz, who around the beginning of the 20th century lived mainly near the city of Turkistan, are considered their descendants.
khopesh: The word khopesh may derive from the Egyptian word for 'leg', as in a leg of beef, because the two share a shape; the hieroglyph for leg is found as early as the time of the Coffin Texts. On the Rosetta Stone of 196 BCE the word appears with a sword determinative, in a passage describing a royal sword of victory to be given to a statue of Ptolemy. The weapon itself evolved from the epsilon and other crescent-shaped axes used in warfare, and also from crescent-shaped swords that came with settlers to the delta region from Western Asia.

A typical khopesh is 50–60 cm long, though smaller examples exist. The blade is sharpened only on the outer edge of its curved end. The inner curve could be used to trap an opponent's arm or to pull a shield out of the way. In the New Kingdom the blades changed from bronze to iron. Some examples have clearly sharpened edges, but many have dull ones that were apparently never meant to cut, and such examples found in high-status graves may have been ceremonial variants.

The khopesh did not originate in Egypt. It was introduced during the Second Intermediate Period, when the Hyksos, who most likely came from the Levant, ruled Lower Egypt and brought composite bows, chariots and curved swords that were precursors of the weapon. Its use was at its height in the New Kingdom, a time of warfare and imperial conquest, when soldiers carried it with axes, spears, maces, daggers, bows and chariots.

Kings are often shown with the khopesh as a symbol of power and conquest. An ostracon of the reign of Ramesses IV shows him smiting enemies with one. A relief on the Hypostyle Hall at Karnack shows Seti I trampling Libyans with a raised khopesh, and the Merneptah Stele shows the god Amun giving the weapon to Merneptah after his victory over the Libyans. A bronze khopesh found in Palestine bears an engraving of Ramesses II, and two ornately carved ones with dull edges were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun.
khor-fakkan: Khor Fakkan, Arabic Khawr Fakkan, means 'Creek of the Two Jaws', a name given for its position on a crescent-shaped bay flanked by two headlands. The city is an exclave of the Emirate of Sharjah on the east coast of the United Arab Emirates, facing the Gulf of Oman and surrounded by the Emirate of Fujairah. After Fujairah City it is the second largest city on that coast. It lies between the Shumayliyah, or Western Hajar, mountains and the sea, with Jebel al Hilqah rising to 1,023 metres. The bay faces north-east and is protected from the prevailing winds by a jetty serving the container terminal.

Settlement is old. Post holes from the wooden uprights of barasti huts resemble those at Tell Abraq, which date from the 3rd to the 1st millennium BCE, and excavators from the Sharjah Archaeological Museum identified 34 graves and a settlement of the early to mid 2nd millennium BCE on rock outcrops above the harbour. Around 1500 Duarte Barbosa described a village with plentiful gardens and farms.

In the 16th century the Portuguese commander Afonso de Albuquerque captured it and called it Corfacão; it was one of a series of fortified places, with Muscat, Sohar and Hormuz, by which the Portuguese controlled access to the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. A walled belt closed the gorge to the interior, with a single door defended by a tower, to guard against tribal attacks.

The Portuguese fort was a ruin by 1666, when the log of the Dutch vessel Meerkat described about 200 small houses of date branches, date palms, fig trees, melons and several wells of fresh water. An Omani invasion of 1623 under Sheikh Muhammad Suhari is one suggested reason for the ruin. In 1737 the Persians invaded with some 5,000 men and 1,580 horses, helped by the Dutch. In 1765 Carsten Niebuhr found Khor Fakkan belonged to a sheikh of the Al Qasimi, the ruling family of Sharjah. Around the turn of the 19th century, Lorimer notes, it had about 5,000 date trees and some 150 houses with about 800 people, who lived by cultivation and pearling.

The Khor Fakkan Container Terminal, inaugurated in 1979, is the only natural deep-sea port in the region and one of the major container ports of the United Arab Emirates. Its project cost Dh 300 million, reclaimed about 150,000 square metres and built quays 16 metres deep for vessels over 400 metres long. The city also draws domestic tourists to its white sand beaches and coral reefs, and the German submarine U-533, sunk off the coast on 16 October 1943, was found by divers in 2009 at a depth of 108 metres.
khorasan: The extent of Khorasan varied over time. In its stricter sense it comprised most of Afghanistan, the present territories of north-eastern Iran and the south of Central Asia as far as the Amu Darya (Oxus), but the name was often used loosely for a wider region including Transoxiana, with Bukhara and Samarqand. The Persian name means 'where the sun arrives from', and it was given to the eastern province of Persia under the Sasanian Empire. The province was often divided into four quarters, centred on Nishapur in the west, Merv in the north, Herat in the centre and Balkh in the east.

The Sasanians established Khorasan as an administrative division in the 6th century, under Kavad I or Khosrow I. After the Arab conquest in the middle of the 7th century it became a province of the Umayyad Caliphate, with military installations at Nishapur and Merv, and Arab armies advanced from it into Transoxiana, where they fought the Turgesh and Khazars. Khorasan was the headquarters of the Abbasid Revolution against the Umayyads, led between 747 and 750 by Abu Muslim, who belonged to the province.

In 821 Tahir founded the first dynasty there independent of Arab rule. Later rulers included the Saffarids, the Samanids of Bukhara, the Ghaznavids, the Seljuqs, the Khwarezmids, the Ghurids and the Timurids, who held it from 1370 to 1506. In 1221 Tolui, a son of Genghis Khan, led the Mongol subjugation of Khorasan, with a thoroughness from which, in one historian's phrase, the region never recovered.

From the early 16th to the early 18th century the Safavids and the Uzbeks contested parts of it. In 1729 Nader Shah recaptured it from the Hotaki dynasty and made Mashhad the capital of Persia. After his assassination in 1747 its eastern parts, including Herat, passed to the Durrani Empire, and the Qajar dynasty took Mashhad in 1796. By the Treaty of Akhal in 1881 Iran gave up its claim to the northern part, mainly Merv, to the Russian Empire.

Khorasan has no political existence as a single region now. The name remains important to many Tajiks of Central Asia, who regard it as part of their national identity. The literary New Persian language developed in Khorasan and Transoxiana, and until the Mongol invasion of the 13th century the region remained the cultural capital of Persia, producing scholars such as Avicenna, Al-Farabi, Al-Biruni, Omar Khayyam and Al-Khwarizmi.
khorat-plateau: The Khorat Plateau takes its name from the short form of Nakhon Ratchasima, historically a barrier controlling access to the area. It averages about 200 metres in elevation and covers about 155,000 square kilometres. Saucer-shaped, it is divided by the Phu Phan Mountains into the northern Sakhon Nakhon Basin and the southern Khorat Basin, and it tilts from about 213 metres in the northwest to about 62 metres in the southeast. The Mun and Chi rivers drain it into the Mekong, which forms its northeastern boundary. The Phetchabun, Dong Phaya Yen, Sankamphaeng and Dângrêk ranges separate it from central Thailand and historically made access difficult.

These mountains catch much of the rain, so the southwest monsoon is weaker here than elsewhere: Nakhon Ratchasima receives about 1,150 millimetres a year, against about 1,500 in central Thailand. The gap between dry and wet seasons is wide, which makes the land less suitable for rice, and the part called Tung Kula Rong Hai was once exceptionally arid.

Many prehistoric sites lie on the plateau, and some bronze relics of the Dong Son culture have been found. The World Heritage site of Ban Chiang, discovered in 1966, yielded evidence of bronze making from about 2000 BCE, without the weaponry often linked with the Bronze Age elsewhere. It was abandoned about 200 CE and not resettled until the early 19th century. Non Nok Tha in Khon Kaen yielded an Iron Age settlement dating from about 1420 to 50 BCE.

The region was once under the suzerainty of the Dvaravati Kingdom and later of the Khmer Empire, and is dotted with ruins of Khmer rest houses set about 25 kilometres apart along the Khmer highways. They served as hospices and libraries and usually had a baray. After the Post-Angkor period and droughts of the 13th to 15th centuries the plateau seems to have been largely depopulated. In 1718 the first Lao muang in the interior of the plateau was founded at Suwannaphum, in present-day Roi Et Province, by an official serving King Nokasad of Champasak.
khorloogiin-choibalsan: Choibalsan was born on 8 February 1895 near the present-day city of Choibalsan, in Dornod Province. He was the youngest of four children of a poor, unmarried herdswoman named Khorloo, from whom his name Khorloogiin comes as a matronymic. His father was probably a Daur Mongol from Inner Mongolia called Jamsu, though Choibalsan claimed not to know who he was. After the October Revolution of 1917 he was called back from Russia to Khüree, joined the revolutionary Consular Hill group, and went to Irkutsk in 1920 with the group later known as the First Seven. In 1921 he fought with Sükhbaatar's partisans and Red Army forces against Ungern-Sternberg.

Through the 1920s Choibalsan remained in second-tier posts, partly because his drinking and violent temper alienated party leaders. In 1929 and 1930 he was titular head of state and supported the Soviet-backed policies of collectivisation, land expropriation and persecution of the Buddhist faith. In 1936 he became head of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and under Moscow's directive had Prime Minister Genden purged for refusing Stalin's demand to eliminate the Buddhist clergy; Genden was executed in Moscow a year later. On the night of 10 September 1937 the arrest of 65 officials and intellectuals, accused of spying for Japan, began the Great Terror. The first show trial in October 1937 sentenced thirteen of its fourteen accused to death.

In March 1939 Choibalsan had the popular Prime Minister Anandyn Amar arrested, and he took the premiership himself that year. In 1939 Soviet forces under Georgy Zhukov defeated the Japanese at Khalkhin Gol, which helped build his cult of personality. During the Second World War Mongolia supplied the Soviet Union with livestock and raw materials. After the war he pursued a five-year plan from 1948 and the unification of Inner and Outer Mongolia, which Stalin would not back. Arrests and executions continued; in the Port-Arthur affair of 1947, eighty people were arrested and 42 executed.

Choibalsan died of kidney cancer in a Moscow hospital on 26 January 1952, and Yumjaagiin Tsedenbal succeeded him as leader. He was widely mourned as a patriot. Official criticisms in 1956 and 1969, and a Central Committee decision of 1962 to end the harmful consequences of his cult of personality, produced little public discussion. His image in Mongolia today remains mixed.
khorramabad: Khorramabad lies in a valley of the Zagros Mountains, about 100 kilometres east of the Iraqi border. It is the capital of Lorestan province and of Khorramabad County. Its population consists of Lurs and Laks, who speak Luri and Laki, and it is the largest Luri-speaking city in the country. The name is a Persian compound of khorram, flourishing or pleasant, and ābād, a cultivated settlement. The valley holds evidence of Middle to Upper Palaeolithic settlement, and excavations led by Frank Hole at the caves of Yafteh, Kunji and Gar Arjeneh found Baradostian blade industries with radiocarbon dates of 32,000 to 38,000 years ago.

In the Neo-Elamite period the area is widely identified with the highland fortress of Khaydalu, which defended the northern approaches of the Elamite kingdom and was plundered by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in 647 to 646 BCE. Under the Sasanian Empire the city was founded or fortified as Shapurkhwast, meaning Shapur's Desire, by Shapur I or perhaps Shapur II. The central citadel, later called Falak-ol-Aflak, was built on a rocky outcrop with thick ramparts and a water well cut 50 metres into bedrock, and the Shapuri Bridge was built across the Khorram-Rud River.

From 1184 Khorramabad was the capital of the atabegs of Little Luristan, who ruled the region until 1596. Mongol and Timurid invasions in the 13th and 14th centuries almost destroyed the town, and the survivors resettled at the foot of the citadel rock. Shah Abbas I ended the atabeg line in 1597 to 1598 by executing Shahverdi Khan and appointed Huseyn Khan Solvizi as the first of the valis of Lorestan, who ruled from Khorramabad. The Ottoman Turks took the city on 6 September 1725 after the Treaty of Constantinople, and it was restored to Persia under Nader Shah. In the 19th century Qajar governors renovated the fortress and gave it the name Falak-ol-Aflak, meaning Sky of Skies.

Khorramabad is still the capital of Lorestan province. Its monuments include the Sasanian Shapuri Bridge, a brick minaret of the Seljuk and Buyid eras in the old city of Shapur Khast, and the archaeological site of Masur Tepe, with layers from the Neolithic to the Islamic periods. Five Palaeolithic cave-dwelling sites near the city were recognised as World Heritage Sites by UNESCO in 2025.
khorramshahr: Khorramshahr is an inland port city in the Central District of Khorramshahr County in Khuzestan province, and is the capital of both the county and the district. It lies about 10 km north of Abadan, on the right bank of the Shatt al-Arab near its meeting with the Haffar arm of the Karun river. The land was once under the waters of the Persian Gulf and later became marshland and tidal flats at the mouth of the Karun.

A small town called Piyan, later Bayan, appeared in the area in the late Parthian period, in the first century CE, though whether it stood on the site of Khorramshahr is highly debatable. In the Islamic centuries the Buwayhid king Panah Khusraw Adud ad-Dawlah ordered a canal dug to join the Karun, which then reached the Persian Gulf separately through the Bahmanshir channel, to the Shatt al-Arab. The extra water made the joint estuary more reliably navigable. The canal was called the Haffar, Arabic for dug out, and became the main channel of the Karun.

The city was the capital of the Sheikdom of Muhammara, ruled by an Arab sheikh. Persia and Turkey alternately claimed and occupied it until 1847, when Article II of the Treaty of Erzurum made it Persian territory.

In the Iran–Iraq War the population fell from 146,706 in the 1976 census to none in 1986. During the first battle of Khorramshahr Iranian propaganda called the city Khuninshahr, the City of Blood, because of the heavy casualties.

Khorramshahr was rebuilt after the war. Its population was 34,750 in 1991 and 123,866 in 2006, and the census of 2016 counted 133,097, close to the figure before the war. The city is home to a Mandaean community, and the Khorramshahr dialect of Neo-Mandaic, spoken by only a few hundred people, survives there; it is one of the last places in the world where Neo-Mandaic is spoken.
khosrow-i: Khosrow was reportedly born between 512 and 514 at Ardestan, in central Iran. He was the youngest son of Kavad I, and his mother was an Ispahbudhan princess, a sister of the general Bawi. About 520 Kavad, wishing to secure the succession against rival brothers and the Mazdakite sect, proposed that Emperor Justin I adopt Khosrow, but the negotiations failed, and Khosrow reportedly felt insulted. Kavad had used the teaching of Mazdak to weaken the nobility and clergy, and in the 520s he withdrew his support from the Mazdakites.

Kavad died in 531 while the Iranian army was besieging Martyropolis, and Khosrow succeeded him. In 532 he signed the Perpetual Peace with Emperor Justinian I, who paid 11,000 pounds of gold. He then dealt with rivals. His elder brother Kawus, a Mazdakite sympathiser, claimed the throne and was defeated, and Khosrow had him killed when he refused to ask forgiveness.

He continued his father's reforms. The great families had owned most of the land and been exempt from tax, and Khosrow centralized the government and strengthened its finances. He created a class of small landowners, the dehqans, who were counted as lower nobility, paid by the central government and used in the administration and the cavalry, so that the army no longer depended on the levies of great lords.

In 540 he broke the peace, sacked Antioch and deported its people to Persia. In 541 he invaded Lazica, beginning the Lazic War, and a fifty-year peace was signed in 562. In the east he allied with the Göktürks and ended the Hephthalite Empire, and Iranian forces under Wahrez defeated the Aksumites in Yemen. After Justin II broke the peace in 572, Khosrow captured the fortress of Dara the following year, and the war lasted until 591. According to Middle Persian sources he ordered the Great Wall of Gorgan, and he had the Derbent Wall fortified.

When Khosrow died in 579 the empire reached from Yemen to Gandhara, its widest extent since Shapur II, and his son Hormizd IV succeeded him. The great families soon recovered the power he had taken from them. The epithet Anushirvan, 'the Immortal Soul', was given after his death to distinguish him from Khosrow II. Later tradition remembered him as a philosopher king and credited him with expanding the Academy of Gondishapur, although the Byzantine historian Agathias thought his philosophical knowledge superficial. Islamic-era works such as al-Tabari's history and Ferdowsi's Shahnameh give much information on his reforms.
khosrow-ii: Khosrow II was born about 570, the son of Hormizd IV and an unnamed noblewoman of the House of Ispahbudhan, one of the Seven Great Houses of Iran. Her brothers Vinduyih and Vistahm strongly influenced his early life. His grandfather was Khosrow I, and before his accession he served as governor of Arbela in Upper Mesopotamia and was also at Partaw, the capital of Caucasian Albania, where he is said to have turned the Kingdom of Iberia into a Sasanian province.

In 590 Hormizd IV disgraced and dismissed his general Bahram Chobin, who rebelled and took Ctesiphon, declaring himself king of kings. Khosrow fled with his uncles, his wives and thirty nobles to Byzantine territory. In 591, with the support of the Byzantine emperor Maurice, he invaded Mesopotamia, and he was proclaimed king again at Mardin in February. He showed tolerance toward his Christian subjects; his wife Shirin, a Christian from Khuzestan, had a church and monastery built near the palace at Ctesiphon. He later put his uncle Vinduyih to death, and in 600 he executed the Lakhmid king Al-Nu'man III, ending the Lakhmid buffer state.

When Maurice was murdered by Phocas in 602, Khosrow began a war on the Byzantines, ostensibly to avenge him. Sasanian forces took Dara and Edessa in 605, plundered Syria and Asia Minor and in 608 advanced into Chalcedon. Heraclius took the field in 622 and in 624 advanced into northern Adurbadagan, sacking cities and temples. After the capture of Dastagird, noble families and generals backed Khosrow's son Sheroe, who seized Ctesiphon on the night of 25 February and imprisoned his father.

Sheroe took the dynastic name Kavad II, and Khosrow was killed. A civil war and interregnum followed. Khosrow's reign is regarded as a golden age of music, with the court musician Barbad, and he restored the erection of rock reliefs after nearly three centuries; the relief at Taq-e Bostan, left unfinished, shows his investiture by Ahura Mazda and Anahita. He restored the title King of Kings to his coins. Persian poets later made him a hero, as in Nizami Ganjavi's Khosrow and Shirin.
khotyn: Khotyn stands on cliffs above the right bank of the Dniester, in the historical region of Bessarabia. A Kievan town of some twenty hectares stood there, and the place later belonged to the Principality of Halych and Halych-Volhynia. Its river crossing made it an important trading centre, and a Genoese trading colony existed there by the 13th century. It was first mentioned in 1310 as the residence of a Catholic bishop, and the Kingdom of Poland held it in the first half of the 14th century. Lithuania conquered the area in 1351 and gave it to the Romanians, who formed Moldavia in 1359.

The present fortress was built after 1400 by the Moldavian ruler Alexander the Good with the help of Vytautas the Great of Lithuania. Poland occupied it after 1433, and Stephen the Great of Moldavia retook it in 1459 after a two-year siege. Strengthened by Stephen, it became the strongest fortress on Moldavia's northern border. As Moldavia weakened, the Ottoman Empire sought the crossing, and the town's later history was dominated by wars between the Ottomans and the expanding Christian powers, first Poland and then Russia.

In the first Battle of Khotyn in 1621 the sultan Osman II advanced towards the Polish frontier. The commander Jan Karol Chodkiewicz entrenched in the fortress with about 35,000 soldiers, helped by 40,000 Ukrainian Cossack forces under Petro Konashevych, and held the sultan off for a month until autumn snow forced him to withdraw. Chodkiewicz died of exhaustion in the fortress on 24 September 1621. In the second battle, on 11 November 1673, forces under Jan Sobieski defeated the Ottomans, a victory seen as a prelude to the Battle of Vienna of 1683.

The Ottomans took the fortress from Moldavia in 1713 and held it until 1812. Russian forces took it four times, in 1739, 1769, 1788 and 1807. The capture of 1739 is remembered through Mikhail Lomonosov's Ode on the Taking of Khotyn from the Turks. The Treaty of Bucharest in 1812 annexed Bessarabia to the Russian Empire, and Khotyn was the seat of Hotin County until 1918.

Khotyn is a town in Chernivtsi Oblast of western Ukraine, with 11,124 inhabitants at the 2001 census. It was part of Romania in 1918-1940 and 1941-1944, and part of the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic from 1940 and 1944 until Ukrainian independence in 1991. The Khotyn Fortress, with the Prince's Palace and clock tower built by Stephen the Great, is its best-known landmark and became a historical-architectural preserve in 2000.
khowar-language: Khowar is the language of the Kho people. Its native name means language (wār) of the Kho, and under the British Raj it was known to the English as Chitrali or Qashqari. Among Pashtuns and Badakhshanis it is called Kashkar. It is the lingua franca of Chitral, and is also spoken in the Gupis-Yasin and Ghizer districts of Gilgit-Baltistan and in Upper Swat. Many speakers have moved to Islamabad, Karachi, Lahore and Peshawar, and the Kalash people also speak it as a second language.

Khowar spread through Chitral from the north, from the Mulkhow and Torkhow valleys. According to Georg Morgenstierne its original home was northern Chitral, around Mastuj, and it began to expand into southern Chitral in the early 14th century. It shares many features with neighbouring Iranian languages of Badakhshan, which points to a very early presence in Upper Chitral, although its links with the Gandhari language suggest that it came from further south in the first millennium BCE, possibly through Swat and Dir.

Morgenstierne considered Khowar the most archaic of the Indo-Aryan languages in several respects, retaining much of Sanskrit case inflection and many words in nearly Sanskritic form. Several sounds, such as q, x and ɣ, which in most Indo-Aryan languages occur only in Perso-Arabic loanwords, occur natively in Khowar. A low-rising pitch contrasts with a high-falling one in a small number of word pairs.

Khowar is written in a form of the Urdu alphabet, usually in a calligraphic script. From the late 19th century writers and rulers of the princely state of Chitral worked to spread literacy in the language. Mirza Muhammad Shakur and Prince Tajumal Shah Mohfi first used the Persian alphabet, but it lacked letters for many Khowar sounds. By the early 20th century Sir Nasir ul-Mulk and Mirza Muhammad Ghafran judged Urdu a better fit, and new letters were created. Settling on a standard took decades, into the 1970s, and six letters were added to the 37 of Urdu to make a 43-letter script. Its nouns inflect for animacy, number and case, and have replaced the three genders of Old Indo-Aryan with a classification by animacy.
khoy: Khoy is the capital of Khoy County in West Azerbaijan province, north of Urmia and 807 km north-west of Tehran. It was named in ancient times for the salt mines that made it an important spur of the Silk Route. A city is said to have stood on the site 3,000 years ago, though the name Khoy came into use only in the 14th century. The region's economy rests on agriculture, especially fruit, grain and timber. Most of the population are Azerbaijanis, with Kurds, largely Sunni and of the Shakkak and Jalali tribes, at its western edge.

In 714 BCE Sargon II passed through the region in a campaign against Urartu. Under Greater Armenia the city belonged to the Nor-Shirakan province. In Parthian times Khoy was the north-western gateway of the Parthian Empire, and under King Tigranes the Great of Armenia it was an important settlement of the Silk Route. About 37 BCE Mark Antony crossed the plain between Khoy and Marand in one of the Roman-Parthian wars. Armenian documents date the church of Surp Sarkis to 332 or 333 CE, and Armenians have long made up a significant part of the population.
Anania Shirakatsi called the place Her in the 8th century. In 1021-2 the Byzantine emperor Basil II led his army as far as Khoy and received the surrender of the royal Artsruni dynasty of Van.

In 1210 forces of the Kingdom of Georgia sent by Tamar the Great under Zakaria and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli conquered the city, in answer to the sack of Ani in 1208, and in the late 1220s Jalal al-Din Mangburni took it. The Ottomans took Khoy on 6 May 1724, after the fall of the Safavids, a gain confirmed with Russia by the Treaty of Constantinople. After the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 most Armenians moved north of the Aras river into Russian territory. Ottoman and Russian troops held the city in the 1910s, and Soviet troops remained until 1946.

Khoy had a population of 198,845 at the 2016 census. It is known for the tomb of Shams Tabrizi, the poet and mystic. Its other sights include Bastam and Bolourabad castles, the Khatoon Bridge, the Old Stone Gate, the old bazaar, the Motallebkhan Mosque and the Surp Sarkis Church.
khudayar-khan: Sayid Muhammad Khudayar Khan was an Uzbek, the son of Shir Ali Khan of Kokand. When his father was killed in an uprising in 1845, Khudayar was in Namangan and survived. Murad Beg Khan was proclaimed khan for a short time, but the supporters of Shir Ali overthrew and later executed him as a puppet of the Emir of Bukhara. The military commander Mingbashi Musulmonqul then declared his son-in-law Khudayar khan, and through the 1840s the young ruler was kept in the palace while the Kipchak nomad elite held power.

In 1853 an uprising against the Kipchaks killed many of them, Musulmonqul among them, and Khudayar ruled in his own right on an anti-Kipchak, pro-Uzbek course. When the northern provinces rebelled in 1858, his brother Malla Bek, sent to put them down, joined the rebels, took Kokand with the help of the Kipchak warlord Alimqul and made himself khan. After Malla Bek was assassinated in 1862, Khudayar, allied with Kanaat, ruler of Tashkent, and helped by an advance of Emir Muzaffar of Bukhara, returned to Kokand, but in 1863 Alimqul set up Muhammad Sultan Khan as khan and took Kokand and Tashkent.

Alimqul was killed opposing the Russians at Tashkent in 1865, and Khudayar entered Kokand without resistance. In 1868 he formally accepted the sovereignty of the Russian Empire. His rule was marked by very high taxes and a failing legal system, and a plot of 1870 to replace him with Seyid Khan, son of Malla Khan, ended in many executions.

Driven out by the uprising of 1875, Khudayar was sent by the Russians to Orenburg. Two years later he fled to Herat; with money from sympathetic Kokand merchants he travelled by Peshawar and Bombay to Mecca and wandered through Arabia before settling, in the early 1880s, in the village of Karukh, east of Herat. He died there in poverty in 1886 and is buried there. On his orders his officer Niaz-Muhammad ibn Ashur-Muhammad Khoqani wrote the Tarikh-i Shahrukhi, a Persian chronicle of the khanate, and his palace remains a landmark of Kokand.
khufu: Khufu was the second pharaoh of the Fourth Dynasty, in the early Old Kingdom. His name, Khnum-khufu, means Khnum protects me and was dedicated to the creator god Khnum. Egyptologists believe that Sneferu was his father, but only because later historians handed down that the eldest son or a chosen descendant inherited the throne. The tomb of queen Hetepheres I, found in 1925 east of Khufu's pyramid, gives her the title mother of a king beside the name of Sneferu. Some doubt that she was Sneferu's wife, since she is not known to have borne the title king's wife.

Khufu's family was large. His wives were Meritites I and Henutsen, and his sons included Kawab, most likely the eldest and crown prince, who died before him, then Djedefre, who became the first successor, and Khafre, who probably followed.

It is unclear how long Khufu ruled. Inscriptions from his last years suggest that he was approaching his 30-year jubilee but may have just missed it. A rock inscription at the Dakhla Oasis dates to his twenty-seventh year, and papyrus fragments known as the Diary of Merer, found at his harbour at Wadi al-Jarf, log the transport of limestone from Tura to the Great Pyramid in the year after the thirteenth cattle count. Few other details of his political activity are recorded. His name appears in inscriptions at Elkab and Elephantine and in the quarries of Hatnub and Wadi Hammamat.

He built his pyramid complex on the north-eastern part of the plateau of Giza, at the high end of a natural plateau so that it would be widely visible, and named it Akhet-Khufu, horizon of Khufu. Sediment cores suggest that a harbour connected to the Nile worked at Giza in his time and that it carried stones and supplies for the complex.

The latest known date of his reign comes from his funeral. Graffiti in a rock-cut pit beside the Great Pyramid record the 28th or 29th year. The only almost completely preserved image of Khufu is a small ivory figurine, found by Flinders Petrie at Abydos in 1903, whose head was recovered three weeks after the body.

His mortuary cult was extensive in the Old Kingdom, with at least 67 attested priests by the end of the Sixth Dynasty, and it was reorganised in the New Kingdom. The Greek historian Herodotus depicts him as a cruel tyrant who closed the temples and forced the Egyptians to work for him. Modern Egyptologists point to the town of Menat-Khufu, nurse of Khufu, and to the long-lasting cult as evidence that Egyptians themselves held a positive view for centuries.
khujand: Khujand, also spelled Khodjent, is the second-largest city of Tajikistan and the capital of its northernmost province, Sughd. It stands on the Syr Darya river at the mouth of the Fergana Valley and was a major city on the ancient Silk Road. It is one of the oldest cities in Central Asia, dating back about 2,500 years to the Persian Empire. Its fortress, built over 2,500 years ago, has been destroyed and renovated several times.

Khujand may have been the site of Cyropolis, said to have been founded by Cyrus the Great on his last expedition against the Massagetae shortly before his death. In 329 BCE Alexander the Great built his furthest Greek settlement near Cyropolis and named it Alexandria Eschate, Alexandria the Furthest. It served as a bastion for Greek settlers against the nomadic Scythian tribes north of the Syr Darya. According to the Roman writer Curtius, it kept its Hellenistic culture as late as 30 BCE.

In the early eighth century the forces of the Umayyad Caliphate under Qutayba ibn Muslim captured the city, and a process of Islamicization began. It passed under the Samanid Empire in the late ninth century and the Kara-Khanid Khanate in 999. The Karakhitans conquered it in 1137, and it passed to the Khwarazmshahs in 1211. In 1220 it strongly resisted the Mongol hordes and was laid waste. It was part of the Chagatai Khanate in the 14th century and then of the Timurid dynasty, under which it flourished greatly. The Shaybanid dynasty of Bukhara annexed it, and the Kokand Khanate took it in 1802. Bukhara regained it in 1842 and lost it a few decades later to Russia.

In 1866 the city became part of the Russian General Governorate of Turkestan. Threats of forced conscription in World War I led to protests in July 1916 that turned violent when demonstrators attacked Russian soldiers. In 1929 the Soviets transferred Khujand and the surrounding area, inhabited mainly by ethnic Tajiks, from the Uzbek SSR to the new Tajik SSR. The city was renamed Leninabad on 10 January 1936 and regained its original name in 1992.

Most of the people of Khujand are ethnic Tajiks, and Sunni Islam is the main religion. The Historical Museum of Sughd is housed inside the Khujand Fortress, and the Sheikh Muslihiddin mausoleum stands on the main square opposite the Panjshanbe Market, one of the largest covered markets in Central Asia. The city also has monuments of the 16th and 17th centuries.
khumarawayh: Abu 'l-Jaysh Khumarawayh was born at Samarra in 864. His father, Ahmad ibn Tulun, the son of a Turkish slave-soldier, became governor of Egypt in 868, took direct control of its revenue in 871 and used it to build his own army of slave soldiers, the ghilmān. Exploiting the rift between Caliph al-Mu'tamid and his brother al-Muwaffaq, he extended his rule over Syria, the Byzantine frontier zone and parts of the Jazira. In 882, after the failed rebellion of his elder brother Abbas, Khumarawayh was named his father's deputy in Egypt and heir.

His succession in May 884 was, in the view of the historian Thierry Bianquis, the first time a governor of so large a territory was openly succeeded by an amir claiming legitimacy by inheritance. The Abbasids attacked his lands in Syria, and al-Muwaffaq's son Abu'l-Abbas, the future al-Mu'tadid, took charge of the invasion; at the Battle of Tawahin Khumarawayh first fled, but his general Sa'd al-Aysar routed the Abbasid prince. He then suppressed al-Aysar's revolt in Damascus and treated the prisoners with clemency, which led to the agreement of December 886. Between 886 and 890 he received the submission of the Jazira, and the governor of Tarsus accepted his overlordship.

When al-Mu'tadid became caliph in 892, the pact was renewed in 893 for an annual tribute of 300,000 dinars and the return of Diyar Rabi'a and Diyar Mudar. At home Khumarawayh built palaces, kept a blue-eyed lion and was rocked to sleep on a basin of quicksilver; he was also a patron of scholars and poets. Unable to command the army as his father had, he bought its loyalty with rich gifts, and by his death the treasury, said to have held ten million gold dinars at his accession, was empty and the dinar had lost two-thirds of its value.

A servant who had been having an affair with Khumarawayh's favourite wife organised a conspiracy and had him killed on 18 January 896. His son Jaysh was deposed and killed in November in favour of his younger brother Harun. Al-Mu'tadid took back the Thughūr and Syria north of Homs, and in 904–905 the caliph al-Muktafi reconquered Egypt. The lavish wedding of Qatr al-Nada remained the stuff of folk legend in Egypt into the Ottoman period.
khurshid-of-tabaristan: Khurshid was born in 734 or 735, the son of Dadhburzmihr and grandson of Farrukhan the Great, the first Dabuyid ruler from whose reign coins are known. By the traditional account the Dabuyids had made themselves autonomous rulers of Tabaristan in the 640s, during the Muslim conquest of Persia, paying only tribute to the caliphate and relying on their country's rough terrain. The historian P. Pourshariati holds instead that Farrukhan founded the family's rule in the 670s. Earlier scholars, misreading the coins, called him Khurshid II.

Khurshid succeeded his father at the age of six, and his uncle Farrukhan-i Kuchak ruled as regent for eight years. When Khurshid came of age, Farrukhan's sons tried to seize the throne; a slave girl, Varmja Haraviya, is said to have betrayed their plot, and with the help of his cousin Jushnas's sons Khurshid imprisoned them and later married her. The historian Ibn Isfandiyar describes a prosperous Tabaristan producing silk and other textiles and trading with the Turks, and Khurshid is said to have built many bazaars and caravanserais. During the Third Fitna he rebelled against Caliph Marwan II and in 746 sent an embassy to the Tang court, which recognised him as a vassal prince.

Forced to submit to Abu Muslim in the Abbasid Revolution, he backed the rebellion of Sunbadh after Abu Muslim's murder in 755. Sunbadh was killed in Tabaristan by one of Khurshid's cousins, possibly at Khurshid's prompting, in the hope of gaining Abu Muslim's treasure. Caliph al-Mansur pressed him to give it up and raised the annual tribute to the level once paid to the Sassanids.

After the generals Abu al-Khaṣīb Marzuq and Khazim bin Khuzaymah took the fortress of al-Tak, Khurshid's family was carried to Baghdad. His daughters became concubines of the Abbasids, one of them of al-Mansur himself. Tabaristan became a province ruled from Amul, though the Bavandids, Karinids and Zarmihrids kept the mountains as tributaries. Coins bore Khurshid's name until 764, which is why some works date his death to 767.
khusrau-khan: According to the Delhi chronicler Amir Khusrau, Khusrau Khan and his brother belonged to the Baradu, a name also given as Barau, Barvari or Parvar; some writers identify the group with the Bharwad, or shepherds. Captured when the Delhi forces under Ayn al-Mulk Multani conquered Malwa, the brothers were named Hasan and Husamuddin in Delhi and brought up by Malik Shadi, an officer of Alauddin Khalji. Mubarak Shah fell in love with Hasan, and the chroniclers describe their relationship as open and public; the chronicler Barani wrote that the sultan did not want to be parted from him for a moment.

Mubarak Shah gave him the former fief of Malik Kafur and within a year made him vazir. In 1317, after the Yadavas of Devagiri had asserted their independence, Khusrau Khan and Malik Qutlugh routed the army of the Yadava minister Raghava, and a force he sent after Harapaladeva captured the Yadava ruler, who was beheaded. In 1318 he besieged Warangal with Malik Qutlugh and Khwaja Haji until Prataparudra surrendered.

Barani writes that Khusrau Khan resented the sultan's use of him and planned revenge. He won leave to raise an army of Baradus, which the Tughluq Nama numbers at 10,000 horsemen, and had hundreds of them admitted to the palace each night. On the night of 9 July 1320 they killed the sultan's teacher Qazi Ziyauddin, and the Baradu leader Jaharya beheaded Mubarak Shah. Two young sons of Alauddin were killed and three others blinded.

By sunrise the nobles in the palace had accepted him as Sultan Nasiruddin, and he married Mubarak Shah's widow. Many of Alauddin's officers kept their posts, while the Baradus received titles, grants and commands. Barani presents the reign as a Hindu bid for power, with idols worshipped in the palace; the historians Mohammad Habib and Kishori Saran Lal reject this, noting that the khutba was read and coins struck in his name. Ghazi Malik, governor of Dipalpur, rose against him, joined by his son Fakhruddin Jauna. Khusrau Khan had the three blinded princes killed, lost the Battle of Saraswati and the Battle of Lahrawat, and fled, but was captured and killed.
khusrau-shah: Khusrau Shah was born in 1121, the eldest and only surviving son of Bahram Shah. He grew up while the Ghaznavid state was at its weakest, worn down by civil wars, a tributary pact with the Seljuk Empire and struggles with the Ghurids. His father's attempt to recover lost lands in India was stopped by Vigraharaja IV of the Chahamana dynasty, and Bahram Shah was defeated by Ghurid rulers, among them Ala al-Din Husayn, who burned Ghazni for seven days. Bahram Shah retook Ghazni from the Ghurids and died in 1157.
Little is known of the young prince beyond a few poems by Hassan Ghaznavi. It seems that he was held as a hostage at the court of the Seljuk ruler Ahmad Sanjar.

Soon after Khusrau Shah became sultan in 1157, Ala al-Din Husayn began a new campaign. The chronicler Minhaj-i-Siraj wrote that the Ghurid had already taken the Ghaznavid lands of south-eastern Afghanistan, including Zamindawar, though the historian Bosworth suggested this may anticipate what happened later. Fakhr-i Mudabbir recorded a battle in which Khusrau Shah was defeated. According to O'Neal, the sultan rebuilt his army and marched west to take the western lands of the Ghurids, but was defeated again by Ala al-Din's army at Herat and had to agree to a pact that gave those lands to the Ghurids.

Little is known of the rest of his reign. The few surviving coins of Khusrau Shah still name Ahmad Sanjar as his overlord, though Sanjar died in 1157, probably because news of his death had not yet reached Ghazni.
khutba: The khutbah (Arabic khuṭba, Persian khotbeh, Turkish hutbe) is the primary formal occasion for public preaching in the Islamic tradition, and the person who gives it is the khatib. It originates in the practice of the Prophet Muhammad, who delivered words of exhortation, instruction or command at gatherings for worship in the mosque, which at Medina was the courtyard of his house. After the conquest of Mecca he presented himself as khatib to the city in 630 CE.

The first four caliphs, the Umayyad caliphs and the provincial governors all delivered sermons. These were not necessarily exhortatory but dealt with practical questions of government and sometimes included direct orders. Under the Abbasids the caliph no longer preached himself but assigned the task to the religious judges, and the Abbasids insisted that they were clearing Islam of the secularism of the Umayyads, which probably strengthened the religious side of the sermon.

Such sermons are prescribed by all legal schools for the Friday congregational prayer, and similar ones are called for on the two festival days, after eclipse prayers and after the rain prayer. The Friday service must be preceded by two sermons, delivered with a pause in between during which the khatib sits. The khatib must pronounce praise of God, invocations of blessing on Muhammad, a recitation from the Quran, admonitions to piety and a prayer for the faithful.

Sermons were traditionally delivered in classical Arabic, and the four Sunni schools of jurisprudence require this. The need for trained preachers contributed to a literary genre of model sermons, such as those of Ibn Nubata, who died in 984. The minimum congregation differs by school: 40 in the Hanbali and Shafi'i schools, three besides the imam in the Hanafi school and 12 local residents in the Maliki school.

In the pre-Islamic Middle East the naming of a ruler in the sermon did not exist; Islam introduced it. In the pre-modern Middle East, mention of a ruler's name in the sermon was one of the two prerogatives of sovereignty, the other being the right to mint coins. Mentioning a ruler meant accepting his sovereignty and suzerainty, and omitting his name was like publicly declaring independence. The sermon was also a main vehicle of communication, announcing the deposition or accession of a ruler, the naming of an heir, and the beginning and end of a war.

Under Mughal rule the sovereign's name was likewise declared, and Babur was styled Zahir-ud-Din Bábar Muhammad in Friday sermons. Sher Khan, an adversary of the emperor Humayun, was content to be given Bengal if the emperor kept the right to mint coins and have the khutbah proclaimed in his name, which would make Sher Khan the emperor's vassal.
khuzestan: Khuzestan is an extension of the Mesopotamian Plain in the south-west of Iran, bordering Iraq and the Persian Gulf, and covers 64,055 square kilometres. Its capital is Ahvaz; the provincial capital was moved there from Shoushtar in 1924. Greek and Roman sources, from the Achaemenid period until the early centuries CE, called the land Susiana, after the city of Susa, once a capital of ancient Elam and one of the Achaemenid imperial capitals. The Achaemenids themselves called the satrapy Ūja or Uvja. Under the Parthians and Sasanians Susiana fell out of use, and in the Middle Persian period the name Khuzistan, from the root hūz, replaced it.

Khuzestan was one of the centres of ancient civilisation and one of the most important regions of the Ancient Near East, based around Susa. The Elamites, whose language was neither Semitic nor Indo-European, ruled the first large empire here, in the 4th millennium BCE, and archaeological ruins show the entire province to have been Elamite. The Sasanians took control in 224 after the Parthians were defeated at the Battle of Hormozdgan. Under Shapur II (reigned 309 or 310 to 379) Arabs crossed the Persian Gulf and raided Fars; he led an expedition through Bahrain, defeated the combined forces of three Arab tribes and resettled them in Kerman and Ahvaz.

In 639 the Rashidun Caliphate's forces under Abu Musa al-Ash'ari defeated the Sasanians at Ahvaz and drove out the satrap Hormuzan. Hormuzan fled to Shushtar, which the Muslims besieged for 18 months until it fell in 642. Under the Qajar dynasty the western part of the province was known as Arabistan. In the two decades before 1925 the western part, the Emirate of Muhammara, functioned as an effectively autonomous emirate under Sheikh Khazʽal. Reza Shah's government dissolved it in 1925 to centralise the state, and put down the rebellion that followed. Iraq invaded Khuzestan in 1980, and the invasion was reversed at the Battle of Khorramshahr in 1982.

Khuzestan is one of the 31 provinces of Iran. It has a large Arab population and contains Iran's largest oil field. Its ancient sites include Susa, modern Shush, and the Sasanian works of Shushtar, and its capital Ahvaz lies where the Mesopotamian Plain meets the Persian Gulf.
khvarenah: The word, Avestan xvarənah and New Persian farr or farrah, most likely means glory and is probably derived from a root meaning to shine; H. W. Bailey proposed instead a link with a verb meaning to eat or partake. Most Iranian languages have forms with an initial f-, such as Old Persian farnah, while the Avestan and Zoroastrian Middle Persian forms begin with xᵛ-. Sasanian inscriptions wrote it with the Aramaic ideogram GDE.

At first khwarrah appears to have been a tribal concept, with parallels among the societies of the Eurasian steppes, and its tie to the myth of Jamshid suggests it began as an expression of royal authority before it was taken into Zoroastrianism and given a wider religious meaning. No explicit reference to it occurs in Achaemenid royal inscriptions, which speak of the king ruling by the favour of Ohrmazd, though some scholars see it in royal imagery.

Zoroastrian tradition knows it mainly from the Yashts, above all Yasht 19, which treats it as a yazata, a divine being worthy of worship, and lists the gods, heroes and Kayanian kings it accompanied. Its powers reach beyond kingship: it enables gods, people and nature to fulfil their proper functions, and the khwarrah of priests was said to be gained through knowledge and study. In the myth of Jamshid, called Yima in the Avesta, his glory leaves him three times when he departs from the righteous path, taking the form of a falcon, and is hidden by Apam Napat in the waters of Lake Vourukasha.

On Kushan coins it appears as an armed, radiant male god named Pharro. Under the Sasanians, diadems and flying ribbons became signs of divine glory, and in the Paikuli inscription the Shahanshah Narseh and his forefathers are said to have received khwarrah and rulership from the gods. Halos and flames on the shoulders, and birds of prey, also stood for it; whether the winged emblem known as the Farr-e Kiyani represents it is disputed.

The idea of a hereditary royal charisma that could be lost came to be associated with the Greek tychē basileōs and Latin fortuna regia in the traditions of the Seleucid, Arsacid and Kushan rulers. The word passed into Armenian as pʿaṙkʿ and into names of Georgian royalty such as Pharnavaz, and in Buddhist Sogdian and Khotanese it came to mean a Buddha's dignity. After the fall of the Sasanian Empire it survived in the literature and epics of Islamic Persia as farr-e īzadī, the glory God grants a sovereign.
khwarazm: Khwarazm, also called Chorasmia, is a large oasis region on the delta of the Amu Darya in western Central Asia. It is bordered on the north by the former Aral Sea, on the east by the Kyzylkum Desert, on the south by the Karakum Desert and on the west by the Ustyurt Plateau. It is the lowest region in Central Asia apart from the Caspian shore.

Like Sogdia, Khwarazm grew out of the Bactria-Margiana culture of the Bronze Age, which fused with Indo-Iranian migrants around 1000 BCE. By the final Saka phase there were about 400 settlements, ruled by the native Afrighid dynasty. The Achaemenid Empire took control under Darius I, who ruled 522 to 486 BCE. When the king of Khwarazm offered Alexander the Great friendship in 328 BCE, Russian archaeologists of the 20th century showed the region to have been a stable and centralised kingdom of agriculture, protected by mailed horsemen.

Under the Sasanian Empire, which spread as far as Khwarazm under Shapur I, the region was a regional capital. The Afrighids of Kath ruled as shahs of Khwarazm, according to al-Biruni, from 305 to 995. The Arab Caliphate conquered the region in 712, and an Afrighid shah first became Muslim around the end of the 8th century. In 995 the Ma'munids of Gurganj overthrew the Afrighids and took the title Khwarazm-Shah, and Mahmud of Ghazni took the region in 1017.

From 1077 the province was governed by Anushtegin Gharchai, a former Turkic slave of the Seljuq sultan, and his descendants. In 1194 Ala ad-Din Tekish defeated and killed Toghrul III, the last Great Seljuq sultan, and under Ala ad-Din Muhammad the Khwarazmian Empire ruled over all of Persia. From 1218 to 1220 Genghis Khan conquered Central Asia and ended it. The Mongols broke the dams of the Amu Darya at Gurganj and flooded the city, killing, Yaqut reports, four inhabitants for every Mongol soldier. Timur destroyed Urganch in 1388, and in 1511 a local Uzbek dynasty took power, with Khiva becoming the capital of the Khanate of Khiva. A treaty in 1873 made Khiva a quasi-independent Russian protectorate.

After the Bolshevik revolution a Khorezm People's Soviet Republic was created from the old khanate, and in 1924 it was incorporated into the Soviet Union and divided among the Turkmen, Uzbek and Karakalpak republics. Today about two thirds of Khwarazm belongs to Uzbekistan and about a third to Turkmenistan, and many ancient towns lie in Xorazm Region of Uzbekistan. Its population is mixed, of Uzbeks, Karakalpaks, Turkmens, Tajiks, Tatars and Kazakhs.
khwarazmian-empire: The empire was culturally Persianate and Sunni Muslim, of Turkic mamluk origin, and was ruled by the Anushtegin dynasty. Its founder, Anush Tigin Gharachai, was a Turkic commander in the service of the Seljuks and governor of Khwarazm from about 1077 until 1097. Under his son Qutb al-Din Muhammad, who became the first hereditary Khwarazmshah, and then under Ala ad-Din Atsiz, who succeeded in 1127, the province ruled by the dynasty grew. Atsiz maneuvered between the Seljuk sultan Sanjar and the Qara Khitai ruler Yelü Dashi, paying tribute to the latter until his death, and added Jand and Mangyshlak to Khwarazm.

Il-Arslan, who ruled from 1156 to 1172, broke away from Seljuk suzerainty after Sanjar's death, and his son Tekish, ruling from 1172 to 1200, shook off the Qara Khitai as well. In 1194 Tekish defeated the Seljuk sultan Toghrul III in alliance with Caliph al-Nasir, and in 1198 the caliph accepted him as sultan of Iran, Khorasan and Turkestan.

Under Muhammad II the empire reached its maximum expansion. He extinguished the Western Kara-Khanid Khanate in 1213, overcame the Ghurids in 1215, and by late 1217 controlled all of Persian Iraq. The empire is estimated to have spanned 2.3 to 3.6 million square kilometres. It was defended by a cavalry army of about 40,000, mostly Turks, and had perhaps 5 million people on the eve of the Mongol invasion. A diarchy had developed, with Muhammad's mother Turkan Khatun holding great influence, a separate diwan and a separate palace.

In 1219 a Mongol force of 100,000 to 150,000 men, under Genghis Khan, crossed the Jaxartes and sacked Samarqand, Bukhara, Otrar and then the capital Gurganj, after the Shah had executed an envoy and put a merchant party to death. Muhammad fled and died of illness in December 1220 on an island in the Caspian Sea. His son Jalal al-Din Mangburni won a victory at Parwan in 1221 but was defeated at the Indus, and he was murdered in 1231 by Kurdish highwaymen, the last Khwarazmshah.

The Khwarazmshahs adopted Persian culture. Persian was the language of administration, history and poetry, Arabic of science and theology, and Turkic the home language of the dynasty. Mina'i ceramics made at Kashan in these decades are among the best-known products of the period.

After the Mongol conquest many Khwarazmians survived as mercenaries, calling themselves the Khwarazmiyya and raiding the Seljuk lands of Jazira and Syria. Hired by the Ayyubid sultan as-Salih Ayyub, they took Jerusalem on 11 July 1244 and, on 17 October 1244, fought at La Forbie, where about 1,200 knights were killed.
khwarazmshah: The title is of Iranian origin, like other Central Asian titles of the time such as Afshin and Ikhshid. Most of what is known of the first line, the Afrighids, comes from the Khwarazmian scholar al-Biruni, who has Afrig founding the dynasty in 305 in succession to the Siyavushids, a line said to have been founded by the Iranian king Kay Khosrow. Soviet archaeology suggests he knew little of pre-Islamic Khwarazm: coins show the region was part of the Parthian Empire, and the Khwarazmian era seems to have begun in the early 1st century, when local shahs freed themselves from Parthian rule. The name Afrighid itself is attested nowhere else.

The Afrighids were most likely adherents of Zoroastrianism; the first Khwarazmshah to convert to Islam was Azkajwar-Abdallah in the early 9th century, and in the early 10th century the shahs became vassals of the Samanids. The Ma'munids of Gurganj, whose court drew Avicenna, Abu Sahl al-Masihi and al-Tha'alibi, were the last ethnically Iranian line: after a revolt killed Ma'mun II in 1017, Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni invaded and took many Khwarazmians to Ghazni as slaves.

Mahmud gave the title to his Turkic slave commander Altuntash, whose line held it until 1041. Under the Seljuks it was unused until about 1077, when Sultan Malik-Shah I made the ghulam Anushtegin Gharchai governor. From his son Muhammad I, appointed in 1097, came the Anushteginids.
