Atsiz pursued autonomy, Ala al-Din Tekish destroyed the Seljuk Empire and threw off the Qara Khitai, and Muhammad II ended Qarakhanid rule in Transoxiana, yet both were content with the titles of Khwarazmshah and Sultan. Jalal al-Din Mangburni could not hold back the Mongol invasions, and the empire collapsed.

The Mongol governors of Khwarazm and the later Sufi dynasty seem not to have used the title. It was revived under the Timurid Empire, for Shah Malik, governor under Shah Rukh, and his son Nasir al-Din Sultan Ibrahim, and the Uzbek Arabshahid dynasty of Khiva used it informally in literary works. Its last official use was by Eltuzar-Inak, founder of the Qungrat line of the Khans of Khiva, who styled himself Heir of the Khwarazmshahs on coins that were never issued before his death in 1806.
khyan: Khyan's royal name, Seuserenre, means The one whom Re has caused to be strong, and his own name is also written Khayan or Khian. He bore the titles of an Egyptian king but also the title ruler of the foreign land (heqa-khaset), the typical designation of the Hyksos rulers. His name has been interpreted as the Amorite Hayanu, which is recorded in the Assyrian king lists for a remote ancestor of Shamshi-Adad I. The name was therefore in use for centuries before the Fifteenth Dynasty.

Khyan ruled from Avaris, where excavations found a strongly fortified palace, seal impressions with his name and a stela of his eldest son, Prince Yanassi, who was probably his designated successor. The palace stood on a high platform of massive brick casemates, with columned halls and monumental staircases. Manfred Bietak holds that Khyan's rule marked the peak of Hyksos power, with direct rule over Lower and Middle Egypt as far as Cusae and indirect domination of the Nile Valley as far south as Thebes. Alexander Ilin-Tomich disputes this and thinks direct Hyksos rule may have been confined to the eastern Delta.

Khyan is one of the better attested Hyksos kings. Objects with his name were found at Knossos and at Hattusha, which suggests diplomatic contacts with Crete and the Hittites. A sphinx bearing his name was bought on the art market at Baghdad and may point to contact with Babylon. Seal impressions found at Edfu in Upper Egypt lay beside those of the 13th Dynasty king Sobekhotep IV, which led some scholars to think the two reigned at about the same time. Robert Porter rejects this reading.

Khyan is identified with the king Iannas in the works of Josephus, which drew on Manetho. Josephus mentions him after Apophis, so that eighteenth-century scholars placed him late in the dynasty. In the version of Manetho by Sextus Julius Africanus he follows a king Pachnan, perhaps Yaqub-Har, whose scarabs his own resemble, and he is now thought one of the earlier rulers of the dynasty.

His date is uncertain. Nearly all carbon-14 analyses of material from the Second Intermediate Period give dates on average 120 years earlier than the prevailing reconstruction, and Egyptologists have accepted that this shows a major problem with the consensus. Bietak proposed that a great ritual feast and the abandonment of the Avaris palace followed the death of its owner, most probably Khyan; the palace may later have been destroyed in the Theban conquest under Ahmose I.
khyber-pass: The Khyber Pass lies in the Khyber District of the Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, along the border with Afghanistan. It connects the town of Landi Kotal to the Valley of Peshawar at Jamrud, crossing part of the Spin Ghar mountains. The pass proper is about 40 kilometres long, and its summit at Landi Kotal, 1,028 metres high, lies 5 kilometres inside Pakistan. Pashtun clans, particularly the Afridis and the Afghan Shinwari, have regarded it as their own preserve for centuries and have levied a toll on travellers for safe conduct, which was long their main source of income.

Before the Kushan era the pass was not widely used for trade. Armies of the Achaemenid and Sassanid empires crossed it, among them Darius I, Ardashir I and Shapur I, as did nomadic invaders from Central Asia such as the Saka, Yuezhi and White Huns. Indian empires rarely extended their control beyond it, with the Maurya king Chandragupta an exception. Greek influence passed through it into India and Buddhism spread the other way. As part of the Silk Road it carried trade, and Gandhara became a regional centre connecting Bagram in Afghanistan with Taxila in India.

In the Islamic period Mahmud Ghaznavi, Muhammad of Ghor, Timur, Babur and Nader Shah used the Khyber and nearby passes to invade the subcontinent. The Mughals tried to control it but met resistance from local tribes, and Ahmad Shah Durrani was the last major conqueror to cross it. In the 19th century the British East India Company wished to secure the pass against Russia during the Great Game. Sikhs under Ranjit Singh captured it in 1837, and their general Hari Singh Nalwa built Jamrud Fort to guard it. After the Second Anglo-Afghan War ended in 1880 the region came under British control, and the British paid local tribes to keep the route secure.

The British built roads, railways and telegraph lines through the pass. The Khyber Pass Railway, heavily engineered, runs from Jamrud to the Afghan border near Landi Kotal and opened in 1925. During the Second World War concrete dragon's teeth were set on the valley floor out of fear of an invasion of India. A common phrase of the colonial period described British India as stretching from Khyber to Kanyakumari. After the partition of India in 1947 the pass became part of Pakistan. Monuments left by British Indian Army units and hillside forts can still be seen from the road.
ki-hajar-dewantara: Soewardi was a grandson of Prince Paku Alam III through his father, GPH Soerjaningrat. His priyayi background gave him access to colonial education, which most of the population of the Indies could not enter. He finished the Dutch primary school (ELS) and went on to STOVIA, a medical school for native students, but did not graduate because of illness. He then worked as a journalist for many newspapers, including De Expres, Kaoem Moeda and Poesara, with a popular, communicative style full of idealism for freedom and anti-colonial feeling.

He was active in Boedi Oetomo from its founding in 1908 and organised its first congress in Yogyakarta. He also joined Insulinde, which advocated self-rule in the Dutch East Indies, and the Indische Party of Ernest Douwes Dekker. In 1913 the colonial government collected money from the population, indigenous people included, for the centennial of Dutch independence from France.

Soewardi's column "If I were a Dutchman" ("Als ik eens Nederlander was"), printed in De Expres on 13 July 1913, criticised this fiercely. Governor General Alexander Idenburg ordered his arrest and exile to Bangka. After protests by Douwes Dekker and Tjipto Mangoenkoesoemo, the three, later called the Tiga Serangkai, were exiled to the Netherlands instead.

In the Netherlands he took part in the Indische Vereeniging and studied education, drawing on Fröbel, Montessori and the Tagore family's school at Santiniketan. Returning to Java in September 1919, he helped his brother found a school in Yogyakarta, and in July 1922 he established Taman Siswa, which provided education for the native population. He later dropped the title Raden Mas and took the name Ki Hadjar Dewantara. During the Japanese occupation he was a leader of Putera from 1943. In the first cabinet of the Republic of Indonesia he was Minister of Education and Culture.

He died in Yogyakarta on 26 April 1959 and was buried in the Taman Wijaya Brata cemetery. Presidential Decree no. 305 of 1959, dated 28 November 1959, declared him a national hero and made his birthday National Education Day. His maxim Tut Wuri Handayani, which asks those behind to give encouragement, is the motto of the Indonesian Ministry of Education. He held that education should be open to all regardless of sex, race, religion or social status. His portrait appeared on the 20,000 rupiah banknote in 1998, and the Taman Siswa movement runs the Dewantara Kirti Griya Museum in Yogyakarta.
kiche-people: The Kʼicheʼ are one of the main Maya peoples and live mostly in the highlands of Guatemala. Their name means many trees; its Nahuatl translation, Cuauhtēmallān, is the origin of the word Guatemala. After the Classic collapse the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom of Qʼumarkaj arose as an independent state and became one of the most powerful in the region. Scholars widely believe that elite warlords reached the highlands in 1225, after the decline of Chichén Itzá, and mingled with local Kʼicheʼ populations. Qʼumarkaj, their political and ceremonial centre, covered about 3.25 square kilometres, and Nahuatl influence is found in their language.

In 1524 the conquistador Pedro de Alvarado, with Kaqchikel allies, defeated the Kʼicheʼ army under Tecun Uman in the valley of Xelajú (Quetzaltenango). Close to 10,000 Kʼicheʼ died, Tecún Umán among them, and he remains a figure of oral tradition; some scholars doubt his historical existence. The Kʼicheʼ then invited Alvarado to Qʼumarkaj, but he suspected an ambush and had the city burned. Spanish clergy, among them Dominicans, sought to convert them and wrote a Kʼicheʼ theological text, the Theologia Indorum.

In the early 1980s the government of Efraín Ríos Montt waged a counterinsurgency campaign against Maya rebellions. As the largest Maya group in Guatemala, the Kʼicheʼ were a major target, in what became known as the Guatemalan genocide. The Guatemalan Historical Clarification Commission found Maya people were 98.4 percent of the victims in southern El Quiché. Ríos Montt was convicted in 2013 and the verdict was overturned; he died in April 2018 during a retrial.

The Popol Vuh, written around the 1550s, is a compilation of Kʼicheʼ mythological and historical narratives, including the creation myth, the story of the divine brothers and the history of the Kʼicheʼ up to the Spanish conquest. It was declared the official book of Guatemala in 1971. According to the 2018 census, the Kʼicheʼ numbered 1,610,551, about 11 percent of the Guatemalan population, mostly in Totonicapán, El Quiché and Quetzaltenango. Rigoberta Menchú Tum, a Kʼicheʼ activist, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992.
kickapoo: The Kickapoo are an Algonquian-speaking people of the Northeastern Woodlands who originated in the Great Lakes region. Their name comes from Kiwigapawa, a word of their own language meaning he who moves about, standing now here, now there. They are closely tied to the Sauk and Meskwaki peoples. Their first recorded contact with Europeans was in 1667 in southern Wisconsin, with Catholic missionaries, and they met the expeditions of La Salle in Illinois Country in 1682.

French fur trading posts were set up near their villages, among them on the Wabash River, where Terre Haute began as an associated French village. The Kickapoo belonged to the Wabash Confederacy with the Piankeshaw, the Wea and the Miami, and after the French and Indian War they moved into southern Illinois. In 1795 they signed the Treaty of Greenville.

As settlers from the east moved into the region in the early nineteenth century, the Kickapoo sold most of their lands in treaties including those of Vincennes, Grouseland and Fort Wayne. Many of their warriors fought beside the Shawnee leader Tecumseh, one of whose closest allies they were, at the Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811 and then on the British side in the War of 1812.

In the Treaty of Edwardsville of 1819 they ceded all their holdings in Illinois, nearly half the area of the state, for a tract on the Osage River in Missouri and goods worth 3,000 dollars. Half of the people travelled south into Spanish territory across the Red River, in present-day Texas, and the United States moved to stop them. The rest stayed in Illinois under Kennekuk, a nonviolent spiritual leader, who led his followers to Kansas during the removals of the 1830s and died there of smallpox in 1852.

Three Kickapoo tribes are federally recognised in the United States, in Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas, and the Mexican Kickapoo live in the Múzquiz Municipality of Coahuila, where they moved after a split between followers of Kennekuk and Chief Kishko. The Texas and Mexican groups are one cross-border nation, and these communities travel each year among the places to keep their ties.

In Kansas, Kennekuk's leadership drew on the religious revivals of the 1820s and 1830s, blending Protestant and Catholic teaching, and his people turned to farming. The Oklahoma Kickapoo received a reservation in 1883, saw it broken into allotments under the Dawes Act in 1893, lost their government under the Curtis Act of 1898, and reorganised in 1936.
kido-takayoshi: Kido was born Wada Kogorō on 11 August 1833 in Hagi, in the Chōshū domain, the son of a samurai physician. At the age of seven he was adopted into the Katsura family and became known as Katsura Kogorō. His adoptive father was on his deathbed, and the family's stipend was cut from 150 koku to 90.

He was educated at the Meirinkan, and in 1849 at the Shōka Sonjuku, the academy of Yoshida Shōin, from whom he took the philosophy of imperial loyalism. In 1852 he went to Edo to study swordsmanship and artillery, made ties with radical samurai from the Mito Domain, and later supervised the building of the domain's first western-style warship.

After 1858 Katsura served at the domain's Edo residence as a liaison between the bureaucracy and the radical young samurai who supported the Sonnō jōi movement. He was in Kyoto when Aizu and Satsuma forces drove Chōshū out in the coup of 30 September 1863. His diary says that he was at the loyalist meeting at the Ikedaya inn on 8 July 1864 but left before the Shinsengumi attacked; rumours told other stories.

He was involved in the Hamaguri Gate rebellion of 20 August 1864, though not present; some 28,000 houses burned and his adopted son was among the Chōshū dead. Using the new name Kido, he was instrumental in the Satchō Alliance of 1866 with Saigō Takamori and Ōkubo Toshimichi, mediated by Sakamoto Ryōma.

After 1868 Kido helped draft the Five Charter Oath and directed the abolition of the han system. He opposed hereditary privilege and favoured appointment by merit. He joined the Iwakura Mission, which left on 23 December 1871, and on returning on 13 September 1873 he advocated constitutional government. He resigned in 1874 in protest at the Taiwan Expedition, returned after the Osaka Conference of 1875, and became chairman of the Assembly of Prefectural Governors.

Kido died on 26 May 1877, during the Satsuma Rebellion, of cancer; his last words to Ōkubo were reported as "Enough Saigō." With Saigō and Ōkubo he was known as one of the Ishin-no-Sanketsu, the Three Great Nobles of the Restoration. His diary shows his conflict between loyalty to Chōshū and the interest of the nation, and it has been published in English translation. He was enshrined at Kyoto Ryozen Gokoku Shrine and at the Kido Shrine in Yamaguchi, and his house in Hagi, a National Historic Site since 1934, is a memorial museum.
kiel: Kiel lies on the Kieler Förde, an inlet of the Bay of Kiel, in the southeast of the Jutland Peninsula, at the mouth of the Schwentine River and about 90 kilometres northeast of Hamburg. The Kiel Canal, which joins the Baltic to the North Sea, has one end in the district of Holtenau and the other at Brunsbüttel. Most of the city belongs to Holstein, while the districts north of the canal are historically part of Southern Schleswig.

Count Adolf IV of Holstein founded the city in 1233 as Holstenstadt tom Kyle, and his eldest son, John I of Schauenburg, granted it Lübeck city rights in 1242. As capital of the county, later the duchy, of Holstein, it belonged to the Holy Roman Empire. It was a member of the Hanseatic League from 1284 until it was expelled in 1518 for harbouring pirates. Kiel University was founded in 1665 by Christian Albert, Duke of Holstein-Gottorp.

From 1773 to 1864 the town belonged to the king of Denmark, who ruled Holstein through a personal union. After the Second Schleswig War of 1864 it was administered briefly by Austria and Prussia, and the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 led to its annexation by Prussia. King William I moved Prussia's Baltic fleet there on 24 March 1865, and as Germany's main naval base the city grew from 18,770 people in 1864 to about 200,000 in 1910.

In late 1918 the fleet stationed at Kiel was ordered to sail for a last battle with the Royal Navy. The sailors, who thought it a suicide mission, refused, took over Kiel and spread the revolt to other northern ports, setting off the revolution that ended the monarchy and created the Weimar Republic. In the Second World War heavy bombing destroyed more than 80 per cent of the remaining old town. British forces seized the city on 5 May 1945, and in 1946 it was named capital of the new state of Schleswig-Holstein.

Kiel is the capital and most populous city of Schleswig-Holstein and Germany's largest city on the Baltic Sea. Its oldest building is the 13th-century Church of St. Nicholas. The shipyard Howaldtswerke-Deutsche Werft, founded in 1838, built the first German submarine, the Brandtaucher, in 1850.
kiel-mutiny: After the Battle of Jutland in 1916 the High Seas Fleet lay mostly at anchor, and as experienced officers left for submarines and light vessels, discipline on the capital ships suffered. Unrest began in the summer of 1917: in August most of the 600-man crew of SMS Prinzregent Luitpold walked off in support of arrested comrades, and two ringleaders were executed. Secret sailors' councils formed on several ships.

In October 1918 the government of Prince Maximilian of Baden asked President Woodrow Wilson to mediate an armistice and ended submarine warfare. Admiral Scheer, Chief of the Admiralty Staff, then on his own authority had Admiral Hipper, commander of the High Seas Fleet, prepare the main fleet for an attack on the British. The historian Michael Epkenhans calls it an admirals' rebellion, planned against the political leadership.

On the night of 30 to 31 October sailors of III Battle Squadron in the Schillig Roads off Wilhelmshaven refused to weigh anchor, with outright mutiny on Thüringen and Helgoland. The command dropped the attack and sent the squadron to Kiel, where Vice Admiral Hugo Kraft had 47 sailors of the Markgraf and nearly 150 other mutineers arrested. Sailors and workers met to demand their release, and on 3 November, led by Karl Artelt and Lothar Popp of the USPD, several thousand marched on the military prison under the slogan peace and bread. A patrol fired into the crowd, killing seven and seriously wounding 29.

On 4 November troops sent to reinforce the garrison joined the demonstrators, Admiral Wilhelm Souchon freed the prisoners, and Artelt organised the first soldiers' council. By that evening about 40,000 sailors, soldiers and workers held Kiel. They presented the Social Democrat Gustav Noske, sent from Berlin, with fourteen demands, among them freedom of speech and the press and that the fleet never sail. They elected Noske chairman of the council, and on 5 November the red flag flew on the ships in the harbour.

Detachments of sailors spread from Kiel to the major cities and met almost no resistance. By 7 November councils held the larger coastal cities, Frankfurt am Main, Stuttgart and Munich, where King Ludwig III of Bavaria became the first German prince to fall. The revolution reached Berlin on 9 November, and the other dynastic rulers abdicated by the end of the month. After street battles in January 1919, the Weimar Republic was established in August 1919.
kievan-rus: Before the 9th century most of the area north of the Black Sea was populated by East Slavic tribes: the Ilmen Slavs and Krivichi around Novgorod, the Poliane, Drevliane and Severiane around Kiev, and the Vyatichi to the north and east, with Baltic Finnic peoples such as the Chud farther north. The name Rus' is most often derived from an Old Norse term for men who row, as rowing was the main way of travelling the rivers of Eastern Europe.

According to the Primary Chronicle, the East Slav lands were divided in the 9th century between the Varangians and the Khazars. The Varangians are first recorded imposing tribute in 859, and in 862 the tribes drove them out and then invited three brothers and their kin to rule. Rurik led the Rus' until about 879 and left his realm to his kinsman Oleg as regent for his young son Igor. Oleg took Smolensk and then Kiev in 882 and forbade the tribes he subjected to pay tribute to the Khazars.

The state's power peaked under Vladimir the Great (r. 980–1015) and Yaroslav the Wise (r. 1019–1054). Vladimir, who had fled to Scandinavia in 977, returned with Varangian warriors, subdued Polotsk and killed his half-brother Yaropolk. He was baptised and extended Christianity by decree to the inhabitants of Kiev and beyond. Yaroslav held Kiev from 1019 and all of Rus' from 1036, promulgated the first law code, the Russkaya Pravda, built the Saint Sophia cathedrals in Kiev and Novgorod, and married his sister and three daughters to the kings of Poland, France, Hungary and Norway.

How the throne passed between Rurik's descendants is unclear, and scholars debate whether any system existed. After Yaroslav's death no adequate system of succession developed, and three of his sons fought each other after a defeat by the Cuman forces at the Alta River in 1068. In 1097 the Council of Liubech tried to settle the quarrels. Through the 12th century the state broke into rival regional powers, weakened further by the decline of the Byzantine Empire, its main economic partner.

At its largest, in the mid-11th century, the realm stretched from the White Sea to the Black Sea and from the Carpathian Mountains to the Taman Peninsula. It fell to the Mongol invasion in the mid-13th century, though the Rurik dynasty continued to rule until the death of Feodor I of Russia in 1598. Belarus, Russia and Ukraine all claim it as their cultural ancestor.
kigali: Kigali lies near the geographic centre of Rwanda, in rolling hills of valleys and ridges joined by steep slopes. Its name comes from the Kinyarwanda prefix ki- and the suffix -gali, meaning wide or broad, and was first applied to Mount Kigali. According to oral history the name dates from the 14th century, when King Cyilima I Rugwe is said to have viewed the territory from a hill and called the country vast. The central business district stands on Nyarugenge Hill, the site of the original settlement.

According to oral history the Kingdom of Rwanda was founded in the 14th century on the shores of Lake Muhazi, about 40 kilometres east of the present city. The early kingdom included Kigali, but it was a small state with larger neighbours, Bugesera and Gisaka. The scholar Alexis Kagame proposed that Kigali was made a capital under Cyilima I Rugwe, but there is little direct evidence, and the later pre-colonial kings are known to have been based at Nyanza.

The founding of the city is generally dated to 1907, when the German administrator and explorer Richard Kandt, the first resident of Rwanda, chose the site for his headquarters for its central location, views and security. Foreign merchants began trading there in the German period, and Kandt opened government schools for Tutsi students.

Belgium took control of Rwanda and Burundi during the First World War, and Kigali remained the seat of colonial administration for Rwanda while Usumbura was the capital of Ruanda-Urundi. At independence in 1962 it had about 6,000 inhabitants. Nyanza and Butare, then called Astrida, were also considered for the capital, but Kigali was chosen for its more central location. In 1973 a bloodless military coup brought Juvénal Habyarimana to power.

In April 1994 he was killed when his aircraft was shot down near Kigali, and the Rwandan genocide followed, which killed over 500,000 Tutsi. The Rwandan Patriotic Front seized Kigali on 4 July 1994. The city lost a large part of its people to killing and flight, and after 1995 refugees returned and much of it was rebuilt.

Kigali is the capital, largest city and a province-level administrative unit of Rwanda, divided into three districts: Gasabo, Kicukiro and Nyarugenge. It had 1,745,555 inhabitants at the 2022 census. It is the country's economic and financial hub and its main port of entry, and houses the president's residence and most government ministries. The Kigali Genocide Memorial hosts the national commemoration on 7 April, and 4 July is observed as Liberation Day. The house in which Kandt lived is now the Kandt House Museum of Natural History.
kigeli-iv-rwabugiri: Rwabugiri, whose birth name is given as Sezisoni Rwabugiri, was a Tutsi of the Nyiginya dynasty, which traced its line back to Gihanga, one of the first kings whose deeds are celebrated in Rwanda's oral chronicles. His year of birth is uncertain and is given as about 1840. He held authority from 1867 to 1895 and was among the last kings of his line.

Around 1870 Rwabugiri established a royal court at Rubengera that collected labour dues and tribute in food. It channelled food across the country and became a centre of commerce. The court managed production so as to keep a surplus as a provision against famine, and on the king's order this was distributed to the poorest in exchange for their labour; in times of shortage, however, the very rich Tutsi living at Rubengera could find food and livestock while most of the country suffered.

As he annexed new lands he placed appointed chiefs over them, drawn into a network that bound the regions to the court. These chiefs sometimes met local resistance: in the north-west the Balera challenged the Nduga whom the court had installed, a contest along lines of clan, since both groups were then counted as Tutsi. Several annexed districts, such as Bugoyi, Bwishaza and Kingogo, had been inhabited entirely by Hutu, and Tutsi moved into them in numbers afterwards. He also killed chiefs of his own Nyiginya lineage who had shown too much independence.

He was the first king of Rwanda to come into contact with Europeans. He built an army equipped with guns obtained from Germans and barred most foreigners, especially Arabs, from the kingdom, defending its borders against neighbouring kingdoms and slave traders. By the end of his rule the country was divided into provinces, districts, hills and neighbourhoods under a hierarchy of chiefs.

Rwanda had been assigned to the German Empire at a conference in Brussels in 1890, but no expedition came until that of Count Gustav Adolf von Götzen in 1894. Rwabugiri died in September 1895 on an expedition in what is now Congo. His son Rutarindwa was proclaimed king as Mibambwe IV, with Kanjogera of the Bega clan, another of Rwabugiri's wives, as queen mother. With her brother Kabare she carried out a coup at Rucunshu in which Rutarindwa was killed, and made her own son king as Yuhi V Musinga. The weakened state opened the way to direct German colonisation in 1897.
kigeli-v-ndahindurwa: Kigeli was born Jean-Baptiste Ndahindurwa on 29 June 1936 in Kamembe, a son of the deposed king Yuhi Musinga and Queen Mukashema, the seventh of his eleven wives. He was Tutsi and had fourteen siblings. When he was four his father was exiled by the Belgian government to Moba in the Congo, and he returned to Rwanda in 1944 after his father's death. He was baptised in the Catholic Church as a teenager and remained devout. After finishing school in 1956 he worked in local government until 1959.

His half-brother Mutara III Rudahigwa died under mysterious circumstances on 25 July 1959, and on 28 July it was announced that Kigeli would succeed him. Mutara had no children, and the suddenness of his death prompted talk of assassination. The Belgian administration had no part in the choice and described it as a coup d'état, as did the Hutu elite. Kigeli was at first favoured by Tutsi traditionalists, Hutu nationalists and the Catholic clergy, but the fact that the Tutsi establishment had engineered his rise limited his ability to act as a neutral arbiter. Hutu and Tutsi militancy grew until hundreds died and many Tutsi went into exile.

In July 1960 he sought refuge in Congo. In 1961 he was in Kinshasa to meet the United Nations Secretary General Dag Hammarskjöld when Dominique Mbonyumutwa, with Belgian support, led a coup, and the monarchy was formally overthrown on 28 January 1961. A referendum held on 25 September 1961 had about 95 per cent turnout, and around 80 per cent of voters opposed the monarchy. Kigeli called it rigged. He was put under house arrest and deported to what is now Tanzania on 2 October 1961. Rwanda became an independent republic on 1 July 1962.

Kigeli lived in Dar es Salaam, Kampala and Nairobi, and was granted political asylum in the United States in July 1992. He settled near Washington, D.C., and then in Oakton, Virginia. He headed the King Kigeli V Foundation, which promoted humanitarian work for Rwandan refugees, and travelled to speak for the Rwandan people and for peace between the groups.

He died of a heart ailment on 16 October 2016 in Washington, aged 81. He never married, in obedience to a rule that bars kings from marrying while out of the country, though he had at least one daughter. On 9 January 2017 the royal house announced his nephew Prince Emmanuel Bushayija as pretender to the throne, to reign as Yuhi VI.
kikaijima: Kikaijima is one of the Satsunan Islands, 56.93 square kilometres in area, about 25 kilometres east of Amami Ōshima and about 380 kilometres south of the southern tip of Kyūshū. It is the easternmost island of the Amami chain and, unlike Amami Ōshima and Tokunoshima, fairly flat, rising to 214 metres. A raised coral island with limestone cliffs, it is one of the fastest rising coral islands in the world. It has a humid subtropical climate with frequent typhoons.

Early Japanese sources name a Kikaijima, though scholars debate whether they mean this island, Satsuma Iōjima or the southern islands as a whole. In 998 the Dazaifu ordered Kikaijima to arrest raiders from the Amami islands, and in 1188 Minamoto no Yoritomo sent troops to pacify it. The Gusuku Site Complex, found on the island's plateau in 2006 and in use from the 9th to the 13th centuries, held goods from mainland Japan, China and Korea and Kamuiyaki pottery from Tokunoshima, supporting the view that Kikaijima was a trade centre of the southern islands.

In 1306 the deputy jitō Chikama Tokiie listed Kikaijima among his family's properties, and the islands later seem to have passed to the Shimazu clan. A record of 1462 in the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty says the island was resisting repeated invasions from Ryūkyū. After the Satsuma Domain's conquest of Ryūkyū in 1609 it came under Satsuma's direct control, and after the Meiji Restoration it joined Ōsumi Province and then Kagoshima Prefecture. With the other Amami Islands it was occupied by the United States after the Second World War until 1953.

The island forms the town of Kikai in Kagoshima Prefecture, and much of it lies in the Amami Guntō Quasi-National Park. Its people live mainly from sugar cane, citrus fruit and fishing, with sugar refining and shōchū distilling. The traditional Kikai language, a Ryukyuan language, is endangered.
kikuyu-people: The Kikuyu, also called Agĩkũyũ or Gĩkũyũ, are a Bantu ethnic group native to central Kenya. They were part of the Thagicu group that settled around Mount Kenya and mainly live in the fertile central highlands. The name Kikuyu is the Swahili borrowing of their own name, Gĩkũyũ. They belong to the Northeastern Bantu branch, and their ancestors were part of the wider Bantu migration that began in West-Central Africa and passed through the Congo Basin, although the exact place they migrated from is uncertain. Traditionally the community was organized into nine clans, among them the Anjirũ, Ambũi, Agacikũ and Aceera.

Before the East Africa Protectorate was established in 1895, the Agĩkũyũ are described as having preserved their geographic and political power from almost all outside influence for many generations. They expanded their territory through land purchases, blood-brotherhood partnerships, intermarriage and the adoption and absorption of others, and they were farmers and traders who also practised small industries such as bridge building, wire drawing and iron chain making. Slavery did not exist among them as an institution, nor did they raid for slaves.

Their traditional way of life was disrupted when they met the British around 1888. Waiyaki Wa Hinga, a leader of the southern Agikuyu who ruled Dagoretti and had signed a treaty with Frederick Lugard of the British East Africa Company, burned down Lugard's fort in 1890. The company captured him two years later and buried him alive in revenge.

In 1946 the Kenya African Union, which the Kikuyu dominated, was formed, a nationalist body demanding access to white-owned land, and in 1947 Jomo Kenyatta, former president of the moderate Kikuyu Central Association, became its president. When the union won no significant reforms, the initiative passed to younger and more militant figures in the trade unions, among squatters on settler estates in the Rift Valley, and in Nairobi and the Kikuyu districts.

Kikuyu is a Bantu language, and many Kikuyu also speak Swahili and English. Until 1888 their literature was expressed in folklore. Missionaries who arrived in that year wrote the language in a modified Roman alphabet, and the Kikuyu responded strongly to missionary education. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o is among the writers who emerged, and his novel Murogi wa Kagogo is the largest known novel in the Kikuyu language.

Engaged couples take part in a dowry custom called Ruracio, in which the bride price is negotiated. Most Kikuyu are Christians today, of varying denominations, though they historically followed indigenous faiths.
kildare: Kildare, in Irish Cill Dara, 'church of the oak', lies about 50 kilometres west of Dublin on the edge of the Curragh, and is close enough to the capital to have become a commuter town. Although it gives its name to the county, the county town is Naas. It had 10,302 inhabitants in 2022. Kildare railway station is on the Dublin–Cork mainline.

Tradition holds that Saint Brigid, reared in her father's household and taught dairying and the care of cattle by her mother, vowed to live in chastity and was consecrated, according to different accounts, by Saint Mel of Ardagh or by Bishop Mac Caille. She then founded a community beneath an oak tree on a hill at the edge of the Curragh. The King of Leinster, who lived at Dún Ailinne, was said to have given her the site. In one story he offered as much land as her cloak would cover, and when she spread it, it stretched over the whole Curragh. The monastery became one of the three most important Christian foundations of Celtic Ireland.

The Annals of Inisfallen record the deaths of abbots and a coarb of Brigit in the 8th century, the plundering of Cell Dara in 964 by the foreigners of Áth Cliath, and the burning of Cell Dara and Port Láirge in 1031. Lord William de Vesci brought the Carmelite friars to Kildare in 1290, established the Franciscans in the Grey Abbey and built the first castle. White Abbey was surrendered on 3 April 1539 under the suppression of the monasteries, and the friars ministered in secret until the Penal Laws eased in the 1750s. The foundation stone of the present Carmelite church was laid on 8 December 1884.

In July 1903 the Gordon Bennett Cup, the first international motor race held in Britain or Ireland, ran through Kildare. Racing was illegal on British public roads, and the straight Kildare roads were judged safer. The British team raced in Shamrock green as a compliment to Ireland, the origin of British racing green, and the 528 km race was won by the Belgian Camille Jenatzy in a Mercedes.

St Brigid's Cathedral and the Norman Kildare Castle stand in the town centre, with the ruins of the Grey Abbey to the south and White Abbey to the north-west. St Brigid's Well lies on the outskirts, and the Solas Bhride centre is dedicated to Saint Brigid. The Irish National Stud and the Curragh Racecourse are nearby.
kilij-arslan-i: Kilij Arslan, whose name means Sword Lion, was the son of Suleiman ibn Qutalmish. After his father's death in 1086 he became a hostage of the Great Seljuq sultan Malik Shah I at Isfahan, and was released when Malik Shah died in 1092 in the wake of a quarrel among his jailers. He then marched at the head of the Turkish Oghuz Yiva tribe army and set up his capital at Nicaea. After Malik Shah's death the Danishmends, Artuqids and other tribes began to compete to found independent states. Kilij Arslan married Ayşe Hatun, daughter of the emir Tzachas, and in 1094 killed his father-in-law at a banquet in his tent at Smyrna.

When the People's Crusade of Peter the Hermit and Walter the Penniless reached Nicaea in 1096, Kilij Arslan sent spies to tempt the crusaders to rush to the fort of Xerigordos and starved them out; those who renounced Christianity were spared and sent east as captives, and the rest were put to death. Near the village of Civetot his army surprised the remaining crusaders, almost entirely unarmed civilians, and around 17,000 of 20,000 were killed.

Believing the main army no threat, he went to war with the Danishmends and was away when the crusaders besieged Nicaea in May 1097. He was defeated on 21 May, the city surrendered to the Byzantines and his wife and children were captured. Allied with the Danishmends, he planned an ambush near Dorylaeum, but his horse archers could not break the line of the crusader knights, and Bohemond's main body captured the Turkish camp on 1 July. In 1101 he defeated crusader armies at Mersivan and Heraclea Cybistra and moved his capital to Konya.

After the crusades he moved east, taking Harran and Diyarbakr. In 1107 Ghazaghli, castellan of Mosul's citadel, asked for his help against Jawali Saqawa, the atabeg appointed by Muhammad I Tapar. Kilij Arslan entered Mosul, appointed his son Malik Shah ruler and set out to fight Jawali near the Khabur River. His army was destroyed. Believing he would not be forgiven for challenging Sultan Muhammad, he rode into the river, shooting arrows at his pursuers, until his horse sank and he drowned. In January 2021 archaeologists from Dicle University identified what they took to be his grave and that of his daughter Saide Hatun at Silvan, Diyarbakır.
kilij-arslan-ii: Kilij Arslan II was the son of Mesud I, sultan of Rum. The Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates described him as maimed in several vital parts of his body, with dislocated hands and a slight limp, so that he travelled mostly in a litter. This was the origin of the Byzantine nickname Koutz-Arslan, "Halt-Arslan". In 1148 he captured the city of Marash, after the surrounding region had been devastated by the Danishmendids in 1136-1137.

In early 1159 the sultan's forces harassed the rear-guard of Emperor Manuel I Komnenos near Kotyaion after Kilij Arslan had refused the emperor passage, which began the Byzantine-Seljuk War of 1158-1162. Kilij Arslan then travelled to Constantinople, in late 1160 or 1161, swore oaths of vassalage, promised to return to the Byzantines any notable cities he conquered, and was ritually adopted as a son by Manuel.

After the Danishmendid emir of Sebasteia, Yaghibasan, died in autumn 1164, Kilij attacked Sebasteia without success but subjugated most of the emirate's lands in 1165, including Albistan, Darende and Geduk. He did not return them to Byzantine control. After Nur al-Din's death in 1174 he occupied Sebasteia, Neokaisareia, Doceia, Comana and other towns in Cappadocia in early 1175.

In 1175 Kilij refused to hand the conquered territory to Manuel, who invaded in 1176 intending to capture Iconium. At the Battle of Myriokephalon the sultan defeated Manuel's army and forced the emperor to negotiate a fragile peace. In 1179 Pope Alexander III wrote to him, and Otto of Sankt Blasien reports that he sought a marriage with a daughter of Frederick Barbarossa. His overtures to pope and emperor were probably less about religion than about balancing the Byzantines through warm relations with the west.

After Manuel's death in 1180 Kilij secured most of the southern coast of Anatolia. In 1186 he divided the sultanate among his eleven sons, who began to fight one another for control. When the armies of the Third Crusade under Frederick Barbarossa crossed his lands, his sons fought them at Philomelion and Iconium, although he had promised free passage. His eldest son Qutb al-Din took Konya, and Kilij took refuge in Kayseri. In 1192 Kilij and his son Kaykhusraw I drove Qutb al-Din out of Konya and besieged him at Aksaray. Kilij died during the siege in August 1192, after promising Kaykhusraw I the succession, and was buried in the Alâeddin Mosque in Konya.
kiliya: Kiliia, also spelled Kiliya or Kilia, is a city in Izmail Raion of Odesa Oblast in south-western Ukraine. It lies in the Danube Delta, in the historic Bessarabian district of Budjak, and across the river lies the town of Chilia Veche, or Old Kiliia, in Romania. The Chilia branch of the Danube, which separates Ukraine from Romania, is named after the town, which is sometimes called Nova Kiliia, or New Kiliia. The name is linked with the Greek kellia, meaning granaries; Chilia Veche was founded by the Greek Byzantines, and its name is first recorded in 1241 by the Persian chronicler Rashid-al-Din Hamadani.

On the site of present-day Kiliia the Republic of Genoa established a large colony called Licostomo, headed by a consul, of which only the defensive ditches of a fortress remain. The area was Byzantine until 1361, then contested until 1412 among the Kingdom of Hungary, Wallachia, Poland, Genoa and the Ottoman Empire. It belonged to the Principality of Moldavia from 1412 to 1448, to Hungary from 1448 to 1465, and again to Moldavia from 1465 to 1484. Stephen the Great of Moldavia built it up as a major Moldavian port to counter the Ottomans, who had taken Chilia Veche in the fifteenth century, but they conquered Kiliia in 1484.

In 1570 the town held Muslims and Christians, with 298 Muslim households in 13 neighbourhoods, one of them Circassian, and 316 Christian households in five neighbourhoods; it was a property held directly by the Sultan. Russian forces under General Ivan Gudovich took it in the Russo-Turkish War of 1787–1792. It was returned to the Ottomans in 1792, retaken in 1806 and awarded to Russia in 1812. The Anglo-French fleet bombarded it in July 1854 during the Crimean War, and in 1878 the Congress of Berlin transferred it, with Budjak, back to Russia.

Kiliia belonged to Romania from 1918 to 1940. After a Soviet ultimatum in July 1940 it passed to the Soviet Union, was held again by Romania from 1941 to 1944, when it was the capital of Chilia County, and then returned to the Soviet Union. In 1941 the Romanian authorities deported its 316 Jews to Transnistria, where a large majority died.

Kiliia was the administrative centre of Kiliia Raion until 2020, when the raion was merged into Izmail Raion; its population was estimated at 18,745 in 2022. Its oldest building is the semi-subterranean church of St Nicholas, which may go back to 1485, though an old inscription says it was founded on 10 May 1647. Historically a trading outpost, it is an important fishing location on the Danube, with Vylkove, and has a ship repair facility. It has been part of independent Ukraine since 1991.
kilkenny: Kilkenny lies in the Nore Valley on both banks of the River Nore, in the centre of County Kilkenny in the province of Leinster, 117 kilometres from Dublin and 48 kilometres north of Waterford. Its Irish name, Cill Chainnigh, means church of Cainneach. The church was built in honour of Saint Canice, an Ulsterman, on the hill that now holds St Canice's Cathedral and its round tower, and it seems to have been the first major settlement.

The town began with an ecclesiastical foundation of the early 6th century within the Kingdom of Ossory, and St Canice's was a major monastic centre from at least the 8th century. The Annals of the Four Masters first record the name in 1085, when the place was for the most part burned. After the Norman invasion of Ireland Kilkenny Castle and a series of walls were built to protect the burghers of a Norman merchant town. William Marshall, Lord of Leinster, gave it a charter in 1207, and by the late 13th century it was under Hiberno-Norman control. The Statutes of Kilkenny, passed there in 1367, aimed to curb the decline of the Hiberno-Norman Lordship of Ireland.

In 1609 James I of England granted the town a royal charter that gave it the status of a city. After the Irish Rebellion of 1641 the Irish Catholic Confederation, known as the Confederation of Kilkenny, was based there until the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland in 1649. Kilkenny was a brewing centre from the late 17th century. Since 1840 it has not been administered as a city under local government law, but a law of 2014 allows the continued use of the description.

The urban centre of Kilkenny had a population of 27,184 in 2022, and it is a well-preserved medieval town. Kilkenny Castle was the seat of the Butler family and was handed to the State in the mid-20th century. St Canice's Cathedral, whose present building dates from the 13th century, is the second longest cathedral in Ireland, and Rothe House, Black Abbey and the Tholsel are among its other historic buildings.
kilkenny-castle: Kilkenny Castle was built to control a fording point of the River Nore and the junction of several routeways, and it was a symbol of Norman occupation. In its original 13th-century form it was a square castle with four large circular corner towers, three of which survive, and a massive ditch, part of which can still be seen on the Parade. The first castle, probably of wood, was built by Richard de Clare, 2nd Earl of Pembroke, known as Strongbow, possibly on the site of an earlier residence of the Mac Giolla Phádraig kings of Osraighe.

Strongbow's daughter and heiress Isabel married William Marshal in 1189, and in 1192 he appointed Geoffrey FitzRobert seneschal of Leinster, beginning a major phase of development at Kilkenny; excavations in 2019 uncovered the foundations of the great gatehouse Marshal built in the early 1200s. Lady Margaret Butler, the paternal grandmother of Anne Boleyn, was born in the castle. From 1642 to 1648 the Supreme Council of Confederate Ireland met there, although its owner, James Butler, 1st Duke of Ormond, was the representative of Charles I. The east wall and north-east tower were damaged in Oliver Cromwell's siege of 1650, and in 1661 the duke remodelled the castle as a château.

Run down by the 18th century, the castle was restored in the 19th towards its medieval appearance, and King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra visited it in 1904. The family sold its landed estates in 1903 under the Wyndham Land Act. In 1922, during the Irish Civil War, Free State forces besieged Republicans in the castle, doing a great deal of damage. In 1935 the family sold its contents for £6,000, moved to London and left the castle empty for thirty years.

In 1967 Arthur Butler, 6th Marquess of Ormonde, sold the castle for £50 to the Castle Restoration Committee for the people of Kilkenny, and the handover also marked the foundation of the Butler Society. The castle and its grounds are managed by the Office of Public Works, and the gardens and parkland are open to the public.
killala: Killala, in Irish Cill Ala, the mottled church, lies north of Ballina, with a harbour at the south end of Killala Bay. The village is in a civil parish of the same name. West of it the townland of Townsplots West, known locally as Enagh Beg, holds a number of ancient forts. Along the river nearby stand the ruins of several monasteries: Rosserk, a Franciscan house of strict observance founded in 1460, the Abbey of Moyne, and the Dominican Rathfran Friary north of the village.

Tradition links the church of Killala with Saint Patrick, who is said to have placed his disciple St. Muredach over it, as early as 442 or 443, and to have baptised 12,000 converts in a single day at a well near the town. Little is known of Muredach's successors before the 12th century. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Killala is one of the five suffragan sees of the Province of Tuam; John MacHale, later Archbishop of Tuam, was its bishop in 1834. By the end of the 18th century Killala had a small sea port where fishing was the main work, and it produced coarse linens and woollens.

In August 1798 the force of General Jean Joseph Amable Humbert, 1,109 French troops sent to support the Irish Rebellion, seized Killala, took Ballina and on 27 August beat a larger government army under General Gerard Lake at the Battle of Castlebar. After the defeat at Ballinamuck, a government force under Major-General Eyre Power Trench attacked Killala on 23 September and drove out the last of the invaders. The town had been under rebel control for thirty-two days.

The village had 562 inhabitants at the 2016 census. Its 12th-century round tower, the last medieval structure of a monastic establishment, and the Cathedral Church of St. Patrick, built in the 1670s and one of two cathedral churches of the Church of Ireland's Diocese of Tuam, Limerick and Killaloe, still stand. A railway from Ballina reached Killala in 1893 and closed to goods in 1934. Since 1998, the bicentenary of the events of 1798, Killala has been twinned with Chauvé in France.
killarney: Killarney, in Irish Cill Airne, meaning church of sloes, lies on the north-eastern shore of Lough Leane in County Kerry. Within and around it are Killarney National Park, St Mary's Cathedral, Ross Castle, Muckross House and Abbey, MacGillycuddy's Reeks, Purple Mountain, Mangerton Mountain, the Gap of Dunloe and Torc Waterfall. Its position on the Ring of Kerry made it a destination for visitors, and it is the second largest town in the county.

Religious settlements dominate the early record. The monastery on Innisfallen Island was founded in 640 by St. Finian the Leper and was occupied for about 850 years, until the monks were dispossessed in 1594 under Elizabeth I. According to tradition, the Irish high king Brian Boru was educated there. The island's ruins were later refurbished by the Kenmare estate as a dining place for visitors.

Thomas Browne, 4th Viscount Kenmare, set the town on its modern course. He founded linen mills in the 1740s to increase the population and the economy. On reaching the estate he had inherited, he found boggy land and considerable debt, but saw the tourist potential of the lakes' islands, Muckross Abbey and Ross Castle. He planted trees, drained bogs, mended roads and encouraged the building of inns. Celebrations of 250 years of tourism used 1747 as the date, though a report dated the start of the resort to 1754, the year Kenmare came into his inheritance. Hosiery and shoemaking later became major industries.

The district was heavily involved in the Irish War of Independence. The best-known engagement was the Headford Ambush of 21 March 1921, when more than thirty men of the IRA's Kerry No. 2 Brigade flying column, led by Dan Allman, attacked a train carrying soldiers of the 1st Battalion Royal Fusiliers at Headford Junction. The fifty-minute fight left two IRA volunteers and nine Fusiliers dead, with three civilian cattle dealers caught in the crossfire.

Tourism is the town's largest industry. Outside Dublin, Killarney has more hotel and guesthouse beds than any other town or city in the state, and its horse-drawn jaunting cars, driven by local families known as jarveys, are among its best-known sights. The 2022 census counted 14,412 inhabitants. The International Football Association Board met at the Lake Hotel in Killarney in 1905, and the Killarney Regatta is held each July and is described as Ireland's oldest surviving regatta.
kilmartin: The village's Gaelic name, Cille Mhàrtainn, means church of Màrtainn. More than 800 monuments lie within six miles (ten kilometres) of it. Kilmartin Glen holds Neolithic, Bronze Age and Iron Age sites, among them the henge monument of Temple Wood, whose two stone circles archaeologists have re-erected, burial and chambered cairns, standing stones and cup and ring marked rocks. One burial cairn has been rebuilt so that visitors can climb down inside it to a stone cist. West of the village lies the Moine Mhòr, a raised bog declared a national nature reserve in 1987.

The churchyard holds the Kilmartin Stones, early Christian and medieval carvings. Inside the church stand two crosses, one of the 9th-10th century and one late medieval, and outside lie West Highland gravestones of the 14th to early 16th centuries, carved with warriors in the dress of their day, fantastic animals and interlace. None is inscribed; they are taken to mark local landowners or minor nobles, and the women among them are often shown by shears. The churchyard was an ancient burial ground of the chiefs of Clan MacTavish, and many Campbells, who owned Kilmartin, lie there too.

Kilmartin Castle, a small Z-plan tower house of about 1580, was the home of John Carswell, Rector of Kilmartin and later titular Bishop of the Isles, before he moved to Carnasserie Castle. Carnasserie was blown up by government forces after Duncan Campbell joined the failed Argyll's Rising of 1685 and was never repaired. The minister John Duncanson was removed in 1662 when episcopacy was re-established and restored in 1670; his son Major Robert Duncanson took a leading part in the Glencoe Massacre of 1692.

The present parish church, designed by James Gordon Davis, opened in 1835 and has since been decommissioned. Kilmartin Museum interprets the glen's monuments and reopened on 3 September 2023 after a £7 million refurbishment. Carnasserie Castle and the hill-fort of Dunadd are in the care of Historic Environment Scotland.
kilo-class-submarine: The Kilo class was designed in the 1970s by the Rubin Design Bureau in the Soviet Union. The first version, Project 877 Paltus ('halibut'), entered service with the Soviet Navy from 12 September 1980 and was built until the mid-1990s. The boats were originally intended for the Warsaw Pact nations, which gave them the Russian nickname Varshavyanka (woman from Warsaw). Production then moved to the quieter and faster Project 636, which was made available for export in 1993, and later to Project 636.3, known in the West as the Improved Kilo II. More than 70 boats have been built.

Project 877 boats were intended mainly for anti-shipping and anti-submarine operations in relatively shallow waters. A boat displaces 2,300–2,350 tons surfaced and 3,000–4,000 tons submerged, is 70–74 metres long, has a crew of 52 and carries six 533 mm torpedo tubes. Anechoic tiles on the casing absorb active sonar and reduce the noise the boat gives off. Project 636 and 636.3 boats can also launch Kalibr cruise missiles through their torpedo tubes. Export prices were high: China paid about US$1.5–2 billion for eight Project 636 boats in 2002.

Besides Russia, the class has served with the navies of Algeria, China, India, Iran, Myanmar, Poland, Romania and Vietnam. Romania commissioned a Project 877 boat, Delfinul, in 1985 and halted its operation in 1995 for lack of support. Poland's ORP Orzeł entered service in 1986. Iran acquired three Project 877EKM boats between 1992 and 1996 for about $600 million each. Myanmar received its first submarine in 2020, a former Indian boat. Vietnam's six Improved Kilo-class boats carry the names of cities.

On 8 December 2015 the Russian Rostov-na-Donu fired cruise missiles at targets near Raqqa in Syria, the first time a Kilo-class boat fired such missiles against an enemy. After the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Black Sea Fleet boats fired Kalibr missiles into Ukraine. Ukrainian forces struck the Rostov-on-Don in drydock at Sevastopol with a Storm Shadow missile on 13 September 2023, and on 2 August 2024 Ukrainian sources claimed it had been sunk, though other sources said it was only hit.
kilwa-kisiwani: Kilwa Kisiwani lies 9 degrees south of the equator, with a circumference of 23 km and a land area of 12 square kilometres. The Mavuji River estuary lies to the west, the Sagarungu sound to the south and the Indian Ocean to the east. The island has no rivers, and its wells have been used for over a thousand years. The topsoil over the limestone is poor, so food on land came from higher ground, while seafood dominated the diet; the soil of the region suited cotton, which was used for sails and for cloth. The monsoon wind reversals shaped the trade of the island with Arabia, India and China.

Radiocarbon dating has confirmed the founding of the settlement at the start of the 9th century CE. Local oral tradition says that in the 11th century the island was sold to Ali bin Hasan, a son of the king of Shiraz, who married the daughter of the local king; research shows he arrived at an already inhabited place, and there is no evidence of Shirazi Shia Islam on the coast. Around the 13th century stone buildings began to replace wattle-and-daub. Kilwa exported spices, tortoiseshell, coconut oil, ivory, cotton cloth, incense and gold, and for about 500 years, from about 1100 to 1600, it minted its own coins, which have been found as far away as Great Zimbabwe.

By the 14th century, under the Mahdali dynasty, it was the most powerful city on the Swahili Coast, and in the 15th century the sultanate claimed authority over Malindi, Mombasa, Pemba, Zanzibar, Mafia, Comoro, Sofala and posts on Madagascar.

Ibn Battuta visited around 1331 and praised the generosity and religion of Sultan al-Hasan ibn Sulaiman, who built the palace of Husuni Kubwa and a large extension to the Great Mosque. Early in the 16th century Vasco da Gama exacted tribute, and in July 1505 a force under Francisco de Almeida besieged and sacked the town; the Portuguese held the island until 1512. In 1784 the Omani rulers of Zanzibar conquered it, and the city was abandoned in the 1840s. It later belonged to German East Africa from 1886 to 1918.

The ruins include the Great Mosque, whose oldest part dates to the 12th century and whose roof once rested on nine hexagonal columns made of single tree trunks, and the palace of Husuni Kubwa, a complex of more than a hundred rooms on a bluff over the ocean, with a pavilion and an octagonal swimming pool. The Gereza Fort stands between the Great Mosque and the Makutani Palace. The island has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981, together with the ruins of Songo Mnara, and about 1,150 people live on it.
kim-busik: Kim Pusik was a scion of the Silla royalty and a member of the Gyeongju Kim clan, which descended from the last Silla king, Kim Pu; Taejo, the first Goryeo king, married into the clan, and it played a leading role in early Goryeo politics. His father, Kim Kun, was an official and poet whose verses, written on an embassy to the Song court, made a deep impression on Song scholars. Kim Kun died when Kim Pusik was about thirteen, and his widow saw to the education of her younger sons; King Yejong later rewarded her for helping each of them pass the state examination.

Kim passed the civil service examination in 1096 and served at the Hallimwon, the Academy of Letters, which also drafted foreign correspondence. In 1115 he was appointed to the Office of Remonstrance. He gave royal lectures on the Book of History and the Book of Changes, where he clashed with Yun Ŏn-i, son of the general Yun Kwan. He drafted much of Goryeo's correspondence with Liao and Song and was part of the embassy to the Song court in 1116–1117. When the Jurchen rose against Liao, he and his brother Kim Puil argued against sending troops to help Liao and stalled the motion.

Under King Injong he opposed the attempts of Yi Cha-gyŏm, the king's maternal grandfather, to enhance his standing, and after a failed coup against Yi in 1126 he was promoted to Chief Censor. After the Myoch'ŏng rebellion he became supreme chancellor in 1136 and dominated the Goryeo government until his official retirement in 1142.

In 1142 Injong ordered the compilation of the Samguk Sagi, a chronicle of the Three Kingdoms and Unified Silla. Kim headed a team of fourteen authors and drew on Chinese histories, above all the Shiji of Sima Qian. One of the most prominent Confucian scholars of his time, he was also a practising Buddhist: he founded the family temple complex Kwallan-sa, which inspired his poem At Kwallan, wrote an inscription honouring the monk Ŭich'ŏn, and became a lay monk in retirement. During the rebellion he swore an oath by heaven and earth, mountains, streams, gods and spirits, and after taking the Western Capital he sacrificed to its guardian deities.
kim-gu: Kim Gu was born Kim Ch'angam on 29 August 1876 in Haeju, Hwanghae Province, the only child of poor farmers. His father belonged to the Andong Kim clan, which had lost its noble status in 1651. In 1893 he joined the Donghak movement, which sought to revise Confucian practice and to end foreign interference, and he took part in the Donghak Peasant Revolution of 1894.

In 1896 he killed a Japanese man at an inn at Ch'ihap'o whom he believed to be connected with the assassination of Empress Myeongseong; the man is now generally thought to have been a civilian merchant. Arrested that summer, he escaped from prison in 1898, spent time as a Buddhist monk, and in 1903 became a Christian and a teacher.

After Korea became a Japanese protectorate in 1905, Kim was arrested in 1911 in the 105-Man Incident, in which more than 700 Koreans were detained on charges of plotting to kill the Governor-General Terauchi Masatake. He was sentenced to 15 years, but pardons shortened the term and he was paroled in 1915. After the March First Movement of 1919 he left for Shanghai, arriving on 13 April, where he was made police commissioner of the Korean Provisional Government. He was its president from 1926 to 1927 and again from 1940.

In 1931 he founded the Korean Patriotic Organization, which aimed at the assassination of Japanese imperial and colonial figures and took about half of the government's budget. After the Shanghai bombing of April 1932 Japanese bodies placed bounties on him totalling 60,000 dayang, and he went into hiding. He later won support from Chiang Kai-shek's Kuomintang, and moved with the government from Nanjing to Changsha, Guangzhou and Chongqing, where he took charge of building the Korean Liberation Army.

Kim learned of Japan's surrender on 10 August 1945 and wrote that he feared Korea's voice would be weak because it had done so little in the war. He reached Gimpo Airport on 23 November and refused to dissolve the provisional government, which disappointed Syngman Rhee and the United States. In April 1948 he went to Pyongyang for unification talks with Kim Il Sung, which produced no agreement.

On 26 June 1949 Lieutenant Ahn Doo-hee shot him four times in his office; Ahn said he regarded Kim as a Soviet agent. His autobiography, the Diary of Kim Ku, is an important source for the independence movement. Kim was awarded the Order of Merit for National Foundation in South Korea in 1962 and a reunification prize by North Korea in 1990.
kim-hong-do: Kim Hongdo was a member of the Gimhae Kim clan and grew up in present-day Ansan. At the age of 7 he studied under the master Pyoam Kang Sehwang, who was then living in seclusion in Ansan. In 1766, at the age of 21, he entered royal service on Kang Sehwang's recommendation as a hwawon of the Dohwaseo, the body of official painters of the Joseon court.

In 1771 Kim painted the portrait of the Royal Heir, the future King Jeongjo, and in 1773 he assisted Byeon Sang-byeok in painting the royal portrait of King Yeongjo. His Nineteen Taoist Immortals of 1776 made his reputation, and Jeongjo, newly on the throne, commissioned many institutional paintings from him. He worked in literati and official painting as well as in genre scenes; his album Danwon pungsokdo holds a series of 25 genre paintings. His scenes of everyday life have been compared with the painters of the Dutch Golden Age, and he introduced Western painting methods, apparently learnt through the Qing dynasty, showing perspective through contrasts of colour.

Kim died in loneliness and poverty, though the circumstances, and even the year, are uncertain. He is remembered as one of the Three Wons, with Hyewon and Owon, and is often named with Owon and the 15th-century painter An Gyeon as one of the three leading painters of Joseon. The Korean Copyright Commission lists 757 paintings, 7 calligraphies and 4 moldings by him.

Ansan, where he spent his youth and learnt his craft, named its district of Danwon-gu and its annual Danwon Art Festival after him. Lee Jung-myung's novel Painter of the Wind is centred on him and Sin Yun-bok, and he was portrayed in the 2008 television series of that name and in the 2008 film Portrait of a Beauty.
kim-il-sung: Kim Il Sung was born Kim Sung Ju on 15 April 1912 near Pyongyang, then called Heijō, to the independence activist Kim Hyong-jik and Kang Pan Sok. He grew up in northeast China. North Korean sources credit him with founding the Down-with-Imperialism Union in 1926, though most scholarly sources reject this. He attended Yuwen Middle School in Jilin until 1930, and at seventeen became the youngest member of the Korean Communist Youth Association, an underground group of fewer than twenty members. Police discovered it three weeks after it formed in 1929 and jailed him for several months. He joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1931 and fought in anti-Japanese guerrilla groups.

In 1942 he was assigned to the Soviet Red Army and stayed in the Soviet Union until 1945. Some sources claim that the name Kim Il Sung had belonged to an earlier resistance leader, Kim Kyung-cheon, but the historian Andrei Lankov has argued that this is unlikely.

Captain Kim Il Sung, a 33-year-old officer of the Red Army, arrived at the port of Wonsan on 19 September 1945 after 26 years in exile. He had only eight years of formal education, all of it in Chinese, and a Soviet officer later said he was essentially created from zero. The Soviet Union designated him premier of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea on 9 September 1948. In June 1949 the Workers' Party of North Korea merged with its southern counterpart to become the Workers' Party of Korea, with Kim as chairman. By 1949 he had consolidated communist rule and begun to promote a personality cult, and the first of many statues of him appeared.

Archival material suggests that the decision to invade South Korea in 1950 was Kim's own initiative, not a Soviet one. A ceasefire was signed in 1953, and the war left North Korea devastated. Kim launched a five-year economic plan on the Soviet model, with state-owned industry and collectivised farming. In 1957 the songbun system divided the population into core, wavering and hostile classes, which decided access to education, housing and employment. In 1966 the promotion of Juche as the state ideology began, and the Monolithic Ideological System was introduced in May 1967. In 1972 North and South Korea signed the July 4 South-North Joint Statement on reunification.

Kim handed the chairmanship of the National Defense Commission to his son Kim Jong Il in 1991 and 1993. He collapsed from a heart attack on 7 July 1994 and died at 2:00 in the morning on 8 July, aged 82; his death was declared 34 hours later. He was succeeded by his son and posthumously declared Eternal President. He had developed Juche, which stressed independence, self-sustenance and self-defence and Korean nationalism.
kim-jong-il: Kim Jong Il was born on 16 February 1941 in the far east of the Soviet Union, generally agreed to be the camp of Voroshilov near Nikolsk. His mother, Kim Jong-suk, was Kim Il Sung's first wife, and the family moved to Pyongyang in 1945. He joined the Workers' Party of Korea in July 1961 and its Propaganda and Agitation Department in 1966.

After the Kapsan faction incident around 1967, the last credible challenge to Kim Il Sung's sole rule, he took part in the investigation and purges that followed, his first official duties. He became director of the department in 1973 and was formally designated his father's successor in October 1980 at the party congress, taking the title Dear Leader as a personality cult was built around him.

Kim Il Sung died on 8 July 1994 and Kim Jong Il became supreme leader. The economy struggled through the 1990s because of mismanagement and severe floods, and North Korea could not import enough to sustain industry, which brought a severe famine. He adopted the Songun, military-first, policy, making the army the central organiser of civil society. In 1996 he launched a purge named the Deepening Group Incident; some 25,000 people are thought to have been purged, about 10,000 of them executed.

South Korea's Sunshine Policy from 1998 led to Kim's meeting with Kim Dae-jung in 2000 and to the Kaesong Industrial Park in 2003, though the sinking of ROKS Cheonan and the bombardment of Yeonpyeong in 2010 ended it. In 2002 the government admitted producing nuclear weapons in violation of the 1994 Agreed Framework with the United States, and it announced an underground nuclear test on 9 October 2006.

After he failed to appear at public events in 2008, observers assumed he was ill, and he began to promote his third son, Kim Jong Un, raising him to high party posts in 2010. Kim Jong Il died of a suspected heart attack on 17 December 2011 while travelling by train, and the government announced it two days later. His funeral took place on 28 December in Pyongyang, and he was declared Eternal General Secretary of the party and Eternal Chairman of the National Defence Commission.
kim-tu-bong: Kim Tu-bong was born in 1889 in South Gyeongsang Province near Busan and was homeschooled in his early years. He moved to Seoul around 1908 and attended Bosung and other schools. There he worked closely with the linguist Chu Sigyŏng, who was beginning his study of Hangul, the script made by King Sejong in the 15th century. Kim also worked as a teacher and joined the Korea Youth organisation in 1913. In 1916 he spent much of his time compiling the Malmoi, the first Korean dictionary. He is remembered in South Korea above all for his work in establishing the Korean linguistic field, especially on Hangul.

After the March First Movement of 1919 he and other members of an independence club fled to China and in April 1919 set up a provisional government in Shanghai. There he met communism and accepted it in 1920, after first supporting the Democratic Party. In 1924 he became president of a children's education department. After the Japanese invasion of China he went with other members of the Korean government to Yan'an, headquarters of the Chinese Communist Party, where he headed the independence club.

He returned to Korea in December 1945 and settled in the north under Soviet occupation. In February 1946 he became chairman of the New People's Party, formed by the Yan'an faction, which merged that year into the Workers' Party of North Korea, and he became its first chairman. He was first head of state of North Korea, as chairman of the standing committee of the Supreme People's Assembly, from 1948 to 1957, though Kim Il Sung held real power.

After the Korean War he was purged, accused of involvement in the August Faction Incident of 1956, and disappeared without record of his fate. He is believed to have been executed or to have died in detention, perhaps in the 1960s.
kim-yu-sin: Kim Yu-sin was born in 595 in Manno county, in present-day Jincheon County, the son of General Kim Seohyeon and Lady Manmyeong, whose father was a younger brother of King Jinheung. He is said to have descended from the last ruler of Geumgwan Gaya, which would have given him a very high place in Silla's bone rank system. Much of what is known of his life comes from the account in the Samguk Sagi and a briefer record in the Samguk Yusa. He became a Hwarang warrior at 15 and was an accomplished swordsman and a Gukseon, a Hwarang leader, by the age of 18.

In 629, at 34, he was given total command of the Silla armed forces. His cousin Princess Deokman became Queen Seondeok three years later and kept him as commander in chief. During her reign he owned ten thousand private soldiers and won many battles against Baekje.

Silla was long in struggle with Baekje over territory. Baekje and Silla had once allied against Goguryeo, with Silla taking the north and Baekje the land south of the Han river, but Silla broke the alliance to claim both, and Baekje then allied with Goguryeo. When the two attacked Silla in 655, Silla joined forces with Tang China. In 660, with a Silla army of 50,000 and some 130,000 Tang troops, Kim attacked the Baekje capital, Sabi, in the Battle of Hwangsanbeol. The Baekje defenders under General Gyebaek numbered about 5,000, and Baekje, already troubled by internal politics, crumbled.

Silla and Tang forces then moved on Goguryeo from two directions and were repelled in 661, but the attack had weakened it. Another offensive in 667 destroyed Goguryeo in 668. Silla then worked to ensure that its Tang allies did not stay on the peninsula, and after hard conflicts forced them out and united the peninsula under its rule.

In 668 King Munmu gave Kim the title Taedaegakgan, and in 669 he reportedly received 142 horse farms. He died on 21 August 673, leaving ten children, and was later awarded the title King Heungmu. His second son Kim Won-sul became a general under Munmu and helped complete Silla's independence from the Tang. His sister Kim Mun-hee married King Muyeol, and his third wife was Muyeol's daughter. Many legends surround him, among them stories of kites used to carry a fire ball into the sky to restore his troops' courage and to send signals. Koreans remember him as one of their best-known generals and as the driving force of the unification. A tomb in Gyeongju is believed to be his, though scholars debate its owner.
kimigayo: The word kimi has been used for the Emperor of Japan or for one's lord since at least the Heian period, and it can also mean "my dear". Before the Nara period the emperor was often called ohkimi, "great lord", so it is disputed whether kimi in the title originally meant the emperor. The poem began with Waga Kimi wa, "my lord", and the opening was changed during the Kamakura period while the rest stayed the same.

In 1869 John William Fenton, bandmaster of a British military band in Yokohama, suggested a national anthem to Iwao Ōyama, an officer of the Satsuma domain, who chose the words and asked Fenton for a melody. The government set it aside because it lacked solemnity. In 1880 the Ministry of the Imperial Household adopted a melody by Yoshiisa Oku and Akimori Hayashi, based on a traditional mode of Japanese court music, and Franz Eckert added Western harmony.

In the Kamakura period the poem was a festive song among samurai, and in the Edo period it became popular among the people. In the later Edo period it was a common New Year song in the Ōoku, the women's quarters of Edo Castle, and in the Satsuma domain. There kimi never meant the emperor: it meant the Tokugawa shōgun, the Shimazu clan as rulers of Satsuma, a guest of honour, or all members of a drinking party. After the Meiji Restoration samurai from Satsuma controlled the imperial government and adopted the song as the national anthem.

By 1893 it was part of public school ceremonies. Around the turn of the 20th century the Christian leader Uchimura Kanzō argued that it was not the anthem of Japan, because it praised the emperor, whereas an anthem should express the feelings of the people. During the Second World War schoolchildren in Japan and its colonies were ordered to sing it and salute Emperor Hirohito every morning.

After 1945 the song remained the de facto anthem. The Ministry of Education gave it no new meaning, which allowed it to be taken as meaning the Japanese people, but it did not formally renounce the prewar one. The Act on National Flag and Anthem passed the House of Representatives by 403 votes to 86 on 22 July 1999 and was enacted on 13 August. Prime Minister Keizō Obuchi said that kimi indicates the emperor as the symbol of the state and the unity of the people, and opposition parties objected. No official translation of the title or words has been set in law.
kimmeridge: Kimmeridge lies on the Isle of Purbeck, about 4.5 miles south of Wareham and 7 miles west of Swanage, on a slope between the English Channel and a curve of hills. Most of the parish lies on Kimmeridge Clay, with Portland stone on Smedmore Hill and Swyre Head. The clay holds bands of bituminous shale and dolomite that form flat ledges in Kimmeridge Bay at low tide. The village gives its name to the Kimmeridgian stage of the Late Jurassic, and the clay is one of the source rocks of the oil and gas of the Wessex and North Sea basins.

In the Iron Age and under Roman rule the black shale, known as blackstone or Kimmeridge coal, was turned on lathes into armlets; the waste discs, found at several sites, were taken by 18th-century antiquaries for coins and called coal money. The Romans also burned the shale to boil sea water for salt. In the medieval period the parish held three settlements, Kimmeridge, Little Kimmeridge and Smedmore, of which only Kimmeridge survives as a village of any size.

Lord Mountjoy tried and failed to make alum here in the mid 16th century. In the first half of the 17th century Sir William Clavell, who moved into his new Smedmore House in 1632, tried salt, then alum, until London merchants holding the sole right from Charles I seized his property and destroyed the works; a port and a glassworks, made with Sir Robert Mansell and Abraham Bigo, failed too, and his pier was wrecked by a storm in 1745. An Act of Parliament of 1847 allowed tramways to carry shale to Weymouth for oil, varnish and dyes, though its sulphurous smell limited its use. In 1959 an oil well was sunk above the bay; it produced 200,000 tonnes between 1961 and 1974.

Kimmeridge's coast is part of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site, designated in 2001, and the parish lies within the Dorset National Landscape. The parish church was mostly rebuilt in 1872 but keeps parts from the 12th century, and the Clavell Tower above Hen Cliff was moved back from the eroding cliff edge. The Museum of Jurassic Marine Life, which opened in October 2016, shows Steve Etches's collection of more than 2,000 fossils.
kimpa-vita: Kimpa Vita was born near Mount Kibangu into a family of the Kongo nobility, probably of the class called Mwana Kongo, and her father was a regional commander of the king's army. Her rank allowed her to study as an nganda marinda, a kind of religious medium, and she was baptised at her father's wish. Some modern scholars link her to King António I of Kongo, whose Kikongo name was Vita a Nkanga.

At her birth the kingdom was divided by the civil wars that followed the death of António I at the Battle of Mbwila in 1665. The old capital, São Salvador (present-day Mbanza Kongo), had been abandoned in 1678, and rival pretenders held different parts of the country.

She lived among colonists whom King Pedro IV of Kongo had sent to reoccupy São Salvador, many of them followers of an old prophet, Appolonia Mafuta.
