After her visions she gave away her possessions, destroyed nkisi charms as false idols and also destroyed non-Kongolese Catholic objects. Before Pedro IV she denounced him for failing to restore the kingdom, and accused the Italian Capuchin Bernardo da Gallo of not wanting black saints in Kongo. Pedro's rival João II at Mbula also refused to listen.

In São Salvador, occupied in 1705, she lived in the ruined cathedral as thousands of mostly peasant followers resettled the city. Noble converts followed, among them Pedro Constantinho da Silva Kibenga, commander of one of Pedro IV's armies, and Pedro's own wife Hipolita. Her prayer the Salve Antoniana, adapted from the Salve Regina, taught that God cared for believers' intentions rather than sacraments or good works, and called Saint Anthony a second God. She taught that black people came from the bark of a fig tree, and her followers wore cloth made from it.

Although she preached chastity, she became pregnant by a man named João Barro and hid the child. Kinlaza envoys found her near her home town when they heard it cry. She was tried under Kongo law as a witch and heretic, with the counsel of the Capuchin friars Bernardo da Gallo and Lorenzo da Lucca, and burned at the temporary capital of Evululu. Lorenzo spared her son and named him Jerónimo.

Her followers held that she was still alive, and the movement's political force was broken only when Pedro IV took São Salvador in 1709. Eighteenth-century Kongo religious art often shows Jesus as an African and gives a prominent place to Saint Anthony as Toni Malau. Some see Kimbanguism, Matswanism and Tokoism as the movement's successors.
kincardineshire: Roughly triangular in shape, the county consists of the largely flat Strathmore area running parallel with the coast and hillier, forested country in the interior, part of the Grampian Mountains. Its highest point is Mount Battock, at 778 m, on the border with Angus. Its rivers include Cowie Water, Carron Water, Bervie Water and the lower reaches of the River Dee. Besides Stonehaven, its burghs were Banchory, Inverbervie and Laurencekirk. The ancient Causey Mounth road crossed its high ground as the only medieval route from the coast south of Aberdeen to the Bridge of Dee.

Anciently the area was the province of Mearns, a name from the Scottish Gaelic for the stewartry, since it was governed by a mere steward (maer) rather than a great steward (mormaer). A sheriff is known to have existed by the 1160s, holding his courts in the town of Kincardine, near Fettercairn, where there was a royal castle. In 1296 King John Balliol wrote his letter of surrender to Edward I of England from Kincardine Castle, after the short war that began the Wars of Scottish Independence.

By 1600 Kincardine was in decline, and the judges complained of its poor facilities and its place away from the centre of the shire. The Stonehaven Act 1600 of the Parliament of Scotland moved the courts to Stonehaven, and by the mid-19th century no trace of the old county town remained. During the Wars of the Three Kingdoms the Honours of Scotland were kept at Dunnottar Castle and later at Kinneff, both in the county, and its coat of arms later showed the crown, sceptre and sword. An elected county council first met on 22 May 1890 at the Stonehaven Sheriff Court.

The county ceased to be an administrative area in 1975, when it became part of the Grampian region. Since 1996 most of it has lain within the Aberdeenshire council area, the parish of Nigg excepted, which is in Aberdeen City. It survives as a lieutenancy area and a registration county, and the name lives on in Aberdeenshire Council's Kincardine and Mearns area committee.
king-cheng-of-chu: King Cheng's personal name was Xiong Yun. In 672 BCE his older brother Du'ao, then ruler of Chu, tried to have him killed. Xiong Yun escaped to the state of Sui, and with Sui's help he attacked and killed Du'ao and succeeded him as king of Chu.

During his reign Chu annexed the state of Huang in the summer of 648 BCE. His wife was Zheng Mao. The Shiji gives a detailed account of the end of his reign. In the forty-sixth year of his reign, 626 BCE, Cheng wished to make his son Shangchen crown prince. The lingyin, the title of Chu's prime minister, Zishang, advised against it: there were many contenders, and if the king later changed his mind a disturbance would follow; Shangchen, he warned, was cruel and fierce. The king did not heed him and made Shangchen crown prince.

Soon the king did change his mind, and rumours spread that Shangchen would be deposed in favour of another son, Zhi. Unsure whether to believe them, Shangchen followed his tutor's advice to hold a banquet for the king's favourite concubine and treat her with disrespect. Angered, she told him it was fitting that the king meant to kill him and make Zhi crown prince. Asked by his tutor whether he could serve under Zhi or go into exile, the prince said no to both, and yes to whether he could do something great.

In the tenth month Shangchen led the palace troops to surround the king and force him to take his own life. According to the Shiji, Cheng asked to eat a bear's paw before he died and was refused. He hanged himself on the day dingwei, and Shangchen took the throne as King Mu of Chu.
king-cheng-of-zhou: King Cheng, whose personal name was Ji Song, was the son of King Wu of Zhou and Queen Yi Jiang. He came to the throne while still a child, at a turbulent time. King Wu had not long before defeated Di Xin at the Battle of Muye, and the new dynasty had yet to assert itself. His paternal uncle Ji Dan, the Duke of Zhou, feared that the Shang might rise again under a weak young ruler and became regent, supervising the government for several years.

During the regency the Duke of Zhou established the capital at Luoyang and taught the king how to run the state. The Duke also wrote treatises for the young king, some of which are recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian. According to the Shuo Yuan, the king once played at giving the State of Tang to the Duke, who held that a king must keep his word and was then formally enfeoffed. When the king fell ill as a child, the Duke is said to have cut off his hair, thrown it in the Yellow River and prayed that any offence against the deities be charged to himself.

The regency was contested. The king's uncles Shu Xian of Guan and Shu Du of Cai, with Wu Geng, the son of Di Xin, thought the regency should be theirs. They conspired together and began the Rebellion of the Three Guards, which the Duke of Zhou put down through campaigns in the east. The Bamboo Annals records that Wu Geng was defeated and killed, the Shang people were relocated to Wey and then to Luoyi, and Chengzhou was established. In the seventh year the Duke stepped down from the regency, and in the eighth the king did true governing for the first time.

Sima Qian tells that when the Duke of Zhou fell ill he asked to be buried at Chengzhou, to show he had never left the king's side. King Cheng did not dare treat him as a subject and buried him at Bi, beside King Wen. A severe storm then struck the autumn harvest. The king and his ministers put on ritual attire and opened a chest holding the Duke's record of his offering of himself for King Wu. The king wept, and the storm stopped.

Near the end of his life King Cheng doubted whether his son Ji Zhao was ready to inherit. Remembering the Duke's care of him, he ordered the Duke of Shao and the Duke of Bi to instruct the heir. The testament known as the Dying Emperor's Will is recorded in the Book of Documents. Ji Zhao succeeded him as King Kang of Zhou.
king-helu-of-wu: Helü's given name was Guang, and before he took the throne he was known as Prince Guang. He was the son of King Yumei of Wu and the nephew of King Liao, who held the throne before him. The prince took the Chu exile Wu Zixu into his entourage, and when he resolved to seize power, Wu Zixu introduced him to Zhuan Zhu, the man who carried out the killing of King Liao.

Once king, Helü gave Wu Zixu charge of designing and building his great city, which forms the basis of the old town of present-day Suzhou. In the campaign of 506 BCE against Chu, Wu won five battles, among them the Battle of Boju, and took the Chu capital Ying. During the sack of the city Helü attempted to sexually assault the Dowager Queen of Chu, who fought him off with a knife and rebuked him, and he left in shame.

Chu then asked the state of Qin for help. After Qin defeated the Wu vanguard, its general Fugai, a younger brother of Helü, rose in rebellion. Helü beat Fugai but was forced to leave Chu, and Fugai later settled in Chu. The king's last war began when he heard that Yunchang of Yue had died and invaded Yue; he was wounded in the fighting and died of his injuries, telling his son to avenge him.

Helü had three sons, Bo, Shan and Fuchai. Bo was at first his heir but died before his father, so the throne passed to Fuchai, who succeeded in 495 BCE, later annexed Yue and captured its king, Goujian. Helü's life is told in the Records of the Grand Historian. A text called Gailu, found in 1983 among eight texts from Tomb 247 at Zhangjiashan in Jingzhou, Hubei, presents a dialogue between Helü and Wu Zixu; a manuscript from Dunhuang gives a parallel conversation but attributes it to Duke Jing of Qi and Yan Ying.
king-huai-of-chu: Xiong Huai succeeded his father, King Wei of Chu, who died in 329 BCE, and the state of Wei used the moment to take Mount Xing. His general Zhao Yang later defeated Wei at Xiangling, seized eight cities and advanced against Qi. In 318 BCE King Huai led a coalition with Yan, Han and Wei against Qin, which ended in the disastrous Battle of Hangu Pass.

In 313 BCE the Qin strategist Zhang Yi offered him 600 li of Shang territory if he broke with Qi; when King Huai did so, Qin handed over only six li. He sent the general Qu Kai with 100,000 troops against Qin, but they were crushed at Danyang, Qu Kai was captured and 80,000 of his men were beheaded. A second offensive with the whole army failed at Lantian, Qin took Hanzhong and then Shaoling in 311 BCE, and Chu began to decline.

By 306 BCE Chu, allied with Qi, had taken the Yue capital, killed King Wujiang and conquered the land from Wu to Zhejiang. When Qi, Han and Wei besieged Chu, King Huai sent Crown Prince Heng to Qin as a hostage to win its aid; the prince killed a Qin official in 302 BCE and fled home, and Qin and its allies attacked Chu in the years that followed.

Invited by King Zhao of Qin to treat for peace at Wuguan, he went against the advice of his ministers Zhao Ju and Qu Yuan and was detained. He refused King Zhao's demand to cede Wu and Qianzhong, and Chu enthroned Crown Prince Heng as King Qingxiang. In 297 BCE he escaped during an attack on Qin, but Zhao refused him entry and Qin pursuers caught him on the way to Wei.

After he died of illness, Qin sent his body back, and the people of Chu were said to mourn him as if for kin. The poem Li Sao in the Chu ci is thought to reflect the relationship between Qu Yuan, or a poet writing in his persona, and the king. A grandson was later made King of Chu under the same regnal name as the Qin dynasty fell into chaos.
king-huiwen-of-qin: King Huiwen, personal name Ying Si and also known as Lord Huiwen of Qin, was the son of Duke Xiao of Qin, ruler of a state of the Eastern Zhou period. As crown prince in his youth he committed a crime, and the minister Shang Yang, then carrying out his Legalist reforms of Qin's laws, insisted that the heir be punished regardless of his rank. Duke Xiao agreed. The prince was banished from the palace, and his tutors were punished for neglecting his education: Prince Qian, the duke's elder brother, had his nose cut off, and Gongsun Gu was branded on the face by tattooing.

Si was believed to bear Shang Yang a personal grudge, and once he came to the throne he had him put to death on charges of treason, while keeping the system his father and the minister had built. Under his rule Qin grew very strong militarily and repeatedly invaded its neighbours. The conquest of Shu and Ba in the Sichuan basin in 316 BCE aimed to annex and colonise weaker independent kingdoms rather than confront the more advanced eastern states, nominally under the Zhou dynasty, with their large armies.

The strategist Gongsun Yan, a student of Guiguzi, persuaded five of the other six major states to ally against Qin. His fellow student Zhang Yi entered Huiwen's service as prime minister and broke up the alliance by sowing discord among the five.

Huiwen ruled Qin for 27 years and died in 311 BCE. His son by Queen Huiwen of Wei, Crown Prince Dang, succeeded him as King Wu of Qin and reigned from 310 to 307 BCE. Another son, Prince Ji, born to Queen Dowager Xuan of the Mi clan of Chu, later ruled as King Zhaoxiang of Qin from 306 to 251 BCE. Two other sons held Shu as marquises after its conquest, Prince Tong from 313 to 311 BCE and Prince Yun from 308 to 301 BCE.
king-james-version: The King James Version was the third translation into English approved by the Church of England, after the Great Bible of 1535 and the Bishops' Bible of 1568. The Geneva Bible, produced in Switzerland in 1560, proved more popular with the laity, but its footnotes represented a Calvinistic Puritanism. In 1525 William Tyndale began translating the New Testament, the first printed Bible in English. He was executed for heresy, but his work became the ultimate basis for all later renditions into Early Modern English.

King James convened the Hampton Court Conference in January 1604, and it proposed a new version in response to problems the Puritans perceived in the earlier ones. The translators were told to follow the ecclesiology of the Church of England and to avoid marginal notes where possible, since the Geneva Bible's notes had been criticised as Puritan and anti-monarchical.

The translators were all members of the Church of England, and all but Sir Henry Savile were clergy. They worked in six committees, two each at the University of Oxford, the University of Cambridge and Westminster, and included scholars with Puritan sympathies as well as high churchmen. Forty unbound copies of the 1602 Bishops' Bible were printed so that each committee could record its changes in the margins. For the New Testament the translators used the Textus Receptus, the Old Testament was revised from the Bishops' Bible with reference to the Masoretic Text, and the Apocrypha was rendered from the Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate.

Robert Barker, the King's Printer, published the first edition in 1611 as a complete folio, sold looseleaf for ten shillings or bound for twelve. Barker fell into debt and sub-leased his privilege to Bonham Norton and John Bill, and bitter financial disputes followed. No record of the authorisation survives, because the Privy Council registers for 1600 to 1613 were destroyed by fire. The version replaced the Bishops' Bible as the lectern Bible in parish churches, and in the 1662 Book of Common Prayer it supplanted the Great Bible in the Epistle and Gospel readings.

By the first half of the 18th century it was effectively unchallenged in Anglican and other English Protestant churches. Misprints and varying modernised texts became a scandal by the mid-18th century, and the Oxford standard text of 1769 became the basis of almost all later printings, often without the Apocrypha. With stereotype printing in the early 19th century the Bible became the most widely printed book in history.
king-kang-of-zhou: King Kang, personal name Ji Zhao, was a son of King Cheng. According to Sima Qian, King Cheng feared near the end of his life that his son would be unfit to rule, and ordered the Duke of Shao and the Duke of Bi to teach him and assist at his enthronement. The Book of Documents preserves this charge as The Dying Emperor's Will: King Cheng died the next day, and after the mourning the new king received a jade tablet commanding him to follow the great statutes and honour the teachings of King Wen and King Wu.

At his crowning King Kang made the Announcement of Kang, also kept in the Book of Documents, which urges study of the better Shang rulers, careful deliberation of important legal cases and a warning that the Mandate of Heaven can be lost. He continued his father's policy and expanded Zhou territory in the north and west. His queen, Wang Jiang, seems to have played a large part in managing the royal treasury, assisting campaigns and rewarding officials.

The Bamboo Annals record the lords paying homage at Fengjing in his first year, the standardising of music in his third, and a southern tour to Lushan on the Jiang River in his sixteenth, and place his death in his twenty-sixth year. The Da Yu ding, cast in his 23rd year, records a speech at Zongzhou in which he praised his predecessors and appointed Yu, grandson of Nangong Kuo, to oversee the army, granting him 659 charioteers and peasants and 1,050 servants. The Zuo Zhuan says he gave the people rest and set up his maternal uncles in fiefs as a barrier for Zhou.

Later rulers such as King Xuan of Zhou looked back to his reign as one of the dynasty's brighter days. In the Han dynasty some scholars held that the Classic of Poetry began in his time and blamed his ministers as lazy and corrupt, while Wang Chong replied that Zhou reached its peak under him. The Book of the Later Han claims the poem Guan Ju was a gentle satire on the king coming late to court, and notes his good relations with the Sushen, who presented stone arrows. He was succeeded by his son, King Zhao.
king-nan-of-zhou: King Nan, personal name Ji Yan and less often called King Yin, was the son of King Shenjing and grandson of King Xian, and the 37th king of the Zhou dynasty. His reign of fifty-nine years was the longest of the dynasty and of all pre-imperial China. By then even the remaining crown land was split between two rival lords: Western Zhou, which held the capital Wangcheng, and Eastern Zhou, centred at Chengzhou. How much ritual standing he kept is disputed: the feudal states took royal titles for themselves, yet inscriptions and some accounts in the Records of the Grand Historian suggest he was still respected as the Son of Heaven.

At the start of his reign he moved the capital from Chengzhou to Wangcheng. Foreign powers then invaded the royal lands repeatedly, beginning with the attack of the State of Qin on Yiyang in 307 BCE. The two Zhou courts survived through shifting alliances and schemes, such as the plan of the Scribe Yan to make Qin suspect Chu while Han ceded land to Zhou. Summoned to the Qin court to debate an attack on the Han city of Nanyang, Nan instead worked with Han to block the road and avoid the war.

The lords of Western and Eastern Zhou also fought each other. Han, nominally allied to Western Zhou, looted Wangcheng and the royal palace. In 273 BCE Ma Fan enlisted King Anxi of Wei to build a fortification wall that would protect the Nine Tripod Cauldrons, the emblems of royal authority. Qin spared the king's land for a time, its rulers believing that destroying the domain of the Son of Heaven would harm their name, and Nan and his officials even reported to Qin on the armies of Han, Wei and Zhao.

When Qin occupied the Han town of Fushu near the old capital, Nan and Western Zhou joined an alliance against it, and Western Zhou's attack was driven back. Nan travelled to Xianyang to submit to King Zhaoxiang of Qin, was made Duke of West Zhou, and died soon after while held in Wangcheng. Qin took the Nine Tripod Cauldrons and exiled his heir Ji Wen to Danhu. In Eastern Zhou, Duke Wen was proclaimed king but recognised nowhere else; he and Nan's son Ji Zhao were defeated in 251 and 249 BCE. The Qin scholars of the Lüshi Chunqiu wrote that there was no greater turmoil than the absence of the Son of Heaven, a title later taken by Qin Shi Huang.
king-of-the-universe: The Akkadian form of the title, šar kiššatim, derives from the Sumerian city of Kish. In Sumerian legend Kish was where kingship was lowered from heaven after the flood, and the city was held to have a kind of primacy over the others. In the Early Dynastic periods rival city-states such as Ur, Uruk, Lagash and Umma fought for standing, and the Mesopotamians believed their land to be the whole world, bounded by the Persian Gulf, the lower sea, and the Mediterranean, the upper sea. Rulers such as Lugal-zage-si of Uruk already claimed to rule from sea to sea.

Sargon of Akkad, once cupbearer to Ur-Zababa of Kish, seized power there and founded the Akkadian Empire. He and his successors used the forms lugal ki-sár-ra and lugal kiš-ki without ruling Kish itself, and from their time the old title King of Kish should be understood as King of the Universe. Sargon's grandson Naram-Sin added King of the Four Corners of the World.

Earlier rulers of Assyria, among them Shamshi-Adad I and Ashur-uballit I, used the title from time to time, and kings of Eshnunna, Babylon and Mari claimed it against them. It was most prominent under the kings of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, though from Sarduri I onwards the kings of Urartu took it too, to claim equality.

The title is not attested for every Neo-Assyrian king and sometimes appears only years into a reign, so it may have had to be earned; Stephanie Dalley proposed in 1998 that seven successful campaigns were needed. Of the Neo-Babylonian kings only Nabonidus used it in his own inscriptions. Cyrus the Great adopted it after taking Babylon in 539 BCE, and its last recorded use is on the Antiochus Cylinder of the Seleucid king Antiochus I Soter.

The Greek counterpart, kosmōkrator, was applied to gods such as Zeus, Helios and Pan, to the planets in astrology, and to rulers: Quintus Curtius Rufus often calls Alexander the Great by it, and from the 2nd century CE it was used of Roman emperors. In Jewish writings king of the universe, melekh haolam, became a title of God, and traditional blessings begin with it; Christians use it for God, and Islam speaks of God as rabbi l-'alamin, Lord of the Universe. In Ephesians and later Christian writings kosmōkrator came to name evil spirits and the Devil.
king-philips-war: About 20,000 Puritans came to New England in the Great Migration of 1620 to 1640, mainly to Plymouth Colony and the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Plymouth claimed rights to all Wampanoag country through early alliances with leaders such as Squanto and Massasoit, a claim that rested on misreading Native leadership, since other leaders such as Weetamoo held territorial claims of their own. Massasoit's younger son Metacom, whom the English called Philip, became sachem in 1662 after the deaths of his father and his brother Wamsutta. He distrusted the colonists and abandoned his father's alliance after repeated violations of it.

Tensions rose after the colonists insisted that the peace agreement of 1671 include the surrender of Native guns. In 1675 three Wampanoags were hanged in Plymouth Colony for the murder of John Sassamon, a Christian Wampanoag schoolmaster and interpreter who had reported that Metacom planned attacks.

On 20 June 1675 a band of Pokanokets attacked homesteads at Swansea, probably without Metacom's approval, and on 24 June launched a full attack there. A colonial expedition destroyed the Wampanoag town at Mount Hope on 28 June. Nipmucs ambushed Thomas Wheeler's party in August and besieged Brookfield, and on 12 September killed at least 40 militiamen and 17 teamsters at Bloody Brook. They burned nearly all of Springfield on 5 October.

In November 1675 a force of 1,000 militia and 150 Native allies under Governor Josiah Winslow attacked the Narragansetts, who had sheltered Wampanoag fighters and families, and killed an estimated 600 in the Great Swamp Fight. The Narragansetts under Canonchet then joined the war. Native forces attacked Lancaster in February 1676 and burned Providence on 29 March. The Mohawk, traditional rivals of the Algonquian people, struck Metacom's winter camp, and Native allies began deserting him. Captain Benjamin Church tracked him to Mount Hope, where John Alderman shot him on 12 August 1676.

More than 1,000 colonists and 3,000 Native people died. More than half of New England's towns were attacked and many were destroyed. Hundreds of Native captives were enslaved, and most were shipped to slave markets as far away as Bermuda, Barbados, Spain, Portugal and the Azores. The Wampanoags were left effectively landless. Metacom's body was beheaded and cut up, and his head was displayed in Plymouth for a generation.

Fighting by the Abenaki continued in the borderlands of New England and Acadia, and conflict in northern New England lasted for decades. Many historians regard it as the deadliest war in colonial American history, and the colonists, who faced it without help from any European government, began to form a group identity distinct from England. Washington Irving wrote an essay on Metacom in 1820.
king-ping-of-zhou: King Ping, personal name Ji Yijiu, was the son of King You of Zhou and Queen Shen, and is counted as the 13th king of the Zhou dynasty. King You became enamoured of his concubine Bao Si, made her queen and her son Bofu his heir, and exiled Queen Shen and Ji Yijiu. Queen Shen's father, the Marquess of Shen, then joined the Quanrong nomads and neighbouring states against King You, who was killed with Bofu at the Battle of Mount Li, while Bao Si was captured.

In the traditional account Ji Yijiu then took the throne, while at about the same time Ji Han, Duke of Guo, raised Ji Yuchen to the throne as King Xie of Zhou, so that Zhou had two kings until Marquis Wen of Jin killed King Xie in 750 BCE. The Xinian manuscript challenges this story: it suggests that many regional lords first accepted King Xie rather than King Ping, that no king was generally recognised for nine years after Xie's death, and that Marquis Wen recognised Ping only in 741 BCE and helped him move to Chengzhou three years later.

The move of the capital east from Haojing to Luoyang ended the Western Zhou and began the Eastern Zhou and the Spring and Autumn period. King Ping is the first Zhou king named in the chronological account of the Zuo Zhuan. His second son, Prince Hu, served as a hostage of Duke Zhuang of Zheng.

King Ping died on 16 April 720 BCE. His eldest son, Crown Prince Xiefu, was the father of his successor, King Huan of Zhou. More than fourteen centuries later Wu Zetian, the Tang dynasty's empress regnant, claimed descent from King Ping through his youngest son, Prince Wu, and renamed her dynasty Zhou; the name reverted to Tang after her death.
king-wei-of-qi: King Wei, personal name Tian Yinqi, reigned from 356 BCE to 320 BCE and was the first ruler of Qi to style himself king. Later stories present him as a judicious ruler. When his spies reported again and again that his general Zhangzi had gone over to Qin, he refused to believe it, and soon word came of a great Qi victory and of the king of Qin's apology. Another story tells that he promised rewards to all who criticised his faults: at first his doorway looked like a marketplace, but after a year no one had any complaint left to bring, and the states of Yan, Zhao, Han and Wei came to his court.

His commander Tian Ji brought to Qi the strategist Sun Bin, whose knees had been mutilated in the state of Wei at the instigation of his rival Pang Juan. Because Sun Bin could not ride, he declined the actual command of the army, but he helped devise the strategy of Qi's victory at the Battle of Maling in 342 BCE, which considerably weakened Wei and in which Pang Juan died. Late in his reign King Wei sent armies against Qin and Zhao.

In the Intrigues of the Warring States the strategist Su Qin is quoted as calling Kings Wei and Xuan of Qi the worthiest rulers of their age, with great power, broad lands, wealthy states and strong troops. King Wei appears in Sun Bin's Art of War, where he and Tian Ji question Sun Bin on strategy and tactics. He cast the ritual bronze vessel known as the Chen Hou Yinqi dui, which bears the earliest attestation of the Yellow Emperor. His eldest son, Crown Prince Pijiang, succeeded him as King Xuan of Qi, and his second son, Tian Ying, Lord Jingguo, served as prime minister of Qi and was the father of Lord Mengchang.
king-wen-of-zhou: Ji Chang, later called King Wen, was the son of Tairen and of Ji Li, the Elder of Zhou, a vassal clan of the Shang kingdom along the Wei River in present-day Shaanxi. In the late 12th century BCE the Shang king Wen Ding is said to have betrayed and executed Ji Li, leaving the young Chang as Elder of the Zhou lineage. The Mencius calls him one of the western barbarians, a phrase commentators read as describing him as close to the Xirong and other non-Huaxia tribes.

According to the Annals of Zhou in the Records of the Grand Historian, he ruled with benevolence, respected the old and welcomed counsellors, among them Jiang Ziya, and mediated quarrels among the regional lords.

The Shang king Di Xin, fearing Wen's growing power, imprisoned him at Youli after the Marquis of Chong slandered him. His eldest son Bo Yikao was executed when he went to plead for his release. Officials such as San Yisheng and Hong Yao gave Di Xin many gifts, and he freed Wen and invested him as Overlord of the West.

Wen then began, in the traditional account, to plot against Di Xin. He settled a land dispute between the states of Yu and Rui, hired Jiang Ziya as military counsellor, repelled the Quanrong and campaigned in turn against Mixu, Li, E and Chong. By then he held about two thirds of the whole kingdom as possessions or sworn allies, and he moved his capital from Mount Qi to Feng.

He is credited with arranging the eight trigrams into the sixty-four hexagrams of the I Ching and with writing the judgments appended to each. He married Taisi, who bore him ten sons and a daughter, among them Ji Fa, later King Wu.

Wen died in 1050 BCE before he could cross the Ford of Meng, although other sources suggest he died in battle against the Shang. Tradition placed his burial at Cheng, near present-day Xianyang. Four years later his second son Fa crushed the Shang at Muye and founded the Zhou dynasty, naming his father Wen, now read as the Cultured. Many of the odes of the Classic of Poetry praise him, and Confucius counted him a great hero. Tradition holds that Heaven gave him the Mandate of Heaven because the virtue of the Shang kings had declined; in 1059 BCE a rare clustering of five planets and an apparition of Halley's comet were seen, and one or more may have been read as a sign.
king-williams-town: Qonce, formerly King William's Town, lies on the banks of the Buffalo River in the Eastern Cape province of South Africa, about 60 kilometres northwest of the Indian Ocean port of East London. It stands 389 metres above sea level at the foot of the Amathole Mountains, in an area known for its agriculture, and has around 35,000 inhabitants. It forms part of the Buffalo City Metropolitan Municipality. The town has one of the oldest post offices in the country, developed by missionaries led by Charles Brownlee.

For thousands of years the area was roamed by Bushman bands and then used as grazing by the nomadic Khoikhoi, who called the Buffalo River Qonce. Xhosa people lived alongside the Khoikhoi and eventually took over the land after Queen Hoho lost a war with King Ngqika kaMlawu. Sir Benjamin d'Urban founded King William's Town in May 1835, during the Xhosa War of that year, on the site of the kraal of the minor chief Dyani Tyatyu, and named it after William IV. It was abandoned in December 1836 and reoccupied in 1846.

The town was the capital of British Kaffraria from the territory's creation in 1847 until its incorporation into the Cape Colony in 1865, and its local government was styled a borough, which was unique in the colony. It was also declared the provincial capital of Queen Adelaide's Province in the 1830s. Many colonists in the neighbouring districts descend from members of the British German Legion, disbanded after the Crimean War and given homes in the Cape Colony, which explains settlement names such as Berlin, Hamburg, Potsdam and Stutterheim.

On 5 May 1877 the Cape Government of Prime Minister John Molteno opened the first railway, linking the town with East London and with the Xhosa lands inland. With this direct railway the town became an important entrepôt for trade with the Xhosa people throughout Kaffraria. In a referendum held on 19 January 1981 by the municipality, the result was overwhelmingly against incorporation into the Ciskei. The Eastern Cape government announced a new name in September 2020, and the town officially became Qonce on 21 February 2021.

The local economy has long rested on cattle and sheep ranching, and the town has an industrial base producing textiles, soap, candles, sweets, cartons and clothing. Its nearness to the provincial capital Bhisho has brought development since 1994. The Amathole Museum in the centre displays Huberta, one of the furthest travelling hippopotamuses in South Africa. A nature reserve of 108 hectares, established in 1973, lies on the outskirts.
king-wu-of-chu: Also known by the personal name Xiong Che, he was the second son of Xiao'ao and brother of the previous ruler, Fenmao, whom he is rumoured to have murdered in 740 BCE to take the throne. He ruled at first as viscount. He married Deng Man, a daughter of the ruler of Deng, made Dou Bobi, son of Ruo'ao, his prime minister, and appointed his son Qu Xia as Mo'ao.

As Chu's power grew, he became dissatisfied with the title of viscount. In the summer of 704 BCE, the thirty-seventh year of his reign and the time of King Huan of Zhou, he called the leaders of the neighbouring vassal states to a meeting at Shenlu. Ba, Pu, Deng, Jiao, Luo, Zhen, Shen, Er, Yun and Jiang sent representatives; only Huang and Sui stayed away. His minister Wei Zhang went to Huang to rebuke it, while the king and Qu Xia attacked Sui and defeated it at the Battle of Suqi, where the minister Dou Dan captured the chariot of the Marquess of Sui.
Chu was one of the few states, with Wu and Yue, whose rulers styled themselves kings before the Warring States period, and all later rulers of Chu kept the title.

In 700 BCE Chu defeated Jiao, which became its vassal. The next year Qu Xia attacked Luo, underestimated the enemy, was trapped between Lu Rong and the Luo army, and after a heavy defeat hanged himself at Huangyu. The king took responsibility and pardoned the surviving soldiers, although he had already ordered their right feet cut off.

In 690 BCE he led a punitive expedition against Sui. After crossing the Han River he fell suddenly ill, sat down under a tree and died soon after. The prime minister Dou Qi, son of Dou Dan, held no funeral and led the army on as planned; when it reached the Sui capital, its rulers submitted and swore allegiance to Chu. Only after the army had recrossed the Han River was the funeral held. His son Xiong Zi succeeded him as King Wen of Chu.
king-wu-of-zhou: King Wu, whose personal name was Ji Fa, was the second son of Ji Chang, later titled King Wen of Zhou, and Tai Si. His older brother Bo Yikao was passed over; modern scholarship links this to an ancient tradition in which younger brothers inherited. Later accounts that Di Xin killed Bo Yikao by lingchi appear only centuries after the events and are very unlikely to be historical. Wu succeeded his father as ruler of the Predynastic Zhou around 1050 BCE, and worked with his father-in-law Jiang Ziya to complete the overthrow of the Shang king Di Xin, alleged to be a cruel and inept tyrant.

The chronology of his reign is disputed. In his ninth year he marched to the Mengjin ford on the Yellow River, where he met more than 800 elders; judging the time unpropitious, he said that the Mandate of Heaven was not yet known and did not attack. In 1046 BCE, leading a coalition that included eight other states, he fought the Battle of Muye. The account says Di Xin deployed 700,000 men, but many Shang soldiers defected and the army was destroyed. Di Xin is said to have set the Deer Terrace Pavilion on fire and died in it, and the Shang capital Yin was captured.

Wu allowed Wu Geng, a Shang heir, to keep a state and Shang religious practices, which later became the state of Song. He moved his court from Feng to the nearby Hao and gave territories to his younger brothers and allied clans: Jiang Ziya at Qi, Duke Dan of Zhou at Qufu, which became Lu, and the Duke of Shao at Yan. His brothers in Guan, Cai and Huo, known as the Three Guards, were placed near Song to watch the Shang royal family.

Wu fell ill in his fourteenth year, and Duke Dan of Zhou composed a prayer for his health. He died about three years after the conquest, in the winter, and his death provoked rebellions against his young heir King Cheng and the regent Ji Dan, including one by three of his brothers allied with Wu Geng. The tomb once identified as his, in Xianyang, Shaanxi, is too recent to be Zhou and is more likely Han. Later Confucians regard Wu as a virtuous ruler, and his overthrow of the Shang is a prominent example of the Mandate of Heaven.
king-wuling-of-zhao: King Wuling, personal name Zhao Yong, was the son of Marquess Su and came to the throne in 325 BCE, about halfway through the Warring States period. Between 325 and 323 BCE he and the rulers of Han, Wei, Yan and Zhongshan declared themselves kings, but after a great defeat by Qin in 318 BCE he reasoned that without a king's power he should not use the title. In the early years of his reign Zhao was harassed by the Donghu, the Linhu, the Loufan and the Beidi, nomadic herding peoples, which may have inspired his later reforms.

In 307 BCE he ordered commanders, the court and the army to adopt the Hu style of dress, trousers, belt, boots and fur caps and clothing, in place of robes, and formed a cavalry trained in the charge and in horse archery. Conservatives in the royal family objected, among them his uncle Lord Cheng, who stayed away from court. The king answered that there was not only one way to rule the world, wore the new clothes at court and gave Lord Cheng a suit of them, until he relented.

The same year Zhao took several cities of Zhongshan. In 306 BCE an expedition to the north made the kings of the Loufan and Linhu submit, their lands placed under a governor of Dai, and their warriors became divisions of his army. In 304 BCE Zhao took the upper reaches of the Yellow River from the Hezong and Xiu, and in 302 BCE he created the prefectures of Yunzhong and Jiuyuan there.

In 299 BCE he abdicated in favour of his younger son, the twelve-year-old Zhao He, who became King Huiwen of Zhao, but remained the real ruler as Zhufu, the Lord Father; he even visited Qin in secret disguised as a Zhao envoy. In 295 BCE his elder son Zhao Zhang rebelled in Handan, was defeated by forces under Lord Cheng and Li Yu, and fled to his father's palace at Shaqiu. There he was killed. Fearing punishment for the siege, Li Yu shut the old king inside without food or water, and after 100 days he starved to death, an event known as the Shaqiu Incident.
king-xuan-of-zhou: King Xuan of Zhou, personal name Ji Jing, was the 11th king of the Western Zhou dynasty and the penultimate one before the change to the Eastern Zhou period. He was born in a troubled time. His predecessor, King Li of Zhou, had imposed heavy taxes on his people and treated them with contempt, and after a period of decadence among the upper class the Zhou people rebelled and exiled him to Zhi. Thereafter Zhou was ruled by He, Earl of Gong, in an era called the Gonghe Regency. After King Li died in exile, power passed to King Xuan. The Stone Drums of Qin were long mistakenly ascribed to him.

King Xuan worked to restore the authority of the royal house. After seeking advice from his ministers he launched campaigns against the surrounding tribes, resettled people and promoted hunting and music again, drawing inspiration from Kings Wen, Wu, Cheng and Kang. The Mao Gong ding, which carries one of the longest Chinese bronze inscriptions, records him speaking of his anxiety about the failing kingdom and charging Duke Yin of Mao to help him stabilise the Mandate of Heaven and not to oppress the common people.

The Guoji Zibai pan records a campaign against the Xianyun along the Luo River, led by Guoji Zibai, in which 50 captives were taken and 500 killed. Classical sources imply that the Xianyun had plundered Haojing and eroded royal authority. Campaigns against Chu followed because it had stopped paying tribute, with a victory recounted in the Classic of Poetry. The Song gui records him ordering a man named Song to take control of 20 storehouses in Chengzhou.

In the ninth year of his reign he favoured the younger son Yi over Kuo as heir to Duke Wu of Lu, against the advice of Zhong Shanfu. Sima Qian wrote that from then on many of the lords mostly rebelled against royal commands. He also records a failed attempt to count the people of Taiyuan and a defeat in the Battle of Qianmu, and repeated defeats by the Rong.

According to Zhang Shoujie's annotation of Sima Qian's Shiji, King Xuan ordered a mass execution of women after a rumour that one woman would bring ruin to Zhou, and killed Du Bo when he protested. Another account says that his concubine Nü Jiu falsely accused Du Bo of rape. In both, three years later King Xuan dreamed of Du Bo shooting him with an arrow, and died. The story is repeated in the Mozi, the primary source today. His son King You was the last king of the Western Zhou.
king-you-of-zhou: King You of Zhou, personal name Ji Gongsheng, was the 12th king of the Chinese Zhou dynasty and the last king of the Western Zhou. In 780 BCE a major earthquake struck Guanzhong, and a soothsayer named Bo Yangfu took it as an omen of the destruction of the Zhou dynasty. In 779 BCE a concubine named Bao Si entered the palace and won the king's favour, and they had a son named Bofu. King You deposed Queen Shen and Crown Prince Yijiu, made Bao Si the new queen and Bofu the new crown prince.

Queen Shen's father, the Marquess of Shen, was furious and attacked the king's palace with the Quanrong. King You lit the warning beacons on Mount Li to call his nobles, but according to the Records of the Grand Historian he had lit them falsely before, to amuse Bao Si, who did not laugh easily, and so none of the nobles answered his genuine call. The earliest warning beacons appeared in the Han dynasty, so this story is considered fabricated. In the resulting battle King You and Bofu were killed and Bao Si was captured. According to the Xinian, preserved on the Tsinghua Bamboo Slips, King You himself attacked the Marquess of Shen, who allied with the Quanrong and defeated the royal army.

After his death nobles including the Marquess of Shen, the Marquess of Zeng and Duke Wen of Xu supported the deposed Prince Yijiu as King Ping of Zhou, so the dynasty continued. Because the capital Haojing was badly damaged and lay near the dangerous Quanrong, King Ping moved the capital eastward in 771 BCE, beginning the Eastern Zhou dynasty and the Spring and Autumn period, which lasted more than 300 years.

In the traditional Mao Commentary to the Classic of Poetry the court hymn Gather the Beans is read as a criticism of King You for squandering the respect of the feudal lords and humiliating them, though this interpretation is disputed.
king-zhao-of-chu: Xiong Zhen was the son of King Ping of Chu and his mother was Bo Ying. He had a sister and at least three elder half-brothers born of concubines, Shen, Jie and Qi, known also by the courtesy names Zixi, Ziqi and Zilü. He married Zhen Jiang, a daughter of the Marquess of Qi, and was succeeded by his son King Hui of Chu.

The invasion of 506 BCE was led by King Helü of Wu, with an army commanded by the strategist Sun Tzu, author of The Art of War, and by Wu Zixu, whose father and brother King Ping had killed. After the rout at the Battle of Boju the Chu commander Nang Wa fled to the state of Zheng. The Chu general Shen Yin Shu defeated the Wu army but was badly wounded, and at his own request a Chu officer killed him.

In his flight King Zhao was wounded by a Chu arrow at Yunmeng, then went through Yun to Sui in northern Hubei. His minister Shen Baoxu went to Qin to ask for help. Duke Ai of Qin was at first non-committal, but after Shen had spent seven days kneeling and wailing in the palace courtyard he agreed to send troops, the Wu army withdrew, and the king returned to Ying.

The Zhuangzi tells of a sheep-butcher named Yue who followed the king into flight and back. Offered rewards, and finally a place among the three highest nobles, he refused them all, saying he had fled from fear and not loyalty, and asked only to return to his stall.

In 491 BCE the king saw the omen known as clouds like numerous red birds pressing the day to fly. Not long afterwards King Fuchai of Wu, Helü's successor, attacked the State of Chen, which asked Chu for help. King Zhao led his troops in person and was killed in a battle that followed.
king-zhao-of-zhou: King Zhao, personal name Ji Xia, was the son of King Kang. By his accession his father and grandfather, King Cheng, had conquered and colonised the Central Plains and forced most northern and eastern peoples into vassalage; only the Dongyi of eastern Shandong still resisted, and they were no longer a threat. Zhao inherited a prosperous kingdom and could afford to build a new ancestral temple for his father, the Kang gong, which grew into one of the two central temples of dynastic worship.

With the north and east at peace, Zhao turned to the Yangtze basin, a region rich in minerals controlled by the Chu confederation, with which Zhou had been on good terms for almost two centuries. As Chu expanded and Zhou's demand for gold, copper and tin grew, border clashes escalated into open war. In 961 BCE Zhao invaded, conquered the region north of the Yangtze and subdued the 26 states of the Han River valley, including Chu, before withdrawing with much loot, most likely because he could not hold the land.

In 957 BCE he launched a second campaign into the middle Yangtze with half the royal forces, the Six Armies of the West, probably to bring the basin under lasting control. The Zhou forces were defeated and almost wholly destroyed.

The defeat damaged the dynasty's reputation, ended its early expansion and was followed by foreign invasions. His son, King Mu, restored stability, but the Yangtze basin remained the southern limit of direct Western Zhou control. Zhao was still honoured for his southern campaigns and became the first Zhou ruler given a sacrificial site in the Kang gong, perhaps because later kings did not wish an ancestor remembered for a shameful defeat. Later moralists portrayed him as a pleasure-loving ruler who died hunting, the Chu poems of the Heavenly Questions mocked his arrogance, and in the seventh century BCE northern lords invading Chu claimed they had come to investigate why he never returned.
king-zhaoxiang-of-qin: Born Ying Ji in 325 BCE, he was a son of King Huiwen of Qin by a low-ranked concubine, Lady Mi, and a younger brother of King Wu. As the son of a concubine he stood low in the succession and held no fief, and as a boy he was sent to the state of Yan as a political hostage. In 307 BCE King Wu died young and childless after breaking his shins while lifting a heavy bronze cauldron in the Zhou palace at Wangcheng, leaving Qin in a succession crisis.

King Wuling of Zhao, seeking a weaker or compliant ruler in Qin, had his official Zhao Gu bring the prince out of Yan and backed his claim, while the prince's maternal uncle, the general Wei Ran, suppressed his opponents. He became king at 18, and his mother, Queen Dowager Xuan, ruled as regent with her brothers Wei Ran and Mi Rong and her sons Prince Yi and Prince Fu, known as the Four Nobles. In 305 BCE a coup by his half-brothers Prince Zhuang and Prince Yong with Queen Huiwen was crushed by Wei Ran; the conspirators were killed and Queen Huiwen executed. The king then came of age and took up state affairs.

In 304 BCE he allied with King Huai of Chu, ceding Shangyong, and when Qi, Wei and Han invaded Chu, Qin took Puban and Fengling from Wei and Wusui from Han, returning them in 302 BCE when the two states gave up their alliance against Qin. Later in the reign Qin captured the Chu capital Ying in 278 BCE, conquered the Xirong state of Yiqu in 272 BCE, defeated a Zhao army of 450,000 at Changping in 260 BCE and overthrew the Eastern Zhou dynasty in 256 BCE.

He died in 251 BCE at the age of 75, having outlived his eldest son, Crown Prince Dao, who died in 267 BCE as a hostage in Wei, and was succeeded by his second son, King Xiaowen of Qin. Historians credit him with policy mistakes in his later years, but his conquests made Qin the dominant military power of the late Warring States period and prepared the unification of China three decades later by his great-grandson Ying Zheng, Qin Shi Huang.
kingdom-of-aragon: Aragon began as a Carolingian feudal county around the city of Jaca, which in the first half of the 9th century became a vassal of the Kingdom of Pamplona, later Navarre. Its own line of counts ended without a male heir in 922. When Sancho III of Pamplona died in 1035 his kingdom was divided in three, and his illegitimate son Ramiro received Aragon. After the death of his brother Gonzalo, who had held Sobrarbe and Ribagorza, Ramiro became the first de facto king of Aragon, although he never used the title. By defeating his brother García Sánchez III he secured the kingdom's independence.

Ramiro's son Sancho Ramírez, who also inherited Navarre, was the first to call himself King of the Aragonese and Pamplonese. As the kingdom expanded south at the expense of al-Andalus, the capital moved from Jaca to Huesca in 1096 and to Zaragoza in 1118. After Alfonso the Battler died childless in 1134, Navarre and Aragon chose different rulers. By 1285 the southernmost lands of present-day Aragon had been taken from the Muslims.

In 1150 the marriage of Queen Petronilla of Aragon and Ramon Berenguer IV, Count of Barcelona, created the Crown of Aragon, which took its name from the kingdom. Their son Alfonso II inherited all their lands, and the crown came to include Catalonia and later the kingdoms of Majorca, Valencia, Sicily, Naples and Sardinia.

In the 14th century the king's power was greatly restricted by the Union of Aragon. When the house of Barcelona died out in 1410, the Aragonese secured the election in 1412 of a Castilian prince, Ferdinand of Antequera, over strong Catalan opposition. The marriage of Ferdinand and Isabella in 1469 was followed by the union of the crowns of Aragon and Castile on the death of John II in 1479. Aragon kept its own parliamentary institutions, the Corts, until the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707 to 1715 ended the kingdom in law. It remained an administrative unit until 1833, and Aragon became an autonomous community of Spain in 1982.

The kingdom's three main groups were Christians, who held power and made up about 70 per cent of the population, Mudéjars, about 15 per cent, and Jews, at most about 10 per cent. Mudéjars were Muslims who stayed after the Reconquista, paid a special poll tax and could keep their communities, religion and language; they worked as craftsmen and farmers and left a lasting architectural tradition. Jews governed their communities, called aljamas, and served as treasurers, doctors, diplomats and translators. Under James I they came under the king's special protection in return for higher taxes. The anti-Jewish violence of 1391 spread from Seville into Aragon, with Valencia a notable target.
kingdom-of-dahomey: Dahomey, in Fon Danhɔmɛ, meaning In the Belly of Chief Dan, developed on the Abomey Plateau among the Fon people in the early 17th century. It was established around 1600 as an offshoot of the royal dynasty of the Kingdom of Allada, and all its kings claimed descent from Allada's royal family as the Alladaxonou dynasty. Houegbadja (c. 1645–1685) is often regarded as the foundational king; he built the Royal Palaces of Abomey and began taking over towns outside the plateau.

King Agaja, Houegbadja's grandson, came to the throne in 1708 and expanded the kingdom with a professional standing army of around ten thousand. He conquered Allada in 1724 and Whydah in 1727, which gave Dahomey the Atlantic coast and a share in the Atlantic slave trade, and made it a regional power. Warfare with the Oyo Empire followed from 1728 to 1740 and left Dahomey in a tributary status. Tegbesu, who ruled from 1740 to 1774, is credited with administrative changes that gave the enlarged kingdom legitimacy.

Ghezo, who ruled from 1818 to 1859, faced political turmoil and financial instability and sought to end Oyo's overlordship. He tried to move trade towards palm oil. In 1851 the Royal Navy blockaded Dahomey, and a treaty of 1852 abolished the export of slaves, though the trade resumed in 1857 and 1858. Disputes with France over Porto-Novo and Cotonou led to the First Franco-Dahomean War in 1890 and a second in 1892. King Béhanzin was overthrown and exiled to Algeria, the kingdom was annexed in 1894, and in 1904 the area became the French colony of French Dahomey.

Early European accounts called the kingdom a despotism, but these were often used as arguments in the British debates on the slave trade and were probably exaggerated. Kings were chosen largely by discussion in the Great Council, which met each year at the Annual Customs of Dahomey. Most court offices had a female counterpart. The army was divided into a right wing under the migan and a left under the mehu, and included a corps of women soldiers that Europeans called the Dahomey Amazons.

Captives taken in wars and raids were sold to Europeans for rifles, gunpowder, cloth, cowrie shells and alcohol, put to work on royal plantations, or killed in sacrifices at the Annual Customs. Cowries were the main currency. Religion combined royal ancestor worship with Vodun, whose chief deity is the combined Mawu-Lisa.
kingdom-of-east-anglia: East Anglia may have been settled by the Anglo-Saxons as early as the start of the 5th century, in the approximate area of the former Iceni and the Roman civitas centred on Venta Icenorum, near Caistor St Edmund. According to Bede, the East Angles descended from people of Angeln, now in Germany. The kingdom was organised in the first or second quarter of the 6th century, with Wehha listed as its first king, followed by Wuffa. It was one of the seven kingdoms later called the Heptarchy, though some modern historians doubt that the seven existed at the same time.
Its ruling dynasty was the Wuffingas, named after Wuffa, and its early centre of power may have been in eastern Suffolk, where the ship burials of Snape and Sutton Hoo lie.

Rædwald, the most powerful of the Wuffingas, was described by Bede as overlord of the kingdoms south of the Humber, and in 616 he defeated and killed the Northumbrian king Æthelfrith at the Battle of the River Idle. He was baptised in 604 but kept pagan gods as well, and he died about 624. Christianity was firmly established under his successor Sigeberht, who founded the first East Anglian see for Felix of Burgundy at Dommoc, probably Dunwich. Penda of Mercia killed Sigeberht and Ecgric in the early 640s, and Anna and his son Jurmin fell at the Battle of Bulcamp in 654.

Mercian power grew until, in 794, Offa had the East Anglian king Æthelberht executed and took the kingdom himself. East Anglian independence was restored by a rebellion against Mercia led by Æthelstan, and Beornwulf and then Ludeca of Mercia died trying to retake it.

The Great Heathen Army landed in 865 and returned in 869; it defeated and killed King Edmund, later venerated as Edmund the Martyr, and installed puppet kings. Guthrum's kingdom was recognised in a treaty with Alfred the Great, and Edward the Elder, after the defeat of the East Anglian Danes in 917, incorporated the region into the Kingdom of England.

The kingdom covered the modern counties of Norfolk and Suffolk and, at its largest extent, parts of eastern Cambridgeshire. In 1017 Cnut the Great made Thorkell the Tall earl of a new earldom of East Anglia. Almost no East Anglian charters survive, because Viking raids and settlement destroyed the kingdom's monasteries and its two sees, so Bede's Ecclesiastical History is the main source for the early period. The Tribal Hidage, probably compiled in the 7th century, assesses the East Angles at 30,000 hides. Place-names ending in -thorp and -by in East Anglia record Scandinavian settlement.
kingdom-of-great-britain: England and Scotland had been in personal union since 1603, when James VI of Scotland became King of England, and James was the first to call himself king of Great Britain. Queen Anne left no clear Protestant heir, and because the laws of succession differed in the two kingdoms, the Roman Catholic House of Stuart might return to the Scottish throne. A Treaty of Union was agreed in 1706 and ratified by separate Acts of Union, which came into effect on 1 May 1707.

Anne became the first monarch of Great Britain. Scotland and England kept their own legal and educational systems and their established churches, and the union followed the English Act of Settlement of 1701, which brought about the Hanoverian succession of George I in 1714.

The early years were marked by Jacobite risings, notably that of 1715, and the Stuart cause ended in defeat in 1746. The weakness of the Hanoverian kings increased the powers of Parliament, and the role of prime minister emerged in the time of Robert Walpole. In the Treaty of Utrecht, which ended the War of the Spanish Succession, Britain gained Newfoundland and Acadia from France and Gibraltar and Menorca from Spain.

In the Seven Years' War the British captured Quebec in 1759 after the Battle of the Plains of Abraham. The loss of the Thirteen Colonies marked a shift of attention towards Asia and the Pacific, and in 1787 the First Fleet left for New South Wales.

From 1793 Britain fought France in the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. The Irish Rebellion of 1798 was quickly suppressed, with a death toll of 10,000 to 30,000. Great Britain was merged with Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland on 1 January 1801.

A single parliament met at the Palace of Westminster, with an unelected House of Lords and an elected House of Commons. The Parliaments of England and Scotland were abolished, and the Privy Council of England and the Privy Council of Scotland were merged in 1708. Ireland stayed formally separate, with its own parliament, which the Declaratory Act of 1719 declared subordinate to the British Parliament; the act was repealed in 1782. Overseas, Britain followed a mercantilist trade policy and maintained a powerful Royal Navy.
kingdom-of-holland: The Batavian Republic adopted a more moderate constitution in October 1801, and a new one drafted by Rutger Jan Schimmelpenninck in March 1805 restored the unitary state, with Schimmelpenninck as Grand Pensionary. Napoleon Bonaparte remained troubled by the instability of the regime. He thought only a monarchy could keep the country from succumbing to British pressure or longing for the old regime, and he found that the Dutch did not meet their military duties and that Schimmelpenninck was not a docile ally. By 1806 the Swiss Confederation and the Batavian Republic were the last remaining sister republics, while Napoleon had already made kingdoms for his family elsewhere.

Schimmelpenninck objected that a hereditary head of state did not suit the Dutch national character. On 28 April 1806 Napoleon gave Dutch diplomats eight days to accept Louis Bonaparte as king. The members of the government ratified a treaty without consulting the people. Louis entered The Hague on 23 June 1806, was never crowned, and had problems with his sovereignty throughout his reign.

Napoleon intended Louis to be little more than a French prefect, but Louis tried to act independently. He learned Dutch, adopted the spelling Lodewijk and declared himself Dutch. He centralised the state, appointing the mayors of the larger cities, and introduced a countrywide tax system, a Civil Registry and Land Registry, and in 1809 a penal code and civil code based on French models that respected Dutch customs. He promoted equality for Jews, Catholics and dissenters, and the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences and the Royal Museum were founded in his reign. After the Leiden gunpowder disaster of 1807 he started a national collection, gave a large sum and opened Huis ten Bosch as a hospital.
In 1807 the kingdom gained East Frisia and Jever, and was divided into eleven departments. After the Walcheren Campaign in 1809 it had to give up all territory south of the Rhine to France.

Louis quarrelled with Napoleon over three matters. He refused to tier the national debt, which would have hurt Dutch investors; he refused conscription, ordering only Dutch orphans to enlist, which provoked a riot in Rotterdam on 14 July 1809; and he enforced the Continental System weakly, since a strict policy would damage Dutch maritime trade. After the Walcheren Campaign Napoleon called him to Paris and annexed the territories between the Meuse and the Scheldt.

Louis abdicated on 1 July 1810 in favour of his son, French troops took Amsterdam on 4 July, and an imperial decree abolished the kingdom and incorporated it into the French Empire, which held the Netherlands until 1813. It was the first formal monarchy on Dutch territory since 1581.
kingdom-of-hungary: The Hungarians, led by Árpád, settled the Carpathian Basin in 895 and established the Principality of Hungary, which lasted until 1000. Their incursions into western Europe were stopped by Otto I, Holy Roman Emperor, at the Battle of Lechfeld. The principality was succeeded by a Christian kingdom when Stephen I, son of the prince Géza, was crowned at Esztergom on Christmas Day 1000. He defeated his rival Koppány with Bavarian help, gave strong support to the Catholic Church and was canonized in 1083. His family, the Árpád dynasty, ruled the kingdom for 300 years, and from 1102 the kings of Hungary were also kings of Croatia in a personal union.

After the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Mohács in 1526 central authority collapsed. Most of the ruling elite elected John Zápolya on 10 November 1526, while a minority elected Ferdinand I, Archduke of Austria, in December, citing earlier agreements that the Habsburgs would take the throne if Louis died without heirs.

Within a few years the kingdom fell into three parts: Royal Hungary in the north and west under the Habsburgs, Ottoman Hungary on the Great Alföld, and an eastern kingdom under the Szapolyai that later became the Principality of Transylvania. The fall of Buda in 1541 confirmed the division, which lasted until the end of the 17th century. The Habsburgs held the Hungarian throne from 1526 until 1918, and Hungarians fought wars of independence against them in 1604–06, 1664–71, 1680–85, 1703–11 and 1848–49.

After the Compromise of 1867 the Habsburg monarchy became the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary. The lands of the Hungarian Crown, comprising the Kingdom of Hungary proper and the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia, received equal status with the Austrian Empire. Each state acted with considerable independence, while the reigning house, defence, foreign affairs and common finances were managed jointly. The unofficial name Transleithania was sometimes used for the Hungarian regions.

The monarchy ended in 1918 with the deposition of the last king, Charles IV. A short-lived Hungarian Soviet Republic held power from 21 March to 1 August 1919 under Béla Kun. On 29 February 1920 the kingdom was restored in name, with Admiral Miklós Horthy as regent, and it lasted until 1946. The Treaty of Trianon cut off most of the old kingdom's territory, which had been multiethnic from its beginning. Stephen I's feast day, 20 August, is a national holiday in Hungary.
kingdom-of-italy: The kingdom was proclaimed on 17 March 1861, when Victor Emmanuel II, King of Sardinia, became King of Italy. It was the result of the Risorgimento, the movement that emerged after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 to join the states of the peninsula and free them from foreign control. The radical journalist Giuseppe Mazzini, who founded Young Italy in the early 1830s, favoured a unitary republic, while monarchists loyal to the House of Savoy worked for a united kingdom.

In the Third Italian War of Independence of 1866, fought with Prussia against Austria, Italy gained Veneto, and in 1870 its troops captured Rome, ending more than a thousand years of papal temporal power. The new lira was introduced by royal decree on 17 July 1861.

In 1882 Italy joined the Triple Alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary, though the tie with Vienna stayed formal because Italy wanted Trentino and Trieste. It joined the Allies in 1915, and in 1919 it annexed Trieste and Trentino-Alto Adige, but it did not receive all the territory promised in the secret London Pact. The liberal era was marked by corruption, government instability and poverty in the south. On 7 May 1898 General Fiorenzo Bava-Beccaris fired on crowds protesting against bread prices in Milan, killing between 82 and 300 people, and in 1900 the anarchist Gaetano Bresci shot King Umberto I at Monza.

Benito Mussolini became prime minister in 1922 and the National Fascist Party took control of the government. The Lateran Treaties of 1929 reconciled the state with the Roman Catholic Church and gave independence to Vatican City. The Second Italo-Ethiopian War began in 1935, and Italy invaded Albania in 1939. Italy entered the Second World War in 1940.

After the Allied invasion of Sicily the new government surrendered at the Armistice of Cassibile in September 1943, and German forces occupying the north and centre set up the Italian Social Republic under Mussolini. Anger at the monarchy for backing Fascism led to a referendum on 2 June 1946, and the monarchy was abolished on 18 June.

The kingdom was a constitutional monarchy that kept the Statuto Albertino of Sardinia as its constitution. Executive power belonged to the king, who governed through appointed ministers, but he could no longer keep a government in office against the will of Parliament. Parliament had an appointive Senate and an elective Chamber of Deputies. From 1936 to 1943 the king's title included Emperor of Ethiopia, and from 1939 King of Albania. Education was compulsory at primary level under the Casati Act of 1859, but illiteracy was nearly 80 per cent in 1861 and took more than fifty years to halve.
kingdom-of-jerusalem: The Kingdom of Jerusalem, also called the Crusader Kingdom, lasted almost 200 years, from the accession of Godfrey of Bouillon in 1099 to the fall of Acre in 1291. Pope Urban II preached the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in 1095, at first to help the Byzantine Empire against Turkish invasions, though control of the Holy Land soon became the main aim. The Seljuk Empire had broken into smaller states after the death of Malik-Shah I in 1092, and the disunity of the emirs of Syria and Anatolia allowed the Crusaders to overcome the opposition they met on the way to Jerusalem.

The kingdom was at first a loose collection of towns taken in the crusade. Under Baldwin I it expanded: with the help of the Italian city-states and King Sigurd I of Norway he captured Acre in 1104, Beirut in 1110 and Sidon in 1111, and held suzerainty over Edessa, Antioch and Tripoli. The historian Thomas Madden calls him the true founder of the kingdom. At its mid-12th-century height it ran in a thin strip from Beirut to the Sinai. The Muslim states of Syria were meanwhile united by Nur ad-Din, who took Damascus in 1154.

A dynastic struggle divided the court of King Baldwin IV. On 4 July 1187 the army of the kingdom was destroyed by Saladin at the Battle of Hattin; King Guy was imprisoned and Raynald of Chatillon executed, and Jerusalem fell. After the Third Crusade the kingdom was re-established in 1192 at Acre, which stayed its capital even when Frederick II won partial control of Jerusalem by diplomacy.

The remaining coastal kingdom was weakened by quarrels, such as the War of Saint Sabas of 1256 to 1258 between the Venetian and Genoese colonies in Acre. After the Mamluks defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260, the sultan Baibars took one coastal city after another, from Caesarea and Arsuf in 1265 to Jaffa in 1268. Acre fell in 1291, and the last outpost on the coast, Ruad, was lost in 1302.

Most settlers came from the Kingdom of France, so the rulers and elite were French. They were a Catholic minority ruling a population that was mostly native Greek and Syriac Orthodox Christians and Sunni and Shi'a Muslims, with a few Jews and Samaritans. Scholars estimate that Crusaders made up 15 to 25 percent of the population. Land was granted to vassals in feudal lordships, and the Italian merchants profited from trade in silk, cotton, spices and sugar. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre was expanded in Gothic style by 1149, and castles such as Kerak and Montreal remain among its monuments.
kingdom-of-kongo: Oral traditions of Kongo's early history were first written down in the late 16th century, with detailed versions recorded in the mid-17th century by, among others, the Italian Capuchin missionary Giovanni Cavazzi da Montecuccolo. The traditions about its foundation changed over time with circumstances. Jean Cuvelier published a KiKongo summary in 1934, but the traditions more probably relate to clan traditions and especially to the period after 1750.

By the 13th century there were three main federations of states in the western Congo Basin. The Seven Kingdoms of Kongo dia Nlaza lay in the east and were considered the oldest and most powerful. To their south lay Mpemba, and west of them across the Congo River a confederation of three small states, Vungu, Kakongo and Ngoyo. A 16th-century tradition said the former kingdoms were now subjects and tributaries of the king of Congo. As centralisation grew, allied provinces lost influence, and by 1620 Mbata, once a co-kingdom, was known only by the title Grandfather of the King of Kongo.

After becoming king in 1509, Afonso I worked to create a viable Catholic Church in Kongo, financed from royal assets and taxation. With advisers from Portugal, among them the royal chaplain Rui d'Aguiar, he created a syncretic Christianity that remained part of Kongo's culture for the rest of its independent existence. Álvaro I's seizure of the throne during the crisis of the Jaga invasion of 1568 began a new royal line, the House of Kwilu.

Relations with Portugal worsened as the governors of Portuguese Angola grew more aggressive. Luis Mendes de Vasconcelos, who arrived in 1617, used mercenary Imbangala to raid southern Kongo provinces, and his successor João Correia de Sousa launched a full-scale invasion of southern Kongo in 1622. From 1636 the House of Kinlaza ruled. After the Battle of Mbwila, the rival Kimpanzu and Kinlaza factions fought a civil war of about 40 years, which increased the number of Kongo people sold across the Atlantic, weakened the monarchy and strengthened Soyo.

The village, called vata, was the basic social unit after the family, headed by a chief called nkuluntu. Villages were grouped into small states led by a mwene. The king, the Mwene Kongo, served for life and was chosen by senior officials, and the succession was one of the central problems of Kongo history. Its universal currency was the nzimbu shell, with 2,000 nzimbu buying a goat. The army was a mass levy of archers with a smaller corps of shield-bearing heavy infantry.
kingdom-of-lombardy-venetia: In the Treaty of Paris of 1814 the Austrians confirmed their claims to the former Duchy of Milan, which the Habsburg monarchy had ruled since 1714, and to the former Republic of Venice, which had been under Austrian rule intermittently since the Treaty of Campo Formio of 1797. The Congress of Vienna combined these lands into a single kingdom ruled in personal union by the Habsburg Emperor of Austria. The emperor was represented day to day by viceroys appointed in Vienna and resident in Milan and Venice.

Emperor Francis I ruled the kingdom from 1815 until his death in 1835, and his son Ferdinand I from 1835 to 1848. On 6 September 1838 in Milan Ferdinand became the last king crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy. After the Five Days of Milan, beginning on 22 March 1848, the Austrians fled the city, which became the capital of a Lombardy Provisional Government, and Venice rose the next day. Field Marshal Joseph Radetzky defeated the Sardinian troops at Custoza on 24–25 July 1848, entered Milan on 6 August and Venice on 24 August 1849, and restored Austrian rule.

Franz Joseph I ruled for the rest of the kingdom's existence, with a governor-general in place of the viceroy: first Radetzky and from 1857 Franz Joseph's younger brother Maximilian, later emperor of Mexico. After the defeat at Solferino in 1859, Austria ceded Lombardy up to the Mincio River to Napoleon III by the Treaty of Zurich, and he passed it to the Kingdom of Sardinia. Venetia and Mantua fell to the Kingdom of Italy by the 1866 Peace of Prague, and a plebiscite on 21–22 October 1866 marked the annexation.

The kingdom had two separate governments, officially declared separate crown lands in 1851. Lombardy had nine provinces, including Milan, Brescia and Mantua, and Venetia eight, including Venice, Verona and Udine. Its population in 1855 was 5,024,117, of whom 4,625,746 were counted as Italians and 351,805 as Friulians. The administration used Italian in its documents, and about 10% of civil servants came from other parts of the empire. German was the command language of the army, and the top police officials and highest governors were Austrian. Local aristocrats, excluded from high office, backed the wars of independence.
kingdom-of-luang-phrabang: The Kingdom of Luang Phrabang, also called the Kingdom of Luang Prabang, was formed in 1707 as a result of the split of the Kingdom of Lan Xang. When the kingdom divided, Muang Phuan became a tributary state of Luang Prabang. The first king was Kitsarat, who reigned from 1707 to 1713, and he was followed by Ong Kham and then by Thao Ang, known as Inthason, who reigned from 1723 to 1749. Over the years the monarchy weakened further and was forced to become a vassal several times to the Burmese and Siamese monarchies.

Sotika-Kuomane, who reigned from 1749 to 1768, was a Burmese vassal from 1765, and his successor Surinyavong II was a Burmese vassal for all of his reign from 1768 to 1788. Siam occupied the kingdom in 1791-1792 and again for a time before June 1794, when Anurutha began his second reign, which lasted until 1819. From 1825 to 1826 the king Manthaturath lived as a monk in Bangkok, and Thai officials administered Luang Phrabang.

A French consulate was established in Luang Prabang in 1885. The kingdom was then a Siamese vassal, and Siam feared that France planned to annex it. A treaty of 7 May 1886 between Siam and France recognised Siamese suzerainty over Luang Prabang and the neighbouring Lao kingdoms. In 1887 a particularly destructive attack by the Chinese Black Flag Army, during the Haw wars, led King Oun Kham to request French protection. This was accepted and signed on 27 March 1889, against Siamese protest.

France and Siam went to war in 1893. The conflict culminated in the Paknam incident, in which France entered Bangkok with warships, and Siam was forced to accept the French ultimatum and cede the lands east of the Mekong. The French Protectorate of Laos was officially established, and the administrative capital moved from Luang Prabang to Vientiane. Luang Prabang remained the seat of the royal family, whose power was reduced to that of figureheads, while real power passed to French officials, including the vice consulate and the Resident-General.

Under French protection the Kingdom of Luang Prabang became the principal kingdom of French Laos. On 11 May 1947 the Kingdoms of Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champassak were reorganised into the Kingdom of Laos, and the king of Luang Prabang, Sisavang Vong, became King of Laos. The Kingdom of Laos gained full independence from France in 1954.
kingdom-of-navarre: The kingdom, originally the Kingdom of Pamplona, took shape around the city of Pamplona in the first centuries of the Iberian Reconquista, in the buffer region between the Carolingian Empire and the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba. The area was inhabited by the Vascones. Tradition holds that the Basque chieftain Íñigo Arista was elected king of Pamplona in 824, which began a dynasty lasting eighty years. Arab sources call him lord of the Vascones, not king, and the region stayed within the sphere of Córdoba, to which it paid taxes. Íñigo rebelled in 841 and was still in rebellion when he died in 851/2.

Sancho Garcés, who ruled from 905 to 925, proclaimed himself king, ended the alliance with Córdoba and extended the kingdom south to the Ebro, taking Nájera and Calahorra. Under Sancho III the Great the kingdom reached its largest extent, covering the modern Spanish province, the Basque provinces, Rioja and the northern slope of the Pyrenees. On his death he divided his possessions among his four sons, and the realm was not united again until Ferdinand II of Aragon.

Navarre passed into French control from 1276, and in 1284 Joan I married the future Philip IV of France. After the death of Queen Blanche I in 1441 disputes over the succession split the country in 1451 into the Agramonts and the Beaumonts. Ferdinand II of Aragon conquered the southern part in 1512, and it was annexed to Castile in 1515 as a separate kingdom with its own Courts, which lasted until 1841.

Lower Navarre north of the Pyrenees survived as an independent kingdom. Jeanne III became a follower of Calvinism in 1560 and commissioned a Basque translation of the New Testament. Her son Henry III inherited the French throne in 1589, and Navarre was merged into the Kingdom of France in 1620.

The kingdom was divided into districts called merindades, each governed by a merino as the king's representative. Its Cortes began as the king's council of churchmen and nobles, and burgesses were added in the 14th century. Today Navarre is an autonomous community of Spain, and Lower Navarre belongs to the French département of Pyrénées-Atlantiques.
kingdom-of-poland: The Polish state grew from the West Slavic tribe of the Polans in Greater Poland in the early 10th century. After the Christianization of Poland in 966 under Duke Mieszko I, his eldest son Bolesław I the Brave of the Piast dynasty was crowned the first King of Poland at Gniezno Cathedral in 1025, with the approval of Pope John XIX. His son Mieszko II Lambert lost the crown in 1031 amid peasant uprisings, the pagan reaction, and an invasion by Yaroslav I the Wise of Kiev, and the realm shrank to a duchy. Casimir I the Restorer moved the capital to Kraków, and Bolesław II the Bold regained the crown in 1076, only to be banished in 1079 for murdering Bishop Stanislaus of Szczepanów.

On the death of Bolesław III Wrymouth in 1138 the country was divided among his sons, beginning more than 200 years of feudal fragmentation. The Silesian Piasts tried to restore the kingdom, but the Mongol invasion of 1241 and the death of Henry II the Pious at the Battle of Legnica ended their attempt.
