Przemysł II was crowned in 1296, and after a vacancy Władysław I the Elbow-High was crowned at Wawel in 1320. His son Casimir III the Great expanded into Red Ruthenia and strengthened towns, administration and army; with his death on 5 November 1370 Piast rule ended.

Under Louis I of Hungary the nobility rose in political life and the idea of the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland took shape: the state was indivisible and lasting, the king its ruler and not its owner. Louis's daughter Jadwiga married Jogaila of Lithuania after the Union of Krewo of 1385, and he was crowned Władysław II Jagiełło on 4 March 1386. The Sejm came to share the Crown's authority, and after Sigismund Augustus died childless in 1572 kings were chosen by free election, in which every nobleman could take part.

In the joint state with Lithuania the Polish part came to be called the Crown. The partitions by Prussia, the Habsburgs and Russia ended the kingdom, and a convention of 1797 declared it abolished forever. The Congress of Vienna created a Kingdom of Poland tied to Russia, which formally lasted until 1915, and after German and Austrian forces occupied central Polish lands a German-dependent kingdom under a Regency Council was proclaimed. When Poland regained independence the Council handed power to an elected government.
kingdom-of-portugal: The nucleus of the Portuguese state was the County of Portugal, established in the 9th century as part of the Reconquista by Vímara Peres, a vassal of the King of Asturias. The county became part of the Kingdom of León in 1097 and was a semi-autonomous county of it. Independence came in three stages. On 26 July 1139 Afonso Henriques was acclaimed King of the Portuguese by his troops after the Battle of Ourique, of uncertain historicity. On 5 October 1143 Alfonso VII of León and Castile recognised him as king through the Treaty of Zamora, generally taken in Portuguese tradition as the founding of the kingdom. In 1179 Pope Alexander III recognised Portugal's independence in the bull Manifestis Probatum.

Afonso I's descendants of the House of Burgundy ruled until 1383, and the Afonsine dynasty gave way to the House of Aviz after the interregnum of 1383–1385. All later monarchs of Portugal were descended from Afonso I in one way or another. Exploration in the 15th and 16th centuries created a vast colonial empire. From 1580 to 1640 the kingdom was in personal union with Habsburg Spain. After the Restoration War of 1640–1668 it passed to the House of Braganza and later to the House of Braganza-Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. After 1471 it was styled the Kingdom of Portugal and the Algarves, and from 1815 to 1822 it was the main part of the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves.

Portugal's influence declined after the Restoration War, but it remained a major power through Brazil. After Brazil's independence it tried to build an empire in Africa until the British Ultimatum of 1890 stopped its expansion. The kingdom was an absolute monarchy before 1822, alternated between absolute and semi-constitutional rule until 1834, and was semi-constitutional afterwards.

Republicanism grew in Lisbon in the early 20th century and gained from the Lisbon Regicide of 1 February 1908, when King Charles and his heir Luís Filipe were assassinated in the Terreiro do Paço. The second son became Manuel II, whose reign ended in the revolution of 5 October 1910, which sent him into exile in the United Kingdom and began the First Portuguese Republic. A Monarchy of the North proclaimed in Porto on 19 January 1919 collapsed within a month. The overseas colonies became provinces of the Republic; Angola and Mozambique became independent in 1975, and the handover of Macau to China in 1999 ended the Portuguese Empire.
kingdom-of-prussia: In 1510 Albert of Brandenburg, of the House of Hohenzollern, became the last grand master of the Teutonic Order in Prussia. In 1525 he adopted Lutheranism, secularised the order's state and made it the Duchy of Prussia, which stayed a Polish fief. When his son Albert Frederick died without issue in 1618, the electors of Brandenburg inherited Prussia and ruled it in a personal union known as Brandenburg-Prussia.

The kingdom was poor in natural resources and still recovering from the Thirty Years' War, and its territory was disjointed, stretching 1,200 kilometres from the Baltic coast to Brandenburg, with the exclaves of Cleves, Mark and Ravensberg in the Rhineland.

Frederick II came to the throne in 1740 and invaded Silesia, which began the War of the Austrian Succession. Austria ceded it formally in the Treaty of Berlin in 1742. When Frederick invaded Saxony and Bohemia in 1756 and 1757, he began the Third Silesian War and the Seven Years' War. Alarmed by Russian influence in Poland, he was instrumental in starting the first Partition of Poland in 1772, in which Prussia annexed most of Royal Prussia.

At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 Prussia received 40 per cent of the Kingdom of Saxony and much of Westphalia and the Rhineland, and became the only great power with a predominantly German-speaking population. The German Customs Union of 1834 excluded Austria and increased Prussian influence. In 1849 the Frankfurt Parliament offered Frederick William IV the crown of a united Germany, and he refused.

The German Confederation collapsed in 1866 in the Austro-Prussian War, and Prussia led the North German Confederation, which became the German Empire in 1871. The kingdom became the Free State of Prussia in the revolution of 1918 and 1919, and Prussia was abolished in 1947.

Prussia was an absolute monarchy until the revolutions of 1848, after which it became a constitutional monarchy. The Constitution of 1850 set up a two-house Landtag, with a lower house elected under a three-class franchise that weighted votes by taxes paid and an upper house appointed by the king. Ministers were responsible only to the king, and the landowning Junkers kept their grip, especially in the east. The population was mostly Lutheran, with Catholics in the Rhineland and Polish-speaking provinces.
kingdom-of-sine: Sine, or Siin in Serer, lay along the north bank of the Saloum River delta. According to the historian Dennis Galvan, the Serer peoples migrated south from the Futa Tooro region from around the eleventh century, some of them fleeing King War Jabi of Takrur, who imposed Sharia law and persecuted those who kept their traditional beliefs. Before the kingdom, some 60 villages were divided among states ruled by lamans, landowners and guardians of Serer spirituality, whose families, among them the Sarr, Joof and Ngom, formed a Great Council of Lamanes to settle disputes.

In the 13th or 14th century Mandinka migrants led by the matrilineal Guelowar clan arrived from Kaabu after losing a dynastic struggle there. The council granted them asylum, and Serer noblemen married Guelowar women, whose children ruled as Serer kings. Serer oral history holds that Maysa Wali, after serving as legal adviser to the council, was chosen to rule and was crowned by Lamaan Jame Ngom of Faajaal; he reigned from about 1350 to 1370. The lamans became provincial chiefs but kept the power to depose a king.

Legend says that Maysa Wali chose Ndiadiane Ndiaye as first Emperor of the Jolof about 1360. Serer tradition holds that Sine never paid tribute, while the historian Sylviane Diouf writes that each vassal kingdom did. Sine and Saloum were the first to leave the Jolof Empire, at least twenty-nine years before the Battle of Danki in 1549. On 18 July 1867 King Kumba Ndoffene fa Maak Joof defeated the Muslim cleric Maba Diakhou Bâ at the Battle of Fandane-Thiouthioune, where Maba was killed. The kings kept their title, Maad a Sinig, through the colonial period until the death of Mahecor Joof in 1969, and in 2019 the monarchy was revived as a ceremonial office.

Sine lived from farming, chiefly millet, and fishing. Rooted in Serer religion, its farmers long refused to grow groundnuts for the French market, and the kingdom was less exposed to hunger and debt than its neighbours. Under the king stood the heirs apparent, the Buumi, Thilas and Loul; the Great Jaraaf, head of the noble council that elected kings from the royal family; the Great Farba Kaba, who commanded the army; and the Lingeer, the queen mother, who headed the female court.
kingdom-of-strathclyde: Strathclyde, in Welsh Ystrad Clud, was also known as Cumbria. It was a Brittonic kingdom of northern Britain, part of what Welsh tribes called Yr Hen Ogledd, the Old North, covering parts of what is now southern Scotland and North West England. It emerged in the post-Roman period as the kingdom of Alt Clud, centred on Dumbarton Rock, and may have been founded by the Damnonii people. Written sources for 400 to 600 are largely Irish and Welsh, and very few are contemporary. Two early kings are known: Coroticus, recipient of a letter from Saint Patrick, and his descendant Rhydderch Hael, named in Adomnán's Life of Saint Columba.

Alt Clut's neighbours were Dál Riata, the Picts and Northumbria, and wars for overlordship were frequent between the 6th and 8th centuries. In 642 the Britons led by Eugein son of Beli defeated Dál Riata at Strathcarron and killed Domnall Brecc. In 750 Teudebur of Alt Clut inflicted a heavy defeat on the Picts, and in 756 Pictish and Northumbrian forces besieged Dumbarton Rock and obtained the submission of Dumnagual. An army led by the Viking chiefs Amlaíb Conung and Ímar besieged Alt Clut for some four months in 870, destroyed its citadel and took many captives. The capital then seems to have moved to Govan.

The kingdom expanded south to the Cumbrian Mountains into lands of Rheged, and in the 10th century stretched from Loch Lomond to the River Eamont at Penrith. King Owain joined Constantine of Scotland and the Vikings against the English and was beaten at Brunanburh in 937. In 945 Edmund of England ravaged Strathclyde. Dyfnwal ab Owain recovered his kingdom and died on pilgrimage to Rome in 975. Owen the Bald is thought to have died at Carham in 1018.

The language of Strathclyde, Cumbric, was closely related to Old Welsh. Some time after 1018 and before 1054 the Scots most probably conquered Strathclyde, in the reign of Máel Coluim mac Cináeda, who died in 1034. By the 1070s the Scots again controlled it, and in 1107 Alexander I granted it to his brother David, Prince of the Cumbrians, later David I. Norse or Norse-Gael settlement left place-names and the hogback graves at Govan. The area around Carlisle was part of Scotland by 1066.
kingdom-of-the-lombards: The Gothic War (535–554), waged by the Byzantine Emperor Justinian against the Ostrogothic Kingdom, left Italy impoverished and sharply depopulated, after a volcanic winter in 536, famine and a plague pandemic in 541–542. In the spring of 568 the Lombards, a Germanic people previously allied with the Byzantine Empire, moved from Pannonia under King Alboin and quickly overwhelmed the small Byzantine army left by Narses to guard Italy. Their arrival broke the political unity of the peninsula for the first time since the Roman conquest.

The kingdom was divided into duchies ruled by semi-autonomous dukes, subdivided into gastaldates at the municipal level. The king was traditionally elected by the dukes, and several attempts to found a hereditary dynasty failed. Its capital and political centre was Pavia. The Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna and the Duchy of Rome separated the northern duchies, called Langobardia Maior, from the southern duchies of Spoleto and Benevento, called Langobardia Minor, which were considerably more autonomous.

The Lombards gradually adopted Roman titles, names and traditions, and by the late 8th century their language, dress and hairstyles had disappeared. They were at first Arian Christians or pagans, which set them against the Roman population, the Byzantines and the Pope, but by the end of the 7th century their conversion to Catholicism had removed a major barrier.

Rothari, an Arian and duke of Brescia, reigned from 636 to 652 and brought almost all of northern Italy under Lombard rule, though he could not force the Exarchate of Ravenna to submit. Liutprand then held the throne from 712 to 744, the longest reign of any Lombard king. The conflict with the Pope caused the kingdom's gradual loss of power to the Franks, who conquered it in 774. Charlemagne adopted the title King of the Lombards but never gained control of Benevento.

A reduced Regnum Italiae continued for centuries as one of the constituent kingdoms of the Holy Roman Empire, and the Iron Crown of Lombardy, which may date from Lombard Italy as early as the 7th century, was used to crown kings of Italy until Napoleon Bonaparte. Lombard law influenced the Italian legal system for a long time.
kingdom-of-the-netherlands: The Kingdom of the Netherlands arose from the defeat of Napoleon I. The Netherlands regained its independence from France in 1813 as the Sovereign Principality of the United Netherlands, after annexation by the First French Empire in 1810. The great powers of Europe, united against Napoleonic France, decided in the secret London Protocol to create a single state from the former Dutch Republic, the Batavian Republic and the Kingdom of Holland, together with the Austrian Netherlands and the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. They gave rule over it to William Frederick, Prince of Orange and Nassau, the son of William V, the last stadholder of the Dutch Republic.

In 1830 the southerners, calling themselves Belgians, seceded from the Kingdom, a step the Netherlands recognised only in 1839 in the Treaty of London. Luxembourg also ceased in 1839 to be part of the Kingdom, continuing as a grand duchy in personal union with the Dutch monarch until 1890.

Slavery was abolished by law in Suriname and the Dutch Caribbean colonies on 1 July 1863. In Suriname, however, many formerly enslaved people had to continue plantation labour under state supervision for another ten years, so for many emancipation was not effectively complete until 1 July 1873. Suriname, Netherlands New Guinea and the Netherlands Antilles remained colonies until the Charter for the Kingdom of the Netherlands was proclaimed in 1954. Aruba left the Netherlands Antilles in 1986, and the Antilles were dissolved in 2010.

The Kingdom is a sovereign state of four constituent countries that participate as equal partners: the Netherlands, Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten. Each of the last three has its own parliament, and the Charter for the Kingdom of the Netherlands takes precedence over their governance and over the Constitution. The Kingdom itself is administered in the country of the Netherlands, which holds roughly 98 percent of its land and population, and foreign policy and defence are conducted for the whole realm. The Council of Ministers of the Kingdom consists of the Dutch ministers plus a minister plenipotentiary from each of the three other countries.
kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies: The name Two Sicilies goes back to the partition of the medieval Kingdom of Sicily. Norman warriors conquered the island from the Saracens, who had ruled it since 827, and in 1131 Roger II made the Duchy of Apulia and the island a Kingdom of Sicily. After the War of the Sicilian Vespers (1282 to 1302) the island passed to the Crown of Aragon, but the rulers on the mainland, though known unofficially as the Kingdom of Naples, never gave up the title King of Sicily. Both realms were thus called the Kingdom of Sicily, and so their reunion was named the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies.

In 1516 Naples and Sicily fell to Charles V. After the War of the Spanish Succession, the peace treaties of 1713/14 left Naples with Austria and gave Sicily to Victor Amadeus of Savoy, who exchanged it with the Habsburgs in 1720 for Sardinia. Both were ruled by Austria until 1735. In 1734 Spanish troops supporting the claims of the Spanish Infante Charles had won at Bitonto.

The Treaty of Casalanza restored Ferdinand IV of Bourbon to the throne of Naples and returned the island of Sicily to him. In 1816 he annulled the Sicilian constitution of 1812, Sicily was fully reintegrated and the state became the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, with Ferdinand as Ferdinand I. Some deeds of the administration of Kings Joseph and Joachim Murat, such as reforms to the civil, penal and commercial codes, were kept and extended to Sicily.

During 1848 and 1849 the kingdom suppressed the revolution and Sicily's attempt at secession with its own forces, including hired Swiss Guards. The Army of the Two Sicilies had also put down the Calabrian revolution of 1847, but it collapsed during the Expedition of the Thousand in 1860. Garibaldi overthrew the king, and a plebiscite voted to join the Kingdom of Sardinia. The annexation completed the first phase of Italian unification, and the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861.

The kingdom held about 36 percent of Italy's population around 1850. Naples was the largest city in Italy and the third largest in Europe. Land was concentrated in the hands of a few families, and villages housed a large, poor rural proletariat. The kingdom had the largest merchant fleet in the Mediterranean. Its achievements include the first steamboat in the Mediterranean in 1818, the first railway on the Italian peninsula in 1839, connecting Naples to Portici, and the first volcano observatory, the Osservatorio Vesuviano, in 1841.
kingdom-of-zimbabwe: The kingdom was a Shona state named after its capital; dzimbabwe is Shona for great house of stone. The site had been occupied since about 1000 by speakers of proto-Karanga and lay on the fringe of the Mapungubwe state. From the 12th century it competed with settlements such as Chivowa, and its ruling dynasty built houses of thick daga and stone walls to shield themselves from view. By 1250 it was an important trading centre, and by 1300 merchants were bypassing the Limpopo for the gold-producing interior, which brought the rapid decline of Mapungubwe and the dominance of Great Zimbabwe.

At its height the capital covered 7.22 square kilometres and had about 10,000 people, and the state, made up of over 150 smaller zimbabwes, likely covered 50,000 square kilometres. It did not control the village mines directly but dominated the trade routes, exporting gold through Swahili cities such as Sofala.

The causes of its decline are unknown. Shona tradition speaks of a shortage of salt, perhaps a figure for exhausted land or resources, and from the early 15th century falling demand for gold hurt the city. Tradition says Nyatsimba Mutota led people north to found the Mutapa Empire, and by the 16th century power had passed to Mutapa and to Khami, capital of the Kingdom of Butua. The site was likely inhabited into the 17th century.

The sacred king, the mambo, was helped by a chosen brother or sister and ruled over a three-tiered class structure, taxing tributary rulers. Royalty lived first in the Eastern and Western enclosures and later in the Great Enclosure, while district chiefs and regional governors had prestige enclosures outside. Wealth rested on cattle, farming and the gold trade, and Persian bowls and Chinese celadon reached the city.

From the 1890s to the 1920s European antiquarians looted the site, and Rhodesians, out of racial prejudice, credited it to anyone but the Shona; its African origin became the consensus only by the 1950s.
kingston-jamaica: Kingston lies on the south-eastern coast of Jamaica and faces a natural harbour protected by the Palisadoes, a long sand spit that connects the town of Port Royal and the international airport to the rest of the island. The city stands on the Liguanea plain, an alluvial plain beside the Hope River, and is surrounded by the Blue Mountains, the Red Hills, Long Mountain and the harbour. It lies in the rain shadow of the Blue Mountains and is very dry compared with parishes on the windward side. Kingston experiences frequent earthquakes. Two districts make up its central area: the historic Downtown and New Kingston.

Kingston was founded on 22 July 1692, shortly after the earthquake that devastated Port Royal. The original section, at the bottom of the Liguanea Plains, was laid out to house survivors, who first camped on the sea front on Colonel Barry's Hog Crawle; about two thousand people died of mosquito-borne diseases. Before the earthquake its functions had been purely agricultural, and the town did not begin to grow until Port Royal was further destroyed by fire in 1703. The surveyor John Goffe drew up a grid plan bounded by North, East, West and Harbour Streets, with main thoroughfares 66 feet across to ease transport between the port and the plantations inland.

Wolmer's, the first free school, was founded in 1729. By 1780 Kingston had 11,000 inhabitants, and its merchants lobbied for the administrative capital to be moved from Spanish Town, which commercial activity had eclipsed. In 1788 the population was 25,000, about a tenth of the island's; one in four was white, two out of five were free, and the remaining three-fifths were enslaved Black people. The government offices were transferred from Spanish Town in 1872. In 1907 an earthquake killed 800 people and destroyed nearly all the historical buildings south of Parade, and a height limit of 60 feet was then set for buildings in the centre. The island-wide riots of the 1930s led to the growth of trade unions and political parties.

Kingston is the capital and largest city of Jamaica, its main transport hub and its largest seaport. Kingston Harbour is described as the seventh largest natural harbour in the world. The local government bodies of Kingston and St. Andrew were amalgamated in 1923 as the Kingston and St. Andrew Corporation, and the Mona campus of the University of the West Indies was founded in 1948. The majority of the population is of African descent, with minorities including East Indians and Chinese, who came as indentured servants in the late nineteenth century. Kingston hosted the Commonwealth Games in 1966.
kingston-ontario: Kingston stands at the north-eastern end of Lake Ontario, at the beginning of the St. Lawrence River and the mouth of the Cataraqui River. It lies between the Prince Edward County and Thousand Islands regions and is nicknamed the Limestone City for its many heritage buildings of local limestone. The region is underlain mostly by Ordovician limestone. Its original name, Cataraqui, derives from an Indigenous name for the area, with many suggested meanings, among them the place where the rivers and lake meet.

Archaeological evidence suggests people lived in the region as early as the Archaic period, and more permanent encampments began about 900 CE. The group that first occupied the area before the French was probably the Wendat, later displaced by the Haudenosaunee. Samuel de Champlain visited in 1615, and in 1673 the French founded a trading post and military fort at Cataraqui, later called Fort Frontenac. After the Conquest of New France the site passed to the British, Cataraqui was renamed Kingston, and Loyalists began settling in the 1780s.

In 1783 Governor Frederick Haldimand directed Major Samuel Holland to lay out a settlement for Loyalists fleeing the American Revolutionary War and to judge whether the site would serve as a naval base, since nearby Carleton Island had been ceded to the Americans. Holland reported that the harbour was good and conveniently placed to command Lake Ontario. During the War of 1812 Kingston, with 2,250 people, was the base of the British fleet on Lake Ontario, which raced the American fleet at Sackets Harbor. The present Fort Henry was built between 1832 and 1836 to defend the Rideau Canal, opened in 1832.

Lord Sydenham chose Kingston as the first capital of the united Canadas, and the Parliament of the Province of Canada first met there on 13 June 1841. The city was judged too small and too near the border, and the capital moved to Montreal in 1844. Kingston's growth then slowed and its national importance declined, though in the early 20th century it housed the Canadian Locomotive Company, the largest locomotive works in the British Empire.

Kingston had 132,485 people at the 2021 census. It is home to Queen's University, founded in 1841 under a royal charter, the Royal Military College of Canada, established in 1876, and St. Lawrence College. It has the largest concentration of federal correctional facilities in Canada, and its heritage register lists 1,211 properties. Fort Henry, garrisoned by the British until 1871, is part of a World Heritage Site. John A. Macdonald, Canada's first prime minister, lived in the city.
kinich-janaab-pakal: Kʼinich Janaabʼ Pakal was born at Palenque on 24 March 603 to Lady Sak Kʼukʼ of the ruling dynasty and her husband Kʼan Moʼ Hix. His birth came in a turbulent time. Calakmul had sacked Palenque four years earlier, and Calakmul's ruler Scroll Serpent led another catastrophic attack in 611. The following year the ruler Ajen Yohl Mat and his heir Janahb Pakal, the boy's maternal grandfather and namesake, both died, which created a crisis of succession. Pakal acceded in July 615 at the age of twelve, after an interim regency by his mother, who slowly ceded power over the years and died in September 640.

Pakal expanded Palenque's power in the western part of the Maya lands and began a building programme at his capital. In March 626 he married Ix Tzʼakbu Ajaw, a descendant of the former Toktahn dynasty from Uxteʼkʼuh, and they had at least two sons, Kan Bahlam and Kʼan Joy Chitam. In 628 Piedras Negras captured one of his officials, and six days later Nuun Ujol Chaak, ajaw of Santa Elena, was taken to Palenque; Santa Elena became a tributary. He captured prisoners from Pipaʼ and Santa Elena in 659 and 663.

His first construction project, in 647, was the temple now called El Olvidado. He greatly enlarged the Palace, adding Building E, called the White Skin House, and Houses B and C in 661 and House A in 668, which is covered with frescoes of prisoners captured in 662. His wife died in November 672, after 47 years of marriage.
Pakal died in August 683 aged 80, having ruled for 68 years and 33 days. He was deified as one of Palenque's patron gods, and his sons Kan Bahlam and Kʼan Joy Chitam each became ruler in turn.

He was buried in a sarcophagus within the Temple of the Inscriptions. The archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier discovered the way into the tomb in 1948, and after four years of clearing rubble from the stairway it was uncovered in 1952. The skeleton lay with a jade mask and bead necklaces, among stucco reliefs of his passage to divinity.

The slight wear on its teeth led Ruz to doubt that the bones were Pakal's, but later analysis of the skeleton showed that the person died in their eighth or ninth decade, in agreement with the inscriptions. The carved sarcophagus lid shows him beneath a world tree, framed by the jaws of a funerary serpent and dressed as the Maize God. Archaeologists reject the claim, made by Erich von Däniken in 1968, that it depicts an astronaut.
kinich-yax-kuk-mo: His name is usually rendered Great Sun, Quetzal Macaw the First, and Maya inscriptions name him the founder and first kʼul ajaw, or holy lord, of the polity centred at Copán in the south-eastern Maya lowlands. On Copán's monuments he is shown with motifs that recall the distant central Mexican city of Teotihuacan, above all a goggle-eyed headdress, seemingly an allusion to the rain deity later peoples such as the Aztecs called Tlaloc. These have been read as claiming an origin in, or a tie to, that city.

Strontium isotope analysis of the teeth from the tomb attributed to him points elsewhere: the man spent his early years near Tikal in the Petén Basin and later lived somewhere between Tikal and Copán, and the signature does not match a Teotihuacan origin. Epigraphic research published in 2022 linked his dynasty to that of Caracol.

The chronology and the inscriptions point to a wider rise, in the late 4th century, of rulers sent into the Maya lowlands from Teotihuacan as invaders or envoys, among them Yax Nuun Ayiin I of Tikal, son of the Teotihuacan lord Spearthrower Owl. This suggests that later kings of Copán, in particular Kʼakʼ Yipyaj Chan Kʼawiil and Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat, gave the founder a Teotihuacan heritage after the fact to strengthen their claim. During his reign he placed Tok Casper on the throne of Quiriguá.

The tomb held to be his, the Hunal tomb inside Temple 16 of the Copán acropolis, was excavated in 2000. He was buried with jade and shell jewellery and his goggle-eyed headdress. The skeleton showed healed fractures of the arm, sternum and shoulder, which have been thought to come from ball-court games. His dynasty ruled Copán until 822, and his portrait stands first on Altar Q, the carved king list of the dynasty, and in prominent places on other monuments of later rulers.
kinkaku-ji: The site was first a villa called Kitayama-dai, belonging to the statesman Saionji Kintsune. In 1397 the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu bought it from the Saionji family and turned it into the Kinkaku-ji complex. When he died, his son converted the building into a Zen temple, according to his wishes. The gold was meant to mitigate and purify pollution and negative feelings about death. During the Ōnin war of 1467 to 1477 every building of the complex except the pavilion burned down.

The pavilion has three storeys, and each is built in a different style. The ground floor, the Chamber of Dharma Waters, is in shinden-zukuri, the residential style of the Heian aristocracy, with unpainted wood and white plaster. The second, the Tower of Sound Waves, is in the style of warrior aristocrats and holds a Buddha Hall and a shrine of the goddess of mercy, Kannon. The third, the Cupola of the Ultimate, is in Chinese Chan style. The upper two floors are covered in gold leaf, and the pavilion serves as a shariden, housing relics of the Buddha. A bronze phoenix tops the roof. It was an important model for Ginkaku-ji and Shōkoku-ji in Kyoto.

The pavilion stands in a strolling garden and extends over a pond called Kyōko-chi, or Mirror Pond, which holds ten smaller islands. Rocks, bridges and plants are arranged to recall notable places in Chinese and Japanese literature. The grounds were laid out after descriptions of the Western Paradise of the Buddha Amida. The garden is regarded as a good example of Muromachi period design.

On 2 July 1950 a 22-year-old novice monk, Hayashi Shoken, burned the pavilion down. The original statue of Yoshimitsu was lost. The monk was sentenced to seven years, released in 1955 because of mental illness and died of tuberculosis in 1956. Yukio Mishima's 1956 book The Temple of the Golden Pavilion fictionalises the events. The present pavilion, 12.5 metres high, dates from 1955 and is said to be a close copy, though some question whether the original had so much gold leaf. In 1984 the gold leaf was found peeling and it was replaced in 1986 and 1987. The temple is a World Heritage Site, one of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.
kinmen: Kinmen lies about 10 kilometres east of Xiamen in Fujian, across Xiamen Bay, and 187 kilometres west of the nearest shore of the island of Taiwan. The county consists of the main island, several surrounding islets including Lesser Kinmen (Lieyu), and the remote Wuqiu Township, 133 kilometres to the northeast. Like the neighbouring mainland, the islands are mostly of Cretaceous granite. Kinmen and Lienchiang County (Matsu) are the two counties of Fuchien Province. The name Kinmen, meaning golden gate, was first recorded in 1387, when the Hongwu Emperor appointed Zhou Dexing to protect the island from pirates.

People have lived on Kinmen for 5,800 to 8,000 years. In 317 CE, during the invasions of the Five Barbarians, six extended families fled south and settled on the island, then called Wuzhou. More settlers came under the Tang dynasty, when the name changed to Kinmen, and under the Ming. Koxinga used Kinmen as a base for his campaign against the Dutch in Formosa and Penghu, and his felling of trees to build a navy led to deforestation and soil erosion. The Prince of Lu, a member of the Southern Ming, fled to Kinmen in 1651 in his resistance to the Qing, who took the island in 1663.

After the Republic of China was founded in 1912 Kinmen became part of Fujian Province. It was made part of Siming County in 1913, became a county of its own in 1914, and in 1928 came under the direct administration of the provincial government. Its position in the Taiwan Strait later brought repeated confrontations. In August 1958 the People's Liberation Army bombarded the islands heavily in the Second Taiwan Strait Crisis. Military administration lasted for decades, and travel restrictions between Kinmen and the main island of Taiwan were lifted in 1994.

Many inhabitants speak Hokkien, with the Quanzhou accent predominant, while Wuqiu speaks Pu-Xian Min. The people of Kinmen see themselves as Kinmenese, people of southern Fujian, or Chinese, and identify as citizens of the Republic of China. Local products include Kinmen Kaoliang liquor and knives forged from the remnants of shells fired in the bombardments. A direct ferry to Xiamen began in January 2001, and the islands opened to tourists from the mainland in 2003. Much of the main island forms Kinmen National Park, which preserves military fortifications, historic dwellings and natural scenery.
kinnaur: Kinnaur is an entirely mountainous district in the north-east of Himachal Pradesh. It borders Tibet to the east, Uttarakhand to the south, Shimla district to the south-west, Kullu to the west, and Lahaul and Spiti to the north. Its altitude runs from about 1,500 metres to over 6,000 metres, and several tributaries of the Sutlej River drain it.

Three ranges run through or touch it: the Zanskar, the Great Himalaya and the Dhauladhar. Leo Purgyil, at 6,816 metres, is the highest peak of Himachal Pradesh, and Kinner Kailash, at 6,050 metres, is a regional pilgrimage site for Hindus. The upper Sutlej valley and part of the Spiti valley lie in a rain shadow with an arid climate like Tibet's, while the lower Sutlej and Baspa valleys receive monsoon rains.

In the 10th and 11th centuries Kinnaur was part of the Guge kingdom. Guge broke apart in the 12th century, and the Bushahr state arose in the western Himalaya, taking over most of present-day Kinnaur. It originated in the village of Kamru in the Sangla valley. The uppermost part of Kinnaur stayed under Tibetan influence until the late 17th century, when the Tibetans handed it to Bushahr as a reward for help in the Tibet-Ladakh-Mughal War.

Bushahr moved its capital to Sarahan and later to Rampur, and so became known as Rampur-Bushahr. The Gurkhas attacked it in the early 19th century, and soon afterwards the British gained supremacy. It was a princely state under the British crown until 1947, and most of present-day Kinnaur was its Chini tehsil.

On 15 April 1948 Rampur-Bushahr joined the Republic of India and became part of the Mahasu district. In 1960 the Chini tehsil and fourteen villages of the neighbouring Rampur tehsil were separated to form the new district of Kinnaur.

Kinnaur has its headquarters at Reckong Peo and a 2011 census population of 84,121, all of it rural. Its people speak about nine language varieties, eight of them Sino-Tibetan, among them Kinnauri, Chitkuli and Jangrami, and one an Indo-Aryan variety called Pahari Kinnauri. Hindi is increasingly the language of choice among young speakers. The district has two protected areas, the Rupi Bhaba Wildlife Sanctuary, established in 1982, and the Lippa-Asarang Wildlife Sanctuary, established in 1974, which shelter species such as the snow leopard, the Himalayan tahr and the wild yak.
kinross-shire: Kinross-shire is Scotland's second smallest county, bordered by Perthshire to the north and by Fife on its other sides. Loch Leven, with an internationally important nature reserve, dominates it; St Serf's Inch is the largest of its islands, and Lochleven Castle stands on another. Rolling farmland round the loch rises to the Ochil Hills in the north-west, where Innerdouny Hill reaches 497 metres, and the Cleish Hills in the south. Most of its people once lived by farming, and Kinross was its only burgh, made a burgh of barony in 1540/1.

The area was once part of the province of Fothriff, joined to the earldom of Fife by the early thirteenth century, and there was a sheriff of Kinross by 1252, first over the parishes of Kinross and Orwell alone. Cleish, Portmoak and Tullibole were added in 1685. From 1426 the county sent a member to the Parliament of Scotland; after the Union of 1707 it alternated with Clackmannanshire in returning a member to Westminster, and the two were merged into one constituency in 1832.

Kinross County Council first met on 22 May 1890 at the County Buildings in Kinross. At the 1921 census the county was the least populous in Scotland, with fewer than 8,000 people, and from 1930 its council worked jointly with Perthshire's. Its population fell from 6,673 in 1891 to 6,423 in 1971 as people left for work in the cities, a decline hastened by the closing of the county's railways after the Second World War. In 1975 it was abolished as an administrative area and became part of the Perth and Kinross district of Tayside.

Kinross-shire lies within the Perth and Kinross council area, and its old boundaries are still used as a registration county. The M90 motorway crosses it from north to south, linking Kinross with Perth and Dunfermline. The arms granted to the county council in 1927 show Lochleven Castle and survive on a small shield in the arms of Perth and Kinross Council.
kinshasa: Kinshasa stands on the southern shore of Pool Malebo, a widening of the Congo River, in a broad crescent of flat, low-lying terrain at an average elevation of about 300 metres. The city-province covers 9,965 square kilometres, and the Congo River forms its western and northern boundary with the Republic of the Congo. Across the river, about four kilometres away and unbridged, lies Brazzaville, so that the two capitals are the closest pair in the world. The river is a transport route across much of the Congo Basin, with barges navigable between Kinshasa and Kisangani.

The site has been inhabited by Teke and Humbu people for centuries. In pre-colonial times it held two trading centres, Ntamo and Ntsaasa, which were part of the Tio Kingdom. Two theories explain the name Nshasa. One links it to a bag of salt, and to a trading post where people from the lower Congo and the Atlantic exchanged salt for goods including ivory and enslaved people; the other derives it from Teke trading terms, in which fishermen exchanged fish for cassava.

The city was founded on 1 August 1881 as Léopold II Station, and Henry Morton Stanley named it Léopoldville in honour of Leopold II of Belgium. A royal decree of 11 April 1914 designated it the capital of the Belgian Congo, and an ordinance of 25 June 1941 gave it city status. Its population grew from 5,000 in 1889 to 39,530 in 1930 and reached 400,000 at independence in 1960.

In 1966, during Mobutu Sese Seko's Zairianisation campaign, it was renamed Kinshasa as a tribute to the village of Nshasa. Its economic prominence peaked in the 1970s, a period known as la belle époque, and in 1974 it hosted the boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman known as the Rumble in the Jungle.

Kinshasa is the capital and largest city of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with a population estimated at about 18 million. It is also one of the country's 26 provinces, divided into 24 communes. French is the language of government, education and the media, while Lingala is the lingua franca of the street. UNESCO designated it a City of Music in 2015, and it has a long-established music scene and a national stadium, the Stade des Martyrs.
kintyre: The peninsula runs about 50 kilometres from the Mull of Kintyre in the south to East and West Loch Tarbert in the north, and the region just north of it is Knapdale. It is never more than 18 kilometres wide and less than three kilometres wide where it meets Knapdale. Its east side is bounded by Kilbrannan Sound, and the southern tip faces the North Channel. The central spine is mostly hilly moorland, rising to Beinn an Tuirc at 454 metres, while the coastal areas are rich and fertile.
The land has long attracted settlers, among them the early Scots from Ulster and the Norsemen, who conquered and settled the area just before the start of the second millennium.

Kintyre has Stone Age sites, such as the Ballochroy megaliths and the cairns at Blasthill, and Iron Age remains, among them the hillfort of Dun Skeig. In the early first millennium an Irish invasion led to Gaelic colonisation centred on the peninsula and to the kingdom of Dál Riata. Its most powerful kin group, the Cenél nGabráin, ruled Kintyre along with Knapdale, Arran and Moyle in Ulster. In 563 Columba came to Kintyre to pay his respects to the kings of Dál Riata before going on to Iona.

Norse Vikings later destroyed the kingdom, and Kintyre came under the Norwegian Kingdom of the Isles. In 1093 King Magnus of Norway had his boat dragged across the isthmus at Tarbert, with himself aboard, to claim Kintyre under an agreement with Malcolm of Scotland, and in 1098 King Edgar of Scotland quitclaimed Kintyre and Knapdale to him.

In the mid 12th century Somerled led a revolt that made the isles independent, and his grandson Donald acquired Kintyre. The Treaty of Perth in 1266 passed Norway's nominal authority to Alexander III of Scotland. Later the MacDonalds combined Somerled's realm into the Lordship of the Isles, and after a plot of the last Lord, John, with the English king came to light, he quitclaimed Kintyre and Knapdale to Scotland. In 1607 James VI ordered the MacDonald lands in Kintyre transferred to the Campbells, and Campbell settlers from the Lowlands founded Campbeltown, diluting Gaelic culture.

Kintyre lies within the council area of Argyll and Bute. Its principal town is Campbeltown, a royal burgh since the mid-18th century, known for single malt whisky such as Springbank, and the economy has long rested on fishing and farming. Medieval remains include Saddell Abbey, founded in 1207 by Reginald, and the castles of Saddell, Skipness and Tarbert. The Mull of Kintyre is the subject of the 1977 song by Paul McCartney's Wings.
kinzig-main: The Kinzig is 87 kilometres long and a right tributary of the Main, and its catchment covers 1,058 square kilometres. Its source, the Kinzigquelle, is a small spring enclosed in sandstone at about 400 metres above sea level, south of Sterbfritz in the municipality of Sinntal, near Schlüchtern. From there the river runs north-west, forming the boundary between the Hessian Rhön Nature Park and the Hessian Spessart Nature Park as far as Schlüchtern.

West of Schlüchtern it turns south-west and separates the Vogelsberg hills to the north from the Spessart to the south. Its main tributaries are the Steinebach, Ulmbach, Salz, Bracht, Orb, Bieber, Birkigsbach, Gründau, Lache and Fallbach. It reaches the Main at Hanau at about 100 metres above sea level.

The river is first recorded in 815 under the name Chinzicha. In October 1813 it played a part in the Battle of Hanau, fought as Napoleon retreated towards the Rhine after his defeat at the Battle of Leipzig. Before Hanau the river flows through the Bulau, a woodland once used by the US Army as an exercise area, which has stayed largely natural because few people live there.

The towns on the river are Schlüchtern, Steinau an der Straße, Bad Soden-Salmünster, Gelnhausen and Hanau, and the Main-Kinzig-Kreis district takes its name from it. The Kinzig Dam lies between Steinau and Ahl, and canoeists use the lower reaches. At the mouth in Hanau an observation platform of two interleaved terraces looks towards Philippsruhe Castle and the Main river port.
kinzig-rhine: The Kinzig is a right tributary of the Rhine, 93 kilometres long, lying wholly within Baden-Württemberg. It rises on the land of Loßburg in the district of Freudenstadt, runs south and then turns gradually west past Alpirsbach, touches the district of Rottweil and spends most of its course in the Ortenau. With its side valleys it forms the largest valley system of the Black Forest, and it is counted either as the border between the Northern and Middle Black Forest or as part of the Middle Black Forest.

The upper river is a true mountain stream that has caused serious floods, while the middle and lower reaches run in a straightened bed between tall levees. At the end of the last ice age the river wound across the Upper Rhine Plain, took in the Murg and joined the Rhine only near Hockenheim. Its largest tributary is the Schutter, which enters near Kehl.

The river is first named in 1099 as ad Chinzechun and in 1128 as Kinzicha; its name is supposed to be of Celtic origin, though the scholars Adolf Bach and Bruno Boesch doubt the proposed derivations. Under Emperor Vespasian, in 73/74, the Romans built the Kinzig Valley road from Offenburg to the newly founded town of Rottweil (Arae Flaviae) and on to Tuttlingen, a shorter link from Mainz to Augsburg after the long detour by Basel had caused trouble during the revolt of the Batavi. After 98 the road lost its wider importance.

Timber rafting on the Kinzig is first recorded in 1339. The rafting corporations of Wolfach and Schiltach held sole export rights from their lords and floated timber to the Rhine and on to Holland, with peaks in the 15th and 16th centuries and again in the 18th, when the Netherlands and England were building their naval and merchant fleets. The railways ended the trade, and the last commercial raft ran in 1896.

The federal highway B 33 and the Black Forest Railway follow the valley from Offenburg, and museums in Gengenbach, Wolfach and Schiltach recall the rafting era. Fruit and wine are grown in the lower valley, and young salmon released since 2002 led in 2005 to the first salmon spawn found in a river of Baden-Württemberg in 50 years.
kipchaks: The Kipchaks are first mentioned in the 8th century as part of the Second Turkic Khaganate, and they most likely lived in the Altai region. When the Khaganate collapsed they entered the Kimek confederation as one of its seven original tribes. They were first clearly named in the Persian geographer Ibn Khordadbeh's Book of Roads and Kingdoms, which says they held autonomy within the Kimek union. A 10th-century source says the Kimek appointed the Kipchak king.

Between the 11th and 13th centuries a complex process of assimilation took place on the Kipchak steppe: the western tribes absorbed people of Oghuz, Pecheneg and Bulgar origin, the eastern ones merged with the Kimek, Karluk and others, and all came to be called Kipchaks. The Kipchaks themselves explained their name as 'hollow tree', after a legend of an ancestress who gave birth inside one.

The Kimek confederation, probably led by the Kipchaks, moved into Oghuz lands, and Sighnaq on the Syr Darya became a Kipchak urban centre. Three groups emerged: Kipchaks of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, of the Syr Darya and of Siberia. From the second half of the 12th century the names Cumans and Kipchaks were used interchangeably for the whole confederation, though how the two peoples were related is unclear.

The Mongols persuaded the Kipchaks to desert the Alans, then attacked the Kipchaks themselves. Under their khan Köten they allied with the Ruthenians, including his son-in-law Mstislav Mstislavich of Galicia, and were defeated at the Kalka River in 1223. When the Mongols crossed the Volga in 1236 the Kipchaks were their main target. Many entered the Mongol ranks and were absorbed into the Golden Horde, while Köten led 40,000 families into Hungary, where King Béla IV gave them refuge in return for their Christianization. Others became mercenaries in Europe or slave warriors. Emperor John III Doukas Vatatzes of Nicaea settled some in Anatolia. The Mamluk Sultanate, founded in 1250, was first ruled by Bahri Mamluks of Kipchak origin.

Their most important written record is the Codex Cumanicus, a late 13th-century dictionary of Kipchak, Cuman and Latin words. The Kipchaks originally practised Tengrism; some converted to Christianity from the 11th century, and many were baptized at the request of King David IV of Georgia, who married a daughter of the Kipchak khan Otrok. Under the Golden Horde, Islam became the official religion in the reign of Özbeg Khan. The Northwestern branch of the Turkic languages is often called the Kipchak branch, and the peoples who speak its languages include the Kumyks, Karachays, Balkars, Nogays, Bashkirs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Volga Tatars and Crimean Tatars.
kirata: Kirāta is a generic term of Sanskrit literature for peoples whose lands lay in the mountains, above all the Himalayas and Northeast India, and who are believed to have been Sino-Tibetan in origin. The name is first found in the Yajurveda and the Atharvaveda, where the Kiratas are often named together with the Cinas, the Chinese, and set slightly apart from the Nishadas. It has been suggested that the word is a Sanskrit form of a Tibeto-Burman tribal name, such as that of the Kirant or Kiranti of eastern Nepal.

Its sense was disputed. Suniti Kumar Chatterji held that it seems to have been used for any non-Aryan hill people. Some writers took it to mean a degraded mountain tribe, while other scholars give it more respectable meanings, people of a lion's character or simply mountain dwellers.

Manu's Dharmashastra calls the Kiratas degraded Kshatriyas, which Chatterji read as a name for people of some military or civilised attainment rather than outright barbarians. In the Mahabharata, Bhima meets the Kiratas east of Videha, where his son Ghatotkacha is born. In the Yoga Vasistha, Rama speaks of a trap laid by Kiratas, picturing them as jungle trappers who dug pits for roving deer, and the same text names King Suraghu, head of the Kiratas, as a friend of the Persian king Parigha. The texts generally call them gold-like or yellow, unlike the Nishadas or the Dasas.

Classical writers knew them too. The Periplus calls them the Kirradai, the same people as Pliny's Scyrites and Aelian's Skiratai, and Ptolemy, though he does not name them, mentions their land, Kirradia; these writers describe them as barbaric in their ways. The Sesatai, who traded the aromatic plant malabathrum, were described in similar terms. Sylvain Lévi concluded that Kirata was a general term used by the Hindus of the plains for the Tibeto-Burman speaking groups of the Himalayas and the Northeast.
kirchheim-unter-teck: Kirchheim unter Teck lies in the foothills of the central Swabian Alb, north of the Albtrauf escarpment, in the valley of the small river Lauter, a tributary of the Neckar. The town is about 35 kilometres south-east of Stuttgart and 10 kilometres from Teck castle. The Lauter flows through the town centre, then north-west through the district of Ötlingen towards Wendlingen am Neckar, where it joins the Neckar.

Traces of settlement from the Neolithic, Celtic and Roman periods have been found, and Alamannic graves show three settlements in the area during the migration period. The first written mention of Kirchheim is from 960, when it came into the possession of Emperor Otto I in an exchange for the diocese of Chur, although the town certainly existed in the 6th and 7th centuries. The market and royal mint date from the mid-11th century.

The Dukes of Zähringen owned the place, and in 1186 it passed by inheritance to a lateral line, the Dukes of Teck. Between 1220 and 1230 they made it a market town under Freiburg law, Duke Louis I of Teck founded a nunnery in 1240, and Duke Conrad II began a city wall in 1270.
Economic difficulties led the Dukes of Teck to give up the town in a process that lasted from 1303 to 1386, by which Kirchheim became part of Austria and later of Württemberg.

In the 14th century the rise of the middle classes brought an economic boom, especially in the textile industry and trade. After Duke Ulrich returned from exile in 1539, Kirchheim was expanded into a Württemberg fortress and the ducal palace was built. Duke Ulrich had introduced Protestantism in 1535. The town owes its present appearance to the rebuilding after a devastating fire in 1690, and in 1864 it became the end of the first private railway in Württemberg.

After the Second World War the population grew markedly with refugees and displaced persons, passing 20,000 in 1948, and on 1 April 1956 the town became a Große Kreisstadt. In 1945 the Luftwaffe built a launch site in the Hasenholz forest for Bachem Ba 349 Natter rocket interceptors, and three concrete launch pads remain.

Kirchheim unter Teck belongs to the district of Esslingen and is a regional centre in the Stuttgart Region. It took in Ötlingen and Lindorf in 1935 and Nabern and Jesingen in 1974. It was long the seat of an Oberamt and was an early centre of industry: by 1911 it made cotton goods, damask, pianofortes, machinery and gliders, and was the most important wool market in southern Germany. Notable people connected with it include the engineer and writer Max Eyth, born there in 1836, and the glider pilot Martin Schempp, who founded Schempp-Hirth.
kiribati: Kiribati has a total land area of 811 km2 spread over 3,441,810 km2 of ocean. Its islands, from Banaba in the west to Kiritimati in the east, straddle the equator and the 180th meridian. They fall into three groups: the Gilbert Islands, sixteen atolls about 1,500 km north of Fiji; the Phoenix Islands, eight atolls and coral islands; and the Line Islands, eight atolls and one reef. Banaba is a raised coral island that was once a rich source of phosphates. The rest of the land is sand and reef rock islets that rise only one or two metres above sea level, with thin, calcareous soil. Kiritimati has the largest land area of any atoll in the world.

The area has been inhabited by Austronesian peoples speaking the same Oceanic language since sometime between 3000 BCE and 1300 CE. Oral historians suggest that seafarers from Melanesia came first, later visited by Austronesian seafarers from the west. Around 1300 CE a mass departure from Samoa added Polynesian ancestry and culture. From about the 15th century the northern islands came under chiefly rule (uea), while the central and southern islands were ruled by councils of elders (unimwaane); Tabiteuea alone is known to have kept an egalitarian society. Clans and chiefs fought over land, and some islands used guns and cannon-equipped ships supplied by Europeans to destroy their foes.

The name Gilbert Islands was given around 1820 by the Russian admiral Adam von Krusenstern and the French captain Louis Duperrey, after the British captain Thomas Gilbert, who sighted some of the islands in 1788. The British annexed the Gilberts as a protectorate in 1892. From 1916 the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony took its name from them, and it lasted until the Ellice Islands became Tuvalu in 1976. Kiribati became independent from the United Kingdom in 1979, with the Gilberts, the Phoenix and Line islands and Banaba. The name is the Gilbertese rendering of Gilberts. Phosphate mining on Banaba was exhausted by independence, and the Banabans mostly live on Rabi in Fiji.

Kiribati is a parliamentary democratic republic under the constitution promulgated on 12 July 1979. Its capital, Tarawa, is made up of islets joined by causeways, and more than half the population lives there. A census of November 2020 counted 119,940 people. The I-Kiribati are a Micronesian people who speak Gilbertese, an Oceanic language; English is the other official language. The country joined the United Nations in 1999.
kirillo-belozersky-monastery: The monastery is dedicated to the Dormition of the Theotokos and was sometimes called the Dormition Monastery of St. Cyril. Its founder, Kirill of Beloozero, a member of the influential Velyaminov clan of boyars, had given up the office of father superior of the Simonov monastery in Moscow. Following the advice of his teacher, St. Sergius of Radonezh, he first dug a cave on the bank of Lake Siverskoye, then built a wooden chapel and a log house for other monks. The area had shortly before come under the Grand Duchy of Moscow, whose rulers seem to have seen the monastery as a strategic point for northern trade and in their struggle with the Novgorod Republic.

Under Hegumen Trifon the community adopted an Athonite cenobitic rule and set up a Byzantine-style school with textbooks on grammar, geography and history; its legacy included the bibliographical work of the elder Yefrosin and the text-critical studies of Nil Sorsky, who founded a skete on the Sora River nearby. In the 16th century the monastery was the second richest landowner in Russia after the Trinity Monastery. Ivan the Terrible kept his own cell there and planned to take vows in it. It also served as a political prison, holding Vassian Patrikeyev, Tsar Simeon Bekbulatovich, Patriarch Nikon and Boris Morozov, and in December 1612 it withstood a siege by the Polish-Lithuanian Lisowczycy.

Its walls, 732 metres long and 7 metres thick, were built in 1654-80, first under the French engineer Jean de Gron, known in Russia as Anton Granovsky, whom the monks replaced with native masters. It was the largest fortress raised in Muscovy after the Time of Troubles.

The walled area holds two priories with eleven churches, most of the 16th century. The Dormition cathedral, built by masters from Rostov in 1497, was then the largest monastery church in Russia, and St. Vladimir's Chapel over the grave of Prince Vorotynsky became the first family mausoleum in Russia. After the Bolsheviks secularised the monastery around 1924, its library went to Moscow and St Petersburg, including the oldest copies of Daniel's Pilgrimage and the Zadonshchina. Monks returned to the Ivanovsky priory in 1998, and the ensemble is a cultural heritage monument of federal significance.
kiritimati: Kiritimati is a raised coral atoll in the northern Line Islands, part of the Republic of Kiribati. Its name is the English word Christmas written in Gilbertese. It has about 312 square kilometres of land and 328 square kilometres of lagoons, which makes it one of the largest atolls in the world by land area and more than 70 per cent of the land area of Kiribati. It lies 232 kilometres north of the equator and 2,160 kilometres south of Honolulu. Kiribati moved the International Date Line in 1995 so that the atoll lies on the western side, in the time zone UTC+14. Rainfall is low and irregular, and severe droughts occur; the island was abandoned in 1905.

Polynesian people first used the island, and radiometric dating places human activity between 1250 and 1450 CE. Archaeological sites on the windward east side include habitation sites, marae, canoe sheds and navigational aids. Researchers suggest that people, probably from Tabuaeran to the north, visited intermittently to gather birds and turtles, and permanent settlement probably began only in 1882. Rats already lived on the island when Captain Cook arrived in 1777. The census of 1931 in the Gilbert and Ellice Islands colony counted 38 inhabitants, most of them workers of the Emmanuel Rougier Company.

During the Cold War the United Kingdom and the United States tested nuclear weapons there. Britain used Kiritimati as the main base of its first hydrogen bomb tests, Grapple 1 to 3, held at Malden Island from 15 May to 19 June 1957. On 8 November 1957 the first British hydrogen bomb was detonated over the south-eastern tip of Kiritimati in the Grapple X test, and the Grapple Y and Z tests of 1958 took place above or near it. The island was not evacuated, so Kiribati residents and British, New Zealand and Fijian servicemen were exposed to radiation. The United States tested weapons there in 1962.

Kiritimati had 7,369 inhabitants at the census of 2020, up from 477 in 1963. The main villages are London, with the port, Tabwakea and Banana, along the northern road, and Poland, which has a Catholic church. The whole island is a wildlife sanctuary, declared in 1975 after a bird sanctuary in 1960, and it is an important breeding ground for seabirds. Its only native land bird is the bokikokiko, Kiribati's endemic reed-warbler. Exports are mainly copra from the state-owned coconut plantation.
kirkuk: Kirkuk lies 238 kilometres north of Baghdad, on the ruins of the original Kirkuk Citadel near the Khasa River. Findings at the Shanidar Cave settlement suggest that Neanderthals occupied the area, and a large quantity of pottery of the Ubaid period has been excavated from several tells in the city. Its ancient name was the Hurrian Arrapha. Since the Seleucid Empire it was known in Aramaic as the Citadel of the House of Seleucid, and the surrounding region appears in Syriac sources as Beth Garmai.

Arrapkha belonged to the Akkadian Empire of Sargon of Akkad and was exposed to raids by the Lullubi in the reign of Naram-Sin. Around 2150 BCE it was occupied by the Gutians, Zagros Mountains dwellers speaking a language isolate, and it was the capital of the short-lived kingdom of Gutium. The Neo-Sumerian Empire drove the Gutians from Mesopotamia around 2115 BCE. In the 1450s BCE the Mittani attacked Assyria and brought Arrapkha under their control, until the Middle Assyrian Empire overthrew them in the mid-14th century BCE.

Arrapha then became part of Assyria proper, the Hurrian population was driven away, and the city rose to prominence in the 11th and 10th centuries BCE and remained important under the Neo-Assyrian Empire. In the Parthian and Sassanid periods it was the capital of the small Assyrian state of Beth Garmai.

Arab Muslims conquered the region in the 7th century CE. Hasanwayhid and Annazid Kurds ruled Kirkuk from 1014 to 1120, then the Seljuk Turks, and the Mongols took it in 1258, after which it belonged to the Ilkhanate. In 1851 it came under direct Ottoman rule. The British occupied Kirkuk on 7 May 1918. Because both Turkey and Britain wanted the Vilayet of Mosul, to which Kirkuk belonged, the question went to the League of Nations, and under the Treaty of Angora of 1926 Kirkuk became part of the Kingdom of Iraq.

The discovery of vast quantities of oil in the region after the First World War was the impetus for annexing the vilayet to Iraq. Pipelines from Kirkuk run through Turkey to Ceyhan on the Mediterranean, with two parallel lines built in 1977 and 1987.

Kirkuk is the capital of the Kirkuk Governorate in northern Iraq and has a diverse population of Kurds, Iraqi Turkmens and Arabs, with smaller numbers of Assyrians. A late 19th-century source gave it about 30,000 inhabitants, and in the early 20th century Turkish was the most common language spoken at home. Its monuments include the Kirkuk Citadel, the Tomb of the Prophet Daniel and the Qaysareyah of Kirkuk. The archaeological sites of Qal'at Jarmo and Yorgan Tepe lie on the outskirts.
kirkwall: Kirkwall stands on the northern coast of Mainland, Orkney, with its harbours in the bay of Kirkwall to the north and Scapa Flow 2.3 kilometres to the south. It is 210 kilometres north of Aberdeen and 850 kilometres north of London. Its parish, St Ola, forms the isthmus between Firth and Holm. On the western edge of the town lies the Grain Earth House, a prehistoric underground passage leading to a small pillared chamber. Such Iron Age earth houses, or souterrains, are characteristic of the Northern Isles, though their purpose remains unknown.

The name comes from the Norse Kirkjuvágr, meaning church bay, the settlement having been established by the Norsemen in the 11th century. It is first mentioned in the Orkneyinga saga in 1046, as the residence of Rögnvald Brusason, Earl of Orkney, who was killed by his uncle Thorfinn the Mighty. The church of the name was not the cathedral, which was originally at Birsay, but an 11th-century church of Saint Olaf of Norway.

St Magnus Cathedral was founded in memory of Saint Magnus Erlendsson, Earl of Orkney from 1108 to 1117, by Earl Rögnvald Kali, later a saint himself. Beside it stand the ruins of the Bishop's Palace and the Earl's Palace. In 1486 King James III of Scotland made Kirkwall a royal burgh, and it later returned a commissioner to the Parliament of Scotland. After the Union with England it joined other towns to form the Northern Burghs, which sent one member to Parliament, and in 1918 the burgh merged into the constituency of Orkney and Shetland.

Steamer services to Kirkwall were run from 1836 by the Aberdeen, Leith, Clyde and Tay Shipping Company. Kirkwall Grammar School has existed since about 1200. The town has many houses and other buildings of the 17th and 18th centuries in the local style, and the town hall was completed in 1884. Tankerness House, one of the best-preserved 16th-century town houses in Scotland, holds the Orkney Museum.

Kirkwall is the largest town in Orkney, with 9,293 inhabitants at the 2011 census, and the seat of Orkney Islands Council. It is technically a cathedral city. Ferries run from its harbour to Aberdeen, Lerwick and the northern islands, and cruise ships call there. The St Magnus International Festival, founded with the help of the composer Peter Maxwell Davies, is held each midsummer, and the Ba Game is played between the Uppies and the Doonies on Christmas Day and New Year's Day.
kirn: Kirn lies in the Bad Kreuznach district of Rhineland-Palatinate, in the valley of the Nahe and of the Hahnenbach, which is cut deeply into the Lützelsoon. It is roughly 10 kilometres north-east of Idar-Oberstein and 30 kilometres west of Bad Kreuznach, and serves as a middle centre for an area on the Nahe and in the Hunsrück. The valley floors are heavily settled, while the steep slopes are forested and topped in places by freestanding quartzite crags, among them the Kallenfels and the Wehlenfelsen. The Hahnenbach flows through the inner town and soon empties into the Nahe.

Kirn was founded at a river crossing where several roads met. Its first documentary mention is from Fulda Abbey on 20 May 841, which calls it Chira. Celtic and Roman finds, including the remains of a villa rustica, point to a much greater age, and the name is believed to be of Celtic origin, probably from kyr, meaning water.

Jews lived in Kirn as early as the Middle Ages. On 21 September 1287 six were murdered in a persecution believed to be linked to the pogroms that followed the Oberwesel blood libel. Jewish life was destroyed again in the persecution of the Plague years, 1348 and 1349. Families settled again from the mid-19th century, and the community had 106 members in 1925. On Kristallnacht, 9 and 10 November 1938, the synagogue's interior was destroyed and 13 Jewish homes were wrecked. The last eleven Jewish residents were deported in July 1942, and 50 people born in or long resident in Kirn are recorded as victims of Nazi persecution.

Kirn is the seat of the Verbandsgemeinde Kirner Land. Its parts are the main centre and the outlying centres of Kallenfels and Kirn-Sulzbach. The Evangelical church on Kirchstraße, the former collegiate church of Saint Pancras, has a Late Gothic choir built after 1467 and a tower of the mid-13th century, with the nave rebuilt in Gothic Revival style in 1891 to 1893. The Catholic parish church of Saint Pancras is a Gothic Revival basilica of 1892 to 1894. The town is twinned with Fontaine-lès-Dijon in France.
kirthar-mountains: The range forms part of the Kohistan region of western Sindh and is held to separate the Iranian plateau from the Indian subcontinent. It extends southward from the Mula River in east-central Balochistan to Cape Monze on the Arabian Sea and covers about 9,000 square kilometres; its coastal sub-ranges, the Khasa and Mulri Hills, reach into the city limits of Karachi. The Gaj and Hub rivers drain it. Barugh Hill is the highest point in the Sindh portion, near the Gorakh Hill Station at 1,734 metres, and peaks above 1,700 metres receive occasional heavy snow in winter.

Geologically the mountains belong to the Kirthar-Sulaiman province, which runs north from the Arabian Sea along the western edge of the Indus Valley. They are parallel ridges, mostly north to south, with plains and dry riverbeds between them, limestone in their upper parts and middle Eocene shale lower down. Of the several passes, only the Gaji Lak Pass, on the road from Zidi and Khuzdar to Jhalawan, is often used.

The name is thought to join an old Sindhi word for mountain, from the Sanskrit giri, with thar, the dry land, so that it means mountains of the desert; the Sanskrit Ramayana calls the region Somagiri. The range holds 21 prehistoric sites and the Taung Tombs of the 16th to 18th centuries, 71 tombs in the lands of the Chhutta tribe. Its people include the Chhutto of the Soomra tribe and Sindhi and Baloch tribes who live by grazing flocks, among them the Burfat, Gabol, Marri, Bugti, Chandio and Lashari. The peak Kutte-Ji-Kabar, the Dog's Grave, takes its name from a Brahui folk tale recorded around 1855.
kirtipur: Kirtipur, in Nepal Bhasa Kipoo, is a municipality and an ancient city in the Kathmandu Valley, 5 km south-west of the city of Kathmandu. It is one of the five dense municipalities of the valley, with Kathmandu, Lalitpur, Bhaktapur and Madhyapur Thimi. The name comes from the Sanskrit kirti, glory, and pur, city, and also from the Kirat kingdom of Yalamber's dynasty. The Newars are the natives of Kirtipur, which remains a centre of Newar culture. Its southern part is surrounded by Champa Devi Hill, to which people around the valley hike on the Nepali New Year.

Kirtipur's history dates from 1099, and it was part of the territory of Lalitpur when the Gorkhali king Prithvi Narayan Shah invaded the Kathmandu Valley in the 18th century. In 1767 Kirtipur was annexed to the Gorkhali kingdom after the Battle of Kirtipur. He took the town on his third attempt, after entering it by trickery, and then cut off the noses of the people, men and women, over 13 years of age.

In the 2006 mass uprising that overthrew the powers of the king, Kirtipur was the site of a peaceful demonstration. Because of its history under the Shah dynasty, whose modern founder conquered the city, it is considered an anti-monarchy city.

The city was listed as a UNESCO tentative site in 2008. Its municipality had 67,171 people at the 2011 census and 81,578 at the 2021 census. Among its temples, the three-storey Bagh Bhairab temple, probably built in the 16th century, is dedicated to the tiger form of Shiva, regarded as the guardian of Kirtipur. The Uma Maheshwor temple stands at the highest point of the town, 1414 metres, and was built in 1655 by Rautra Vishwanath Babu, a son of a king. The Chilancho Stupa carries an inscription of Nepal Samvat 635. Tribhuvan University, the oldest and largest university in Nepal, is located in Kirtipur.
kisaeng: Kisaeng, also called ginyeo, were enslaved women from outcast or enslaved families who were trained as courtesans to provide artistic entertainment and conversation for men of the upper class. The origin of the kisaeng is unclear. A theory linking them to the Silla wonhwa, female predecessors of the hwarang, has little support, since the wonhwa seem to have been aristocrats. Many scholars instead trace them to the early years of Goryeo, when many people were displaced after the end of the Later Three Kingdoms period in 936. The first king of Goryeo, Taejo, considered these wanderers a threat and ordered them made slaves of the government, and the first kisaeng were probably drawn from them.

Kisaeng emerged as a class during the Goryeo dynasty and are first mentioned in the early 11th century, when they were engaged mainly in skilled trades such as needlework, music and medicine. Training academies called gyobang were set up for court entertainers, and they entertained the king and visiting dignitaries and, from the reign of Munjong, performed at state ceremonies.

The system continued under the Joseon dynasty, although the Confucian scholars of the time took a dim view of professional women. Proposals to abolish the kisaeng failed. Under Yeonsangun, between 1494 and 1506, kisaeng became symbols of royal excess: he brought 1,000 women and girls from the provinces to serve as palace kisaeng. In 1908 the Kisaeng Regulation Order grouped them with licensed prostitutes under Japanese rule.

Kisaeng held the status of cheonmin, the lowest in society, and it was hereditary, so that daughters of kisaeng became kisaeng. Women also entered the class by being sold by families who could not support them. A kisaeng could be released only by payment of a heavy price to the government, usually by a wealthy patron. Most careers were short, peaking at 16 or 17 and generally over by 22, and all kisaeng had to retire at 50. Many former kisaeng worked in or managed a local tavern.

In later Joseon a three-tiered system developed, with the ilp'ae who sang and danced at upper-class feasts at the top and the samp'ae at the bottom. Kisaeng were trained in music, dance, poetry and prose, and many sijo composed by them survive. Kisaeng also acted as sources of intelligence, and some, such as Nongae of Jinju, are remembered for killing or attempting to kill Japanese commanders during the invasions of 1592-1598.
kisangani: Kisangani stands on the Congo River in the eastern part of the central Congo Basin, in the north-east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, about 80 kilometres from the equator. It lies at the junction of the Congo, Tshopo and Lindi rivers, below a series of seven cataracts spread over 100 kilometres between Kisangani and Ubundu with a total drop of 61 metres. Its position at the northernmost navigable point of the Congo River for large cargo made it a trading city, and it has been the commercial capital of the northern Congo since the late 19th century. It is the capital of Tshopo Province.

Before Henry Morton Stanley, working for King Leopold II of the Belgians, founded what became Stanley Falls Station in 1883, the Wagenya people lived in the area and fished at Wagenia Falls. Stanley had first passed through in 1877, mistakenly believing he was descending the Nile. Arab-Swahili slave traders from Zanzibar reached the falls from the east, and relations between Free State officials and the slavers were tense. In October 1884 Lieutenant Arvid Wester made a treaty with them, signed by a son of Tippu Tip, which was short-lived. Tippu Tip himself became governor of the Stanley Falls District on 24 February 1887 and held it until June 1888. Arab-Swahili influence in the district was not decisively ended until 1893.

A decree of 6 September 1958, in force from 1 January 1959, established the city of Stanleyville. Late in the colonial era a boom in coffee, cotton and rubber brought prosperity, and the population grew from slightly over 15,000 to 121,765 by 1958. The city was the political base of the Mouvement National Congolais of Patrice Lumumba, who had worked there as a clerk at the central post office. In 1964 it was under siege by the Simbas. In the 1990s it served as the forward base of foreign forces advancing with Laurent-Désiré Kabila towards Kinshasa to overthrow Mobutu Sese Seko.

Kisangani is the most important inland port of the country after Kinshasa and a commercial centre for the north-east. Its people come from many ethnic groups, and none dominates. French is the official language, and Lingala, Swahili and Pa-Zande are common local languages. Since the 1950s it has been a centre of higher education and research, with the Université de Kisangani among its institutions. The Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Kisangani and many other churches stand in the city.
kissamos: Kissamos, in Greek Κίσσαμος, lies in the north-west of Crete and is part of the Chania regional unit. It is often called Kastelli, after the Venetian castle that stood there. It is now a port and fishing harbour, with a regular ferry from the Peloponnese via Kythira. The town museum is in the old Venetian governor's palace.

Strabo said that ancient Cisamus depended on Aptera and served as its naval arsenal. The Peutinger Table shows two port towns in Crete called Cisamus, and modern Kissamos lies much further west than Aptera. In 1837 Pashley already excluded it as the Cisamus associated with Aptera, which is placed far to the east.

The ancient city became a Christian bishopric, a suffragan of the metropolitan see of Gortyna, the capital of the Roman province of Crete. Of its bishops in the first millennium, Theopemptus or Nicetas appears at the Trullan Council in 692 and Leo at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787. After the Venetian conquest of Crete in 1212, Kissamos became a Latin diocese, and more than twenty Latin bishops are known until the end of the 16th century, among them Angelo Barbarigo (1383–1406) and Prospero Santacroce (1548–1572). The Latin see was suppressed about 1600, and only a titular bishopric remains. The Orthodox bishopric is still a residential see of the Church of Crete.

The municipality of Kissamos was formed in 2011 by merging three former municipalities, Kissamos, Inachori and Mythimna. It covers 341 square kilometres and includes the Gramvousa peninsula and its islets. It forms the extreme western part of Crete. The former province of Kissamos was abolished in 2006. Excavations in the town have uncovered Roman houses with fine mosaics.
kissi-people: According to Kissi tradition, as recorded in The Peoples of Africa, the Kissi lived in the Upper Niger region before the seventeenth century, south of the Futa Jallon, until the Yalunka people drove them out. After 1600 they moved westward, expelling the Limbas as they went, while living under constant threat from the Kurankos. They are also known by many other names, among them Assi, Gissi, Gizi, Kisi and Kizi.

In Guinea the warrior Kissi Kaba Keita united many Kissi chiefdoms under his rule and resisted French conquest. Before the French attacks he had rallied the Kurankos of Morige and the Leles of Yombiro. When the French arrived in 1892 he left the largely autonomous local chiefs to defend their own areas and fought mainly by guerrilla tactics, which delayed the conquest. By 1893 he judged that resistance would fail and submitted, and the French recognised him as chief of the northern Kissi territory. Relations worsened, the French appointed his rivals in several of his chiefdoms, and he was eventually executed at Siguiri.

The Kissi are the fourth largest ethnic group in Guinea, about 6.2 per cent of its population, and also live in Liberia and Sierra Leone. Their language belongs to the Mel branch of the Niger–Congo family. They are known for making baskets and weaving on vertical looms, and in the past their smiths, working the rich iron deposits of the region, produced the Kissi penny.

Many Kissi have converted to Christianity, but most continue to practise their traditional religion, in which ancestor worship and prayer to deceased relatives are common. Before colonial contact they carved many soapstone figures and heads. Their purpose is unclear: some scholars link them to ancestor worship, others think they may represent gods meant to increase harvests. A large number are held in the British Museum.
kit-carson: Christopher Houston Carson, known as Kit, was born on 24 December 1809 into a large family: his father Lindsay Carson was a farmer and cabin builder who had fought in the American Indian Wars.
