In August 1826 Carson ran away from an apprenticeship against his mother's wishes and went west with a caravan of fur trappers over the Santa Fe Trail, reaching Santa Fe in November 1826. He settled in Taos, lived with the trapper Mathew Kinkead, who taught him the trade, and became fluent in Spanish and several Native American languages. He joined Ewing Young's trapping expedition of 1829.

In April 1842 Carson met John C. Frémont aboard a Missouri River steamboat, and Frémont hired him as a guide at $100 a month. He guided Frémont's expeditions of 1842, 1843 and 1845. Frémont's reports, rewritten as romantic accounts by his wife Jesse Benton Frémont, made Carson known across the United States. In June 1846 Carson took part in the Bear Flag Revolt, and under Frémont he took part in the conquest of California and in the massacres on the Sacramento River and at Klamath Lake. By his own account Frémont ordered him to kill José de los Reyes Berreyesa and two of his nephews, who had been captured.

In December 1846 General Kearny ordered Carson to guide him and his troops from Socorro, New Mexico, to San Diego, and Mexican soldiers attacked them near the village of San Pasqual. His rescue mission after the Battle of San Pasqual is one of his best-known adventures.

After the war Carson ranched at Rayado, east of Taos, and in the 1850s served as Indian agent to the Ute and Jicarilla Apache. In the Civil War he led a regiment of mostly Hispanic New Mexican volunteers for the Union at the Battle of Valverde in 1862. When the Confederate threat in New Mexico was over, he led forces against the Navajo, Mescalero Apache, Kiowa and Comanche by destroying their food sources, and he oversaw the Navajo Long Walk. He was breveted a brigadier general and took command of Fort Garland, Colorado, but poor health forced him to retire.

Carson died of an aortic aneurysm at Fort Lyon on 23 May 1868 and is buried in Taos beside his third wife, Josefa. About 70 dime novels used his name between 1860 and 1901, and he became a symbol of the frontier. Historians have written that he did not like or want his fame. His legacy is contested, particularly because of his brutal treatment of Native Americans.
kitabatake-chikafusa: Kitabatake Chikafusa belonged to the Murakami branch of the Minamoto clan and over his life served as adviser to five emperors. His best-known work came under Emperor Go-Daigo, to whom he proposed a series of reforms amounting to a revival of political and economic systems of several centuries earlier. He held the Ashikaga clan, who held the office of shōgun and kept the rival Northern Court, in strong distaste: they were warriors rather than nobles, and of a less distinguished branch of the Minamoto than his own.

He disliked above all Ashikaga Takauji, the first Ashikaga shogun, who had first backed Go-Daigo's claim to the throne and then headed the Northern Court. When Go-Daigo died in 1339, Chikafusa was under siege in his stronghold in Hitachi Province. A capable commander, he held off the superior forces of the shogunate on many occasions over a siege of four years. When the fortress fell he escaped to Yoshino, the capital of the Southern Court, and advised the emperor there until his death in 1354.

From the siege he sent copies of his major works to the new ruler, the twelve-year-old Emperor Go-Murakami, and his advisers. The Jinnō Shōtōki tells the history of Japan reign by reign, from the earliest, semi-mythical emperors to Go-Daigo and Go-Murakami, and was meant chiefly as a guide to the young emperor and a defence of the Southern Court's legitimacy. Largely written on the road, it was recompiled and edited in 1343. The Shokugen-shō, also of 1339, was written largely from memory and described the origins and organisation of government offices.

Land ownership runs through his writing. He denounced the provincial shugo and jitō, the constables and stewards, as land-hungry, holding that their creation in 1190 had cost the country the art of government, and he blamed the chaos of feudalism on unlimited claimants to a limited amount of land. The details of his reform plans are unknown, but he probably sought a return to the structures of the Taihō era of 702, abolishing the systems of land tenure and taxation that supported the bushi, the great warrior families.

Historians count Kitabatake, together with his rival Ashikaga Takauji, among the foremost figures of his age. His works are heavily coloured by personal bias and political motive, yet they remain among the most detailed accounts available of the history of Japan's feudal government and imperial line. On 2 April 1908 he was raised posthumously to the Senior First Rank.
kitbuqa: Kitbuqa Noyan, also spelled Kitbogha, Kitboga or Ketbugha, was an Eastern Christian of the Naimans, a group subservient to the Mongol Empire. He became a lieutenant and confidant of the Ilkhan Hulagu. In 1252 Möngke Khan ordered him to lead the advance guard of Hulagu's army against the fortresses of the Nizari Ismailis. He advanced with Hulagu into western Persia, mounting a series of sieges, and commanded one of the flanks that sacked Baghdad in 1258.

Kitbuqa then assisted in the conquest of Damascus in 1260. Accounts based on the writings of Templar of Tyre often describe the three Christian rulers Hethum I of Armenia, Bohemond VI of Antioch and Kitbuqa entering Damascus together in triumph, but modern historians regard the story as apocryphal. When Hulagu withdrew the bulk of his forces after the death of his brother, the Great Khan Möngke, Kitbuqa was left in charge of the Mongol army remaining in the Middle East, and he was responsible for further raids southward towards the Mamluk Sultanate in Cairo.

Hayton of Corycus wrote in 1307 that Kitbuqa held Syria and Palestine in peace, greatly loved and honoured the Christians because he was of the lineage of the Three Kings of the Orient, and worked at recovering the Holy Land.

Commanding a force estimated at 10,000 to 20,000 men, Kitbuqa tried to continue the advance towards Egypt. The Mamluks had agreed a passive truce with the Crusaders, which let them move north through Crusader territory and camp near Acre for supplies. They engaged the depleted Mongol army near Galilee at the Battle of Ain Jalut in 1260. The Mongols were defeated and Kitbuqa was captured. Brought bound before the Mamluk sultan, he is said to have been defiant, describing the vengeance the Mongols would take and taunting the emirs for having betrayed their master. He was executed by the veteran Mamluk Jamal al-Din Akoush al-Shamsy.

Mamluk histories speak of him with respect, as a great warrior who refused to retreat. Hulagu was expected to avenge him, but a conflict with his cousin Berke of the Golden Horde prevented it. The defeat marked the beginning of the end of the Mongol Empire's westward expansion, although the Mongols went on invading Syria, Japan, Hungary, Poland and Southeast Asia for several decades.
kite: In China the kite has been claimed as the invention of the 5th-century BCE philosophers Mozi and Lu Ban, who flew wooden kites called muyuan. After paper was invented in the Han dynasty, paper kites, called zhiyuan, became popular. Silk for the sail, fine and strong silk for the line and resilient bamboo for the frame were all readily available. By the Tang dynasty, bamboo flutes, whistles and ribbons were attached to kites to make sound, a forerunner of the modern fengzheng, named for that sound. The earliest known Chinese kites were flat and often rectangular, and later tailless kites carried a stabilising bowline. They were decorated with mythological motifs and figures.

Ancient Chinese texts describe kites used for measuring distances, testing the wind, lifting men, signalling and communication in military operations. By 549 a kite was used to carry a message for a rescue mission. During the Song dynasty the Fire Crow, a kite carrying incendiary powder, was made as a weapon. According to the Samguk Sagi, the Korean general Kim Yu-sin of Silla rallied his troops in 647 with flaming kites that also frightened the enemy.

In India the kite evolved into the fighter kite, the patang, and thousands are flown every year at festivals such as Makar Sankranti. Kites were known throughout Polynesia as far as New Zealand, probably carried from China with the people. Polynesian kites of cloth and wood in human form were used in religious ceremonies to send prayers to the gods.

Kites reached Europe late, although the Romans knew windsock-like banners. Marco Polo brought stories of them in the late 13th century, and sailors brought kites back from Japan and Malaysia in the 16th and 17th centuries. Konrad Kyeser described dragon kites in Bellifortis about 1400. At first they were regarded as curiosities, but by the 18th and 19th centuries they served scientific research. Benjamin Franklin published an account of a kite experiment in 1752 to show that lightning was electrical, and kites aided the Wright brothers' research toward the first airplane. The years from 1860 to about 1910 became the European golden age of kiting. Powered aircraft then reduced interest in them.
kittery-maine: Kittery lies in York County, at the mouth of the Piscataqua River, opposite Portsmouth, New Hampshire. It is the southernmost town in Maine and includes Badger's Island, the seaside district of Kittery Point, the village of Kittery and part of the Isles of Shoals. Of its area of 195 square kilometres, about three quarters is water. Its population was 10,070 at the 2020 census, and it is a tourist destination known for its outlet stores.

English settlement around the harbour of the Piscataqua estuary began about 1623. By 1632 the community was protected by Fort William and Mary on the New Hampshire side of the river, and in 1689 defensive works that later became Fort McClary were added on the Maine side. Kittery was incorporated in 1647 and was named after the manor of Kittery Court at Kingswear in Devon, the birthplace of the founder Alexander Shapleigh, who arrived in 1635 on the Benediction, a ship he co-owned with Captain Francis Champernowne. With the Pepperrell family they established fisheries at the Isles of Shoals, where fish were caught, salted and exported to Europe. Other settlers hunted, trapped and worked the timber.

Kittery developed into a centre of trade and shipbuilding. The township originally reached inland up the Salmon Falls River and included the present towns of Eliot, South Berwick, Berwick and North Berwick. In 1652, after the death of Sir Ferdinando Gorges, Maine became part of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. In 1663 John Josselyn called Kittery the most populous town in the province. The Maine Historical Society calls Sir William Pepperrell, who lived at Kittery, the state's most prolific and infamous slave owner, and as many as 500 enslaved people were brought to Kittery Parish in the colonial era. In 1705, during Queen Anne's War, Wabanaki raiders killed six residents and took five prisoners.

The first vessels of the United States Navy were built on Badger's Island during the Revolution, among them the USS Ranger of 1777, commanded by John Paul Jones. The Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, the nation's first federal navy yard, was established in 1800. In the Civil War it rebuilt the USS Constitution and built the USS Kearsarge. The Treaty of Portsmouth, which formally ended the Russo-Japanese War, was signed at the shipyard in 1905.
kittur-chennamma: Chennamma was born on 14 November 1778 at Kakati, a small village in the present Belagavi District of Karnataka, a small deshgat or princely state. Her father was Dhulappa Desai and her mother Padmavati. She was born into a family that followed Jainism, and later descendants of the family converted to Lingayatism. She was trained in horse riding, sword fighting and archery from a young age, and at 15 she married Raja Mallasarja of the Desai family, whom she had looked up to since the age of 9.

Her husband died in 1816, leaving her a son and a volatile state, and her son died in 1824. She then adopted a Lingayat boy, Shivalingappa, and made him heir to the throne. This displeased the East India Company, which ordered his expulsion. Kittur came under the administration of the Dharwad collectorate, headed by St John Thackeray, with Mr Chaplain as commissioner. Neither recognised the new regent's rule, and they told Kittur to accept British control. This is seen as a forerunner of the doctrine of lapse that Lord Dalhousie introduced from 1848, by which a state whose ruler died childless reverted to the suzerain.

In 1823 she wrote to Mountstuart Elphinstone, lieutenant-governor of Bombay, pleading her case. The request was refused and war broke out. The British put sentries round Kittur's treasury and crown jewels, valued at about 1.5 million rupees, and mustered 20,797 men and 437 guns. In October 1824 the British lost heavily in the first round, and Thackeray was killed, mainly through her lieutenant Amatur Balappa. Two British officers, Sir Walter Elliot and Mr Stevenson, were taken hostage and released on an understanding with Chaplain that the war would end, but Chaplain continued it with more forces. In the second assault the sub-collector of Solapur, Munro, nephew of Thomas Munro, was killed.

With the help of her deputy Sangolli Rayanna, Chennamma fought fiercely but was captured and imprisoned in Bailhongal Fort, where she died on 21 February 1829 as her health failed. Rayanna continued a guerrilla war until 1829, wanting to install Shivalingappa as ruler, but he was caught and hanged, and Shivalingappa was arrested.

She is remembered as a folk heroine in Karnataka and is sung of in ballads. Kittur marks her first victory with the Kittur Utsava on 22 to 24 October each year, her samadhi is at Bailhongal, and a statue of her was unveiled at the Indian Parliament complex on 11 September 2007. A commemorative stamp was issued on 23 October 1977 and Rani Channamma University in Belagavi is named after her.
kiva: A kiva, also called an estufa, serves for rites and political meetings, many of them tied to the kachina belief system. Similar underground rooms appear in ruins across the Southwestern United States, built by the Ancestral Puebloans, the Mogollon culture and the Hohokam. For the Ancestral Puebloans such rooms are believed to have served as homes and as places for social and ceremonial life. Those of the Pueblo I period and later, in the Pecos Classification archaeologists use, were usually round.

Great kivas differ from ordinary, Chaco-style kivas. They are always larger and deeper, their walls rise above the surrounding ground, and they always stand apart from the core buildings, whereas Chaco-style kivas are flush with the ground and often built into the room blocks of great houses. Great kivas almost always have a bench around the inner space and often floor vaults, which may have served as foot drums for dancers.

Mesa Verde protokivas were 3 or 4 feet deep and 12 to 20 feet across, and the round kivas that followed were usually 12 to 15 feet across. During the Pueblo III Period, between 1150 and 1300, kivas held a prominent place in the community. Their architecture grew more elaborate, with tower kivas and great kivas carrying special floor features; those in Mesa Verde National Park were generally keyhole-shaped. In most larger communities there was one kiva for every five or six rooms. The Great Kiva at Aztec Ruins National Monument is ringed by fifteen rooms, and four massive pillars held up a roof estimated at 95 tons.

Calling an ancient room a kiva involves assumptions about how its uses compare with modern practice. The kachina belief system appears to have emerged around 1250, long after kiva-like rooms, which suggests their older functions were adapted to the new religion. The burning of kivas is read as a strong sign of conflict in the Pueblo III Period. After 1325 or 1350, outside the Hopi region, there were 60 to 90 rooms for each kiva, a change that may point to new religious or social organisation, perhaps in the status and number of clans.
kizil-caves: The Kizil Caves are Buddhist rock-cut caves on the northern bank of the Muzat River, 65 kilometres west of Kucha in Baicheng County, Aksu Prefecture, Xinjiang. In Uyghur the name means the Thousand Red Houses. There are 236 caves carved along a cliff 2 kilometres long, of which 135 are relatively intact, and they form the largest of the Buddhist cave sites linked to the Tocharian kingdom of Kucha and the largest in Xinjiang. The earliest, dated partly by radiocarbon, belong to about 300 CE, and most researchers think the site was abandoned around the beginning of the 8th century after Tang influence arrived.

Many caves have a central pillar for walking round. Murals show the Buddha's life, Jataka stories and legends, and use blue pigments including ultramarine from Afghan lapis lazuli. Early paintings show Gandharan influence, later ones Iranian and Sogdian, and only two caves show Tang influence. In 648 a Tang force under Ashina She'er conquered Kucha, and one record says he had eleven thousand people executed. The caves were explored by a Japanese expedition in 1902–1904 and by the Third German Turfan Expedition under Albert Grünwedel in 1905–1907. In 1912 Grünwedel proposed two styles, dated 500–650, but radiocarbon work of 1979–1981 pushed the first caves back to about 300.

Around 5,000 square metres of wall paintings remain, though the site was damaged and looted, and many murals were removed by Western expeditions. Most went to the Museum of Asian Art in Berlin, where many were destroyed in the Second World War, and some others were taken to Russia, Japan, Korea and the United States. The caves were inscribed in 2014 on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Silk Roads: Chang'an-Tianshan Corridor.
kizlyar: Kizlyar lies in the delta of the Terek River in the Republic of Dagestan, on the border with the Chechen Republic, 221 kilometres north-west of Makhachkala. Several explanations of its name are given. According to some researchers it comes from an old name of the Terek, and a folk etymology from an unspecified Turkic language gives girls. Vyacheslav Nikonov holds that the correct translation of the Turkic name is red cliff. The first documented reference to Kizlyar dates to 1609, although some historians associate the place with Samandar, the capital of Khazaria in the 8th century.

In 1735 the Russian government built a fortress at Kizlyar and laid the foundations of the Caucasus fortified borderline. In the 18th and 19th centuries it served as one of the trading posts between Russia and the Middle East and Central Asia. Its population was then largely Armenian and Russian, and in 1796 some 2,800 Armenians and 1,000 Russians lived there. Under the Russian Empire it was the administrative capital of the Kizlyarsky Otdel of the Terek Oblast. In the early 19th century it became a centre of viticulture and wine making, and the local brandy factory still produces a regional brandy that is sold across Russia as cognac. The town is also known for making traditional knives, daggers and sabres.

German forces briefly took Kizlyar in 1942. In January 1996 Chechen separatists raided the local airbase in the Kizlyar raid, which claimed the lives of seventy-eight Russian soldiers. The generals Pyotr Bagration, born in 1765, and Roman Bagration, born in 1778, were natives of the town.
klagenfurt: Klagenfurt lies in southern Austria near the border with Slovenia, at 446 metres above sea level, on the Wörthersee and the Glan river. To the south the Karawanken range separates Carinthia from Slovenia and Italy. The name means ford of lament. Two Carinthian linguists took it to translate a Slovene name for the neighbouring wetland, a place haunted by a wailing female ghost; a later view derives the Slovene word from an Italic phrase meaning a place at or in the water.

Legend tells that the city was founded after a group of men killed a winged lindwurm that preyed on the duchy from the moors beside the lake. A watchtower was built at the edge of the moor, the dragon was baited with a bull fitted with a chain and hook, and a village arose on the battlefield. The Renaissance monument in the city centre, the Lindwurmbrunnen, commemorates it.

After a great fire Emperor Maximilian I, unable to rebuild the city, ceded Klagenfurt in 1518 to the Estates, the nobility of the duchy, over the protests of the citizens. The new owners dug a canal to the lake to bring timber, built town houses, and enlarged the city on a chequerboard plan following the ideas of the Italian architect Domenico dell'Allio. Fortifications that took half a century to build made it the strongest fortress north of the Alps. French troops under Napoleon destroyed the walls in 1809, and the railway of 1863 strengthened its place as the centre of the region. During the Second World War the city was bombed 41 times, killing 612 people.

Klagenfurt is the capital and largest city of Carinthia and the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Gurk-Klagenfurt. It is regarded as the cultural centre of the Carinthian Slovenes. Its old city has Renaissance arcaded courtyards, the Landhaus, once the palace of the Estates, and a Baroque cathedral built by the then Protestant Estates. The Ingeborg Bachmann Prize for literature is awarded there.
klaipeda: Klaipėda lies on the Baltic Sea coast, in Lithuania Minor, at the mouth of the river Akmena-Danė, whose usually ice-free port gave the city its regional importance. The old town stands on the left bank of the Danė, and its streets form a rectangular network laid out in the 13th to 15th centuries, with half-timbered buildings that reflect its German past. The Curonian Spit lies across the water, and a small part of it, Smiltynė, belongs to the city. Settlement by Baltic tribes is said to date from as early as the 7th century, when the Balts used the site as a trading centre for goods and annual fairs with the Germans.

In the 1240s, after Grand Duke Mindaugas of Lithuania accepted Christianity, crusaders moved into Sambia and founded a fort, Memelburg, in 1252. Its founding documents were signed on 29 July and 1 August 1252. In the 13th to 15th centuries the settlement was attacked by Sambians and Samogitians and burned or ruined about 20 times.

In 1525 it adopted Lutheranism when the Duchy of Prussia was created as a fief of the Polish crown, beginning a long period of prosperity for the port, which exported wheat from Lithuania through the mouth of the Neman. Sweden occupied the town at times between 1629 and 1635. In 1701 it became part of the Kingdom of Prussia and was one of its strongest fortresses. Russia held it from 1757 to 1762, and after Germany's unification in 1871 it was the German Empire's northernmost city.

Under the Treaty of Versailles the Klaipėda Region was detached from Germany and placed under French administration. Lithuanians staged the Klaipėda Revolt in January 1923, presenting the Entente with a fait accompli, and the League of Nations accepted the transfer in February 1923. The Klaipėda Convention of 8 May 1924 secured the region extensive autonomy. Nazi Germany annexed it in 1939. The Soviet Red Army took the nearly empty city on 28 January 1945, when only about 50 people remained, and the region was incorporated into the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic.

Klaipėda is the third-largest city of Lithuania and its only major seaport, the busiest in the Baltic states. It was named Memel officially from 1252 to 1923 and again from 1939 to 1945, and both names were in official use between 1923 and 1939. The Lithuanian name has been used since 1945. Its old town is known for its half-timbered fachwerk architecture, and the Lithuanian Sea Museum stands in the old Prussian star fort at Kopgalis.
klaipeda-revolt: The Klaipėda Region, north of the Neman River, was part of Lithuania Minor, with a large population of Lutheran Prussian Lithuanians and a port that was Lithuania's only viable access to the Baltic Sea. Under the Treaty of Versailles it was detached from Germany on 10 January 1920 and placed under the League of Nations, and French troops under General Dominique Joseph Odry arrived in February; Gabriel Jean Petisné then headed the civilian administration. Poland hoped to gain influence through a union with Lithuania, and after Lithuania refused a British offer in March 1922 to trade its claim to Vilnius for the region, France and Britain favoured a free city like Danzig.

After a Prussian Lithuanian delegation failed before the Conference of Ambassadors, the Lithuanian government decided in secret on 20 November 1922 to stage a local revolt, on the model of Żeligowski's Mutiny. Prime Minister Ernestas Galvanauskas kept the plan even from the First Seimas, and the Lithuanian Riflemen's Union under Vincas Krėvė-Mickevičius provided the men. Germany let it be known it would not interfere, and the Soviet Foreign Minister Georgy Chicherin offered support.

On 10 January 1923, 1,090 volunteers in civilian clothes crossed the border under Jonas Polovinskas, who had taken the name Jonas Budrys. A Supreme Committee for the Salvation of Lithuania Minor under Martynas Jankus claimed power, and Erdmonas Simonaitis formed a new Directorate. By 11 January the rebels held the region except the city of Klaipėda, where fighting broke out on 15 January; 12 insurgents, two French soldiers and one German policeman were killed before a ceasefire.

France protested and threatened force, but Britain and Italy supported the transfer, and the League, which was then dividing the neutral zone of the Vilnius Region, treated Klaipėda as Lithuania's compensation. On 17 February 1923 the Conference of Ambassadors transferred the region to Lithuania, on condition of autonomy, payment of Allied administration costs and an internationalised Neman. The Klaipėda Convention, prepared by a commission under the American Norman Davis, was hailed as a Lithuanian diplomatic victory, but it limited the central government's powers. Nazi Germany exploited its weaknesses, and a German ultimatum took the region in March 1939.
klarjeti: Klarjeti was traversed by the Chorokhi (Çoruh) and stretched from the Arsiani Range westwards towards the Black Sea, bordered by Shavsheti and Nigali to the north and by Tao to the south. Its centre was the fortified trading town of Artanuji, now Ardanuç. The region roughly corresponds to the Cholarzene of classical sources and probably to the Kaţarza or Quturza of earlier Urartian records; the Armenians knew it as Kļarjk'. With Tao and several smaller districts it formed the region conventionally called Tao-Klarjeti.

Klarjeti was one of the south-westernmost provinces of the Kingdom of Iberia, ruled according to the medieval Georgian chronicles by the Pharnavazid dynasty. From the 2nd century BCE to the 3rd century CE it was contested between Iberia and Armenia and passed back and forth between them. In the division of Iberia between the Roman and Sasanian empires in the 370s it passed to the Roman side, though whether as a province or a vassal is unknown. The marriage of King Vakhtang I of Iberia to the Roman princess Helena seems to have let the Iberians regain it about 485.

Vakhtang's younger sons and their descendants, the Guaramids, then held Klarjeti and Javakheti until their possessions passed to their Bagrationi cousins. Under the Bagrationi the area prospered: the taxes collected at Artanuji fed their rise, and the land, deserted in an Arab invasion, was repopulated and became a centre of Christian culture through the monastic movement begun by the monk Gregory of Khandzta (759–861). Around 870 it became the hereditary fief of one branch of the family, the Sovereigns of Klarjeti, until their cousin Bagrat III, the first king of a unified Georgia, dispossessed them in 1010 and granted the area to the Abuserisdze family.

Klarjeti never fully recovered from Seljuk attacks later in the 11th century and declined further during the Mongol invasions and those of Timur in the 13th and 14th centuries. After the partition of the Kingdom of Georgia in the 15th century it passed to the princes of Meskheti, who lost it to the Ottoman conquest in 1551.
klaus-stortebeker: Klaus Störtebeker, also known as Klaas Störtebecker, Johann Störtebecker or Nikolaus Storzenbecher, was a German pirate, born around 1360. A large number of myths and legends surround the few facts known about his life. His name is both a nickname and a surname, meaning empty the mug with one gulp in Low German, and refers to his supposed ability to empty a four-litre mug of beer at once. At this time pirates and other fugitives often took colourful names.

Störtebeker was reputed to be the leader of the Victual Brothers, who were hired to assist in a war between Sweden and Denmark and went on to capture merchant vessels, mainly in the Baltic and the North Sea. They shared the spoils equally and called themselves Likedeelers, equal sharers. He entered public consciousness around 1398, after the Victual Brothers were expelled from the Baltic island of Gotland, where they had a stronghold in the town of Visby. In the following years he and fellow captains, among them Gödeke Michels, Hennig Wichmann and Magister Wigbold, captured Hanseatic ships regardless of their origin.

Störtebeker had a stronghold at Marienhafe in East Frisia from about 1396 and married a daughter of the East Frisian chieftain Keno ten Broke. A tower bearing his name still stands at the Marienkirche there.

According to legend a Hamburg fleet led by Simon of Utrecht caught Störtebeker near Heligoland, and he and his 73 companions were beheaded on the Grasbrook in Hamburg. He is said to have offered a gold chain long enough to enclose Hamburg for his life, and, after his own beheading, to have walked past eleven of his men before the executioner tripped him. The Hamburg records differ from this story in its details; the Hanseatic fleet was commanded by Hermann Langhe and Nikolaus Schoke, and no reliable source describes the course of the battle.

No authentic portrait is known; a skull said to be his was displayed in Hamburg from 1922. In German folklore he is a figure like Robin Hood, said to steal from the rich to help the poor. Statues stand in Hamburg, Verden an der Aller and Marienhafe, and an open-air Störtebeker Festival takes place each year at Ralswiek on Rügen.
klemens-von-metternich: Klemens Metternich was born on 15 May 1773 into the old Rhenish House of Metternich, the son of Franz Georg Karl, a diplomat who had passed from the service of the Electorate of Trier to that of the imperial court. He was named after Prince Clemens Wenceslaus of Saxony, the archbishop-elector of Trier and his father's former employer.

He spoke French better than German and later studied at the universities of Strasbourg and Mainz. In October 1794 a French army annexed all the family estates except Königswart in Bohemia. On 27 September 1795 he married Countess Eleonore von Kaunitz-Rietberg, a match arranged by his mother that introduced him to Viennese society.

Metternich served as Austrian minister in Dresden from 1801 and then as ambassador to Napoleon's France from August 1806. After the Austrian defeat at the Battle of Wagram in 1809, Johann Philipp Stadion resigned as foreign minister, and Metternich became foreign minister on 8 October. He arranged a détente with France that included the marriage of Napoleon to the archduchess Marie Louise, then brought Austria into the War of the Sixth Coalition on the Allied side.
He was made a prince in October 1813. At the Congress of Vienna, which gathered from autumn 1814, he had his aide Friedrich von Gentz named secretary to the negotiations.

After 1815 he sought to preserve the existing social hierarchy and the authority of legitimate sovereigns. Wanting a strong Ottoman Empire to counterbalance Russia, he opposed Greek nationalism. At home he used censorship and a wide-ranging spy network to suppress unrest, and he crushed nationalist revolts in Austrian northern Italy.

In late February 1848 Joseph Radetsky placed Lombardy-Venetia under martial law as disturbances spread, and the revolution forced Metternich to resign. He travelled through the Netherlands to London, arriving on 20 April, and lived in exile until 1851. Vienna's press accused him of embezzlement and bribery, but an investigation cleared him of the more extreme charges.

He returned to the Viennese court to advise Emperor Franz Josef and died on 11 June 1859, aged 86. Historians agree on his skill as a diplomat and his dedication to conservatism. Supporters note that his system helped prevent major wars in Europe, while critics call him a stumbling block to reform in Austria.
klement-gottwald: Gottwald was born on 23 November 1896, either at Dědice, now part of Vyškov, or at Hoštice-Heroltice. His mother was an unmarried maidservant. He trained in Vienna as a carpenter. He served in the Austro-Hungarian Army from 1915 to 1918 and deserted in the summer of 1918. In the 1920s he edited communist magazines in Slovakia and Ostrava.

From 1926 Gottwald was a functionary of the Communist Party of Czechoslovakia (KSČ). He helped form a pro-Moscow opposition within the party and from 1928 was a member of the Comintern. At the Fifth Congress in February 1929 he was elected general secretary. In 1938 he led opposition to the Munich Agreement. After the party was banned he emigrated to the Soviet Union in November 1938. In 1943 he agreed with the government-in-exile in London and President Edvard Beneš to unite resistance in a National Front.

Gottwald returned to Prague on 10 May 1945 as deputy premier. In the same year he became party chairman. The KSČ won 38 percent in the free election of 1946, the best result of any Czechoslovak party to that point, and he became prime minister. By the summer of 1947 its popularity had fallen, particularly after the Soviets pressed Czechoslovakia to refuse Marshall Plan aid, and Stalin ordered Gottwald to act against parliamentary opposition. In February 1948 twelve non-Communist ministers resigned over the Communist interior minister Václav Nosek's packing of the police. Gottwald refused to resign and threatened a general strike, and on 25 February Beneš accepted the resignations. Beneš resigned on 2 June, and Gottwald was elected president on 14 June.

After a meeting with Stalin, Gottwald imposed the Soviet model: industry was nationalised and the collectivisation of farms began. Resistance in the government was met with purges, and perceived opponents were jailed or sentenced to forced labour. Show trials included that of the non-Communist politician Milada Horáková, executed in June 1950, and of the Communist leaders Rudolf Slánský and Vlado Clementis, both executed in December 1952.

Gottwald died on 14 March 1953, five days after returning from Stalin's funeral, and was the first Czechoslovak president to die in office. Antonín Zápotocký succeeded him as president and Antonín Novotný as party leader. His embalmed body was displayed in a mausoleum in Prague until 1962, and his ashes were moved in 1990 to a common grave at Olšany Cemetery. The city of Zlín was named Gottwaldov from 1949 to 1989.
kletorologion: The work belongs to the Byzantine lists of offices and court precedence known as Taktika. Its author, Philotheos, held the dignity of prōtospatharios and the post of atriklinēs, which made him responsible for receiving the guests at the imperial banquets and conducting them to their proper places. In his preface he describes the treatise as a precise exposé of the order of imperial banquets and of the name and value of each title, compiled from older lists, and recommends its adoption at the imperial table.

The text survives in the last chapters, 52 to 54, of the second book of the De Ceremoniis, the later treatise on imperial ceremonies associated with Emperor Constantine Porphyrogennetos (r. 913–959). It was published in the reign of Emperor Leo VI the Wise (r. 886–912).

The first section gives a brief overview of all the court ranks and state offices of the Byzantine Empire, divided into five categories: orders of rank for bearded men, that is men who were not eunuchs; the great offices of state; the minor offices of the various bureaus and ministries; orders of rank for eunuchs; and the great offices of state reserved for eunuchs.

The second and third sections set out the order in which officials were to be introduced to the banquets. The second covers the highest dignitaries, those who could be seated at the emperor's own table. The third deals with middle-ranking and lower-ranking officials and with embassies, both from the other patriarchates of Rome, Antioch and Jerusalem and from foreign peoples, the Arabs, Bulgars and Germans.

The fourth and longest section advises the atriklinēs on arranging the banquets of the year, beginning with the celebrations for Christmas. It carries two memoranda, one on the largesses the emperor gave to officials on certain occasions and one on the salaries of the atriklinai. A short appendix, chapter 54 of the De Ceremoniis, lists the church officials and their precedence and adds the Notitia Episcopatuum of pseudo-Epiphanius, a list of episcopal sees.
kleve: Kleve lies in the Lower Rhine region near the Dutch border and the River Rhine. Its name probably derives from the Middle Dutch clef or clif, a cliff or bluff, referring to the promontory on which the Schwanenburg castle was built. Its massive Schwanenturm, 55 m high, is associated in legend with the Knight of the Swan, whom Richard Wagner took up in Lohengrin. Medieval Kleve grew together from four parts: the castle, the village below it, the first town on Heideberg Hill and the Neustadt of the 14th century.

Kleve received city rights in 1242. The County of Cleves was united with the Duchy of Mark in 1368 and became a duchy itself in 1417. In 1521 it was joined with the duchies of Jülich and Berg, when John III, Duke of Cleves, married Mary, heiress of Jülich-Berg-Ravenburg. His daughter Anne of Cleves (1515–1557) was briefly the fourth wife of Henry VIII of England. The ducal dynasty died out in the male line in 1609, which led to the War of the Jülich Succession (1609–1614); after the Thirty Years' War ended in 1648, Cleves passed to the elector of Brandenburg.

During the Thirty Years' War the town was held by the Dutch Republic, which in 1647 gave Johann Moritz von Nassau-Siegen administrative control. He had the castle renovated in the baroque style, built the Prinzenhof and laid out gardens that influenced European landscape design. In 1701 Cleves became part of the Kingdom of Prussia. French Revolutionary troops captured it in 1794, and Prussia regained it in 1815. In the 19th century its mineral waters made it a fashionable spa, Bad Cleve. In the Second World War over 90 per cent of its buildings were badly damaged, most of the destruction coming in a bombing raid in 1945 before Operation Veritable.

Kleve is the capital of the district of Kleve in North Rhine-Westphalia. Most of the Schwanenburg and the Stiftskirche were reconstructed after the war. The official language is Standard High German, though the native dialect of the region is the Low Franconian Kleverlandish. The Haus Koekkoek museum shows the work of the Dutch landscape painter Barend Cornelis Koekkoek, who settled there.
klis-fortress: Klis Fortress stands above the village of Klis, near Split in Croatia, on a pass between the mountains Mosor and Kozjak, at an altitude of 360 metres and 11 kilometres from the Adriatic Sea. It is built on an isolated rocky eminence that is inaccessible on three sides. Historically it controlled access to and from Bosnia, Dalmatia and inland Croatia.

The Illyrian tribe of the Dalmatae held a stronghold on the spot, and the Romans annexed it in 9 CE. From 537 it belonged to the Byzantine Empire. After Salona was sacked in 614 by Avars and Slavs, Croats drove out the Avars in the 7th century. In the 9th century Duke Mislav made Klis the seat of his throne. His successor Trpimir I, who moved the duke's main residence from Nin to Klis, expanded the fortress and built a church and the first Benedictine monastery in Croatia in the valley below. From 1102 the fortress was governed by Croatian nobility under the Hungarian kings.

In March 1242 the Tatars under Kadan, hunting Béla IV of Hungary, attacked the fortress believing he was there. The defenders hurled stones and killed many, and the Tatars looted the outskirts but failed to take Klis and rode off towards Trogir when they learned that the king was elsewhere.

In the 16th century the Croat lord Petar Kružić gathered a garrison of refugees, the Uskoks, who held the Ottomans at bay for more than two and a half decades. Reinforcements of about 3,000 infantry landed in March 1537, but a great number of Turks overwhelmed them on 12 March, and the fortress passed to the Ottomans. It became the centre of a sanjak of the Bosnia Eyalet. In 1596 Split noblemen and Uskoks seized it for a few weeks until the Ottomans retook it on 31 May. In 1648, in the Ottoman-Venetian war, the Venetian commander Leonardo Foscolo compelled the garrison to surrender.

Its present stone appearance dates from the restructuring by the Venetians in the 17th century. The fortress has three parts enclosed by walls with separate entrances. The Austrians built the first main entrance in the early 19th century. It has been developed as a visitor attraction by the Kliški uskoci re-enactment association with the Ministry of Culture's conservation department in Split, and a former Austrian armoury displays arms, armour and uniforms.
klodzko: Kłodzko stands in the centre of the Kłodzko Valley, on the Eastern Neisse, and is the seat of Kłodzko County. The area has been populated since at least the 1st century BCE, and archaeological sites suggest a settlement on the ancient Amber Road that traded widely with the Roman Empire. It was established as a settlement in the 10th century and received city rights in 1233. Culturally and traditionally the town belongs to Bohemia.

The earliest mention is in Cosmas of Prague's Chronicle of Bohemians, which names Cladzco as belonging in 981 to Duke Slavník, father of Adalbert of Prague. The town passed between Poland and Bohemia in a series of conflicts, and in 1114 the Bohemian Duke Soběslav I captured and burnt it, then rebuilt it. By the Peace of Kłodzko of 1137 Bolesław III Wrymouth of Poland gave up all claims to the Kłodzko Land. A Mongol raid reached the town in 1241, and King Wenceslaus I drove the Mongols out. In 1334 Bohemia bought the town back from the Dukes of Ziębice, and King John of Luxembourg relocated it, which brought fast growth and German settlers.

In 1459 George of Poděbrady raised the whole Kłodzko Land to a county, and in 1526 it passed with Bohemia to the Habsburgs. During the Thirty Years' War the fortress was besieged several times between 1619 and 1649. It was never captured, but over 900 of the town's 1,300 buildings were destroyed and the population fell by more than half. The Austrian authorities then ended local self-government and made it a small garrison town attached to the growing fortress. The Kingdom of Prussia annexed Glatz during the Silesian Wars and continued the fortress, and the town joined the German Empire in 1871.

During the Second World War the fortress was a prison and a subcamp of the Gross-Rosen concentration camp. The Red Army took the town without a major battle on 9 May 1945, and under the Potsdam Conference's border changes it became part of Poland. Its German inhabitants were deported in February 1946, and Poles settled the town. It is the commercial centre of its valley and counted 25,717 inhabitants in 2021. Its Gothic stone bridge of 1390, often called a Charles Bridge in miniature, survived the war.
klooga-concentration-camp: Klooga lay in Harju County near the village of Klooga, in German-occupied Estonia, then part of the Reichskommissariat Ostland, the German civilian administration of the Baltic states and western Belorussia. It was one of the 20 field camps of the Vaivara concentration camp complex, some of which existed only briefly, commanded by the German officers Hans Aumeier, Otto Brennais and Franz von Bodmann. The whole camp was enclosed by barbed wire, and the men's and women's camps, some 600 yards apart, had large two-storey buildings for the prisoners.

The camp was set up in September 1943 and held between about 1,500 and 2,500 men and women at a time: Soviet prisoners of war, Estonian political prisoners and, after mass transfers in August and September 1943 from the Kovno and Vilna ghettos in Lithuania and the Salaspils ghetto in Latvia, a large majority of Jews. German SS units and the 287th Estonian Police Battalion guarded them. Prisoners cut peat and worked in the cement works, sawmills, brickworks and a clog factory under extremely harsh conditions, and a group of some 75 tried to organise resistance.

As the Soviet army advanced in September 1944, the SS sent many prisoners west by sea to Stutthof and to Freiburg in Schlesien. The killing of those left began on 19 September; according to Soviet sources the victims were shot and their bodies stacked on wooden pyres and burned. When Soviet troops reached the camp on 22 September, only 85 of the 2,400 prisoners left after the evacuation had survived, by hiding or fleeing into the forest. Hans Aumeier was sentenced to death in Kraków on 22 December 1947 and executed on 28 January 1948.

On 1 September 1994 a memorial to the Jews killed in the Second World War was unveiled on the site, at the initiative of the Jewish Cultural Society and with the support of the Estonian Government. In May 2005 Prime Minister Andrus Ansip visited Klooga and apologised that Estonian citizens had taken part in the killings, and in July 2005 President Arnold Rüütel unveiled a grey marble memorial stone.
klosterneuburg: Klosterneuburg stands on the Danube immediately north of Vienna, from which it is separated by the Kahlenberg and Leopoldsberg hills of the Vienna Woods. Archaeological finds show settlement in the Neolithic period, and in the Roman era a fort of the Danubian limes stood on the site, on the north-western border of Pannonia. The place is first recorded as Nivvenburc, meaning New Castle, in a deed of 1108. It lies in a wine-growing area, and Fritz Zweigelt bred the Zweigelt and Blauburger red grapes at its Federal Institute for Viticulture and Pomology.

In 1113 the site became a residence of the Babenberg margrave Leopold III. A princely castle with a collegiate church was built on a hill rising from the Danube in 1114, and in 1133 Leopold transferred it to Augustinian canons. The order became one of the oldest and richest of its kind in Austria and owned much of the land on which the north-western suburbs of Vienna now stand. Duke Leopold VI of Austria also lived there for parts of his reign.

A market grew on the opposite bank, and by the late 13th century the monastery town of Klosterneuburg and the market town of Korneuburg had grown apart. King Albert I of Germany granted Klosterneuburg its own town privileges in 1298. Ottoman forces devastated the unfortified lower town in the Siege of Vienna of 1529 and again in 1683, while the fortified upper town was defended both times. In 1730 building began on a Baroque rebuilding of the monastery modelled on the Escorial, planned under Emperor Charles VI, but the project did not survive its first phase. Napoleonic troops occupied the town from 1805 to 1809, and from 1938 to 1954 it formed the 26th district of Vienna.

Klosterneuburg has about 27,500 inhabitants and belongs to the Tulln District of Lower Austria. The monastery complex includes the old chapel of 1318 with Leopold's tomb, the Verdun Altar, a treasury and relic chamber, a library of 30,000 volumes with many manuscripts, a picture gallery, a coin collection and a wine cellar holding a very large tun. The Institute of Science and Technology Austria was established in the town in 2006.
kneiphof: The town stood on an island of about 10 hectares, bounded to the north by the Neue Pregel and to the south by the Alte Pregel, two branches of the Pregel River. Its name, known in medieval forms such as Knipaw and Knypabe, was of Old Prussian origin and referred to swampy land flushed by water. Early in the 14th century the island was called Vogtswerder in German, after a vogt of the Teutonic Knights who used it, but the townspeople kept the Prussian name of the 1327 charter.

Kneiphof was the youngest of Königsberg's three towns, beside Altstadt and Löbenicht, each with its own charter, market rights, church and walls. Grand Master Werner von Orseln granted it Kulm rights on 6 April 1327 and gave the eastern third of the island to the Bishopric of Samland for the cathedral. Bridges such as the Krämerbrücke and the Grüne Brücke joined it to its neighbours; five of them belong to the seven bridges of Königsberg problem, which Euler proved to have no solution. As a Hanseatic town it joined the Confederation of Cologne against King Valdemar IV of Denmark in 1367.

Kneiphof was a founding member of the Prussian Confederation in 1440 and rose against the Teutonic Knights in the Thirteen Years' War, accepting King Casimir IV Jagiellon of Poland. When Altstadt and Löbenicht returned to the Order in 1455, Kneiphof held out behind its water and walls, helped by ships from Danzig, until hunger forced its surrender to Komtur Heinrich Reuß von Plauen on 14 July. By the decree of 13 June 1724 King Frederick William I of Prussia merged the three towns into the united city of Königsberg, and Kneiphof Town Hall served the whole city until 1927.

Devastated by the bombing of 1944, the quarter passed with Königsberg to the Soviet Union in 1945, and material from its buildings went to rebuild cities such as Leningrad. From the 1970s the island was turned into a park with many sculptures, and the cathedral was rebuilt from the 1990s. Now called Kant Island after the philosopher Immanuel Kant, it lies in the Moskovsky District of Kaliningrad, Russia.
knighthood: The idea of knighthood may have been inspired by the ancient Greek hippeis and the Roman equites, the Roman Ordo Equestris being a class of mounted nobles. The Franks generally fielded masses of infantry with an elite, the comitatus, that rode to battle but dismounted to fight, as at the Battle of Tours in 732.

In the Early Middle Ages any well-equipped horseman could be called a knight, or miles in Latin. The first knights appeared under Charlemagne in the 8th century, as the Franks took to horseback in wide campaigns of conquest and, with the stirrup, increasingly fought as true cavalry. The word knight comes from the Old English cniht, meaning boy or servant, and its sense moved to household retainer.

By the 10th century the institution was well established. Higher nobles granted vassals fiefs in return for loyalty, protection and service, and supplied knights with lodging, food, armour, weapons, horses and money. A knight generally held his land by military tenure, usually 40 days of service a year. In the 12th century knighthood became a social rank, separating milites gregarii, non-noble cavalrymen, from milites nobiles, true knights, while the armoured cavalryman took the separate name of man-at-arms.

The knighting ceremony, the accolade, was usually held at a great feast such as Christmas or Easter. It involved a ritual bath, a prayer vigil through the night, an oath, and a blow with a sword on the shoulders. The first military orders, the Knights of the Holy Sepulchre and the Knights Hospitaller, were founded shortly after the First Crusade of 1099, followed by the Knights Templars in 1118, Santiago in 1170 and the Teutonic Knights in 1190. They began as monastic orders protecting pilgrims and grew powerful with the crusader states.

By the Late Middle Ages knighthood was associated with chivalry, a code for the courtly Christian warrior, spread by the Matter of France and the Matter of Britain, the cycles about Charlemagne's paladins and King Arthur's Round Table. Gunpowder weapons such as the culverin began to make armoured knights obsolete, though the titles remained, and Maximilian I is often called the last knight. Orders of knighthood continue today, among them the Order of the Garter and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, and a knighthood is granted by a head of state, monarch or prelate for meritorious service.
knights-hospitaller: The Hospitallers arose in the early 12th century, at the height of the Cluniac reform movement within the Benedictine order. Earlier, in the 11th century, merchants from Amalfi had founded a hospital in Jerusalem dedicated to John the Baptist, where Benedictine monks cared for sick, poor or injured Christian pilgrims. Blessed Gerard, a lay brother, became its head. After the Christian conquest of Jerusalem in 1099 the hospital rose in prominence, and Pope Paschal II recognised the Hospitallers as a distinct order in 1113.

In the 1120s and 1130s the order was militarised and hired knights who later became Hospitallers. It received its own papal charter and was charged with the care and defence of the Holy Land. Its members were organised as priest brothers, knight brothers and sergeant brothers; sergeants were at first hired as mercenaries to defend pilgrims and were formally listed as brothers in the statutes of 1204. The Grand Master commanded the order, with the marshal responsible for war and the hospitaller for its main hospital.

The order fought in the Crusades until the fall of Acre in 1291, then took refuge in Cyprus. Its Master, Guillaume de Villaret, chose Rhodes, then part of the Byzantine Empire, as a domain of its own and reorganised the order into eight langues: Aragon, Auvergne, Castile, England, France, the Holy Roman Empire, Italy and Provence. The knights governed Rhodes from 1310 to 1522. In 1530 Pope Clement VII and the Emperor Charles V arranged that they receive Malta, Gozo and Tripoli in perpetual fiefdom, for the yearly tribute of a Maltese falcon.

On Malta the knights stayed 268 years and built the fortified capital Valletta. The island's people were at first wary of them, and most knights were French, but the two groups coexisted peacefully. After their successful defence of the island in 1565 and the victory at Lepanto in 1571, the knights turned to protecting Christian shipping against the Barbary corsairs. In 1651 they bought four Caribbean islands from the Compagnie des Îles de l'Amérique and sold them to the French West India Company in 1665. In June 1798 Napoleon invaded Malta, and Grand Master Ferdinand von Hompesch zu Bolheim surrendered on 12 June.

The Reformation cost the order much of its European property. Its English holdings were confiscated in 1540, and the Bailiwick of Brandenburg became Lutheran in 1577 yet remained attached to the order. After the loss of Malta the knights dispersed through Europe, and in 1834 the main body settled in Rome, where hospital work again became its chief concern. Five organisations now continue the Hospitaller tradition and recognise one another, among them the Sovereign Military Order of Malta and the Most Venerable Order of Saint John, whose St John Ambulance is its best-known work.
knights-templar: After the Franks of the First Crusade captured Jerusalem from the Fatimid Caliphate in 1099, many Christians made pilgrimages to the Holy Land, but the roads beyond Jerusalem were not safe. Bandits preyed on pilgrims travelling from the coast at Jaffa to the interior, and some were killed by the hundreds. In 1119 the French knight Hugues de Payens approached King Baldwin II of Jerusalem and Warmund, Patriarch of Jerusalem, and proposed a monastic order to protect them.

The king and patriarch agreed, probably at the Council of Nablus in January 1120, and Baldwin gave the order a headquarters in a wing of the royal palace on the Temple Mount, in the captured Al-Aqsa Mosque. The first group numbered about nine knights and had few resources, relying on donations. Its emblem showed two knights on a single horse, a sign of poverty.

The order's work soon grew from escorting pilgrims to regular campaigning. Its first castle, Bagras in the Amanus Mountains, lay on the northern frontier of the Principality of Antioch, and from 1143 the Templars also took part in the Reconquista in Iberia. In the mid-12th century the tide turned. Saladin united much of the Islamic world, the Christian factions quarrelled, and the Templars were sometimes at odds with the Knights Hospitaller and the Teutonic Knights. Jerusalem fell to Saladin in 1187, after the Battle of Hattin.

The order moved its headquarters to Acre, which was lost in 1291. Its last foothold, the island of Arwad, fell to the Mamluk Sultanate in 1302 or 1303. In 1307 King Philip IV of France, who owed the order large debts according to some historians, had Jacques de Molay and many other French Templars arrested on Friday 13 October. Pope Clement V, under pressure from Philip, disbanded the order in 1312.

The Templars were organised like a monastic order, on the model of Bernard's Cistercian Order. A grand master, appointed for life, directed the military effort in the East and the financial holdings in the West, and each province had its own master. There were three ranks: noble knights in white mantles, non-noble sergeants in black or brown, and chaplains.

The Latin Rule, devised by Bernard de Clairvaux and Hugues de Payens, set out 72 clauses on dress, horses and conduct. After 1312 some knights and property passed to the Order of Christ, founded in Portugal in 1319 under King Denis, and to the Order of Montesa in Spain.
knin: Knin lies in the northern Dalmatian hinterland of Croatia, 56 kilometres east of Šibenik, on the foothills of the Dinaric Alps, where the Krka river rises on the outskirts of the town. The fortress stands on these foothills. The Roman town of Burnum, a military camp in the 1st century BCE, lay about 18 kilometres away, and its amphitheatre, built in 77 CE under Vespasian, could hold 8,000 people. The villages of Biskupija and Kapitul nearby are archaeological sites of the 10th century with churches, graves and inscriptions of medieval Croatian culture.

The settlement grew on the Spas hill and later formed the castle. A monastery of Saint Bartholomew was built at Kapitul in the 9th century, in the time of Trpimir I. Knin is first mentioned in the 10th-century De Administrando Imperio as the centre of a county and one of the populated towns of Croatia. Around 1040 the Croatian kings had a seat of the royal bishop established in the nearby village of Biskupija, and the bishops served at court until 1102, when Croatia entered its union with Hungary.

Knin fell to the Ottomans in 1522 and later became the centre of the Sanjak of Kırka, founded in 1574. The Republic of Venice briefly occupied it in 1648 during the Cretan War and took it again in 1688. Franciscans built a monastery and church there in 1708, and a siege by the Ottomans in 1715 was repulsed. Knin passed to the Habsburgs with Dalmatia in 1797 under the Treaty of Campo Formio, was part of the French Illyrian Provinces from 1809, and returned to Austria in 1813. By the end of the 19th century it had become an important commercial, road and railway centre, and the Lika railway linked it with Zagreb in 1925.

In the Second World War the area lay in the Italian occupation zone, administered by the Independent State of Croatia, and was the scene of the Ustaša campaign of genocide against the local Serb population. Before the Croatian War of Independence, Serbs made up 87 percent of the municipality and 79 percent of the town. During the war most of the non-Serb population was displaced, and in its last days most Serbs left, fearing the incoming Croatian forces. The International Court of Justice stated in 2015 that a substantial part of the Serb population fled as a direct consequence of military actions.

Knin is a city in Šibenik-Knin County and an important junction of the rail and road routes between Zagreb and Split, with lines running on to Zadar and Šibenik. The 2021 census counted 11,755 people in the municipality and 8,317 in the town itself. It has a hot-summer climate modified by the nearby mountains.
knossos: Settlement on Kephala hill began around 7000 BCE, and growth into an urban centre accelerated at the start of the second millennium BCE. The first palace, built around 1900 BCE, appears to have served administration, storage, ritual and craft production, with writing and sealings pointing to a complex bureaucracy. It was destroyed around 1700 BCE, probably by earthquakes, and rebuilt on a larger scale. The Second Palace period, from about 1700 to 1450 BCE, was the height of Minoan Knossos, with a central court, staircases, magazines, light wells, drainage and richly painted walls.

The palace was partly destroyed about 1450 BCE, and Knossos then became a Mycenaean administrative centre. Its Linear B tablets, written in an early form of Greek, record land, labour, livestock, textiles and offerings. A major destruction by fire is conventionally dated about 1350 BCE, though the date of the final destruction is debated. Knossos stayed occupied through the Iron Age, was a major Cretan city-state in the Archaic and Classical periods, issued coins showing the Labyrinth, and in the Roman period was called Colonia Iulia Nobilis Cnossus. It declined as nearby Heraklion rose.

Minos Kalokairinos made the first known modern excavation in 1878 and 1879, exposing part of the west wing and storage magazines with large pithoi. In 1900 Arthur Evans began large-scale work and uncovered most of the palace. He named the Bronze Age civilisation of Crete Minoan after the myth of King Minos. He also reconstructed parts of the palace in reinforced concrete, work that has been criticised where it goes beyond what the evidence supports. The Knossos Urban Landscape Project later surveyed the surrounding valley and showed a long-lived urban landscape rather than a palace alone.

The palace covered about 20,000 square metres around a rectangular Central Court. Its plan probably contributed to the Greek image of the Labyrinth. Its tablets were central to the decipherment of Linear B by Michael Ventris and John Chadwick. In 2025 Knossos was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List with Phaistos, Malia, Zakros, Zominthos and Kydonia as the Minoan Palatial Centres.
knowth: The great mound, 9 kilometres west of Drogheda, is about 12 metres high and 67 metres across, covers roughly a hectare and is surrounded by 17 smaller tombs. It is ringed by 127 kerbstones. Its two passages run east and west to separate chambers: the eastern one to a cruciform chamber with three recesses and basin stones that held the cremated dead, the western one to an undifferentiated chamber. Their orientation suggests an alignment with the equinoxes, though later disturbance makes it hard to establish.

Over 200 decorated stones were found. Besides spirals, lozenges and serpentine forms they include crescents and what is held to be the oldest known depiction of the moon, and much of the carving is on the hidden backs of stones, either deliberately concealed or reused.

After the mound fell into disuse, a timber circle near the eastern entrance served as a ritual site in the late Neolithic and Bronze Age, and some 35 cist graves were later dug there, but the site then lay largely unused for about two thousand years. In the late Iron Age and early Christian period it became a hill fort with ditches and souterrains, its passages were entered and four names were cut in ogham, and it grew into the capital of the Kingdom of Northern Brega. The medieval Triads of Ireland list its caves among the three darkest places in Ireland.

The Normans used it as a motte in the 12th century; it then passed to the Cistercian monks of Mellifont Abbey as a grange, and after the dissolution of the monasteries it was farmland until the state took over most of the site in 1939.

George Eogan of University College Dublin led excavations from 1962, finding the western and eastern passages in 1967 and 1968, and parts of the monument were then reconstructed. Unlike at Newgrange, the white quartz found at the entrances was left on the ground, a decision some archaeologists dispute. The site is visited by guided tour from the Brú na Bóinne Visitor Centre at Donore.
kobayakawa-clan: The Kobayakawa claimed descent from the Taira clan, through its Kanmu-Heishi branch, which traced itself to Emperor Kanmu, the 50th emperor of Japan. Nakamura Munehira, son of Taira no Tsunemune, founded the Nakamura clan of Sagami Province. His second son, Dohi Sanehira, who died in 1191, founded the Dohi clan, and Sanehira's second son, Kobayakawa Tohira, who died in 1237, founded the Kobayakawa. Two sons of the third head of the family, Kobayakawa Shigehira, who died in 1264, divided the clan: Masahira, his third son, made his base at Numata and began the Numata-Kobayakawa, and Masakage, his fourth son, settled at Takehara and began the Takehara-Kobayakawa.

The two branches continued side by side for some three centuries; the lists of their heads end with the same man, Kobayakawa Takakage, born in 1533, the third son of Mōri Motonari. Takakage was the uncle of Mōri Terumoto, and his brother headed the allied Kikkawa clan, so that the Kobayakawa held great power in the politics of western Japan. Toyotomi Hideyoshi regarded Takakage as one of the best statesmen and appointed him to the Council of Five Elders, but Takakage died in 1597, before Hideyoshi.

At the end of the 16th century the Kobayakawa fought beside the Kikkawa, Mōri, Toyotomi and Ōtomo clans against the Shimazu for control of Kyūshū, and after the defeat of the Shimazu they were awarded Chikuzen Province as their fief. Takakage's successor, Kobayakawa Hideaki, born in 1582, was a nephew of Hideyoshi.

A powerful clan of the Sengoku period, the Kobayakawa were disbanded in the Edo period, after the Battle of Sekigahara. In the Meiji period the Mōri clan restored the house, which was given the title of baron in the new nobility. The Kusai clan of Takehara, a branch of the Kobayakawa, was also granted noble rank.
kobayakawa-hideaki: He was the fifth son of Kinoshita Iesada. Toyotomi Hideyoshi first adopted him, and he called himself Hashiba Hidetoshi; he was then adopted again by Kobayakawa Takakage and became Kobayakawa Hidetoshi, taking the name Hideaki after Takakage's death. He received the rank of Saemon no Kami at his coming-of-age ceremony and held the court title of Chūnagon, so that he was also known as Kingo Chūnagon.

During the Siege of Ulsan he led reinforcements to relieve Ulsan Castle from the besieging Joseon and Ming forces, fighting on the front line with a spear, capturing an enemy commander and breaking the siege. Hideyoshi rebuked him for a reckless charge by an overall commander and took his domain of Chikugo from him. Hideaki believed a rumour spread by Tokugawa Ieyasu that a jealous Ishida Mitsunari was behind this, and never forgave Mitsunari.

Before Sekigahara he aided Mitsunari in the Siege of Fushimi while in secret contact with Ieyasu. Mitsunari and Ōtani Yoshitsugu promised him two more domains near Osaka and the post of kampaku if they won. Later accounts say he hesitated during the battle until Ieyasu had shots fired at his troops, and then attacked Ōtani's men, prompting other commanders to change sides; some recent historians argue that the earliest accounts place his switch at the start of the battle and call the story of the shots a myth. Afterwards he defeated Mitsunari's father, Ishida Masatsugu, at the Siege of Sawayama.

His reward was the former fiefs of the defeated Ukita clan in Bizen and Mimasaka, assessed at 550,000 koku. Two years later he drank himself to death, having supposedly lost his sanity. With no one to succeed him the Kobayakawa clan was disbanded. The historian Junji Mitsunari has argued that the defection at Sekigahara was not his decision alone but that of the whole clan, whose vassals urged him to change sides.
kobe: Kobe lies on the north shore of Osaka Bay in the Kansai region of Honshu, about 35 km west of Osaka and 70 km south-west of Kyoto. Wedged between the coast and the mountains, it is long and narrow, with Mount Rokko, 931 metres high, overlooking it. The shape of the coast at Wada Cape led to the development of a port, which has remained the economic centre of the city. The name comes from kamube, later kanbe, an archaic word for those who supported the city's Ikuta Shrine.

In the Nara and Heian periods the port was known as Owada Anchorage and was one of those from which imperial embassies were sent to China. In 1180 Taira no Kiyomori moved his grandson, Emperor Antoku, to Fukuhara-kyo in present-day Hyogo Ward, and the city was briefly the capital for about five months. In 1184 the Genpei War battle of Ichi-no-Tani was fought at the Taira fortress and the Ikuta Shrine, and the Minamoto prevailed. In the Kamakura period the port grew into a hub of trade with China and other countries and was known as Hyogo Port.

For most of its history the area was not a single political entity. Hyogo Port was opened to foreign trade, together with Osaka, on 1 January 1868, just before the Boshin War and the Meiji Restoration. Soon afterwards, in the Kobe Incident, troops from Bizen wounded several Western soldiers with gunfire. Many foreign residences from the period remain in the Kitano district. Kobe in its present form was founded on 1 April 1889.

On 16 and 17 March 1945 B-29 bombers attacked Kobe with incendiary bombs, killing 8,841 residents and destroying 21 percent of the urban area. On 17 January 1995 a magnitude 6.9 earthquake killed about 6,434 people in the city, made 212,443 homeless and toppled sections of the Hanshin Expressway.

Kobe is the capital of Hyogo Prefecture, with about 1.5 million people, and part of the Keihanshin metropolitan area with Osaka and Kyoto. Its port is one of Japan's busiest container ports. The city keeps a cosmopolitan character, with Western-style ijinkan residences in Kitano and Japan's first mosque, built in 1935. It is known for Kobe beef, the Arima Onsen hot springs and sake from the Nada district.
koblenz: Koblenz lies in a narrow flood plain between high hill ranges, where the Moselle meets the Middle Rhine. Its name comes from the Latin ad confluentes, meaning at the confluence. The meeting point of the rivers is the German Corner, which carries an equestrian statue of Emperor William I as a symbol of the unification of Germany. On the opposite bank of the Rhine the hill of Ehrenbreitstein bore early fortifications around 1000 BCE and is crowned today by a citadel.

In 55 BCE Roman troops under Julius Caesar reached the Rhine and built a bridge between Koblenz and Andernach. The military post Castellum apud Confluentes was one of those set up by Drusus. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the city was conquered by the Franks and became a royal seat, and Carolingian heirs met there to discuss what became the Treaty of Verdun in 843, by which it passed to Lotharingia. A synod of 922 condemned slavery. The Norsemen sacked the city in 882. In 1018 Emperor Henry II gave it to the archbishop-elector of Trier, whose successors held it until the end of the 18th century.

After the fall of the Bastille in 1789 the archbishop-elector, uncle of Louis XVI, welcomed French royalist émigrés, among them the Count of Provence and the Count of Artois. The Prince of Condé formed an army of aristocrats there. In 1792 the Duke of Brunswick began to march from Koblenz in an unsuccessful invasion of France, and the French Revolutionary army took the city in 1794. The Treaty of Lunéville of 1801 made it the capital of the French department of Rhin-et-Moselle. The Congress of Vienna assigned it to Prussia, and in 1822 it became the seat of government of the Prussian Rhine Province.

Koblenz is a city of Rhineland-Palatinate. The city was heavily bombed in the Second World War and rebuilt, and it served as the seat of government of Rhineland-Palatinate from 1947 to 1950. The Rhine Gorge was declared a World Heritage Site in 2002, with Koblenz marking its northern end. The city marked its 2,000th anniversary in 1992.
koca-sinan-pasha: Koca Sinan Pasha, "Sinan the Great", was born in Topojan in Luma territory and was of Albanian origin. A Ragusan document of 1571 describes him as coming from a Roman Catholic family that had converted to Islam. His father was named Ali Bey, and he had family ties with Catholic relatives such as the Giubizzas. The Austrian orientalist Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall called him the "unbridled Albanian", and Mustafa Ali of Gallipoli repeatedly criticised him for promoting an Albanian clique in the administration.

Sinan was appointed governor of Ottoman Egypt in 1569 and until 1571 took part in the conquest of Yemen, which earned him the name Fātiḥ-i Yemen, "Conqueror of Yemen". In 1580 he commanded the army against the Safavids and was appointed grand vizier by Murad III, but he was disgraced and exiled the next year after the defeat of his lieutenant Mehmed Pasha at Gori. After serving as governor of Damascus he became grand vizier a second time in 1589, after the great revolt of the Janissaries. He oversaw the execution of Petru Cercel in March 1590, having sided with Mihnea Turcitul in the contest for the throne of Wallachia. He was dismissed in 1591 after another revolt of the Janissaries.

Recalled in 1593 for a third term, he commanded the Ottoman army in the Long War against the Habsburgs. He took Veszprém and Palota after a siege of three or four days, took Sisak and returned to Belgrade through Novi Sad. In 1594 he captured Győr. During the uprising in Banat in 1594 he ordered the relics of Saint Sava brought from Mileševa to Belgrade, where he had them burned in order to discourage the Serbs. He was deposed in February 1595 and banished to Malkara. Recalled in August to lead the expedition against Michael the Brave of Wallachia, his defeats at Călugăreni and Giurgiu and the fall of Esztergom cost him the seal of office on 19 November.

The death of his successor Lala Mehmed Pasha three days later made Sinan grand vizier for the fifth time. He died suddenly in the spring of 1596, on 3 April, and left a large fortune. He is buried in Istanbul near the Grand Bazaar. He married Esmehan Hanımsultan, a granddaughter of Selim I, and had a son and three daughters. Contemporary critics, among them Mustafa Âlî, wrote that he preferred Albanians for high office. At his request, in 1586, Murad III exempted five villages in Luma from all taxes. He was a major builder of caravanserais, bridges, baths and mosques, including the fortress and mosque of Kaçanik and the Pearl Kiosk of 1590.
kocel: Kocel was the second son of Pribina, a Slavic dux installed by the Franks in Lower Pannonia around 838 or 840. The historian Bowlus believes he was born around 820. He ruled the Principality of Lower Pannonia as an East Frankish vassal with the title of comes, count, from Mosapurc, known in Old Slavonic as Blatnograd, at modern Zalavár near Lake Balaton. A Latin gift deed of 861 calls him "Count of Slavs".

In 861 Kocel made a significant donation to the Freising monastery, which shows that he had a solid social and political standing. According to Bowlus, the document indicates that Pribina had died and that Kocel had succeeded him. Louis the German installed Kocel as ruler in Lower Pannonia in 864. In 865 Kocel held "Lower Pannonia" (Pannonia inferioris) when Archbishop Adalwin of Salzburg visited his lands twice.

Kocel asked for the Byzantine missionary Methodius to be sent into Pannonia as a papal legate. In midsummer he sent Methodius to Rome with twenty men to petition for his elevation to bishop. Pope Hadrian II raised Methodius to archbishop and sent confirmations to several people, among them Kocel, whose land lay within the new jurisdiction. In 871 Frankish Pannonia was held by Kocel and Bavarian margraves, and his talks with the pope show that he enjoyed independence. In 874, after the Moravian conflict, Kocel continued to rule the Drava Valley, presumably under Carloman of the March of Pannonia.
Kocel disappears from the sources after 874. He was either dead or removed from office around 876, and certainly dead by 880. A posthumous source of between 876 and 880 calls him "Duke" (Chezil dux).

Some historians identify Kocel with the Frankish commander Kotzil or Kotzilis, mentioned in the De Administrando Imperio in connection with a revolt of the Croats in which all the Franks and their archon Kotzil were killed, most probably in 874, the year Kocel disappears from the sources. Francis Dvornik thought the account may combine several events, in which Kocel perished in 876, while Neven Budak concluded that the Croatian revolt cannot be connected to Kocel.
kocher: The Kocher is a river 169 kilometres long, a right tributary of the Neckar in the north-eastern part of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Its name comes from the Celtic cochan and probably means winding, meandering river. Its drainage area is 1,960 square kilometres. It rises in the eastern foothills of the Swabian Alb from two karst springs, the Schwarzer Kocher (Black Kocher) and the Weißer Kocher (White Kocher), which join at Unterkochen near Aalen. The Black Kocher is about 8 kilometres long and flows slowly, its covered ground giving the water a dark colour. The 3.3-kilometre White Kocher is named for the white foam on its water as it rushes over stones.

From Unterkochen the river flows north through Aalen and Wasseralfingen to Hüttlingen, where it turns west towards Abtsgmünd and receives the Lein. It winds north-west to Unterrot, where the Rot joins it, and continues to Gaildorf and Schwäbisch Hall. Near Geislingen the Bühler flows in. The river then curves west again, cutting into the plain of Hohenlohe and passing Künzelsau, and at Neuenstadt am Kocher it takes in the Brettach. It enters the Neckar near Bad Friedrichshall, a few kilometres upstream from the mouth of the Jagst, which runs roughly parallel to it.

Many industrial sites in the upper valley and poor sewage plants caused heavy pollution of the Kocher. In 1984 it was declared the most polluted river in the administrative district of Stuttgart. A remediation project of only six years improved the water quality significantly. The river's mostly brown colour comes from mud in the water and does not indicate poor quality.
kochi: Kochi, formerly Cochin, lies on the south-west coast of India, bordering the Laccadive Sea, in the district of Ernakulam in Kerala. The city straddles the backwaters and takes in the northern end of a peninsula, several islands and part of the mainland. Much of it lies at sea level. The name is thought to come from the Malayalam kochu azhi, meaning small lagoon. Arab merchants called the place Kashi, and the Cochin Jewish community called it Kogin. The city reverted to its original Malayalam form Kochi in 1996.

Muziris, a port north of Kochi mostly identified with Kodungallur, was the centre of the Indian spice trade for many centuries. Kochi became a significant trading centre after the massive flooding of the Periyar in 1341 destroyed Muziris.
