The earliest documented references to Kochi are in the writings of the Chinese voyager Ma Huan, who visited in the 15th century with Admiral Zheng He's treasure fleet, and in the accounts of the Italian traveller Niccolò Da Conti, who visited in 1440. The Chinese fishing nets that are a symbol of the city were introduced by the Chinese in the 14th century.

The ruler of Perumpadappu fled to Kodungallur after the Zamorin of Calicut annexed the Ponnani region, and his family later moved to Kochi and established the Kingdom of Cochin. When Vasco da Gama landed at Kozhikode and the Zamorin fought the Portuguese, the ruler of Cochin aligned with the Portuguese. From 1503 to 1663 the Portuguese held Fort Emmanuel, before the Dutch took it over, and the Dutch later ceded the area to the United Kingdom. The construction of the Cochin Port and the reclamation of Willingdon Island in 1928 made Kochi a major seaport.

Kochi is a port city and the financial, industrial and commercial centre of Kerala, with 677,381 inhabitants in the municipal corporation at the 2011 census. It is the seat of the High Court of Kerala. Cochin Shipyard is the largest shipbuilding and maintenance facility in India in terms of capacity. The city once had a large Jewish community, known as the Malabar Yehuden and now increasingly as the Cochin Jews, who owned several synagogues. Landmarks include Mattanchery Palace and the Church of Saint Francis.
kodagu: Kodagu, also known by its former name Coorg, lies on the eastern slopes of the Western Ghats and covers 4,102 square kilometres. The name derives from the root koḍa, meaning western, with the suffix gï, meaning place. It is hilly: the lowest elevation is 50 metres above sea level, and the highest peak, Tadiandamol, rises to 1,750 metres, with Pushpagiri second at 1,715 metres. The Kaveri originates at Talakaveri on the eastern side of the Ghats and with its tributaries drains the greater part of the district. Kodagu has three wildlife sanctuaries, Pushpagiri, Talakaveri and Brahmagiri, and shares Nagarahole National Park.

The Kodavas were the earliest inhabitants and agriculturists of Kodagu and lived there for centuries. They were also a warrior community who carried arms in war and had their own chieftains. The earliest mentions of Coorg appear in works of the Sangam period, which place part of Kodagu in Karkanadu, one of the two nadus under the Ezhimala dynasty, along with the Wayanad-Gudalur region.

The Haleri dynasty, an offshoot of the Keladi Nayakas, ruled Kodagu between 1600 and 1834. Raja Veerarajendra, who escaped captivity under Tippu Sultan in 1788, gave lands, tax breaks and a church to Konkani Catholics who fled Tippu's roundup. In 1834 the East India Company annexed Kodagu into British India as Coorg, after deposing Chikka Virarajendra following the Coorg War. British rule brought educational institutions and scientific coffee cultivation. An armed struggle against the British began in 1837, which they called the Coorg Rebellion. Coorg stayed a separate state until 1956, when it was merged into an enlarged Mysore State, now Karnataka.

Madikeri is the capital. The 2011 census counted 554,519 people. Hindus are the vast majority, with Muslim and Catholic minorities, and the languages spoken include Kannada, Malayalam, Kodava, Tulu, Are and Yerava. Kodava, a language native to the district, has used a script devised by I. M. Muthanna in 1970. The economy rests on agriculture, with paddy, coffee, rubber, pepper, cardamom and oranges among the main crops. Talakaveri, where the Kaveri rises, has a temple to Brahma, and the Omkareshwara Temple at Madikeri was built by Lingarajendra II in 1820.
kodama-gentaro: Kodama was born on 16 March 1852 in Tokuyama in Suō Province, the first son of Kodama Hankurō, a mid-ranking samurai with a landholding of 100 koku. He began his military career fighting for the Meiji Restoration against the forces of the Tokugawa shogunate in the Boshin War of 1868. In the new Imperial Japanese Army he rose quickly, from non-commissioned officer in 1870 to major in 1874, and saw combat in the suppression of the Shinpūren and Satsuma rebellions before enrolling at the Osaka military training school.

Promoted colonel in 1883 and major-general in 1889, Kodama headed the Army Staff College, where he worked with the German Major Jakob Meckel to reorganise the Japanese army on the Prussian model. He studied military science as an attaché in Germany and became Vice-minister of War in 1892. After the Sino-Japanese War of 1894 and 1895 he became Governor-General of Taiwan, where he did much to improve the island's infrastructure, and he served as Minister of the Army and, under Prime Minister Katsura Tarō, also as Minister of Home Affairs and of Education.

Made a full general on 6 June 1904, he accepted Marshal Ōyama Iwao's request to become chief of staff of the Manchurian Army, a step down in rank that drew public applause. He guided the strategy of the whole campaign against Russia. The postwar writer Shiba Ryōtarō credited him entirely with the victory at the Siege of Port Arthur, but there is no historical evidence for this, and Kodama himself kept quiet about his part.

After the war Kodama was named Chief of the Army General Staff, and he was raised to baron in 1895 and viscount in April 1906. He died of a cerebral haemorrhage on 23 July 1906, a death regarded as a national calamity. At his son Hideo's petition the Meiji Emperor made Hideo a count, and Kodama himself was later raised to the rank of a Shinto kami. Shrines to him stand in his home town, now Shūnan in Yamaguchi Prefecture, and on the site of his summer home on Enoshima.
kodava-people: The names Kodava, for the people, language and culture, and Kodagu, for the land, share the root koda, which some take to mean mist, others hills or west, all fitting the Western Ghats. In their own language the land is Kodava Naad; the British Raj anglicised the people's name as Coorgs. Works of the Sangam period place parts of Kodagu in Karkanadu, the hilly eastern district of the Ezhimala dynasty.

The region later passed under the Kadamba and the Gangas, briefly the Cholas, then the Hoysalas and the Vijaynagara rulers. From around 1600 the Haleri Rajas ruled Kodagu, and under them the Kodavas began to keep Hindu festivals such as Ugadi, Ayudha Puja and Mahashivaratri.

In 1834 the last Haleri Raja, Chikka Vira Raja, fell out with the East India Company, which invaded Kodagu. The campaign was short but bloody; resistance was fiercest near Somwarpet, where the Coorgs were led by Mathanda Appachu, but it ended when the Raja sent his Diwan, Apparanda Bopu, to surrender and lead the British from Kushalnagar into Madikeri. Kodagu was annexed, the Raja exiled, and large numbers of European planters settled in its forests to grow coffee, which changed the economy and land management of Kodava society. Kodavas later fought in both World Wars and in India's wars with China and Pakistan.

Kodavas live in okka family groups scattered over farms and forest holdings, with the ancestral ainmane houses as their meeting points; most towns of Kodagu are recent and largely home to non-Kodavas. Under the Jamma tenure instituted by the Rajas, lands were held almost wholly by Kodavas as a hereditary right, indivisible and inalienable, together with the adjoining woods. Each village keeps at least one devarakadu, a sacred grove believed to be an abode of the gods, where poaching and felling are forbidden.

Their festivals follow the farming year. Kail Poldh, the festival of arms on 3 September, marks the end of rice transplanting, when the weapons kept in the prayer room were taken out to guard the crops from wild boar. At Kaveri Sankramana in mid-October pilgrims gather at Talakaveri, the source of the Kaveri, and carry its holy water home, and Puttari, the festival of new rice, falls on a full-moon night in late November or early December. Because of their militia duties, the Indian Arms Act of 1878 exempted all persons of Kodava race from its restrictions on firearms.
kodiak-island: Kodiak Island is a large island on the south coast of Alaska, separated from the mainland by the Shelikof Strait. It is the largest island of the Kodiak Archipelago, about 160 kilometres long and between 16 and 97 kilometres wide, with an area of 9,311 square kilometres, slightly larger than Cyprus. It is mountainous and heavily forested in the north and east and fairly treeless in the south, with many deep, ice-free bays that give boats sheltered anchorage. The Kodiak bear and the king crab are native to the island, and the Karluk River is known for its salmon run.

Kodiak is the ancestral land of the Sugpiaq, an Alutiiq nation, whose people lived by hunting marine mammals, fishing and gathering. The Russian fur trader Grigory Shelikhov founded a settlement at Three Saints Bay in 1784, and in 1792 it was moved to the site of the present town of Kodiak, which became the centre of Russian fur trading with Alaska Natives. In 1784 Shelikhov and 130 Russian fur traders massacred several hundred Qik'rtarmiut Sugpiat men, women and children at Refuge Rock, a small island off Sitkalidak Island, which the Alutiiq now call Awa'uq, to become numb.

Russian traders conscripted the Alutiiq to hunt, gather and process food and furs, taking labour by hostage taking, physical threat and punishment. Men were forced to meet quotas of otter pelts and bird skins, and families went hungry and were separated. The Orthodox mission was authorised by Catherine II in 1793 and established on the island in 1794 by monks from the Valaam Monastery. A smallpox epidemic from 1837 to 1839 destroyed an estimated one-third of the Native population. After the 1867 Alaska Purchase the island became part of the United States. On 6 to 8 June 1912 the eruption of Novarupta, about 160 kilometres to the northwest, covered the island in ash, collapsed roofs and devastated wildlife.

The city of Kodiak is the main settlement among seven communities on the island, and ferry and air services connect it with the outside world. Fishing for Pacific salmon, halibut and crab is the most important economic activity. Most of the southwestern two-thirds of the island lies in the Kodiak National Wildlife Refuge, and the island hosts a large United States Coast Guard base.
kodungallur: Kodungallur lies on the banks of the Periyar on the Malabar Coast, 36 kilometres north of Kochi and 38 kilometres from Thrissur. As a port at the northern end of the Kerala lagoons, it was a strategic entry point to the backwaters. It has had many names, among them Cranganore (anglicised) and Cranganor in Portuguese, Mahodayapuram, Shingly and Vanchi. Several of the foreign forms, such as Shinkali and Jangli, derive from the name of the River Changala, a tributary of the Periyar. Scholars believe that the ancient harbour of Muziris, at the mouth of the Periyar, coincides with modern Kodungallur.

In early historic times the harbour was visited by navigators from across the Mediterranean world. The Roman Empire traded continuously with the west coast of India, and sailors acquired black pepper, pearls, muslin, ivory, diamonds, silk and perfumes from central Kerala. Traditions of several faiths attach to the town. Saint Thomas Christians hold that Thomas the Apostle landed here in the middle of the first century CE and founded seven churches. According to Kerala Muslim tradition the first mosque in India was built here in 624 CE with the consent of the last Cheraman Perumal.

In the medieval period the town was part of Mahodayapuram, seat of the imperial Cheras. The Chola rulers sacked the port in the 11th century, and after the Chera Perumal rule ended in the early 12th century Kodungallur became a principality allied to Cochin or Calicut. A flood or earthquake in 1341 is postulated to have silted the river's harbour so that large vessels could scarcely enter, and trade moved to Cochin and Calicut.

On 1 September 1504 the Portuguese under Suarez de Menezes almost completely destroyed the port, and in October of that year Lopo Soares attacked it again with a combined force of about 1,000 Portuguese and 1,000 soldiers of Kochi, which captured and burned the city. Reports say the Saint Thomas Christian quarters were spared. The Portuguese built Fort Cranganore in 1523 and enlarged it in 1565. The Dutch took it in 1663, and on 31 July 1789 they handed their holdings in Kodungallur to Travancore for 300,000 Surat silver rupees.

Kodungallur is a municipality in Thrissur district, headquarters of its own tehsil. The Thiruvanchikulam Mahadeva Temple, dedicated to Shiva, was the patron shrine of the Chera Perumals and is still the family deity of the Cochin royal family. The Kodungallur Bhagavathy Temple to the goddess Bhadrakali heads 64 Bhadrakali temples in Kerala. The Muziris Heritage Project, launched by the government of Kerala in 2006, works to recover and preserve the heritage of the region from North Paravur to Kodungallur.
koffiefontein: In the 19th century the place was a stopover for transport riders travelling between the coast and the diamond fields and gold mines to the north. Its name, Afrikaans for coffee spring or fountain, recalls the strong coffee the riders brewed there, grinding their own beans and boiling the water of a natural spring. When diamonds were found near the spring in 1870, a town grew up quickly as prospectors came to work the ground, and its stones were known for clarity of the first water.

Because it lay near Kimberley and Mafeking, the district saw much fighting in the Second Anglo-Boer War of 1899-1902. After Boer forces under General Brand and Commandant Hertzog attacked the town and its mine, the British built blockhouses in October 1900, which still stand. At one point the Boers looted the town and its people took refuge in the mine. During the Second World War a large internment camp held 2,000 Italian prisoners of war, some German prisoners and some 800 South African internees suspected of being pro-Nazi, among them Frans Erasmus and John Vorster, prime minister from 1966 and president from 1978 to 1979.

Koffiefontein is a small farming town where cattle and sheep are raised and lucerne, potatoes and ground nuts grown; the Kalkfontein Dam on the Riet River supplies its water. The mine was closed in 2006 and acquired by Petra Diamonds in 2007. The barracks of the internment camp and murals by its Italian prisoners survive, as do San rock paintings in the district and the homestead and grave of the Afrikaans novelist Etienne Leroux.
kofu: Kōfu lies in north-central Yamanashi Prefecture in central Honshu, in the Kōfu Basin, 250 to 300 metres above sea level and surrounded by mountains on all sides. Three quarters of its territory is part of Mount Kinpu in the north, and Mount Fuji can be seen in the distance to the south. Its name means capital of Kai Province. Archaeologists have found evidence of settlement from the Japanese Paleolithic period, continuing through the Jōmon, Yayoi and Kofun periods.

In the Nara period the provincial temple of Kai Province was established in what is now Kōfu, which suggests that the provincial capital stood nearby. In the Heian period the Kai-Genji, a branch of the Minamoto clan, ruled large estates there and developed a military force noted for its cavalry. By the Muromachi period the Takeda clan, a branch of the Kai-Genji, dominated the area and built a castle in what is now part of the city.

Under Takeda Nobutora Kōfu was rebuilt as a castle town from 1519, and it remained the capital of the Takeda under his successors Takeda Shingen and Takeda Katsuyori. During the Edo period Kai Province was territory ruled directly by the Tokugawa shogunate, and Kōfu Castle remained its administrative centre. In 1705 the domain was conferred on Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu, a favourite of the fifth shōgun, and in 1724 it passed to Yamato-Koriyama, after which the shogunate held the castle directly again.

The town of Kōfu was proclaimed on 1 July 1889, after the Meiji Restoration. A typhoon and the felling of forests brought a great flood in August 1907, in which 233 people died in Yamanashi Prefecture, the largest natural disaster of modern times there. On the night of 6 July 1945 United States B-29 bombers destroyed much of the city.

Kōfu is the capital of Yamanashi Prefecture and a commercial and transport centre for its central part, with 187,985 inhabitants in 2019. Local industries include food processing, wine, textiles and crystalware. Historic sites include Kōfu Castle, Tsutsujigasaki Castle, Takeda Shrine and the temple Kai Zenkō-ji. Each April the Shingen-ko Festival celebrates the memory of Takeda Shingen with parades.
koga-ibaraki: Koga lies in the extreme southwestern corner of Ibaraki Prefecture, almost in the centre of the Kanto Plain, and the city is very flat. The Tone River flows eastward through its southern part, and the Watarase River runs through the west and joins the Tone north of the Tonegawa Bridge. The city borders Saitama and Tochigi prefectures. Its climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers and cool winters with light snowfall, and an annual rainfall of about 1,229.9 mm.

The area was settled in the Jōmon period. By the Nara period Koga was known as a ferry port on the Watarase River and was mentioned in the Man'yōshū. In the Heian period it was the site of an iron smelter and of kilns producing ceramics and roof tiles, and it was one of the largest centres of iron production in eastern Japan. In the Muromachi period it was the seat of the Koga kubō, a secondary government created by the Ashikaga shogunate to rule eastern Japan.

In the Sengoku period Koga developed into a castle town. In the Edo period it became the seat of the daimyō of Koga Domain under the Tokugawa shogunate, and a station on the Nikkō Kaidō highway. The modern town of Koga was established on 1 April 1889 and became a city on 1 August 1950. On 12 September 2005 it absorbed the towns of Sanwa and Sōwa to form the present, larger city.

From the Meiji era to the early Shōwa era Koga was a centre of silk-raising. KDDI's Yamata Transmitting Station, which began broadcasting on 1 January 1941, stands in the city, and the announcement of Japan's surrender by Emperor Hirohito in 1945 was sent from it to Japanese forces overseas. Local sites include the sites of Koga Castle and of the Koga Kubo residence, the Hase Kannon temple, the Koga History Museum and Sogo Koen Park, a former summer palace of a local daimyō with two restored 17th-century farmhouses. The artist Kawanabe Kyōsai was among the people of Koga.
kogi-people: The Kogi call themselves Kágaba, a name meaning jaguar in their language, which belongs to the Chibchan family and is close to the languages of the Arhuaco and Ika of the same mountains. They descend from the Tairona culture, which built stone structures and paths in the forest and made gold objects. Around 1000 CE, before the Spanish arrived, invading Caribs drove the Tairona into the highlands, a refuge that later proved strategic. The view, associated above all with Gerardo Reichel-Dolmatoff, that their culture has continued unbroken since the Pre-Columbian era has been criticised for passing over centuries of contact and for picturing the Kogi as noble eco-savages.

Missionaries later built chapels and churches among their villages, but life in the mountains spared the Kogi the worst effects of colonisation. They keep outsiders out of their ancestral lands, and only men deal with strangers. To warn the outside world, whom they call Younger Brother, of ecological ruin, the mamos let a small BBC crew film them for the 1990 documentary, then withdrew again. Twenty years on they called on the same film-maker, Alan Ereira, and in the 2012 film Aluna they gave a second warning, linking reckless change to ecosystems and the desecration of tombs with climate change.

Kogi belief rests on Aluna, the thought of the Great Mother, who created the world from images in her mind; the Earth is a living being and humanity its children. The Kogi see themselves as Elder Brothers guarding the Heart of the World, the peak of Gonawindua, also called Pico Cristóbal Colón. Mamos, priests trained from early childhood in isolation through abstinence from food, sleep and sex, bless seeds and marriages and make offerings to keep the world in balance.

Villages of round huts of stone, mud and palm leaves each have a men's temple, the nuhue, where decisions are taken. Everyone wears white, the colour of the Great Mother. On coming of age a man receives a poporo, a gourd of lime powder taken with chewed coca, and men greet one another by exchanging coca. Families farm plots at several altitudes, raise cattle on the highlands and trade sugar and coffee.
kogi-state: Kogi State lies in the North Central region of Nigeria and borders ten other states, the only state in the country to do so. Its name comes from the Hausa word for river, and it is nicknamed the Confluence State because the River Niger and the River Benue meet next to its capital, Lokoja. The two rivers meet in the centre of the state and bisect it southward. The state lies within the tropical Guinean forest–savanna mosaic ecoregion, with a rainy season from April to October and a dry season from November to March marked by the harmattan.

Before colonial rule the area was divided among various states, some tiny and village-based, others part of larger realms. The Nupe Kingdom held much of what is now western Kogi until the early 1800s, when the Fulani jihad annexed it and placed the area under the Sokoto Caliphate. The eastern half of the modern state was the ancient Igala Kingdom. British expeditions occupied the area in the early twentieth century and made it part of the Northern Nigeria Protectorate, whose capital was Lokoja until 1903. According to the account given of Lokoja, the name Nigeria was coined there by Flora Shaw, later the wife of Baron Lugard, as she looked out over the Niger from Mount Patti.

After independence in 1960 the area was part of the Northern Region until 1967, when the region was split, and then of the Benue, Niger and Kwara states. Kogi State was formed on 27 August 1991 from parts of Benue State, Niger State and Kwara State.

The state is home to the Ebira, Gbagyi, Nupe subgroups such as the Kakanda and Kupa, and Oko in the centre, the Igala and Bassa in the east and the Yoruba, mainly the Okun, Ogori, Oworo and Magongo, in the west. About 45% of the population is Muslim, about 40% Christian and the remainder follows traditional ethnic religions. Agriculture is the mainstay of the economy, with coffee, cocoa, palm oil, cashews, groundnuts, yams and rice among the crops. The state has twenty-one local government areas, and its landmarks include Mount Patti, Lord Lugard House and the confluence of the two rivers.
koh-i-noor: In 1310 the Delhi Sultan Alauddin Khalji acquired a large diamond after subjugating the Kakatiya dynasty of southern India, and the 18th-century chronicler Khafi Khan identifies the stone as the Koh-i-Noor. The diamond first appears in the historical record in the late 15th century and later came into the possession of Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire. After Babur's son Humayun defeated Ibrahim Khan Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, the family of Bikramjit, the ruler of Gwalior, presented Humayun with a diamond. Babur wrote that its value could feed the whole world for a day.

Under Shah Jahan the stone was set in the Peacock Throne. Nader Shah took it with the throne from Delhi in 1739 after defeating Muhammad Shah at the Battle of Karnal. After Nader Shah's assassination in 1747 it passed to Ahmad Shah, who founded the Durrani Empire; accounts differ on how. His grandson Shah Shuja Durrani fled with it to Lahore, in the Sikh Empire, and in 1813 Ranjit Singh took it from him. Shah Shuja's memoirs state that Ranjit Singh extorted it by having his son tortured in front of him.

The Last Treaty of Lahore of 29 March 1849, after the Second Anglo-Sikh War, annexed the remaining territories of the Sikh Empire. Its third article required the eleven-year-old Maharaja Duleep Singh to surrender the gem to the Queen of England. It was shown at the Great Exhibition of 1851, where its flawed appearance disappointed viewers. Prince Albert had it recut in 1852, which took 38 days and reduced it from 186 old carats to 105.6 carats.

Since reaching Britain the diamond has been worn only by women of the royal family. Queen Victoria wore it as a brooch and circlet, and it was later set in the crowns of Queen Alexandra, Queen Mary in 1911 and Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother in 1937. It is displayed in the Jewel House at the Tower of London. India asked for its return in 1947 and again in 1953, Pakistan in 1976, and Iran and Afghanistan have also made claims, while the British government holds that it was acquired legally under the Last Treaty of Lahore. Wilkie Collins drew on its history for his novel The Moonstone of 1868.
koine-greek: Koine, from a Greek phrase meaning the common dialect, arose within the armies of Alexander the Great. Under Macedonian leadership this common variety was spoken from the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt to the Seleucid Empire of Mesopotamia, and it replaced the older Greek dialects with an everyday form that people anywhere could understand. The post-classical period of Greek is defined as beginning with Alexander's death in 323 BCE. Ancient Macedonian contributed some military terms and changes in grammar to the new language.

Its roots were unclear even in antiquity. Hellenistic scholars thought it a mixture of the four main dialects, a view Paul Kretschmer supported in 1901, while Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff and Antoine Meillet saw a simplified Ionic. Most scholars now follow Georgios Hatzidakis, who showed that its stable nucleus is Attic with admixtures, above all from Ionic.

Koine ran from conservative literary styles to the spoken vernaculars of the time. Literary Koine was the medium of much post-classical writing, including the works of Plutarch and Polybius, and the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote his private thoughts in it in the work now called Meditations. In the Roman Empire's eastern provinces local elites and communities in Asia Minor, Arabia, Judaea, Syria and Egypt used Greek for inscriptions, documents and official announcements, even where it was not the main spoken language. A decree of the Roman Senate to the town of Thisbae in Boeotia in 170 BCE survives in it.

Its sounds changed greatly over the period. From the second century BCE the distinction between long and short vowels was lost and a stress accent replaced the ancient pitch accent. Several diphthongs became single vowels, and pronunciation moved from close to Ancient Greek towards Modern Greek.

Koine is the language of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible made in the 3rd century BCE, of the Christian New Testament and of most early Christian theological writing by the Church Fathers, and in this setting it is called Biblical, New Testament or patristic Greek. Scholars have debated how far Biblical Greek reflects ordinary spoken Koine and how far Hebrew or Aramaic influence shaped it. As the dominant language of the Byzantine Empire it developed into Medieval Greek, which informed Modern Greek, and it continues as the liturgical language of the Greek Orthodox Church and some Greek Catholic churches.
kojiki: According to its preface, Emperor Tenmu, who reigned from 673 to 686, ordered a review of the clan records and commissioned a court attendant of exceptional memory, Hieda no Are, to memorize the records and oral traditions of the imperial line. On the 18th day of the 9th month of 711 Empress Genmei ordered Ō no Yasumaro to write down what Hieda no Are had learned, and he presented the work on the 28th day of the 1st month of 712. Earlier compilations of 620 had been lost when Soga no Emishi's estate burned in 645.

The Kojiki collates different traditions into one official mythology. It justifies the rule of the Yamato court and gives other groups a place in the national genealogy, as when it absorbs the local traditions of the Izumo lineage in order to subordinate them to Yamato. It does not mention Buddhism, and scholars tend to treat it as myth rather than history.

The book is written mostly in Classical Chinese, but its songs and poems are in Old Japanese, written phonetically with Chinese characters. The first of its three volumes covers the creation and the age of the gods. Izanagi and Izanami form the islands of Japan and bear many deities, and Izanami dies giving birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi. Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi and Susanoo are born as Izanagi washes his left eye, his right eye and his nose. Ninigi, a grandson of Amaterasu, descends to Kyūshū and becomes the ancestor of the imperial line.
The second volume begins with the conquests of Jimmu, the first emperor, and ends with the 15th emperor, Ōjin. The third volume covers the 16th to 33rd emperors and has far fewer dealings with gods.

During the Heian period the Nihon Shoki was widely studied, while the Kojiki was treated as a secondary text. By the Kamakura period few people had access to it, and its earliest manuscript, the Shinpukuji-bon, dates from 1371 to 1372. It reached a wide audience only in print, with the Kan'ei Kojiki published in Kyoto in 1644.

In the Edo period scholars of nativist studies such as Kada no Azumamaro and Kamo no Mabuchi saw it as a record of a Japanese identity that could be recovered, and it gained the standing of a sacred text. Its myths, with those of the Nihon Shoki, inspired Shinto practices such as the misogi purification ritual.
kojo-no-tsuki: Rentarō Taki's music was inspired by the ruins of Oka Castle, while Bansui Doi drew his words from the ruins of Aoba Castle and Aizuwakamatsu Castle. Taki wrote the song in B minor. A later version by Kosaku Yamada, slower, nostalgic in mood and set in D minor, is also popular as a song with accompaniment. Taki's original uses an E sharp in the second bar, but the modern version usually has an E, probably because the original did not fit traditional Japanese music.

The tenor Yoshie Fujiwara recorded the song in 1925 and was the first Japanese singer to make it known throughout the world. Thelonious Monk recorded a jazz arrangement under the title Japanese Folk Song on his 1967 album Straight, No Chaser, and that version is heard in the 2016 American film La La Land.

The German heavy metal band Scorpions sang it live as a power ballad at the Nakano Sun Plaza in Tokyo, released on their 1978 album Tokyo Tapes, in one of the rare renditions that follow Taki's original closely. Yngwie Malmsteen played it as an instrumental on the Alcatrazz tour of Japan in 1984, and the Japanese band Takeshi Terauchi & Blue Jeans recorded an instrumental rock cover on Let's Go Blue Jeans.

The guitarist Eduardo Falú recorded it as La luna sobre las ruinas del castillo on his 1974 album Palabras para mi guitarra, and the pianist George Winston arranged it for his 2004 album Montana: A Love Story. The enka singer Kiyoshi Hikawa sang it live in 2008, and Jackie Evancho recorded it in Japanese in 2012 for the Japanese release of Songs from the Silver Screen. The 2020 video game Cyberpunk 2077 has the character Hanako Arasaka sing a version on a parade float. In 1998 the asteroid 8957 Koujounotsuki was named after the song.
koka-shiga: Kōka occupies the entire southern end of Shiga Prefecture and is long from east to west, with an area of 481.62 square kilometres. At its eastern end the southern ridge of the Suzuka Mountains, with an elevation of 1,000 metres, runs from north-east to south-west and forms the boundary with Mie Prefecture; the highest point of Kōka is Mount Amagoi in this range. It borders Iga, Kameyama, Komono, Suzuka and Yokkaichi in Mie Prefecture, three municipalities in Kyoto Prefecture, and six others in Shiga. The climate is humid subtropical, with warm summers, cool winters and light or no snowfall, and an annual rainfall of 1,673 mm.

Kōka was part of the ancient province of Ōmi. During the Sengoku period it was an ikki, a league effectively self-governed by local ninja families. In the Edo period it became a centre of the Kōga-ryū school of ninjutsu, in rivalry with the Iga-ryū. The area lay on the route of the Tōkaidō highway connecting Kyoto with Edo. Minakuchi-juku was both a post station and the castle town of Minakuchi Domain, which ruled parts of the area during the Edo period.

The village of Minakuchi was established on 1 April 1889 in Kōka District with the creation of the modern municipalities, and was raised to town status on 18 August 1894. On 1 October 2004 Minakuchi merged with the towns of Kōka, Kōnan, Shigaraki and Tsuchiyama, all of Kōka District, to form the present city.

Kōka has a mayor-council government with a directly elected mayor and a city council of 24 members. It is traditionally known for ceramics, most notably Shigaraki ware, as well as agriculture and forestry, and its light manufacturing is concentrated in pharmaceuticals. It is served by the JR West Kusatsu Line, the Ōmi Railway and the Shigaraki Kōgen Railway, and by the Shin-Meishin Expressway and National Route 1. Its sights include the Miho Museum, Minakuchi Castle, Minakuchi-juku and Tsuchiyama-juku, and two national historic sites: the site of Shigaraki Palace and the Tarumi Saiō Tongū Site.
kokand: Kokand lies at the south-western edge of the Fergana Valley, 228 km south-east of Tashkent. It stands at the crossroads of the two main ancient routes into the valley, one leading north-west over the mountains to Tashkent and the other west through Khujand, which has made it the valley's main transport hub. Its name belongs to the family of Central Asian city names ending in kand, meaning a city in Sogdian and other Iranic languages, and one reading takes it to mean good city. The city is nicknamed the City of Winds.

Excavations at Muyi Mubarak, Tepakurgan and Eski Kurgan show that part of the city's territory was used for irrigated agriculture not later than the 7th century BCE. The settlement appeared not later than the second half of the 2nd century BCE as the centre of the Sokh oasis, within the confederal state of Fergana that Chinese annals call Dayuan. Arab geographers of the 10th century, al-Istakhri and Ibn Haukal, mention a city called Khavakand or Khokand. It lay on the Silk Road, and the Mongols destroyed it in the 13th century.

The present city began as a fort in 1732, on the site of an older fortress called Eski-Kurgan. In 1740 it became the capital of an Uzbek kingdom, the Khanate of Kokand, which reached as far as Kyzylorda in the west and Bishkek in the north-east. Kokand was also the main religious centre of the Fergana Valley, with more than 300 mosques. The palace of Khudayar Khan, built between 1863 and 1874, was described by the American diplomat Eugene Schulyer as much larger than any other palace in Central Asia.

Imperial Russian forces under Mikhail Skobelev captured the city, which became part of Russian Turkistan. In 1917 and 1918 it was the capital for 72 days of the anti-Bolshevik Provisional Government of Autonomous Turkistan, known as the Kokand Autonomy. In September 1918 the Bolsheviks burned the city and killed over ten thousand of its people in their campaign against the Basmachi movement. In the 1920s Kokand was included in the Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic.

Kokand is a district-level city in Fergana Region of Uzbekistan, with about 322,100 people in 2022. The Juma Mosque, built between 1812 and 1818 by Muhammad Umar Khan, has a 100 m long iwan on 98 carved columns. The Amin Beg Madrassah dates from the 1830s, and the Narbutabey Madrassah, built in the 1790s, holds the tomb of Muhammad Umar Khan and his wife, the poet Nodira. Nineteen rooms of Khudayar Khan's palace survive, the Soviets having demolished most of it.
kokoda-track-campaign: After the fall of Singapore many Australians feared an invasion of the mainland. The 8th Division had been lost or broken in Malaya, Ambon, Timor and Rabaul, and Prime Minister John Curtin brought the 6th and 7th Divisions home from the Middle East against Winston Churchill's wish to send them to Burma. Following the Battle of the Coral Sea, the Japanese 17th Army at Rabaul planned to take Port Moresby overland, relying on pre-war reports of a road from Kokoda. The task went to the South Seas Detachment under Major General Tomitarō Horii, who doubted it could be supplied but did not press his objection.

Japanese troops landed near Gona on the evening of 21 July 1942 and pushed inland against Maroubra Force, made up of four platoons of the 39th Battalion and men of the Papuan Infantry Battalion. Kokoda and its airfield fell on 29 July, and the 39th Battalion's commander, Owen, was mortally wounded. The Australians were driven back through Isurava and Eora Creek, and the 21st Brigade narrowly escaped capture at Mission Ridge and Brigade Hill from 6 to 8 September. Brigadier Kenneth Eather's 25th Brigade halted the advance at Ioribaiwa and withdrew to Imita Ridge.

Within sight of Port Moresby, the Japanese, who had outrun their supplies and were ordered back after reverses at Guadalcanal, withdrew on 26 September. Pursuing Australians met strong prepared positions at Templeton's Crossing and Eora Village from 11 to 28 October, reoccupied Kokoda unopposed and won the battle around Oivi and Gorari from 4 to 11 November. Horii drowned in the flooded Kumusi River, and by 16 November two brigades of the 7th Division had crossed it at Wairopi to advance with United States troops on the beachheads.

The Japanese at Buna–Gona held out until 22 January 1943. About 6,000 Japanese fought in the forward areas of the track, and all Australians captured in the campaign were executed. The jungle fighting led to wide changes in Australian doctrine, training and equipment, and a crisis of command under General Douglas MacArthur and General Sir Thomas Blamey cost three senior officers their posts. Damien Parer's newsreel Kokoda Front Line! won an Oscar, and the campaign entered the Anzac legend as a battle that saved Australia, though the idea that the Australians were far outnumbered has since been shown to be wrong.
kokopo: Under the German New Guinea administration, which controlled the area from 1884 and formally until 1919, Kokopo was known as Herbertshöhe, or Herbert's Heights. The name honoured Herbert, the eldest son of the German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. The settlement was the capital of German New Guinea until 1910.

Rabaul, the provincial capital, lay about 20 km to the north-west by the Kokopo–Rabaul Highway. The capital was moved from Rabaul to Kokopo in 1994, when the volcanoes Tavurvur and Vulcan erupted. Kokopo's population then grew more than sixfold, from 3,150 in 1990 to 20,262 in 2000, while the remains of Rabaul came to hold around 4,000 inhabitants, down from over 17,000 before the eruption.

Kokopo is administered under the Kokopo/Vunamami Urban LLG. It has a tropical rainforest climate, with heavy rainfall and hot temperatures through the year. Rabaul Airport, also called Tokua Airport, a domestic airport, lies a few kilometres east of the town.

The PNG Hunters, a rugby league club founded in 2013, are based in Kokopo and play at Kalabond Oval; their colours are red, black and gold. On 29 March 2015 a strong earthquake of a preliminary magnitude of at least 7.5 was recorded near Kokopo and a tsunami warning was issued. In the same year a research and conservation project was suggested to study the spinner dolphins living around Kokopo beach, a population that might be threatened if a new port for larger shipping were built.
kokstad: The town lies on the outer slopes of the Drakensberg at 1,302 m above sea level, with Mount Currie rising behind it to 2,224 m. Stad is the Dutch and Afrikaans word for city. It stands about 10 km from the Eastern Cape border on the N2 national road, which runs east to Port Shepstone and Durban and south to Mthatha. The surrounding countryside is mostly cattle farms, and the town is a centre for cheese and other dairy products.

The Griqua had split at Griquatown in 1820, and one section under Adam Kok III moved first to Philippolis. Facing growing conflict with the Voortrekkers, who took Griqua land on lease and refused to return it, several hundred Griquas crossed the Drakensberg by Ongeluks Nek in 1861 into a region known as Nomansland. They arrived eighteen months later exhausted, most of their livestock dead, and named the mountain after Sir Walter Currie, who had supported their settlement. Each Griqua man could secure a farm of 3,000 acres, but most sold their land cheaply to white settlers.

In 1869 the Reverend William Dower agreed to found a mission for the Griqua on condition that they resettle on the banks of the Mzimhlava river. In 1874 the trading store of George Brisley and Donald Strachan, Strachan and Co, issued trade tokens that circulated as money across a wide region, described as the first indigenous currency of South Africa. Adam Kok died after a fall from a cart in 1875. After East Griqualand passed to the Cape Colony, the town gained its first hotel, The Royal, and in 1881 a newspaper, the Kokstad Advertiser, both started by an African-American. It became a municipality in 1892, and in 1904 a third of its 2903 people were Griquas.

The town was transferred to Natal province in 1978 and lies in the Harry Gwala District Municipality of KwaZulu-Natal, with just over 50,000 people. Its heritage sites include the Adam Kok Monument, a cast-iron bandstand of 1912 declared a national monument in 1983, and the old town hall, while the East Griqualand Museum is devoted chiefly to Griqua history.
kokura: During the Edo period (1603 to 1868) the Hosokawa and Ogasawara clans were the daimyo at Kokura Castle. Hosokawa Tadaoki hoped to create at Kokura a town that resembled Kyoto, including its grid-like layout. The swordsman Miyamoto Musashi, author of The Book of Five Rings and founder of the Hyoho Niten Ichi-ryu school, noted for its use of two swords, lived in Kokura Castle briefly in 1634 under the patronage of the Ogasawara and Hosokawa clans.

After the end of the Tokugawa Shogunate Kokura was the seat of government of Kokura Prefecture. When the municipal system of cities, towns and villages was introduced, Kokura Town was one of 25 towns in the prefecture, which later merged with Fukuoka Prefecture. Kokura became a city, Kokura City, in 1900.

On the morning of 9 August 1945 Kokura was the primary target of the atomic bomb known as Fat Man, but the city was obscured. The reconnaissance missions of the day before had also mistaken Kokura for the neighbouring city of Yahata. Major Charles Sweeney, the mission commander, had orders to drop the bomb by sight and not by radar, so he diverted to the secondary target, Nagasaki. The aircraft did fly over Kokura and came very close to carrying out the drop there. The meteorologist Tetsuya Theodore Fujita lived in Kokura during the war.

In 1963 Kokura merged with four other cities to form Kitakyushu. It made up the Kokura ward of the new city until 1974, when it was divided into Kokura Kita ward in the north and Kokura Minami ward in the south.

Kokura is the centre of the city of Kitakyushu, and Kokura station is the penultimate station on the southbound San'yo Shinkansen line, which is owned by JR West. The main dojo of Miyamoto Musashi's sword school stands in the city. The Gion Festival of Kokura, called the Gion of Drums, celebrates the life of the local folk hero Muhomatsu. The writers Matsumoto Seicho and Mori Ogai are counted among its notable residents.
kolkata: Kolkata lies on the eastern bank of the Hooghly River in the lower Ganges Delta, at an elevation of 1.5 to 9 metres. Much of the city was originally a wetland, reclaimed over the decades to accommodate a growing population. Excavations at Chandraketugarh, 35 kilometres to the north, show that the region has been inhabited for over two millennia. The name derives from Kôlikata, the Bengali name of one of three villages that predated the British, the others being Sutanuti and Govindapur. One explanation is that it varies Kalikshetra, the area of the goddess Kali.

The earliest mention of the village of Kalikata is in Bipradas Pipilai's Manasa Vijay of 1495. The three villages were part of an estate belonging to the Sabarna Roy Choudhury family of zamindars, sold to the East India Company in 1698. The city's recorded history began in 1690 with the arrival of the Company. Job Charnock is often regarded as its founder, but in 2003 the Calcutta High Court ruled, in response to a petition, that the city has no founder.

The Company developed the area into Fort William. Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah occupied the fort in 1756 but was defeated at the Battle of Plassey in 1757. Under Company and then crown rule Calcutta was the de facto capital of India until 1911 and, after London, the second largest city of the British Empire. It was the centre of bureaucracy, politics, law, education, science and the arts, was associated with the Bengali Renaissance and was a hotbed of the Indian nationalist movement. The first newspaper in India, the Bengal Gazette, began publishing there in 1780.

The partition of Bengal in 1947 affected the city's fortunes, and Hindu refugees from East Bengal arrived in the following decades. In 1971 it hosted Bangladesh's government-in-exile. Its official name, Calcutta, was changed to Kolkata in 2001.

Kolkata is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of West Bengal, with a city population of about 4.5 million and a metropolitan area of over 15 million. Its landmarks include the Victoria Memorial and the Howrah Bridge. The University of Calcutta was the first modern university in South Asia, and the Port of Kolkata is India's oldest operating port. The city's celebrations of the festival of Durga Puja are recognised by UNESCO.
kolkhoz: The word kolkhoz is a contraction of the Russian for 'collective farm'. Soon after the first Soviet state farms were created in 1918 the first collective farms were organized. There were three main types: partnerships for joint cultivation, in which only labour was shared; agricultural artels, the commonest form, which pooled land, equipment and livestock but let members keep a plot and small livestock for themselves; and agricultural communes, the most radical form, in which even housing and everyday consumption were shared. By 1938, as a result of complete collectivization, the artel was the only official form.

The Standard Charter, which had the force of law from the early 1930s, described the kolkhoz as a voluntary cooperative managed by its members. In practice the general assembly and elected management only approved the plans and targets of district and provincial authorities, and members had no right to leave freely or to take their share of assets with them. By July 1929 a large kolkhoz of 200 to 400 households was usually divided into work units of 15 to 30 households, headed by a brigade leader.

A member, a kolkhoznik, received a share of the produce according to the number of labour days worked, and many farms paid no cash. The farm had to sell its grain to the state at fixed prices. In 1948 the government charged wholesalers 335 rubles for 100 kilograms of rye and paid the kolkhoz roughly 8. The difference was a major source of state income, used to buy foreign machinery for industrialisation. Private plots of about one acre were only 3.9 percent of the sown land in 1938, yet in 1937 they gave 21.5 percent of gross agricultural output.

After the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991 the number of kolkhozes and sovkhozes declined rapidly from 1992, and other corporate forms gained ground. Surveys in the 1990s found that many of the new corporate farms still behaved like the old kolkhozes. In the Transcaucasian and Central Asian states the kolkhoz almost disappeared. Turkmenistan reorganized its kolkhozes into peasant associations by decree in 1995, and Uzbekistan renamed them shirkats in its Land Code of 1998.
kollam: Kollam, formerly Quilon, lies at the southern end of the Malabar Coast on the banks of Ashtamudi Lake, 71 kilometres north-west of Thiruvananthapuram. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities of India, with evidence of habitation from the megalithic period, and a maritime entrepôt for millennia. Arabs, Phoenicians, Chinese, Ethiopians, Syrians, Jews, Chaldeans and Romans all traded at its port. It was called Koolam in Arabic, Coulão in Portuguese and Desinganadu in ancient Tamil literature, and the name may derive from koyillam, a compound meaning royal palace and noble house, or from a Sanskrit word for pepper.

In the ninth century the Persian merchant Sulaiman al-Tajir found Kollam the only Indian port visited by huge Chinese junks. Two East Syriac bishops, Mar Sabor and Mar Proth, settled there with their followers, and the port is said to have been founded at Tangasseri in 825 under the king of Venadu. The Malayalam calendar, the Kollam era or Kollavarsham, was introduced at meetings in the city in 825 CE.

Envoys of Yuan China came in 1280 to establish relations with the local ruler, and Marco Polo visited in 1275. Ibn Battuta counted Kollam among the five Indian ports he saw. The Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows it as Columbo, a Christian city under a Christian king. A Pandya ruler, Maravarman Kulasekara Pandyan I, fought a war in Venadu and captured the city in the 13th century.

The Portuguese set up a trading centre at Tangasseri in 1502, centred on pepper, and built St Thomas Fort there in 1517. The Dutch East India Company took the city in 1661. The Thambiran Vanakkam, printed in Tamil at Kollam on 20 October 1578, was the first book published in an Indian language. In 1809 forces of Travancore under Velu Thampi Dalawa fought the East India Company at the Battle of Quilon and lost in six hours.

Kollam is the seat of the administrative offices of Kollam district and a trading city known for cashew processing and coir. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Quilon is described as the first diocese in India, and the Infant Jesus Cathedral at Tangasseri, founded by the Portuguese in 1614, is its pro-cathedral. Excavations at the Kollam port premises since 2014 have found Chinese porcelain and coins that show trade links with China.
kolobrzeg: Kołobrzeg lies on the Parsęta River on the south coast of the Baltic Sea, in the West Pomeranian Voivodeship, and is the seat of Kołobrzeg County. Its Polish name means 'by the shore'. The first Slavic settlements near the site, centred on local salt deposits, date to the 6th and 7th centuries. In the late 9th century Pomeranian tribes built a fortified settlement at the place now called Budzistowo, where salt was boiled in salt pans and used to preserve herring for trade. A market and a tavern, forum et taberna, are mentioned in 1140.

The chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg names the see of Kołobrzeg, set up at the Congress of Gniezno in 1000 by Bolesław Chrobry and Emperor Otto III. The missionary work of Bishop Reinbern did not last, and the Pomeranians revolted in 1005. Bolesław III Wrymouth took the stronghold in the winter of 1107/08, and Otto of Bamberg later led the Christianization of the area.

German settlers founded a new town a few kilometres from the old stronghold, which Duke Wartislaw III of Pomerania chartered under Lübeck law on 23 May 1255; the old site became a village called the Old Town. In 1276 the bishops of Kammin became lords of the town and moved their residence there. It joined the Hanseatic League in 1361 and passed to Brandenburg-Prussia under the Treaty of Westphalia in 1648. From mid-March to 2 July 1807 French forces and Polish insurgents besieged it, and the defence led by Lieutenant-Colonel August von Gneisenau held until the Treaty of Tilsit ended the war.

Soviet and Polish forces fought German troops for the town between 4 and 18 March 1945. German naval forces evacuated most of the inhabitants and many refugees in Operation Hannibal. On 18 March the Polish Army re-enacted Poland's Wedding to the Sea. After the war the town became part of Poland, its remaining German inhabitants were expelled, and Polish settlers came in, many of them displaced from the east.

Kołobrzeg is a port and spa city of about 43,000 inhabitants. It became a popular Baltic spa town in the late 19th century and is now a seaside resort and tourist destination. The Museum of Polish Arms and a museum of the city's history stand in the town, and the Millennium Memorial, unveiled to mark the year 1000, stands outside the Basilica Cathedral.
kolomna: Kolomna is a historic city in Moscow Oblast, at the confluence of the Moskva and Oka rivers, 114 kilometres south-east of Moscow by rail. The 2010 census counted 144,589 people. The old city stands on a sharp bend of the Moskva, and its name may come from an Old Russian term meaning on the bend of the river. It lies on three rivers and has passenger and cargo berths, and it is on the Ryazan line of the Moscow railway.

Kolomna was first mentioned in 1177, but the latest archaeological surveys suggest that it was founded between 1140 and 1160. In January 1238 it was destroyed by the Mongol invasion. In 1301 it became the first town incorporated into the Moscow Principality. The statue of Dmitry Donskoy in front of the kremlin commemorates the gathering of his troops at Kolomna before the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380.

Like some other ancient Russian cities, Kolomna has a kremlin, a citadel of red brick like the better-known one in Moscow. The stone Kolomna Kremlin was built from 1525 to 1531 under the Russian Tsar Vasily III and formed part of the Great Abatis Border. Much of its wall was removed in the eighteenth century and its materials used for other public buildings, but a stretch of wall, several towers and some interior buildings survive, and a museum is housed inside.

The city's arms were granted by Empress Catherine II, who was influenced by the similar sound of the name of the Colonna family of Rome. The resemblance has no historical basis. Because of the production of sensitive missile components, Kolomna was a closed city until 1994.

Kolomna is the administrative centre of Kolomensky District, though it is not part of it, and it is incorporated as a city under oblast jurisdiction. It is not listed among the cities of the Golden Ring, despite its kremlin and its many well-preserved churches and monasteries. Among its attractions are Kolomna Cathedral, the New Golutvin Monastery, the Bobrenev Monastery and the Old Golutvin Monastery near the confluence of the rivers. The Church of John the Baptist is one of the oldest surviving buildings in the Moscow region and can be dated to the 14th century. A museum is devoted to pastila, a local fruit candy.
kolyma: Kolyma, or Kolyma Krai, was never formally defined and was split over time among various administrative units. It is bounded on the north by the East Siberian Sea and the Arctic Ocean and on the south by the Sea of Okhotsk, and it includes the Kolyma Mountains. Part of it lies within the Arctic Circle. Winters last up to six months, with average winter temperatures from −19 to −38 °C, and permafrost and tundra cover much of the land. There are rich reserves of gold, silver, tin, tungsten, mercury, copper, antimony, coal, oil and peat. The Evens, Koryaks, Yakuts, Chukchis, Chuvans, Yukaghirs and Itelmens traditionally lived from fishing on the coast or reindeer herding in the Kolyma valley.

Gold and platinum were found in the early 20th century. During the first five-year plan of 1928 to 1932 the Soviet Union needed capital, and a government agency, Dalstroy, the Far North Construction Trust, was founded on 13 November 1931 to exploit the gold. Eduard Berzin, its first director, arrived on 4 February 1932 with the first ten prisoners. Prisoners came in large numbers, notably from the anti-kulak campaign and the drive to collectivize the peasantry, and they built the town of Magadan and the Kolyma Highway, known as the Road of Bones. About 80 camps eventually lay across the taiga. Prisoners crossed the Sea of Okhotsk in crowded ships, and thousands died in transit.

The inmate headcount rose from 30,000 in 1934 to over 70,000 in 1937 and reached 199,726 in 1952, the highest ever. Berzin was shot in 1938 during the Great Purges. The camps used mostly free labour after 1954, a general amnesty came in 1956, and Dalstroy was liquidated in 1957. Estimates of the death toll from 1930 to the mid-1950s range from 250,000 to over a million, and no final figure is possible. Varlam Shalamov's Kolyma Tales and Yevgenia Ginzburg's Journey into the Whirlwind are among the survivors' accounts.

The Magadan Oblast was established in 1953, and industrial gold mining began in 1958. Today the region roughly comprises Magadan Oblast, north-eastern areas of Yakutia and the Bilibinsky District of Chukotka. Magadan, its principal town, is a port on the Sea of Okhotsk that stays open year-round with icebreakers. The Mask of Sorrow monument in Magadan commemorates those who died in the forced-labour camps.
komi-peoples: The Komi are a Permian people living around the basins of the Vychegda, Pechora and Kama rivers. Linguistic reconstruction suggests that the prehistoric Permians split into two peoples during the first millennium BCE, the Komi and the Udmurts. By the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the Komi had divided further into the Komi-Permyaks, who remained in the Kama basin, and the Komi-Zyryans, who migrated north. The name Komi is their endonym for all subgroups, first recorded by ethnographers in the eighteenth century, and comes from a Finno-Ugric word meaning man or human.

From the twelfth century Russians expanded into the Perm region, and the Komi came into contact with Novgorod, whose traders sought furs and hides. Komi dukes unified the Great Perm with its centre at the stronghold of Cherdyn. Novgorod claimed the territory but had little control and gave up its rights in 1471. In 1365 Dmitry Donskoy, prince of Moscow, gave Stephen of Perm the task of converting the region to Christianity, and the eparchy of Perm was created in 1383. Stephen also devised an alphabet for the Komi language, the Old Permic script.

Moscow seized Cherdyn in 1472, leaving the duke of Perm a vassal. The duchy lasted until 1505, when a Russian governor replaced the duke's son Matvei and Komi independence ended. Russian migrants moved into the region in growing numbers from the 1500s, and there were several Komi rebellions against Russian rule, especially after freed serfs began arriving in the 1860s. Under the Soviet Union the policy of korenizatsiya promoted Komi culture, but industrialisation damaged the traditional way of life, the purges of the 1930s devastated the Komi intelligentsia, and gulags and wartime industrialisation left the Komi a minority in their own lands.

The Komi are divided into two main groups, the northern Zyryans and the southern Permyaks, and traditionally take their subgroup names from the rivers where they live. Hunting, gathering and fishing have long been the main sources of food, and wood is the main building material in their forested lands. The Komi language belongs to the Permian branch of the Uralic family. Old Permic was used until the sixteenth century, Cyrillic from the nineteenth, and the first book printed in Komi, a vaccination manual, appeared in 1815. Most Komi myths concern shamanism and paganism, and the most widespread tell of the creation of the world through the struggle of two gods, En and Omöl'.
komnenian-dynasty: The Komnenos family was Byzantine Greek. The historian Michael Psellos reported that it came from the village of Komne in southern Thrace, a view commonly accepted by modern scholars. The first known member, Manuel Erotikos Komnenos, acquired large estates at Kastamon in Paphlagonia, which became the family stronghold. The family thus became associated with the powerful military aristocracy of Asia Minor, so that although it came from Thrace it was considered eastern. Isaac I Komnenos, his son, led a coup against Michael VI in 1057 and reigned until 1059, when courtiers pressed him to abdicate and become a monk.

The dynasty returned to the throne with Isaac's nephew Alexios I Komnenos, who married Irene Doukaina, grandniece of Constantine X Doukas. The two clans were afterwards often called Komnenodoukai. Under Alexios and his successors the empire was fairly prosperous and stable. Alexios moved the imperial palace to the Blachernae quarter of Constantinople, and much of Anatolia was recovered from the Seljuk Turks. The First Crusade crossed Byzantine territory, and the family intermarried with the ruling houses of the Principality of Antioch and the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

Alexios ruled for 37 years, his son John II for 25, and John's son Manuel I for another 37. Succession followed no fixed order, and after Manuel's reign the family fell into conspiracies. Alexios II ruled for three years, and his conqueror Andronikos I for two, before the Angelos family took the throne under Isaac II, who was dethroned and blinded by his own brother Alexios III. Andronikos executed many relatives who opposed him, and opposition to Isaac II also cost family members their lives.

Weeks before the crusaders took Constantinople in 1204, one branch fled to Paphlagonia and the Pontic Alps and founded the Empire of Trebizond. Its rulers, the Grand Komnenoi, held it until 1461, when it fell to the Ottomans, and the last emperor, David Komnenos, and his family were executed two years later by Mehmed II. Another branch, using the name Komnenos Doukas, founded the Despotate of Epirus in 1204. A renegade, Isaac Komnenos, ruled Cyprus from 1184 until Richard I of England took the island in 1191.

The Palaiologoi, a closely related family, ruled the restored empire from 1261 until 1453. John Komnenos Molyvdos, a scholar and physician who died in 1719, is often considered the last descendant. Many later claims of Komnenian descent are almost certainly fiction.
komotini: Komotini stands at 32 to 38 metres on the Thracian plain near the foothills of the Rhodope Mountains. Its history is closely tied to the Via Egnatia, the Roman road from Dyrrhachium to Constantinople. The Roman emperor Theodosius I built a small rectilinear fortress on the road at a junction with a route across the Rhodope towards Philippopolis, and an inscription on the Byzantine wall reads the building of Theodosius. Archaeological finds show a settlement from the 2nd century CE.

For most of its early life the place was overshadowed by the larger town of Mosynopolis to the west, and by the end of the 12th century it had been abandoned. The present settlement dates from 1207, when the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan destroyed Mosynopolis and its survivors took refuge inside the walls of the abandoned fortress. The Ottoman Empire conquered it between 1361 and 1362/3, apparently under Gazi Evrenos Bey, and it was known in Turkish as Gümülcine throughout the Ottoman period. Evrenos built a mosque, an imaret, a bath and shops that formed the nucleus of Islamic life in Western Thrace.

The census of 1519 counted about 2,500 people, mostly Muslims, with smaller Christian and Jewish communities. The Yeni Mosque, built in the 1600s, is the only building in Greece with Iznik tiles of the 1580s. In the 19th century the city profited from the processing and trade of tobacco, and by the 1880s it had 13,560 inhabitants.

In the Balkan Wars Bulgarian forces captured it, and it passed to the Greek army on 14 July 1913. It was briefly the capital of the Provisional Government of Western Thrace, but the Treaty of Bucharest returned it to Bulgaria, and Greece received it after the First World War. During the Second World War it was under Bulgarian control, and the Bulgarian authorities arrested 863 Jews of the city and sent them to Treblinka, from which 28 survived.

Komotini is the capital of the region of East Macedonia and Thrace and of Rhodope, and its municipality had 65,243 inhabitants in 2021. The Democritus University of Thrace was founded there in 1973. The Muslim minority of Western Thrace, which dates from the Ottoman period, was exempted from the Greek-Turkish population exchange of 1922 to 1923.
komuch: After the revolt of the Czechoslovak Legion, Ivan Brushvit persuaded the legion to occupy Samara on 8 June 1918, and a committee of five Socialist Revolutionaries, members of the dissolved Constituent Assembly, Vladimir Volsky as chairman with Brushvit, Prokopiy Klimushkin, Boris Fortunatov and Ivan Nesterov, took civil and military power in the city and province. The name Komuch is formed from the initials of its Russian title. It proclaimed itself the highest authority in Russia, acting for the Constituent Assembly until a new assembly met, and its executive was a council of department heads led by Yevgeny Rogovsky.

Komuch announced the reinstatement of democratic freedoms. It set an eight-hour working day, permitted factory committees, trade unions and congresses of workers and peasants, revived city dumas and zemstva, abrogated Soviet decrees and returned industry and banks to their former owners. While speaking of the socialisation of land, it allowed landowners to recover confiscated land and harvest the winter crops, and sent expeditions into the countryside to protect landowners and later to mobilise its People's Army. The committee grew as deputies arrived in Samara, reaching 96 members by the end of September 1918.

From June to August its authority spread into the provinces of Simbirsk, Kazan, Ufa and Saratov, but in September the People's Army suffered a series of defeats by the Red Army. During the State Conference at Ufa, held from 8 to 23 September with the Provisional Siberian Government and about 170 delegates, Komuch lost Kazan on 10 September and Simbirsk two days later. The conference set up the short-lived Provisional All-Russian Government, and after Admiral Aleksandr Kolchak's coup in November 1918 General Vladimir Kappel dissolved its remaining institutions.
konark-sun-temple: Konark, called Kainapara in Indian texts, was a significant trading port by the early centuries of the common era, and a sun temple is thought to have stood in the area by at least the 9th century. The present temple is attributed to Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, who reigned from 1238 to 1264. Planning and construction records written in Sanskrit in the Odia script survive on palm leaf manuscripts found in a village in the 1960s, which is unusual for a Hindu temple. The king sponsored the work, and Shiva Samantaraya Mahapatra oversaw it.
It was built near an older Surya temple, whose sanctum sculpture was re-consecrated in the new temple. Copper plate inscriptions of the era call the Konark temple the great cottage.

The temple takes the form of the chariot of Surya, who in Vedic iconography rides across the sky behind seven horses, driven by the charioteer Aruna. The seven horses are named after the seven metres of Sanskrit prosody, and the chariot's twelve pairs of wheels correspond to the twelve months of the Hindu calendar. The wheels are nearly 3.7 metres across and also serve as sundials. The temple faces east, so that the first rays of the sunrise strike its entrance. It was built from three kinds of stone: chlorite, laterite and khondalite.

The complex had a main sanctuary, the deul, which was estimated at some 70 metres high, and in front of it the jagamohana or assembly hall, about 39 metres tall, which still stands. The dance hall, the Nata mandira, and the dining hall also survive. Its walls carry reliefs of deities, musicians, animals, scenes of daily life and couples in erotic scenes. A pillar to Aruna that stood before the eastern stairs was moved in the last quarter of the 18th century to the Lion's Gate of the Jagannath temple in Puri.

Why the temple fell is uncertain. An inscription of 1384 shows it was complete and in worship, and a text of the 16th century describes it as prosperous, with no mention of ruins. Some attribute damage to attacks by Muslim armies between the 15th and 17th centuries, among them one by the general Kalapahar. A Maratha holy man later found it abandoned and overgrown. The main tower collapsed, leaving the sanctum without a roof.

Removal of stones was forbidden in 1803, but later some stones and sculptures were taken to Puri and, in 1894, thirteen sculptures to the Indian Museum in Calcutta. In 1903 the jagamohana was sealed and filled with sand to prevent its collapse. The Mayadevi temple was discovered in 1909, and the temple was made a World Heritage Site in 1984. European sailors had called it the Black Pagoda from as early as 1676.
konavle: Konavle is a municipality and small Dalmatian subregion southeast of Dubrovnik, in Dubrovnik-Neretva County. It is a narrow field between the Sniježnica mountain and the Adriatic Sea, running from the coastal town of Cavtat to the Montenegrin border at Prevlaka. Only Cavtat, the largest settlement, and the southernmost village, Molunat, lie on the coast; the other 30 villages are inland. Sniježnica, at 1,234 metres, is the highest point of the county. The municipality had 8,577 inhabitants in 2011, of whom 97.1 per cent were Croats, and its historical inhabitants were called Canalesi.

The area has been inhabited since the Paleolithic and Neolithic. In the 5th and 4th centuries BCE the Illyrian tribes of the Pleraei and Ardiaei settled there, and in the 2nd century BCE the Romans developed a trade and maritime centre at the site of the Greek colony of Epidaurus. The name comes from the Latin canalis and refers to irrigation canals that brought water from the spring at Vodovađa to Epidaurus. Remains include a Roman aqueduct, villae rusticae and a Mithraic monument at Močići. In the Middle Ages Konavle was part of Travunia, at various times a vassal of Serbian, Dioclean and Bosnian rulers, and it has necropolises of Bogomil stećak tombstones.

At the start of the 15th century powerful Bosnian lords held Konavle: Sandalj Hranić in the east and the brothers Petar and Radoslav Pavlović in the west. The Republic of Ragusa bought the eastern part from Sandalj on 24 June 1419 and the western part, with Cavtat and Obod, from Radoslav Pavlović a few years later. Ragusa made it a feudal estate governed by a count seated at Pridvorje, elected by its Grand Council for six months and later a year. A First Konavle War followed from 1430 to 1433. In 1427 Ragusa set out to eradicate Bogomilism, and Franciscans restored Catholicism, converting the whole population.

Konavle remained part of the Republic of Ragusa, as its largest granary, until the republic was abolished in 1808. After a short French occupation it was ravaged by Montenegrin and Russian invaders, and after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 it passed to Austrian rule. A railway opened there in 1901. In the Croatian War of Independence the region was occupied by Yugoslav Army forces from Montenegro from October 1991 to May 1992.

Dubrovnik's airport lies near the Konavle village of Čilipi. Remains from the Ragusan period include the Count's Palace in Pridvorje and the Soko Tower at Dunave. The painter Vlaho Bukovac and the jurist Baltazar Bogišić come from Konavle.
kondapalli: Kondapalli lies to the west of Vijayawada in NTR district, and its closest neighbouring locality is Ibrahimpatnam. In the 18th century the town was known by the name Mustafanagar. Kondapalli Fort, also called Kondapalli Kota, stands to the west of the town. Around it lies the Kondapalli Reserve Forest, one of the last remaining pristine forests of the Krishna district, which covers about 30,000 acres (120 km2) of varied ground and is home to leopards, wild dogs, jackals, wild boar and wolves. The state government also planned a zoological park at the village.

The town's best-known craft is the making of Kondapalli Toys, known locally as Kondapalli bommalu. Local artisans chisel them from light local softwoods called Tella Poniki and paint them with vegetable dyes and bright enamel colours. Among the most popular are sets of the Dasavatarams, the ten incarnations of the god Vishnu, elephants carrying an ambari, palanquin-bearers carrying a bride and bridegroom, a toddy tapper and sets of village craftsmen, as well as many kinds of animals. A swinging doll of papier mache is a favourite with many buyers.

Kondapalli is a municipality and an industrial suburb of Vijayawada, with an industrial estate of about 450 acres (1.8 km2) that supports more than 800 enterprises. The Dr Narla Tata Rao Thermal Power Station, also called the Vijayawada Thermal Power Station, stands between Ibrahimpatnam and Kondapalli, and the town is a hub for the storage, bottling and transport of petroleum products. Kondapalli railway station lies on the Kazipet–Vijayawada section of the South Central Railway zone, and NH 30 passes through the town.
kongo-language: Kongo, or Kikongo, is a tonal Bantu language with roughly seven million native speakers and an estimated five million more who use it as a second language. It is spoken in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and Angola. Malcolm Guthrie placed it in the group H10, the Kongo languages. Not all its varieties are mutually intelligible, and its grammar rests on a system of 18 noun classes marked by prefixes. Kikongo was the language of the Kingdom of Kongo before the Portuguese Crown created Angola in 1575, and the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 divided the rest of the kingdom into three territories. The creole Kituba, also called Kikongo ya Leta, is based on it.

Kongo was the earliest Bantu language written in Latin characters. A catechism prepared under the authority of the Jesuit Diogo Gomes, born in Kongo in 1557 to Portuguese parents, has not survived. In 1624 another Portuguese Jesuit, Mateus Cardoso, edited and published a Kongo translation of the catechism compiled by Marcos Jorge. Its preface says that Kongo teachers from São Salvador did the translation, probably with part of the work by Félix do Espírito Santo.

A dictionary of about 10,000 words followed around 1648 for Capuchin missionaries. Its principal author was Manuel Robredo, a Kongo secular priest who took the name Francisco de São Salvador on becoming a Capuchin. French Catholic missionaries on the Loango coast produced further dictionaries in the 1780s. British Baptist missionaries who arrived in 1879 developed a modern orthography, and in 1887 W. Holman Bentley published a Dictionary and Grammar of the Kongo Language, crediting the help of Nlemvo. With João Lemvo he completed a Christian Bible in 1905.

Many of the Africans taken captive and sold across the Atlantic spoke Kikongo, and creolised forms of the language survive in the ritual speech of Afro-American religions in Brazil, Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Haiti and Suriname. Kongo is also one of the sources of the Gullah language of the American Southeast and a major source of Palenquero in Colombia. Southern Black American English words such as goober, from nguba, meaning peanut, and mojo come from Kongo.
kongsberg: Kongsberg lies on the river Numedalslågen at the entrance to the valley of Numedal, in Buskerud county. The river divides the town and has three waterfalls within it. The name was formerly spelled Konningsberg and means King's Mountain. According to official records, silver was first found in the summer of 1623 by the shepherd children Helga Verp and Jacob Grosvold, although signs of earlier silver mining show that deposits of precious metals were already known.

To build the mining company, Christian IV of Denmark and Norway invited engineers and other specialists from Saxony and the Harz region. In the first years nearly half of the population were German immigrants, and German was used in mining business and in religious services. The Germans brought the Knappschaft, a guild-like association of miners that provided free medical assistance, a pension plan and a Saturday break, and the German mining law gave the town its own jurisdiction. In 1636 the mines employed 1,370 Germans and 1,600 Norwegians; by 1648 there were 1,500 Germans and 2,400 Norwegians. Gunpowder was officially introduced in 1681.

Silver from Kongsberg helped to pay for the wars of Denmark-Norway against Sweden, and the Royal Mint moved there from Akershus in 1686. At the peak of mining in the early eighteenth century, the mines and related industries contributed about 10 per cent of the gross national product of Denmark-Norway. The ore also held gold, copper, cobalt, lead-zinc and fluorite, and roughly 15,750 tonnes of silver were taken out between 1623 and 1957.

In 1716, during the Great Northern War, the town was the main target of the advance of Karl XII. The 1769 census counted about 4,000 mine workers among 8,000 inhabitants, making Kongsberg the second largest town in Norway after Bergen.

Output then fell, and a fire in 1810 destroyed 56 houses. The government set up a defence industry in 1814 to complement mining, and by 1835 the population had declined to 3,540. Kongsberg received its royal charter of trade in 1802 and became a municipality on 1 January 1838.

The silver mines are now a museum and the main tourist attraction, and the mint still produces Norwegian coins. Kongsberg Church, inaugurated in 1761, holds about 2,400 people and has a baroque organ built by Gottfried Heinrich Gloger. The defence industry of 1814 grew into a high-technology cluster, and the town is known for its ski jumpers, among them Birger Ruud.
kongu-nadu: The name combines two Tamil words, Kongu country. Kongu may come from the konganam flowers worn as garlands by the early Kongars, or from kangu, edge or boundary, since the area lay on the borders of the ancient Tamil kingdoms; it was also called Kongu Mandalam. The Western Ghats run down its western side and meet the Eastern Ghats in the Nilgiri mountains, and most of the region lies on the Deccan Plateau, which slopes from west to east. The Kaveri, Bhavani, Amaravati and Noyyal rivers rise in the Western Ghats and flow east, and the Palghat Gap links the region to the west coast.

Excavations at Kodumanal on the Noyyal show settlement from the 4th century BCE, and the Patiṟṟuppattu of the 1st century CE describes it as a thriving industrial and commercial centre. The region was the eastern entrance to the Palakkad Gap on the trade route called Rajakesari Peruvazhi, which ran from Muziris on the west coast to Arikamedu on the east. Early Tamil Brahmi writing has been found on coins, seals and rings from the Amaravati river bed near Karuvur, which was the Chera capital when the Cheras ruled the region between the 1st and 4th centuries.

The Pandyas made incursions in the 7th century, and Rashtrakutas and Western Gangas held parts of it. Under Rajaraja I the whole region came under Chola influence in the late 10th century; it was directly ruled by the Imperial Cholas until 1064 and then autonomously by the Kongu Cholas, who bore the title Konattar.

Later came the Pandyas, the Hoysalas, the Delhi Sultanate and, in the 15th century, the Vijayanagara Empire. After its fall Nayak governors divided the region into 24 palayams.
