Mysore gained it in the late 18th century, and after the defeat of Tipu Sultan and the Polygar Wars the East India Company annexed it to the Madras Presidency in the early 19th century; in the Second Polygar War of 1801 Dheeran Chinnamalai fought the Company here.

The region covers roughly 60,895 square kilometres of western and north-western Tamil Nadu, with a population of over 27.4 million at the 2011 census; its borders have never been officially defined. Coimbatore, Tiruppur and Salem are the largest urban areas, and most people speak Kongu Tamil, a dialect of Tamil. Mudumalai, established in 1940 as the first national park in India, lies within it.
konigsberg: Königsberg was preceded by a Sambian, or Old Prussian, fort called Twangste and by several Old Prussian settlements, among them the fishing village and port of Lipnick. During the Teutonic Order's conquest of the Sambians in 1255 Twangste was destroyed and replaced by a new fortress, Conigsberg, meaning King's Hill, which honoured King Ottokar II of Bohemia, who paid for its erection during the Prussian Crusade. In Polish the city is called Królewiec and in Lithuanian Karaliaučius.

Through the preaching of Georg von Polenz, Bishop of Samland, Königsberg became predominantly Lutheran. In 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg secularised the Teutonic Knights' remaining territories in Prussia and converted to Lutheranism. By paying feudal homage to his uncle, King Sigismund I of Poland, he became the first duke of the Duchy of Prussia, a fief of Poland, and the city became an influential centre of the Reformation. On 18 January 1701 Elector Frederick III was crowned Frederick I, King in Prussia, in Königsberg Castle, although Berlin and Potsdam were the main royal residences.

Plague killed 9,368 people, roughly a quarter of the population, between September 1709 and April 1710. Russian forces occupied Königsberg without resistance in January 1758 during the Seven Years' War, and by the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 5 May 1762 Russia gave up its claim. After the First Partition of Poland the city became in 1773 the capital of the province of East Prussia. By 1800 it had 60,000 inhabitants, including a garrison of 7,000. On 9 November 1918 about 1,000 revolutionary soldiers occupied the military command centres and set up a soviet-style workers' and soldiers' council. Under the Potsdam Agreement of 1 August 1945 the city became part of the Soviet Union pending a peace settlement.

The city is now Kaliningrad, renamed in 1946 in honour of the Soviet head of state Mikhail Kalinin, and is the capital of the Kaliningrad Oblast, a Russian exclave bordered by Lithuania to the north and Poland to the south. It was largely repopulated with Russians and, to a lesser degree, Ukrainians and Belarusians from the Soviet Union, and the Soviet government demolished the historic centre. In the treaty of 12 September 1990 Germany renounced all claims to the city and to lands east of the Oder–Neisse line.
konkan-coast: The Konkan is bounded in the north by the Daman Ganga River at Daman and extends south to Anjediva Island next to the town of Karwar, with the Arabian Sea to the west and the Deccan Plateau to the east. Its hinterland holds numerous river valleys, riverine islands and the hilly slopes of the Western Ghats, also called the Sahyadri, which lead up into the tablelands of the Deccan.

The region runs through the western coasts of Maharashtra and Goa. In the south it reaches the Gangavalli River in the district of Uttara Kannada in present-day Karnataka, whose northern bank forms its southernmost portion; the towns of Karwar, Ankola, Kumta, Honnavar and Bhatkal fall within it. Its best-known islands are the Ilhas de Goa, site of the Goa state capital at Panjim, and the Seven Islands of Bombay, on which Mumbai lies.

The limits of the Konkan have always been flexible, and it has carried other names such as Aparanta and Gomanchal, the latter meaning the coastal area between the Daman Ganga and the Gangavalli. The ancient Sapta Konkan was a larger area that stretched from Gujarat to Kerala and took in coastal Maharashtra and coastal Karnataka, including Tulunad, though it overlaps the Kanara and Malabar coasts.

The region has been recognised by name since at least the time of Strabo, in the third century CE. The Chinese Buddhist monk Xuanzang mentioned it as Konkana Desha, Varahamihira's Brihat-Samhita described it as a region of India, and a 15th-century author, Ratnakosh, used the word Konkandesha. From the 10th century it had a thriving mercantile port with Arab tradesmen.

According to the Sahyadrikhanda of the Skanda Purana, Parashurama threw his axe into the sea and commanded the Sea God to recede up to the point where it landed. The land thus recovered was called Saptah-Konkana, from the Sanskrit koṇa, corner, and kaṇa, piece.

The coast's districts run from north to south through Daman, Palghar, Thane, Mumbai Suburban, Mumbai City, Raigad, Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg to part of Uttara Kannada. Its largest city is Mumbai, the capital of Maharashtra and the headquarters of the Konkan Division.

The main ethnolinguistic group is the Konkani people, alongside many castes and communities and tribal groups such as the Katkari, Warli and Mahadev Koli. The Jewish Bene Israel live mainly in Raigad district, and Christian communities include the Bombay East Indians and the Goan Catholics. Konkani Muslims and Nawayaths are descended, reportedly, from people who came from Hadhramaut and other parts of Arabia and the Middle East, while the Siddi have their roots in Africa.
konrad-adenauer: Konrad Adenauer was born on 5 January 1876 in Cologne, in Rhenish Prussia, the third of five children of Johann Konrad Adenauer and Helene Scharfenberg. A formative influence was the Kulturkampf, the struggle of the Prussian state with the Catholic church, which left him with a lifelong dislike of Prussianism, as it did many Catholic Rhinelanders. A devout Catholic, he joined the Centre Party in 1906 and was elected to Cologne's city government the same year. In 1909 he became vice-mayor, and in 1917 he was unanimously elected Mayor of Cologne for twelve years, re-elected in 1929.

Adenauer opposed Adolf Hitler and the Nazis, but in the early 1930s he thought they should be brought into the Prussian and Reich governments. The Nazis came to power on 30 January 1933, and his term as mayor ended that year. After the war the American army reinstalled him as Mayor of Cologne, but when the city passed into the British zone, General Gerald Templer dismissed him for incompetence in December 1945. The dismissal helped his later career, since he could pursue alliance with the Allies without being called a sell-out. From 1946 to 1966 he led the Christian Democratic Union.

The first Bundestag election, on 15 August 1949, made the Christian Democrats the strongest party, and Adenauer became chancellor. His rival, the Social Democrat Kurt Schumacher, wanted a united, socialist and neutral Germany; Adenauer preferred integration with Western states, especially France and the United States, even at the price of continued division. West Germany joined NATO, and the Bundeswehr was established in 1955 and 1956. He refused to recognise East Germany or the Oder-Neisse line as Poland's frontier. In 1957 he signed the Treaty of Rome, and from 1958 he built a close friendship with Charles de Gaulle. In 1961 the Berlin Wall was built, and his relationship with John F. Kennedy was strained.

Adenauer resigned as chancellor at 87 and led the CDU until he was 90, and he was often called Der Alte, the old one. He died on 19 April 1967, aged 91, at his home in Rhöndorf. His requiem mass in Cologne Cathedral was attended by guests from over a hundred countries and organisations, and he is buried at Rhöndorf. He is considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union.
konrad-henlein: Konrad Henlein was born on 6 May 1898 in Maffersdorf in Bohemia, then part of Austria-Hungary, the son of an accounts clerk. He attended business school in Gablonz and in the First World War served in the Austro-Hungarian Army on the Italian front. Severely wounded and gassed, he was captured by Italian soldiers and spent the rest of the war as a prisoner on Asinara Island, where he studied the history of the German gymnastics movement of Friedrich Ludwig Jahn. After the war the Sudetenland, where he lived, became part of the new Czechoslovakia. By 1923 he was promoting nationalist völkisch ideas in his local gymnastics club, and in May 1931 he was elected president of the Turnerbund.

On 1 October 1933, knowing that the Czechoslovak authorities were about to ban the two main völkisch parties in the Sudetenland, Henlein founded the Sudeten German Home Front, a movement for the autonomy of the German minority. Under pressure from the government it was renamed the Sudeten German Party on 19 April 1935. In the election of May 1935 it won 15.2 per cent of the vote, making it the strongest party in Czechoslovakia, with about 68 per cent of the ethnic German vote. It was secretly subsidised by the German foreign ministry. Henlein presented himself abroad as loyal to Czechoslovakia, and in December 1935 he lectured at Chatham House in London.

After the Anschluss of March 1938 he met Hitler in Berlin and agreed to provide a pretext for a German attack by demanding autonomy for the Sudetenland. He was told always to appear moderate and never to negotiate in good faith. On 24 April 1938 he announced the eight-point Karlsbad programme. The crisis that followed led to the Munich Agreement of 30 September 1938.

When the Wehrmacht entered the Sudetenland on 1 October 1938, Henlein was appointed Gauleiter and Reichskommissar, and he became an SS-Gruppenführer. He organised the pogrom of 9 November 1938 in the Sudetenland and took part in confiscating Jewish businesses and property. He joined the Nazi Party on 26 January 1939 and became Reichsstatthalter of Reichsgau Sudetenland on 1 May 1939, holding the post until the end of the war. On 10 May 1945, in American custody at Pilsen, he killed himself by cutting his veins with his broken glasses.

After the war the annexation of the Sudetenland was reversed, and almost the entire ethnic German population was transferred to Germany and Austria in 1945–46 under the Beneš decrees. In Czech, Henleinovci, 'Henleinists', is a term of abuse meaning a traitor or fifth-columnist.
konrad-i-of-masovia: Konrad was the youngest son of the High Duke Casimir II the Just of Poland and Helen of Znojmo, daughter of the Přemyslid duke Conrad II of Znojmo. After his father's death in 1194 he was brought up by his mother, who acted as regent of Masovia. He received Masovia in 1199 and the neighbouring lands of Kuyavia in 1205. In 1205 he and his brother Leszek I the White of Sandomierz won their largest victory at the Battle of Zawichost, where the Ruthenian army of Prince Roman the Great of Galicia–Volhynia was crushed and Roman was killed. His wife was Agafia of Rus, daughter of Prince Svyatoslav III Igorevich, and they had ten children.

Konrad tried to enlarge his lands by conquering the pagan land of Chełmno in Prussia, first in a crusade of 1209 with the consent of Pope Innocent III. In 1215 the monk Christian of Oliva became missionary bishop among the Old Prussians, but his residence at Chełmno was devastated the next year. Campaigns in 1219 and 1222 also failed and brought Prussian raids across his borders, which even threatened his residence at Płock. In 1226 he invited the Teutonic Knights to fight the Prussians. In March 1226 Emperor Frederick II issued the Golden Bull of Rimini, granting Prussia to the Order's Grand Master Herman of Salza. In 1228 Konrad also founded the Order of Dobrzyń.

A Treaty of Kruszwica of 1230, by which Konrad granted Chełmno Land to the Order, is attested only by a document that is believed never to have been signed and probably was forged by the Order. The Knights crossed the Vistula, conquered Chełmno Land and built the castle of Toruń in 1231, and in 1234 Pope Gregory IX confirmed their holdings in the Golden Bull of Rieti. Konrad also claimed the title of High Duke of Poland in 1229, but Henry I the Bearded prevailed in 1232. After the death of Henry II the Pious at the Battle of Legnica in 1241 he took the title again, and yielded it two years later to his nephew Bolesław V the Chaste.

Konrad died on 31 August 1247. Poles consider him responsible for the Teutonic Knights' control of most of the Baltic coastline, which undermined Polish authority there. Casimir III of Poland had to accept the Order's rule in Toruń and Chełmno by the Treaty of Kalisz of 1343, and after the Thirteen Years' War Casimir IV Jagiellon gained Chełmno Land, as part of Royal Prussia, in the Second Peace of Toruń of 1466.
konrad-i-of-olesnica: Konrad was the second son of Henry III, Duke of Głogów, and Matilda, daughter of Albert I, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg. When his father died in 1309 he succeeded to all his lands with his brothers, but as a minor he stayed under the care of his mother and his elder brother Henry IV the Faithful until 1312. On 3 March 1310 in Berlin he was present when his brothers Henry IV and Bolesław renounced their rights over Gdańsk Pomerania to Brandenburg for money.

In the division of 29 February 1312 Konrad and Bolesław received as co-rulers Oleśnica, Namysłów and Kluczbork with the regions of Kalisz and Gniezno, while their mother kept Głogów as her dower. A year later the two divided their share and Konrad took Namysłów and Kalisz, but he lost Kalisz in 1313 after a revolt of the nobility, and in 1314 Władysław I the Elbow-high took almost all of Greater Poland.

When Bolesław died without issue in 1321, Konrad inherited Oleśnica. While Władysław I and Bolesław III the Generous plundered the duchy, he married Elisabeth, daughter of Henry VI the Good of Wrocław, which removed any threat from that duchy. The peace of Kraków on 10 August 1323 gave him Wołów, Lubiąż and Smogorzów but forced him to give Namysłów to Bolesław III.

In the summer of 1343 King Casimir III the Great of Poland attacked him, but Konrad defeated the Polish army before the walls of Oleśnica and made peace. He took control of the Duchy of Koźle in 1355, shared the Duchy of Bytom with Duke Casimir I of Cieszyn from 8 December 1357, and bought Milicz the next year. A dispute with his nephew Henry V of Iron over the inheritance of Jan of Ścinawa, begun in 1361, was settled in 1365 through Ludwik I the Fair, Duke of Brzeg.

Konrad died on 22 December 1366 and was buried in the Chapel of St. Hedwig in the monastery of Trzebnica. His first marriage was childless. By his second wife, Euphemia, daughter of Władysław, Duke of Koźle-Bytom, he had a daughter, Hedwig, married to Duke Nikolaus II of Opawa, and a son, Konrad II the Gray.
konrad-of-marburg: Little is known of Konrad's early life. He may have been of aristocratic descent, which fits church sources of his time that describe him as well educated and learned. He bore the title magister, a sign that he had completed a course at a university, perhaps Paris or Bologna, and he was noted for strict asceticism. Much of his early work for the church was against heresy, and he took an active part in the Albigensian Crusade in southern France, with Pope Innocent III among his early supporters.

Back in Germany, the land of his birth, he became spiritual director to Elizabeth of Hungary, wife of Louis. With a commission from Archbishop Siegfried II of Mainz he hunted heresy in Thuringia and Hesse and soon gained a name for injustice. By most accounts he accepted almost any accusation and treated suspects as guilty until proven innocent; the accused were told to repent or be burnt, and were urged to denounce others in the hope of saving themselves.

He spared neither nobles nor priests: Heinrich Minnike, Provost of Goslar, was among his first victims and was burnt at the stake. He once tricked a widow into unwitting disobedience and had her and her maids flogged. In 1231 Pope Gregory IX allowed him to set aside the usual procedure for investigating heresy, and in answer to his reports issued the bull Vox in Rama. With Conrad Dorso and John the One-Eyed he burnt many people in the Upper Rhineland with barely the semblance of a trial.

When the bishops at Mainz postponed their verdict on Count Henry III of Sayn, Konrad demanded a decision, then gave up and set out for Marburg. Knights attacked him on the road on 30 July 1233, killing him and his assistant, the Franciscan friar Gerhard Lutzelkolb.

Pope Gregory called him an upholder of the faith and ordered his killers punished, but in the German Empire his memory turned opinion against the Inquisition for many years, and his name spread through Europe as that of an overly harsh judge. His letter to the pope on the miracles of Saint Elizabeth was first printed at Cologne in 1653. A stone marks the place of his death at Hof Kapelle near Marburg, and Charles Kingsley put him in The Saint's Tragedy.
konstantin-dragas: Konstantin, also called Kostadin Dejanović, was the son of the despot and sevastokrator Dejan, who held the Kumanovo region under Stefan Dušan, and of Teodora Nemanjić, a half-sister of Dušan. Through his mother he was a grandson of King Stefan Dečanski and Queen Maria Palaiologina. Around 1365 his elder brother Jovan Dragaš held Štip and Strumica, and Emperor Uroš V raised Jovan to the rank of despot, as Dušan had raised their father.

Konstantin helped his brother govern their lands during the fall of the Serbian Empire. The Battle of Maritsa in 1371 devastated part of the Serbian nobility, and the brothers became vassals of the Ottoman Empire, while keeping close links with their Christian neighbours, among them the Byzantine Empire. When Jovan died in 1378 or 1379, Konstantin succeeded him and governed large parts of north-eastern Macedonia and the Struma valley. Like his brother he minted coins in the Nemanjić style, and the family gave generously to monasteries on Mount Athos, among them Hilandar, Pantaleimon and Vatopedi.

He married twice. His first wife's name is unknown; his second was Eudokia of Trebizond, daughter of Emperor Alexios III of Trebizond. On 10 February 1392 his daughter Jelena married Manuel II Palaiologos, and the next day the couple were crowned emperor and empress by the patriarch. A son, Jakov, converted to Islam and became lord of Velbužd.

Konstantin was killed at the Battle of Rovine near Craiova on 17 May 1395, fighting for Sultan Bayezid I against Mircea cel Bătrân of Wallachia alongside Stefan Lazarević and Marko Mrnjavčević, king of Prilep. The Ottomans named his capital Velbužd Köstendil after him, the present Kyustendil in Bulgaria. His grandson Constantine XI was named after him and added Dragaš to his own name. In Serbian epic poetry he appears as Beg Kostadin, usually a negative figure set against Marko Kraljević: both were Ottoman vassals, but Marko is shown accepting Ottoman rule for the good of his people and Kostadin for the sake of his own position and privileges.
konstantin-pats: Konstantin Päts was born on 23 February 1874 (11 February O.S.) near Tahkuranna. His father, Jakob Päts, was a housebuilder, and his mother, Olga, had been raised in the Eastern Orthodox faith, to which her husband converted from Lutheranism. Päts attended the Orthodox parish school at Tahkuranna and the Riga Clerical Seminar from 1887 to 1892, left it after deciding not to become a priest, and studied law at Tartu University from 1894 to 1898. In 1900 he moved to Tallinn to begin a political career.

In Tallinn, Päts founded the newspaper Teataja, whose first issue appeared on 23 October 1901. The authorities took it for a paper loyal to the empire, but its content was radical, and it began a long rivalry between Päts and Jaan Tõnisson, editor of Postimees. In 1904 Päts and Jaan Poska organised an electoral bloc of Estonians and liberal Russians that won the Tallinn municipal elections, and in April 1905 he became deputy mayor. During the Revolution of 1905 his newspaper was closed and he fled to Switzerland, where he learned he had been condemned to death. After returning he served a prison sentence in 1910 and 1911.

In 1917, after the February Revolution, Päts headed the provincial government of the autonomous Governorate of Estonia, and on 19 February 1918 he became one of three members of the Salvation Committee that issued the Estonian Declaration of Independence on 24 February. He led the Provisional Government of 1918 and 1919 and, as Minister of War, organised the army in the War of Independence. In the 1920s he led the Farmers' Assemblies, was Speaker of the Riigikogu from 1922 to 1923 and held the office of State Elder several times.

In 1934, during his last term as State Elder, he organised a self-coup with army and parliamentary support, aimed at the right-wing Vaps Movement. In the following years, called the Era of Silence, he ruled with General Johan Laidoner's support and postponed the return of constitutional order, until a new constitution of 1938 made him the first President of Estonia.

After the Soviet Union delivered an ultimatum on 16 June 1940 and occupied Estonia the next day, Päts remained formally in office for over a month. On 21 July 1940 he sent his son Viktor to the United States embassy to ask for asylum for his family, but he was arrested and deported to the Soviet Union. Sources differ on the date of his resignation. He died on 18 January 1956 in a hospital in the village of Burashevo, near Tver. Estonians located his grave in 1988, and his remains were reburied at Tallinn's Metsakalmistu cemetery on 21 October 1990.
konstantin-stanislavski: Konstantin Sergeyevich Alekseyev was born on 17 January 1863 into the Alekseyevs, one of the richest families in Russia. He adopted the stage name Stanislavski in 1884 to keep his acting secret from his parents. His family's two private theatres gave him a stage. After his debut at one of them in 1877 he began a lifelong series of notebooks of critical observations on his acting, and this habit of self-analysis later gave rise to his system.

He chose not to attend university and worked in the family business. At twenty-five he co-founded a Society of Art and Literature, in which he acted in plays by Molière, Schiller, Pushkin and Ostrovsky and directed for the first time. In 1889 he married Maria Lilina. His family's discouragement kept him an amateur until the age of thirty-three.

On 4 July 1897 Stanislavski met the playwright and teacher Vladimir Nemirovich-Danchenko, and an eighteen-hour discussion led to the Moscow Art Theatre. Stanislavski brought a gift for vivid stage images and telling detail, Nemirovich his skill at literary analysis and managing a theatre. Their production of Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in 1898 was a milestone, praised for its delicate representation of everyday life and its ensemble playing.

The company's European tour of 1906 won it an international reputation, but it also brought on an artistic crisis. Stanislavski found that he was acting without inner impulse and that his performance had become mechanical. His attempt to resolve this led to his system. In 1912 he created the First Studio, whose members included Yevgeny Vakhtangov and Michael Chekhov. After a heart attack on stage in 1928 he stopped acting but kept directing, teaching and writing.

His early work was director-centred: he planned every role and movement in advance. From 1908 he stressed that rehearsal should have a stage of experiment in which the cast helps the director. His manual An Actor's Work, written as a fictional student's diary, was published in 1938.

Late in life he developed the Method of Physical Action, in which actors explore a play through active analysis, improvising its simplest physical actions instead of discussing it at length around a table. He argued that if actors commit to the truth of their actions, truthful thoughts and feelings follow.
Under Stalin he lived in a kind of internal exile in Moscow, and his system was attacked in 1931 but later held up as a model of Socialist realism. He died on 7 August 1938.
konstantin-von-kaufmann: Kaufmann was born on 2 March 1818, the second of four sons of Lieutenant General Peter Feodorovich von Kaufmann. His family, German in origin, had served the tsars for over a century and had become Russian Orthodox. He graduated from the Nikolayev Engineering Institute as a military engineer, served in the Caucasus campaigns, commanded the sappers at the siege of Kars in 1855 and settled its surrender terms with General William Fenwick Williams. From 1861 he helped the war minister Dmitry Milyutin reorganise the army, and from 1864 he was Governor-General of Vilna, where the state was expropriating the Polish aristocracy.

His campaign of 1868 against the Emirate of Bukhara took Samarkand. In the Khivan campaign of 1873 he took Khiva, where the slaves had risen as his army approached; he made the khan, Muhammad Rahim Khan II, a vassal and demanded that he abolish slavery and the slave trade, which he did. In 1875 he defeated Nasreddin, who had led an uprising against the previous khan of Kokand, and the rest of the khanate in the Ferghana Valley was annexed. The reception of his envoys by Sher Ali Khan of Afghanistan was a main cause of the Second Anglo-Afghan War.

The temporary statutes under which Turkestan was governed gave him unusual independence: he negotiated with neighbouring states, set taxes, controlled the budget and could confirm or revoke death sentences of the military courts, ruling through a military bureaucracy laid loosely over a largely unreformed local administration.

Kaufmann also had the new territory studied. He brought in Alexei and Olga Fedchenko, whose three expeditions between 1868 and 1872 documented its natural history, with statisticians, the war artist Vasily Vereshchagin and later the educationalist Nikolai Ostroumov, set up a Tashkent branch of a Moscow scientific society and showed the findings at the 1872 Moscow technical exhibition. He could not persuade the government to back all his plans of further conquest. He died in office on 16 May 1882, and several plants, among them Tulipa kaufmanniana, are named after him.
konstantin-von-neurath: Konstantin von Neurath was born on 2 February 1873 at the manor of Kleinglattbach in Württemberg, into a Swabian noble family and political dynasty. He studied law at Tübingen and Berlin, graduated in 1897 and entered the Foreign Office in Berlin in 1901.

He served as an infantry officer until he was badly wounded in 1916. In the Ottoman Empire he wrote a memorandum on the German embassy's position on the Armenian genocide, which justified the actions of the Ottoman government while presenting Germany as protesting against its excesses. After the war he was minister to Denmark from 1919, ambassador to Rome from 1921 to 1930, and then ambassador in London.

Neurath became Reich foreign minister in June 1932 under Chancellor Franz von Papen and kept the post under Kurt von Schleicher and then Adolf Hitler. He lent an aura of respectability to Hitler's expansionist policy and took part in the German withdrawal from the League of Nations in 1933, the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 1935 and the remilitarisation of the Rhineland. In 1937 he joined the Nazi Party by accepting the Golden Party Badge and received the honorary SS rank of Gruppenführer.

At the conference recorded in the Hossbach Memorandum on 5 November 1937, Neurath, Werner von Blomberg and Werner von Fritsch objected to Hitler's plans, but only on the ground that Germany could not start a war without drawing in France and Britain and needed more time to rearm. Neurath was dismissed on 4 February 1938 and replaced by Joachim von Ribbentrop.

In March 1939 he became Reichsprotektor of Bohemia and Moravia. He imposed harsh press censorship, banned political parties and trade unions and, after student protests in October and November 1939, sent 1,200 students to concentration camps and had nine executed. He also supervised the persecution of Czech Jews under the Nuremberg Laws. In September 1941 Hitler judged his rule too lenient and gave the real power to Reinhard Heydrich, and Neurath's resignation was accepted in August 1943.

The Allies tried Neurath at Nuremberg in 1946, where Otto von Lüdinghausen defended him. The tribunal found that most of his crimes against humanity occurred during his short tenure as nominal protector, especially in suppressing Czech resistance, and found him guilty on all four counts. It sentenced him to 15 years in prison. He was held in Spandau Prison until 6 November 1954, when he was released on grounds of ill health. He died on 14 August 1956 at his family's estates in Enzweihingen, aged 83.
konstantinos-karamanlis: Konstantinos Karamanlis was born on 8 March 1907 in the village of Proti, near Serres in Macedonia, then part of the Ottoman Empire. He became a Greek citizen in 1913, when Macedonia was annexed by Greece after the First and Second Balkan War. He studied law in Athens, practised in Serres, and in 1936, at the age of 28, was first elected to parliament for the conservative People's Party. After the war he rose quickly, becoming Minister of Labour in 1947 and, in 1952, Minister of Public Works under Alexandros Papagos, when the Greek Rally won the election.

When Papagos died in October 1955, King Paul appointed the 48-year-old Karamanlis prime minister, bypassing two senior party figures. He extended full voting rights to women, and won elections in 1956, 1958 and 1961. He also gave up enosis, union with Cyprus, in favour of independence for the island, through the Zurich and London agreements. On 9 July 1961 his government signed an association treaty with the European Economic Community.

The assassination of the leftist deputy Grigoris Lambrakis in May 1963 weakened his position, and that summer he resigned after a clash with King Paul over a royal visit to Britain. He then spent eleven years in self-imposed exile in Paris, while a military coup took place on 21 April 1967.

After the junta collapsed in July 1974 he was recalled to Athens to lead a national unity government. He legalized the Communist Party of Greece, freed political prisoners and held elections in November 1974, in which his new party, New Democracy, won 54.4 percent. A plebiscite then abolished the monarchy, and the junta's leaders were tried. A Turkish invasion of Cyprus on 14 August 1974 led him to withdraw Greece from the military side of NATO until 1980.

Karamanlis signed the treaty of accession to the European Economic Community in May 1979, and Greece became its tenth member on 1 January 1981, while he was president, a post he held from 1980 to 1985 and again from 1990 to 1995. He won the Karlspreis in 1978. He died in 1998 at 91 and was buried on the grounds of the foundation he had founded.

Assessments differ. Supporters called him the Ethnarches, or national leader, and he is credited with restoring democracy and with Greek entry into Europe. Left-wing opponents accused him of condoning right-wing para-state groups. He has also been criticized for his handling of Cyprus in 1959 and 1974.
konstantinos-logothetopoulos: Konstantinos Logothetopoulos was born in Nafplion in 1878. He studied medicine in Munich and stayed in the German Empire, practising and teaching medicine until 1910, when he moved to Athens and founded a private clinic. He served as a doctor in the First Balkan War of 1912 to 1913 and the Second Balkan War of 1913, and was discharged in 1916. Called up again in 1922 during the Greco-Turkish War, he served in the Army Hospital of Athens.

After the war he became professor of gynaecology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and in time Dean of the University, where he taught many young doctors, among them the future politician Grigoris Lambrakis. He spoke German fluently, had chaired the Greek-German Council and was married to a niece of Field Marshal Wilhelm List.

After the Battle of Greece he became Vice President and Minister of Education in the first collaborationist government of Georgios Tsolakoglou. When Tsolakoglou was removed, Logothetopoulos served as prime minister from 2 December 1942 until 7 April 1943, when Ioannis Rallis replaced him. His short tenure saw the start of the deportation of Greek Jewry, in which he played an ambiguous role.

When the Wehrmacht left Greece in 1944, he went with it to Germany and lived with his wife and daughter in the Bavarian town of Vilshofen an der Donau, practising medicine. The United States Army captured him and handed him over to the Greek authorities in 1946. Convicted of collaborating with the enemy, he was first sentenced to life imprisonment but was released in 1951. He died in Athens on 6 July 1961.
konstanty-ostrogski: Ostrogski began his military career under John I Albert, King of Poland, fighting against the Tatars and the Grand Principality of Moscow. For a victory near Ochakiv over the forces of Mehmed I Giray he was made Grand Hetman of Lithuania on 11 September 1497, the first person to hold the title. Defeated at the Battle of Vedrosha in 1500, he was held captive for three years until he escaped in 1503 and joined King Sigismund I the Old, who let him keep his post.

In 1508 he defeated the rebellious prince Michael Glinski, who fled with his supporters to Moscow. With Mikołaj Firlej and Mikołaj Kamieniecki he was one of the main commanders of the Polish-Lithuanian alliance, and in 1512 he won a victory over the Tatars at the Battle of Wisniowiec. When war with Muscovy resumed in 1514 he commanded all the Polish and Lithuanian forces, up to 35,000 soldiers, with Jerzy Radziwiłł and the future Hetman of the Crown Jan Tarnowski among his subordinates, and on 8 September defeated the army of Vasili III at Orsha. His siege of the Russian fortress of Opochka in 1517 failed badly and ended hopes of retaking Smolensk.

Ostrogski died on 10 August 1530, a respected commander. Though loyal to Catholic Poland and long at odds with Orthodox Russia, he remained devoutly Orthodox in the traditions of his family, gave generously to build Orthodox churches and sponsored church schools for Orthodox children. One of the wealthiest Orthodox nobles, he was buried in the Dormition Cathedral of the Kiev Pechersk Lavra, where his restored tombstone was inaugurated on 24 August 2021 in the presence of Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda. He married Tatiana Koretska and later Aleksandra Słucka, and had a son by each, Illia and Konstanty Wasyl Ostrogski. The town of Starokostiantyniv bears his name, as does the Lithuanian–Polish–Ukrainian Brigade, and he appears in Jan Matejko's painting Prussian Homage.
konstanz: Konstanz lies at the western end of Upper Lake Constance, where the Rhine leaves the lake and flows under the Old Rhine Bridge as the Seerhein. The old town, with the Dominicans Island, the port and the main railway station, stands south of the river, while the larger part of the modern city lies to the north on the Bodanrück peninsula. The Altstadt and Paradies are the only parts of Germany south of the Rhine. The border with Switzerland runs along the southern edge of the city, which adjoins the Swiss town of Kreuzlingen.

The first Romans settled the site around 40 CE, in the province of Raetia. Its later name, Constantia, comes either from the emperor Constantius Chlorus, who fought the Alemanni in the region and built a strong fortress around 300, or from his grandson Constantius II, who visited in 354.

Konstanz grew as a spiritual centre, and by the late Middle Ages about a quarter of its 6,000 inhabitants were exempt from taxation on account of clerical rights. It owned the only bridge over the Rhine in the region, and in 1192 became an Imperial City, subject only to the Holy Roman Emperor.

During the Council of Constance, Jan Hus was burned at the stake on 6 July 1415. The council also elected Pope Martin V, in the only conclave ever held north of the Alps, and Ulrich von Richental's illustrated chronicle records its events and the everyday life of the city. In 1460 the Swiss Confederacy conquered Thurgau, the city's hinterland, and the forest cantons voted against admitting Konstanz, which joined the Swabian League instead. The Reformation took hold in the 1520s under Ambrosius Blarer, but in 1548 Emperor Charles V imposed the Imperial Ban, and Habsburg Austria took the city, which lost its imperial status.

The new Habsburg rulers were eager to re-Catholicise the town and opened a Jesuit College in 1604. The city passed to the Grand Duchy of Baden in 1806, and the bishopric was dissolved in 1821. On 22 October 1940, 110 of the last Jewish residents were deported to the Gurs internment camp in France. Konstanz was not bombed in World War II.

Konstanz has about 83,000 inhabitants and the University of Konstanz, founded in 1966. The Konzilgebäude, where the conclave met, stands by the harbour, near the Imperia statue of 1993, a satirical memorial to the council. Prehistoric pile-dwelling settlements here belong to the Prehistoric Pile dwellings around the Alps World Heritage Site.
kontor: The word kontor is Middle Low German, from the French comptoir and ultimately the Latin computāre, to calculate. The kontors were set up in cities outside the Hanseatic League as corporations of senior merchants, a universitas mercatorum, chiefly for security, though they also inspected goods and dealt with local and regional authorities. The Peterhof in Novgorod came first, in the early 13th century; the kontor of Bruges, which later moved to Antwerp, and Bryggen in Bergen were the last. In the mid 14th century the League made all its trading posts subject to the decisions of the Hansetag, the Hanseatic diet, where kontor envoys could speak but not vote.

Each kontor had its own seal and its own code of rules, written in Middle Low German and read aloud to the merchants once a year, governing trade, taxes, duties and contact with locals and outsiders. Every resident and visiting Hanseatic trader came under its authority. Most were enclaves, Bruges being the exception. Aldermen, usually chosen for a year, held legal authority: Bruges had first six and later three, the Steelyard one Hanseatic and one English alderman, the Peterhof one. They were assisted by the achteinen, usually eighteen officials.

From the middle of the 15th century the kontors of Bruges, London and Bergen employed a clerk trained in law at a university to advise the aldermen and keep their correspondence. In Novgorod a priest did this work, and in the 15th century the Livonian towns replaced the alderman there with a resident appointee who spoke Russian, the hofknecht. Smaller posts with a single merchant and a warehouse, called factories, were not kontors.

Most kontor buildings are lost. Bryggen in Bergen, now on UNESCO's list of World Heritage Sites, and the Oosterlingenhuis in Bruges survive. The Hanseatic kontor at Bryggen closed in 1754 and was replaced by a Norwegian kontor run by Norwegian citizens. The word itself still means office in the Scandinavian languages and Estonian, and as kontora it is a term for an office or bureau in Russian and Ukrainian.
kontorhaus-district: The district lies in the south-eastern part of Hamburg's Altstadt, between Steinstraße, Meßberg, Klosterwall and Brandstwiete. From the 17th century the area was a densely built Gängeviertel, a corridor quarter of narrow alleys, which grew denser still during the housing shortage after the Hamburg fire of 1842. When cholera spread through its poor housing in the epidemic of 1892, the city decided to redevelop it and resettled many inhabitants. Fritz Schumacher, director of construction from 1909, planned large office buildings for Hamburg's merchants around Burchardplatz, at first with some housing as well.

The buildings mostly have a reinforced concrete frame behind facades of clinker brick and copper roofs. Each was designed individually, and upper floors are often set back to open the street canyons to the sky. Ornament is in clinker brick and in ceramics, often sculptures tied to Hamburg's trades and crafts.

The first finished was the Miramar-House of 1921/22 by Max Bach, with its rounded corner and entrance sculptures by Richard Kuöhl. Fritz Höger's Chilehaus, built in 1922–1924 for the shipowner Henry B. Sloman, who made his fortune in Chile saltpetre, is regarded as Höger's main work. The Sprinkenhof, built between 1927 and 1943 to designs by Hans and Oskar Gerson and Höger around three courtyards, was then Hamburg's largest office complex. Hans and Oskar Gerson also designed the Meßberghof, and Rudolf Klophaus the Altstädter Hof, the Bartholomayhaus and the Pressehaus, now the Helmut-Schmidt-Haus. The Mohlenhof, with Kuöhl's Hermes at its entrance, came through the Second World War almost unscathed.

Most of the district's buildings are listed. Later buildings of the 1990s, such as the Danske Hus and the Neue Dovenhof, follow the style of the clinker brick blocks. On 5 July 2015 the World Heritage Committee, meeting in Bonn for its 39th session, added parts of the district and the neighbouring Speicherstadt to the list of World Heritage Sites.
konungs-skuggsja: Konungs skuggsjá, Speculum regale in Latin and Kongsspegelen or Kongespeilet in modern Norwegian, belongs to the speculum literature, the mirrors for princes that treat politics and morality. The most important manuscript is AM 243 a fol., copied in Norway, probably in Bergen, around 1275. The relations between the surviving manuscripts were studied by Ludvig Holm-Olsen, whose findings underpin his edition of 1983.

The seventy chapters consist of a prologue and two main parts, the second of which may be divided into a section on the king's court and one on the king's justice. In the prologue the speaker sets out to discuss merchants, kingsmen, the clergy and peasants, but the book barely goes beyond the first two; the last two chapters may have been meant for a separate treatment of the clergy. The son asks about trade, the hird, chivalric behaviour, strategy and tactics, and parts of the work deal with the relations of church and state. The merchant, the father warns, must often put his life at stake, at sea or in heathen lands, and so must always behave well wherever he finds himself.

Several chapters describe marvels of other countries. One tells of a creature caught in a forest, human in shape but covered in hair, with a long mane down its back, of which no one could say whether it was a man or an animal. Another tells how, after mass at a church in Ireland, people found an anchor hanging on a rope from the sky, caught on the church door, and saw a ship above, from which a man came down through the air to free it.

The first printed edition, by Hálfdan Einarsson at Sórey in 1768, gave Latin and Danish translations. Rudolf Keyser and others published the text at Christiania in 1848, and Laurence Marcellus Larson's translation, The King's Mirror, was published in New York in 1917. A line from the work stands on the gravestone of the Danish linguist Rasmus Rask: if you wish to become perfect in knowledge, learn all the languages, but do not neglect your own.
konya: Konya stands on the south-western edge of the Central Anatolian Plateau. It was known as Iconium in antiquity and into Seljuk times, in Greek Ikónion, and the Rum Seljuks called it Dârülmülk. The name is believed to correspond to Ikkuwaniya, a Late Bronze Age place known from Hittite records.

The region has been inhabited since the third millennium BCE, and excavations show settlement in the Late Copper Age, around 3000 BCE. It fell at different times to the Hittites, the Phrygians, the Persians and the Romans, and Xenophon describes Iconium as the last city of Phrygia. After Alexander the Great defeated Darius III in 333 BCE, the town came under Seleucus I Nicator, and later under the kings of Pergamon. Under the emperor Claudius it was renamed Claudiconium, and under Hadrian it was Colonia Aelia Hadriana.

Paul and Silas probably visited it around 50 CE, and the apocryphal Acts of Paul and Thecla make it the birthplace of Saint Thecla. Under the Byzantine Empire it became a bishop's seat and, around 370, a metropolitan see for Lycaonia.

From the eighth to the tenth century it was a frequent target of Arab attacks. The Seljuk Turks conquered it in the 11th century, and it became the capital of their Sultanate of Rum. It was briefly occupied by the army of the First Crusade in 1097 and by Frederick Barbarossa in 1190. Konya reached the height of its wealth and influence in the second half of the 12th century, when the sultans subdued the Danishmend beyliks and took ports on the Mediterranean and Black Sea.

After the sultanate fell, the Karamanids took Konya, and in 1420 their beylik fell to the Ottoman Empire. Under Ottoman rule it was governed by the sultans' sons and was the capital of the Karaman Eyalet until 1864. İbrahim Paşa occupied it in 1832, and it went into decline afterwards.

Konya is a major city of central Turkey and the capital of Konya Province. It was the last home of Rumi, whose turquoise-domed tomb is its main tourist attraction. In 1273 his followers established the Mevlevi order, known as the Whirling Dervishes, and Konya is its spiritual centre.
koos-de-la-rey: Jacobus Herculaas de la Rey was born on 22 October 1847 on Doornfontein Farm in the Winburg District of the Orange Free State, a Boer of French Huguenot, Spanish and Dutch descent. After the Battle of Boomplaats the British confiscated the family farm, and the family trekked into the Transvaal and settled at Lichtenburg. He had very little formal schooling and as a young man worked as a transport rider serving the diamond diggings at Kimberley. He married Jacoba Elizabeth (Nonnie) Greeff; they had twelve children and cared for six orphans.

He fought in the Basotho War of 1865 and Sekhukhune's War of 1876, and in the First Boer War took over Piet Cronjé's siege of Potchefstroom when Cronjé fell ill. Elected commandant of the Lichtenburg district, he joined the Transvaal Volksraad in 1883, where he backed the progressive faction of General Piet Joubert and warned that Paul Kruger's policies towards the uitlanders would lead to war with Britain.

When war came he led the attack on a British armoured train at Kraaipan, where the first shots of the war were fired. At the Modder River he had his men dig in along the riverbanks, the first use of trench warfare in the war; his son Adriaan was killed there. After the fall of Pretoria he took command of the guerrilla war in the western Transvaal, winning at Moedwil, Nooitgedacht and Ysterspruit with commandos of up to 3,000 men. He released Lord Methuen, who had broken his leg, after capturing him at Tweebosch.

De la Rey urged peace at Vereeniging, and in 1907 he was elected to the colonial Transvaal Parliament. A delegate to the National Convention, he became a senator of the Union and supported Louis Botha's efforts to unite Boer and British. When the First World War began he argued for neutrality over the invasion of German South West Africa.

On 15 September 1914 he was travelling with Christian Frederick Beyers, who had just resigned as Commandant-General, when their car ran through police roadblocks set to catch the Foster gang, and a police bullet killed him at Langlaagte. Many Boers believed he had been deliberately assassinated, and his death had a major role in sparking the Maritz rebellion. A bronze bust by Fanie Eloff marks his grave at Lichtenburg, and a song about him by Bok van Blerk revived interest in 2005.
kopek: The silver kopeck was introduced in Russia in 1535 as a result of the monetary reform of Elena Glinskaya, who was serving as regent for her son Ivan IV. It was equal in weight to the Novgorodian denga, or novgorodka, at 0.68 to 0.69 grams, a coin that had circulated throughout Russia from 1478. From 1535 to 1718 kopeck coins bore the image of a horseman carrying a spear, in Russian kopyo, which gave the coin its name.

The weight of the silver kopeck fell over time: to 0.54 to 0.56 grams in 1610, 0.46 to 0.47 grams in 1626 and 0.38 grams in 1698. In 1610, during the Time of Troubles, the government of Vasily Shuisky briefly minted gold coins, including a kopeck. From 1656 to 1663 the government tried to replace silver coins with copper ones, which led to devaluation and ultimately to the Copper Riot, and in 1663 the minting of copper coins ceased.

Peter I began minting copper coins again in 1704, and the last wired silver coins were struck in 1718. His monetary reform also introduced the grivennik, worth 10 kopecks, and the poltina, worth 50. The denga, worth half a kopeck, and the polushka, worth a quarter, were minted periodically for centuries until 1917.

From 1704 to 1916 the obverse of the kopeck usually showed a double-headed eagle or a horseman with a spear and the monarch's monogram. Minting resumed in the Soviet period in 1924, with the State Emblem of the Soviet Union and the motto Workers of the world, unite on copper coins. After the Russian monetary reform of 1997 new coins again showed the horseman with a spear.

The kopeck is equal to one hundredth of a ruble and is not subdivided in any country. It is called kopeyka in Russia, kapeyka in Belarus, in use since 1992, and kopiyka in Ukraine, in use since 1996. Latvia used a kapeika from 1919 to 1922 and again from 1992 to 1993, and the Azerbaijani gapik, a hundredth of a manat, is derived from it.
koporye: Koporye is a historic village in Leningrad Oblast, Russia, about 100 km west of St Petersburg and 12 km south of the Koporye Bay of the Baltic Sea. Its population in 2017 was 1,603. Its Finnish name is Kaprio and its Swedish name Koporje, and under Swedish rule it was also known as Caporie or Capurien.

The Teutonic Knights built the first wooden fortress on the coast of the Koporye Bay in the winter of 1240, and Alexander Nevsky destroyed it the next year. The second fortress was built in stone by Alexander's son Dmitry Alexandrovich in 1280. The Novgorodians, enraged by the prince's independence, razed it two years later. The Swedes took advantage of the lack of a fortress and occupied the banks of the Narva River, and in 1297 the Novgorodians restored the stone fort. Koporye was the strongest stronghold in the region and survived numerous attacks during the Swedish-Novgorodian Wars.

In the 14th and 15th centuries the town was given several times to mercenary princes invited by the Novgorodians to protect the northern territories of the republic. It had an important fortress, the residences of a prince and several lesser landowners, and was the centre of an iron-working district, but it remained very small, with only 18 households by the end of the 15th century. After Novgorod was incorporated into Muscovy, the fortress was strengthened and rebuilt to withstand cannon fire, and most extant structures belong to that period.

Russian forces surrendered Koporye during the Livonian War but regained it under the Treaty of Tyavzino. During the Time of Troubles some 2,000 Swedes attacked it and the Russian garrison had to surrender. Russia tried unsuccessfully to retake it in 1656. Koporye remained Swedish until 1703 and formed an important part of Swedish Ingria. As the Gulf of Finland grew shallow and receded to the north, the site began to lose its maritime importance. In 1703, during the Great Northern War, a major Russian army under Boris Sheremetev regained Koporye from its defenders, 80 Swedish soldiers under Captain Wasili Apolloff.
The fortress survives in a ruined state, despite some repairs in the 19th century. Huge gaps in the walls from the fire of the Russian artillery in 1703 may still be seen. Today it is a museum.
koppany: Koppány, called Cupan in the chronicles, was the son of Zerind the Bald, according to the 14th-century Illuminated Chronicle. No primary source says he descended from Álmos or Árpád, but his claim to the throne shows that he belonged to the Árpád dynasty, and historians debate which of Árpád's sons was his ancestor: Gyula Kristó, László Szegfű and György Szabados favour the eldest, Tarkatzus, while Kornél Bakay argues for the youngest, Zoltán. He was probably born between about 950 and 965.

Under Grand Prince Géza, who came to the throne around 972, Koppány held a duchy, described in the Illuminated Chronicle as Symigium, or Somogy; two later sources add Zala. Modern historians agree that he ruled south-western Transdanubia, most likely between Lake Balaton and the river Dráva. Géza was remembered as cruel, and the historian Pál Engel suggests he murdered most of his kinsmen, a purge Koppány survived. Szabados holds that Koppány's father had already dominated Somogy and Zala; László Kontler that Géza gave him the duchy as compensation after making his own son Stephen heir.

Koppány's claim followed the traditional principle of seniority, against the Christian law of primogeniture on which Stephen's right rested, and his wish to marry Géza's widow, Sarolt, followed the pagan custom of levirate marriage, which Christians saw as incest. Both claims suggest that he was a pagan or inclined to paganism. Stephen's deed of foundation for Pannonhalma Archabbey says that a county named Somogy tried to dethrone him, and the Lesser Legend of King St Stephen has Koppány destroying Stephen's castles and murdering his servants before laying siege to Veszprém.

German knights who had come to Hungary after Stephen's marriage to Gisela of Bavaria in 996 played a leading part in the royal victory, and their commander Vecelin killed Koppány, near Veszprém according to one chapter of the Illuminated Chronicle and in Somogy according to another. On Stephen's orders his body was quartered and hung over the walls of Esztergom, Veszprém, Győr and Gyulafehérvár.
koraku-en: In 1687 the daimyō Ikeda Tsunamasa ordered Tsuda Nagatada to begin building the garden. Apart from changes made by later daimyōs, it has kept its original appearance, reaching its modern form in 1863. It was first called Kōen, the later garden, because it was laid out after Okayama Castle. In 1871 it was renamed Kōrakuen after the spirit of senyukoraku, grieve earlier than others and enjoy later than others, taken from Fan Zhongyan's Memorial to Yueyang Tower.

The daimyōs used the garden to entertain important guests and as a place of rest, though ordinary people could visit on certain days. Many Edo-period paintings and records of the Ikeda family survive, so that it is one of the few provincial daimyō gardens whose changes over time can be traced. After the transfer to Okayama Prefecture in 1884, the garden was badly damaged by floods in 1934 and by bombing in 1945, and it was restored from the Edo-period paintings and diagrams. In 1952 it was designated a Special Scenic Location under the Cultural Properties Protection Law.

The garden stands on the north bank of the Asahi River, on an island between the river and the city. It is laid out in the Kaiyu or scenic promenade style, in which each turn of the path opens a new view of lawns, ponds, hills, tea houses and streams. It covers about 133,000 square meters, of which about 18,500 are lawn, and a stream 640 meters long runs through it. Its central pond, Sawa-no-ike, holds three islands said to recall the scenery around Lake Biwa near Kyoto.
korce: Korçë stands on a plateau some 850 m above sea level, surrounded by the Morava Mountains. The current name is of Slavic origin: gorica means hill in the South Slavic languages and is a very common toponym. The city is known by other names, among them Goritsa in Bulgarian, Macedonian and Serbian, Korytsa in Greek, Coriza in Italian and Görice in Turkish. The Old Bazaar, with the Mirahori Mosque, is regarded as the urban core, and the town's actual physiognomy was realised in the 19th century.

Korçë's foundation is closely tied to Ilias Bey Mirahori, an Albanian convert to Islam, Master of the Stables to Sultan Bayezid II. In 1484 the Sultan rewarded him with seven villages in the Korçë area, and a series of firmans replaced these in 1497 with the locality of Piskopiye, whose boundaries correspond to the territory of today's city. When the nearby town of Moscopole was destroyed by Ali Pasha's men in 1769, some of its commerce moved to Korçë, and part of its population came from there. Greek schools were founded from 1724, and on the eve of the Balkan Wars 2,115 students attended Greek education in the city.

Ottoman rule lasted until 1912, when Albania declared its independence. Armed Albanian bands under Sali Butka, Spiro Bellkameni and Kajo Babjeni briefly liberated Korçë in August 1912. Because of its proximity to Greece, the city was fiercely contested in the Balkan Wars, and Greek forces captured it on 6 December 1912. After 1916 the city came under French control, which lasted until 1920. Albanian bands led by Themistokli Gërmenji and Sali Butka fought for Albanian self-administration against the Venizelist forces.

Korçë is the seat of Korçë County in south-eastern Albania, with 51,152 inhabitants in the city at the 2011 census. It has been regarded as the intellectual capital of southern Albania. Fan Noli University was founded in 1971, and the National Museum of Medieval Art holds about 7,000 icons. Aromanian and Greek communities remain, and the largest carnival in Albania takes place there before Orthodox Easter.
korcula: Korčula lies off the Dalmatian coast, separated from the Pelješac peninsula by a strait between 900 and 3,000 metres wide. It is about 47 kilometres long and 8 wide, with an area of 279 square kilometres, and its highest peaks are Klupca and Kom. The main settlements are the towns of Korčula, Blato and Vela Luka. The climate is Mediterranean and the island is largely covered with Mediterranean flora, including extensive pine forests, which gave the Greeks their name for it, Black Korkyra.

Mesolithic and Neolithic peoples left remains at Vela Spila and Jakas Cave. Illyrians settled about 1,000 BCE and left stone fortresses. Greek colonists from Corfu founded a colony in the 6th century BCE, and the Lumbarda Psephisma, the oldest written stone monument in Croatia, records another founded from Issa (Vis) in the 3rd century BCE. After the Illyrian Wars the island became part of the Roman province of Illyricum and later of Dalmatia. In the 6th century it came under Byzantine rule, and in the early Middle Ages its Croatian population was grouped with the Narentines, who turned to maritime skills and to piracy against Venetian shipping.

In 1214 the island first drafted the Statute of Korčula, which guaranteed its relative autonomy against outside rulers, including Zachlumia, Serbia, Hungary-Croatia, Ragusa and Venice. In 1298 Genoa defeated Venice in the Battle of Curzola off the coast; a later tradition holds that Marco Polo was captured there, though other scholars place his capture elsewhere. Venice held the island until 1797, using its timber and, from 1776, its arsenal. It then passed to the Habsburg monarchy, was held by the French from 1806 and by British forces from 4 February 1813, and returned to Austria in 1815. Italy ruled it from 1918 to 1921 and again from 1941, and since 1991 it has been part of Croatia.

Korčula's stonemasonry tradition reached its peak under Venetian rule. The Moreška sword dance, which arrived in the 16th century, is performed in the town of Korčula, and the island has a long history of klapa, a cappella singing. The poet and dramatist Petar Kanavelić, a leading Croatian writer of the 17th century, came from there. Korčula is the second most populous Adriatic island after Krk and is known for Grk, a white wine produced only on the island.
kordofan: Kordofan is a region in central Sudan covering some 376,145 square kilometres. It is largely an undulating plain, with the Nuba Mountains in the southeast. The rainy season from June to September makes the area fertile, but in the dry season it is virtually desert. The region is known for gum arabic, and its crops include groundnuts, cotton and millet. Its chief town is El Obeid. Kordofan was originally inhabited by Nubian-speaking peoples and in antiquity was part of the Kingdom of Kush, and in the Middle Ages of the Nubian kingdoms of Alodia and Makuria. By the 14th century Arabs from Egypt were expanding southwards into it, and most of its inhabitants are now Arabs, among them the semi-nomadic Baggara and camel-raising Kababish.

For centuries Kordofan largely escaped control by any one of the region's major states, though the Funj Sultanate of Sennar had influence over its east. In 1734 Isawi of the Musabba'at, an exiled faction of Darfur's royal family, dislodged the Funj administration there. Abu Likaylik later conquered it, and about 1772 Hashim of the Musabba'at led an insurgency that retook it. The Funj ousted Hashim in 1780 and held Kordofan for about five years. After a decisive defeat of Sennar in 1784 the country was under Darfur viceroys and enjoyed prosperity: tribute was a voluntary present to the Sultan of Darfur, merchants paid no duties, and caravans brought goods from Abyssinia and Egypt to El Obeid and Bara.

This ended in 1821, when Muhammad Ali Pasha, Ottoman viceroy of Egypt, sent his son-in-law Mahommed Bey the Defturdar with about 4,500 soldiers and eight pieces of artillery to subject Kordofan; the monopoly of the Egyptian governors then impeded trade. The Mahdi captured El Obeid in 1883, and an Egyptian force under the British general William Hicks was ambushed and annihilated at Sheikan to its south. After the British reoccupation in 1898 Kordofan became one of the provinces of the Sudan.

Kordofan was split in 1973 into the provinces of North Kordofan and South Kordofan, which became states in 1994 together with West Kordofan. West Kordofan was abolished in August 2005, under the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, and re-established in July 2013. Its population was estimated at 3.6 million in 2000. Armed conflict broke out in South Kordofan in June 2011, ahead of the independence of South Sudan, and the war in Sudan from 2023 brought fighting to the region again.
korea: Korea consists of the Korean Peninsula, Jeju Island and smaller islands in East Asia. The peninsula extends southward about 1,100 km from the continent, between the Sea of Japan to the east and the Yellow Sea to the west, and the Korea Strait lies between it and Japan. The Amnok (Yalu) River separates it from China in the northwest and the Duman (Tumen) River from China and Russia in the northeast. The name Korea is a modern spelling of Corea, attested in English from 1614, which comes from the kingdom of Goryeo.

According to Korean legend, Dangun founded Gojoseon in 2333 BCE. The Han dynasty defeated it in 108 BCE and installed four commanderies in the north, and Goguryeo annexed them all by 313. In the Three Kingdoms period Goguryeo held the north and Manchuria, while Baekje and Silla held the south. Silla allied with the Tang dynasty in the 640s to conquer Baekje and Goguryeo and drove the Tang from the peninsula in 676. Goryeo, founded in 918, replaced Silla, and in the 13th century it became a vassal state of the Mongol Empire.

In 1392 General Yi Seong-gye overthrew Goryeo and founded the Joseon dynasty, with its capital at Hanseong, now Seoul, and in 1394 he adopted Confucianism as the official ideology. The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was created in the 15th century. Japanese and Qing invasions later devastated Joseon. After Japan's victory in the First Sino-Japanese War in 1895, China lost suzerainty over Korea, and in 1897 Joseon became the Korean Empire. Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910. In 1945 Soviet and American zones were set at the 38th parallel, two governments were established in 1948, and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953, in which more than 1.2 million people died, ended in an armistice.

Korea is divided between North Korea and South Korea, with a demilitarized zone approximating the original partition. Korean is the official language of both and is written almost entirely in Hangul. Confucian tradition has dominated Korean thought, alongside Buddhism, Taoism and Korean Shamanism. Surviving works of its early history include Cheomseongdae, an astronomical observatory built in 634, and the Great Dharani Sutra, the earliest known surviving Korean woodblock printing, believed to date from 750-51.
korean-liberation-army: After Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and crushed the March First Movement of 1919, Korean exiles in Shanghai founded the Korean Provisional Government, which wanted an army from the start but lacked money and men. In 1933 Kim Gu won leave from Chiang Kai-shek to train Korean fighters at the Luoyang branch of the Republic of China Military Academy, disguised as an all-Chinese class; 62 of its 92 students graduated before it closed on 9 April 1935, and most later joined the army. The government fled with the Kuomintang across China after war broke out in July 1937 and reached Chongqing around 1939.

Chiang approved Kim's proposal on 11 April 1940 but then withdrew funding over the army's independence, and Kim went ahead. The army was proclaimed on 17 September 1940 at a dawn ceremony in the Jialing Hotel, timed to avoid Japanese air raids, with General Chi Ch'ŏngch'ŏn as commander and General Lee Beom-seok later as chief of staff. It moved its headquarters to Xi'an and grew to 3,600 troops by 1943, though it suffered from funding problems and infighting. The Kuomintang recognised it on 28 May 1941 and placed it under the Chinese commander-in-chief, while the United States declined to recognise the government in exile.

In 1942 the Korean Volunteers Army of Kim Won-bong, Kim Gu's left-leaning rival, was merged into it, to the displeasure of both sides. At British request, for Japanese speakers, nine men went to Calcutta on 29 August 1943 and served on the edges of Burma and India, notably at the Battle of Imphal. On 1 May 1945 the government in exile won full control of the army, and with the Office of Strategic Services it prepared the Eagle Project, a mission into Korea set to leave on 20 August under Lee. Japan's announced surrender on 15 August ended the plan.

The army was disbanded in June 1946, and its members returned to Korea in late 1945 and 1946. Many of them, including Generals Chi and Lee, joined the Government of the Republic of Korea, and some of its generals and officers helped form the ROK Armed Forces. There has long been a campaign in South Korea to move the National Armed Forces Day from 1 October to 17 September, the army's founding day.
korean-war: Korea had been a colony of the Empire of Japan from 1910 to 1945. As the Second World War drew to a close, two American colonels, Dean Rusk and Charles H. Bonesteel III, chose the 38th parallel on 11 August 1945 as the line dividing the peninsula into a Soviet and an American occupation zone. The zones formed their own governments in 1948: North Korea under Kim Il Sung in Pyongyang and South Korea under Syngman Rhee in Seoul, each claiming to be the only legitimate government of all Korea. Border clashes were extensive, and Kim Il Sung began seeking Stalin's support for an invasion in March 1949.

On 25 June 1950 the Korean People's Army crossed the 38th parallel behind artillery fire, with tanks against a South Korean army that had none. The UN Security Council denounced the invasion the same day; the Soviet representative, whose government was boycotting the council, was absent and could not veto. UN forces comprised 21 countries, with the United States providing around 90 per cent of the military personnel. Seoul fell on 28 June, and by early August the South Korean army and its allies held only the Pusan Perimeter in the south-east.

On 15 September UN forces landed at Incheon, well behind the North Korean lines, and broke out of the perimeter soon afterwards. They retook Seoul and invaded North Korea in October. On 19 October the Chinese People's Volunteer Army crossed the Yalu and entered the war. Chinese and North Korean forces took Seoul a second time on 4 January 1951, before a UN counter-offensive regained it two months later. The fighting then became a war of attrition with little change of territory, while armistice talks began on 10 July 1951 and were delayed for two years by the repatriation of prisoners of war. Throughout, the United Nations Command bombed North Korea.

Combat ended on 27 July 1953 with the signing of the Korean Armistice Agreement, which allowed the exchange of prisoners and created a demilitarised zone four kilometres wide along the front line. The war caused around one million military deaths and an estimated 1.5 million to 3 million civilian deaths. Alleged war crimes include the mass killing of alleged communists by South Korea, the Seoul National University Hospital massacre by North Korea and the carpet bombing of North Korea by the United Nations Command. No peace treaty has been signed. The war saw armoured offensives, tunnel warfare by Chinese forces and the first large jet aircraft battles.
koreans: The origin of the Koreans has not been well clarified. Linguistic, archaeological and genetic evidence places it somewhere in Northeast Asia, but the pattern of their expansion and arrival on the peninsula remains unclear. Archaeological evidence suggests that Proto-Koreans were migrants from Manchuria in the Bronze Age, and some scholars connect the arrival of early Koreans with the Bronze Age dagger culture that expanded from the West Liao River region. Whitman suggests that Proto-Koreans reached the south of the peninsula around 300 BCE and lived alongside, or absorbed, the descendants of Japonic Mumun cultivators. Other scholars reject the idea that Korean speakers were not native to the peninsula and say that no solid evidence of a migration has been found.

The names Koreans use for themselves recall their past states. South Koreans say Hanguk-in, people of the Han, a name taken from the Three Kingdoms of Korea. North Koreans say Joseon-in, people of Joseon, the last dynastic kingdom. Ethnic Koreans in Russia and Central Asia call themselves Koryo-saram, after Goryeo, the dynasty of 918 to 1392 that also gave rise to the word Korea.

Large-scale emigration began in the mid-1860s, mainly into the Russian Far East and Northeast China. These populations later grew to more than two million Koreans in China and several hundred thousand Koryo-saram in Central Asia and the former Soviet Union. During Japanese rule, from 1910 to 1945, Koreans were often recruited or forced into labour in mainland Japan, Sakhalin and Manchukuo. Those who stayed in Japan after the war became the Zainichi Koreans, and about 40,000 trapped in Sakhalin after the Soviet invasion are called Sakhalin Koreans. Many Koryo-saram descend from Koreans forcibly deported under Stalin.

The Koreans speak Korean, written mainly in Hangul, which was invented by Sejong the Great. Hanja, the Chinese characters, are now used mostly for academic, historical and religious purposes. North and South Korea share a common heritage, though the political division since 1945 has led to some divergence in modern culture.

The historian Eugene Y. Park observes that many Koreans have a memory blackout of their genealogy before the twentieth century. Only a small share of Koreans had surnames and ancestral seats at first, and the rest took them in the last two or three hundred years. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries families devised master narratives that trace one surname and ancestral seat to a single ancestor, a practice that became universal in the nineteenth century.
korla: Korla, also known as Kurla or Kuerle, is the second largest city by population in Xinjiang and a county-level city. It is the seat of the Bayingolin Mongol Autonomous Prefecture, the largest prefecture of China, and lies about 200 kilometres south-west of Ürümqi, though the Tian Shan between them makes the road distance much longer. The Kaidu River, also called the Konqi or Kongque River, flows through the centre of the city, a rare feature among cities in Xinjiang. The Iron Gate Pass, about 7 kilometres to the north, was easily defended and protected the ancient Silk Roads from raiding nomads. The climate is cold desert, with about 59 millimetres of rain a year.

Korla has existed since at least the Han dynasty, when it was known as Yuli. The Hanshu records that it had 1,200 households and 9,600 people, 2,000 of them able to bear arms, and that it adjoined Shanshan and Qiemo. In 94 CE the general Ban Chao sent soldiers against Yanqi (Karashahr), Weixu, Yuli and Shanguo; the heads of the kings of Yanqi and Yuli were sent to Luoyang, and the kings of Yuli, Weixu and Shanguo were replaced. After the rebellion of the Western Regions of 106 to 125 CE, only the kings of Korla and Hoxud refused to submit, and Ban Yong, son of Ban Chao, defeated them.

The historian Musa Sayrami stated that Yaqub Beg of Yettishar was poisoned in Korla on 30 May 1877 by the former hakim Niyaz Hakim Beg of Yarkand, although Niyaz Hakim Beg and other sources said he died by suicide or in battle against the Qing. Francis Younghusband, passing through in 1887, found the town prosperous, with more land under cultivation than any other town on his journey and maize as the main crop. It was incorporated as a city on 30 September 1979.

The census of 2010 counted 549,324 people, up from 381,943 in 2000, and the city is home to 23 ethnic groups. PetroChina's Tarim oil fields operations are headquartered in Korla, which is also known for its fragrant pears. It is a regional transport hub served by the national highways G218 and G314, the Southern Xinjiang Railway and an airport. Among its sights are the Iron Gate Pass, the Lotus Pond, the Jiamai Mosque and the ruins of the Yuzigan Old City.
korntal: Korntal was first documented in 1297 in the records of Sindelfingen. Until 1819 it was an estate belonging to the municipality of Weilimdorf, which is now part of Stuttgart. In 1819 the town of Korntal was founded as a civic-religious community on the model of the communities established in Germany by the Moravian Church. In connection with the construction of the Great Hall of Württemberg, William I of Württemberg granted the community certain special rights. These were lost in 1919 with the Weimar constitution, by which time the community was no longer connected to the Moravian Church.

Korntal station opened in 1868 on the Black Forest Railway between Zuffenhausen and Calw, and on 30 June 1958 Korntal received the status of a city. Its neighbour Münchingen was first documented in 1130 in the Zwiefalter Chronicle and was ceded in 1336 by the sons of Ulrich von Asperg to Count Ulrich of Württemberg. It had St Catharine's Hospital from 1278 and a mill from 1381, and much of the village was destroyed in the Thirty Years' War. Münchingen received a rail connection, the Strohgäubahn, in 1906.

Korntal-Münchingen was created on 1 January 1975, in the district reform of Baden-Württemberg, by combining the city of Korntal and the community of Münchingen, against the declared will of most of the citizens of Münchingen. The merger was seen as a better alternative to Korntal being absorbed by Stuttgart. The town lies in the Strohgäu on the northwestern border of Stuttgart, in the district of Ludwigsburg, and has three districts: Korntal, Münchingen and Kallenberg. At Liegnitzer Straße the border with Stuttgart runs through a built-up area, so that houses on one side of the street belong to Korntal and those on the other to Weilimdorf. The missionary Johann Ludwig Krapf died there, and Rosina Widmann, an educator and missionary in Ghana, came from Korntal.
koroni: Koroni was founded in ancient times, and the geographer Pausanias places the original town at modern Petalidi, a few kilometres to the north. The town later moved to its present site, where ancient Asini had stood, and the Byzantines built a fortress there in the 6th and 7th centuries. After the fall of Constantinople to the Fourth Crusade in 1204 the Peloponnese passed to Frankish crusaders. A Venetian fleet took the fortress and nearby Methoni in 1206 or 1207, and Geoffrey of Villehardouin, Prince of Achaea, recognized the possession in the Treaty of Sapienza in June 1209.

For three centuries Coron and Modon, the first Venetian possessions on the Greek mainland, served as a base for galleys and ships on their way to the Levant, and a Venetian document called them the chief eyes of the Republic. Merchants and pilgrims to the Holy Land stopped there, and Koroni was noted for cochineal, from which crimson dyes were made. It became the seat of Latin bishops, one of whom, Angelo Correr, became Pope Gregory XII. Sultan Bayezid II stormed Methoni in 1500 and Koroni surrendered in August of that year.

Andrea Doria retook the town in 1532, but Hayreddin Barbarossa forced the Spanish garrison to surrender in 1534. Venice recaptured it after a siege from 25 June to 7 August 1685, held it as part of the Kingdom of the Morea until 1715, and the Ottomans then retook it. Koroni became part of the modern Greek state in 1828, liberated by the French general Nicolas Joseph Maison. Today it is a town of 1,193 people in 2021 on the southwest peninsula of the Peloponnese, on the Gulf of Messinia, below a Venetian castle, and part of the municipality of Pylos-Nestor. Between 1966 and 1989 a sounding-rocket launch facility near the town sent up 371 rockets.
koror: Koror is a state of the Republic of Palau, made up of many islands, the best known being Koror Island, also called Oreor. It stretches across a large part of the lagoon from Babeldaob Island in the north almost to Beliliou Island in the south. Its land area is small, but it includes hundreds of islands and islets, among them most of the Rock Islands. In the northern part are three volcanic islands: Koror, Ngerekebesang and Ngemelachel. The Rock Islands are uplifted coralline limestone reef with sheer cliffs above a sea-level notch, covered in forest, with marine lakes in some sinkholes. The state has a tropical rainforest climate, with rainfall averaging around 3,750 millimetres a year. Its official languages are Palauan and English.

In the oral tradition of Palau, Koror is one of the children of Milad and has an important place in traditional belief. It is the home of the clan of the Ibedul, the high chief of Palau. Several traditional villages span the volcanic and rock island areas. Many stone platforms, called odesongel, served as clan cemeteries, and other stone features served as shrines. The lagoon was an important resource area and was probably exploited intensively in prehistoric times.

Koror was the capital of the South Seas Mandate, a League of Nations mandate administered by the Empire of Japan. Malakal Harbor, a sheltered deep-water anchorage, has been in continual use since the 1840s. Prince Lee Boo, who lived from 1764 to 1784, is among the town's notable residents. The state adopted its own constitution in 1983, and its government was established the same year.

More people live in Koror than in the rest of Palau, and it is the main commercial centre of the country. The second largest settlement is Meyuns. The islands are linked by bridges, and the Koror-Babeldaob Bridge connects the island to the state of Airai, where Palau International Airport is located.
