The school has existed since at least 1549, and the writer Adalbert Stifter was a pupil. In 2010 several monks were suspended over abuse at the boarding school, and in July 2013 an Austrian court sentenced its former director, August Mandorfer, to twelve years in prison.
kriegsmarine: Under the 1919 Treaty of Versailles Germany was allowed a minimal navy of 15,000 personnel, six capital ships of no more than 10,000 tons, six cruisers, twelve destroyers and twelve torpedo boats, with no submarines, aircraft carriers or naval aviation. The ships and men were taken over from the Kaiserliche Marine, which was renamed the Reichsmarine. Germany worked from the outset to circumvent the limits, keeping up U-boat design through an office in the Netherlands and developing the G7e torpedo in Sweden. On 15 November 1932 the government decided on a prohibited naval re-armament.

The Anglo-German Naval Agreement of 18 June 1935 allowed Germany a navy equal to 35 per cent of British surface tonnage and 45 per cent of British submarine tonnage, and that year the Reichsmarine became the Kriegsmarine. Its first military action came in the Spanish Civil War, when ships were sent to Spanish waters from July 1936 under the cover of non-intervention while covertly supporting Francisco Franco's Nationalists. After Republican bombers attacked the Deutschland off Ibiza on 29 May 1937, killing 31, the Admiral Scheer shelled Almeria, killing 19 or 20 civilians.

In January 1939 Adolf Hitler approved Plan Z, a programme of about 800 ships for 1939 to 1947, built around six H-class battleships and meant to give parity with the Royal Navy. The outbreak of war in September 1939 shelved it in favour of U-boats, and resources went first to the army and air force. In the first months the Kriegsmarine sank the carrier HMS Courageous and the battleship HMS Royal Oak, and lost the Admiral Graf Spee at the Battle of the River Plate.

Wolfpacks of submarines attacked British convoys in the Battle of the Atlantic, but the tactic was largely abandoned by May 1943 as U-boat losses mounted. After the failure at the Battle of the Barents Sea, Hitler concluded that large warships were useless, and Erich Raeder was replaced as commander-in-chief by Karl Dönitz on 30 January 1943. Dönitz became President of Germany on Hitler's suicide in April 1945.

Hitler was supreme commander, exercising authority through the Oberkommando der Marine. The Luftwaffe held a near-monopoly on military aviation, a source of rivalry with the navy. Kriegsmarine personnel also manned coastal artillery, flak batteries and radar. From mid-1944 surplus personnel were formed into about 40 land regiments and, from January 1945, six divisions. After Germany surrendered, the surviving ships were divided among the victors. At Liepāja in Latvia, in July 1941, its commandants ordered hostages shot and issued anti-Jewish regulations.
kris: The word kris comes from an Old Javanese term meaning dagger. A Chinese source of the 10th century, under the Song dynasty, records that an envoy from She-po, or Java, arrived at court in 992 with gifts that included a small dagger with a hilt of rhino horn and gold. Although the peoples of Southeast Asia already knew stabbing weapons of this type, the kris most probably developed in Java and spread through the archipelago, Malaysia, southern Thailand and the Philippines by diplomacy and trade. A Sundanese manuscript dated to 1518 CE describes the kris as the weapon of kings. Claims of forms older than the Majapahit kris cannot be verified.

A kris has three parts: the blade (bilah or wilah), the hilt (hulu) and the sheath (warangka), each treated as a work of art in carved wood, metal, gold or ivory. Blades are between 38 and 127 cm long and are not normally sharpened, as the weapon is for stabbing. The number of curves, or luk, is always odd, and blades from the Majapahit era are straight, as were more than half of all kris before modern times. The pamor pattern comes from iron with a little nickel, perhaps iron ore from Sulawesi, forged in layers.

The maker was a specialist smith called an empu, a title in Java for those with the skill, and with knowledge of literature, history and the occult as well as spiritual power, since a kris is believed to have a presence of its own. Some blades take years to complete. Heirloom kris, or pusaka, are considered to have good or bad luck, and tales such as that of Empu Gandring's unfinished kris, told in the Pararaton, give some of them supernatural powers.

Although many assume the kris was the main weapon of fighters, warriors carried it as a secondary arm if they lost their main weapon, usually a spear. Commoners wore it daily, especially when travelling, and in peacetime it formed part of ceremonial dress. Men usually wore one, women a smaller one, and heirloom blades were handed down and worn at weddings and other ceremonies. It signalled status, heroism and authority. Javanese, Balinese and Sundanese traditionally wear it at the back, to show that violence is the last resort, whereas elsewhere in the archipelago it is worn at the front or the left hip.

In Bali the kris dance in the Barong performance shows men in trance stabbing themselves unhurt. Kris-making is preserved in the courts of Yogyakarta and Surakarta and in the principalities of Mangkunegaran and Pakualaman, though it nearly came to a standstill before the 1990s and has since revived. In 2005 UNESCO listed the Indonesian kris on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
krishna: The tradition of Krishna appears to have grown from the merging of several independent deities of ancient India, the earliest attested being Vāsudeva, a hero-god of the Vrishni tribe, whose worship is attested from the 5th to 6th centuries BCE in the writings of Pāṇini and from the 2nd century BCE in inscriptions such as the Heliodorus pillar. The Vrishnis were later thought to have merged with the Yadavas, whose hero-god was Krishna, and the two deities became one, who was identified with Vishnu in the Mahabharata. Around 180 BCE the Indo-Greek king Agathocles issued coins whose images are now read as Balarama and Vāsudeva-Krishna. The Mahabharata is the earliest text to describe Krishna as a personality in detail.

Hindus worship Krishna as the eighth avatar of Vishnu and, in Krishnaite traditions, as the Supreme God. His name is a Sanskrit word meaning black, dark or dark blue, and he is usually shown with dark or blue skin. The Mahabharata, the Harivamsa, the Bhagavata Purana and the Vishnu Purana tell his life, and agree on the main story. He is born in a prison at Mathura to Devaki and Vasudeva and raised by Nanda and Yashoda, because Devaki's brother, the tyrant Kamsa, has been told that her eighth child will kill him. As a boy he is a cowherd and a prankster, the butter thief, who lifts Govardhana hill to shelter Vrindavana from rain.

As an adult he kills Kamsa and leads the Yadavas to the city of Dwaraka. In the Kurukshetra War he serves as Arjuna's charioteer on condition that he raise no weapon, and his counsel to Arjuna forms the Bhagavad Gita.

Krishna is a central figure of bhakti, devotional worship, within Vaishnavism, and devotees see lila, divine play, as the central principle of the universe. His birth is observed each year at Krishna Janmashtami, in late August or early September, with fasting, singing, night vigils and temple visits. Mathura and Vrindavan, where there are about 5,500 temples, are major pilgrimage sites, and regional forms include Jagannatha in Odisha, Vithoba in Maharashtra and Guruvayoorappan in Kerala. His stories inspired dance forms such as Bharatanatyam, Kathakali and Odissi, and reliefs at Prambanan in Java, dated to the 9th century, show episodes of his life.
krishna-raja-sagara: Mysore, and Mandya in particular, was dry country. A severe drought in 1875–76 killed a fifth of the population of the Kingdom of Mysore, and crop failures kept recurring for want of irrigation water. Any major new works on the Kaveri needed the consent of the downstream Madras Presidency under an agreement of 1892, and the dispute over the river's water, carried on today between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, shaped the dam's height and operation from the start.

The first chief engineer for the project, Captain Dawes, drowned in the Kaveri in 1909 while surveying the site near Kannambadi village. The Diwan T. Ananda Rao then brought in M. Visvesvaraya, who took up his post on 15 November 1909 and drew up the design. Mysore's finance ministry argued the project would serve no purpose, and the Maharaja hesitated over so large a sum before sanctioning it. The order to begin was issued on 11 October 1911, with ₹81 lakh set aside, a cost that later rose to about ₹1.03 crore.

The dam is a gravity dam built of surki mortar, standing just below the point where the Kaveri meets its tributaries the Hemavati and the Lakshmana Tirtha in Mandya district. In place of ordinary spillways Visvesvaraya fitted 48 automatic gates in six sets of eight, which open and close as the reservoir rises and falls. He had invented and patented the mechanism for Lake Fife near Khadakvasla in the Bombay Presidency. The cast-iron gates were made at Bhadravati. An arbitration award by H. D. Griffin on 12 May 1914 allowed Mysore to build to the full planned height of 124.80 feet.

Ten thousand workers were employed, and the First World War cut the supply of cement imported from Britain just as the main masonry began. A fifty-year agreement of 1924 between Mysore and Madras permitted both the dam and the Madras government's Mettur dam and set out how the water would be shared; a supplementary agreement of 1929 fixed the quantities to be released.

The reservoir became the main source of drinking water for Mysore, Mandya and nearly all of Bengaluru, and its canals turned rain-fed fields of ragi and maize to rice and sugarcane. The Mysore Sugar Company opened at Mandya on 30 January 1933, and the district became known as Sakkare Nagara, Sugar City. Visvesvaraya later called the scheme a miniature version of the Tennessee Valley Authority.
krishna-river: The Krishna River, in full Krishnaveni, is the third-longest river in India after the Ganga and Godavari, and the fourth-largest in water inflow and basin area. It rises in the Western Ghats near Mahabaleshwar in Maharashtra at an elevation of about 1,300 metres, flows past the town of Wai and continues east until it empties into the Bay of Bengal. It passes through Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana and is a major source of irrigation in all four states.

It has 13 major tributaries, among them the Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Bhima, Tungabhadra and Musi. The Bhima is the longest, at 861 kilometres. The basin covers 258,948 square kilometres, nearly 8 per cent of India's area, and most of it is rolling country, bounded on the west by the unbroken line of the Western Ghats. Its soils include black and red soils, laterite and alluvium, and the Krishna-Godavari delta is known as the Rice Granary of India.

Jain literary sources, including the Kalpasutra and the Nisithacurni, describe the region near the Krishnavena as Abhiradesa, the land of the Abhiras, which points to an early association with that people. Hindus revere the river as sacred and believe that it removes the sins of those who bathe in it. Every twelve years the Krishna Pushkaram fair is held on its banks. The first holy place on the river is Wai, known for the Mahaganpati Mandir and the Kashivishweshwar temple, with seven ghats on the river.

Kudalasangama, where the Krishna meets the Malaprabha, holds the samadhi of Basavanna, the founder of the Lingayat sect. Other holy places include Srisailam, with the Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga, and the Kanaka Durga Temple at Vijayawada. The three tributaries Panchganga, Warana and Yerla meet the Krishna near Sangli, and Hindus consider these places holy. The Bhilawadi Krishna Ghat is believed to date from 1779.

The basin holds oil and gas in the Krishna-Godavari Basin, coal at Yellandu, iron ore and other minerals. The Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary protects the last surviving mangrove forests in its estuary. Many dams and barrages cross the river, among them the Almatti, Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar and Tungabhadra dams and the Prakasam Barrage. Bridges built under British rule, such as the Irwin Bridge at Sangli, still cross it.
krishnadevaraya: Krishnadevaraya was born on 17 January 1471, the son of Tuluva Narasa Nayaka, an army commander, and his queen Nagamamba, and came to the throne after the death of his half-brother Viranarasimha. In 1513 he fought Sultan Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda in person at Pangal, where the Vijayanagara army was defeated and obliged to retreat. His army laid siege to Udayagiri in 1512 and, after a campaign of about a year, took Kondaveedu through a night attack found by his prime minister Timmarusu. The Gajapati king Prataparudra Deva was driven to Cuttack, surrendered and gave his daughter Jaganmohini in marriage to Krishnadevaraya, and the Krishna River became the boundary of the two kingdoms.

He established friendly relations with the Portuguese in Goa in 1510, obtaining guns and Arabian horses and Portuguese help with the capital's water supply. On 19 May 1520 he secured Raichur Fort from Ismail Adil Shah after a difficult siege in which 16,000 Vijayanagara soldiers were killed, helped by a Portuguese contingent under Cristovão de Figueiredo. His reply to the Sultan's envoys was haughty, and he then occupied Bijapur and proclaimed the eldest of three imprisoned Bahmani princes king of the Deccan. At home he abolished taxes such as the marriage fee and made annual tours of the empire. The travellers Paes, Nunez and Barbosa praised the efficiency of his administration.

Krishnadevaraya composed the Telugu poem Amuktamalyada, on which he based his view that a king should rule with an eye to dharma, and several Sanskrit works including Madalasa Charita and Jambavati Kalyana. His reign is regarded as a golden age of Telugu literature, and eight Telugu poets known as the Ashtadiggajas, among them Allasani Peddana and Mukku Timmana, adorned his court. He also patronised Kannada, Sanskrit and Tamil poets; the court language was Kannada. The Madhva saint Vyasatirtha was his rajaguru, though Sri Vaishnavas claim that Venkata Tathacharya held the role.

He rebuilt the Virupaksha Temple and made land grants to Tirumala, Srisailam, Chidambaram and other temples. He visited the Tirumala Venkateswara Temple seven times, and 229 of its roughly 1,250 published inscriptions are attributed to him.

In 1524 Krishnadevaraya made his son Tirumala Raya crown prince; the prince was poisoned soon afterwards, and the king, suspecting Timmarusu, had him blinded. He fell ill while preparing an attack on Belgaum and died on 17 October 1529, succeeded by his brother Achyuta Deva Raya. The Mughal emperor Babur considered him the most powerful ruler in India, and Mukku Timmana praised him as the destroyer of the Turks.
krishnaraja-wodeyar-iii: He was born at Srirangapatna on 14 July 1794, the son of Maharaja Chamaraja Wadiyar IX and his first wife, Maharani Kempananjammani Devi. His adoptive grandmother, Maharani Lakshmi Devi, oversaw his education and upbringing. Through the years of Hyder Ali and Tipu she had sent feelers to the British, hoping to see the kingdom returned to the Wadiyars, and she informed them of Tipu's treaty with the French. After Tipu's death in 1799 she negotiated the handing over of the throne.

The boy was installed on 30 June 1799 in a pavilion built near the Lakshmiramana Swamy temple in Mysore, under her regency. Arthur Wellesley led Lakshmi Devi to the ceremony, and she arranged for Tipu's adviser Purnaiah to stay on as Dewan, loyal to the king until he came of age.

At sixteen, in early 1810, he was no longer counted a minor, and after discussion with Arthur Cole, the British Resident, the government passed from Purnaiah to the young Maharaja. His grandmother died that year and Purnaiah in 1812. Relations with the British were cordial until the 1820s. In 1825 Thomas Munro, governor of Madras, found no substance in Cole's charges of financial impropriety, but the Nagar revolt changed matters. In 1831, citing maladministration, the British set up the Mysore Commission; Mark Cubbon headed it from 1834 to 1861. The Maharaja died on 27 March 1868 and was succeeded by his grandson and adopted son, Chamarajendra Wadiyar X.

The Maharaja was himself a writer, credited with more than 50 works, among them Sritattvanidhi, Saugandhika Parinaya and Surya Chandra Vamsavali, which retells a hundred episodes from the Ramayana and the Mahabharata and the deeds of the dynasty's founders. He knew Sanskrit, Kannada, Tamil, English, Telugu and Urdu, played the veena, and is credited with reviving the game of Ganjifa. His court helped shape modern Kannada prose and the survival of Yakshagana. Basavappa Shastri translated Othello into Kannada as Shurasena Charita, and the royal workshop produced murals and illustrated manuscripts of the Bhagavata Purana and the Ramayana.
krishnaraja-wodeyar-iv: Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV was born on 4 June 1884 in Mysore Palace, the son of Maharaja Chamarajendra Wadiyar X and Maharani Kempananjammanni Devi. After his father died suddenly in Calcutta in 1894, his mother ruled as regent while he was a boy. As the fourth king of the name he is known in Kannada as Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wadiyar, from nālvaḍi, the fourth.

He was educated at Lokaranjan Palace in Mysore under P. Raghavendra Rao, studying Kannada and Sanskrit beside Western subjects, horse-riding and Indian and Western classical music. Sir Stuart Fraser of the Bombay Civil Service trained him in administration, and long tours of the state taught him the country. George Curzon, the Governor-General of India, invested him with full ruling powers in 1902 at Jaganmohana Palace.

The Mysore Representative Assembly, founded in 1881, was enlarged in his reign and became bicameral in 1907 with the creation of the Mysore Legislative Council. Bangalore had street lights from 5 August 1905, and princes from other parts of India were sent to Mysore for administrative training. He abolished child marriage for girls below the age of eight, promoted girls' education, offered scholarships to widows and encouraged spinning, for which Gandhi praised him.

He founded the University of Mysore, the first university chartered by an Indian province, co-founded Banaras Hindu University, and was first chancellor of both. The Indian Institute of Science at Bangalore began its work in 1911 with his gift of 371 acres of land and funds. He played eight instruments, among them the veena, sitar and saxophone, wrote poems in Kannada, and hosted musicians of the Agra Gharana and Abdul Karim Khan.

In 1900 he married Pratapa Kumari Devi, youngest daughter of Rana Bane Singh of Vana in Kathiawar, the first marriage between the Mysore royal family and a Rajput house of northern India; they had no children. He died of a heart attack on 3 August 1940, when his fortune was estimated at US$400 million, and was succeeded by his nephew Jayachamaraja Wadiyar. In 1930 John Sankey called Mysore the best administered state in the world, and he is often regarded as the father of modern Mysore.
krivichs: The Krivichs, also written Kryvichs, were a tribal union of early East Slavs between the 6th and the 12th centuries. It is suggested that they were originally native to the area around Pskov and that they moved into mostly Finnic areas in the upper reaches of the Volga, the Dnieper and the Dvina, south of the lower Velikaya and into parts of the Neman basin. According to Max Vasmer, their name probably comes from that of their forefather Kriv, an interpretation that stems from East Slavic mythology. The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus mentions the tribe in De Administrando Imperio under forms such as Κριβιτζοί.

The Krivichs left many archaeological monuments: the remains of agricultural settlements with traces of ironworking, jewellery-making, blacksmith's work and other crafts, long burial mounds of the 6th to 9th centuries with cremated bodies, mounds of rich warriors with weapons, and distinctive jewellery such as bracelet-like temple rings and glass beads made of stretched wire. By the end of the first millennium they had well-developed farming and cattle-breeding.

They settled along the trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks and traded with the Varangians. Their chief tribal centres included Gnezdovo, Izborsk and Polotsk. As a tribe they took part in the military campaigns of Oleg and Igor against the Byzantine Empire.

The name outlived the tribe. In Latvian, Krievs means a Russian and Krievija means Russia, and through the Baltic lands the word became known in Central Europe: a German chronicler from Duisburg wrote in 1314 of the land of Crivitae, and a Polish publication of 1687 called the Polotsk saint Paraxedis the queen of the Kryvians. In Latvian a Belarusian is a Baltkrievs, and Belarus is Baltkrievija. The Belarusian historian Vaclau Lastouski published a magazine called Kryvich in Kaunas from 1923 to 1927. Places called Kryvičy in modern Belarus may be named after the tribe, though this is contested.
krnov: Krnov lies in the historic region of Czech Silesia, on the border with Poland, at the confluence of the Opava and Opavice rivers. It is about 21 kilometres northwest of Opava and 49 kilometres northwest of Ostrava. The town proper lies in the Zlatohorská Highlands, and the western and southern parts of its territory reach into the Nízký Jeseník range. The highest point is the hill Bednářský vrch, at 588 metres. It is a town of the Bruntál District in the Moravian-Silesian Region and has about 22,000 inhabitants.

The first written mention of Krnov dates from 1240, and it was a town by 1269 at the latest, perhaps from 1253. Fortifications were built in the second half of the 13th century, and the Minorites came in 1273 and founded a monastery. Krnov belonged to the Duchy of Troppau until 1377, when the Duchy of Krnov separated and the town became its capital. In 1523 the duchy passed to the Hohenzollern family, who built a castle; the town reached its peak of prosperity and growth under their rule.

The Thirty Years' War brought decline, and after the war the duchy passed to the Liechtenstein family, who began the re-Catholicisation of the duchy. After the War of the Austrian Succession Krnov became a border town, and a fire in 1779 destroyed almost the whole town. Industrialisation in the 19th century, with textile factories and a railway opened in 1872, more than doubled its population in a few decades. In 1910 about 98 percent of its 16,681 people gave German as their native language. From 1938 to 1945 Germany occupied it, and after the war the German population was expelled under the Potsdam Agreement.

The Neo-Renaissance town hall, built in 1901 to 1903, was designed by Leopold Bauer, a native of Krnov. The Church of Saint Martin was first documented in 1281, and the Krnov Synagogue is the only one in the region to survive in its original form. The former cotton mill and the pilgrimage site on the Cvilín hill, with its Church of Our Lady of the Seven Sorrows built in 1722 to 1727, are protected as national cultural monuments. The town is known for the drink Kofola, and its pipe-organ firm Rieger-Kloss was founded in 1873.
kromeriz: Kroměříž lies on both banks of the Morava River in the Zlín Region, about 20 kilometres north-west of Zlín, where the Haná River flows into the Morava on the town's northern edge. Its name comes from the personal name Kroměžir, meaning Kroměžir's property. In the Middle Ages it was a market village at the crossing of the Amber and Salt roads, at a ford across the Morava where a toll was collected.

The first written mention, under the Latin name Cromezir, is in a document written between 1107 and 1125, when the Olomouc bishop Jan II bought the settlement. In the thirteenth century it became the centre of a dominion of the Olomouc bishopric. Raids by Tatars, Cumans and Hungarians in 1241 and 1253 depopulated the settlement. Bishop Bruno von Schauenburg then rebuilt it, founding the market square on the hill above the old settlement, surrounding it with walls, building the Church of Saint Maurice and planting vineyards. The place was first called a town in 1266 and was officially promoted to a town in 1290.

Jews were allowed to settle in the town in 1322, and in the mid-sixteenth century its Jewish community was the largest in Moravia. The bishops lost control of the town during the Hussite Wars in 1423 and regained it in 1455. Bishop Stanislav I Thurzo rebuilt the bishop's residence as a castle in late Gothic and Renaissance style.

Swedish troops under Lennart Torstensson plundered the town in 1643, burning most of its buildings, and a large fire struck in 1656. Bishop Karl II von Liechtenstein-Kastelkorn then rebuilt the town and had the castle completely rebuilt by 1686, founding a mint and ornamental gardens between 1666 and 1675. The Constitutive Imperial Congress sat in Kroměříž in 1848, and in August 1885 the Austrian and Russian emperors met there.

Kroměříž is a town of about 28,000 inhabitants in the Czech Republic and is best known for its Baroque castle and gardens, added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1998. The historic centre is protected as an urban monument reservation. The Castle Gallery holds about 500 paintings, including a late work by Titian, the Flaying of Marsyas. The Church of Saint Maurice retains its early Gothic appearance and holds the grave of Bishop Bruno von Schauenburg.
kronborg: The castle began as a fortress called Krogen, meaning the Hook, built in the early fifteenth century by the Danish king Eric of Pomerania. He insisted that ships entering or leaving the Baltic Sea through the Øresund pay sound dues, and built a strong fortress at the narrowest point of the strait to enforce them. Denmark then held both shores, and with Helsingborg Castle opposite and a guard ship it could control all navigation.

Krogen stood on Ørekrog, a sandy tongue of land, and consisted of a square curtain wall with stone buildings inside. Large parts of its walls survive within the present castle, and Christian III added corner bastions in 1558 and 1559.

After the Northern Seven Years' War ended in 1570, Frederick II extended the bastions to meet the improved power of artillery. The works, led by the Flemish architect Hans Hendrik van Paesschen, were completed in 1577, and the castle then took the name Kronborg, Crown Castle. Its buildings were extended into three wings between 1574 and 1585. From 1578 Anthonis van Obbergen took over as master builder, and the south wing gained a storey and a ballroom measuring 62 by 12 metres, the largest hall in Northern Europe when finished in 1582.

The walls were clad in sandstone from Scania and the roof in copper. James VI of Scotland stayed there in 1590 after marrying Anne of Denmark. A fire on the night of 24 to 25 September 1629 destroyed much of the castle, sparing only the chapel. Christian IV rebuilt the exterior without major changes by 1639, though the interior never fully regained its former glory. During the war of 1658 to 1660 a Swedish army under Carl Gustaf Wrangel besieged and took Kronborg, and the Swedes carried off many art treasures, including the courtyard fountain.

The Crownwork and new ramparts followed in 1688 to 1690. From 1739 the castle also served as a prison, where Queen Caroline Mathilde was held in 1772. It was under military administration from 1785 to 1922, and the army left in 1923.

Kronborg is among the most important Renaissance castles in Northern Europe and was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2000. It was opened to the public in 1938 after a thorough renovation. As Elsinore, the anglicised name of the surrounding town of Helsingør, it is the setting of Shakespeare's Hamlet, which was first staged at the castle in 1816 by soldiers of the garrison and has been performed there many times since. A legend also places the sleeping Danish hero Ogier the Dane, or Holger Danske, at Kronborg, waiting until his homeland needs him; a statue of him lies in the casemates.
kronstadt-rebellion: Kronstadt, on Kotlin Island in the Gulf of Finland, was the main base of the Baltic Fleet and defended Petrograd. Its sailors had taken part in the October Revolution and the civil war, and Leon Trotsky had earlier called them the adornment and pride of the revolution. The island held about 50,000 civilians and 26,000 sailors and soldiers, most of them veterans of 1917.

As the Russian Civil War ended, the country was in ruin, and war communism and the forced seizure of peasants' grain deepened the hardship. A January cut of one third in bread rations led to demonstrations in Moscow and strikes in Petrograd, where about 60 percent of the large factories closed for lack of fuel. When the crews of the Petropavlovsk and Sevastopol heard of the repression in Petrograd, they passed a resolution of fifteen demands, including new elections to the soviets by secret ballot, freedom of speech and press for workers, peasants, anarchists and left socialists, and the release of political prisoners.

The rebels called their movement a third revolution, meant to restore power to freely elected soviets. They sought reform of the Bolshevik party, not its end, and rejected help from émigrés. The authorities presented them as agents of the Entente and counter-revolution, and issued an ultimatum on 5 March. Operations began on 7 March, when some 60,000 troops took part. Tukhachevsky's units advanced over the ice in a snowstorm; many soldiers drowned, others defected or refused to advance, and the attack failed.

On 16 March Tukhachevsky's reinforced army of 50,000 prepared to take the island and its 15,000 rebels, beginning with heavy artillery fire. Cadets and Red Army units attacked before dawn, and after heavy fighting on 17 March the last northern forts fell by 1 a.m. The revolt was suppressed on 18 March after it had lasted sixteen days. No power agreed to give the rebels military support, and no aid reached the island.

There were no public trials. Of about 2,000 prisoners, 13 were tried in private as leaders and sentenced to execution two days after the fall of Kronstadt. Hundreds of rebels were killed at Kronstadt and hundreds more shot in Petrograd, and the rest were sent to prisons and forced labour camps, where many died of hunger or disease.

Lenin called the crisis the most critical the Bolsheviks had yet faced. The rebellion did not meet its demands, but it hastened the New Economic Policy, which replaced war communism. Emma Goldman and other supporters of the regime lost their faith in it. Historian Paul Avrich judged that the rebels had little chance of success.
krosno-odrzanskie: Krosno Odrzańskie is a town in Lubusz Voivodeship in western Poland, on the east bank of the Oder at its confluence with the Bóbr. It is the capital of Krosno County. Its position at a point of passage across the Oder made it important on the western border of the Polish kingdom with the Holy Roman Empire from the 11th to the 13th centuries.

The town was first mentioned as Crosno in 1005, when Duke Bolesław I Chrobry of Poland had a fortress built there in his conflict with Emperor Henry II and the West Slavic Veleti confederation. In 1163 it belonged to the Duchy of Silesia, ruled by Bolesław I the Tall, and in 1201 his son Duke Henry I the Bearded gave it a town charter. Henry built a stone castle there, where he died in 1238 and where his widow Hedwig of Andechs took refuge during the first Mongol invasion of Poland in 1241. When the Duchy of Wrocław was divided in 1251, the town became part of the new Duchy of Głogów under Konrad I.

When the last Piast duke of Głogów, Henry XI, died without issue in 1476, his widow Barbara of Brandenburg, daughter of Elector Albert Achilles, inherited the territory. His cousin Duke Jan II the Mad of Żagań devastated the town in opposition, but in 1482 he signed an agreement with Albert Achilles, who kept the area. It remained formally a lien of the Bohemian kingdom until 1538, when King Ferdinand I renounced all rights, confirming its place in the Neumark of Brandenburg. With Brandenburg, Crossen became part of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701, of the Province of Brandenburg in 1815 and of the German Empire in 1871. A whirlwind devastated the town in May 1886.

The Red Army took the town in 1945, and it became Polish again. Polish communists from Poznań arrived on 2 May to take over its administration, and a second group of 66 members who also meant to rule it caused a conflict that was resolved by June. The adjective Odrzańskie, after the Oder, was added to distinguish it from other settlements of the same name, notably Krosno. From 1975 to 1998 it lay in Zielona Góra Voivodeship. It had 11,319 inhabitants in 2019. People born there include the painter and architect Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff and the Mesoamerica scholar Eduard Seler.
kru-people: Oral tradition is the main key to Kru origins. Traditions recorded in the mid-19th century by James Connelly tell that the core Kru communities came down from the interior, from a place he called Claho, some three generations earlier; travelling down the Poor River, they learned the value of salt, founded Bassa and moved on to Little Kroo, where more Kru-speaking communities joined them. These moves probably took place in the 18th century, linked to growing European trade, and the settlers founded five towns, Little Kroo, Setra Kroo, Kroo-Bar, Nana Kroo and King Will's Town. The name Kru is an anglicised form of their own name, Klao, not a sailor's crew.

During the Atlantic slave trade Kru men were valued as traders and sailors rather than as slaves, and Kru oral traditions hold that they were never enslaved; they tattooed their foreheads and noses with indigo to mark themselves as free men. By the 1790s they were hired as free sailors on European ships, and when legitimate trade replaced the slave trade they served as seamen, navigators and interpreters, including on American and British warships against the slave trade. Kru communities grew up beside the trading factories from Sierra Leone to the mouth of the Congo, and Krumen served in the Royal Navy from 1820 to as late as 1924.

They also resisted outside control. In 1856, with the Grebo, they opposed the Maryland settlers' efforts to control their trade, and in the Kru Coast Revolt of 1915-1916 many Kru were killed in American and Liberian reprisals.

Sailors worked in small companies under a headman, who paddled out to meet ships and negotiated employment on the spot. Late 19th-century reports describe small commonwealths, each with a hereditary chief who dealt with strangers, while power lay with elders who wore iron rings on their legs; property and land were held in common. Their spiritual world includes a high creator god, Nyesoa, spirits of territories and family guardians, reached in parts of Liberia through trained specialists called deya. The Kru make up about 7% of Liberia's population.
kruje: Krujë stands at about 600 metres on the foot of Mount Krujë, between the mountain and the plain of the Ishëm River, 20 kilometres north of Tirana. Its name is related to the Albanian word kroi, meaning 'fountain' or 'water source', and it first appears as Kroai in Byzantine documents of the early 9th century. In ancient times the region was inhabited by the Illyrian tribe of the Albani, and the town lies near the Iron Age site of Zgërdhesh. A middle-sized fortress grew into a town probably between the 6th and the 9th century.

In 1190 Krujë became the capital of the Principality of Arbanon, founded by Progon, the first Albanian state of the Middle Ages. Later it belonged to the Kingdom of Albania, and by 1395 it was under Ottoman vassalage. On 28 November 1443 Skanderbeg took the town by deceiving its governor with a forged letter of the sultan and raised the first Albanian flag there. In 1444 he made it part of the League of Lezhë.

In 1450 a force of 1,500 to 2,000 men under Vrana Konti and Skanderbeg defeated an Ottoman army of about 100,000 led by Sultan Murad II. Ballaban Pasha and Sultan Mehmed II besieged the town without success in 1466 and 1467, with about 150,000 men between them. After Skanderbeg died in 1468 troops of the Republic of Venice joined the garrison. The Ottomans took the town in 1478 after besieging it for over a year.

The town revolted against Ottoman rule in 1906. On 20 September Ottoman troops ambushed the rebel leaders who had come to negotiate, and about 30 people died. Krujë was captured on 14 August 1912 during the revolt that led to the Declaration of Independence. In the Second World War the resistance leader Abaz Kupi, a native of the town, built one of the first permanent resistance forces in Albania there.

Krujë is a town and municipality of north-central Albania. The Roman Catholic bishopric of Krujë was founded in 1167. The Skanderbeg Museum, founded in 1982, stands beside the castle, and the national ethnographic museum, founded in 1989, occupies a villa of the Toptani family built in 1764.
krum: Krum was born around the middle of the 8th century, but his family background and the circumstances of his accession are unknown. It has been speculated that he descended from Khan Kubrat through Kubrat's son Kuber. His name is probably of Turkic origin and may reflect a shortened form of an Old Turkic word for rule, leadership or authority. He became khan sometime between 796 and 803.

Around 805 Krum defeated the Avar Khaganate and advanced north into the Tisza region, which gave Bulgaria a common border with the Frankish Empire. Bulgarian forces defeated a Byzantine army in the Struma valley in 807. In 809 he forced the surrender of Serdica and, despite a guarantee of safe conduct, slaughtered its garrison of 6,000. In 811 the emperor Nikephoros I advanced into Bulgaria, took Pliska on 20 July and burned it. Krum armed as many men as he could, women and peasants included, and on 26 July trapped the retreating Byzantines in the Varbitsa Pass. The army was wiped out and Nikephoros killed. It is said that Krum had the emperor's skull lined with silver and used it as a drinking cup.

In 812 Krum took Develt and Mesembria. At the Battle of Versinikia on 22 June 813 he routed the army of Michael I Rangabe, and then advanced on Constantinople, where he performed a pagan ceremony before the walls, sacrificing people and animals. He ordered a moat and rampart dug from Blachernae to the Golden Gate. Michael was forced to abdicate, the third emperor to lose his throne to Krum in as many years. Leo V the Armenian then tried to ambush Krum during talks; Krum escaped wounded, and in revenge burned churches and monasteries in Eastern Thrace and took Adrianople.

Krum was preparing a great attack on Constantinople, with Slavs, Avars and siege engines, when he died on 13 April 814, most likely of a hemorrhage and stroke. During his reign Bulgarian territory doubled in size, reaching from the middle Danube to the Dnieper. He is remembered for the first known written Bulgarian law code, which gave subsidies to beggars and state protection to the poor and severely punished drinking, slander and robbery. Through these laws he became known as a strict but just ruler who brought Slavs and Bulgars into a centralised state.
krupp: Friedrich Krupp (1787–1826) built a steel foundry in Essen, and after his death his widow and sons ran it in partnership. His son Alfred Krupp (1812–87), sole owner from 1848 and known as the Cannon King, invested in steel rollers, railway tyres, the Bessemer process and mines in Germany and France. Unusually for the time, he gave his workers subsidised housing and health and retirement benefits. Krupp was the first to patent a seamless railway tyre strong enough for freight, and many American railroads used its rails.

Steel cannon followed from the 1840s, above all for the Russian, Turkish and Prussian armies, and by the late 1880s arms made up around half of output. The firm had five employees when Alfred began and twenty thousand at his death.

Krupp artillery counted at Wissembourg and Gravelotte in the Franco-Prussian War and at the siege of Paris. By 1912 the Ottoman Empire had bought 3,943 Krupp guns and Romania 1,450. In the First World War Krupp made most of the German army's artillery, including the Big Bertha of 1914 and the Paris Guns, while its Germaniawerft at Kiel built warships and submarines. Gustav Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach headed the firm after marrying the heiress Bertha Krupp, and from 1933 its works were the centre of German rearmament.

In the Second World War Krupp built tanks, guns, the 88 mm anti-aircraft gun, the Schwerer Gustav railway gun and 130 U-boats. It used workers conscripted from across Europe, later held as slave labourers who were beaten and starved; its senior doctor, Wilhelm Jaeger, described atrocious conditions in the camps. The Nuremberg tribunal convicted Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach of plunder and slave labour and sentenced him to 12 years, but he was released in 1951 and resumed control in 1953.

Krupp steel built the pressure sphere of the bathyscaphe Trieste and the Effelsberg 100-metre radio telescope. In 1968 the firm became a joint-stock company owned by the Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach Foundation. Under Gerhard Cromme it took over Hoesch AG, merging with it in 1992, before joining Thyssen. Its arms sales to many sides and its role in Nazi Germany have drawn lasting condemnation.
krusevac: Kruševac lies in the valley of the West Morava, on the Rasina river, in central Serbia. Its name comes from the Serbian word krušac, meaning river stone, which was widely used in building at the time. Lord Lazar Hrebeljanović founded it in 1371 as a fortified town and used it as his seat.

Lazar built the Lazarica Church, also called the Church of St Stephen, between 1375 and 1378 in the Morava style of architecture. An edict of 1387, in which he confirmed the rights of Venetian merchants on Serbian territory, names the town as his seat. The Serbian army assembled there before the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. According to legend, crows brought news of the defeat to Lazar's wife, Princess Milica, from the tower of her palace, and after the battle she held the town as her seat. Little remains of Lazar's city apart from the fortress, which was declared a Cultural Monument of Exceptional Importance in 1979.

From 1427 until 1833, and nominally until 1867, the town was under Ottoman rule, and it was the seat of the Sanjak of Kruševac. Austrian occupations from 1688 to 1690 and from 1717 to 1739 interrupted this. A monument to the Serbs who fell at Kosovo, sculpted by Đorđe Jovanović, was unveiled by King Petar I Karađorđević in 1904.

In September 1941 Yugoslav Army units under Dragutin Keserović, with a detachment of communists, attacked the German garrison but failed to take the town after four days of fighting. Mass executions of patriots and anti-fascists took place on the hill of Bagdala, the largest in the summer of 1943, and a monument named Slobodište now stands there. The town was liberated on 14 October 1944. In the Yugoslav socialist period it became one of the main industrial centres of Serbia, and the machine factory 14. oktobar employed around 7,000 workers.

Kruševac is the administrative centre of the Rasina District. In 2022 its urban area had 53,746 inhabitants and its city administrative area 113,582. The Kruševac Fortress, the Lazarica Church and the Kosovo monument recall its medieval and national past.
krusevo: The name Kruševo comes from the Slavic word for pear and means place of pear trees. The town lies at more than 1,350 metres above sea level, overlooking the region of Pelagonia, 33 kilometres from Prilep and 53 kilometres from Bitola. It is the highest town in North Macedonia and one of the highest in the Balkans, and the seat of Kruševo Municipality.

The area was first part of the Byzantine Empire, was conquered by the First Bulgarian Empire in the 9th century and was taken back by the Byzantines in the 11th. It then fell to the short-lived Lordship of Prilep in the 14th century, before coming under Ottoman rule in 1395. A large part of the Macedonian population descends from the Mijaks, a Macedonian subgroup who came from Lazaropole and settled beside Aromanians by the middle of the 18th century. Orthodox Albanian refugees, fleeing the crises of southern Albania, also settled there, often in groups of families led by a priest.

In the 19th century Kruševo grew into a commercial centre with links across the Balkans and beyond, and local merchants such as the Nitsiotas brothers and five other companies were active in Vienna. Bulgarian, Greek and Romanian schools operated in the town, the Romanian one opening in 1876. Early in the 20th century the Bulgarian geographer Vasil Kanchov counted 4,950 Bulgarians, 4,000 Vlachs, who are Aromanians, and 400 Christian Albanians.

During the Ilinden Uprising of 1903 the rebels proclaimed the short-lived Kruševo Republic. Its leader, Nikola Karev, formed a council with twenty members from each of the town's three main groups: Slavic speakers, Albanians and Vlachs. The Kruševo Manifesto called on all the people of Macedonia, whatever their nationality or religion, to fight together against the Ottoman Empire for an independent Macedonian republic. When the uprising was suppressed, the Ottoman army almost completely destroyed the town. The band of Pitu Guli tried to defend it at Mečkin Kamen.

The 2021 census counted 4,104 inhabitants, of whom 74.4 per cent were Macedonians and 21.1 per cent Aromanians. Since 2006 Macedonian and Aromanian have been the town's official languages, and Kruševo is the only place where Aromanian has any official status. The town is known for its 19th-century Ottoman architecture. Mečkin Kamen and the Makedonium monument commemorate the Ilinden Uprising, and on 2 August each year Kruševo is one of two sites where the Macedonian Day of the Republic is observed.
kruszwica: Kruszwica lies in the Inowrocław County of the Kuyavian-Pomeranian Voivodeship, on the shores of Lake Gopło in the historic region of Kuyavia. It is described as the oldest town in the region, initially founded in the 6th century. Historians of the early 20th century held that the lake was once a very large body of water, standing at least ten feet higher than later, and that it may have been linked by small navigable streams to the Warta, the Oder and the Vistula. The Polish historian Jan Długosz described a vast lake, larger than the one that remained.

Kruszwica is called the first historical fortified town (gród) of the region. Such towns grew up under the protection of military bands and their chiefs in answer to raids, and served as places for barter, common worship and the storage of goods in time of invasion. Some historians attribute the change of the Polanie tribe, from a communal tribal order in the second half of the eighth century to a strong princely power in the ninth, to the influence of commerce, picturing Pomeranian merchants from Szczecin meeting traders from the east and south on the Gopło, so that Byzantine, Roman and Scandinavian cultures met there.

Kruszwica formed part of Poland from the 10th century, and later became a county seat and royal town of the Kingdom of Poland. Germany occupied Kruszwica from September 1939 until 1945, and its administration ran a forced labour camp for Jewish women there from 1940 to 1942 and one for Jewish men from 1942 to 1943. The Polish resistance was active in the town, and Władysław Kostuj, who organised the local branch of the Secret Teaching Organization, was arrested in 1944 and murdered by the German gendarmerie.

Kruszwica is a small town with a medieval castle and a 12th-century Romanesque church beside the lake. It has a sugar works and a plant making cooking oil and margarine. Visitors come for boat trips on the lake, and the town hosts rowing championships every year. The nearest railway station is in Inowrocław.
krzeszow-abbey: Krzeszów Abbey, Kloster Grüssau in German, stands in Krzeszów in Lower Silesia. It was founded on 8 May 1242 by Duchess Anna of Bohemia, widow of the High Duke of Poland Henry II the Pious, who had been killed at the Battle of Legnica during the first Mongol invasion of Poland, and was settled with Benedictine monks from the abbey of Opatovice in Bohemia. Anna's grandson, Duke Bolko I of Świdnica, later acquired its lands again and gave them to the Cistercians of Henryków, who consecrated the new Assumption of Mary Monastery Church in 1292.

The Duchy of Świdnica passed to the Kingdom of Bohemia in 1392. The abbey was destroyed in the Hussite Wars and again in the Thirty Years' War, and rebuilt each time; it was closely connected with the Silesian mystic Angelus Silesius. From 1728 the church was rebuilt in Baroque style, with sculptures by Ferdinand Brokoff and paintings by Petr Brandl and Michael Willmann. Frederick II of Prussia conquered Silesia in 1742, and Prussia secularised the abbey in 1810, during the Napoleonic Wars.

In 1919 German monks forced to leave Emmaus Abbey in Prague resettled the empty buildings, and Pope Pius XI raised the house to an abbey again in 1924. The Nazi government suspended it in 1940 and used it as a detention camp, and from 1942 large parts of the Berlin State Library collection were stored there. After the region passed to Poland, the German monks were expelled on 12 May 1946 and moved in 1947 to Bad Wimpfen in Baden-Württemberg, while Polish Benedictine nuns expelled from Lviv settled at Krzeszów.

The abbey's Basilica of the Assumption holds the mausoleum of the dukes of the Świdnica line of the Piast dynasty. Since 1 May 2004 the abbey has been one of Poland's official national Historic Monuments, recorded by the National Heritage Board of Poland. In 1946 a convoy carried thousands of manuscripts away from the monastery, among them autograph scores by Mozart, Beethoven and Bach; several volumes were returned to East Germany in 1965, and the remaining Berlinka collection at the Jagiellonian University in Cracow is disputed as looted art.
ksar-es-seghir: Ksar es-Seghir lies in a sheltered bay on the right bank of the river of the same name, about halfway between Tangier and Ceuta, in the Jebala region. The coast there is hard to reach by sea or land, so the town never grew to rival the other ports of northern Morocco, but its shelter made it a safe landing ground for troops. Its Arabic name means The Small Castle, set against Ksar-el-Kebir, The Big Castle, farther south. Under the Almoravids and Almohads it was called Qasr al-Majaz, the castle on the way, as a port of embarkation for Spain.

In antiquity the settlement was known as Lissa or Exilissa, probably a Phoenician colony that was annexed by the Carthaginians and later came under Roman control, when it was a salting post. Ksar Masmuda, named after the local Berber tribe, was founded after the Umayyad conquest of 708–709. In 1287 the Marinid sultan Abu Yaqub Yusuf gave the round town new walls with 29 bastions and three gates, Bab al-Bahr, Bab Sebta and Bab Fes. By the 15th century it had become a base for corsairs preying on shipping in the strait.

King Afonso V of Portugal took it on 23–24 October 1458 with 25,000 men and 200 ships, and the Marinid sultan Abd al-Haqq II besieged it in vain in 1458 and 1459. From 1502 the Portuguese extended its walls into the sea to shield a landing ground, and the town's resident population reached about 800. King John III of Portugal decided in 1533 to give it up, finding his Moroccan holdings costly; the departing Portuguese removed the people, dismantled much of the town and dumped sand into the harbour.

Moriscos expelled from Spain settled there in 1609, but the town shrank into a fishing village amid the ruins, and a newer town grew up across the river from the old citadel. It belongs to Fahs-Anjra Province and had 10,995 inhabitants at the census of 2004. A naval base of the Royal Moroccan Navy opened there in 2010, and the cargo port of Tanger-Med was built about twelve kilometres to the northeast.
kshatriya: The word comes from the Sanskrit kshatra, meaning rule or authority, and the class is also called Rajanya. In early Rigvedic society the administration was headed by a tribal king, the Rajan, whose position may or may not have been hereditary. He may have been elected in a tribal assembly, the Samiti, protected the tribe and its cattle, was assisted by a priest and did not keep a standing army. The fourfold varna system is not yet recorded in this period.

The Purusha Sukta of the Rigveda describes the symbolic creation of the four varnas through cosmic sacrifice. It uses the term rajanya rather than Kshatriya and is the first extant Vedic text to name the four classes together; some scholars consider it a late addition to the Rigveda. By the end of the Vedic period the word rajanya, which stressed kinship with the ruler, had been replaced by Kshatriya, which denotes power over a specific domain.

In the period of the Brahmanas, from 800 to 700 BCE, the rank of the varna was uncertain. The Panchavimsha Brahmana places the Rajanya first, before the Brahmana and Vaishya, while one passage of the Shatapatha Brahmana puts them second and another puts them third. The order Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra became fixed from the time of the dharmasutras, between 450 and 100 BCE.

Kshatriyas were often considered pre-eminent in Buddhist circles. In Hindu society they were sometimes rivals of the Brahmins, but they generally acknowledged the superiority of the priestly class. Their ritual duties were to study the Vedas, give gifts and perform fire sacrifice, and in ritual the staff of the banyan tree is assigned to them.

During the period of the Mahajanapadas, about 600 to 300 BCE, the oligarchic republics called gana sanghas were ruled by Kshatriya clans. Brahmanical sources sometimes called these clans degenerate Kshatriyas or Shudras, since they did not follow the Vedic religion, and they were often patrons of Buddhism and Jainism. After that period most prominent royal dynasties in northern India were not Kshatriyas; the rulers of the Nanda Empire were said to be Shudras.

Between 300 and 700 CE, Brahmins bestowed Kshatriya status on new royal dynasties by linking them to the Kshatriyas of the epics and Puranas, through the Solar dynasty (Suryavamsha) and the Lunar dynasty (Chandravamsha). In return the new Kshatriyas patronised and rewarded the Brahmins. Other claimed lineages include the Agnivanshi, descended from Agni, and the Nagavanshi, descended from the Nagas.
ku-hawaiian-god: Hawaiian ideas of deity allow a god many forms, and Kū is invoked under many names, each naming a lesser manifestation. In the forest and the rain he is Ku-moku-haliʻi, Ku spreading over the land, Ku-olono-wao, Ku of the deep forest, and Ku-ka-ohia-laka, Ku of the ʻōhiʻa lehua tree. In farming and fishing he is Ku-ka-o-o, Ku of the digging stick, Ku-kuila and Ku-keolowalu, of dry and wet farming, and Ku-ula, Ku of the abundance of the sea. In war he is Ku-nui-akea, Ku the supreme one, and Ku-kaʻili-moku, and in sorcery Ku-waha-ilo, Ku of the maggot-dropping mouth.

Believers hold that Kū takes bodily forms, his kinolau: among animals the shark, man, the Hawaiian hawk, the dog and certain red fish; among plants the ʻieʻie vine, the ʻōhiʻa lehua flower, the breadfruit, the trunk of the coconut tree and the noni fruit.

Kū was also called Akua. In Hawaiian belief he, Kāne and Lono are primordial gods who have existed for eternity and who caused light to shine upon the world. He was the husband of the goddess Hina. It has been suggested that the pair express a complementary dualism, since kū means to stand and one meaning of hina is to fall, but evidence from other Polynesian languages does not support this, and the name Hina is more likely linked to a silvery-grey colour, as in Mahina, the Moon.

Some feathered god images, kiʻi or akua hulu manu, are considered to represent Kū, though it is unclear whether all of them do; one in the Bishop Museum is thought to be Kamehameha I's own image of his god. Kamehameha raised monuments to Kūkaʻilimoku at the royal complex of Hōlualoa Bay and at his residence at Kamakahonu. The three colossal statues of Kū he dedicated, the only ones known, had passed to the Bishop Museum, the Peabody Essex Museum in Salem, Massachusetts, and the British Museum in London.
kuala-kangsar: Kuala Kangsar stands where the Kangsar River joins the Perak River, about 25 km north-west of Ipoh and 98 km south-east of George Town. It is the main town of the Kuala Kangsar administrative district. The name is believed to derive from Kuala Kurang-Sa, literally 100 minus one, usually taken to mean the 99th small tributary to flow into the Perak River. The Sultan of Perak officially resides in the town, which has been Perak's royal seat since the eighteenth century and is one of four towns that play a role in Perak's complex system of succession.

Sultan Yusuf Sharifuddin Mudzaffar Shah, who ruled from 1877 to 1887, built his first palace, Istana Sri Sayong, beside the riverbank, where it was exposed to monsoon floods. After the Big Flood of 1926 the palace was moved to a knoll, the site of the present royal palace, Istana Iskandariah, whose Art Deco architecture is rare in Malaysia.

The town was the seat of the first British Resident in the Malay Peninsula, James W. W. Birch, from October 1874 until he was murdered on 2 November 1875, and it was the capital of Perak until 1876. In 1897 it hosted the first Conference of Rulers of the Federated Malay States, the Durbar. By the 1890s the tin mining towns of Ipoh and Taiping had eclipsed it. The English botanist Henry Nicholas Ridley planted the first rubber tree in Malaysia here, and Ridley helped Malaya become the largest rubber producer in the world. The first Malaysian scout troop was also founded in the town.

The town is administered by the Kuala Kangsar Municipal Council. Its landmarks include the Ubudiah Mosque and the Royal Mausoleum, Istana Kenangan, the old palace that is now the Perak Royal Museum, the Kuala Kangsar Clock Tower and the Victoria Bridge, built in 1900. Its schools and colleges include the Malay College Kuala Kangsar and Sultan Azlan Shah University. Two bridges connect the town with Sayong, and it can be reached by the North–South Expressway and by train.
kuala-lumpur: Kuala Lumpur lies in the Klang Valley, bordered by the Titiwangsa Mountains in the east and the Strait of Malacca in the west. It stands at the confluence of the Klang and Gombak rivers, in the centre of Selangor on the central west coast of Peninsular Malaysia. The municipality covers 243 square kilometres, and its highest point is Bukit Nanas at 94 metres.

The name means muddy confluence in Malay, from kuala, the point where two rivers join, and lumpur, mud. Its origin is uncertain. One suggestion is that it was named after a Sungai Lumpur, a muddy river. Others propose Pengkalan Lumpur, muddy landing place, or a Cantonese word, lam-pa, for flooded jungle, but there is no firm contemporary evidence for these.

Kuala Lumpur was first developed around 1857 by Raja Abdullah as a town serving the tin mines of the region. Yap Ah Loy and Frank Swettenham were instrumental in its early development in the late 19th century. In 1872 Swettenham described the settlement beside the Klang River as a purely Chinese village, though a Malay stockade already stood at Bukit Nanas. It was the capital of Selangor from 1880 until 1978. Most of its notable colonial-era buildings date from the end of the 19th century and the early 20th, among them the railway station and the Jamek Mosque.

The city belonged to the Federated Malay States from the late 19th century, was under the Empire of Japan from 1942 to 1945, and became part of the Malayan Union in 1946 and the Federation of Malaya in 1948. It was the founding capital of the Federation of Malaya and of Malaysia, formed in 1963. It received city status in 1972, and in 1974 it was separated from Selangor to become the first Federal Territory. Its federal executive and judicial branches moved to Putrajaya in early 1999.

Kuala Lumpur is the capital and most populous city of Malaysia, with 2,111,536 people. It is the seat of the Parliament of Malaysia and of the Istana Negara, the official residence of the monarch. Its population includes the Malays, Chinese and Indians as well as Eurasians, Kadazans, Ibans and other Indigenous peoples. The Petronas Towers are the tallest twin buildings in the world, and the University of Malaya, established in 1949, is the oldest university in Malaysia.
kuala-selangor: The name Kuala Selangor means the estuary of the Selangor River. The town stands where the river drains into the Strait of Malacca, about 55 kilometres north-west of central Kuala Lumpur and 42 kilometres north-west of Shah Alam, the state capital. It is the largest town and the administrative centre of the Kuala Selangor District, which also contains the adjacent towns of Tanjung Karang, Ijok, Puncak Alam, Bestari Jaya and Jeram.

Before the 18th century the area was ruled by the Malacca Sultanate. In the late 17th century it was invaded by the Bugis. Kuala Selangor was then made the capital of the Sultanate of Selangor during the 18th century, a seat that was relocated three times in the years that followed.
In 1784 the Dutch conquered Kuala Selangor and destroyed its fortifications. A branch railway once linked the town to Padang Jawa. It was built in stages in 1913 and 1914 and closed in 1933.

The residents are mostly Malays, followed by Indians and ethnic Chinese. Most of the Chinese residents come from southern Fujian, and the Hokkien dialect predominates among them. The town is reached from Kuala Lumpur by Federal Route 54 and the Kuala Lumpur to Kuala Selangor expressway, and from the royal capital Klang by Federal Route 5.

Visitors come to Bukit Melawati, to the fireflies of Kampung Kuantan, where firefly tourism began in the early 1970s, and to the Kuala Selangor Nature Park. The park opened in 1987 and covers 296 hectares, divided between 201 hectares of tropical rainforest and a swamp forest. The town appears in the films Mukhsin (2007) and Ngangkung (2010).
kubadabad-palace: Until its remains were found, the palace was known only from the contemporary historian Ibn Bibi, who wrote that toward the end of his reign Kayqubad I drew up the plans himself and gave the task of completing it to his vizier Sa'd al-Din Köpek. The site lies just over 100 kilometres west of the Seljuq capital at Konya. The remains were found in 1949 and excavated, first in the 1960s by the German archaeologist Katharina Otto-Dorn and later by a team from Ankara University led by Rüçhan Arık.

The complex comprises sixteen buildings, among them two palaces. The larger, the Great Palace, measures fifty by thirty-five metres and is an asymmetrical building with a courtyard, guest rooms, a harem and an eyvan. Its layout, modelled on the caravanserai, broke with the pavilion plan of earlier palaces. The site also had a game park and a small wooden dockyard copying the Tersane at Alanya.

Unlike the palaces at Konya and Kayseri, Kubadabad stood far from any fortified town. Protection seems to have come from a fortress on the nearby island of Kız Kalesi. The important Hittite site of Eflatunpınar lies in the same area.

The tiles found in the excavations are painted under the glaze in blue, purple, turquoise and green, with white star-shaped figural panels alternating with turquoise crosses. No other palace in the Islamic world has so varied a tile decoration. Similar tiles were found at the Roman theatre of Aspendos, which Kayqubad had turned into a palace. Two tiles are thought to show a portrait of the sultan, and another shows a double-headed eagle inscribed al-sultān, a symbol that also appears on the city walls of Konya.

The court scenes show the sultan, harem women, courtiers and servants seated cross-legged, often holding pomegranates or opium branches as symbols of eternal life. In 2012 bearded, turbaned figures of a different physical type were found in both palaces, holding pomegranates or inscribed tablets; they are thought to represent high officials or scholars. Other tiles show hunting scenes and imaginary animals.
kublai-khan: Kublai was the second son of Tolui and Sorghaghtani Beki, and a grandson of Genghis Khan. In 1224, near the Ili River, Genghis Khan performed a hunting ceremony on the nine-year-old Kublai and his brother Möngke, and is reported to have said that the boy's words were full of wisdom. Kublai was twelve when Genghis died in 1227.

After his brother Möngke became Khan in 1251, Kublai received the viceroyalty over northern China and moved his camp to central Inner Mongolia. He is said to have managed his territory well, raising the agricultural output of Henan and increasing spending on social welfare, which won him the respect of Han warlords and helped prepare the founding of the Yuan dynasty.

Learning that his younger brother Ariq Böke had been raising troops, Kublai returned north to find that an assembly at Karakorum had named Ariq Böke Great Khan. Kublai summoned his own assembly, which proclaimed him Great Khan on 15 April 1260 with the support of most senior princes in northern China and Manchuria. The Toluid Civil War that followed lasted until 1264 and began the division of the Mongol Empire. His real power was limited to the Yuan realm.

Within a decade Kublai saw that China was his main base. He adopted Chinese political and cultural models, worked to reduce the influence of regional lords, and relied on advisers such as Liu Bingzhong and Xu Heng. He proclaimed the dynastic name Great Yuan in 1271, completed the conquest of the Song dynasty by 1279, and became the first non-Han emperor to rule all of China proper. His capital Khanbaliq, also called Dadu, was designed by the architect Ikhtiyar al-Din.

He made Goryeo a tributary state in 1260, and ordered invasions of Japan, Vietnam, Burma and Java. The attempt on Japan in 1274 used a fleet of 900 ships, and both attempts failed, partly from bad weather or poorly designed ships. These costly campaigns and the issue of paper currency caused inflation.

In his last years Kublai sent his grandson Gammala to Burkhan Khaldun in 1291 to secure his claim to the sacred burial ground of Genghis Khan. He died on 18 February 1294. His seizure of power in 1260 pushed the Mongol Empire in a new direction and hastened its disunity, but his willingness to present the Mongol realm as China brought it international attention. Yuan rule of Tibet, Manchuria and Mongolia from modern Beijing set a precedent for the later expansion of the Qing dynasty into Inner Asia.
kubrat: Kubrat was the ruler of the Onogur-Bulgars. His name is derived from the Turkic words qobrat, meaning to gather, or qurt, wolf. The Nominalia of the Bulgarian khans calls him Kurt, a member of the Dulo clan, who succeeded Gostun of the Ermi clan and is credited with a reign of 60 years.

The Bulgars were Turkic nomads who took part in the Hunnic confederation of the 5th century. After Attila's death the tribes that later formed the Bulgars withdrew east into the Black Sea and Caspian steppe. By the end of the 6th century the western Bulgar tribes had joined the Avar Khaganate, while the eastern Bulgars came under the Western Turkic Khaganate. Byzantine writers named him in various ways: Theophanes the Confessor called him king of the Onogundur Huns, and Patriarch Nikephoros I called him ruler of the Onuğundur-Bulğars.

Kubrat spent his early life at the imperial palace in Constantinople. John of Nikiu, a 7th-century historian, writes that he was baptised there, received into the Christian community in childhood and grew up in the palace, and that great affection and peace prevailed between him and Emperor Heraclius. Whether he was a child or a young adult is unclear. His or his uncle Organa's conversion is placed around 619, and he may have formed part of a coalition against the Sasanian-Avar alliance that Heraclius or Organa had planned.

According to Nikephoros I, Kubrat revolted successfully against the Avars and concluded a treaty with Heraclius, and the state of Old Great Bulgaria, or Magna Bulgaria, was formed. Nikephoros says he died during the reign of Constans II (641 to 668), and that he told his five sons, among them Batbayan, Kotrag and Asparukh, never to separate their dwellings, so that their power might thrive. The loose tribal union nonetheless broke up under internal tensions and pressure from the Khazars to the east.

The Pereshchepina Treasure, found in 1912 by Ukrainian peasants near Poltava, comprises over 50 kg of gold and silver objects of the migration period. Three rings bear monograms, and one is inscribed in Greek with the name Kubrat and the dignity of patrikios, which led scholars to identify the site as his grave. The bracelets show Byzantine influence or workmanship. The latest coins in the hoard date to about 650, under Constans II.

Reading the Nominalia's 60 years as a lifespan places his death in 653 or 665; historical and archaeological sources place it between 650 and 665, and his birth between 590 and 615 on one theory. Kubrat Knoll on Livingston Island in Antarctica is named after him.
kuching: Kuching is the capital and most populous city of the state of Sarawak in Malaysia. It stands on the Sarawak River at the south-western tip of Sarawak on the island of Borneo, and the river divides it into a northern and a southern half. The city covers 431 square kilometres and has about half a million people. Its highest point is Mount Santubong, on the Santubong peninsula 35 kilometres north of the centre. The climate is tropical rainforest, and Kuching is the wettest populated area in Malaysia.

Sarawak was part of the Bruneian Empire from the reign of the first Sultan of Brunei, Sultan Muhammad Shah. Kuching was its third capital, founded in 1827 by the Sultan's representative, Pengiran Indera Mahkota. The earlier capitals were Santubong, founded by Sultan Pengiran Tengah in 1599, and Lidah Tanah, founded by Datu Patinggi Ali in the early 1820s. The founding was spurred by the discovery of antimony ore on the upper Sarawak River in 1824, which was in demand in Singapore. A Dutch report mentioned about a hundred Malays and three Chinese houses in the area shortly before. Mahkota's rising tax and labour demands were unpopular, and the local Malay chiefs moved upriver, allied with Dayaks and rebelled against Brunei.

Neither side gained the upper hand until 1840, when the Bruneian prime minister, Pengiran Raja Muda Hashim, offered the governorship of Sarawak to the British adventurer James Brooke in return for his help. In 1841 Kuching became the capital of the Kingdom of Sarawak under Brooke. Most of the Land Dayak rebels were pardoned and became his followers. The name Kuching was already in use by the time Brooke arrived in 1839, and its origin is uncertain: it may come from the Malay word for cat, kucing, or from Cochin, an Indian trading port.

Under Charles Brooke the town received a sanitation system, a hospital, a prison, a fort and a bazaar. The Brooke administration held a centenary celebration in Kuching in 1941. During the Second World War Japanese forces occupied the city, and they set up the Batu Lintang camp nearby for prisoners of war and civilian internees. The town survived the war intact. In 1946 the last Rajah, Sir Charles Vyner Brooke, ceded Sarawak to the British Crown, and Kuching remained capital of the colony.

Kuching remained the state capital when Malaysia was formed in 1963 and received city status in 1988. It is the only city in Malaysia run by two local authorities, one for the north and one for the south. Its people include Chinese, Malays, Iban and Bidayuh, and the Sarawak Malay dialect is spoken alongside Hokkien and Mandarin. It is a member of UNESCO's Creative Cities Network for gastronomy.
kuchlug: Kuchlug was the son of Taibuqa, the Tayang khan of the Naimans, a Mongol-speaking tribe. In 1204 Jamuqa, the chief Mongol rival of Temüjin, the future Genghis Khan, fled to the Naimans, and Temüjin followed and attacked them in the battle of the thirteen sides. Taibuqa wished to fall back to the Altai Mountains, but Kuchlug favoured a direct assault on open ground and dismissed his father's plan as cowardly. The battle was a disaster. Jamuqa fled, Taibuqa was mortally wounded, and the rest of the tribe surrendered to Temüjin. Kuchlug escaped with a few soldiers and fled west towards the Kara Irtysh.

Genghis Khan remained wary of him. In 1208 they met in battle again, and Kuchlug was pushed further west into Zhetysu. After this second defeat he turned to the Qara Khitai, based at Balasagun, for protection.

Yelü Zhilugu, emperor of the Qara Khitai or Western Liao, welcomed him. Kuchlug became his adviser, married his daughter Princess Hunhu, received the title of khan and was allowed to reorganise the Naimans as a military unit under his command. The empire was then facing rebellions in the east and a struggle with Muhammad II of the Khwarazmian Empire in the west, and Kuchlug apparently allied himself with the Khwarezm-Shah. In 1210, while Yelü Zhilugu dealt with a Karakhanid revolt at Samarkand, Kuchlug rebelled and seized the treasury at Uzgen.

In 1211 he ambushed and captured Yelü Zhilugu while the emperor was out hunting. Yelü Zhilugu was made taishang huang and Kuchlug became emperor. Many historians regard this usurpation as the end of the Qara Khitai, though the realm kept the official name Great Liao until 1218.

Kuchlug came from a Nestorian tribe, but his Buddhist wife convinced him to adopt Buddhism. Unlike earlier Qara Khitai rulers, he was reported to have instituted anti-Muslim policies. According to the Persian historian Ata-Malik Juvayni, he made a town's Muslim population choose between Nestorianism, Buddhism or Khitan dress, and he is said to have crucified the imam of Hotan on the door of his madrassa.

When he attacked Almaliq, the Karlugs appealed to Genghis Khan, who sent the general Jebe. The Mongols defeated a Qara Khitai force of 30,000 near Balasaghun. Kuchlug fled to Kashgar, where he found no support, and then across the Pamirs to the border between Badakhshan and Wakhan. Hunters caught him there and handed him to the Mongols, who beheaded him in 1218. According to the Yuan Shi, his head was displayed across his former realm.
kuchuk-muhammad: Muḥammad bin Tīmūr was born on 28 June 1391, the son of Tīmūr Khan, possibly by a daughter of the powerful beglerbeg Edigu, and descended from Genghis Khan through Jochi. His name, Little Muḥammad, set him apart from his older rival Ulugh Muḥammad, Big Muḥammad. From about 1428 he was a claimant to the throne at Astrakhan, backed by Ghāzī and Nawrūz, the sons of Edigu and possibly his uncles, until a quarrel drove Nawrūz over to Ulugh Muḥammad.

When the emirs Tekne and Ḥaydar deserted Ulugh Muḥammad and raised Sayyid Aḥmad as khan in 1432, Ulugh Muḥammad came to terms with Küchük Muḥammad, and the two divided the Golden Horde along the Volga, the west to Ulugh Muḥammad and the east to Küchük Muḥammad. With Sayyid Aḥmad holding his own, the Horde had three khans; in 1434 Grand Prince Vasilij II of Moscow sent tribute to all three. Nawrūz's return to Küchük Muḥammad in 1437 broke the deadlock. Ulugh Muḥammad was attacked by both rivals and escaped only because Küchük Muḥammad had to expel Ghiyāth ad-Dīn, son of Shādī Beg, from Sarai; he later established himself at Kazan.

Large parts of the Horde stayed outside Küchük Muḥammad's control: the north under Ulugh Muḥammad, the south-west under Sayyid Aḥmad, and the east under Abu'l-Khayr of the Uzbeks and Maḥmūdāq of Sibir. His rivalry with Sayyid Aḥmad continued, and because the Russians and Lithuanians dealt more with his rivals, the later years of his reign are obscure.

Judging by his last coins and the first mention of his sons as khans, he died in 1459. Of his several sons, Maḥmūd and Aḥmad mattered most. According to Sabitov's reconstruction of a corrupt list, Maḥmūd was khan of the Great Horde from 1459 to 1465 and then of Astrakhan, and Aḥmad ruled the Great Horde from 1459 to 1481. His descendants held the Great Horde and Astrakhan in turn for decades, the polity of Küchük Muḥammad and his line, apart from the line in Astrakhan, being sometimes known as the Great Horde.
kuchum: Kuchum was the son of Prince Murtaza of the Shayban dynasty and a descendant of Hadji Muhammad. In 1554 he contested the throne of the Siberian Khanate against the brothers Yadegar and Bekbulat, who held it and were both Russian vassals. In 1563 Yadegar was defeated and Kuchum took the throne.

Kuchum took an anti-Russian stance on the basis of religion and sought military help from the Crimean Khanate and the Ottoman Empire. His attempts to convert his non-Turkic subjects, among them the Mansi, Khanty and Selkup, by force may have alienated them instead. In 1572 Ivan the Terrible ordered the Stroganovs to have a Cossack ataman lead an expedition to force the natives into submission, and approved the use of guns for it. In 1582 the Cossack ataman Yermak defeated Kuchum's forces and captured the capital Qashliq.

Kuchum withdrew to the steppe and regrouped. On 6 August 1584 he attacked Yermak at night, killing him and most of his army, and regained the ruined Qashliq. He tried to unite the rival factions of the khanate's nobility but met resistance, and after an unsuccessful attempt on his life by Qarachi Sayet Khan he moved his horde to the steppe south of the Irtysh and fought the Russian governors from there. In 1590 he raided the Tatars around Tobolsk, who paid yasak, or tribute, to the Russians. In 1591 Koltsov caught him on the Ishym River and took two of his wives and his son Abdul-Khair, and in 1594 a fort was built at Tara partly to watch him.

In 1597 Kuchum asked for negotiations, and the tsar and Abdul-Khair wrote from Russia offering estates in return for surrender. Before September 1598 Andrey Voyeykov caught a large group of his followers at Ub Lake and then Kuchum himself on the Ob. He fled, but the Russians killed two of his sons and captured five other sons, eight wives and eight daughters. A Muslim cleric sent to negotiate received a reply in which Kuchum described himself as deaf, blind and without subsistence and said that he had not submitted before and would not now. It was his last contact with the Russians. He is believed to have died in Bukhara.

Abdul-Khair converted to Christianity in 1591, the first of the dynasty to do so, and his family eventually assimilated into the Russian nobility. About 1620 Kuchum's son Ishim-khan married a daughter of the Torghut prince Kho Orluk, and Ishim's descendants continued resistance with Oirat support; in 1661 his sons fought the Russians in Bashkiria. In 2025 a monument to Kuchum's wife Suzge Khanum was installed in Tobolsk and then removed by the authorities, who said the installation had not been approved.
kudowa-zdroj: Kudowa-Zdrój, often shortened to Kudowa, lies below the Table Mountains in Kłodzko County, Lower Silesian Voivodeship, on the Czech-Polish border, just across from the Czech town of Náchod.
