It is about 40 km west of Kłodzko and 140 km from Prague, and has a population of around 10,000.

It is counted among the oldest spa towns of Europe, where heart and circulatory diseases were treated. Its centre has a park in a style recalling the 17th century, with exotic plants and a mineral water pump room. The Chapel of Skulls in the district of Czermna is an ossuary holding the remains of thousands of people, one of a few of its kind in Europe.

The village was first mentioned in a document by Henry the Elder, son of the Hussite Czech king George of Podebrady. Its original name was Lipolitov, which in the mid-16th century became Chudoba, later Kudoba, Bad Kudowa and, in 1945, Kudowa-Zdrój. Its oldest part is Czermna, dating from the 16th century. The first record of its mineral waters, under the name Cermenske Lazne, comes from the chronicles of Louis of Náchod in 1580, and in 1625 (some sources say 1621) the Lutheran monk G. Aelurius praised their taste in his Glaciografia.

Kudowa belonged to Bohemia under the Holy Roman Empire until 1742, when the county of Kladsko passed to Prussia. From 1818 to 1945 it was Bad Kudowa in the Prussian province of Lower Silesia. The chemist Adolf Duflos analysed the waters in 1850, and a local doctor, J. Jacob, helped establish the spa's name for heart disease. The town received 300 patients in 1847 and 4,150 visitors in 1900. German, Polish and Czech were all heard there, and Jewish guests came in considerable numbers.

In the Second World War the Germans ran a subcamp of Gross-Rosen for Jewish women in the Zakrze district, along with other forced labour camps. The town was spared fighting and destruction. After 1945 most German inhabitants were expelled and Polish settlers, many expelled from former Eastern Poland, arrived. Kudowa received municipal rights for the first time and became one of the most popular spa towns in Poland. Small groups of Germans and Czechs stayed until 1960, with a Czech school until 1955 and a German school until 1960. Since 1962 the town has held the annual International Moniuszko Festival, dedicated to the composer Stanisław Moniuszko.
kudur-mabuk: Kudur-Mabuk first appears in the reign of Sin-Iddinam of Larsa (c. 1849–1843 BCE), at Mashkan-shapir in the Emutbal province, in the northern part of the kingdom of Larsa. His name means that the god Mabuk is a protector; nothing is known of Mabuk except from personal names. His father, Šimti-šilhak, and his daughter Manzi-wartaš also bore Elamite names. Late in the reign of his son Warad-Sin he became governor of Emutbal, and he styled himself Father of the Amorite land and Father of Emutbala.

He led a number of military campaigns for Larsa, especially in the reign of Rim-Sin I. An inscription recording his building of the Emetegira for the god Nergal says that he smote the army of Kazallu and Muti-abal and seized Kazallu, tore down its wall and made it submit, and he restored Maškān-šāpir and Kār-Šamaš to Larsa. He called Ṣillī-Ištar, leader of Maškān-šāpir, the enemy of Larsa, and a lost stele known from a copy showed him smiting him. A fortress in the kingdom bore his name, Dur-Kudur-Mabuk.

He restored or rebuilt several shrines, among them the Eeškite for Nanna, the Ekuga for Nergal and the Etilmun for Inana, as well as the Nanna-ḫul canal. His sons honoured him in their year names: Warad-Sin brought a golden statue of him into the temple of Shamash, and Rim-Sin I placed copper statues of him in the temple of Nanna.

He is not mentioned after the 8th year of Rim-Sin I and is presumed to have died then. His daughter En-ane-du, possibly Manzi-wartaš under a Sumerian name taken on her accession, was high priestess of the moon god Nanna at Ur. It has been proposed that another son, Sîn-muballiṭ, was the governor of Maškān-šāpir when Hammurabi of Babylon captured it. Centuries later Nabonidus, the last Neo-Babylonian ruler, found an inscription of Enanedu, daughter of Kudur-Mabuk, while rebuilding the Egipar at Ur.
kuelap: Kuélap, also written Cuélap, is a walled settlement in the mountains near the towns of María and Tingo, in the southern part of the region of Amazonas, Peru. It was built by the Chachapoyas culture on a limestone ridge overlooking the Utcubamba Valley, at an elevation of 3,000 metres on the left bank of the Utcubamba River, in the district of Tingo, Luya Province. The area is covered with cloud forests of trees, orchids and epiphytes. The protected zone covers 218.33 hectares and a buffer zone 609.67 hectares, which together protect about twelve archaeological sites and the main site of Kuélap.

The abandoned settlement covers about six hectares, 584 metres from north to south and 110 metres at its widest. Its walls are 10 to 20 metres high, built of finely worked limestone blocks, some of which may weigh three tons. It has three entrances, two on the east and one on the west, and the main entrance is trapezoidal and narrows until it allows the passage of one person. All but five of its 421 structures are circular, and some have friezes of rhomboid and zigzag shapes.

An inverted-cone structure 5.5 metres high, known as El Tintero or the Templo Mayor, had ceremonial remains and may have served as a solar observatory. Many stones carry designs in relief, and burials have been found in the walls and inside the circular structures.

The majority of the structures were built between 900 and 1100 CE, and the city may have had some 3,000 inhabitants. It was abandoned in 1570 because of the Spanish Conquest. The judge Juan Crisóstomo Nieto of Chachapoyas accidentally rediscovered it in 1843, and Antonio Raimondi surveyed it in 1870. Charles Wiener visited in 1881, and Louis Langlois described the main buildings in 1939. Ernst Middendorf, Adolf Bandelier, Henry and Paule Reichlen and Arturo Ruíz also studied the site.

Since 2013 Kuélap has suffered structural instabilities, which culminated in the collapse of a section of the perimeter wall in April 2022. The Ministry of Culture launched emergency conservation measures and research with Peruvian and foreign experts. In 2026 archaeologists uncovered a stone funerary structure holding the remains of five individuals, four adults and an infant, with ceremonial offerings in a Regional Inca style, dated to the Late Horizon period (c. 1470-1532 CE). Visitors now reach the site by a cable car that takes them to within 2 km of the fortress.
kufa: Kufa lies on the banks of the Euphrates in Iraq, about 170 kilometres south of Baghdad and 10 kilometres north-east of Najaf. It was one of the two amsar, garrison cities, of Iraq, with Basra, serving as a military base and administrative centre. It was founded in 637 or 638 as an encampment by the Companion Saʻd ibn Abī Waqqas beside the Lakhmid Arab city of al-Hirah, after the Arab victory at al-Qadisiyyah in 636 and the fall of the Persian Empire, and was laid out in a circular plan according to the Partho-Sasanian model, with seven divisions.

Kufa was restless from the start. In the 640s its commons complained that the governor shared out the spoils of war unfairly, and in 642 Umar summoned Saʻd to Medina, found him innocent, but deposed him to avert ill feeling. Governors followed one another under Uthman, and in 656 Kufan agitators joined the Egyptian instigators who marched on the caliph. After Uthman was killed, Ali ibn Abi Talib moved the capital from Medina to Kufa. He was attacked in the Great Mosque by the Kharijite Abd-al-Rahman ibn Muljam while praying.

In the Umayyad era Muawiyah I appointed Ziyad ibn Abihi governor and he put down opposition among the followers of Hasan. When Yazid I became caliph, the Kufans turned to Muhammad's grandson Husayn for leadership, and Yazid sent Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad as governor, which led to the Battle of Karbala. In 749 the Abbasids under al-Hasan ibn Qahtaba took Kufa and made it their capital, before moving their seat to Baghdad in 762. The Qarmatians sacked it in 905, 924 and 927, and it never fully recovered. From the 11th century it came under constant attack, shrank and lost its importance.

Kufa is a holy city of Shia Islam, with Najaf, Karbala and others. The Great Mosque contains the shrines of Muslim ibn Aqil, Hani ibn Urwa and al-Mukhtar, and the place where Ali was struck. Other sites include Ali's house and the tomb of Zayd ibn Ali. The city was a major centre of scholarship: Abu Hanifa, a founder of a Sunni school of law, was a Kufan, and Shia theology began there. The Kufic script is named for the city, and is regarded as the earliest form of Arabic script, derived from the script of al-Hirah. Its population was estimated at 110,000 in 2003.
kufra: Kufra is a basin and group of oases in the Kufra District of southeastern Cyrenaica in Libya, in the middle of the Sahara. The basin is elliptical, with a major axis of 50 kilometres and a minor axis of 20, bordered by hills at most 100 metres high. Al Jawf, the largest oasis, lies at its northeast end and is rich in palms and gardens. Buma and Buema lie east of it, and Ez-Zurgh, Et-Tleilíb and Et-Talláb lie to the south and southwest. On the north edge is the village of El Tag, which has no oasis.

Surrounded on three sides by depressions, Kufra dominates the passage of east-west traffic across the desert. A folk etymology derives the name from the Arabic kafir, meaning disbeliever, in reference to the Toubou people native to the region.

In 1154 al-Idrisi described a place that has been identified as Kufra, once flourishing but then in ruin. Gerhard Rohlfs reached the oasis from the north in 1879. In 1895 the Senussi, seeking greater independence, moved from Jaghbub and made Kufra their main centre, and El Tag, founded by Sayyid Muhammad al-Mahdi as-Senussi, became their holy place.

General Rodolfo Graziani conquered Kufra in 1931, leading about 3,000 soldiers supported by about twenty bombers. The Italians built an airfield at Buma and a fort at El Tag, and the oasis became a station on the air route to Italian East Africa.

After the Suez Canal closed to Italian shipping in the Second World War, Kufra grew more important as a link with Italian East Africa. Free French forces from Chad under General Leclerc, with Chadian troops, attacked and took it in the Battle of Kufra in 1941.

In May 1942 three South African Air Force Bristol Blenheim aircraft became lost, and after landing safely their crews died of thirst. During the 2011 Libyan Civil War, fighting for the town ended with it in rebel hands by 6 May 2011.

At the beginning of the 1970s Libya launched a large agricultural project at Kufra, using fossil water from the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer System to irrigate circles about a kilometre in diameter that can be seen from space. Kufra receives only about 1 millimetre of rain a year. The town is still dominated by the fort of El Tag, built by the Italians in the mid-1930s, and Kufra Airport lies at Buma.
kuge: The word comes from Middle Chinese kuwng-kæ, ducal family, and first meant the emperor and his court; over time it came to mean the court's officials. In the relative peace of the Heian period most kuge lived in Kyoto and were free to pursue cultural interests. In the Kamakura period, from 1185 to 1333, kuge became the opposite of buke, the warrior nobles who swore loyalty to the shogunate, and the word was used for all who worked at court, nobles and commoners alike.

The kuge had two classes: the dōjō, who sat on the floor with the emperor, and the lower jige, who could not. In the 12th century the dōjō were divided into groups according to the highest office open to them. The sekke, five families descended from Fujiwara no Michinaga, could become sesshō and kampaku. The seigake, of Fujiwara or Minamoto descent, could become ministers up to daijō-daijin, the chancellor. Below them came the daijinke, the military urinke and the civilian meika, who could reach dainagon, and the hanke, created in the late Sengoku period. The jigeke handled the palace's cooking, cleaning and other business, and like the others held their ranks by inheritance.
Besides the Fujiwara and Minamoto, kuge families came from clans such as the Sugawara, Kiyohara and Ōe. Buddhist priests, Kyoto patrons of culture, geisha and actors were also associated with them.

Though they lost most of their political power, the kuge kept up the court's culture. As masters of fields such as waka poetry and the biwa they took disciples among the daimyō and sometimes rich commoners, and issued them licences to perform in public or to teach. Each licence carried a fee, and in the Edo period these fees were an important part of kuge income. In the kazoku peerage created in 1869 the former court families regained some of their status.
kuito: Cuíto stands in the historical heart of the Ovimbundu kingdom, whose ruler was named Viye. According to tradition he married a Songo woman named Cahanda, and together they built the city; the Portuguese later named Bié Province after the ruler. The Ovimbundu were known for selling captives from neighbouring peoples to European slave traders, which made the area a centre of that trade and brought colonists to it. The Portuguese founded the city in 1750 and later called it Silva Porto after António da Silva Porto, who built his home, Belmonte, in the area.

The mild climate of Bié Province attracted Portuguese settlers, and many made their home in Silva Porto in the early 1900s after the Benguela Railway connected it to the coast. In the 1960s the Portuguese used the town as a training centre for black soldiers of the Portuguese army, to be sent to northern Angola against nationalist guerrillas in the Portuguese Colonial War.

After independence from Portugal in 1975 the city suffered its worst times in the Angolan Civil War. UNITA laid siege to it from 6 January 1993. Nobody was permitted to enter or leave, the city was heavily damaged, and over 30,000 people were killed, both by the fighting and by starvation. UNITA was eventually driven out, and a second attempt to capture the city, with heavy artillery and tanks, was made in 1998.

Cuíto, the capital of Bié Province, lies on the eastern flank of the Bié Plateau, where its elevation gives it an unusually cool climate for the tropics, with an average annual temperature of 18 °C. The municipality had a population of 450,881 in 2014. The city is served by the Benguela Railway, whose station lies a few kilometres north of the town, and by flights from Luanda.
kujula-kadphises: The origins of Kujula Kadphises are obscure. He is usually believed to be a descendant of the Kushan ruler Heraios, or possibly identical with him. His name Kujula is shared with some of the last Indo-Scythian rulers, such as Liaka Kusulaka and his son Patika Kusulaka, which might suggest a family connection. On his coins, inscribed in the Indian Kharosthi script, he styled himself Maharaja Rajarajasa Devaputra Kujula Kara Kadphises, meaning Great King of Kings, Son of the Divine Being. He is described as the prince who united the Yuezhi confederation in Bactria in the 1st century CE.

The chronology of the Kushan rulers remains uncertain, and the dates proposed for Kujula's reign differ among scholars. He was a contemporary of Roman emperors from Claudius to Domitian. Latin sources mention Indian ambassadors received by some of them, though it is unclear whether these were independent merchants or officials of the Kushan Empire. Roman influence shows in his coinage, among it a series of copper tetradrachms with a bust modelled after Augustus and a curule chair on the reverse.

In their expansion eastward, Kujula and his son Vima Takto seem to have displaced the Indo-Parthian kingdom founded in northwestern India by Gondophares. The invasion is thought to have come some time after 45 CE, under Gondophares's successors Abdagases and Sases. A Chinese account says that his son defeated Tianzhu, placed generals to govern it, and that the Yuezhi then became extremely rich. It adds that all the kingdoms called their king the Guishuang, or Kushan, king, while the Han called them by their original name, Da Yuezhi. Statues at the palace site of Khalchayan in Bactria, dated to about 50 CE, probably belong to his rule.

The Rabatak inscription, found in 1993 in what was once Bactria and set up by Kanishka, names Kujula Kadphises as his great-grandfather, Vima Taktu as his grandfather and Vima Kadphises as his father, and records that Kanishka ordered images made for them. Kujula's first coin issue bears the debased portrait and name of Hermaeus with Heracles on the reverse, in the Greek tradition, though Heracles may be the Greek rendering of the Iranian god Verethragna. Earlier scholars took him for a Buddhist because of the epithet satyadharmasthita, but a Mathura inscription of Huvishka, who bears the same epithet, shows that it belonged to a devotee of Shiva, and he is now regarded as a Shaivite.
kuk-swamp: Kuk Swamp lies in the Wahgi Valley of the Papua New Guinea highlands, at an altitude of about 1,550 metres and some 12–13 kilometres north-east of Mount Hagen, the capital of Western Highlands Province. The swamp developed in a former lake basin that was filled by an alluvial fan, a deposit of water-borne material. Kuk Creek flows through the whole of the fan to a catchment in the lower hills to the south, and channels were built to carry water past the reach of the fan. If they were blocked, the area turned into a swamp that diverted water into smaller channels.

Evidence of early agricultural drainage, beginning about 9,000 years ago, has been found at the site. Pits, postholes and runnels point to planting, digging and the tethering of plants. The ditches fall into three classes: major disposal channels, which diverted water flowing south from the fan towards the north-east, and large and small field ditches, which are more uniform, surround the planting areas and connect with the major channels. With them the people of Kuk turned the swamp into an anthropogenic grassland suited to agriculture, where plants including taro were grown at the edge of their cultivable limit in the highlands.

Excavation of the channels yielded wooden digging sticks and a grindstone. Layers of clay in the ditches show that people built them deliberately. Further evidence, dated between 6,900 and 6,400 years ago, shows the cultivation of bananas and sugar cane. Banana phytoliths are numerous in the cultivation plots; since bananas do not produce phytoliths in the quantity grasses do, researchers concluded that their abundance in a managed grassland between 6950 and 6550 years ago indicates deliberate planting. The bananas were Eumusa bananas, the largest group of banana domesticates.

The site was studied by the Australian archaeologist Jack Golson. UNESCO designated Kuk Swamp a World Heritage Site in 2008, as one of the places in the world where people developed agriculture independently. The Kawelka, a Melpa-speaking people, live in the area.
kukai: Kūkai was born on 27 July 774 in the precinct of Zentsū-ji temple in Sanuki province on Shikoku, into the aristocratic Saeki family, a branch of the ancient Ōtomo clan, and was originally named Saeki no Mao. At fifteen he began to study the Chinese classics under his maternal uncle, and in 791 he went to Nara to study at the government university. His family's fortunes had fallen after the clan was accused of the murder of a rival. He became disillusioned with Confucian studies and turned to Buddhist practice, chanting the mantra of the bodhisattva Kokūzō in remote mountains. At twenty-four he published his first major work, Sangō Shiiki, which quotes the classics of Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism.

A dream led him to the Mahavairocana Tantra, much of which he could not understand, so he resolved to go to China. In 804 he joined a government expedition there, and in 805 at the Qinglong Monastery in Chang'an the monk Huiguo initiated him into esoteric Buddhism. He returned to Japan in 806 with many texts new to Japan.

In 809 the court ordered him to reside at Takao-san temple, now Jingo-ji, and Emperor Saga supported him. In 816 Saga accepted his request for a mountain retreat at Mount Kōya, consecrated in 819, though it was not complete until after his death. In 823 Saga gave him Tō-ji in Kyoto, which became the first esoteric Buddhist centre there; an imperial decree gave Kūkai its exclusive use for the Shingon school.

In 821 he restored the Manno Reservoir, still the largest irrigation reservoir in Japan. In 827 he became Daisōzu of the Office of Priestly Affairs, and in 828 he opened a school open to all regardless of social rank, which taught Daoism and Confucianism as well as Buddhism and gave pupils free meals. He completed his major work, the Jūjūshinron, in 830.

Kūkai spent most of his last years at Mount Kōya and died there in 835, at the age of 62. In accordance with his will he was entombed on the eastern peak rather than cremated. The faithful believe that he is still alive, in deep meditation, awaiting the Buddha Maitreya, and his mausoleum at Okunoin is the main site of devotion to him. Modern Shingon sees him as a bodhisattva, and the Shikoku Pilgrimage is the most important pilgrimage route associated with him. Many legends surround him: he is said to have been welcomed on Mount Kōya by two Shinto deities of the mountain, and one legend credits him with inventing the kana syllabary.
kukawa: The town was first called Kuka, the Kanuri name for the African baobab, which grew widely in the countryside around it. The name has caused some confusion, since the geographers Muhammad al-Idrisi in the 12th century and Ibn Khaldun in the 14th both mention towns called Kaou Kaou, one of them very close to the present town. Kuka stood at the end of one of the main trans-Saharan routes to Tripoli. Rainfall is only 400–500 mm a year, with hot, rainy summers and dry winters.

Al-Kanemi moved to Kuka from his former seat at Ngurno as he took a more independent line towards the mai, Dunama IX Lefiami, and adopted the style of shehu. In 1846 Mai Ibrahim IV Lefiami tried to restore royal power against al-Kanemi's son Umar Kura; his allies from the Wadai Sultanate captured and destroyed Kuka, but Ibrahim and his son Ali V Minargema were defeated. Umar Kura took sole power, the mais' capital at Kafela was destroyed, and Kuka became the capital of the Kanem–Bornu Empire.

Umar Kura rebuilt it as two walled towns, Kuka Futebe (West Town) and Kuka Gedibe (East Town), where the shehu and the elite lived, about half a mile apart inside a 20-foot mud wall; the plural form Kukawa may come from this. In the late 19th century it held between 60,000 and 200,000 people and grew rich from caravans and pilgrims bound for Mecca. The French explorer Parfait-Louis Monteil came in 1892. When Rabih az-Zubayr took the town in May 1893 it was plundered and burned, and its people were killed, enslaved or dispersed; he then made Dikwa his capital.

In 1903 Shehu Abubakar Garbai settled in the ruins, by then a British garrison town, and Frederick Lugard invested him there in 1904. With poor water and no trade route, the site was abandoned for Yerwa (modern Maiduguri) in 1907.

Kukawa is one of the sixteen Local Government Areas of the Borno Emirate, and Baga lies within it. Its people are mainly Kanuri and Shuwa Arabs, living by farming, fishing and trade. The area suffered from the Boko Haram insurgency: a massacre took place in Kukawa in July 2015, and in August 2020 the Islamic State West Africa Province held hundreds of its people hostage.
kul-oba: The name means hill of ash in Crimean Tatar, and the mound is now also called the Royal Kurgan. It stands near Kerch, beside the M25 road to Feodosiya. The stone tomb inside was probably built by a team of Greek masons from Panticapaeum. Its plan is almost square, 4.6 by 4.2 metres, under a stepped vault 5.3 metres high. The timber ceiling seems to have been designed to imitate a Scythian wooden tent and was hung with a canopy of gold plaques.

Kul-Oba was the first Scythian royal barrow to be excavated in modern times, and its finds drew wide public interest to the Scythian world. The principal burial lay by the east wall on a wooden couch. The dead man wore a diadem with a pointed felt cap hung with gold pendants and, at his neck, a gold disk weighing 461 grams, with one to three bracelets on each wrist. Beside him were a phial, a whip, a knife and a quiver, all inlaid with gold or precious stones.

To the left of the couch stood a sarcophagus of cypress wood and ivory holding a woman in a brocaded dress, with an electrum diadem, open-work earrings, a gold necklace and bracelets and a bronze mirror with a gilded handle. The remains of a man buried by the south wall are thought to be a charioteer. A niche held horse bones, a helmet and two spearheads, and silver bowls, bronze cauldrons with lamb bones and amphorae with traces of wine lined the walls.

One of the best-known finds is a granulated earring with two figures of Nike, now in the Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg. The excavators did not suspect a secret room beneath the tomb. Treasure hunters found and plundered it, though the Russian government later recovered some of the missing objects.
kul-tigin: Kül Tigin (684-731) was a general and a prince of the Second Turkic Khaganate. He was the second son of Ilterish Qaghan, the founder of the khaganate, and the younger brother of Bilge Qaghan, born Ashina Mojilian, the fourth qaghan. He was seven when his father died. His name is read kül rather than köl, since Chinese sources used the character 闕 (què), though Bazin and Hamilton preferred köl.

During the reign of Qapaghan Qaghan, Kül Tigin and his older brother earned a reputation for military prowess. They defeated the Yenisei Kyrgyz, the Türgesh and the Karluks, extended the territory of the khaganate to the Iron Gate south of Samarkand, and subjugated all nine of the Toquz Oghuz tribes. In 705 Turkic forces under Ashina Mojilian entered Lingwu and defeated Shazha Chongyi, and Kül Tigin commanded a unit in the battle, in which he lost three horses. In 711 he took part in the Battle of Bolchu, which was disastrous for the Türgesh.

In 712 the Arab general Qutayba ibn Muslim besieged Samarkand. Qapaghan Qaghan sent Kül Tigin at the head of a combined army of Eastern Turks, Tashkent forces and Ferghana troops to relieve the city. Qutayba ultimately defeated the army, and the Umayyads entered Samarkand and established a garrison. In 713 Kül Tigin and his brother and uncle took part in the subjugation of the Karluk tribes.

After Qapaghan Qaghan died, his son Inel Qaghan tried to take the throne in defiance of the traditional lateral succession. Kül Tigin refused to recognise the takeover, raised an army, and killed Inel, Ashina Duoxifu and their trusted followers. He placed Mojilian on the throne as Bilge Qaghan and took the title of shad, the equivalent of commander-in-chief, for himself.

Kül Tigin died suddenly on 27 February 731. A stele in his memory, inscribed in Turkic and in Chinese, was erected at his memorial complex at Khöshöö Tsaidam, the site of the Orkhon inscriptions. His burial ceremony took place on 1 November 731, and Bilge Qaghan posthumously named him Inanču Apa Yarğan Tarqan. He is also mentioned in the inscription for Bilge Qaghan at the neighbouring site of Khöshöö Tsaidam-1. The Czech archaeologist Lumir Jisl found the head of his sculpture in 1957-1958, carrying a bird with spread wings.
kulak: The word kulak was first used in the 19th century as a pejorative for wealthier peasants who owned land and offered credit to poorer ones. After the abolition of serfdom in 1861, and again in the Stolypin reform of 1906 to 1914, some peasants became landowners and lenders. Ivan Koshko, governor of Penza, wrote in 1899 that kulaks had exploited the inactivity of state rural banks to force poorer peasants into predatory loans. By 1912 about 16 per cent of peasants held over 3 hectares per male family member, the statistical threshold for prosperous farmers. Such farmers were about 20 per cent of the rural population and produced almost half the grain sold on the market.

Soviet terminology divided the peasants into poor peasants, mid-income peasants and kulaks, with landless seasonal workers as a fourth group. The Bolsheviks regarded the middle peasants as hesitant allies and the kulaks as class enemies, though the legal criteria shifted often after 1917 and officials applied them arbitrarily. Historian Robert Conquest argues that peasants with a couple of cows or a few acres more than their neighbours came to be labelled kulaks.

In May 1929 a decree defined a kulak household by criteria such as permanent hired labour, ownership of a mill or processing equipment, renting out equipment, or trade and moneylending, and in 1930 local authorities were allowed to add criteria. In Ukraine in 1930 and 1931 the label podkulachnik, or sub-kulak, was applied to those close to kulaks or who urged others to resist quotas.

In August 1918 Lenin sent his Hanging Order, calling for at least one hundred known kulaks to be hanged publicly. In July 1929 Stalin called for an offensive to eliminate the kulaks as a class, and on 30 January 1930 the Politburo approved their dissolution, sorting them into three categories: those to be sent to the Gulag, those to be moved to distant provinces and those to be resettled within their home provinces. Officials seized farms and executed many, and peasants slaughtered millions of animals rather than hand them over.

Soviet archives, published internationally in 1990, record 1,803,392 people sent to labour colonies and camps in 1930 and 1931, of whom 1,317,022 are recorded as reaching their destinations. Estimates of deaths range from 700,000 in Soviet sources to as many as six million, the figure Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn gave. The famine of 1932 and 1933 complicates the count.
kullervo-manner: Kullervo Achilles Manner was born on 12 October 1880 in Kokemäki, the son of the minister Gustaf Manner and of Alma Limón, a pastor's daughter. After leaving high school in 1900 he worked as a journalist in Porvoo and Helsinki. In 1906 he founded the Porvoo newspaper Työläinen (Worker) and edited it until 1909. An article it published in 1909 brought him, by then a member of parliament, a six-month prison sentence for lèse-majesté against Nicholas II. His brother Arvo Manner later governed the provinces of Viipuri and Kymi.

Manner was elected to parliament for Uusimaa as a Social Democrat in 1910 and 1917, and chaired the Social Democratic Party of Finland in 1917–1918. He was named chairman of the Finnish People's Delegation on 28 January 1918. On 10 April 1918 he became commander-in-chief of the Red Guards and head of their short-lived government, with dictatorial powers, while the White Guards under General Mannerheim and the Senate held northern Finland.

In Soviet Russia he succeeded Yrjö Sirola as chairman of the Finnish Communist Party and became an official of the Comintern. His decline began in 1929, when he and his wife Hanna Malm lost a briefcase of secret papers in Stockholm; the Swedish police seized it on a tip from the Finnish state police, and sixty-five communist agents in Finland were arrested and prosecuted. The Comintern then rebuked the party for its passivity towards the far-right Lapua Movement, and Malm was removed from the central committee.

Manner and Malm blamed the failure of 1918 on the slow Social Democratic leaders, Manner among them, and on the Bolsheviks, who under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk had withheld promised aid. When Malm made this public in 1932 and named Otto Wille Kuusinen, the party reacted severely; Manner recanted, and she was exiled for a year to Uhtua in Soviet Karelia. He lost most of his posts in May 1934. Arrested in 1935, both were sent to labour camps. Malm drowned herself at Solovki on 8 August 1937, and Manner died at the Ukhtpechlag camp on 15 January 1939, officially of tuberculosis, though the historian Alexander Popov suggests radiation sickness from work with radium-bearing water. He was rehabilitated in 1957.
kullu: Kullu is a municipal council town and the administrative headquarters of Kullu district. It stands on the banks of the Beas River in the Kullu Valley, about 10 km north of the airport at Bhuntar, at an average elevation of 1,278 m. The valley lies between the Pir Panjal, Lower Himalayan and Great Himalayan ranges, and the river, which rises at Beas Kund, passes a series of hillside settlements among forests of deodar, with pine on the lower rocky ridges. The town is 497 km from India's capital.

The valley appears in ancient Hindu literary works, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Puranas. During the Vedic period several small republics known as janapadas existed there. They were later conquered by the Nanda, Mauryan, Shunga, Gupta, Pala and Karkoṭa powers. After a brief period of supremacy under King Harshavardhana the region again divided among local chieftains, including some Rajput principalities, which were later conquered by the Mughal, Maratha and Sikh empires.

The Buddhist pilgrim monk Xuanzang visited the valley in 634 or 635 CE. He described a fertile region completely surrounded by mountains, with about twenty Buddhist monasteries and about 1,000 monks, most of them following the Mahayana tradition, and some fifteen Hindu temples. Both faiths used meditation caves near the mountain passes. The country was said to produce gold, silver, red copper, crystal lenses and bell-metal. In 1650, during the reign of Jagat Singh of Kullu, the Raghunath Temple was established after a priest, Pandit Damodar, took the idol of Rama from the Tretanath Temple at Ayodhya to Kullu.

Kullu's offices include those of the Deputy Commissioner, the Superintendent of Police and the district courts. The people speak the Kullui language. The 2011 census recorded a literacy rate of 79.4 per cent.
kulmbach: Kulmbach lies in the middle of Upper Franconia, about 25 kilometres north-west of Bayreuth. South of the town the River Main begins where the White Main and the Red Main meet. A small settlement around 900 CE, with a forest lodge and a fortified tenant farm guarding the Main crossing, preceded the town. Kulmbach is first mentioned as Kulma in a deed of gift between 1028 and 1040, and the name comes from a stream that runs down the mountain.

The area passed from the Counts of Schweinfurt to the Andechs family through a marriage, and the counts built the first Plassenburg in the early twelfth century. In 1180 Emperor Barbarossa raised the house to an imperial princedom with the title Duke of Merania. Around 1231 Kulmbach received town rights, and the rule of the Meranian dukes ended in 1248. The Thuringian counts of Orlamünde held it from 1260 and finished the new Plassenburg. In 1340, after the last Orlamünde died, the burgraves of Nuremberg, of the Hohenzollern family, took over. Trade flourished on the roads to Bamberg, Nuremberg, Eger, Hof and Leipzig, and the Hussites sacked the town on 31 January 1430.

The first Protestant service was held in St. Peter's Church in 1528 under Margrave George the Pious. In the Second Margrave War a league against Margrave Albert Alcibiades invaded Kulmbach on 26 November 1553 and burned it. Many citizens were massacred or fled, and the Plassenburg was destroyed in October 1554. Rebuilding began in 1557 under Margrave George Frederick, and the new Plassenburg, a major Renaissance building, was begun in 1559. In 1604 Margrave Christian moved his residence to Bayreuth, though the court returned several times, and Kulmbach lost its political importance. It passed to Prussia, was occupied in 1806 and went to Bavaria in 1810.

The Plassenburg houses the German Tin Soldiers Museum, with more than 300,000 tin figures. The railway arrived in 1846 and brought a boom for the breweries, which numbered 26 by 1882. Kulmbach became a free town in 1890 and the county town in the local reforms of 1972. The Kulmbacher Bratwurst and the strong beer known as EKU 28 are among its food specialities, and the Plassenburg is regarded as one of the great Renaissance castles in Germany.
kulob: Kulob is a city in Khatlon Region in southern Tajikistan, 203 km south-east of the capital Dushanbe on the river Yakhsu, a right tributary of the Panj. It is one of the largest cities in the country, with a population estimated at 106,300 for the city proper and 214,700 with its outlying communities (2020). It has a hot-summer Mediterranean climate, with an annual average temperature of 15.8 °C.

In the Hellenistic period the region was part of the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom. A Greek inscription of 200–195 BCE records a man named Heliodotos dedicating a fire altar to Hestia for the sake of King Euthydemus I and his son Demetrius I. The historian al-Tabari mentions Khatlon as early as 737 CE, though the city's founding is said to be much earlier. The Sufi mystic Mir Sayyid Ali Hamadani, who died while travelling through Central Asia in 1384, was buried in Khatlon, and his tomb still stands.

The city was conquered by the Mongol Empire under Genghis Khan and then formed part of the Timurid Empire. It was incorporated into the Khanate of Bukhara in 1559 and after the eighteenth century usually sided with the Emirate of Bukhara against Kokand and Afghanistan. Its name was changed to Kulob in 1750. In 1861 the local lord Surrah Khan imprisoned Abdul Mejid, a British and Kokand agent, on behalf of Bukhara, before disorder in the emirate led him to release the party.

Agreements between the British and Russian Empires over Afghanistan brought Kulob and its hinterland under the Russian Empire. After the Russian Revolution it was incorporated into the Soviet Union only in March 1921 and in 1929 became part of the Tajik Soviet Socialist Republic.

During the Tajikistani Civil War in the early 1990s the city was the main base of the Popular Front militias. Danghara, a village in the Kulob area, is the birthplace of the president Emomali Rahmon. After independence in 1991 the Russian 201st Motor Rifle Division was stationed in Kulob, as in Dushanbe and Qurghonteppa. In September 2006 the city marked its 2,700th anniversary. It is served by Kulob Airport.
kulottunga-i: Kulottunga, whose name means the Exalter of His Clan, was born around 1025 under the star of Pusya. His mother Ammangadevi was a daughter of Emperor Rajendra Chola I, and his father Rajaraja Narendra was himself the son of Kundavai, a daughter of Rajaraja Chola I. The poem Kalingattuparani describes his birth as an incarnation of the god Vishnu and says he was brought up at Rajendra's court in Gangaikondacholapuram.

As a prince he fought in the wars of Rajendra Chola I and his successors Rajadhiraja I, Rajendra Chola II and Virarajendra Chola. In his inscriptions he claims that, while still heir-apparent, he captured herds of elephants at Vayiragaram, conquered Sakkarakottam, the Chakrakota region around modern Bastar, and took tribute from its Nagavanshi ruler Dharavarsha.

Kulottunga succeeded his cousin Athirajendra Chola in 1070. That year Vijayabahu of Lanka attacked the Chola forces on the island from Rohana and took Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa; after further indecisive fighting the Cholas withdrew. On the mainland Kulottunga fought the Western Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI and then campaigned against the Pandyas, who had used the confusion of his accession to reassert their independence.

His reign saw wide overseas contacts. An embassy of 1077 to the Chinese court, which the historian Nilakanta Sastri attributes to him, returned with more than 81,000 strings of copper cash, and the Khmer king Suryavarman II presented him with a precious stone in 1114. An inscription of 1079 in a Taoist temple in Guangzhou calls him supreme chief of Srivijaya. At home he carried out a land survey that became the basis of taxation, replaced the Chola-Pandya viceroys in the south with military cantonments, and with his son enlarged the Nataraja Temple at Chidambaram sixfold.

Kulottunga died around 1122, at about 97, though this is disputed, and was succeeded by his son Vikrama Chola. Late in his reign the northern half of Vengi seems to have passed to Vikramaditya VI, and some historians hold that Gangavadi was lost to the Hoysala Vishnuvardhana. The poet Jayamkondar composed the Kalingattuparani at his court. Historians dispute whether he was Krimikanta Chola, the persecutor of the Vaishnavite acharya Ramanuja, and his records also show gifts to Vishnu shrines. Nilakanta Sastri judged that he avoided unnecessary wars and that his reign laid the foundation for the empire's well-being over the next 150 years.
kulturkampf: The Kulturkampf, or cultural struggle, was fought between the Catholic Church in Germany, led by Pope Pius IX, and the Kingdom of Prussia under Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. It was about the church's direct control of education and of ecclesiastical appointments. The years 1871 to 1878 mark only its culmination in Prussia, for the dispute over the separation of church and state was older. Predominantly Catholic Baden had been in the forefront of curbing church power, in the Baden Church Dispute of 1852 to 1854 and in its own Kulturkampf from 1864 to 1876. The name itself came into use on 17 January 1873, when the Progressive deputy Rudolf Virchow spoke in the Prussian legislature of a great cultural struggle.

From 1871 to 1876 the Prussian parliament and the Reichstag, both with liberal majorities, passed 22 laws. The Pulpit Law of 10 December 1871 punished clerics who discussed state affairs in a way that endangered public peace. The School Supervision Act of 11 March 1872, at the heart of the campaign, ended church oversight of Prussian primary schools. Prussia suspended relations with the Holy See in December 1872, after Rome had rejected Cardinal Hohenlohe as German ambassador. Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths followed in 1874 for Prussia and in 1875 for the empire.

On 13 July 1874 Eduard Kullmann tried to shoot Bismarck at Bad Kissingen, citing the church laws, and the attempt led to harsher measures. In 1875 the encyclical Quod Nunquam declared the May Laws invalid, the Payment Law stopped state payments to clerics who would not accept all the laws, and the Congregations Law dissolved all orders except those caring for the infirm. Even many liberals saw the later laws as an encroachment on civil liberties. In the Province of Posen the conflict took on a more nationalistic character, with Bismarck attempting to Germanise Polish areas.

The laws proved ineffective and even counterproductive against the Centre Party. The British ambassador Odo Russell reported in October 1872 that the German bishops, once politically powerless, had become powerful leaders and enthusiastic defenders of the Church of Rome. Strict supervision of schools was applied only in Catholic areas, which alienated Protestant conservatives as well.

After Germany formed the Dual Alliance with Austria in 1879, the danger of war with France or Russia receded, and Bismarck turned to the popularity of the socialists and to import duties, on which he could not rely on the liberals. He had never been comfortable with the growing ferocity of the campaign, and he had achieved more separation of church and state than he wanted. In later usage the term describes any conflict between a secular government and religious authorities, or between factions holding opposed values.
kumamoto: Katō Kiyomasa, a contemporary of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, was made daimyō of half of the old administrative region of Higo in 1588, and afterwards built Kumamoto Castle. Its many innovative defensive designs led to its being considered impenetrable, and Kiyomasa had a reputation as one of the finest castle-builders in Japanese history. After he died in 1611 his son Tadahiro succeeded him, until Tokugawa Iemitsu removed Tadahiro in 1632 and replaced him with the Hosokawa clan.

Hosokawa Tadatoshi, the third lord of Kumamoto, was the patron of the artist and swordsman Miyamoto Musashi, who lived the last part of his life in the city and wrote Go Rin no Sho, The Book of Five Rings, there. He died in 1645.

The castle was assaulted during the Satsuma Rebellion and sacked and burned after a 53-day siege. The tradition of eating basashi, raw horse meat, is said to have originated at that time. The present municipal administration was founded on 1 April 1889. The writers Lafcadio Hearn, from 1891 for three years, and Soseki Natsume, from 1896 to 1900, lived in Kumamoto. On 1 July 1945 an Allied air raid destroyed one square mile, 20 per cent of the city's area. A series of earthquakes struck the area from 14 April 2016, including a tremor of magnitude 7.1 on 16 April.

Kumamoto is the capital of Kumamoto Prefecture, on the island of Kyushu, and has been a designated city since 1 April 2012, with five wards. Its main landmark is Kumamoto Castle. The central keep is a concrete reconstruction built in the 1970s, but several wooden ancillary buildings of the original castle remain. Within the outer walls stands the Hosokawa Gyobu-tei, the former residence of the Higo daimyō, with a Japanese garden.

About three kilometres south-east is Suizen-ji Jōju-en, a formal garden. The Buddhist monk Nichidatsu Fujii began a peace pagoda on Mount Hanaoka in 1947, inaugurated in 1954, the first of more than 80 he and his followers built around the world. The downtown commercial district centres on two shopping arcades, Shimotori and Kamitori.
kumamoto-prefecture: Kumamoto Prefecture lies in the centre of Kyūshū, the southernmost of the four major Japanese islands. It borders Fukuoka and Ōita prefectures to the north, Miyazaki to the east and Kagoshima to the south, and its western side faces the Ariake Sea and is separated from the East China Sea by the Amakusa Archipelago. It covers 7,409 square kilometres.

Mount Aso, an extensive active volcano standing at the centre of the Aso caldera in the east of the prefecture, rises to 1,592 metres and is among the largest active volcanoes in the world. A fifth of the land is designated as natural parks, among them the Aso Kujū and Unzen-Amakusa National Parks.

The area was called Higo Province, and the province was renamed Kumamoto during the Meiji Restoration. The creation of prefectures was part of the abolition of the feudal system. The current Japanese spelling of Kumamoto literally means bear root or origin of the bear, but the Kuma River and Kuma District are written with other characters used for their sound, and the element also appears in the ancient name Kumaso.

Kumamoto is the capital and largest city, and other major cities include Yatsushiro, Amakusa and Tamana. The prefecture has fourteen cities. The largest motorcycle production facility in the world is in Kumamoto. Its sights include Kumamoto Castle, Suizenji Park and the Tsūjun Bridge at Yamato, the largest stone aqueduct in Japan. The prefecture's mascot, a black bear with red cheeks named Kumamon, was created to attract tourists after the Kyushu Shinkansen line opened.
kumarajiva: Kumārajīva was born in 344 in the Kingdom of Kucha, a Tocharian-speaking city-state of the Tarim Basin. His father, the Indian monk Kumārāyana, probably came from Kashmir or Gandhāra and became royal priest after the king gave him his younger sister Jīva in marriage. When Kumārajīva was seven his mother joined a nunnery. From the age of nine he studied the Agamas and the Sarvastivada Abhidharma in North India, Kashmir and Kucha, and he later turned to Mahayana under Buddhayaśas in Kashgar. He was ordained at 20 and became known for his skill in debate.

In 379 a Chinese monk's report brought his fame to China, and Emperor Fu Jian of the Former Qin sent the general Lü Guang to take Kucha and bring him to Chang'an. Fu Jian's main army was defeated, however, and Lü Guang set up his own state. Being no Buddhist, he held Kumārajīva prisoner for many years and forced him to marry the daughter of the king of Kucha, so that he gave up his monastic vows. He is thought to have learned Chinese then. Yao Xing of the Later Qin defeated the Lü family and brought him to Chang'an in 401.

There Yao Xing treated him as his teacher and gave him the title National Preceptor. He led a court-sponsored translation team that included Daosheng, Sengzhao, Daorong and Sengrui, working before audiences of more than a thousand monks. Within about twelve years the bureau had translated some thirty-five sutras in 294 scrolls.

The team rendered the Lotus Sutra, the Diamond Sutra, the Vimalakirti Nirdesa Sutra and the Prajñāpāramitā sutras, together with the main Madhyamaka treatises, and Kumārajīva introduced Madhyamaka to China, where it became the Sanlun school. The text was read aloud with his commentary, discussed and revised many times. The team replaced the older geyi method, which matched Buddhist terms to Daoist and Confucian ones, with clearer Chinese. His versions have often remained more popular than later, more literal ones such as Xuanzang's. Jan Nattier argues that their apparent abbreviations reflect earlier Indian source texts. He died in 413.
kumari-goddess: The word Kumari comes from Sanskrit, where it means a virgin or young unmarried girl. The worship of young girls as embodiments of divine energy has ancient roots in the Kathmandu Valley. The practice is first recorded in a 1280 inscription from the reign of King Ananta Malla, though oral and ritual traditions point to an origin in the Lichhavi period, about 400 to 750 CE, and a formal royal cult is widely linked to the later Malla kings.

The most popular foundation story concerns King Jaya Prakash Malla of Kantipur. According to legend, the goddess Taleju visited him nightly to play the dice game Tripasa, on condition that he tell no one. His daughter followed him and discovered the goddess, who was angered and vanished. Taleju later appeared to the king in a dream and told him to look for a young Shakya girl in whom she would manifest.

Believers hold that the Kumari is a living embodiment of Shakti, the cosmic energy, and that the goddess inhabits the body of a chosen girl; a young girl is chosen because of her purity and because she has not been touched by bleeding that could cause the goddess to leave. Candidates are drawn from the Shakya and Bajracharya castes of the Newar community and must be in excellent health, without scars or birthmarks, and have all their teeth. After approval, priests perform secret tantric purification rites until Taleju is believed to enter the girl.

The Royal Kumari's life is strictly regulated. Her feet never touch the ground outside her residence, and she is carried in a palanquin when she goes out. Devotees view her through a latticed window, and her silence and composure are read as omens. Her tenure ends when she loses blood, most commonly at her first menstruation, and the search for a successor begins.

During the Shah dynasty the king bowed before the Kumari each year at Indra Jatra and received a tika from her, reinforcing royal legitimacy. After the monarchy was abolished in 2008, the president of Nepal took over a similar ceremonial role. Besides the Royal Kumari of Kathmandu there are Kumaris at Patan, Bhaktapur and Bungamati, among other places.

In 2007 temple authorities declared the Kumari of Bhaktapur tainted after she travelled to the United States to attend a documentary screening, but reversed the decision after international attention. Child-rights activists criticised the isolation of a girl and her limited education, and in 2006 Nepal's Supreme Court directed the government to consider whether the tradition violated the rights of the child while respecting its religious significance. Since then reforms have included formal education and a state pension for former Kumaris.
kumasi: Kumasi lies in a rain forest region near Lake Bosomtwe, about 200 kilometres from Accra, on the eastern slopes of a ridge rising from the marshes of the Nsuben rivers. Its name comes from the Twi word Kumase, meaning "under the kum tree", after an Okum tree in Kwaman planted by Okomfo Anokye. The city was planned according to the traditional land settlement patterns of the Asante Empire, and some areas were declared sacred. A visitor in 1817 recorded 27 streets.

Traditions differ on the city's foundation. Most oral sources credit Okomfo Anokye with choosing the site: he is said to have planted two kum seeds, one in Kwaman and one in Kumawu, and decreed that the one that grew would be the capital of Osei Tutu's empire. Other accounts say Osei Tutu negotiated for land under a kum tree, or that Nana Oti Akenten bargained with the chief of Tafo for it. The Asantehene ruled both city and empire. In 1718–19 the Aowin king Ebirimoro invaded Kumasi and sacked it, and Asantehene Opoku Ware I beat back the invasion.

European visitors around 1873 described broad, clean streets shaded by banyan trees, though William Butler called it a more filthy and blood-stained collection of mud and wattle hovels than any other village in the forest. Estimates of the early 19th-century population ranged from 12–15,000 in European sources to 100,000 in Ashanti sources. The British burned parts of the city, including the royal residence, in the Third Anglo-Ashanti War of 1874, and took over Kumasi in 1896; Fort Kumasi was built that year. In 1926, after King Prempeh I returned from thirty years of exile in the Seychelles, the city was given ceremonial control over the Ashanti sub-states.

Kumasi is the capital of the Ashanti Region of Ghana and the second largest city in the country, with 443,981 inhabitants in the 2021 census. It remains the seat of the Asantehene and the centre of Asante culture, and legend says Okomfo Anokye received the Golden Stool here. The Manhyia Palace, dating from 1925, is a museum, and the Centre for National Culture holds Asante regalia. Kumasi is known for kente cloth and for the Kejetia Market.
kumbakonam: Kumbakonam, also called Kudanthai, lies about 40 km from Thanjavur and 282 km from Chennai, in the old delta region watered by the Kaveri and its tributaries. It is bounded by the Kaveri to the north and the Arasalar to the south and is the second-largest city of the district. Its name, roughly Pot's Corner, recalls the mythical pot of the creator god Brahma, which held the seeds of all living beings. Tradition holds that it was displaced during a cosmic dissolution and came to rest at the site of the city, an event commemorated in the Mahamaham festival held every twelve years.

The region was inhabited in the Sangam period. Kumbakonam is identified with the ancient town of Kudavayil, where the early Chola king Karikala held court, and it is linked with Malaikūrram, a Chola capital in the 7th century CE. According to the Sinnamanur plates, the Pandya king Srimara Srivallabha defeated a confederacy of Pallavas, Cholas and Western Gangas there in 859. The region grew in importance under the medieval Cholas between the 9th and 12th centuries. The Pandyas took the town in 1290, and after their decline in the 14th century it was conquered by the Vijayanagara Empire. The Vijayanagara emperor Krishnadevaraya visited in 1524 and bathed in the Mahamaham tank.

The Madurai and Thanjavur Nayaks ruled the town from 1535 until the Marathas annexed it in 1673. After the fall of Vijayanagara in 1565 poets, musicians and scholars came to the town. Tipu Sultan's invasion in 1784 caused heavy economic disruption, from which recovery took until the early 19th century. In 1799 the Thanjavur Maratha ruler Serfoji II ceded Kumbakonam to the British East India Company. It was made a municipality in 1866 and became a municipal corporation on 24 August 2021.

Kumbakonam is known as the temple city, with about 188 Hindu temples within the municipal limits. The Adi Kumbeswarar Temple is its oldest Shaivaite shrine, with origins in the 7th-century Chola period, and the Sarangapani temple, with a twelve-tiered gateway tower of the Nayak period, is its largest Vaishnavite shrine and one of the 108 Divya Desams. At nearby Darasuram the Airavatesvara Temple of the 12th century, built by Rajaraja Chola II, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Under British rule the city became a centre of Hindu scholarship and Western education, which earned it the name Cambridge of South India. The Government Arts College, founded as a provincial school in 1854, counted the mathematician Srinivasa Ramanujan among its alumni, and the Tamil scholar U. V. Swaminatha Iyer taught there. The 2011 census gave the city 140,156 inhabitants.
kumbaya: According to Stephen Winick of the Library of Congress, the song almost certainly arose among African Americans in the south-eastern United States, with a Gullah version appearing early even if it did not begin in that dialect. The two oldest versions of certain year were both collected in 1926 and are kept in the American Folklife Center: a manuscript of words without music, gathered in Alliance, North Carolina, by the student Minnie Lee for her teacher Julian P. Boyd, and a wax cylinder recorded by the folklorist Robert Winslow Gordon of a singer named H. Wylie, within a few hours' drive of Darien, Georgia.

Members of the Society for the Preservation of Spirituals collected a Gullah version, Come by Yuh, on the South Carolina coast at some time between 1922 and 1931, and in May 1936 John Lomax found Ethel Best singing Come by Here with a group in Raiford, Florida. These records contradict the long-standing attribution to the Reverend Marvin V. Frey, who claimed to have written the song around 1936 and said the title Kum Ba Yah came from Angola in 1946. Winick points out that in Wylie's dialect here is pronounced yah, which gives the phrase directly.

The Cooperative Recreation Service published the song in its Song Sampler pamphlet of January 1956, and it became a standard campfire song in Scouting and summer camps. The Folksmiths, among them Joe Hickerson, recorded it in 1957 and Pete Seeger in 1958, and Little Sugar and the Hightower Brothers released a gospel version on the Savoy label that year. Joan Baez's recording of 1962 spread it widely during the folk revival, and it became associated with the civil rights movement: marchers were recorded singing it during the Selma to Montgomery march of 1965.

From the 1990s the title entered the idiom of American politics, often used sarcastically to suggest that someone is too eager to compromise; Richard Vatz described such references as criticism of a consensus that does not examine the issues. President Barack Obama, Mike Huckabee and Herman Cain were among the politicians who used the phrase.
kumbhalgarh: Kumbhalgarh stands on a hilltop 1,100 metres above sea level on the western range of the Aravalli Hills in Rajsamand district, Rajasthan, about 84 kilometres from Udaipur. It has been called the Great Wall of India. Its perimeter walls extend 36 kilometres, among the longest continuous walls in the world, and the frontal walls are 4.5 metres thick. There are seven fortified gateways, and the palace known as Badal Mahal stands at the highest point of the fort. The name comes from Rana Kumbha, who ruled Mewar from 1433 to 1468 and commissioned the fort.

Rana Lakha had won the plains of Godwar from the Chauhan Rajputs of Nadol in the late 14th century. According to the Kumbhalgarh inscription, Rana Kumbha ordered the fort built in 1448, and its chief architect was Mandan, who described his methods in his text Rajvallabh. The fort was Kumbha's second most favoured capital. Of the 84 forts in his dominion he is said to have built 32, and Kumbhalgarh is the largest and most elaborate. Ahmad Shah II of Gujarat attacked it in 1457 and found the effort futile; local belief held that the deity Banmata protected the fort, and he destroyed her temple. Mahmud Khalji failed in further attempts in 1458–59 and 1467.

Akbar's general Shahbaz Khan besieged the fort in October 1577 and took it in April 1578, after a siege of six months. The Badshahi Bavdi, a stepped tank, was built after his invasion to supply his troops with water. Maharana Pratap recaptured the fort in 1583. In 1818 an armed band of sanyasis formed a garrison, but James Tod persuaded them to yield, and the British took the fort and later returned it to Udaipur State.

More than 360 temples, Jain and Hindu, stand within the walls, among them the Ganesha temple built by Maharana Kumbha, the Neel Kanth Mahadeva temple of 1458 with a black stone Shiva of twelve hands, and the Parsva Natha Jain temple of 1513. Maharana Pratap was born at the fort. Kumbhalgarh was inscribed in 2013, with five other forts of Rajasthan, as the Hill Forts of Rajasthan World Heritage Site, and the state tourism department holds a three-day annual festival there.
kumbo: Kumbo, also known as Kimbo, lies about 2,000 m above sea level on the Bamenda Highlands Ring Road, some 110 km from Bamenda, and is the capital of Bui Division. It is spread over three hilly settlements, Tobin, Mbveh and Squares, and had 80,212 inhabitants at the census of 2005. Lamnso is the common language, beside Pidgin, English, Oku, Djottin, Fulfulde, French and Hausa. The Mbve market sells goods from the region, from Nigeria and from other parts of Africa.

The Fon's palace, seat of the paramount ruler of the Nso people, is the centre of the town's social and cultural life: carved wooden buildings around two courtyards where the Fon receives his people and advisers, and a statue of Ngonso, held to be the first queen of the Nso. Beside it stand the houses of the Ngwerong and Nggiri societies, which help the Fon in his task. The Missionaries of the Sacred Heart arrived in 1912 and founded their mission in 1913, and most of the Nso are Christians.

The stone cathedral, built in the 1950s on a hilltop that dominates the town, became the seat of a bishop when the diocese of Kumbo was created. In May and June 2021, during the Anglophone Crisis, the Cameroonian Army carried out Operation Bui Clean to drive Ambazonian separatists from the town and its surroundings, with heavy casualties on both sides, and insurgents attacked the town again in April 2024.

Kumbo is the second-largest town of the North West and is known for its horse racing, a custom brought by the Mbororo cattle herders, whose annual race is held at the Tobin Municipal Stadium. The Musa Heritage Gallery, founded in 1996, keeps over 400 carved masks, statues and other works of the Western Grassfields. The statue of Ngonnso, founder of the kingdom, is held in a museum in Germany, and people in Nso have called for its return.
kumo-xi: The Göktürks called them the Tatabi. Chinese histories place them among the peoples of Donghu origin: the Book of Sui says the Xi were originally called the Kumo Xi, and the New Book of Tang says that after a defeat by the Xiongnu they took refuge in the Wuwan Mountains and that the leader Tadun, killed by Cao Cao, was of their line. The Book of Wei records that the Kumo Xi and the Khitans spoke the same language and fled together to the region of Songmo.

The meaning of the name is disputed. Omeljan Pritsak reconstructed it as qu(o)mâġ-ġay, the first part related to Mongolian and Turkic words for fine sand; Peter Benjamin Golden reads it as desert Qay or sand Qay, after their earlier homeland. Yury Zuev derived Tatabi from an Iranic phrase for falling waters.

In 388 the Kumo Xi and the Khitans fought the Northern Wei dynasty. The war weakened the Kumo Xi far more than the Khitans, and the two peoples split into separate polities. By the early Tang dynasty, in about the 7th century, the Xi were subordinate to the Khitans, but after the Khitans' Li-Sun Rebellion of 696–697 and the revolt of Ketuyu in 730–734 they regained the upper hand.

A period of strength followed, from about 755 to 847. The Xi were friendly with An Lushan, backed his rebellion and often raided Han territory. These raids drew heavy Tang responses, and battles in the 760s and in 795 went badly for them; after 795 they paid tribute to the Tang. When the Uyghur Khaganate collapsed in the 840s, the Xi rebelled in 847 and were crushed by Zhang Zhongwu, frontier commander of Lulong. They never recovered, and in the late ninth century the rising Khitans absorbed what remained of them, founding the Liao dynasty in 907.

The Xiqin, a bowed string instrument, is believed to derive from an instrument of the Xi. It is regarded as the ancestor of the Chinese erhu and of the Mongolian khuuchir and morin khuur. The history of the Kumo Xi is closely linked to that of the better-known Khitans, who absorbed them.
kumtor-gold-mine: Kumtor is one of the largest gold mines in Central Asia, and at 13,000 feet one of the highest anywhere. The deposit is worked as an open pit by drilling and blasting, with trucks and loaders or shovels carrying the ore to a crusher and then to a mill, where the gold is extracted by the carbon-in-leach process. The mill is rated to treat about 16,000 tonnes of ore a day. By 30 June 2022 the mine had produced over 13.8 million ounces of gold. In 2020 its operations accounted for 12.5% of the gross domestic product of Kyrgyzstan and 23.3% of its industrial output.

A geophysical expedition of the State Geological Committee of the Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic discovered the deposit in 1978. In 1992 the new Government of Kyrgyzstan and the Cameco Corporation signed an agreement forming the Kumtor Gold Project, and Cameco became its full owner that year. Construction began in 1993, and commercial production started in May 1997. The government's dealings with Centerra Gold over the mine were long in dispute: in 2013 Parliament rejected a draft memorandum for a 50/50 joint venture, demanding a Kyrgyz share of 67 percent, and in December 2015 the government withdrew from the talks.

The disputes went to international courts until the Strategic Environment and Investment Agreement between Centerra Gold and the government settled the arbitration and environmental claims. On 16 November 2016 amendments to the Water Code permitted commercial activity near the Davydov and Lysyi glaciers. From 2012 campaigners called for nationalisation, accusing Centerra Gold of environmental violations and corruption. On 14 May 2021 President Sadyr Japarov signed a law allowing temporary state control, and on 17 May the Cabinet of Ministers placed the Kumtor Gold Company under external management, appointing Tengiz Bolturuk to run it. Centerra Gold answered with arbitration, and one source described the action as an expropriation.
kumul-rebellion: Jin Shuren became governor of Xinjiang after the assassination of Yang Zengxin in 1928. He openly antagonised the Uyghurs and Kyrgyz with travel restrictions, higher taxes, seizures of property and frequent executions. Pressed for money and crowded with Han refugees from warlord fighting elsewhere in China, he annexed the semi-autonomous Kumul Khanate, whose khans were Chagataids, last ruling descendants of Genghis Khan. Kumulik land was taken and given to Han settlers, and rebellion broke out on 20 February 1931, with many Han killed by the local population.

Yulbars Khan, an adviser at the Kumul court, appealed to Ma Zhongying, a Hui warlord in Gansu, who had a secret understanding with the Kuomintang that he would be recognised as ruler of the province if he won it. Ma besieged Kumul but could not take the city and, wounded in October, withdrew to Gansu. Jin bought two Soviet biplanes and signed a secret treaty with the Soviet Union in October 1931, and provincial troops relieved Kumul on 30 November 1931.

In the south a separate rising in Khotan, led by Muhammad Amin Bughra and his brothers, sought complete independence and was hostile to both Han and Hui. On 20 February 1933 a provisional government was set up there with Sabit Damulla Abdulbaki as prime minister. Its forces expelled Swedish missionaries, persecuted Christian converts and killed Hindus in Karghalik and Khotan. In April 1933 White Russian troops in Ürümqi overthrew Jin and installed Sheng Shicai. Ma Zhongying returned, his troops notorious for looting and burning villages, and with Zhang Peiyuan attacked Sheng in the Second Battle of Ürümqi.

Sheng called on the Soviet Union, whose troops crossed the border in January 1934 and drove Ma back from Ürümqi with aerial bombing; Zhang Peiyuan was defeated and took his own life. Ma's retreating Hui forces turned south and destroyed the East Turkestan government at Kashgar, Yarkand and Yangi Hissar. In February 1934 between 1,700 and 2,000 Uyghur civilians in Kashgar Old City were massacred in revenge for the Kizil massacre of Han and Hui. Ma Zhongying's brother-in-law Ma Hushan then governed southern Xinjiang in the name of the central government.
kumulipo: Hawaiian kahuna and priests recited the Kumulipo during the makahiki season, which honoured the god Lono. When James Cook arrived in Kealakekua Bay on the island of Hawaiʻi in 1779, during that season, he was greeted with its recitation; some stories say Cook was taken for Lono because of the type of sails on his ship and his pale skin. In 1889 King Kalākaua printed it as a sixty-page pamphlet, with a two-page paper on how it was first composed and recited.

The chant runs to 2,102 lines and tells of the world created over a cosmic night, not one night but many over time. It is a cosmogonic genealogy in sixteen wā, or ages, in each of which something is born. The first seven belong to pō, darkness, the age of spirit, in which the plants and animals of sea and land appear in stages like the growth of a child, each sea creature paired with a land cousin of similar name: limu seaweed with ferns, 73 kinds of fish, 52 kinds of flying creatures.

The remaining nine wā form ao, opened by the arrival of light and the gods. The four divinities Laʻilaʻi, Kiʻi, Kāne and Kanaloa are born, and the first humans come from Laʻilaʻi. Later ages honour the lineage of Wākea, whose son Hāloa is the ancestor of all people, tell of Māui, and trace his line for forty-four generations down to Piʻilani, after which comes the genealogy of Kalaninuiamamao to the late 18th century.

Queen Liliʻuokalani, who described it as a prayer of the development of the universe and the ancestry of the Hawaiians, translated it while under house arrest in ʻIolani Palace. Other translations include Adolf Bastian's German and Martha Warren Beckwith's English of 1951. Bastian and Roland Burrage Dixon read a recurring verse as describing the octopus as the sole survivor of an earlier age, a reading Beckwith translated differently. The name Pōwehi, a poetic phrase for generative darkness from the chant, was informally given to the black hole M87*.
kumyks: The Kumyks are the largest Turkic people of the North Caucasus and live in Dagestan, Chechnya and North Ossetia. They traditionally populate the Kumyk Plateau in northern Dagestan and north-eastern Chechnya, along the Caspian Sea and the banks of the Terek River. Most researchers derive the name from a Turkic ethnonym, Kimak, or from another name for the Kipchaks, the Cuman. Scholars disagree about their origin. Some see the population of the Kumyk plains in the 8th to 10th centuries as their ancestors, others link them to the Khazars, and others hold that Kumyk identity appeared in the 12th and 13th centuries with Kipchak migration.

Kumyks were historically linked with the Caucasian Huns, the Khazars, the Cuman-Kipchaks and the Golden Horde, and all their lands were once part of the Tarki Shamkhalate. In the 16th century their rulers balanced between three neighbouring states, the Ottoman Empire, Persia and Russia, and the Shamkhalate became a considerable regional power. Russian campaigns began in the 1560s, when the commander Cheremisinov seized and plundered Tarki in 1560. In 1594 Kumyk forces turned back a Russian and Cossack expedition under Khvorostinin.

Kumyks were among the main forces of Sheikh Mansur's rising in the late 18th century. The Russian authorities abolished the Tarki Shamkhalate in 1867, which may be seen as the end of Kumyk statehood. In mid-July 1916 Kumyks rose at Aksay against conscription, and the rising ended on 24 July when the draft was cancelled. On 12 April 1944 Soviet authorities deported the Kumyk inhabitants of Tarki and neighbouring villages to Central Asia.

The Kumyk language is a Kipchak language and was the lingua franca of the North Caucasus, from Dagestan to Kabarda, until the 1930s. It was an official language of communication between the peoples of the north-eastern Caucasus and the Russian administration. In 1848 Timofey Makarov published a Kumyk grammar, the first written in Russian for any language of the North Caucasus. Leo Tolstoy and Mikhail Lermontov, who both served in the Caucasus, studied the language. Kumyks make up about 14 percent of the population of Dagestan, and more than 500,000 lived in Russia at the 2010 census.
kunene-river: The Cunene, spelled Kunene in Namibia, flows from the highlands of Angola southwards to the border with Namibia, and then west along the border until it reaches the Atlantic Ocean. It is one of the few perennial rivers in the region, about 1,050 kilometres long, with a drainage basin of 106,560 square kilometres. Its mean annual discharge at the mouth is between 174 and 222 cubic metres per second. It runs generally north to south through four degrees of latitude and finally turns west to the sea through a break in the outer highlands.

Between the mouths of its two tributaries the river crosses a swampy plain, flooded at high water. Divergent branches run to the southeast, mostly intermittent, and one of them, the Kwamatuo, flows into a large marsh or lake called Etosha. After the swampy region the Cunene descends to the coast plain through a number of cataracts, the chief of which has a fall of 330 feet. The river shrinks as it crosses an almost desert region, and near the sea it passes through sand-hills, its mouth being completely blocked at low water.

The Epupa Falls lie on the river, and the Olushandja Dam, on the tributary Etaka, helps to supply the Ruacana Power Station with water. Namibia proposed in the late 1990s the Epupa Dam, a controversial hydroelectric project, and in 2012 Namibia and Angola announced plans for the Orokawe Dam in the Baynes Mountains. The Himba, who would have been most affected, objected that the dam would threaten the local ecosystem and their economic basis. Himba chiefs issued a declaration against it to the African Union and the United Nations in February 2012, and in 2012 and 2013 Himba and Zemba marched in protest at Okanguati and Opuwo. Tourists visit campsites and lodges at Epupa, where ancient baobab trees grow beside the gorge.
kunlun-mountains: From the Pamirs the Kunlun Mountains run east through southern Xinjiang to Qinghai province, along the southern edge of the Tarim Basin, which holds the Taklamakan Desert. South of the range lies the sparsely populated Changtang region of the Tibetan Plateau. The chief northern ranges are the Altyn Tagh and its north-eastern extension, the Qilian Shan; the Min Shan is the main extension in the south. The Bayan Har Mountains, a southern branch, form the watershed between the Yangtze and the Yellow River.

The highest peak, the Kunlun Goddess Peak in the western range, reaches 7,167 m. In the centre stands the Arka Tagh, whose highest points are Ulugh Muztagh and Bukadaban Feng, and in the east Amne Machin is the main peak. The range formed on the northern edge of the Cimmerian Plate, when it collided with Siberia in the Late Triassic and closed the Paleo-Tethys Ocean.

What the name Kunlun covers has varied. Older sources used it for the belt running across the centre of China, taking in the Altyn Tagh, the Qilian and the Qin Mountains. Sima Qian records that Emperor Wu of Han sent men to find the source of the Yellow River and gave the name Kunlun to the mountains at its source. The name seems to have begun as a semi-mythical place in the Classic of Mountains and Seas.

Kunlun entered Chinese thought in the Warring States period (475-221 BCE) and became closely woven into Chinese culture. It was held to be a Taoist paradise, the centre of heaven and earth and the staircase to the sky. According to legend, King Mu of Zhou was the first to visit it, found the Jade Palace of the Yellow Emperor and met Xi Wang Mu, the Queen Mother of the West, who had her abode there. She was the object of a cult that peaked in the Han dynasty. The scholar Gu Jiegang set the Kunlun myths of the western plateau against the Penglai myths of the eastern coast.

Important rivers flow from the range, among them the Karakash, the Black Jade River, and the Yurungkash, the White Jade River, which flow through the Khotan Oasis into the Taklamakan. The range has very few roads: in 3,000 km it is crossed by only two, Highway 219 from Yecheng in Xinjiang to Lhatse in Tibet, and Highway 109 between Lhasa and Golmud. More than 70 volcanic cones form the Kunlun Volcanic Group, the last known eruption of which was on 27 May 1951.
kunming: Kunming lies at an altitude of about 1,900 metres in the middle of the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, just north of the Tropic of Cancer, on the northern edge of Lake Dian. Its low latitude and high elevation give one of the mildest climates in China, and it is nicknamed the City of Eternal Spring. The name comes from the Kunming Yi, a people of the Di-Qiang group who lived near Erhai Lake in the Western Han period. The Yuan government set up Kunming County in the area, and the name has continued since.

The city long profited from its position on the caravan route to South Asia and Southeast Asia. Settlements around Lake Dian go back to Neolithic times, and the Dian Kingdom, whose language probably belonged to the Tibeto-Burman family, was established near the area. The Han dynasty took over its territory and set up Yizhou Commandery in 109 BCE. A city founded in 765 was known as Tuodong in the Kingdom of Nanzhao, and later belonged to the Kingdom of Dali.

The Yuan dynasty took Tuodong in its invasion of the south-west in 1252–1253. Under the governor Ajall Shams al-Din Omar a city in the Chinese Style named Zhongjing was founded, with a Buddhist temple, a Confucian temple that doubled as a school, and two mosques. He is largely credited with the sinicization of the region. The Ming defeated the Yuan in the 14th century and later built a wall around the city. Wu Sangui held Kunming as a Qing governor and ruled all of Yunnan and Guizhou from it; after his death in 1678 his grandson Wu Shifan resisted for two more months before the Qing recovered the city.

The Kunming–Haiphong railway, completed in 1906–1910 by the French, began the city's modern growth, and Kunming became a treaty port in 1908. During the Second World War refugees brought dismantled factories and universities from the north and east, and the city became an industrial base for the wartime government in Chongqing. It was also the terminus of the Burma Road and home to the Flying Tigers. Its walls stood until 1952, when young people were ordered to pull them down.

Kunming is the capital and largest city of Yunnan, with a population of 8,460,088 at the 2020 census. It is a centre of education and research, and the Golden Temple, the largest copper building in China, dates from 1602 in the Ming dynasty. The city links Yunnan by rail and road to Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Thailand.
