kunta-kinteh-island: The first record of European contact with the island is from May 1456, when a Portuguese expedition led by the Italian explorers Alvise Cadamosto and Antoniotto Usodimare moored off it. They buried a sailor named André there and so gave it its first European name, St Andrew's Island. The first European settlers came from the Duchy of Courland and Semigallia, a vassal of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, although the English Crown had granted the island to two companies in 1588 and 1618. In 1651 the settlers built a fort, named Jacob Fort after Jacob Kettler, Duke of Courland, and used it as a trade base. It had no water supply and depended on the goodwill of the King of Barra.

Two expeditions sent by the duke failed, one because of the conduct of its Dutch director and one because its leader abandoned it in Hamburg. In 1658 the duke himself was captured in the Swedish invasion known as the Deluge, and communication with the island was cut for about two years. The Dutch West India Company took the island over, and the English captured it in 1661; the Dutch ceded the fort to the English in 1664.

The English renamed the island James Island and the fort Fort James, after James, Duke of York, later King James II. The Royal Adventurers in Africa Company administered it, using it first for the gold and ivory trade and later for the slave trade. In 1684 the Royal African Company took over. The French captured the fort in 1695, but by 1702 it was again under English control. It was destroyed and rebuilt several times in this period, in clashes between English and French and by pirates.

After the Slave Trade Act of 1807 made the trade illegal in the British Empire, the Six-Gun Battery (1816) and Fort Bullen (1826) were built at the mouth of the Gambia River to thwart slaving. They are the only known defensive structures in the region built to stop slaving interests rather than enforce them. These sites and the island were abandoned in 1870.

The island lies in the Gambia River about 30 kilometres from its mouth, near Juffureh, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with related sites including a ruined Portuguese chapel in Albreda and the Maurel Frères building in Juffureh. It was renamed Kunta Kinteh Island on 6 February 2011, after a character in Alex Haley's Roots. Heavy erosion has reduced it to about a sixth of its size in the time of the fort. Ruins of English administrative buildings, a cell, a small jetty and some baobab trees remain.
kuntillet-ajrud: Kuntillet Ajrud, also known by the Hebrew name Horvat Teman, was one of the few water sources along the Darb el-Ghazza, the Gaza Road, which ran from the site of ancient Eilat or Ezion-Geber past Kuntillet Ajrud and Kadesh Barnea up to Gaza. Carbon-14 dating indicates that the site was occupied from 801 to 770 BCE.

The main building is fortress-like and divided into two rooms, one large and one small, both with low benches. Both rooms held paintings and inscriptions on the walls and on two large water jars, or pithoi, one found in each room.

What the site was for is disputed. It is frequently described as a shrine, though this is not certain. The excavator, Ze'ev Meshel, first argued for a religious function from the inscriptions and drawings with religious themes and from an unusual amount of linen, which he connected with the dress of priests. Other scholars point out that the site has no temple, shrine or cultic objects, and that similar textiles have since been found at Kadesh Barnea. Four inscriptions carry the military title Commander of the Fortress, three on storage jars and one on the plastered walls, which supports the view that it was a state-sponsored fortress or a caravanserai.

Although its position in the Sinai would normally point to the Kingdom of Judah, the occupants are usually taken to have come from the northern Kingdom of Israel. The evidence is the pottery, the personal names with the ending -yaw, the northern spelling of some inscriptions and the references to Yahweh of Samaria.

Edward Henry Palmer identified the place in 1869, when it was known as Contellet Garaiyeh, with the station Gypsaria on the Tabula Peutingeriana, and noted the remains of an ancient fort. Ze'ev Meshel of Tel Aviv University excavated it in 1975 and 1976, and the excavation report was published in 2012.

The paintings on the pithoi show animals, stylised trees and human figures. They appear to have been made over a considerable period by several artists and form no coherent scenes. Talley Ornan has argued that all the drawings have parallels in Neo-Assyrian palace reliefs and were preliminary sketches for wall paintings, and Schniedewind has read the inscriptions as scribal exercises of soldiers stationed at the fortress. Mordechai Gilula's theory that two figures on one jar represent Yahweh and the goddess Asherah has been almost abandoned: the scholars who have analysed the images in most detail hold that they are Bes or Bes-like figures.
kuomintang: The Kuomintang traces its roots to the work of Sun Yat-sen, a proponent of Chinese nationalism and democracy. On 20 August 1905 Sun joined other anti-monarchist societies in Tokyo to form the Tongmenghui, a group committed to overthrowing the Qing dynasty and establishing a republic. The party's charter was adopted on 28 January 1924. Its guiding ideology was Sun's Three Principles of the People, namely Chinese nationalism, democracy and the people's economic livelihood, and it was organised on the Leninist principle of democratic centralism and supported by the Soviet Union.

When Sun died in 1925, leadership passed formally to Wang Jingwei, the left-wing leader, and Hu Hanmin, the right-wing leader, but real power lay with Chiang Kai-shek, who controlled the military as superintendent of the Whampoa Military Academy.

From 1926 to 1928 the party under Chiang Kai-shek unified China in the Northern Expedition against regional warlords, which led to the fall of the Beiyang government. It had at first allied with the Chinese Communist Party in the First United Front, but on 12 April 1927 Chiang violently purged the communists in what became known as the Shanghai massacre, which started the Chinese Civil War.

The Nationalist government led five campaigns against the Chinese Soviet Republic and forced the communists into the Long March, until the Second Sino-Japanese War brought a Second United Front. The party sought to build a one-party ideological state, called Dang Guo, and included the Blue Shirts Society, an ultranationalist paramilitary group modelled on Mussolini's blackshirts.

After Japan's defeat in 1945, the KMT general Chen Yi accepted the Japanese surrender in Taiwan on 25 October. On 28 February 1947 the party put down an uprising there, and the White Terror began to purge suspected communist spies. In December 1949 the party retreated to Taiwan. It occupied assets formerly owned by the Japanese, and it oversaw rapid economic development, but lost the country's seat in the United Nations and diplomatic recognition by many states in the 1970s.

In the late 1980s Chiang Ching-kuo lifted martial law and the ban on opposition parties. His successor Lee Teng-hui continued democratic reforms and was reelected in 1996 in the first direct presidential election. The 2000 presidential election ended 72 years of KMT presidencies.

The party's constitution designated Sun Yat-sen as party president, a title kept in his memory, with Chiang Kai-shek as Permanent President. The party was headed by a director-general from 1927 to 1975 and has had a chairman since 1975. It is run by a National Congress and Central Committee, and it has been divided into factions, among them the Whampoa Clique, the CC Clique and the Blue Shirt Society. Its support in Taiwan is concentrated in the urban north and ranges across social groups, largely determined by age.
kupang: Kupang lies on the south-western tip of the island of Timor, with the Savu Sea on its northern shore. It is the largest city and port on the island, and the southernmost large city in Indonesia, as well as the closest to Australia. Its position let the Dutch watch shipping along Timor's south coast, and the Koinino River supplied fresh water. The climate is tropical savanna, with extreme wet and dry seasons: January is the wettest month and August and September the driest.

When representatives of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) first encountered Kupang in 1613, after conquering the Portuguese fort on Solor, the area was governed by a Raja of the Helong people. Because the VOC had little presence on Timor, the Portuguese mestizo Topasses of Flores influenced the area strongly, and by the 1640s a Portuguese stronghold stood there. By 1646 the VOC was established on Solor and renewed its agreement with the Raja, and in January 1653 it built Fort Concordia on the left bank of the river estuary. Kupang then became the base of the Dutch struggle against the Portuguese.

After Dutch defeats between 1655 and 1657, refugees from the allied Sonbai and Amabi principalities settled around the town on Helong land, followed by the Amfoang in 1683 and the Taebenu in 1688. The Helong Raja stayed Lord of the Land but depended closely on the VOC. In 1749 the Topasses were decisively defeated by the Dutch and their allies, which extended VOC influence over wide areas of western and central Timor. Chinese traders and artisans had settled by the early 18th century and became indispensable to the local economy.

William Bligh, set adrift after the Mutiny on the Bounty, reached Kupang on 14 June 1789 after 41 days and 3,618 nautical miles in an open boat. The British attacked in 1797 and 1811 and were driven off, but Kupang surrendered in January 1812 after the British took Java, and was returned to the Dutch in 1816. It was opened to foreign trade in 1825 and was a free port after 1866. Japan occupied it from 1942 to 1945, and Allied bombing destroyed much of the Old Town. It joined the Republic of Indonesia in 1950.

Kupang is the capital of East Nusa Tenggara province and a city of 442,758 people at the 2020 census. Its population is largely Christian, with Muslim, Hindu and Buddhist minorities. The University of Nusa Cendana is the oldest university in the province. It is the seat of an archdiocese, the diocese having been founded in 1967 and raised in 1989. Ruins and remnants of the colonial period survive in the city.
kurapaty: The executions at Kurapaty were carried out between 1937 and 1941 by the Soviet secret police, the NKVD, during the Great Purge and the wider Soviet repressions in Belarus. The exact count of victims is uncertain, because the NKVD archives are classified in Belarus. According to those archives, up to 35,000 people were shot in Byelorussia under Stalin, the vast majority of them during the Great Purge. Estimates of the number who perished at Kurapaty itself differ widely between the officials, writers and historians who have given them.

The remains were discovered by the historian Zianon Paźniak and exhumed in 1988. The discovery gave added momentum to the pro-democracy and pro-independence movement in Belarus in the last years of the Soviet Union. Investigations by both the Soviet and the Belarusian governments concluded that the perpetrators were the NKVD, on the basis of confessions by former NKVD members and the testimony of 55 villagers from Cna, Cna-Yodkava, Drazdova, Padbaloccie and other villages, who said that the NKVD brought people in trucks and executed them between 1937 and 1941.

In 2004 the mass graves at Kurapaty were entered in the register of the Cultural Properties of Belarus as a first-category cultural heritage site. Bill Clinton, then President of the United States, visited the forest in 1994 and left a small granite monument inscribed To Belarusians from the American people, which unidentified vandals damaged three times before it was restored. In 2001 young people from the Belarusian Popular Front, Zubr and smaller organisations occupied the site, living in tents through a bitter winter, to try to stop a widening of the Minsk Ring Road that threatened it; the construction went ahead.

On 29 October 2004 the Jewish community of Belarus set up a monument to the Jews and others murdered in the forest, with inscriptions in Yiddish and Belarusian addressed to fellow believers, Jews, Christians and Muslims, victims of Stalinism. Each November, on Dziady, when Belarusians commemorate their dead forefathers, hundreds of people visit the site.
kuressaare: Kuressaare is the only city on the island of Saaremaa and the westernmost town in Estonia. It lies on the southern coast, facing the Gulf of Riga, and is the administrative centre of Saaremaa Municipality and the seat of Saare County. Its historic name Arensburg comes from the Middle High German word for eagle and renders the Latin arx aquilae, the castle of the eagle. The fortress and the eagle, the symbol of Saint John the Evangelist, appear on the town's coat of arms. The Estonian name combines Kure saar, an ancient name of the island, with linn, meaning city or fortress.

The German crusading order of the Sword Brethren conquered the whole island in 1227. Its western and southern parts became part of the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek in 1228. The prince-bishop's castle is documented in Latin texts of 1381 and 1422, and a town grew around it. Johann von Münchhausen, bishop since 1542, turned Protestant and sold his lands to the King of Denmark in 1559. The king sent his younger brother Prince Magnus, who was elected bishop the following year and obtained the German civic charter for the town in 1563. The bishopric was secularised in 1572, and Saaremaa became part of Denmark.

In 1645 the Treaty of Brömsebro passed the island to Sweden, and the queen made her favourite Magnus Gabriel de la Gardie Count of Arensburg. During the Great Northern War the town suffered heavily from plague and was burnt to the ground by invading Russian troops in 1710. The Treaty of Nystad of 1721 incorporated Saaremaa into the Governorate of Livonia of the Russian Empire.

Large reserves of healing mud were found near the town in the middle of the 19th century, and the first mud spa was built in 1840. Kuressaare became a seaside resort and spa town. German forces invaded the island in 1917 in Operation Albion and held it until November 1918. From 1952 to 1988, during the Soviet occupation, the town was officially called Kingissepa. Over 90 civilians were killed in Kuressaare Castle in 1941 by Soviet naval forces and the NKVD, and under Soviet rule the island was a closed border zone.

Kuressaare Castle, a medieval episcopal fortress, houses the Saaremaa Regional Museum. The original wooden castle was built between 1338 and 1380, and the present square building has four wings around a courtyard, with a gate and the towers Pikk Hermann and Sturvolt. It is one of the best preserved castles in the Baltic States. The old town keeps mainly 18th- and 19th-century buildings, including the baroque town hall of the 17th century, and the town remains a resort.
kurgan: The word kurgan comes from a Turkic word meaning a fortified place, embankment or high grave. The earliest confirmed kurgans date to the fourth millennium BCE in the Caucasus, and some researchers associate them with the Proto-Indo-Europeans. Some archaeologists suggest that flat graves of the Varna and Suvorovo cultures were once covered by mounds that eroded away, which would put the first kurgans in the fifth millennium BCE, but this is not widely accepted.

From the Pontic–Caspian steppe the custom spread across Central Asia and much of Europe. By the Iron Age kurgans marked the dead of the Scythians, Sarmatians, Thracians, Getae and Dacians. In 1956 Marija Gimbutas introduced the Kurgan hypothesis, which named a Kurgan culture after these mounds and identified it with the Proto-Indo-European people.

A kurgan is a mound of earth and stone built over one or more graves. Most contain a single burial, though some were collective tombs reopened over generations; at Ipatovo, excavations showed thirteen phases of burial from the fourth millennium BCE into the second millennium CE. The chamber, built above or below ground before the mound was raised, varied widely. Bronze Age tombs of timber or stone sometimes had timber roofs, double walls or passageways, and other kurgans had stone circles, ditches or altars. The Arzhan tumulus in Tuva (late ninth or early eighth century BCE) had radially arranged chambers with stone-slab walls and human and horse burials.

Kurgans were chiefly funerary monuments, and they show differences of rank. In the Yamnaya culture a few richly furnished burials stood apart from modest graves. Horses were buried in many Iron Age steppe kurgans: Berel Kurgan 11 held thirteen harnessed horses preserved by permafrost, and the Kostromskaya kurgan of the seventh century BCE held twenty-two. Elite Scythian and Saka kurgans contained gold ornaments, weapons and drinking vessels; the Issyk kurgan in Kazakhstan held a young Saka buried with more than 4,000 gold ornaments, and the fourth-century BCE Tovsta Mohyla in Ukraine yielded the Golden Pectoral. At Noin-Ula in northern Mongolia a kurgan is the tomb of Uchjulü-Chanuy, head of the Hun confederation.
kurigalzu-i: Kurigalzu I was the 17th king of the Kassite, or third, dynasty that ruled Babylon, and he died around 1375 BCE. An inscription known as his autobiography names his father as Kadashman-Harbe I. Galzu was the name by which the Kassites called themselves, and the king's name may mean Shepherd of the Kassites, as a Babylonian name-list glosses it.

A second Kassite king, Kurigalzu II, ruled about 45 years later. Regnal numbers were not customary and both kings reigned long, so it is hard to tell for which of them an inscription was made. The later king is better known for campaigning against the Assyrians than for building.

When the Elamite ruler Hur-batila raided Babylon and challenged him to battle, Kurigalzu defeated and captured him, then conquered Susiana and advanced to Susa, which was sacked. Two inscriptions bearing his name were found there, and he may have installed Igi-Halki, the founder of a new Elamite dynasty, as his vassal. Chronicle P records the campaign out of sequence and credits it to the later king of the same name.

He kept up diplomacy with Egypt. His daughter was given to the pharaoh Amenhotep III, who made several diplomatic marriages. Letters from Amarna recall earlier exchanges with Thutmose IV, and Burna-Buriash II later reminded Tutankhamun that Kurigalzu had refused a request from the Canaanites to join an alliance against Egypt.

His building works are attested at no fewer than eleven Babylonian cities. At Ur he rebuilt the Ningal Temple and set fragments of the Ur-Nammu Stela in buildings on the ziggurat terrace. Around 1390 BCE he founded Dur-Kurigalzu, the fortress of Kurigalzu, over an older settlement in the far north of Babylonia. It was the first royal residence to bear its king's name, and it guarded a trade route east across the Iranian plateau to Afghanistan, the source of lapis lazuli.

The ziggurat of Enlil, about 170 feet high, still stands on the western outskirts of Baghdad. Rawlinson identified the site in 1861 from its brick inscriptions, and Seton Lloyd and Taha Baqir began excavating it in 1942. The city covered 225 hectares and held a vast palace and administrative complex called the Palace of the Whole World. The so-called autobiography of Kurigalzu was probably composed in late Babylonian times, and how far it preserves tradition from his reign is not known.
kuril-islands: The Kuril Islands are a volcanic archipelago of 56 islands and many islets, running north-east from Hokkaido to the Kamchatka Peninsula and separating the Sea of Okhotsk from the North Pacific. They form a Greater Kuril Chain and, at the south-western end, a parallel Lesser Chain. The islands are summits of stratovolcanoes; the chain has around 100 volcanoes, some 40 of them active, and frequent earthquakes. Winters are long, cold and stormy and summers short and foggy. The name Kuril comes from the Ainu word kur, meaning man; Russians later linked it to the verb kurit', to smoke, because of the volcanic plumes.

The Ainu inhabited the islands from early times, although few records predate the 17th century. They traded among themselves for centuries before either Japanese or Russians appeared, and Japanese goods carried by the Menashi Ainu reached Kamchatka. Japanese merchants entered the islands in the 17th century, and by the 18th century the Ainu were subject to the lord of Matsumae. A Tokugawa map of 1644 shows 39 islands north-east of Hokkaido. A Dutch expedition under Maarten Gerritsz Vries explored them in 1643, and Russian Cossacks landed on Shumshu in 1711.

In the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1875 Russia renounced its claims to the Kurils in exchange for Japan renouncing its claims to Sakhalin. Japanese administration then forcibly assimilated the Ainu, who were granted Japanese citizenship but had to adopt Japanese names, while many Japanese moved onto the islands. Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto assembled the strike force for the attack on Pearl Harbor in Hitokappu Bay on Iturup in 1941, and the fleet sailed on 26 November. The Yalta Agreement of February 1945 promised the Kurils and South Sakhalin to the Soviet Union in return for joining the Pacific War.

Soviet forces invaded the North and South Kurils between 18 and 31 August 1945. By 1946 the Soviets had expelled the entire Japanese civilian population, roughly 17,000 people. The Kuril Islands dispute over the four southernmost islands has continued since, and Japan has never accepted the Soviet claim.

The islands are administered by Russia as three districts of Sakhalin Oblast, with a population of roughly 20,000. Japan claims Kunashir, Iturup, Shikotan and the Habomai islets as its Northern Territories, and holds that the other islands are undetermined under international law because the San Francisco Peace Treaty names no owner and the Soviet Union did not sign it. Seabirds nest on the islands in millions, and the surrounding waters are among the most productive in the North Pacific.
kurkh-monoliths: The two stelae were found in 1861 by John George Taylor, British Consul-General in the Ottoman Eyalet of Kurdistan, at Kurkh, now Üçtepe Höyük in the district of Bismil, on the right bank of the Tigris. Taylor described a slab bearing the image of an Assyrian king, covered on both sides with cuneiform inscriptions and left bare at the base so that it could be set upright as a trophy, with a second found a little below it on the mound. He gave both to the British Museum in 1863. Henry Rawlinson identified Kurkh as the ancient city of Tushhan; in 1980 Karlheinz Kessler proposed Tidu instead.

The Shalmaneser III stela, of limestone with a round top, is 221 centimetres tall. It shows the king before four divine emblems, the winged disk of Ashur, the star of Ishtar, the crown of Anu and the disk and crescent of Sin, with a gesture of the right hand that has been read as a kiss of worship, a ritual or a sign of authority. Its inscription follows his campaigns in western Mesopotamia and Syria against Bit Adini and Carchemish and ends with the Battle of Qarqar, fought against a coalition led by Irhuleni of Hamath and Hadadezer of Damascus.

The Ashurnasirpal II stela, 193 centimetres tall, shows the king in worship and describes his campaign of 879 BCE against the lands of the upper Tigris. The Qarqar account is also the oldest document that mentions the Arabs, among them Gindibu' with 1,000 camels.

Julius Oppert first proposed in 1865 that A-ha-ab-bu Sir-ila-a-a was Ahab of Israel, and James Alexander Craig published the first full translation in 1887. Some scholars dispute the reading, since Assyrian records usually call the kingdom the House of Omri, and Werner Gugler and Adam van der Woude have argued that this Ahab was a king from northwestern Syria; Nadav Na'aman suggested a scribal error of 2,000 for 200 chariots. The text claims twelve kings but lists eleven, and its Gu-a-a may be Que or, as H. Tadmor held, Byblos.
kuroda-nagamasa: Kuroda Nagamasa, whose childhood name was Shojumaru, was held as a hostage in 1577, when Oda Nobunaga tried and sentenced his father as a spy; he was nearly killed but was rescued by Takenaka Hanbei. After Nobunaga's death in the Honnō-ji Incident in 1582 he served Toyotomi Hideyoshi with his father, fought at the Battle of Shizugatake in 1583 and took Takarabe castle in Hyuga during the Kyūshū campaign of 1587.

In 1588 he invited the local lord Ki Shigefusa, who had angered Hideyoshi, to Nakatsu Castle and had him assassinated while drinking. His men then killed the Ki clan's vassals, took its castle and killed Shigefusa's father, Ki Nagafusa, and Nagamasa had the hostage Tsuruhime crucified with 13 maids on the banks of the Yamakuni River. In 1589 he succeeded his father as head of the Kuroda clan. A Christian like his father, he renounced his faith when Hideyoshi expelled the missionaries.

In the first invasion of Korea (1592–1593) he commanded the 3rd Division of 5,000 men and took part in the first Siege of Pyongyang, entering the city with Konishi Yukinaga after its defenders had left. On 16 October 1597 he fought 6,000 Ming soldiers at the Battle of Jiksan, and in the second campaign he led reinforcements to the defence of Ulsan. In Jeolla Province he and other generals carried out the killings known as Nadegiri, mutilating their victims and collecting the noses of the Koreans they killed.

After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 he was among the generals who confronted Ishida Mitsunari, and in the Sekigahara campaign he sided with the Eastern Army of Tokugawa Ieyasu. With his father he negotiated, through Kikkawa Hiroie, the Mōri clan's promise to change sides, and at Sekigahara his men targeted Shima Sakon, who was fatally wounded. Ieyasu rewarded him with Chikuzen in exchange for Nakatsu in Buzen. He later fought in the Osaka campaigns of 1614–1615.
kuroda-yoshitaka: Kuroda Yoshitaka was born at Himeji on 22 December 1546, named Mankichi, the son of Kuroda Mototaka. The family is believed to have come from Ōmi Province; his grandfather Shigetaka brought it to Himeji as a senior retainer of Kodera Masamoto, the lord of Himeji, and lived at Gochaku Castle. Mototaka was allowed to marry Masamoto's adopted daughter and use the Kodera name. Yoshitaka became head of the family at 21, when his father retired.

In 1577 he pledged loyalty to the Oda as Hideyoshi led their advance into the Chūgoku region, and with Takenaka Hanbei he served as Hideyoshi's strategist against the Mōri clan. In 1578 he went to Arioka Castle to dissuade Araki Murashige from revolting, but Araki imprisoned him. Oda Nobunaga, believing he had defected, sentenced his son Shōjumaru, later Kuroda Nagamasa, to death, but Hanbei saved the boy. Rescued at the Siege of Itami in 1579, Yoshitaka was left lame and blind in one eye.

He fought at the Siege of Takamatsu and the Battle of Yamazaki in 1582, at Shizugatake in 1583 and Komaki-Nagakute in 1584, and led Toyotomi forces in the conquest of Shikoku in 1585. In Kyushu, under the influence of Takayama Ukon, he was baptised as Dom Simeão and arranged the rescue of a Jesuit mission from Bungo. After Hideyoshi's edict of 1587 against the missionaries he gave up the faith and took the name Josui, perhaps from Josué, the Portuguese form of Joshua.

Before Sekigahara he and Nagamasa allied with the Tokugawa general Ii Naomasa, holding a grudge against Ishida Mitsunari from the invasions of Korea. In 1600 he fought Ōtomo Yoshimune at the Battle of Ishigakibaru and took part in the Siege of Yanagawa; one theory holds that he meant to win Kyushu for himself, briefly holding seven of its provinces. He died in 1604 after Nagamasa had succeeded him, and his grave is at Namazuta in Iizuka. Known as frugal, he took part in building the castles of Himeji, Nagoya, Osaka and Hiroshima.
kursk: Kursk stands at the confluence of the Kur, Tuskar and Seym rivers and is the administrative centre of Kursk Oblast. Its name comes from the Kur River, a name derived from kurya, meaning channel. The city was first built as a fortress on a hill dominating the plain. Its position on the shortest routes from Moscow to the Crimea and from Moscow to Kiev later made it an important trading town.

Kursk probably emerged as a fortified settlement of the Severians by the 9th century and became part of Kievan Rus' in the late 10th century, as a stronghold of the Kievan princes on the south-eastern border. The Life of Theodosius of the Caves mentions it in 1032, and the Tale of Igor's Campaign praises the Kursk warriors. In the early 12th century it became the seat of a separate appanage principality. Polovtsians raided it, and the Mongols under Batu Khan devastated it; it was rebuilt, but the Golden Horde had again ruined it by the end of the 13th century.

Its revival began with a new fortress built under Feodor I of Russia. Kursk was captured in 1604 by supporters of False Dmitry I and withstood Polish–Lithuanian sieges in 1612, 1616 and 1617 and another in 1634. After the Belgorod Line was built it became one of the largest trade and craft centres of southern Russia, with an annual fair held under the walls of the monastery of Our Lady of Kursk. It received city status in 1779, became the centre of Kursk Governorate in 1797 and by the mid-18th century was among the ten largest Russian cities. A fire in 1781 led to a regular plan in 1782.

German forces occupied Kursk from 4 November 1941 to 8 February 1943. In July 1943 they launched Operation Citadel, their last major offensive against the Soviet Union, and the village of Prokhorovka near Kursk became the centre of one of the largest tank battles in history. Rebuilding began in February 1944, and by 1950 the urban economy was fully restored.

Kursk had 440,052 inhabitants at the 2021 census and is the oldest city of its oblast. Its stone churches include the baroque Sergiev Cathedral and Trinity-Sergius Cathedral, both completed in 1778. The Soviet government developed it as a railway hub on the strength of nearby iron ore deposits.
kurt-eisner: Kurt Eisner was born in Berlin on 14 May 1867 to Emanuel Eisner and Hedwig Levenstein, both Jewish. He studied philosophy and then became a journalist in Marburg. From 1890 to 1895 he was a contributing editor of the Frankfurter Zeitung, and an article attacking Kaiser Wilhelm II earned him nine months in prison. From 1892 to 1917 he was married to the painter Elisabeth Hendrich, with whom he had five children; he later married the editor Elise Belli, and they had two daughters.

He was an open republican as well as a Social Democrat and joined the SPD in 1898, although German Social Democracy, for tactical reasons, held back from republican propaganda. He became editor of Vorwärts after the death of Wilhelm Liebknecht in 1900, but in 1905 a majority of the editorial board, which favoured more orthodox Marxists, called on him to resign.

Afterwards his work was mostly in Bavaria. He was chief editor of the Fränkische Tagespost in Nuremberg from 1907 to 1910 and then a freelance journalist in Munich. In 1917, at the height of the First World War, he joined the Independent Social Democratic Party of Germany. In 1918 he was convicted of treason for inciting a strike of munitions workers, and spent nine months in Stadelheim Prison before the general amnesty of October released him.

He then organised the revolution that overthrew the Wittelsbach monarchy in Bavaria, and became the first republican premier of the People's State of Bavaria. On 23 November 1918 he made public documents from the Bavarian representative in Berlin in July and August 1914, which he thought showed that the war was caused by a small horde of mad Prussian military men together with industrialists, politicians and princes. At the Berne Conference of Socialists he attacked moderate German socialists for refusing to acknowledge Germany's part in causing the war. For that speech and his hostility to Prussia, large sections of the German people came to hate him bitterly.

On 21 February 1919 Anton Graf von Arco auf Valley, a far-right Bavarian nationalist, shot Eisner in the back in Munich as he was on his way to resign before the Bavarian parliament. The elected government fled Munich, and the short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic followed. Arco-Valley was sentenced to death in January 1920, but the sentence was reduced to life imprisonment, and he was pardoned in 1927.

Eisner was buried in the Munich Ostfriedhof. A monument to the dead of the revolution, commissioned in 1922, held his urn; it was demolished on 22 June 1933 and the urn moved to the New Jewish Cemetery. After World War II the artist Konstantin Frick re-created the monument. A plaque set in the pavement in 1989 marks the place where he was murdered.
kurt-hahn: Kurt Hahn was born in Berlin on 5 June 1886 to Jewish parents. He attended school in the city and then the universities of Oxford, Heidelberg, Freiburg and Göttingen. During the First World War he worked in the German Department for Foreign Affairs, analysing British newspapers and advising the Foreign Office. He was private secretary to Prince Max von Baden, the last Imperial Chancellor of Germany, and in 1919 joined the German delegation to the Paris Peace Conference as secretary and speechwriter to the foreign minister, Graf Brockdorff-Rantzau, where he witnessed the making of the Treaty of Versailles.

In 1920 Hahn and Prince Max founded Schule Schloss Salem, a boarding school in Baden-Württemberg, where he was headmaster until 1933. After the Potempa murder of 1932, in which Stormtroopers killed a young communist in front of his mother, Hahn spoke out publicly against Hitler and asked Salem's students, staff and alumni to choose between Salem and Hitler. He was imprisoned from 11 to 16 March 1933, released after an appeal by the British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, and forced to leave Germany in July.

In Scotland Hahn founded Gordonstoun on principles like those of Salem. He became a communicant member of the Church of England in 1945 and also preached in the Church of Scotland. He helped to found the Outward Bound organisation with Lawrence Holt, Atlantic College in Wales, the first of the United World Colleges, and the Duke of Edinburgh's Award. Later he founded or inspired several more boarding schools, among them Anavryta in Greece and Louisenlund in Germany (both 1949), Rannoch in Scotland (1959) and The Athenian School in the USA (1965).

Hahn resigned the headship of Gordonstoun on health grounds and returned to Hermannsberg, near Salem, in 1953. He died there on 14 December 1974, aged 88, and was buried in Salem's Stefansfeld cemetery. His philosophy rested on respect for adolescents, whom he believed to have an innate decency that society corrupted as they aged, and on giving them chances of leadership, outdoor adventure and what he called Samaritan service. He listed six declines of modern youth, among them fitness and self-discipline, and four remedies: fitness training, expeditions, projects and rescue service. Through Alec Peterson his ideas reached the International Baccalaureate programme.
kurt-schuschnigg: Kurt Schuschnigg was born on 14 December 1897 in Reiff am Gartsee, now Riva del Garda, in the Tyrolean crown land of Austria-Hungary. In the First World War he was taken prisoner on the Italian Front. He studied law at Freiburg and Innsbruck, and after graduating in 1922 practised as a lawyer in Innsbruck.

He joined the right-wing Christian Social Party and in 1927 was elected to the Nationalrat as its youngest deputy. From January 1932 he was Minister of Justice, and from May 1933 also Minister of Education, under Karl Buresch and then Engelbert Dollfuss. He openly discussed abolishing the parliamentary system, restored the death penalty, and after the socialist February Uprising of 1934 had eight insurgents executed at once.

After the Nazi Otto Planetta assassinated Dollfuss in the July Putsch, Schuschnigg became chancellor of the authoritarian Federal State of Austria on 29 July 1934. He ruled mostly by decree and his policies differed little from those of his predecessor, though his rule was milder. He had to manage a near-bankrupt state while armed paramilitary forces owed loyalty to rival parties and the Austrian Nazis grew stronger. His overriding concern was to preserve Austria's independence.

He sought to balance Germany by aligning with Italy and Hungary, a policy that failed once Mussolini sought Hitler's support. In July 1936 he signed an agreement with Germany that released imprisoned July Putsch insurgents and put the Nazi contact men Edmund Glaise-Horstenau and Guido Schmidt in the cabinet. On 12 February 1938 he met Hitler at the Berghof, where he was presented with what amounted to an ultimatum, including the appointment of Arthur Seyss-Inquart as minister of security, and was coerced into agreeing.

On 24 February he told the Federal Diet that Austria would go thus far and no further. He then proclaimed a plebiscite for 13 March. Hitler demanded its cancellation and then Schuschnigg's resignation. He resigned on 11 March, German troops entered Austria the next day, and he was placed under house arrest.

Schuschnigg was held in solitary confinement and then spent the war in Sachsenhausen and Dachau. In late April 1945 he narrowly escaped an execution order, was freed by Wehrmacht officers in South Tyrol and passed to American troops on 4 May 1945. He emigrated to the United States, where he was professor of political science at Saint Louis University from 1948 to 1967 and became a citizen in 1956.

The Austrian People's Party would not admit him, because it wished to distance itself from the dictatorship. On returning to Austria he downplayed his time of dictatorial power and tried to justify the regime. He died at Mutters, near Innsbruck, in 1977.
kuru-kingdom: The Kuru kingdom was a tribal union of the Bharata and Puru tribes, formed in the Middle Vedic period as a result of their alliance and merger after the Battle of the Ten Kings. With its centre of power in the Kurukshetra region, it was the first recorded state-level society in the Indian subcontinent and dominated roughly from 1200 to 800 BCE. Its first capital was at Āsandīvat, identified with modern Assandh in Haryana. Later literature names Indraprastha, identified with Purana Qila in Delhi, and Hastinapura as the main Kuru cities. The kingdom corresponds with the archaeological Painted Grey Ware culture.

The Atharvaveda praises Parikshit as King of the Kurus, ruler of a prosperous realm, and the Shatapatha Brahmana commemorates his son Janamejaya as a conqueror who performed the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice. These two kings played a decisive part in consolidating the state and developing the srauta rituals. The Kurus later declined after being defeated by the non-Vedic Salva tribe, and the centre of Vedic culture shifted east to the Panchala kingdom. Post-Vedic literature says the capital was moved to Kaushambi after floods destroyed Hastinapur.

By the 6th century BCE the dynasty had divided into Kuru and Vatsa kingdoms. Buddhist sources describe Kuru as a minor state under a chieftain called Koravya, and by the time of the Buddha its small states had been replaced by a Kuru republic.

The clans that formed the kingdom were largely semi-nomadic and pastoral, but as settlement moved into the western Ganges plain, farming of rice and barley became more important. The fourfold varna system replaced the older twofold division of arya and dasa. Kings ruled with a rudimentary administration of a priest, village headman, army chief, emissary, herald and spies, and took tribute from commoners and weaker neighbours. A common council, the Samiti, could elect or dethrone the king, and a smaller assembly of elders, the Sabhā, advised him.

The Kurus arranged the scattered hymns of different clans into the Vedas, forming the bulk of the Rigveda, and developed the srauta rituals. The Mahabharata centres on a conflict between two branches of the Kuru dynasty, possibly around 1000 BCE, though archaeology has not shown whether its specific events have a historical basis.
kuruc: The word kuruc was first used in 1514 for the armed peasants led by György Dózsa. Today's etymologists derive it from the Turkish kurudsch, 'rebel' or 'insurgent'. In 1671 Meni, the beglerbeg pasha of Eger, applied it to the mostly noble refugees from Royal Hungary, and from 1671 to 1711 it was used in Hungarian, Slovak and Turkish texts for the rebels against the Habsburgs. The opposite term, labanc, widespread after 1678, meant the Austrians and their loyalist supporters; it comes from a Hungarian word for 'long hair', referring to the wigs of Austrian soldiers.

After the magnate conspiracy and the rebellion of Francis I Rákóczi, Emperor Leopold I introduced absolutist government in Royal Hungary. The court tried again to suppress Protestants, and in 1673 it set up a governing council under Johann Caspar von Ampringen. Soldiers dismissed from frontier castles, nobles who lost their estates and Protestants fled east and gathered by the Tisza. In 1672 these 'fugitives' (bújdosók) invaded Upper Hungary and took the castles of Diósgyőr, Ónod, Szendrő and Tokaj, but on 26 October 1672 a Habsburg army defeated them at Gyurke. In 1674 a trial of Protestant pastors ended in sentences of death, and the pastors were sold as galley slaves in Naples, which caused public outcry across Europe.

Between 1674 and 1678 the fugitives were led by Count Paul Wesselényi, and in May 1677 France, Poland, Transylvania and the fugitives signed a treaty in Warsaw. In 1678 Mihály Teleki took the lead, and the same year Emeric Thököly declared war on the Habsburgs and his army occupied almost all of Lower and Upper Hungary. The fugitives elected him their leader at Szoboszló in January 1680. In 1681 Leopold I restored the constitution and the Palatine of Hungary.

From then on the history of the kurucs is that of the Thököly Uprising of 1680–85 and Rákóczi's War of Independence of 1703–1711, which had a wider social base and more complex aims than the original movements. Rákóczi himself did not use the word, preferring the French term insurgents or malcontents. After 1711 many former kuruc soldiers joined the Habsburg army, and in the first half of the 18th century 'kuruc' came to mean Hungarian hussars in that service. By the end of the century it was only a historical term. Today it can denote Hungarians who stand for strict national independence, in a positive sense of patriotic or a negative sense of chauvinistic. The South German oath Kruzitürken joins Kuruzen and Türken.
kurukh-people: According to Edward Tuite Dalton, Oraon is a name given by their Munda neighbours, meaning to roam, while Kurukh may derive from a word meaning to shout, so that it would mean a speaker. Their origins are debated. The Indian Anthropological Society places their first home in the Konkan, and they are said to have settled on the Chota Nagpur Plateau by 100 CE. Sarat Chandra Roy suggested a migration from Coorg in South India, another hypothesis links them with the Brahui of Baluchistan, and a third places them in the Indus Valley Civilisation.

Oraon traditions recorded by Dalton tell of expulsion from Gujarat, defeat at Kalinjar, and a stay at Rohtasgarh before they were driven out by Muslims in the reign of Akbar and settled in Chotanagpur.

Under British rule the Kurukh rose against the East India Company and local zamindars over taxation: Budhu Bhagat led the Lakra rebellion, also known as the Kol uprising, in 1832. Colonial policies left most of the tribe working as agricultural labourers for zamindars by the early 20th century, and many migrated to the tea gardens of Assam, West Bengal and Bangladesh and to Fiji, Guyana, Trinidad and Tobago and Mauritius, where they were called Hill Coolies. From 1914 to 1920 Jatra Bhagat led the Tana Bhagat movement of civil disobedience, whose followers later supported Mahatma Gandhi.

The Kurukh are patrilineal and patrilocal, divided into exogamous clans named after plants, animals and objects, such as Lakra (tiger), Tirkey (an eagle) and Toppo (woodpecker), which also serve as surnames. A village is governed through offices such as the Pahan, the village priest; young people were taught in the youth dormitory, the Dhumkuria, and disputes are settled at the Akhra, the meeting place. Twelve to thirty villages form a Parha council, presided over by the headman of the Raja village.

Just under half still speak Kurukh as their mother tongue, many having adopted Sadri or Odia. Unlike many neighbouring peoples who practise shifting cultivation, they plough their fields. Of the 3,623,512 counted in the 2011 census, about 36 per cent were Hindu, 30 per cent Christian and 29 per cent followers of Sarna, the nature religion of the plateau, whose rituals are held in sacred groves and whose supreme god is Dharmesh.
kurukshetra: Kurukshetra is a historical region of India, also called Dharmakshetra, the realm of duty, and the Land of the Bhagavad Gita. The name also refers to the city of Kurukshetra, the administrative headquarters of Kurukshetra district. In the Vedas it is described as a region, not a city, and kshetra means region in Sanskrit. Its boundaries correspond roughly to the central and western parts of present-day Haryana and Punjab, and one account places it between two rivers, the Sarasvati and the Drishadvati.

According to the Puranas, the region is named after King Kuru, ancestor of the Kauravas and Pandavas of the Mahabharata, and the Kurukshetra War of that epic is believed to have taken place here. The Vamana Purana says that Vishnu blessed Kuru with two boons: that the land would be known as holy after his name, and that anyone dying there would go to heaven.

The Kuru kingdom, a union of Vedic Indo-Aryan tribes of the northern Iron Age (c. 1200 to c. 900 BCE), developed into the first recorded state-level society in the Indian subcontinent. It collected its ritual hymns into the Vedas and developed the Srauta rituals, which contributed to the roots of Hinduism. It dominated the middle Vedic period under Parikshit and Janamejaya, but had become something of a backwater by the 5th century BCE. Its traditions supplied the basis of the Mahabharata.

The Mauryan empire conquered Kurukshetra in the late 4th century BCE, after which it became a centre of Buddhism and Hinduism. The Kushans later took the region, and the Gupta empire conquered it in the early 4th century CE, when it saw a cultural and religious revival. The Pushyabhuti dynasty ruled after the Gupta empire, and the town reached its height under King Harsha (c. 590 to 647 CE), when the Chinese scholar Xuanzang visited Thanesar. Civil war followed Harsha's death without a successor.

Tomara A Kashmiri army briefly held the area in 733, and the Tomara dynasty took over from 736. Mahmud of Ghazni sacked it in 1014, and it joined the Delhi Sultanate in 1206. Babur put down a local rebellion in 1526 and made it part of the Mughal Empire. Under Akbar it became a spiritual centre for Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims. Maratha forces controlled it until the British took it in 1805, after the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

Kurukshetra is an important Hindu pilgrimage destination. The 48 kos parikrama is a traditional circuit of about 90 km round the holy city, made on foot to all its sites. Brahma Sarovar, one of Asia's largest man-made ponds, draws many pilgrims to bathe on Somavati Amavasya and at solar eclipses, and Jyotisar is the site where the Bhagavad Gita is said to have been delivered to Arjuna.
kurultai: The word kurultai, also spelled quriltai, literally means 'gathering'. The oldest recorded mention of its root, before the time of Genghis Khan, is the verb Qur in the Dīwān Lughāt al-Turk of the 11th century, where it meant to assemble, to assemble into a formation, or to build. Another hypothesis derives it from the hypothetical Proto-Mongolic verb *kura-, *kurija-, 'to collect, to gather', from which comes khural, 'meeting, assembly'. The same root gives the Mongolian khurim, 'feast', which first referred to large festive gatherings on the steppe.

A kurultai was a medieval political and military council made up of members of a Mongol khan's family, imperial sons-in-law, captains of the army and others. All Great Khans of the Mongol Empire were formally elected at one, and khans of subordinate states such as the Golden Horde were chosen by a similar regional assembly. The Secret History of the Mongols records that in the year of the tiger, 1206, the people gathered at the source of the Onan river, hoisted the white standard with nine tails and gave Chinggis Qa'an the title of Qan.

Chiefs also assigned critical positions and titles at a kurultai and decided the military direction the new khan would follow. Most major campaigns were first planned at such assemblies, and lesser ones met under subordinate leaders and generals. No laws were written down there, but the decisions set policy.

A kurultai needed senior members from across the empire, who were generally also military leaders. Without them its decision was viewed as illegitimate or no action was taken. The deaths of Ögedei in 1241 and Möngke in 1259 drew Mongol leaders and troops away from the outskirts of Vienna and Venice and from Syria, which halted operations against the Austrians and the Mamluks.

The Golden Horde's enthronement was described by the 15th-century German traveller Johann Schiltberger: the khan was seated on white felt and raised in it three times, carried round the tent, seated on a throne, given a golden sword and sworn in. The gathering was also a festival with feasting and traditional games, many of which continue in the modern Mongolian Naadam. Women attended, though they could not vote.
kurume: Kurume lies on the Chikugo Plain in southern Fukuoka Prefecture, about 40 kilometres from the prefectural capital at Fukuoka City. The Chikugo River flows from the north-east to the south-west of the city and marks much of its boundary, and the Minou Mountain Range, with Mount Takatori, Mount Hatsushin and Mount Mino, rises along its southern and south-eastern side. Its climate is humid subtropical, with the most rain in July. In 2005 the surrounding towns of Kitano, Jōjima, Mizuma and Tanushimaru were merged into it, giving the city a long east-west shape.

The area was part of ancient Chikugo Province and was the site of its provincial capital, its kokubun-ji and its ichinomiya. During the Edo period it came under the Kurume Domain, ruled for most of its history by the Arima clan, whose policy of promoting industry developed the castle town around Kurume Castle into a commercial centre. The clan's family temple, Bairin-ji, was founded near the castle. The modern city was established on 1 May 1889, with the creation of the modern system of municipalities.

From 1915 to 1919 over 1,000 German and about 50 Austro-Hungarian prisoners of war, taken after the surrender at Tsingtao, were held in an internment camp at Kurume, the largest in Japan. Exchanges between the prisoners and local people left a lasting mark on the city, and the prisoners' work and skills contributed to the local rubber industry that became the basis of the tyre maker Bridgestone. Kurume was a garrison town for the Imperial Japanese Army and from 1922 a centre of the rubber and chemical industries. On 11 August 1945 an air raid by 53 B-24 bombers killed 212 people and destroyed much of the urban centre.

Kurume is a regional commercial centre. Bridgestone was founded here by Shōjirō Ishibashi (1889–1976), whose family made jika-tabi, the sock-like shoes of farmers, and found that rubber soles protected the wearers from parasitic worms in the rice paddies; the company's original plant remains in the city. Traditional products include kasuri, an indigo-dyed woven cloth, and rantai shikki, lacquered bamboo trays and bowls. The city has many National Historic Sites, among them Kofun burial mounds and the Chikugo Kokufu ruins, and attractions such as Kurume Castle, Kōra taisha, Kurume Suitengū and Zendō-ji, the head temple of the Jōdo sect in Kyushu.
kurunegala: Kurunegala is the capital of the North Western Province and of Kurunegala District. It lies at the junction of several main roads, about 94 km from Colombo, 42 km from Kandy and 51 km from Matale, at an altitude of 116 metres and surrounded by coconut plantations and rubber estates. Eight large rocks encircle and dominate the city, and six of them take their names from the animals they are imagined to resemble, among them Ibbagala, the Tortoise Rock, and Wanduragala, the Monkey Rock. The largest is Ethagala, the Elephant Rock, which reaches 325 metres.

The city is named after that rock: kurune means tusker and gala means rock in Sinhala. Its old name was Hasthishaila-pura, Sanskrit for the City of the Elephant Rock. A folk legend says that in a long-ago drought a witch turned some of the water-consuming animals into stone.

Kurunegala had a citadel in the 13th century, and its rise as a capital followed events at Yapahuwa. The sacred tooth relic was taken from the Yapahuwa kingdom to the Pandyan country by an Aryacakravarti from the Jaffna Kingdom during the rule of Buwaneka Bahu I (1272 to 1284). King Parakrama Bahu III, who ruled from Kurunegala between 1287 and 1293, brought it back.

Kurunegala remained the seat of government for three further kings: Buwanekabahu II (1293 to 1302), Parakramabahu IV (1302 to 1326) and Buwanekabahu III (1326 to 1335), also called Wanni Buwanekabahu, the son of Pandit Parakramabahu II and believed to be the last king to rule from the city. Vijayabahu V ruled from Dambadeniya and Yapahuwa from 1335 to 1341, after which the kingdom shifted to Gampola. Under the Kurunegala kings the economy rested on agriculture, trade and taxes, and the royal income came chiefly from farmers' shares of their harvest and from gems such as pearls and moonstones.

Little survives of the royal complex: a stone entrance, steps, rock pillars and ruined walls of the palace and of the Palace of the Tooth Relic. Nearby are the archaeological cities of Parakramapura, with the remains of a moated palace and monasteries of the 12th century, Dambadeniya and Yapahuwa.

Most of the people of Kurunegala are Sinhalese, with sizeable Moor, Tamil, Burgher and Malay communities. Buddhism is the main religion, alongside Hinduism, Christianity and Islam. The Athkanda Raja Maha Viharaya and the Ibbagala Raja Maha Viharaya are among its Buddhist temples, and the city is the seat of Roman Catholic and Anglican dioceses. A large reservoir built by ancient kings, Kurunegala Lake, lies at the edge of the centre, and a clock tower of 1922 commemorates officers from the Wayamba province killed in the First World War.
kurunta: Kurunta was a younger son of the great king Muwatalli II, brother of Muršili III, nephew of Ḫattušili III and cousin of Tudḫaliya IV. His Luwian name referred to a patron god of the Hittite pantheon, and like other later Hittite princes he also bore a Hurrian name, Ulmi-Teššub, though scholars debate whether the treaties naming Ulmi-Teššub and Kurunta concern one man. Muwatalli entrusted him young to Ḫattušili, and he grew up with Ḫattušili's sons. When Muršili III and Ḫattušili fought for the throne, Kurunta supported his uncle.

Ḫattušili III rewarded him with the vassal kingdom of Tarḫuntašša, which his father had made the royal residence, and he founded a junior line of the royal house there. An early treaty promised that his son and grandson would succeed him, fixed his frontiers and listed his military duties. The future Tudḫaliya IV interceded to enlarge his lands, and Kurunta seems to have sworn loyalty to him, support that may have helped Tudḫaliya to the throne. The later treaty gave him the highest rank at court below the king and crown prince, and promised him lands the great king might conquer around Parḫā, Classical Perge in Pamphylia. An Egyptian physician, Pariamaḫu, was sent by Ramesses II to treat him.

At some point he took the title of Great King on his seal and on a rock inscription at Hatip, southwest of Konya, which calls him the son of Muwatalli. His seal impressions were found in Ḫattuša itself, and the bronze treaty tablet had been deliberately buried near the southern Sphinx Gate. Scholars generally suppose that he usurped the throne from Tudḫaliya IV or Arnuwanda III, but they do not agree on the course of events; others suggest he only declared his independence.

No names of his descendants are recorded, though a later king of Tarḫuntašša corresponded with Niqmaddu IV and Ammurapi II of Ugarit. His treaties are important to modern scholars for the geography of Bronze Age Anatolia. Some place Great King Ḫartapu as his successor, but Ḫartapu's date remains controversial.
kusaila: Kusaila, also known as Aksel, was a 7th-century Berber Christian ruler of the kingdom of Altava and leader of the Awraba, a Christianised sedentary Berber tribe of the Aurès, and possibly also king of the Sanhaja. Ibn Khaldun, writing in the 14th century, some 700 years later, gave Tlemcen as his homeland, but sources closer to his time, the earliest from the ninth century, link him only with the Aurès Mountains. He grew up in Berber tribal territory during the time of the Byzantine Exarchate of Africa.

According to the historian Gabriel Camps, his name may come from the Roman name Caecilius, common among Christianised Berbers and found on graves at Volubilis, which would point to a noble family. The historian Yves Modéran considered this fragile, since the name follows a regular Berber consonant pattern and is close to Berber names such as Aksil.

Later Muslim accounts, from the 11th century to Ibn Khaldun, say that Abu al-Muhajir Dinar invited him to his camp in 678 and persuaded him to accept Islam and join his army with a promise of equality with the Arabs, after which the Awraba took part in his campaigns. Some historians prefer the earlier ninth-century sources, which describe Kusaila as a Christian and give him no dealings with either Abu al-Muhajir or Uqba ibn Nafi before the ambush.

In the later accounts Uqba, who replaced Abu al-Muhajir, treated Kusaila and his men with contempt. As Uqba returned from Morocco with a small remnant of his troops, about 300 men, Kusaila joined the Byzantines and ambushed them at Tahudha near Biskra with a force of about 5,000, in what became known as the Battle of Vescera. The Arabs lost their lands west of Cyrenaica for more than a decade, and Kusaila took Kairouan as his capital, his domain stretching from Volubilis to the interior of Ifriqiya.

Arab reinforcements arrived under Zuhayr ibn Qays, and Kusaila met them in 688 at the Battle of Mamma, where the outnumbered Awraba were defeated and Kusaila was killed. The Awraba eventually submitted to the reorganised Arab army. Resistance passed to the Jerawa of the Aurès, and Kahina succeeded Kusaila as war leader of the Berber tribes. In 693 Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan sent Hassan ibn al-Nu'man with 40,000 men, who captured Carthage.
kusel: Kusel lies on the Kuselbach in the southwest of Rhineland-Palatinate, in the North Palatine Uplands, about 30 kilometres northwest of Kaiserslautern. The floor of the dale is roughly 220 metres above sea level, and hills close it in on both sides. Lichtenberg Castle stands just beyond the town's limits to the west, and the Remigiusberg and the Potzberg to the east. With about 5,000 inhabitants, Kusel challenges Cochem for the title of Germany's smallest district seat. Until 1865 its name was written Cusel, and its oldest form, Cosla, is a Celtic word for a brook.

Celtic graves of the Iron Age have been found around Kusel, and after the Battle of Tolbiac in 496 the area came under Frankish rule. A Frankish royal estate of the 7th century stood on the ruins of a Roman one, and the Remigiusland around it was given to the Archbishopric of Reims, probably between 575 and 590. In 931 the estate passed to the Abbey of Saint-Remi in Reims. In 1127 monks from Reims founded a Benedictine house on the Remigiusberg. The Counts of Veldenz, who had been hired to protect the Remigiusland, built Lichtenberg Castle about 1214 in rivalry with the owners, and it is now known as Germany's biggest castle ruin.

Charles IV is known to have granted Kusel town rights in 1347. In 1444 it passed to the Duchy of Palatine Zweibrücken, which bought the Remigiusland in 1552 for 8,500 Rhenish guilders. In 1635, during the Thirty Years' War, Croatian troops of the Imperial army under General Matthias Gallas entered by cunning, killed more than half the townsfolk and burned the town. It took 40 years to rebuild it, and it was burned again in the Franco-Dutch War. A fire in 1794 burnt out almost all the old buildings.

Kusel is the seat of the Kusel district and of the Kusel-Altenglan Verbandsgemeinde. The medieval street layout survives in the old town, and the centre has Classicist and Historicist buildings of the 19th century, among them the Classicist Protestant parish church of 1829 to 1831. Cloth-making was the main industry from the mid-19th century until after the Second World War. The tenor Fritz Wunderlich was born in Kusel, and the Fritz-Wunderlich-Halle in its cultural centre bears his name. The Kuseler Herbstmesse, held in early September, is said to be one of the biggest folk festivals of the Western Palatinate.
kushan-empire: Chinese sources describe the Kushans as one of five aristocratic tribes of the Yuezhi. Many scholars believe the Yuezhi were an Indo-European people, and some suggest a Tocharian origin, while others propose an Iranic Saka origin. The Records of the Great Historian and the Book of Han place them in the grasslands of eastern Xinjiang and north-western Gansu, until the Xiongnu beheaded their king and forced them west between 176 and 160 BCE.

Traces of the Kushans in Bactria and Sogdiana date to the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, where they displaced the Sakas and built fortresses on the ruins of Hellenistic cities such as Ai-Khanoum. The earliest documented ruler, Heraios, called himself a tyrant in Greek on his coins. Kujula Kadphises later welded the Yuezhi tribes into a tight confederation.

Kushan rulers are recorded for about three centuries, from around 30 to around 375 CE. Vima Takto expanded the empire into north-western South Asia, and his son Vima Kadphises added conquests in Bactria. Kanishka the Great, the fourth king, ruled a huge territory from his accession. According to the Rabatak inscription it reached south to Ujjain and Kundina and east beyond Pataliputra. His successor Huvishka's rule was a period of retrenchment and consolidation, in which he devoted effort to controlling the city of Mathura.

Vasudeva I was the last of the Great Kushans, and the end of his rule coincides with the Sasanian invasion as far as north-western India. The empire fragmented into semi-independent kingdoms in the 3rd century, which fell to the Sasanians, who established the Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom. In the 4th century the Guptas pressed from the east, and the last Kushan and Kushano-Sasanian kingdoms were overwhelmed by invaders from the north, the Kidarites and later the Hephthalites.

The Kushans initially used Greek for administration, then adopted the Eastern Iranian Bactrian language, written in an adapted Greek script. Their gold, silver and copper coins carried more than thirty gods, drawn from Iranian, Greek and Indian worlds, together with images of kings and the Buddha. Kushan rulers were patrons of Buddhism, and Kanishka is remembered in Buddhist tradition for convening a great council in Kashmir. Between the mid-1st and mid-3rd century, Buddhism, patronised by the Kushans, spread to China and other Asian countries along the Silk Road.

The art of Gandhara, at the crossroads of Kushan power, developed Greco-Buddhist traditions. The Kushans also had diplomatic contacts with Rome, and in the 1st and 2nd centuries they collaborated militarily with the Han general Ban Chao, though in 86 they marched against him and were defeated.
kushano-sasanian-kingdom: The Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom, also called the Indo-Sasanian Kingdom, was a polity established by the Sasanian Empire in Bactria in the 3rd and 4th centuries. The Sasanians, shortly after their victory over the Parthians, extended their rule into Bactria under Ardashir I, around 230 CE, and then to the eastern parts of their empire in western Pakistan under his son Shapur I (240 to 270). The Kushans thus lost their western territory, including Sogdia, Bactria and Gandhara, to Sasanian nobles who took the title Kushanshah, or King of the Kushans (Koshano Shao in the Bactrian language), and minted coins. They are sometimes considered a sub-kingdom inside the Sasanian Empire.

The Kushanshahs are known mainly from their coins, which were minted at Kabul, Balkh, Herat and Merv and so show the extent of the realm. Its farthest extent to the east appears to have been Gandhara. They seem not to have crossed the Indus, since almost none of their coinage has been found at Taxila just beyond it. Hormizd I Kushanshah issued coins with the title Kushanshahanshah, King of kings of the Kushans, probably in defiance of Sasanian rule, and seems to have led a failed rebellion against the emperor Bahram II (276 to 293).

Around 325 Shapur II was directly in charge of the southern part of the territory, while the Kushanshahs kept their rule in the north. Sasanian coins found at Taxila begin only with Shapur II (r. 309 to 379) and Shapur III (r. 383 to 388), which suggests that Sasanian control beyond the Indus resulted from Shapur II's wars with the Chionites and Kushans in 350 to 358, described by Ammianus Marcellinus. The administration continued until 360 to 370, when the Kidarites invaded and took much of the Kushano-Sasanian lands; the rest was incorporated into the Sasanian Empire proper. The Hephthalites later displaced the Kidarites.

The coinage carried legends in Brahmi, Pahlavi or Bactrian, sometimes inspired by Kushan coins and sometimes more clearly Sasanian. The obverse usually shows the ruler in an elaborate headdress and the reverse either a fire temple or Shiva with Nandi. Coins of Shiva and Nandi point to a strong influence of Hinduism, and the cult of Mithra also flourished, Mithra being regarded as a divine protector of the rulers. The prophet Mani followed the Sasanian expansion to the east, which exposed him to the Buddhist culture of Gandhara, and he is said to have visited Bamiyan. Sasanian art influenced Kushan art for several centuries.
kushinagar: Kushinagar, in Pali Kusinārā and in Sanskrit Kuśinagara, is a town in the Kushinagar district of Uttar Pradesh. Alexander Cunningham held that the name came from the abundance of kusha grass in the region. According to the Mahāparinibbāṇa Sutta (Sutta 16 of the Dīgha Nikāya), the Buddha in his eightieth year travelled with disciples for months from Rājagṛha through Pāṭaliputta, Vesāli, Bhoganagara and Pāvā to Kushinagar. At Pāvā a resident named Cunda invited them to a meal that included sūkaramaddava, and soon afterwards the Buddha fell ill with a painful complaint resembling dysentery. He crossed the Kakkuttha River, now the Khanua, and reached Kushinagar, where he lay down between sala trees on his right side and attained parinirvana. His body was cremated seven days later.

The Sakya clan was to receive the ashes, but six other clans and a king claimed them too. A Brahmin named Drona divided them into eight portions: for Ajātasattu of Magadha, the Licchavis of Vesāli, the Sakyas of Kapilavastu, the Bulis of Allakappa, the Koliyas of Rāmagāma, the brahmin of Veṭhadīpa, the Mallas of Pāvā and the Malla king of Kushinagar. According to Buddhaghosa each portion was placed in a reliquary and buried in a tumulus, later enlarged into stupas; of these only the Ramagrama stupa in Ramgram, Nepal, is said to remain intact.

The ruins were first mentioned in modern literature in 1837 by D. Liston, who noted that they were already a place of worship. Alexander Cunningham excavated the Matha Kuar shrine and the Ramabhar stupa in 1861–1862 and was the first archaeologist to identify the site as the place of the Buddha's parinirvana. In 1876 Archibald Carlleyle uncovered the Mahaparinirvana stupa and a reclining Buddha 6.1 metres long. A Burmese monk, Sayadaw U Chandramani, asked the English Governor of India in 1901 for permission for pilgrims to worship the image. J. Ph. Vogel conducted campaigns between 1904 and 1907. Laurence Waddell suggested in 1896 that the death took place near Rampurva, but archaeology and the sutta both support Kushinagar.

The red sandstone reclining Buddha lies in the Parinirvana Temple, on its right side with its head to the north. The Parinirvana Stupa stands behind it, and the Ramabhar stupa, 1.5 km east, marks the cremation place. The Matha Kuar shrine holds a seated Buddha in blue stone, with an inscription of the 10th or 11th century. Modern temples in Thai and other Buddhist styles also stand there.
kusunoki-masashige: Kusunoki Masashige's origin has not been validated. He is believed to have been born in 1294 in Kawachi Province as a well-to-do member of the rural gentry, and he claimed descent from Tachibana Moroe, a nobleman of the eighth century. His birthplace has been linked to the village of Chihaya-Akasaka. He was a scholar and a devout Buddhist, and much of his early education took place at Kanshin-ji Temple in present-day southern Osaka Prefecture, where he also studied strategy under a man named Oe Tokichika.
According to legend, Emperor Go-Daigo dreamed that he was sheltering under a camphor tree (kusunoki in Japanese), and the dream led him to the surname of the warrior who would support him.

Only six years passed between the start of Masashige's military campaign in 1331 and his death in 1336. His defence of two loyalist fortresses, at Akasaka and at Chihaya, helped allow Go-Daigo to return briefly to power in the Genkō War against the Kamakura shogunate. In 1333 the emperor rewarded him with the governorship of Izumi Province and Kawachi Province, promoted him to Fifth Rank and later appointed him to the Records Office and Settlements Board.

He is also thought to have built smaller castles in southern Osaka, among them Eboshigata Castle and Ishibotoke Castle, along the Koya Kaido pilgrimage trail. They protected the route from bandits and brought in tolls and news, since travellers paid to pass and the garrisons listened for rumours.

Ashikaga Takauji turned against Go-Daigo. Masashige and Nitta Yoshisada drove Takauji out of Kyoto, but by 1336 he was a threat to the city again. Masashige proposed that the emperor withdraw to Mount Hiei and let Takauji enter Kyoto, then trap him there with the help of the monks. Go-Daigo refused to leave the capital and ordered a pitched battle. At Minatogawa, in present-day Kobe, Masashige's army was surrounded and reduced to 73 of its 700 horsemen. He withdrew to a house with his brother Kusunoki Masasue and others, and the brothers stabbed each other. His head was buried at Kanshin-ji.

Under the Tokugawa shogunate, scholars influenced by Neo-Confucianism made him a hero of loyalty, and Minatogawa Shrine was established in 1871. In 1880 the Meiji government awarded him the Senior First Rank posthumously.
kutadgu-bilig: The author speaks of himself at several points in the poem. Named Yūsuf, he was born in Balasagun, then the winter capital of the Karakhanids, near present-day Tokmok in Kyrgyzstan, and was about 50 when he finished the work in 1069-1070. He presented it to Tavghach Bughra Khan, the prince of Kashgar, and was given the title Khāṣṣ Ḥājib, roughly Privy Chamberlain, by which he is often known. Some scholars suspect that the prologue, far more openly Islamic than the rest and partly in prose, is by another hand.

The poem is built around four main characters, each standing, as the author says, for an abstract principle. Robert Dankoff suggests that Yūsuf sought to reconcile the urban Islamic and the nomadic Turkic traditions of wisdom among the Karakhanids, at a time when a move away from nomadic life had changed what was asked of a good ruler; Dankoff also sees some Greek and Buddhist influence.

The language is Karakhanid, a Karluk form of Middle Turkic close to the Old Turkic of the Orkhon inscriptions but with many Persian words and calques from Arabic and Persian. Though it draws on the wisdom of the hadiths and the Qurʻān, it cites no Islamic text by name, which has been taken to support the view that Islam reached Central Asia through wandering Sufis.

Yūsuf wrote in the Arabic mutaqārib metre, in rhyming couplets of 11-syllable lines, the earliest known use of that metre in a Turkic language. As Turkic did not distinguish long and short vowels, he worked with open and closed syllables instead. The dialogue form has been compared with Turkic song contests such as the Kazakh and Kyrgyz aytış and the Uzbek askiya.

The work was well known through the Timurid era, but only three manuscripts survive, each named after the city where it was found: Vienna, Fergana and Egypt. Facsimiles of all three were printed in Istanbul in 1942 and 1943.
kutahya: Kütahya lies on the Porsuk River in western Turkey, at 969 metres above sea level, and is the seat of Kütahya Province. The surrounding region has broad areas of gentle slopes with agricultural land, rising to high mountain ridges to the north and west. Its population is 263,863. Old sources name the ancient city Kotiaeon, Cotiaeum or Koti, and its history is said to reach back to 3000 BCE, although the date of its founding cannot be fixed.

In the Iron Age the area was settled by the Phrygians. In 676 BCE the Cimmerians defeated the Phrygian king Midas III and dominated the region, until Lydian rule replaced theirs in the time of Alyattes. Alexander the Great established control there in 334 BCE, and after his death in 323 BCE the region passed to Antigonos I. In 133 BCE Cotyaeum came under Roman rule and became part of the province of Phrygia Salutaris. Menas, a soldier turned hermit, declared himself a Christian before the prefect Pyrrhus in 304 CE and was tortured and beheaded on a rock outside the city. Under Justinian I the town was fortified with a double line of walls and a citadel.

Kotyaion fell briefly to the Seljuks in 1071 and was sacked by them again some time after 1180. It was later taken by the Germiyanids and by Timur, until the Ottomans conquered it. It was first the centre of Anatolia Eyalet, and the troops of Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt briefly occupied it in 1833. Kütahya was occupied by the Greek Army on 17 July 1921 during the Turkish War of Independence, and the Turkish Army captured it in ruins on 30 August 1922.

Under the Ottomans, many Armenians settled in the town and came to dominate tile-making and pottery. Kütahya became a major centre of the Ottoman ceramic industry, producing tiles and faience for mosques, churches and official buildings across the Middle East. A small ewer now in the British Museum, inscribed in Armenian script with a date of 1510, gave its name to Abraham of Kütahya ware. Arthur Lane proposed in 1957 that this ware was made from 1490 until about 1525, and his chronology has been generally accepted.

During the Armenian genocide of 1915 the Ottoman governor, Faruk Ali Bey, went to great lengths to protect the Armenians of the district from deportation. He was removed in March 1916, and the community suffered under his successor. The ceramicist David Ohannessian, a master of a Kütahya workshop, was deported in early 1916 and later travelled to Jerusalem to help restore the Dome of the Rock, where Armenian ceramics continue today.
kutaisi: Kutaisi lies on the Rioni River, 221 kilometres west of Tbilisi, in the Imereti region of Georgia, and is the capital of Imereti. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Archaeological evidence indicates that it was the capital of Colchis in the sixth to fifth centuries BCE. It is believed that in the Argonautica, the Greek epic poem about Jason and the Argonauts, Apollonius Rhodius took Kutaisi to be their final destination and the residence of King Aeëtes.

Kutaisi was later the capital of the kingdom of Lazica until a brief Arab occupation. An Arab invasion of western Georgia was repelled in 736 by Abkhazians together with Lazic and Iberian allies. Around 786 Leon II won full independence from the Byzantine Empire and moved his capital to Kutaisi, uniting Lazica and Abasgia in a dynastic union that led to the unification of the Georgian monarchy in the 11th century. From 1008 to 1122 it was the capital of the Kingdom of Georgia, and from the 15th century until 1810 the capital of the Kingdom of Imereti.

During the 17th century the Imeretian kings repeatedly appealed to the Russian Empire for help against the Ottomans, and were ignored. In 1768, under Catherine the Great, troops under General Gottlieb Heinrich Totleben joined King Heraclius II of Georgia, and Totleben helped King Solomon I of Imereti recover Kutaisi on 6 August 1770. The Russian–Turkish wars ended in 1810 with Russia's annexation of the Imeretian kingdom, and Kutaisi became the capital of the Kutaisi Governorate, which covered much of western Georgia.

In March 1879 the Kutaisi Circuit Court tried nine Georgian Jews from Sachkhere who were falsely accused of killing a Christian girl for religious purposes. After ten days and nearly 70 witnesses they were acquitted, as their lawyers showed that the accusation rested largely on false testimony. The trial drew attention across the Russian Empire.

Kutaisi is the third-largest city of Georgia, with 160,971 inhabitants in 2025. The ruined Bagrati Cathedral, built by King Bagrat III in the early 11th century, is its landmark, and the Gelati Monastery a few kilometres east is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Motsameta Monastery is named for the brothers David and Constantine, dukes of Margveti, who were martyred by Arab invaders in the 8th century. The city also holds the Sataplia Cave, with dinosaur footprints, and the Kutaisi Synagogue, built in 1885.
kutaisi-governorate: The Kutaisi, or Kutais, Governorate was a province (guberniya) of the Caucasus Viceroyalty of the Russian Empire. It roughly corresponded to most of western Georgia throughout most of its existence, and between 1878 and 1903 it also took in most of what is now the Artvin Province of Turkey, except the Hopa and Yusufeli districts. It was named for its administrative centre, Kutais, present-day Kutaisi. The governorate bordered the Sukhumi Okrug to the northwest, the Kuban Oblast to the north, the Terek Oblast to the northeast, the Tiflis Governorate to the southeast, the Batum Oblast to the southwest and the Black Sea to the west.

The governorate was created in 1846 out of part of the former Georgia-Imeretia Governorate. It also included the Akhaltsikhe uezd until that district was ceded to the Tiflis Governorate in 1867. In 1883 it included the Sukhumi Okrug and two districts, Artvin and Batum, of the then-abolished Batum Oblast.
